title: US claims of Cuba’s ‘unique threat’ jar with reality of hunger and blackouts
body_text: The US government’s latest allegations that Cuba is behind “many of the most significant upheavals in recent American political history” and that its leaders pose “a unique threat to American homeland security” have come as startling revelations to those living under the six-month-long US oil blockade in Havana, where desperate people search through piles of uncollected rubbish for food, or else swelter at home in 24-hour-plus blackouts. The unsigned 100-page report, Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism, published by the US state department on Monday, blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”. It is the latest push in a maximum-pressure campaign to bring down the island’s government that began with the abduction of Nicolás Maduro, the president of Cuba’s ally Venezuela, on 3 January. Since then, Cuba has been brought to a standstill by the oil blockade, sanctions on foreign businesses and threats of a military intervention. It also seems to be an attempt to “other” those on the US left before November’s midterm elections. “Cuba’s assault on the United States was never, at root, a quarrel over economic policy or sovereignty or even ownership of a particular territory,” the report reads. “It was a revolution against western civilisation itself – waged, in part, via the novel and insidious method of persuading the children of the west to turn against their own inheritance.” “Fidel would have been quite proud of this,” said one amused Cuban as he read it. The US state department, run by the Cuban-American Marco Rubio, refused to name the author, but it is clearly someone who knows their history. “Almost immediately after taking Havana in January 1959, Castro began plotting armed assaults against neighbouring governments – launching expeditions against Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua and Panama in just that year alone,” it reads. What it fails to mention is that Haiti was then run by François “Papa Doc” Duvalier, who killed an estimated 60,000 of his own people; the Dominican Republic by Rafael Trujillo, who launched the “parsley massacre”, killing between 20,000 to 35,000 Haitians; and Nicaragua by the Somoza family, who are credited with the murder of up to 50,000 Nicaraguans. Although the report provides no new evidence, there is a suspicious emphasis on race. The supposedly remarkable success of Cuban intelligence at infiltrating US institutions was due to a soft spot for “glamorous Latins”, it quotes an intelligence officer saying to the Miami Herald in 2002: “‘We’re much more open to Latins than we are to people with steel teeth and a Slavic accent.’” It also bemoans the ideological commitment of the spies Cuba recruited, while failing to mention either that several were inspired by the CIA’s attempts to assassinate Castro, or the shelter the US offered to the exiles Luis Posada Carriles and Orlando Bosch, who organised the bombing of Cubana flight 455 in 1976, killing 73 people. Most jarringly, the report groups together the US’s long internal struggle around civil rights and social reform and reframes it as a battle between the forces of foreign actors and “western civilisation”, lingering over groups such as the Black Panthers, which it credits to Cuba. While several black revolutionaries found sanctuary on the island, most famously Assata Shakur, who had a $2m price on her head for the killing of a New Jersey state trooper, the experience was not perhaps as conspiratorial as the author suggests. In interviews, Nehanda Abiodun, one of the mentioned fugitives, said her politics and revolutionary rage came from her experience growing up in 1970s New York, not out of any love for Cuba, whose government she came to resent for muzzling her in return for refuge. She used to say that the first thing that happened on landing was being racially profiled by the Cuban police. If she was part of a well-oiled international conspiracy, it didn’t show. For five years the Cuban government has not even been able to afford to feed its 9.5 million people, who mostly blame it for the crisis. But the report is ready for this: “To mistake Cuba’s poverty for harmlessness is to misunderstand the threat entirely. Its material weakness was never the measure of its danger.” It concludes: “Today, Cuban agents and operatives maintain a foothold in hundreds of front groups, activist organisations, solidarity centres, and ideological NGO and nonprofit networks. These groups collectively represent one of the single largest, most sophisticated and dangerous vectors for hostile foreign influence in modern American history.” In the run-up to the report’s release, Miguel Díaz-Canel, Cuba’s president, said the US had fallen prey to a “new and more dangerous version of McCarthyism”. But perhaps the more damning criticism came from a Cuban academic who preferred to remain nameless: “It reads just like a report Cuba’s state media might write about the United States.”

title: Hunter Biden for president? Stranger things have happened
body_text: What sort of longshot candidate do we reckon is going to run for US president in 2028? The Rock? Kim Kardashian? Kermit the Frog? US politics has become so debased that being rich, famous and a natural-born citizen (sorry, Zohran Mamdani) now seem to be the only qualifications required for a job in the White House. Which is why you shouldn’t entirely write off murmurings that Hunter Biden might be interested in following in his daddy’s presidential footsteps. When asked by a Fox News reporter about Hunter’s 2028 odds last month, Donald Trump suggested Joe Biden’s prodigal son might “do well”. If other “basket case[s]” in the Democratic party could do well, Trump added, then Hunter probably had a shot. Various analysts appear to agree. “Could Hunter Biden run for office? Don’t rule it out,” a recent Times headline blared. The article quotes a Biden biographer saying: “With a character like Hunter Biden in a populist, social media-driven political environment, you have to never say never.” You would definitely have said “never” a couple of years ago: Hunter wasn’t exactly the US’s favourite person during his dad’s presidency. His various scandals made him a target for Maga and a headache for Democrats. But in recent months, Hunter has reinvented himself as a social-media star. Since reactivating his X account in May, the former first son has posted an average of 23 times a day – Elon Musk-levels of posting. Except while Elon is tweeting about how “whites are a rapidly dying minority”, Hunter is cracking self-deprecating jokes about drugs and gaining fans across the political spectrum, with some calling him the “Maga whisperer”. Writing on X in June, Biden said he’d gladly take the title. “Left, right, D or R we all want the same things,” Hunter added. “We’re being divided on purpose by the Epstein Elite Oligarch class because as long as we’re at each other’s throats, they get fat and rich off of our misery.” Amen to that. Still, despite his refreshing political commentary, I’m not sure we should be treating the man as a folk hero or a Maga whisperer quite yet. It seems to me Hunter’s comeback isn’t so much motivated by political ambitions as by his millions of dollars of debt. He’s always been good at capitalising on his last name, and I suspect he’s realised he can parlay being provocative online into monetisable opportunities. To that end, Hunter has been going on every podcast that will have him, including sitting down with the far-right conspiracy theorist Candace Owens and the white nationalist Nick Fuentes. He’s also launched a paid Substack called Where’s Hunter? (a reference to one of Trump’s favourite catchphrases) and joked about starting an OnlyFans. Look, if you’re going to milk your famous name, at least make sure you’re not boring. (Trump’s spawn have failed spectacularly in this regard.) And Hunter’s new Extremely Online persona may be occasionally unhinged, but it’s not boring. On Saturday, for example, Hunter went on the progressive commentator Jennifer Welch’s podcast and joked that America’s biggest problem wasn’t “oligarchy”, but “closetocracy”, or the angry “closeted gay mafia” of Republicans in DC. This is relevant, Hunter said, because he believes the “internal conflict creates so much vitriol inside a person that they take it out on the rest of the world”. Hunter added that while he didn’t get a “gaydar ping” from Senator Ted Cruz, the man definitely gave him a “really kinky weird” vibe. I don’t know that this particular conversation was big or clever, but I’m sure it annoyed Cruz, so there’s that. Speaking of things that aren’t big or clever, Hunter’s also been trolling JD Vance following the vice-president’s creepy comments about Biden’s “suggestive” ice-cream licking. (I’ll spare you JD’s thoughts on corn dogs.) On Sunday, which was National Ice Cream Day for those who celebrate, Hunter posted a photo of himself licking an ice-cream with the caption: “Hey @JDVance. I wish I knew how to quit you.” And Hunter hasn’t minced his words when it comes to Vance’s boss. In a recent interview, he said that if he were sitting next to Trump, he’d tell him to “go fuck his fucking self”. He then noted that he’d challenged Donald Trump Jr to a UFC fight “three times” but hadn’t heard back. He added: “That’s how I’m going to pay all my debt.” Good luck with that, mate. Hunter has zero chance of ever winning a presidential nomination, but I’d bet good money he’d beat Don Jr in a cage fight. The US may be divided, but that’s a Biden-Trump rematch I think everyone in the country could get behind. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Writing on X in June, Biden said he’d gladly take the title. “Left, right, D or R we all want the same things,” Hunter added. “We’re being divided on purpose by the Epstein Elite Oligarch class because as long as we’re at each other’s throats, they get fat and rich off of our misery.” Amen to that. Still, despite his refreshing political commentary, I’m not sure we should be treating the man as a folk hero or a Maga whisperer quite yet. It seems to me Hunter’s comeback isn’t so much motivated by political ambitions as by his millions of dollars of debt. He’s always been good at capitalising on his last name, and I suspect he’s realised he can parlay being provocative online into monetisable opportunities. To that end, Hunter has been going on every podcast that will have him, including sitting down with the far-right conspiracy theorist Candace Owens and the white nationalist Nick Fuentes. He’s also launched a paid Substack called Where’s Hunter? (a reference to one of Trump’s favourite catchphrases) and joked about starting an OnlyFans. Look, if you’re going to milk your famous name, at least make sure you’re not boring. (Trump’s spawn have failed spectacularly in this regard.) And Hunter’s new Extremely Online persona may be occasionally unhinged, but it’s not boring. On Saturday, for example, Hunter went on the progressive commentator Jennifer Welch’s podcast and joked that America’s biggest problem wasn’t “oligarchy”, but “closetocracy”, or the angry “closeted gay mafia” of Republicans in DC. This is relevant, Hunter said, because he believes the “internal conflict creates so much vitriol inside a person that they take it out on the rest of the world”. Hunter added that while he didn’t get a “gaydar ping” from Senator Ted Cruz, the man definitely gave him a “really kinky weird” vibe. I don’t know that this particular conversation was big or clever, but I’m sure it annoyed Cruz, so there’s that. Speaking of things that aren’t big or clever, Hunter’s also been trolling JD Vance following the vice-president’s creepy comments about Biden’s “suggestive” ice-cream licking. (I’ll spare you JD’s thoughts on corn dogs.) On Sunday, which was National Ice Cream Day for those who celebrate, Hunter posted a photo of himself licking an ice-cream with the caption: “Hey @JDVance. I wish I knew how to quit you.” And Hunter hasn’t minced his words when it comes to Vance’s boss. In a recent interview, he said that if he were sitting next to Trump, he’d tell him to “go fuck his fucking self”. He then noted that he’d challenged Donald Trump Jr to a UFC fight “three times” but hadn’t heard back. He added: “That’s how I’m going to pay all my debt.” Good luck with that, mate. Hunter has zero chance of ever winning a presidential nomination, but I’d bet good money he’d beat Don Jr in a cage fight. The US may be divided, but that’s a Biden-Trump rematch I think everyone in the country could get behind. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Senate committee advances nomination of Trump intelligence pick Jay Clayton
body_text: The Senate intelligence committee on Tuesday advanced the nomination of Jay Clayton to serve as the US intelligence director, despite criticism from Democrats. Donald Trump had nominated Clayton, now the top federal prosecutor in the southern district of New York, for the role of the director of national intelligence (DNI) last month after the departure of Tulsi Gabbard. Intelligence committee members questioned Clayton at a hearing last week, and its Republican chair, Tom Cotton, announced that it had reported his nomination favorably by a 9-8 vote, teeing him up for a future vote on his confirmation by the full Senate. “Jay Clayton is a highly qualified nominee with a deep experience combatting a wide range of national security threats,” Cotton said in a statement. “I’m pleased that the Senate Intelligence Committee voted to advance his nomination to be Director of National Intelligence,” he added. Cotton did not provide a breakdown of how lawmakers voted. The committee is composed of nine Republicans and eight Democrats, and Mark Warner, a spokesperson for the Democratic vice-chair, said he had opposed the nomination. Democratic senator Ron Wyden released a statement announcing his no vote, accusing Clayton of “spreading conspiracies” about mail-in voting and denying Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election. “From start to finish, Mr Clayton has proven himself incapable of telling the truth or demonstrating an iota of independence from Donald Trump,” Wyden said. At his hearing last week, members of the Democratic minority criticized Clayton, a former Wall Street attorney who served as the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), for previous statements he made echoing Trump’s claim that US elections have been marred by fraud. They also aired concerns about politicization at the office of the DNI, which serves to coordinate the nation’s intelligence agencies. It is unclear when his nomination will be voted on by the Senate. If confirmed, he would take over from Bill Pulte, a federal housing official who Trump appointed as acting DNI following Gabbard’s departure. Democrats strenuously objected to Pulte’s installation in that office, decrying him as a loyalist to the president who may try to use its powers to retaliate against his enemies. As director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency director, Pulte had last year referred several Democratic officeholders as well as the Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook for mortgage fraud. His predecessor, Gabbard, had raised similar concerns when she appeared alongside FBI agents who raided an election office in Georgia earlier this year. Administration officials later said she was running her own investigation of the 2020 election. Clayton’s confirmation may nonetheless clear a path for Congress to renew the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), a key spy tool that had its legal authorization expire last month in part due to a blockade by Democrats incensed by Trump’s appointment of Pulte. Since taking over as acting DNI, Pulte has reportedly fired dozens of staffers from the office. In his statement, Cotton signaled support for those purges, saying he looked forward to working with Clayton to “continue reforming the Office of Director of National Intelligence”.

title: Hegseth tells Senate war on Iran has so far cost $37.5bn at hearing to request more funds
body_text: The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth told the Senate on Tuesday that the US-Israel war on Iran had cost $37.5bn so far, as he faced lawmakers furious over the conflict’s soaring price tag and the deaths last week of three American service members. During an appearance before the Senate appropriations committee, Hegseth, whose opening remarks were repeatedly interrupted by protesters, provided an updated account of the war’s cost – up from previous estimates – and defended the Trump administration’s roughly $88bn supplemental funding request, calling it “urgent, necessary”. Alongside the chair of the joint chiefs, Gen Dan Caine, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon was running low on cash to keep the fight going. Of the total request, as much as $67.1bn is earmarked specifically to cover the costs of the Iran war effort. “Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Hegseth told the Senate panel, warning that it would threaten the defense department’s ability to “pay our service members, rapidly replenish equipment and munitions, and sustain vital operations without disruption”. It was the defense secretary’s first sustained public questioning since a brief ceasefire collapsed and the war roared back to life. At least two US soldiers were killed in an Iranian attack on Friday, and another died in Iraq destroying an Iranian drone, pushing the American death toll since February to 17. Nearly 100 troops have been wounded in the conflict, officials confirm, though most injuries were minor. Patty Murray, the committee’s Democratic vice-chair, demanded Hegseth explain what the war had actually achieved, accusing the administration of shifting its rationale by the week and warning the conflict risked becoming “another forever war”. “We hear a different rationale for this war every few days,” Murray said in her opening remarks, noting the justification had moved from pre-empting threats that “did not exist” to regime change, then to dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme and navy, and now, she said, to simply reopening the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was “fully open, toll-free, before this war began”. “Here we are, five months later”, she continued. “The strait is closed. The ceasefire hasn’t just disintegrated – this war is now spiraling out of control again.” Under questioning from lawmakers, Hegseth cast the funding request as the price of deterrence rather than admitting failure, and framed the Pentagon’s overhaul under the US president as a break from what he described as years of slow bureaucracy. “The best way to create peace is to prepare for war, to deter it,” Hegseth told the panel, arguing the department was “building a force so capable that it would be absurd for anyone to challenge it”. Hegseth said the $21bn readiness portion of the request would cover military pay, replace equipment used in recent operations and stabilize fuel shortfalls, while the $46bn capability portion would expand production of “solid rocket motors, Jdams [joint direct attack munitions], hypersonics and counter-drone capabilities”. Without the funds, he warned, the department faced “critical shortfalls” that threaten its ability to pay troops and replenish munitions, and he cautioned that failing to fund the Pentagon at $1.5tn was “the greatest threat that our nation faces”. Some Democrats, including Chris Coons of Delaware, plan to direct criticism at Russell Vought, director of office of management and budget, who is not testifying but who earlier told US Congress that the war’s running cost was about $30bn, a figure that is largely believed by experts to be a severe undercount. Hegseth and Caine faced potential threats from within their own party. Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the committee, and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski, two prominent Republicans, have both crossed the aisle to back war-powers resolutions aimed at reining in the president’s authority over the conflict. Collins, who is facing a competitive re-election contest, has previously voiced frustration that the administration’s strategy for the war seems to shift almost daily. During the hearing, she asked Hegseth about the effect on military exercises if the supplemental funding is not provided. The defense secretary said that current and future training “would have to be curtailed” if the Pentagon does not get its budget needs met urgently. Senator John Kennedy, a Republican of Louisiana, pressed the panelists on the situation in the strait of Hormuz, asking if Iran will impose tolls on commercial vessels passing through the vital waterway which carried about a fifth of global oil and gas supplies before the war. “That’s a hypothetical question,” Caine replied, “and I don’t know the answer to that.” “Guys, we need straight answers,” Kennedy shot back. Both congressional chambers have passed a war-powers resolution urging the president to seek congressional authorization to continue military operations in Iran. Asked why the administration had not yet sought congressional approval for the war, Hegseth said it was the view of his department that “standalone Article II authorities exist for us to conduct this operation on behalf of the defense of the American people”. The defense secretary evaded the lawmaker’s question about whether he would use the approval of any supplemental funding as a “substitute for explicit congressional authorization”. House representatives have separately accused the Pentagon of stonewalling on basic figures: Betty McCollum, the top Democrat on the House defense appropriations panel, said the department has missed a deadline to detail war costs and has not disclosed how many precision munitions remain after the military burned through thousands of them in Iran.

title: House passes spending bill to head off government shutdown before midterms
body_text: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday approved a stopgap measure to head off a government shutdown until early December, with its Republican leaders seeking to defuse a volatile issue in the run-up to the November midterm elections. The continuing resolution authorizing government spending until 4 December passed by a vote of 220-205, roughly along party lines. It next heads to the Senate, where it will need to win bipartisan support to clear the chamber. The government’s current spending authority expires on 30 September, but top Republicans had argued the measure’s passage was necessary to ensure that Democrats do not block government funding measures in the Senate. They did so last year for a record 43 days in protest against the expiration of tax credits that lowered some healthcare costs, and twice again this year, to push for reforms to immigration enforcement operations after the killings of two US citizens in Minneapolis. “Our conference refuses to let the obstruction and inaction of Senate Democrats trigger another manufactured shutdown at the end of September. That is why we are acting before a funding lapse crisis, not in response to it,” said Tom Cole, the House appropriations committee chair who spearheaded the resolution. Earlier on Tuesday, lawmakers agreed to move forward on the stopgap measure and a budget framework paving the way for a $95bn party-line package, in a 214-211 vote roughly along party lines. The constitution tasks Congress with authorizing government spending, and the Senate and House every year attempt to pass 12 appropriations measures granting those authorities. But lawmakers often miss those deadlines, forcing them to resort to passing continuing resolutions that extend governmental departments’ ability to operate. While the House has passed three appropriations measures for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October, the Senate – where the top Democrat and Republican say they remain far apart in government spending talks – has approved none, nor have any advanced through committees, a key procedural step. Republican leaders ‌in the chamber said they were negotiating with Senate Democrats on their own short-term funding bill. Rosa DeLauro, the Democratic ranking member on the House appropriations committee, denied that her party was seeking a shutdown, and called passage of a stopgap funding measure “necessary”. However, she opposed the Republican-backed measure, calling it “hastily” conceived and noting it appropriated funds for the border patrol without “substantial reforms” to the agency that plays a major role in Donald Trump’s crackdown on undocumented immigrants. “We are putting the cart before the horse by considering this legislation without understanding the full scope of what is needed to continue operations through December 4,” DeLauro said. Should the Senate fail to pass the measure, funding negotiations will intensify from September, when Congress returns to Washington DC after spending most of August in recess with the end-of-the-month deadline to prevent a shutdown near. Those talks could be complicated by the approaching midterm elections, in which Democrats hope they can retake control of the House and potentially the Senate, where they can only win a majority by picking up at least three seats in states that backed Trump two years ago.

title: Three speeches on a single day signaled a dying American democracy
body_text: The presumption that US elections are legitimate died last week in Washington. It was 237 years old. It did not die of one wound. It died of three, inflicted in a single day, in daylight, on the record. And the country, running to the loudest of them, never examined the one most likely to kill. In critical care we distinguish the mechanism of death from its cause. The mechanism was a Thursday. The cause was chronic, progressive and untreated. The morning belonged to the secretary of state. Before officials of more than 60 countries, he announced that the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left. He named a transnational enemy defined by hatred of the west, “a revolt of the worst against the best”. He tied it to Iran and to Cuba and offered no evidence for either link. He said the journalists and thinktanks who might check the claims often agree with the enemy’s goals. The move is old and reliable: discredit the second opinion in advance. Midday belonged to the White House deputy chief of staff. What he said deserves to be quoted rather than summarized, because summary is a mercy it has not earned. He called “leftwing political terrorism” a “fatal cancer of civilization”. He said that its politics, left to run its course, “always becomes a gulag”. He said antifa demonstrators are “all deformed in some way, in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism”, that “their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred”, and he asked why there is “not one normal-looking person among them”. He said that when the leftist protests that his rights are being violated, those appeals “must fall on deaf ears”. He urged the assembled governments to be “completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization”. And he described the work already under way in six verbs: “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute”. I have been practicing medicine for four decades. Cancer is my vocabulary, not his. And I know what happened the last time a government borrowed it. The Nazi state’s central perversion was the medicalization of killing: the enemy as tumor, as bacillus, the nation as patient, extermination as cure. Robert Jay Lifton called it the biomedical vision. It recruited my profession first, and my profession answered willingly. When a government describes citizens as a cancer, it has written the first line of a treatment plan. On Thursday, the plan was read aloud, from a state department podium, in six verbs. One disclosure belongs in the chart. My family left Russia in 1917. My relatives left Germany in 1933. In both generations, leaving was called excessive; staying was the reasonable position. But an alarm that was right both times it sounded is not overcaution. On Thursday, it sounded a third time. The evening belonged to the president. In primetime he called the American election system indefensible, claimed a foreign power held 220 million voter files, declared mail voting inherently corrupt, accused his own intelligence services of concealment, and told Congress that the only reason to oppose his bill is the intent to cheat. That framework converts every future outcome into evidence. Pass the bill and win: the bill worked. Fail and lose: the cheaters blocked it. A presumption of legitimacy cannot survive inside a belief system engineered to be unfalsifiable. It was just a Thursday. Netflix’s forecast disappointed Wall Street. A rocket aborted on the pad. No sirens sounded, because this is not how they sound. Democracies do not die to soundtracks. They die on ordinary weekdays, between the earnings reports, while the country is at work. Then came the response, and the response was a triage error. Nearly all of it ran to the evening. The factcheckers parsed the voter files. The law professors graded the bombshells. Real work, spent on the loudest injury. The morning’s remarks, the ones that declared a class of Americans a cancer and read enmity on their bodies, drew the attention of an ordinary news cycle: straight coverage in the mainstream, horror at the margins, and in a portion of the press, open applause. I have watched teams run to the dramatic patient while the quiet one, the one not crying out, exsanguinates behind a curtain. The most dangerous words spoken in Washington on Thursday were not spoken in primetime. They were spoken before lunch, to more than 60 countries. The official transcript records the applause. The decedent is survived by the federal courts, still open. By 50 secretaries of state, still certifying. By a general election, still on the calendar, 108 days out. And by an electorate that has not yet been asked the only question that matters, which is whether it will accept a count its president has pre-declared corrupt, counted among citizens its government has pre-declared malignant. In 40 years of intensive care, I have pronounced death many times. The criteria are strict because the declaration is irreversible, and so we are taught to be certain before we speak. I have also, more than once, seen a rhythm return after the room had gone quiet, when someone refused to stop compressions on schedule. This notice is filed in the knowledge that pronouncements can be premature. It is filed in the fear that this one is not. Robert B Shpiner is a clinical professor of medicine in pulmonary and critical care at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

The morning’s remarks, the ones that declared a class of Americans a cancer and read enmity on their bodies, drew the attention of an ordinary news cycle: straight coverage in the mainstream, horror at the margins, and in a portion of the press, open applause. I have watched teams run to the dramatic patient while the quiet one, the one not crying out, exsanguinates behind a curtain. The most dangerous words spoken in Washington on Thursday were not spoken in primetime. They were spoken before lunch, to more than 60 countries. The official transcript records the applause. The decedent is survived by the federal courts, still open. By 50 secretaries of state, still certifying. By a general election, still on the calendar, 108 days out. And by an electorate that has not yet been asked the only question that matters, which is whether it will accept a count its president has pre-declared corrupt, counted among citizens its government has pre-declared malignant. In 40 years of intensive care, I have pronounced death many times. The criteria are strict because the declaration is irreversible, and so we are taught to be certain before we speak. I have also, more than once, seen a rhythm return after the room had gone quiet, when someone refused to stop compressions on schedule. This notice is filed in the knowledge that pronouncements can be premature. It is filed in the fear that this one is not. Robert B Shpiner is a clinical professor of medicine in pulmonary and critical care at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

title: Nicaragua’s congress announces ‘work plan’ to suspend elections
body_text: Nicaragua’s congress, controlled by the country’s long-serving president, Daniel Ortega, has announced a “work plan” to implement the authoritarian leader’s order that the country should no longer hold elections. The UN and the US strongly condemned Sunday’s announcement by Ortega, who has been in power since 2007 and, after a controversial constitutional change last year, now governs alongside his wife, Rosario Murillo, as “co-president”. During the ceremony marking the 47th anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista revolution, in which he helped overthrow the brutal dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza García, Ortega said he would work with congress to pass new laws that would “build a wall” against the opposition. On Tuesday, the Ortega-controlled National Assembly issued a statement saying that, under the pretext of “ensuring peace, security, stability and the continuity of achievements in the fight against poverty”, it was “beginning the necessary analysis to draw up a work plan to implement the president’s directives”. Although the Ortega-Murillo regime has already overseen a profound erosion of democracy – marked by the violent suppression of protests, the imprisonment of thousands of people and the forced exile of nearly 1 million Nicaraguans – Sunday’s announcement marked a significant rhetorical escalation that is now being put into practice by congress. On Wednesday, the UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, called on the Nicaraguan authorities to “reopen civic space, and restore the rule of law. People of all political viewpoints must be allowed to vote and run for office, in line with the state’s international human rights obligations.” The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who refers to the country’s government as the “Murillo-Ortega dictatorship”, said in a statement on Tuesday that “the Nicaraguan people have the right to choose their own leaders through democratic elections” and the US “calls on the international community to join forces” against the regime. Ortega’s uninterrupted period of almost 20 years in office is not his first spell in power. He led the junta that took office after the Sandinista revolution and, in 1984, was elected president, remaining in office until 1990. His current term, to which he was elected after he outlawed opposition parties and jailed all opposition presidential hopefuls before the 2021 election, had been due to end next November. However, last year’s constitutional changes extended the presidential term from five to six years. Despite the National Assembly’s announcement, it remains unclear whether the 2027 elections will be scrapped altogether or whether Ortega and Murillo will run unopposed.

title: Democrats need to hammer Trump on his unprecedented corruption
body_text: If the Democrats hope to maximize their chances of winning in this November’s elections, there’s a subject they need to scream far and wide about: Donald Trump’s immense and unprecedented corruption. The Democrats need to make clear to every American that Trump has shamelessly used his second term to increase his wealth by an astounding amount – by more than $2bn – all while millions of Americans are struggling to make ends meet, their struggles made worse by Trump policies that have pushed up inflation and gas prices. Every day through election day, the Democrats should convey loud and clear that America’s billionaire president has focused far more on making himself richer than on improving the lives of average Americans. Trump’s corruption and conflicts of interest are so vast and outrageous that many Americans have little idea how vast and outrageous they are: ranging from Trump’s making more than $1.4bn from crypto last year to granting pardons to criminals whose families have donated to Trump’s campaign to his sons’ investing in startup companies that receive generous help from the Trump administration. Democrats should repeatedly hammer Trump for his greed, corruption and conflicts of interest the same way that Hungary’s opposition repeatedly attacked Viktor Orbán for his immense corruption – a strategy that caused Orbán’s popularity to plummet and caused Hungarian voters to oust their country’s authoritarian leader last April. Peter Magyar, Orbán’s challenger, defeated Orban by focusing on three issues the Democrats would be smart to focus on: the cost of living, the lack of economic opportunities, and the fact that their country’s leader and his family grew ever richer even as many people grew poorer. Trump’s corruption and continuous push for self-enrichment are by far the worst of any president in US history. “It is completely unprecedented,” Megan Gorman, author of All the Presidents’ Money, a book on the history of presidential wealth since 1776, told the New York Times. Gorman said Trump’s focus on enriching himself is “a betrayal of the American social contract: that those who lead the country prioritize country over self”. Norm Eisen, the White House ethics czar under Barack Obama, told the Washington Post: “It’s corruption on a scale that, to be honest, has few rivals in world history.” Before Trump won a second term, the Teapot Dome was considered the worst presidential financial scandal in US history. Every US high school student studies that ugly scandal, which occurred under Warren Harding (president from 1921 to 1923). But Teapot Dome is peanuts compared with Trump’s cornucopia of scandals. Harding wasn’t even involved in Teapot Dome, nor did he profit from it. It instead involved his secretary of the interior, Albert B Fall, who took $400,000 in bribes and gifts to lease government-owned oil reserves. In today’s dollars, those bribes and gifts would be worth about $8m – that’s chump change compared with Trump’s corruption. By enriching himself by $2.2bn last year, according to White House financial disclosures, Trump has in effect jacked up his wealth by about $8m every two days since returning to the White House. Trump’s corruption and conflicts have taken many forms. After originally denouncing cryptocurrencies as “a scam”, Trump, in a stunning about-face, worked with his sons to create World Liberty Financial, a crypto company that enriched him by $799m last year. Trump and his sons enjoyed a huge windfall when a member of the United Arab Emirates’ royal family paid $500m for a secret 49% stake in their company. Not long after, Trump agreed to do something the UAE badly wanted; he let the UAE buy leading-edge Nvidia AI chips, a move that some national security officials opposed because they feared that China would ultimately get many of those chips. Trump cashed in big-time in another way – he made an astounding $636m last year by selling $Trump memecoins, a speculative cryptocurrency with little practical value. Trump urged his fans to buy those coins, writing: “It’s time to celebrate everything we stand for: WINNING … GET YOUR $TRUMP NOW.” Nearly a million people, many of them Maga loyalists, lost a total of $3.8bn from investing in $TRUMP coins, which have lost 97% of their value since their peak. At the same time Trump has won big in crypto, his administration reduced regulations on crypto, disbanded its crypto enforcement unit, and terminated some legal cases alleging crypto fraud. The US constitution’s emolument clause prohibits presidents from accepting gifts from foreign states, but in a blatant violation of that clause, Trump accepted a retired $400m luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar’s royal family. Trump is already using it, and after his second term ends, it will go to Trump’s presidential library, and presumably his personal use. Trump has called the Qatari gift “the world’s most luxurious plane”, while Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut called the gift “the definition of corruption”. Trump has turned presidential pardons of criminals into an ethically dubious pay-to-play game. He pardoned Changpeng Zhao, the billionaire founder of the world’s largest crypto exchange, after Zhao had quietly helped boost the value of the Trump family’s crypto company by nearly $2bn. Zhao had spent four months in prison after pleading guilty to money laundering. Trump also pardoned Trevor Milton, founder of the Nikola electric vehicle company – he had been sentenced to four years in prison for defrauding investors. Before Trump granted that pardon, Milton and his wife had donated more than $1.8m to Trump’s campaign. Similarly, Trump pardoned Paul Walczak, a nursing home executive who pleaded guilty to stealing more than $10m in employee payroll taxes. That pardon came after Walczak’s mother attended a $1m Trump fundraiser. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, has vigorously defended Trump against allegations of corruption, saying: “Neither the president nor his family has ever engaged, or will ever engage, in conflicts of interest.” Anna Kelly, a White House spokesperson, added that Trump “only acts in the best interests of the American public”. Trump’s repeated use of no-bid contracts also raises big ethical questions. Trump awarded a secret $500m no-bid contract to build the East Wing ballroom. His administration also awarded a $1.7m no-bid contract to a business owned by Trump’s longtime ally John Cafaro, who had given more than $300,000 to political committees tied to Trump. That no-bid contract was for installing a water-purification system for the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which had a huge algae bloom after the renovations Trump ordered. (In 2001, Cafaro pleaded guilty to conspiracy to bribing a congressman.) Trump’s sons are also cashing in on Trump’s power and presidency. After Trump helped persuade Kazakhstan’s leader to give a little-known US company access to the world’s largest untapped reserve of tungsten, a metal crucial for making missile warheads and AI chips, Trump’s sons Don Jr and Eric took an ownership stake in the project days before the deal was announced. The Export-Import Bank and a second federal agency have pledged to lend $1.6bn to the little-known US company that got access to the mine, which by one estimate holds up to $80bn worth of tungsten. Not stopping there, Don Jr and Eric have invested in a drone manufacturer that is seeking to sell drones to Gulf states that Iran has attacked and that rely on the Trump administration for military aid. In a move that Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized as “corruption in plain sight”, the Pentagon awarded a $24m contract to a startup company whose chief strategy officer is Eric Trump to test an android for the marines. Warren said: “Is the Pentagon just a cash machine for Trump’s kids now?” The Washington Post found that Don Jr and Eric have invested in more than a dozen defense-related startups and that those companies have generated at least $3.2bn in direct government business since Trump’s sons made those investments. Unlike previous presidents, Trump has refused to set up a blind trust for his holdings. That has raised serious concerns because Trump’s investment accounts made more than 21,000 trades last year, with many appearing to be timed to take maximum advantage of Trump’s public statements that moved the stock markets. (The White House defends the trades and says Trump’s investment accounts are managed by professional advisers who do not regularly communicate with him.) On 23 July, the day before Trump issued a plan that largely deregulated AI, his investment accounts bought up to $5m in stock each in numerous AI companies, including Broadcom, Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia (he also purchased stocks unrelated to AI that day). In an unprecedented deal for a president – one widely condemned as corrupt self-dealing – Trump got his justice department to promise that the IRS would drop any existing audits of Trump, his family and his business while also dropping efforts to pursue back taxes from him even though, by some estimates, Trump owes more than $100m in back taxes. Last week, a federal judge denounced that deal as improper self-dealing. The list goes on and on. Indeed I could detail many more scandals and conflicts, including the Trump family’s pursuit of branding deals in Saudi Arabia and a South Korean aluminum company paying $2m to Trump’s holding company as it faced a trade investigation. If any previous president had done one-tenth of these things, the public would be up in arms. Meanwhile, Republicans in Congress have inexcusably turned a blind eye to Trump’s corruption, giving him a pass on his unprecedented self-enrichment and self-dealing. And while Trump has enriched himself handsomely, he has enthusiastically backed legislation that cut Medicaid and food stamps to millions of struggling Americans, while also forcing up healthcare premiums for millions by blocking an extension of Obamacare subsidies. Importantly, the US public is growing increasingly upset with Trump’s corrupt shenanigans. An Economist/YouGov poll this week found that 49% of voters said they would use the word “corrupt” to describe Trump, while 19% wouldn’t describe him that way. Voters should remember all this corruption and unethical self-enrichment when they vote in November – and Democrats need to do their best to make sure that voters don’t forget. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: Trump’s war on Iran is unpopular and expensive. He’s perfectly OK with that
body_text: Could it be … that Donald Trump isn’t a team player? The midterm elections are less than four months away, and Republicans in the House and the Senate – hampered by a deeply unpopular president and what might be an even less popular war – are increasingly fearful of losing their jobs. Even Trump’s base is beginning to turn against the conflict. Yet asked on Tuesday if Iran is trying to affect the midterm elections by threatening the strait of Hormuz, the Republicans’ de facto leader was pretty blase. “Probably. It won’t have any impact on me. I’m just going to do the right thing. I don’t view it as: ‘Gee, we’re having an election in a period of time.’ You know, everyone says: ‘Oh, I’m doing something before’ – no. The election – I can’t think about that having to do with this,” Trump said. He added: “I think people are very impressed.” Unfortunately for Trump – and for Republicans in swing districts – all available evidence suggests people are very unimpressed with the president’s nearly five-month war in Iran. Just 28% of Americans think the Iran war is worth fighting, a Washington Post-Ipsos poll found last week; 68% believe it is not worth fighting. The same survey found that 29% of people believe “America’s leadership in the world has gotten stronger” under Trump; 52% think it has weakened. Amid surging prices linked to the Iran war, just 17% of Americans said they were better off financially than they were when Trump became president. Even Trump’s most hardcore supporters – the ones who heckle journalists at his rallies and wear T-shirts that say things like “Stomp my flag [and] I’ll stomp your ass” – are souring on the war. About 37% of self-identified Maga Trump voters say the US should continue the war in Iran only if it doesn’t increase costs, according to a Politico poll released on Wednesday. Moreover, 57% of voters who self-identify as Maga blame the war in Iran for the increase in gas prices. It is Not Good News, in other words, and this week some Fox News pundits issued urgent warnings to Trump to end the war. “With the midterm elections a little more than 100 days away, the clock is ticking for President Trump to get out of this war before voters head to the polls. It’s making a lot of Republicans nervous. It’s already, as we know, unpopular,” Laura Ingraham, usually a staunch Trump supporter, said on her show on Monday. “Republicans cannot let this become an endless distraction, especially if they want to win in November.” With no clear exit strategy, news of mounting injuries and more deaths of service members, there are good reasons for voters to focus on the war. And then there is the financial cost. During a contentious Senate hearing on Tuesday, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – he of alleged strip club stage-storming fame – said the Iran war had cost $37.5bn so far, as he asked Congress to approve an $88bn supplemental funding request. With gas prices running at more than $4 a gallon – up from about $3 when Trump took office – the spiraling costs are hardly likely to be a vote-winner. It might be making Republicans in Congress nervous. But Trump, a president in his second term who is not eligible to run for re-election, arguably has less to lose. A Democratic-majority House could impeach him for the third time, but the Senate would be highly unlikely to convict. Whenever and however Trump leaves the White House, his landing will probably be softened by his soaring personal wealth – his income last year was $2.2bn. With a president embroiled in a costly war, and seemingly ambivalent about how it affects his colleagues, could the midterms be a disaster? Maybe. Would Trump get over that? Probably.

title: Election deniers win Republican primaries in Arizona
body_text: Donald Trump-backed candidates in Arizona prevailed in key primary contests on Tuesday, setting up a fall campaign that will test whether Republicans can reverse some of their recent losses in the presidential battleground state. Andy Biggs, the hard-right congressman endorsed by Donald Trump, easily won the Republican nomination to challenge the incumbent Democrat, Governor Katie Hobbs. The race is expected to be among the most fiercely contested in the country, with control of the governor’s office carrying outsized national significance in a state that became “ground zero” for election denialism after Trump’s narrow loss there in 2020. Biggs, a former chair of the House Freedom caucus who was a central figure in the effort to overturn Trump’s election defeat, trounced fellow congressman David Schweikert, by appealing to the party’s deeply conservative base. Hobbs, who flipped the seat from red to blue in 2022, ran unopposed. Alex Kolodin, a Republican state representative and attorney who helped lead failed legal efforts to overturn Arizona’s 2020 and 2022 election results, also won the party’s primary to become its secretary of state: Arizona’s top election official. Kolodin will face the Democratic incumbent, Adrian Fontes, in November for the office that will oversee elections in a swing state during the 2028 presidential race. Fontes has cast himself as a bulwark against Trump’s election denialism, while overseeing elections in one of the nation’s most closely watched battleground states. In an all-caps social media post on Wednesday, Trump declared “A COMPLETE SWEEP!!!” “MAGA CANDIDATES WON EVERYTHING LAST NIGHT IN ARIZONA,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He added: “AFTER DECADES, ARIZONA IS BECOMING A REPUBLICAN STATE.” In fact, Arizona was long a Republican stronghold and only recently transformed into a competitive swing state, fueled by rapid population growth, shifting suburban voting patterns around Phoenix and an influx of college-educated voters. In the decade since Trump’s 2016 election, Arizona Democrats have gained control of the top three statewide offices – governor, attorney general and secretary of state – as well as both US Senate seats. But Trump still narrowly carried Arizona in 2024 after losing the state four years earlier – a shock defeat he unsuccessfully sought to overturn. Throughout the Republican gubernatorial campaign, Biggs and Schweikert offered contrasting visions for reclaiming the governorship. Schweikert, who gave up his toss-up congressional seat to run for governor after eight terms, argued that Biggs’s hard-right politics and unswerving embrace of the president had allowed Democrats to make gains in once-ruby-red Arizona. But Republican voters in Arizona, as they have across the country. This year, Republicans are contending with unfavorable national political conditions. Historically, the president’s party loses ground in the midterm elections, and Democrats are hopeful they can seize control of the House – and possibly the Senate, riding a wave of discontent over high gas prices and an unpopular Iran war that have dragged down Trump’s approval ratings. Two toss-up House districts in Arizona are key to that effort. Arizona’s first congressional district, anchored in affluent Scottsdale, has long been a Democratic target as the suburbs shifted away from the Republican party over the past decade. Two years ago, Schweikert won re-election with just under 52% of the vote, narrowly defeating Amish Shah, a former state lawmaker who Democrats appeared poised to renominate on Tuesday. His challenger, the former local news anchor Marlene Galán-Woods, also sought the nomination two years ago. This year, Galán-Woods, the widow of Grant Woods, the former Republican attorney general who publicly broke with his party over Trump, earned the controversial backing of the Democratic congressional campaign committee. Shah will face Republican Jay Feely, a former Arizona Cardinals kicker, in November. Feely faced Joseph Chaplik, a former state lawmaker, and John Trobough, a technology and telecommunications executive, in his party’s primary. In the sixth congressional district, which extends from the suburbs of Tucson to the US-Mexico border, encompassing much of south-eastern Arizona, Democrats hope national headwinds facing the president’s party will dislodge Republican congressman Juan Ciscomani, who is seeking a third term. Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a Marine Corps veteran, was running unopposed. Meanwhile, the contest to succeed Biggs in the safely Republican fifth congressional district has drawn unusual attention. The Trump-backed Republican nominee, Mark Lamb, the former Pinal county sheriff, spent the closing weeks of the primary campaign confronting allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of power reported in a multi-part investigation by the Arizona Republic. Prosecutors found no basis for criminal charges, and Trump has reaffirmed his support for Lamb, who has denied wrongdoing. He will face Democrat Elizabeth Lee, a nurse, in the general election. Elsewhere, Republicans chose their nominees for two top state positions that Democrats see as critical to pushing back against the Trump administration. Warren Petersen, president of the Arizona senate, won the Republican primary race to take on Democrat Kris Mayes for attorney general. Mayes, an outspoken critic of Trump, won the office in 2022 by just 280 votes after an automatic recount, making it one of the closest statewide races in Arizona history. He was competing for the nomination against Rodney Glassman, a former Democrat who was the party’s Senate nominee against John McCain in 2010 before joining the Republican party. Tuesday’s primary also settled tight contests in legislative races across Arizona, where Republicans hold slim majorities in both chambers of the state capitol.

title: House passes $1.15tn defense bill despite standoff over Israel and Trump’s voter agenda
body_text: The US House of Representatives passed a $1.15tn defense policy bill in a near-party-line vote on Wednesday, after Democrats refused to back the measure amid the war with Iran and Donald Trump’s push to impose new restrictions on voting nationwide. A key plank of the president’s plan to spend $1.5tn on the military in the 2027 fiscal year, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), passed the Republican-controlled chamber by a 216-212 vote, with all but six Democrats opposing its passage. Seven House Republicans broke ranks to oppose the measure, which now goes to the Senate. The NDAA is a mammoth bill with effects across the armed services, and Congress passes it each year with bipartisan margins. This year’s version includes pay raises of 5-7% for the military, as well as the codification of the name “Department of War” for the Pentagon. The bill’s large overall cost is itself a key feature, which top House Republicans say is necessary to make generational investments in the armed forces. “For the first time in 40 years, we’ve been presented a budget that accounts for the true cost of American deterrence. This topline begins to reverse the damage caused by decades of underinvestment in the US military,” Mike Rogers, the House armed services committee chair, said before the vote. The NDAA’s path to enactment has been complicated by the president’s decision to join Israel in attacking Iran without first seeking authorization from Congress. Last week, Senate Democrats blocked the advancement of that chamber’s version of the NDAA in protest of the war, which has flared anew after a memorandum of understanding meant to spur peace talks between the US and Iran collapsed. Democrats also soured on the bill after Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, acceded to the demands of rightwing lawmakers and inserted into the legislation the Save America Act, a Trump-backed proposal to ban mail-in ballots and impose new identification restrictions on voters at the polls and when they register. The party also objected to the overall prospect of allocating $1.15tn to the military while slashing funding elsewhere in the federal government, just a year after Congress’s Republican majorities approved extending an array of lower tax rates indefinitely. “The annual NDAA used to be a consistently bipartisan, substantive piece of legislation,” said Rosa DeLauro, the top Democratic appropriator. “I am disappointed that under Republican leadership, it has become just another partisan bill that is written to satisfy the most extreme Republican voices rather than a serious, nonpolitical framework for our national defense.” Adam Smith, the Democratic ranking member on the House armed services committee, had voted to advance the measure out of panel, but opposed its passage on the House floor, saying it had been “loaded with toxic, partisan amendments that continue the rightwing culture war assault on the LGBTQ+ community and preempt state and local laws under the guise of military readiness”. “Our country faces threats and [the defense department] has modernization needs, but I will not support making massive cuts to critically important domestic programs and slashing taxes to meet those needs,” Smith said. Amid a wider backlash within the party over US support for Israel, some Democrats said they opposed the NDAA because of its inclusion of provisions that would deepen cooperation between the two countries’ defense industries. “This amendment is an existential threat to American sovereignty and democracy,” said the progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was among the no votes. The House’s passage of the bill came after the chamber considered dozens of amendments. While many were agreed to unanimously, others offered barometers for how far the Republican-controlled chamber was willing to go on the most divisive issues before the parties. A proposal by the Republican Eli Crane to halt all military aid to Ukraine was resoundingly defeated by a 76-350 vote, while an amendment from Republican Lauren Boebert to codify Trump’s executive order banning transgender service members failed by a 212-217 tally. However, the House agreed to amendments from Nancy Mace barring the military health insurer from offering some gender-related care, and banning transgender athletes from girls’ sports at defense department-run schools. Beyond the NDAA, House Republicans on Wednesday approved a budget plan that will authorize $73bn for the war with Iran while circumventing the Democratic filibuster in the Senate. But that blueprint falls far short of the $350bn the Pentagon originally proposed to bring overall defense spending to $1.5tn for the upcoming fiscal year.

title: House Republicans to write $95bn bill to fund Iran war and aid farmers
body_text: House Republicans on Wednesday agreed to begin the process of writing a $95bn bill to fund the war with Iran as well as provide new aid to farmers, while making a long-shot attempt to impose new restrictions on voting nationwide. In a virtually party-line 216-214, the Republican-controlled chamber passed a budget resolution that paves the way for the creation of a reconciliation bill, which can advance through the Senate under special rules that circumvent the Democratic filibuster and requires only a simple majority to pass. Two Republicans – Warren Davidson of Ohio and Thomas Massie of Kentucky, as well as Kevin Kiley, an independent of California who aligns with the GOP – joined all Democrats in opposing the measure. The resolution’s passage comes amid an intensification of the conflict with Iran, which Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, told the Senate on Tuesday had thus far cost $37.5bn. The Trump administration last month asked Congress to authorize approximately $88bn in supplemental funding, the majority of which – up to $67.1bn – will go to pay for the war. The budget resolution passed by the House largely answers that call by authorizing the armed services committee to propose $60bn in spending for the fiscal years through 2036, and the intelligence committee an additional $13bn. The $73bn sum is expected to go towards military operations against Iran. The agriculture committee has been allocated $12bn in spending changes, which it is expected to propose using on measures to help farmers rocked by the global effects of the conflict with Iran, as well as Trump’s tariff regimen against major trading partners. The House administration committee, which counts federal elections in its jurisdiction, is authorized to propose spending $10bn, and will probably use that to attempt to pass the Save America Act into law. The measure, championed by Donald Trump, would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose enhanced strict identification requirements on voters when they cast ballots and register. But legislation seeking to advance through the Senate under the rules of budget reconciliation can only deal with spending, revenue and the debt limit, making it likely that the Save America Act’s policy changes will be stripped out when the chamber takes up the measure. Mike Johnson nodded to that fact on Tuesday, when he told reporters the goal of the bill was to pass the Save America Act into law “as much of that as possible”. “As always, Republicans support our troops, our farmers and election integrity and we will demonstrate that again this week,” the Republican House speaker said. The budget resolution is the third attempt Republicans have made in Trump’s second term to use the party-line reconciliation procedure to enact their agenda. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed last year, was a reconciliation bill, as was the measure the GOP approved last month that funded agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation campaign through the remainder of his term. Democrats blasted the budget proposal, with Hakeem Jeffries saying before the vote: “President Trump and Republicans in this House continue to act indifferent to the economic wellbeing of the American people and to actively do things that are hurting everyday Americans financially, like this reckless and costly war of choice. “Republican extremists apparently have money for wars, but can’t feed the poor,” the House minority leader added. The House’s approval of the resolution came two days before the chamber recesses until the end of August. But John Thune, the Senate’s Republican majority leader, signaled no urgency in passing the blueprint. At a press conference on Tuesday, he said he would “hold” the measure in case negotiations with Democrats on funding the government break down before the 30 September deadline. If that happens, Thune said, the Senate could repurpose it to pass a stopgap funding measure along party lines. “I hope that’s not necessary,” he said. Even if that scenario were avoided, the budget resolution could face headwinds in the Senate Republican conference, where some lawmakers have blanched because it does not bring total defense spending to the $1.5tn the Trump administration has requested for the 2027 fiscal year. Others have objected to the lack of offsets to the new spending the bill will approve, amid the US’s rising debt load.

title: Trump scoffs at ‘affordability’ as he touts economic policies at Georgia rally
body_text: Donald Trump scoffed at the word “affordability” as a political message, describing it at a campaign rally on Wednesday as a term concocted by Democratic political consultants to criticize his presidency. Yet even as the president dismissed the notion of affordability, he devoted much of his speech at Wheeler high school to touting the bread-and-butter benefits of his economic policies. “So I just want you to remember that if you’re paying a little bit more – a lot of it’s come down now, we got it coming down very rapidly actually,” Trump said in Marietta, an Atlanta suburb, casting higher prices today as a lingering effect of the Biden administration. Americans are broadly disappointed with Trump’s handling of the economy, with just 33% of voters approving in a recent Washington Post-Ipsos poll, an assessment that could hurt his party’s hopes of bucking historical precedent and retaining control of Congress in November’s midterm elections. The president was in Georgia, a politically divided state where high-profile contests for governor and Senate are playing out, to promote his newly funded “Trump accounts”, which establish tax-free investment funds for every child born through 2028, seeded with $1,000 from the federal government. Speaking before the president, the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, described the accounts as the “triumph of capitalism over socialism”, taking a swipe at the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. “Look around our campuses and classrooms today – apart from those here at Wheeler, of course – you will find that our students are being sold the seductive lie that government can solve every problem, redistribute every dollar and supplant its judgment for our own,” Bessent said. “In New York, the current mayor rose to power by repackaging failed ideals of the past as a moral cause of the future. But in Georgia, you know that beneath that youthful veneer lies the oldest impulse in politics which is to concentrate power and then to call it compassion.” Several Republican candidates joined Trump in Marietta, where the president likened the US senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat seeking re-election in one of the most closely watched races of the cycle, to the character Pee-wee Herman, portrayed by the late actor Paul Reubens. Polling shows Ossoff with a lead over the Republican nominee in the Senate race, US congressman Mike Collins, who was in Washington where his vote was needed to help pass a budget bill to fund the Iran war and other White House priorities. Rick Jackson, Georgia’s Republican candidate for governor, pledged to ask the state legislature to match the $1,000 federal contribution to childhood Trump investment accounts if elected. If they failed to do so, Jackson said he would match the figure himself. Jackson is the founder of Jackson Healthcare, a medical staffing company. His personal net worth has been estimated to be more than $3bn. In 2024, the state of Georgia recorded more than 126,000 live births, which equates to $126m in annual contributions for Trump accounts. Georgia began the 2026 fiscal year with an unprecedented budget cushion of about $15bn in the bank, with $9bn in unrestricted funds. This surplus resulted from conservative budgeting that began in 2021 as a reaction to pandemic pressures. That money has become an intense political question, with Republicans looking for ways to provide property tax relief while Democrats argue for a broader investment in healthcare and childcare support. Parents, friends and employers will be able to deposit as much as $5,000 a year into the Trump accounts, which will be controlled by parents and guardians until their children turn 18, after which the account holder gains control and can use saved-up funds to pay for college, buy a home or start a business. The $1,000 contributions will cost the government $17bn through 2028, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. “For decades, Washington politicians gave our children absolutely nothing but debt,” Trump said. “But the Trump accounts, we’re finally seeing and ensuring that every young American gets a great start in life and a really fair shot at the American dream, which is what we all want. They all aspire to that.” Trump increased the national debt by about $8tn in his first term, more than any other president on an inflation-adjusted basis and nearly as much as the government accrued during Barack Obama’s two terms in office. Spending during Trump’s second term is on pace with his first-term mark, with an additional $3bn accrued so far. Inflation currently stands at about 3%, with a decrease of 0.4% last month, driven primarily by a nearly 10% drop in gasoline and oil prices following the short-lived truce in the Iran war. Core inflation was flat for the first time in five years. But gasoline prices have again risen above $4 a gallon in the US, according to AAA tracking, a direct result of oil prices climbing after reawakened hostilities with Iran and the contested strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global oil and gas shipments. Trump said he had just come from Dover air force base in Delaware where he attended the dignified transfer ceremony for US service members killed in the conflict with Iran. The family of 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii accompanied the president on Air Force One to Georgia and attended the event in Marietta, Trump said. Trump continued to claim that his policies had drawn pledges of $19.2tn into the US economy, a figure that economists from the libertarian Cato Institute and elsewhere consider inflated by illusory investment promises.

Rick Jackson, Georgia’s Republican candidate for governor, pledged to ask the state legislature to match the $1,000 federal contribution to childhood Trump investment accounts if elected. If they failed to do so, Jackson said he would match the figure himself. Jackson is the founder of Jackson Healthcare, a medical staffing company. His personal net worth has been estimated to be more than $3bn. In 2024, the state of Georgia recorded more than 126,000 live births, which equates to $126m in annual contributions for Trump accounts. Georgia began the 2026 fiscal year with an unprecedented budget cushion of about $15bn in the bank, with $9bn in unrestricted funds. This surplus resulted from conservative budgeting that began in 2021 as a reaction to pandemic pressures. That money has become an intense political question, with Republicans looking for ways to provide property tax relief while Democrats argue for a broader investment in healthcare and childcare support. Parents, friends and employers will be able to deposit as much as $5,000 a year into the Trump accounts, which will be controlled by parents and guardians until their children turn 18, after which the account holder gains control and can use saved-up funds to pay for college, buy a home or start a business. The $1,000 contributions will cost the government $17bn through 2028, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. “For decades, Washington politicians gave our children absolutely nothing but debt,” Trump said. “But the Trump accounts, we’re finally seeing and ensuring that every young American gets a great start in life and a really fair shot at the American dream, which is what we all want. They all aspire to that.” Trump increased the national debt by about $8tn in his first term, more than any other president on an inflation-adjusted basis and nearly as much as the government accrued during Barack Obama’s two terms in office. Spending during Trump’s second term is on pace with his first-term mark, with an additional $3bn accrued so far. Inflation currently stands at about 3%, with a decrease of 0.4% last month, driven primarily by a nearly 10% drop in gasoline and oil prices following the short-lived truce in the Iran war. Core inflation was flat for the first time in five years. But gasoline prices have again risen above $4 a gallon in the US, according to AAA tracking, a direct result of oil prices climbing after reawakened hostilities with Iran and the contested strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global oil and gas shipments. Trump said he had just come from Dover air force base in Delaware where he attended the dignified transfer ceremony for US service members killed in the conflict with Iran. The family of 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii accompanied the president on Air Force One to Georgia and attended the event in Marietta, Trump said. Trump continued to claim that his policies had drawn pledges of $19.2tn into the US economy, a figure that economists from the libertarian Cato Institute and elsewhere consider inflated by illusory investment promises.

title: What is the US-Saudi Arabia nuclear deal and why is it causing concern?
body_text: The US and Saudi Arabia have agreed a landmark deal that would use American technology and expertise to establish a civilian nuclear program in the Gulf country, a move that has caused alarm across the Middle East and through the corridors of power in Washington. Much of the deal remains unclear, but concerns centre on whether Saudi Arabia would have the capability to enrich uranium domestically, and what that means for nuclear proliferation. What is the nuclear deal that’s agreed? The 30-year deal is designed to meet the “energy needs” of oil-rich Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from US energy secretary Chris Wright. Under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s economic plan, Saudi Arabia aims to use nuclear power for some electricity generation, thereby boosting oil sales by freeing up more supplies for export. The deal would make American companies central in the development of the country’s nuclear infrastructure, while denying competitors like China and Russia a foothold in the country. The deal is thought to be worth tens of billions of dollars, and is the continuation of a plan first conceived during the Biden administration. That deal would have seen the US agree to nuclear cooperation in exchange for Saudi Arabia establishing formal ties with Israel. The prospect of normalisation between Israel and Riyadh has been derailed by the 7 October attack by Hamas, and the resulting years-long war in Gaza. The Trump administration has chosen to push the deal through without the wider agreement with Israel. Will Saudi Arabia be able to enrich uranium on its soil? The deal reportedly paves the way for the building of a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia, but this would be contingent on a joint US-Saudi study determining such a facility is necessary. The study would run for two years, potentially leaving Donald Trump’s successor in the White House with the decision on whether to sign off on allowing domestic enrichment in Saudi Arabia. Many countries with nuclear energy industries do not enrich uranium domestically – a process which could theoretically produce highly enriched uranium for a nuclear weapon. They instead rely on importing the fuel for reactors. Part of the US justification for going through with the deal, is that Washington would have oversight of any enriched uranium and spent fuel from reactors, ensuring they could not be reused to make a bomb. Why is it controversial? Nuclear nonproliferation groups have warned for years that such a deal could set Saudi Arabia on the path to develop a nuclear weapon. Riyadh has in the past said it would need a nuclear weapon if its regional rival, Iran, acquired one. The US is engaged in a war with Iran that is in part being fought to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb or enriching uranium to weapons-grade level. US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed concerns about the Saudi deal, saying the US is “not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation”. The Trump administration’s nuclear cooperation agreement was signed alongside a separate “bilateral safeguards agreement” which it said would provide for adequate monitoring. But experts have expressed alarm that Wednesday’s deal lacks the oversight and guardrails of previous nuclear agreements. Saudi Arabia will reportedly not be subject to the most rigorous monitoring from the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). The IAEA’s “Additional Protocol” has been implemented by dozens of countries, and was one of the requirements of the Obama-era nuclear deal with Iran from which Trump withdrew in 2018. It involves inspection and verification to ensure that countries are using nuclear material solely for peaceful purposes. When the US struck a similar deal with the United Arab Emirates, the UAE agreed not to seek enrichment or process spent atomic fuel, a measure that became known as the “gold standard” for nations wanting atomic power. The Saudi-US agreement reportedly does not include this gold standard. Can this deal be blocked? Opponents have long argued that providing Saudi Arabia with a domestic nuclear program will set off a race across the Middle East for other countries to pursue similar capabilities. Israel – which is known to have a secretive nuclear weapons program – has reportedly raised concerns that the deal could launch a regional arms race. Democrats in Congress have expressed similar concerns. Senator Chris Murphy said the agreement would “set off a nuclear race in the region, further disincentivizing Iran from limiting its own program”. However, Murphy and his colleagues in Congress will probably have difficulty blocking the deal. The deal is expected to be submitted to Congress for approval in the coming days, but to block the agreement, Congress would need to pass a joint resolution and have a two-thirds majority to override the president’s veto.
