title: What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countries
body_text: Just before a temporary levy on global imports was set to expire, the Trump administration issued a fresh wave of tariffs on more than 80 countries late on Thursday, ranging from 10% to 12.5%. The new tariffs take effect on Friday morning. It’s Donald Trump’s latest effort to continue imposing global levies without congressional approval, despite the supreme court ruling in February that found the US president had illegally used his executive power to implement his global trade policies. Trump has long maintained that the US has been paying more than its fair share in tariffs, and that increased duties are necessary to boost American manufacturing and jobs. Here’s what to know about Trump’s latest round of tariffs. Which countries are affected? The US’s largest trading partners, including Canada, Mexico and China, were included among the more than 80 countries that will face the latest tariffs. The United Kingdom, Australia, India and the 27 countries that make up the European Union will also be affected. All of these countries were investigated for their labor practices, according to the office of the US trade representative, who apparently determined whether they were effectively blocking goods that had been produced with forced labor from being imported to the US. How much will they have to pay? These countries will be subject to either a 10% or 12.5% duty. The trading partners that will be subject to a 10% tariff are those who “have made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions”, said the US trade representative. This includes Canada, the European Union, India, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Those that have “failed to adopt a forced labor import prohibition”, including Australia, Brazil, China and Japan, will be subject to a 12.5% tariff rate. What did the supreme court decide on tariffs? In February, the supreme court ruled 6-3 that the 1977 law that Trump had invoked a year earlier was not a sufficient legal justification for the president’s “Liberation Day” tariffs. The law was designed to grant the president greater authority during a national emergency to regulate international trade, but the court said that the power to enact during times of peace belongs solely to Congress. “And they gave Congress ‘alone … access to the pockets of the people’,” the majority opinion reads. “The Framers did not vest any part of the taxing power in the executive branch.” Are the latest tariffs legal? Even after the supreme court found that many of Trump’s tariffs were illegal, the administration had signaled it was determined to find an alternate solution to make tariffs permanent. Trump immediately issued a 150-day 10% global tariff under section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 after the court’s ruling, scheduled to expire at 12.01am, on 24 July. The latest tariffs fall under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which had been used sparingly before Trump’s presidency. It allows the president to impose tariffs if the US trade representative has conducted the required investigations and found sufficient evidence of unfair labor practices that affect American commerce. It is likely that the latest tariffs will be challenged in court. Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics and the former deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization, wrote in an analysis on Thursday that the “new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach”. “If they were challenged in court, the supreme court would likely overturn them,” he added. How have tariffs affected Americans? The New York Federal Reserve estimated that 90% of the economic burden imposed by tariffs was passed on to US consumers and businesses, even though Trump’s administration has maintained they have benefited Americans. Tariff policy has also proved unpopular among many Americans, including Republicans. A recent survey from Harris Poll found that 72% of Americans believe tariffs have had a negative impact on consumers, including 64% of Republican voters. For some American small businesses, however, tariffs have become a non-issue compared with other pressing concerns about the economy, including higher costs and artificial intelligence. Since the February supreme court ruling, the government has also paid companies back tens of billions of tariff revenue.

title: Trump imposes fresh tariffs on UK, EU and dozens of other trading partners
body_text: Donald Trump has imposed a fresh round of tariffs on more than 80 countries to replace a 10% global duty that was due to expire, provoking a wave of criticism and protests from US allies and major trading partners. In the latest attempt to instate aggressive trade policies despite challenges from the US supreme court, the president has imposed tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on dozens of countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the 27 countries that make up the European Union. It in effect replaces the blanket 10% tariff that Trump imposed in February, right after the supreme court declared many of his earlier tariffs were illegal. The newest levies, announced late on Thursday by the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, would fall under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is aimed against countries that engage in forced labor. Trump had said his administration would investigate unfair trading practices to impose permanent tariffs as soon as the February supreme court decision was announced. “The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” Greer said in a statement. “I am encouraged by the trading partners who have moved quickly to adopt forced labor import prohibitions, and look forward to ensuring their effective enforcement.” Australia and Brazil described the new tariffs as unjustified and said they would seek to have them removed, while Norway’s foreign minister said there was no basis for the new tariffs. The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc would seek clarification from Washington, adding that it had honoured commitments under a transatlantic trade agreement reached last year and viewed ⁠the new tariffs as a shock. Canada, one of America’s largest trading partners, immediately responded that it “should not be targeted”, adding it was a leader against the practice of importing goods produced with forced labor. “If the intent is truly to address forced labour, the focus should be a coordinated approach through a multilateral mechanism,” Matthew Holmes, executive vice-president of the Canadian chamber of commerce, said in a statement. “The timing of this is somewhat suspect as previous rounds of tariffs sunset.” Trump had long viewed tariffs – border taxes levied on imports – as a core tool to protect American jobs and manufacturing, reduce trade deficits and reverse what he sees as “unfair” practices by US trading partners. Tariff, he has said many times, is “the most beautiful word in the dictionary”. Only Congress has the authority under the constitution to levy taxes. But last April, on what he declared was “liberation day”, Trump announced a baseline 10% tariff under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, a trade law that grants the president the authority to regulate international transactions during a national emergency. That policy, however, suffered a damaging blow in February when the US supreme court ruled 6-3 that the ability to enact tariffs during peacetime still belongs to Congress. Trump immediately announced another 10% tariff regime under another trade law that had never been used before, which limited the tariffs to a period of 150 days. Those tariffs expired a minute past midnight on Friday morning US eastern time. The latest round of tariffs invoke section 301, which has long proved controversial and so far been used sparingly, according to a Brookings analysis of the law in March. Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics and the former deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization, wrote in an analysis on Thursday that the latest tariffs “again raise the question of whether the president has the legal authority to determine and implement US tariff policy – an authority that the constitution vests in Congress”. “The answer is no: Congress did not delegate authority of such breadth to the president. It cannot constitutionally do so,” he said. “These new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach. If they were challenged in court, the supreme court would likely overturn them.” Outside courtroom setbacks, Trump’s tariffs have also proved unpopular among Americans, potentially presenting a threat to Republicans at the midterms this November. A Harris Poll survey, conducted exclusively for the Guardian, found earlier this year that seven in 10 Americans said they paid higher prices because of Trump’s tariffs, and 72% of voters believe the tariffs have had a negative rather than a positive impact on consumers. This belief persisted even among Republican voters: 64% agreed that Trump’s tariffs had led to higher prices, and 60% said tariffs had had a negative impact. American consumers have also been pummeled by the effects of the war in the Middle East, which have sent energy costs and gas prices soaring. The rise in energy prices has also led to a surge in inflation, which jumped to a three-year high this May. Trump and his administration, however, are adamant that his policies have only improved the lives of American consumers. During a heated exchange before US senators on Wednesday, Greer appeared to claim Trump’s policies had not driven prices higher. Asked by the Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren if the tariffs had increased prices for American families, Greer said: “No.” “Core inflation fell to 2.6% year on year, much better than in January 2025,” he added. Core inflation excludes food and energy. Overall inflation is slightly higher than it was when Joe Biden left office.

title: Trump says he will dismantle the ICC ‘brick by brick’. It could be his most chilling move of all
body_text: Barely a month appears to go by without Donald Trump making a fresh attempt to destroy the international rules-based order. The US has pulled funding from dozens of international institutions, shut down USAID and withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement. Nato may survive on paper, but Trump has made clear that he has little interest in coming to the aid of any ally that is attacked. The Board of Peace is clearly an attempt to sideline the United Nations. But the state department’s announcement last week that it wishes to dismantle the international criminal court “brick by brick” could be Trump’s most frightening move of all. This is not an idle social media post sent out late at night; there is no chance that the next person to speak to Trump might change his mind. It is now official US policy to destroy the ICC, and the administration is prepared to go to extraordinary lengths to do so. Nations that do not fall into line will be punished. The state department has promised “increased scrutiny of nations that refuse to reject the ICC’s false authority while relying on US assistance”, particularly targeting those countries that “enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella”. That will include the UK, a country that contributes just over £15m a year to the ICC, making it the fourth largest donor after Japan, Germany and France. Travel and sanctions bans have already been imposed on judges and senior officials; now more will be targeted. As one of those previously threatened with sanctions told me, it can result in individuals being completely cut off from modern life. Personal bank accounts are shut down, while a whole host of US apps and websites, from Uber to booking.com, are off-limits. Email accounts can be blocked – Microsoft and Google are US companies. For the court itself, it means backing up evidence previously held on Microsoft systems. The state department campaign also includes working with other nations that are not part of the ICC, suggesting that the US could ally itself with Russia and China. Make no mistake, this is an existential crisis not just for the ICC but the very idea of international justice. The most powerful nation on Earth and the supposed leader of the democratic west is aligning itself with dictators and autocrats to prevent those accused of genocide, ethnic cleansing and war crimes from ever facing justice. The US has had a complicated history with international justice. It was integral in the establishment of the post-second world war Nuremberg trials but was reluctant to ratify the genocide convention, only doing so in 1988, four decades after it was passed by the UN general assembly. The issue was always one of self-preservation, rather than principle. For generations of US politicians, mainly Republicans but including some Democrats, the very idea that judges in other countries could hold American citizens to account was a non-starter. Until now, successive US presidents have generally accepted the idea of international justice even if, hypocritically, they did not want it to apply to them. The US refused to sign the Rome statute that created the ICC in 2002, but it did not use its power to prevent its birth. In 2005, at the height of the Darfur genocide, it allowed the UN security council to pass a resolution authorising the ICC to investigate, and if necessary prosecute, those accused of war crimes in Sudan. Under Joe Biden’s presidency, it also encouraged the ICC to prosecute Vladimir Putin for alleged war crimes committed in Ukraine. For Trump, though, the ICC has always been a threat. He imposed sanctions on court officials during his first term, following an investigation into alleged war crimes committed by US troops in Afghanistan. The campaign against the court ratcheted up after his return to office last year. The ICC’s chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, had issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes in Gaza. In response, Trump imposed fresh sanctions on ICC officials including Khan. The threats to the ICC are not just coming from its enemies – many of them are self-inflicted. Two women, one a staffer at the ICC, have accused Khan of sexual abuse. The executive committee of the ICC’s governing body last month voted to suspend Khan, who denies any wrongdoing, after concluding that he had committed serious misconduct. The court’s 125 member states will, this Friday, vote on whether to remove him from office. Staff in The Hague say the ICC has become an increasingly high-pressure place to work, with one former senior official describing the atmosphere as toxic. There are also concerns from international law and human rights experts over its record. It has botched many of its big cases, including against Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto, two opposing politicians who were both accused of fomenting Kenya’s post-election violence in 2007-8. As the ICC dithered, witnesses disappeared and the two men joined forces to run for election. Their election as president and vice-president in 2012 eventually led to the case collapsing. The question now is what the “rest of the west” will do in response to Trump’s attacks. The court’s biggest donors need to stay strong and not give in to intimidation. It will be an early test for Ed Miliband, who said upon his appointment as foreign secretary on Monday that “we face a time of greater instability and threat to international law … than at any time since the second world war”. The ICC’s imperfections undoubtedly make it a harder institution to defend. Those weaknesses can be magnified and targeted, making the court’s natural defenders reluctant to man the barricades. Yet that is exactly what needs to happen. Even when it is badly run or cases are poorly constructed, the ICC’s very existence can have an impact. Netanyahu and Putin will for ever be referred to as men indicted for war crimes. Their worlds have shrunk thanks to the threat of arrest. The Philippines’ former president, Rodrigo Duterte, is on trial, accused of crimes against humanity during his “war on drugs”. This is why Trump is so determined to shut it down, argues Luis Moreno Ocampo, the court’s first chief prosecutor. “Trump knows he could be a target after he leaves office,” he told me. “The ICC is a huge obstacle for him.” And that’s another reason why it’s so important the ICC is saved. Actions need to have consequences. After the midterm elections in the US, a Democrat-led Congress is likely to hold hearings and open investigations into a whole host of Trump’s actions, from his murky dealings to his use of paramilitaries against his own citizens. But the rest of the world needs to hold him accountable too – whether it’s for bombing boats in the Caribbean, striking a school in Iran or indeed any fresh horror he commits in the next two and a half years. Just as Putin and Netanyahu will live out the rest of their days knowing the threat of arrest could lie just around the corner, Trump fears this might be his fate. He cannot be allowed to escape it. Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

title: Trump administration drive to seize election powers sparking ‘chaos’ despite pushback
body_text: The Trump administration continues to expand its authoritarian and radical drive to revamp voting rules and seize state election powers, though it faces growing resistance from US courts, state officials and Democrats, who warn the moves are sparking “chaos” and endangering voting rights and the rule of law. Donald Trump’s unprecedented drive to change election rules, which states legally set, is fueled by his obsession with his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, which he falsely attributes to voting fraud, coupled with his fear that Democrats will “find a reason to impeach me” if they take control of the House in November’s midterms elections, say former election officials and legal experts. Given Trump’s dark mindset, his administration has used justice department legal moves and threats, FBI raids and investigations, and other federal agencies to coerce states to change voting rules in key ways, including curtailing voting by mail and machines that Trump and Maga allies have vilified, baselessly, as riddled with fraud. Legal experts say the administration is intimidating election workers and voters before the November elections, and laying the groundwork for potentially challenging election results where Republican candidates lose to ensure the GOP keeps control of Congress. In a conspiratorial 25-minute televised talk on 16 July, Trump presented a hodgepodge of selective intelligence and misleading allegations about Chinese efforts to influence the 2020 elections to hurt him, plus debunked claims of increased voting by noncitizens, flawed voting machines and other threats, to argue that the US elections system needs drastic changes. Trump asserted without hard evidence that American elections were rife with “hacking, manipulation and corruption. Great damage has been done to our country.” In a sharp rebuttal, the nation’s 24 Democratic governors said: “It’s deeply alarming that President Trump continues to try to undermine free and fair elections. No amount of lies and conspiracy theories can change the fact that our country’s elections have repeatedly been proven to be safe and secure.” Trump’s goal, say critics, is to instill fear in voters’ minds, and push for radical measures pre-election including congressional passage of the Save America Act, which would sharply limit voting by mail and require voters to present proof of US citizenship. It lacks the votes in the Senate to pass. Over the past few months, for example, the Department of Justice has demanded that 30 US states provide unredacted voter lists, which contain personal and sensitive information. In July, top justice department official Harmeet Dhillon threatened state election officials with criminal investigations and prosecutions if they knowingly permitted noncitizens to register to vote. The FBI has taken extraordinary steps to again investigate the Georgia election results in 2020 that Trump bitterly contested after his loss there: early in 2026, the FBI seized hundreds of boxes of 2020 ballots from Fulton county, and in July sent 200 agents there to investigate the 2020 results and election workers. The administration’s hardball tactics have sparked strong criticism from experts, and resistance including legal rebuffs from courts nationwide as well as state officials and Democrats. Voting rights advocates and former election officials point out that courts have overwhelmingly rebuked justice department lawyers for their claims seeking to justify administration moves to obtain unredacted voting lists from the states and information about election workers in Georgia and other states. Eileen O’Connor, who spent eight years as an attorney in the justice department’s voting section in the civil rights division and is now with the Brennan Center for Justice, said: “[The] DoJ has had case after case seeking unredacted voter rolls from the states rejected by judges. The DoJ has filed 30 of these cases and has now lost 15 of them.” In another election-related matter where the Department of Justice sought detailed information on every election worker in Fulton county, Georgia, in the 2020 election, O’Connor noted the judge “openly excoriated the DoJ” and called the subpoena an “arbitrary fishing expedition”. Although the justice department is not winning in courts, O’Connor stressed, “they’re injecting chaos” into this year’s elections. More broadly, O’Connor said, the administration’s strategy was “to decrease confidence in the elections and possibly lay the groundwork for possible challenges” post-election. Former election officials are also raising red flags about Trump’s multiple moves to undermine confidence in the fall elections and intimidate voters and election workers. “Trump is trying to intimidate state election officials and threatening actions aimed at suppressing the Democratic vote,” said Larry Noble, a former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission who teaches law at the American University. “It’s also likely he thinks he’s laying the groundwork to claim that any Republican loss is due to fraud.” Noble said several of Trump’s recent actions – including his “firing the members of the non-partisan Election Assistance Commission, and suggesting he is open to possibly sending ICE agents and national guard troops to polling places” – were “a continuation of his efforts to exert control over the midterm elections”. He added: “It’s not clear what, if any, limits he has on how far he will go to prevent Democrats from gaining back power. I fear it’s even possible he will order actions to try to disrupt voting or vote counting during the election to avoid Republican losses.” Democratic and Republican election officials and congressional Democrats have been pushing back hard on the Trump administration’s multifront fight to change election rules. In a social media post, for instance, Deidre Henderson, Utah’s top election official and lieutenant governor, condemned the tone and tactics used by Dhillon in her threatening letter to states. “Got another love letter this morning from the DoJ, sprinkled throughout with threats of criminal prosecution,” Henderson wrote. “This is truly bizarre behavior by the federal agency that is supposed to be protecting civil rights.” In another pressure move, Dhillon told Michigan officials this month that the justice department plans to send federal monitors to three cities, including Lansing, that are Democratic-leaning while the state’s 4 August primaries are held. Likewise, the Federal Emergency Management Agency promulgated new rules late last month that demand states change how they conduct elections to avoid losing federal counter-terrorism funding from the Department of Homeland Security, Fema’s parent agency. Markwayne Mullin, in a press briefing the day after Trump’s speech, upped the ante by threatening local election officials with jail time if they failed to comply with the administration’s moves to change election policies. The DHS secretary reiterated several of Trump’s unsubstantiated assertions about the security of American elections. Voting experts and former justice department officials say the administration’s multifaceted blitz to overhaul voting rules is a dangerous political exercise aimed at boosting Trump’s powers and keeping the GOP in control of Congress. “Six years after the 2020 election, after audits, recounts, litigation and now internal investigation, Donald Trump has failed to produce any evidence of election tampering that changed votes,” said Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney who teaches law at the University of Michigan. “While foreign adversaries have conducted propaganda campaigns to influence public opinion, those operations have favored Trump as much as his opponents. Reducing foreign influence in our elections is a valid goal, but stopping voting by mail will not advance that goal. With an estimated one in four Democrats and one in five Republicans voting by mail, ending voting by mail has only one effect, and that is to favor Republican candidates.” McQuade added: “Trump’s speech revealed no new evidence and merely served to lay the groundwork for baseless claims of election fraud in November, when election outcomes will almost certainly be disastrous for a president with a dismal 37% approval rating.” Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Law School and a former top official in the justice department’s civil rights division, said: “The administration is trying desperately to project power that it simply doesn’t have. That includes trying to intimidate state and local officials who aren’t going to be intimidated.” Still, that intimidation drive is especially acute in the FBI’s efforts in Georgia. “The assignment of hundreds of FBI personnel to look at the 2020 election is doing nothing more than allowing a puppet FBI director to be dangled about by the president,” said Michael Moore, a former US attorney in Georgia. Some Republicans also worry that Trump’s obsession with his 2020 loss and his non-stop attacks on election rules and voting rights will backfire and hurt GOP candidates. “Trump simply has an unhealthy obsession with the 2020 election that he lost,” said Charlie Dent, the former Republican House member of Pennsylvania. “He’s using the levers of the federal government to investigate an election that’s already been well investigated. “Trump seems very determined to prevent losing congressional control by the GOP. But he’s doing so much that makes it difficult for the GOP to win.” In historical terms, some voting rights experts say the Trump administration’s attacks on voting rules are unprecedented and foresee other dangerous moves ahead. “The Trump administration is doing everything they can to stack the deck in their favor. This is the most hostile administration towards voting rights and democracy we’ve seen in our lifetimes,” said Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy at the non-partisan Campaign Legal Center. Looking ahead, Diaz warned: “We have very real concerns that they’ll try to weaponize law enforcement either to disrupt or interfere with the elections while they’re in progress, or after ballots have been cast before they’re certified.”

Former election officials are also raising red flags about Trump’s multiple moves to undermine confidence in the fall elections and intimidate voters and election workers. “Trump is trying to intimidate state election officials and threatening actions aimed at suppressing the Democratic vote,” said Larry Noble, a former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission who teaches law at the American University. “It’s also likely he thinks he’s laying the groundwork to claim that any Republican loss is due to fraud.” Noble said several of Trump’s recent actions – including his “firing the members of the non-partisan Election Assistance Commission, and suggesting he is open to possibly sending ICE agents and national guard troops to polling places” – were “a continuation of his efforts to exert control over the midterm elections”. He added: “It’s not clear what, if any, limits he has on how far he will go to prevent Democrats from gaining back power. I fear it’s even possible he will order actions to try to disrupt voting or vote counting during the election to avoid Republican losses.” Democratic and Republican election officials and congressional Democrats have been pushing back hard on the Trump administration’s multifront fight to change election rules. In a social media post, for instance, Deidre Henderson, Utah’s top election official and lieutenant governor, condemned the tone and tactics used by Dhillon in her threatening letter to states. “Got another love letter this morning from the DoJ, sprinkled throughout with threats of criminal prosecution,” Henderson wrote. “This is truly bizarre behavior by the federal agency that is supposed to be protecting civil rights.” In another pressure move, Dhillon told Michigan officials this month that the justice department plans to send federal monitors to three cities, including Lansing, that are Democratic-leaning while the state’s 4 August primaries are held. Likewise, the Federal Emergency Management Agency promulgated new rules late last month that demand states change how they conduct elections to avoid losing federal counter-terrorism funding from the Department of Homeland Security, Fema’s parent agency. Markwayne Mullin, in a press briefing the day after Trump’s speech, upped the ante by threatening local election officials with jail time if they failed to comply with the administration’s moves to change election policies. The DHS secretary reiterated several of Trump’s unsubstantiated assertions about the security of American elections. Voting experts and former justice department officials say the administration’s multifaceted blitz to overhaul voting rules is a dangerous political exercise aimed at boosting Trump’s powers and keeping the GOP in control of Congress. “Six years after the 2020 election, after audits, recounts, litigation and now internal investigation, Donald Trump has failed to produce any evidence of election tampering that changed votes,” said Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney who teaches law at the University of Michigan. “While foreign adversaries have conducted propaganda campaigns to influence public opinion, those operations have favored Trump as much as his opponents. Reducing foreign influence in our elections is a valid goal, but stopping voting by mail will not advance that goal. With an estimated one in four Democrats and one in five Republicans voting by mail, ending voting by mail has only one effect, and that is to favor Republican candidates.” McQuade added: “Trump’s speech revealed no new evidence and merely served to lay the groundwork for baseless claims of election fraud in November, when election outcomes will almost certainly be disastrous for a president with a dismal 37% approval rating.” Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Law School and a former top official in the justice department’s civil rights division, said: “The administration is trying desperately to project power that it simply doesn’t have. That includes trying to intimidate state and local officials who aren’t going to be intimidated.” Still, that intimidation drive is especially acute in the FBI’s efforts in Georgia. “The assignment of hundreds of FBI personnel to look at the 2020 election is doing nothing more than allowing a puppet FBI director to be dangled about by the president,” said Michael Moore, a former US attorney in Georgia. Some Republicans also worry that Trump’s obsession with his 2020 loss and his non-stop attacks on election rules and voting rights will backfire and hurt GOP candidates. “Trump simply has an unhealthy obsession with the 2020 election that he lost,” said Charlie Dent, the former Republican House member of Pennsylvania. “He’s using the levers of the federal government to investigate an election that’s already been well investigated. “Trump seems very determined to prevent losing congressional control by the GOP. But he’s doing so much that makes it difficult for the GOP to win.” In historical terms, some voting rights experts say the Trump administration’s attacks on voting rules are unprecedented and foresee other dangerous moves ahead. “The Trump administration is doing everything they can to stack the deck in their favor. This is the most hostile administration towards voting rights and democracy we’ve seen in our lifetimes,” said Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy at the non-partisan Campaign Legal Center. Looking ahead, Diaz warned: “We have very real concerns that they’ll try to weaponize law enforcement either to disrupt or interfere with the elections while they’re in progress, or after ballots have been cast before they’re certified.”

title: New York Chinatown fears impact of $8bn casino development, calling it ‘predatory project’
body_text: On Main Street in Flushing’s Chinatown, shoppers weave between fruit stands, restaurants and family-run businesses that have served the New York City neighborhood for decades. But behind the bustle, many residents fear the working-class immigrant community is under threat from an $8bn casino development that could displace thousands of renters and force small businesses to close. “A predatory project is being dumped in our community that disproportionately harms our people,” said Jack Hu, 35, a Flushing resident and member of the No Casino in Flushing Meadows Corona Park campaign. “This community is really upset about this project and how it was pushed through without our consent.” Metropolitan Park is a casino and entertainment project backed by the New York Mets owner, Steve Cohen, and Hard Rock International through Queens Future LLC. The development would turn parking lots next to Citi Field at Willets Point into a casino, hotel, restaurants, an entertainment district and a public park between the Flushing and Corona neighborhoods. Chinese immigrant communities have higher rates of problem gambling than the general population, studies have found. This is due to a number of issues, including cultural beliefs around luck and fortune, immigration-related stresses and isolation, barriers to accessing mental healthcare, and casino marketing targeting Chinese-speaking clients. In Flushing, the community is already burdened by gambling addiction, and a casino on its doorstep could make things worse, especially among its elderly populations, said some residents. “This is a working-class community and the Metropolitan Park casino is also going to extract wealth from the most vulnerable,” said Hu, who says his father has a gambling addiction, which he developed soon after immigrating to the US. “Casino operators use things like meal coupons, free bus vouchers, free gambling vouchers to lure working-class Asians into casinos so that they can take their money.” In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson for Metropolitan Park said: “We take our responsibility to be a good neighbor and a good partner seriously. Metropolitan Park includes over $1bn in community benefits. This includes a community impact fund and specific funding for responsible gaming, addiction and mental health services.” The project has also signed memorandums of understanding with local organizations such Elmcor Youth & Adult Activities; Hamilton-Madison House, which provinces clinical mental health services; Korean Community Services; and the Korean American Family Service Center to create “culturally sensitive and community-adapted addiction services”, the spokesperson said. According to the Urban Institute, a DC-based thinktank focused on economic and social policy research, the Metropolitan Park proposal could displace almost 16,000 renters who spend more than half of their income on housing in Corona and Flushing due to rising rents. “It will make the whole town worse. Gambling is not a good thing, people get addicted to it,” said Xiang, an employee of a bakery who moved to Queens from China seven years ago. “Tourists might bring money, but the casino could also bring trouble here.” The Metropolitan Park spokesperson said: “A comprehensive environmental impact study (EIS) was conducted, finding that Metropolitan Park will not directly displace any existing businesses or residents. This study was reviewed and accepted by the city planning commission.” Many business owners in the community have recently been affected by the Trump administration’s sanctions against China, making imported goods more expensive. If commercial rents were to rise as a result of the casino, many of these businesses could also be displaced, said some residents. Residents also said they were skeptical that casino visitors would patronize Flushing’s independent businesses, noting that the resort will have its own restaurants and amenities. As evidence, they pointed to the limited spillover from nearby Citi Field and the US Open, which they said have brought few sports fans into the neighborhood. “If you look around here, you’ll see just locals,” said Hu. “There’s nobody that comes here and drops a load of money at a local restaurant. These events do not pull business into Flushing.” A new poll, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found that 61% of likely Democratic voters in New York’s sixth congressional district oppose the project, compared with 20% who support it. The remaining 19% were undecided. The poll was conducted by Public Policy Polling in June. It was commissioned by the Democratic congressional candidate Chuck Park as part of a broader survey conducted during his campaign for the Democratic nomination to challenge Grace Meng, the incumbent representative in New York’s sixth congressional district primary, in June. Park ultimately lost the nomination to Meng, who has represented the district in Congress since 2013. Separately, Park said he knocked on the doors of 6,000 residents during his campaign, many of whom raised their objections to the casino with him. “We heard over and over and over again that people did not want the casino. This spanned from really socially conservative first-generation immigrants who thought that the casino would bring crime, human trafficking, and lead to major quality-of-life concerns,” said Park. “We also heard from young progressive leftist activists that this casino is a giveaway of public land to a billionaire who just wants to make himself even richer.” During the project’s public approval process in March 2025, the casino’s backers told the New York City council that Metropolitan Park had “actively engaged with community leaders” and that community involvement had been central to the proposal. The project won one of New York’s three downstate casino licenses in December 2025. “With nearly four years of community engagement, over 30 public meetings and approvals from six community boards, the city council, the state legislature, the community advisory committee and the gaming commission, Metropolitan Park has undergone one of the most rigorous and transparent public reviews of any project. The community has been heard, and their message is clear: they want Metropolitan Park,” said a spokesperson for the project. “Metropolitan Park will be an economic gamechanger for the local community, bringing over 23,000 new jobs, a dedicated Queens vendor food hall and over $100m in anticipated local spending annually.” The casino developers highlight they have adopted a “community-first” approach on the Metropolitan Park project’s website, and claim the project will provide jobs, green space and entertainment for residents. “Casinos are the worst form of regressive tax,” said Park. “They lure in low-income members of local communities. They get them addicted to gambling, and then they just milk money.” The casino project received a major boost from the state senator John Liu, who introduced Senate Bill S7121A, known as the “parkland alienation” bill, last year, which allows a local government to sell or repurpose public parkland for non-park uses. Without the legislation being signed into law, Cohen’s project may never have been realized, critics say. Liu was able to introduce the bill because a small area of the proposed project falls in the 16th senate district he represents. In exchange for the parkland alienation bill, Cohen pledged to build a bridge, similar to Manhattan’s High Line, connecting downtown Flushing to Willets Point, which Liu has called “Flushing Skypark”. “Given the inevitability of three casinos in NYC resulting from the 2012 state referendum, all within a stone’s throw of Senator Liu’s district, he appropriately turned his focus toward mitigating potential harms and maximizing public benefits to his constituents,” said Liu’s spokesperson. “Senator Liu appreciates the passion with which some advocates oppose the casino, but he has received far greater demand to allow the bid to be submitted for consideration by the gaming commission.” Public campaign finance records show that Liu received a $5,000 donation from the New York Hotel and Motel Trades Council committee on political education political action group in 2025. The Pac receives the majority of its funding from the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council (HTC) labor union. “Senator Liu has been proud to receive substantial support for over two decades from a union that has been particularly successful in fighting for record-breaking wage and benefit increases for its members, mostly immigrant women of color,” said his spokesperson. Liu’s move was met with backlash, including protests from the community. In 2024, one year earlier, Liu penned an op-ed in Daily News, stating the three New York casino projects would exact “disproportionate harm” on “this historically marginalized and increasingly vulnerable community”. “It’s clear they have Asian-Americans squarely in their sights,” Liu said of the casino developers in the article. The spokesperson for Liu said: “Senator Liu has been clear about his opposition to casinos and gambling in general anywhere, but if they are in fact going to be sited downstate (a decision made by voter referendum in 2012), the maximum amount of public benefit must be provided. That is what Senator Liu negotiated, under the assumption that casinos will be sited downstate – whether at the Mets site or the others, which are all in close proximity to the Asian community.” Having watched his father struggle with gambling for more than three decades, Hu fears that a casino in his neighborhood will deepen his father’s addiction. “He wants to retain a little bit of hope to become wealthy,” said Hu, whose parents moved to Flushing from Guangzhou in the 1980s. “It’s like you’ve grown up your entire life with nothing. You come here seeking to build a better life for yourself and for your family, and it’s these types of people that fall victim to these predatory businesses that tell you that you can get wealthy quickly.”

title: Justice Elena Kagan decries idea that US supreme court ‘rubber-stamps’ Trump’s agenda
body_text: The liberal justice Elena Kagan has said it was “wrong” to accuse the US supreme court of becoming a rubber stamp for Donald Trump in his second term, amid criticism of its authorization of some of the president’s most controversial actions. Pointing to rulings against the president on key issues such as tariffs, Kagan – one of three liberals on a court that has in recent years been defined by rulings authored by members of its six-justice conservative majority – defended it at an annual gathering of attorneys and judges for the ninth judicial circuit in Bellevue, Washington, on Thursday. “Is this a really conservative court? The answer is yes. The second question is: is this a court that does whatever the current administration wants? The answer is no,” Kagan said. It comes after the court allowed Trump to have his way on a string of issues. These include on immigration policy, where they upheld his effort to end temporary deportation protections for Haitians and Syrians, and also issued an order on the shadow docket that strips Venezuelans of those same protections. Conservatives have also recently allowed Trump and future presidents to fire the heads of independent agencies, while boosting his Republican allies’ chances of keeping control of the House of Representatives by weakening the Voting Rights Act. Three members of the court’s conservative majority were appointed by Trump during his first term. But Kagan pointed to the court’s February ruling, in which she and the liberals joined three conservative justices to strike down Trump’s use of executive authority to impose tariffs on a host of countries. “Tariffs is probably the key policy issue for this president,” said Kagan, who joined the court in 2010 after being appointed by Democratic president Barack Obama. “I don’t think that there are all that many decisions in recent times where a court strikes down such an important policy to a sitting president.” Beyond trade policy, the supreme court has also scuppered Trump’s attempt to fire the Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, and blocked his administration’s effort to end birthright citizenship. Kagan added: “I don’t see this as a court that is … going to rubber-stamp what the current administration does. You know, quite the opposite. I actually think that there are significant times with respect to very significant issues where the court has checked the executive branch.”

title: Democrats move to keep South Carolina as first state to vote in 2028 presidential primaries
body_text: Democrats moved to keep South Carolina as the first state to vote in their party’s 2028 presidential primary process, while moving up several other states, in an effort to better represent the views of the party’s racially diverse voter base. At a meeting in Washington DC of the Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) rules and bylaws committee on Friday, South Carolina received a slim majority of votes to take the first spot, scheduled for 22 January 2028, with Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia set to follow, in that order. The selections must still be confirmed by the full DNC at a meeting set for next month. Minyon Moore and James Roosevelt Jr, who co-chair the committee, called the proposal “a rigorous, fair, and efficient calendar that will win Democrats back the White House in 2028”. South Carolina was the state whose primary voters revitalized Joe Biden’s presidential campaign in 2020, and as president he returned the favor by encouraging the DNC to make the state the first to vote in the 2024 nominating calendar. That supplanted New Hampshire, the site for decades of the first primary for both parties, as well as Iowa, which holds caucuses that have traditionally been the first nominating contest of presidential election years. However, both states are overwhelmingly white, and with Democrats increasingly relying on Black, Latino and other minority voters to elect their candidates, the party has sought to move states with larger populations of those groups towards the front of the nominating calendar, where they can play a crucial role in selecting the presidential frontrunners. Making the case for South Carolina, the long-serving congressman James Clyburn said in a statement ahead of the meeting: “We have a record that all of us can point to and be proud of. It’s a relatively small state. It has four distinct cultures, a relatively cheap media market, and demographics that reflect what our voter population needs to be in order for our candidates to be successful in the general election.” During the meeting, the Nevada Democratic chair, Daniele Monroe-Moreno, argued that her state offers the ideal racial mix and nodded to Donald Trump’s success there in 2024, when he became the first Republican in two decades to win its electoral votes. “When we go into the next presidential cycle, my state, the state of Nevada, is that coalition that we need to win back,” she said. The new early voting states are either presidential battlegrounds or home to hotly contested US Senate races and House districts. They also have substantially more Black and Latino voters than the states that led the 2020 nominating calendar, as well as larger populations of voters in unions or without college degrees, both constituencies with which many Democratic candidates have struggled to win in recent elections.

title: Trump administration admits canceling clean energy grants to Democratic states
body_text: The Trump administration has admitted scrapping more than $7.5bn in federal grants for clean energy projects to states “based solely” on whether they backed Donald Trump in the 2024 election. US federal officials appeared to acknowledge in court documents last week that they had terminated the funding last October “based solely” on political criteria, targeting projects in states that were represented by Democrats and had voted for Kamala Harris. The administration previously framed the move as safeguarding taxpayer dollars from “waste” and continues to insist it was not politically motivated. “[The Department of Energy] accepts that neither the inclusion of the ARCHES grant nor any other grants in the October notice tranche was based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor,” government lawyers said in the filing. “[The Department of Energy] accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, ie, whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State. “[The Department of Energy] will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.” The apparent admission was first reported by the New York Times. In a statement on Friday, a spokesperson for the US energy department said of the report: “That is a misrepresentation of the court filing. None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.” The acknowledgment of political considerations “was referring to the timing of the announcement, not of the decisions themselves”, the spokesperson claimed. The filings stem from a lawsuit, filed last June, by a group of six University of California faculty and other researchers challenging various federal agencies that halted Biden-era funding. The plaintiffs said in a press release at the time that the abrupt cancellations of already-awarded grants had been a part of a “political ‘cost-cutting’ agenda and ideological purity campaign” waged by the administration. It comes as the White House seeks to exert even greater control over billions of dollars in annual federal grants, aiming to have Trump’s political appointees review all federal grants, with the power to block or revoke vast amounts of funding if they did not conform to or align with Trump’s priorities. According to a 400-page proposed rule for federal financial assistance published on 29 May, “Discretionary awards must, where applicable, demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities.” They must also adhere to further standards set out by the White House, including not promoting “anti-American values”, the denial of “the sex binary in humans” and the use of “racial preferences” in selection criterion. Per last week’s court filing, the energy department had reviewed its financial assistance awards and created a list last September that recommended canceling more than 600 grants awarded by the Biden administration for a wide range of clean energy projects in states represented by both Republicans and Democrats. However, in October, the White House budget office, led by Russell Vought, terminated only 284 of those grants. Vought announced on X: “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled. The projects are in the following states: CA, CO, CT, DE, HI, IL, MD, MA, MN, NH, NJ, NM, NY, OR, VT, WA.” Last week, federal officials appeared to concede that the decision had been purely informed by politics. “With one exception, the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators (“Blue State” grants),” the court filing says. Meanwhile, the energy department left in place hundreds of other energy grants in state represented by Republicans and that had voted for Trump in 2024 – despite the department having also recommended that they too be scrapped. Last month, Trump’s energy secretary, Chris Wright, appeared before the House science, space and technology committee to defend his department’s fiscal 2027 budget request. “No decisions were made on politics,” he insisted. The Guardian has reached out to the White House.

title: ‘Proxy for Trump’ Milei tours Latin America to meet far-right leaders
body_text: Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, is not particularly fond of travelling to multilateral forums – it is not unusual for him to skip Mercosur summits, as he did a few weeks ago. But on Saturday he begins a tour of Latin America to meet far-right leaders, starting in Brazil with the launch of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign against the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, ahead of October’s election. Milei will then attend Keiko Fujimori’s inauguration in Peru on Tuesday, followed by Abelardo de la Espriella’s inauguration in Colombia on 7 August, from where he will travel to Ecuador to meet president Daniel Noboa. The self-styled libertarian has justified the trips as those of “a president willing to open up to the world, seeking to triple the country’s trade”. But analysts point to the timing: amid his declining popularity at home, the tour comes in the wake of a wave of far-right victories in presidential elections across Latin America. “As someone who has been in power for a little longer, Milei is trying to establish himself as a leader of that group,” said Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, a researcher and professor at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. “I’ve never seen Milei take much interest in official visits to other countries,” said Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, a sociologist and professor at Universidad Torcuato Di Tella in Buenos Aires. “What interests him are figures from the world of big tech and the far right, but in neither case is there any real interest in opening trade negotiations,” he added. Benjamin Gedan, a senior fellow and director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said a constant in Milei’s trips has been his effort to remain “deferential to the US president, Donald Trump, and never trying to upstage him”. When Trump took office in January 2025, Milei faced relatively little competition for his affection in Latin America, where fewer than a dozen other far-right presidents were in office, most notably El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. Trump described Milei as his “favourite president”. Since then, however, rightwing or far-right candidates have won all seven presidential elections held in the region, with the US president accused of attempting to influence some of them. Almost all of the winners also interacted with Milei during their campaigns through public exchanges of praise or video calls but, according to Tokatlian, there is no doubt about whom they were really trying to please. “All these rightwing leaders see Milei as a kind of proxy for Trump, who is the one who is really in charge. They don’t want to be under any kind of Argentine leadership. It’s Milei who’s trying, but there’s no great eagerness for him,” he said. Tokatlian believes that any contest for Trump’s favour, if one exists at all, will be decided by “whoever gives the US the most on drug trafficking, migration, military cooperation and containing China’s influence”. The US has signed a series of military cooperation agreements with countries across the region. In March, Trump launched the Shield of the Americas, a “counter-cartel coalition” made up exclusively of far-right leaders aligned with him. Notably absent were key countries for drug production and trafficking in the region – Mexico, Brazil and Colombia – all of which are governed by leftwing administrations. After being elected, De la Espriella said that Colombia would join the initiative and establish a local Shield of the Americas office in Medellín. Ariel Goldstein, a researcher and professor at the University of Buenos Aires, believes Milei nonetheless remains ahead of the others in the race for Trump’s attention. “He has already spent the past two or three years building an intense relationship of friendship and subordination with the US,” he said. When Trump was re-elected, Milei travelled to Palm Beach to become the first foreign leader to meet him after his victory. The Argentinian president has also emulated a number of policies from his US counterpart, including withdrawing from the World Health Organization and tightening immigration policies. Last year, Trump offered a $40bn US bailout that was widely seen as crucial to the libertarian party’s victory in Argentina’s midterm elections. However, Milei’s path to re-election next year is far from looking smooth: although inflation has fallen, purchasing power has also declined, while unemployment and informality have risen and his administration has been hit by corruption scandals. Meanwhile, Goldstein believes that Milei and Trump are now heavily invested in winning the next major prize on the electoral calendar: Latin America’s largest country, Brazil. Besides attending the launch of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, the Argentinian president had hoped to visit the senator’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest after being convicted over an attempted coup, but the request was denied by a justice. Milei has never held a bilateral meeting with Lula. “A Bolsonaro victory would be hugely important to Milei and Trump because it would allow them to reorganise the whole region around an axis of subordination to the US,” said Goldstein.

title: Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results
body_text: Donald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates. According to a new report called Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’s nearly 150% higher than the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”. High-profile departures, like that of homeland security secretary Kristi Noem’s, have had a lot of media coverage. But as the Partnership for Public Service note in their report, there has been “remarkably little public attention” when it comes to overall departures in Trump 2.0. Indeed, the narrative has largely been that while Trump’s first term was a chaotic mess marked by constant personnel changes, his second presidency has been far more stable. And that narrative isn’t entirely wrong. In Trump’s first term the rapid turnover was a sign that the reality TV host and real estate nepo baby had no idea what he was doing. In Trump 2.0, however, the departures point to something far more insidious. Rather than signaling incompetence, they are fueling a power grab by a president who seems to think of himself as a king. “Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government’s leadership ranks – it concentrates power in the president,” Chris Piper from the Partnership for Public Service writes in a blog post. “Each seat left to an acting official is one the president can fill on his own terms without the Senate’s advice and consent: no vetting, no confirmation hearing, no vote.” Trump himself has said he likes acting officials because the temporary nature of the position gives him more control. “And so, Acting gives you much greater flexibility,” the president said in his first term. “A lot easier to do things.” Last month Trump similarly told the Wall Street Journal that he thought the non-permanent status of Bill Pulte, his incoming acting director of national intelligence and a man sometimes referred to as “Little Trump”, was an asset. “You’re less shackled,” he said. “It sort of gives you more power, you know, for a somewhat limited period of time.” Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term. The conservative supermajority in the supreme court, which Trump helped create, has been invaluable to him in this regard. In July 2024, the court ruled that former presidents are entitled to some degree of immunity from criminal prosecution, nullifying the chance of an election subversion case against him before the election. Then, last month, the supreme court gave the president another gift: the power to fire leaders of independent agencies or commissions. The decision in Trump v Slaughter overturned Humphrey’s Executor, a 1935 ruling that the US constitution did not grant “illimitable power of removal” to the president. Trump doesn’t quite have carte blanche to remove whomever he likes. On the same day as that decision, the supreme court ruled in Trump v Cook that the Federal Reserve was an exception to Trump’s power. Nevertheless, it is hard to overstate the significance of the Slaughter ruling, which upended almost a century of well-settled law curbing executive power. “Today, the court discards that democratic regime in favor of one that distorts the structure of government to fit the majority’s theory of unitary, total executive control. The result is a president who emerges with far greater power than ever before,” justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent. Trump, meanwhile, wrote on Truth Social that it was “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years”. I highly doubt that Trump has spent significant portions of his life thinking about the constitutionality of the Humphrey’s Executor decision. But do you know who has? The people at the Heritage Foundation, who are behind Project 2025, which is widely seen as the playbook for Trump’s second term. Overturning Humphrey’s Executor is right there on page 560 of Project 2025. Also in that playbook are steps to interfere with election administration and weaponize the Department of Justice against election officials who make decisions the Trump administration disagrees with. In other words: a strategy for influencing the upcoming election. Make no mistake: the masterminds behind Trump’s second term haven’t overseen “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years” just to easily cede that power to a Democratic president at the next election. A bunch of losers are still complaining that the Odyssey isn’t white enough Elon Musk has been whining about Christopher Nolan casting Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy for months now. This week, following rave reviews of the Odyssey, Musk announced that his AI image and video generator Grok Imagine would create its own “historically accurate” version of the film. Perhaps Musk should listen to Colman Domingo, who recently said on Jimmy Kimmel Live that he has a message for everyone upset about diversity in The Odyssey: “If you want to see a film with a cast of all white people who are cursed by the gods, the ‘Melania’ movie is currently streaming.” Record 384 World Cup-linked reports of domestic abuse in England and Wales The data was collected as part of a strategy to better understand the link between football tournaments and domestic abuse. A police chief cited extended pub opening hours as one of the factors in the surge in violence. AOC is leading Kamala Harris in a new 2028 presidential poll by a long way A University of New Hampshire poll has AOC leading the field with 22% support while Pete Buttigieg has 21%. Harris only has 5%. Model scout for Jeffrey Epstein found dead at his home near Paris Daniel Siad, who was found dead at his home on Monday, compared his work trying to source women with fishing. “In This busyness I feel like fisherman some time I cache (sic) quick, some time no fish,” he wrote in an email to Epstein in 2014. Australian politician Pauline Hanson thinks domestic violence is a ‘two-way street’ The senator also suggested women experiencing abuse should simply “not put up with it”. Israeli rights groups warn of ‘mass pogroms’ in occupied West Bank While violence by Arabs is called “terrorism”, the media tends to downplay attacks by Jewish settlers in Israel by characterizing it as “settler violence”. This violence, enabled by the Israeli military and ignored by many in the US, has been intensifying. Following a deadly settler attack on Friday, Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem and 19 other Israeli human rights organisations condemned the international community’s “silence and inaction” and called for “immediate action to stop Israel’s violence and prevent pogroms by settler militias”. Why middle-aged women are raving Women are putting the internalized ageism aside and realizing you’re never too old to go out clubbing. People are watching porn based on ICE raids Rule 34 of the internet is that if something exists, there is porn of it. The dystopian machinations of the Trump administration are no exception. Wired has a disturbing piece on the rise of Maga-themed porn. The week in pawtriarchy Meet Jimothy, who appears to be the internet’s new favourite racoon. Seattle-based Jimothy hasn’t won hearts and minds by passing out drunk in a Virginia liquor store like some of his compatriots. Rather, he has gone viral because of his distinctive body shape, which may be the result of a rare genetic condition called short spine syndrome. He looks a bit like a furry goblin, basically. I reckon Jimothy’s lack of a well-functioning backbone means he has a promising political career ahead of him. Perhaps Trump could make him Secretary of Trashury. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Troy Jackson: the Maine lumberjack Democrats believe can beat Susan Collins
body_text: As cinemagoers flock to The Odyssey, Democrats in Maine are hoping that their long and perilous quest for a political hero ends in Troy. They have nominated lumberjack Troy Jackson this weekend as their candidate to challenge Susan Collins, a veteran Republican in the US Senate, after the implosion of the party’s original candidate left them scrambling for a replacement less than four months before the midterm elections. Jackson, a former president of the Democratic-controlled Maine senate, i secured the nomination at a special party convention in Bangor on Saturday. He inherits a race transformed by the abrupt withdrawal of the primary winner, Graham Platner, following allegations of sexual assault made by a former girlfriend, accusations he has denied. While Kamala Harris infamously had only 107 days to build a presidential campaign in 2024, Jackson would have even less time for a battle that could decide control of the 100-member Senate. The fifth-generation logger from Aroostook county in northern Maine combines an unusual political biography with an unapologetically progressive platform. He first came to prominence in the late 1990s when he led a week-long blockade by Maine loggers protesting the employment of Canadian workers, whom they accused of depressing wages. The demonstration ended with police escorting him away but established his reputation as a champion of rural workers, which would continue into his time as a legislator. Jackson initially ran as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat in Maine’s house of representatives. He lost but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic party in 2004 and went on to serve three terms in the house before being elected to the state senate, where he was president from 2018 until 2024. In contrast to Platner, the biggest scandal attached to him so far is that he displayed flashes of temper such as cursing, shouting and throwing a water bottle in a meeting when he could not persuade someone to vote his way, according to a Washington Post report based on interviews with more than two dozen people. Jackson’s political views have shifted significantly over the years. Earlier in his career he opposed abortion rights and same-sex marriage, positions he has since abandoned. He has emerged as one of Maine’s leading progressives, backing policies such as Medicare for All and calling for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). For those seeking an economic populist and working-class champion, he appears to fit the bill. Tim Fullerton, a Democratic strategist from the southern part of the state, recently spent time with him and came away impressed. “Troy is as Maine as they come, Maine through and through,” he said. “He shoots from the hip. Federal campaign filings show she has raised more than $16m, while Jackson’s campaign says it has brought in just over $1m. Jackson has framed Collins – viewed as one of her party’s most vulnerable figures in the 2026 cycle – as an enabler of Trump, accusing her of siding with Republicans and corporate interests at decisive moments, including over Trump’s war in Iran. Collins has sought to portray Jackson as an ideological extremist. Speaking to the Associated Press this week, she described his political evolution as that of a “Bernie bro”, arguing that his record placed him firmly on the socialist wing of American politics. Republicans have also attacked the circumstances of Jackson’s expected nomination. Jim Deyermond, chair of the Maine Republican party, criticised Democrats for selecting a long-serving political insider after insisting the replacement process would be open following Platner’s withdrawal. The Platner saga left Democrats pointing fingers at each other and tarnished the party’s brand. But they cling to the hope that, with inflation and the Iran war driving down Trump’s approval rating, Collins could be swept aside in a blue wave. And a lot can happen between now and November. Earlier this month, for example, a 26-year-old Colombian national, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, was shot dead by an ICE officer in Biddeford, Maine. The Department of Homeland Security claimed that Guerrero was fleeing and threatened “public safety”. Jackson condemned ICE as a “rogue agency that goes around doing things that they’re being told to on high”. Fullerton, who is also cofounder and chief executive of Find Out Media, commented: “The situation with ICE and Biddeford has changed the game for Mainers. You heard from Susan Collins: oh, they need to be reformed, and she was pretty mealy about it. Troy and the rest of the Democrats were rightly angry and very direct. Luckily, we’re not building a cult of personality like Maga, one where you wonder, how does this go beyond Trump? It’s a great asset that we’re building around ideas and not individuals.”
