title: Trump revives old tropes as he pushes warnings of ‘communist menace’
body_text: Perhaps above all else, Donald Trump is a child of the cold war. Three months before the US president was born, Winston Churchill delivered a historic speech in Fulton, Missouri, that ushered in a generations-long existential struggle between western capitalism and Soviet communism. Lamenting the spread of Soviet communism across eastern Europe following the allied victory in the second world war, Churchill – by then no longer British prime minister – warned his audience on 5 March 1946 that “an iron curtain has descended across the continent”. It was the prelude to a nuclear-armed standoff between Washington and Moscow that triggered a hysteria-driven “red scare” in the US – leading to the execution of convicted spies and exemplified by witch-hunts instigated by the Republican senator Joe McCarthy, who claimed he had obtained lists of communist agents working in the state department and other key areas of American life. The hunt for communists would have been a ubiquitous theme of Trump’s early childhood. Strikingly, Roy Cohn – McCarthy’s chief counsel, who had masterminded the federal prosecution of the convicted Soviet spies, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, subsequently executed for treason – became Trump’s mentor in later decades, as he rose in the New York real-estate world. “For many years, communism and communists were the major enemy of the United States,” said Harvey Klehr, an emeritus professor at Emory University and an expert in the US’s history with communism. “There were obviously times it might have gotten exaggerated or or got out of hand, but there was a darn good reason for people to be alarmed about it.” Paranoia waned in relative terms after McCarthy was censured by the Senate in 1954, but only abated after the collapse of eastern European communist regimes in 1989 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union two years later. Now, 37 years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and the end of the cold war, Trump is reviving it. In a series of high-profile addresses, Trump has identified an ideology that millions of Americans are too young to recall as the US’s biggest threat. “A generation after we fought and won the cold war against the menace of communism, there is now a resurgence of the communist menace in our land, including from newcomers to our country who embrace ideas totally opposed to our way of life and our great success,” he said in a speech at Mount Rushmore on 3 July, on the eve of the US’s 250th birthday. He vowed to “vanquish communists quickly” and “send them into exile”. That the topic was no one-off was confirmed by a new 100-page report from the state department published this week, titled Cuba: the Capital of 21st Century Communism. “For nearly seven decades, the Cuban regime has waged a sustained campaign of subversion against the United States,” states the report, claiming that the “highest reaches” of the US government have been “infiltrated”. “Today, that network continues to maintain ties to powerful leftist nonprofits, anti-ICE collectives, socialist groups, and Marxist militant organizations across the United States.” The rebirth of anti-communist animus has been fueled by the recent success of Democratic candidates identifying as “democratic socialists” – most notably the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. A succession of leftwing candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have followed Mamdani’s triumph by winning Democratic primaries, including Darializa Avila Chevalier, who ousted the veteran New York representative, Adriano Espaillat, in June. Chevalier has drawn scrutiny over a now deleted Twitter account that praised Marxist ideology and historical communist figures, such as Vladimir Lenin. Several high-profile Democrats and liberal-leaning figures have ridiculed Trump’s attacks for falsely conflating socialism – a term which can describe democratic governments in several European countries – with Soviet-style communism. “Not subtle: new party line is to associate Communists with every crime, every offense,” wrote Ruth Ben-Ghiat, a historian of fascism, on X. “Create a sense of Communist threat to justify a rightwing crackdown. Old playbook used with coups and Fascist takeovers.” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic representative for New York and a member of the DSA, called the communist label “very silly”. “They want to call it communist because they don’t want you to know that Germany, Italy, the UK, Canada – everybody else – has it better than us, and we spend the most money for the worst care in the developed world,” she told reporters. Cara Tobe, a spokesperson for the DSA – asked whether the association’s membership included communists – said: “Our organization’s dues-paying members range in political beliefs, but we are all united under the banner of democratic socialism. “It’s concerning but not surprising that Donald Trump would like to send his opponents into exile, because it’s increasingly evident our ideas win with the American people: socialism beats fascism.” Yet some commentators say Trump’s charge is not baseless. “The communist issue is not entirely a bugaboo,” said Klehr, who said the DSA had a “very significant communist component”. Formed by Michael Harrington, the leftwing activist and writer, in 1982, the DSA was founded under a constitution that excluded members of “democratic centralists” organizations – code for Soviet-style communist parties founded on Lenin’s model. Klehr said that provision had been repealed – resulting in an influx of radical new members that he compared to the “entryist” infiltration of Britain’s Labour party by the Trotskyite Militant tendency in the early 1980s, which resulted in the adoption of leftwing policies and led to an overwhelming election defeat at the hands of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservatives. The faction was expelled in 1985 by Labour’s then leader, Neil Kinnock. “The DSA has changed, and a significant number of people who unapologetically call themselves Marxist-Leninists or communists have moved into DSA and attained some significant positions,” said Klehr. Bill Galston, a fellow at the Brookings Institution and a former White House domestic policy adviser under Bill Clinton, said: “There are people who’ve been in the DSA for decades and can remember the struggle between the democratic and the undemocratic left, and in particular between communists and socialists, and so they are definite. “They are responding to the perception that there are various communist or communist-adjacent factions that have joined the DSA, and that they don’t want to be part of that.” Two recent articles in the Atlantic have highlighted the fierce debate over the credentials of DSA candidates and their potential to be catalysts for an ideological shift within the Democratic party. However, Galston – a self-proclaimed “red diaper baby” whose grandfather stood multiple times as a communist candidate in New York – questioned the ability of Trump’s “communist” tag to resonate beyond his Maga base. He cited a recent Economist/YouGov poll asking voters how much of a threat communism posed to the US. Some 18% termed it a “major threat” and another 25% a “minor threat”, while 33% said it was “not a threat”. “Trump is 80 years old, and for him, the epithet ‘communist’ rolls off his lips quite naturally, because it was part of the conflict with internal communism and the Soviet Union as an external communist foe that was part of his formation,” said Galston. “Older Americans, those who do have a memory of the cold war, are more responsive to this alleged threat than are younger Americans. He’s speaking to a political party that is disproportionately supported by older Americans. “So one way of looking at this is as part of Trump’s overall strategy of base mobilization. He’s preaching to the choir here and he knows intuitively who makes up that choir.” Galston also attributed the resurgence of fears of communism to an age-old popular American failure to make fine distinctions in political terminology – a confusion Trump’s critics say applies to him. But Klehr argued that the trend signaled a broader threat to democracy and liberal values that he said emanated from the extreme left and far right. “Donald Trump wouldn’t know a communist from a democratic socialist from a Martian, but there are other very smart people that do understand the difference, and the significance,” he said. “It’s the same sort of thing that occurred on the political right not that many years ago, when various kinds of rightwing lunatics, neo-Nazis and racists began to move into the Republican party, they won some primaries, they established a beachhead and they’re still there. “I think some of that is happening in the Democratic party, and it’s dangerous on both counts. It raises serious concerns for the health of a democratic society. “The memory of communism is fading, and yet … some of the things they call for, it’s like they’ve forgotten the history.”

title: Republicans head home for the summer after a string of losses in Congress
body_text: When the chief Republican budget writer took to the floor of the House of Representatives this week to tout a plan to spend tens of billions of dollars on the war with Iran, he avoided using the words “war”, “conflict” or even “Iran”. “Just baseline battlefield readiness” is what Jodey Arrington said the money in the $95bn budget blueprint would be used for. “Bullets and bombs to finish the job and come home safely and victoriously, strengthen our food supply, and ultimately safeguard the integrity of our elections.” It was a rosy depiction of a risky proposition for House Republicans three months before they face voters in November’s midterm elections amid sticky inflation, signs of a Democratic resurgence , and poor approval ratings both for the war with Iran and Donald Trump’s presidency in general. Under the leadership of the speaker, Mike Johnson, House Republicans in their final week of work before a long summer recess opted not to alter course. In addition to passing the war spending plan along party lines, they approved a super-sized military budget and made multiple attempts to forge new restrictions on voting nationwide. “Many of you like to say that major legislating can’t happen in an election year. We just proved you wrong,” Johnson told reporters on Wednesday, after the votes. Not 24 hours later came a reminder of how Democrats can leverage divisions within the House GOP’s historically small majority, when four dissident Republicans joined with the minority to pass a symbolic war powers resolution that would mandate Trump withdraw troops from combat against Iran. “You’re about to have hundreds of members of Congress go home to their constituents, and a lot of folks are about to get crushed, rightfully so, by their constituents,” the Democratic congressman Jason Crow told reporters following that vote in an articulation of the affordability agenda his party is counting on to return it to power. “They’re going to hear that people are losing healthcare, they’re losing their homes, they’re losing their farms, they’re losing their small businesses. As they have done twice prior since Trump returned to office, the House had written the budget blueprint to comply with the reconciliation procedure, which can circumvent Democrats’ use of the filibuster in the Senate and pass with a simple majority. But senior Republicans have shown little enthusiasm for a third such bill, and before the House even approved the budget blueprint, the Republican Senate majority leader, John Thune, said he would put it on “hold” in case he needed the measure as leverage over the Democrats in negotiations to continue government funding beyond its 30 September expiration. That raised the likelihood that the question of how much to spend on the Iran conflict will remain undecided in September. And while the House’s passage of the annual Pentagon budget, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), is typically a major accomplishment, Johnson complicated its chances in the Senate by bowing to pressure from rightwing lawmakers and merging it with the Save America Act. A fixation of Trump, the legislation would ban mail-in ballots and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and cast ballots. But that’s not the only headwind the defense budget faces: Democrats have objected to its $1.15tn cost, and earlier this month they halted the advancement of the Senate’s version of the bill, in protest of the renewed hostilities with Iran. As they departed the Capitol for the five-week recess, House Republicans nonetheless believed they had a credible case to make for why the opposition should stay in the minority for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. “Joe Biden and the Democrats are the ones that ran this country into the ditch, and we’re on a rescue mission to save it. And we passed some really good policies that are actually working, and so we got a great story to tell to the voters,” said Richard Hudson, who chairs the National Republican Congressional Committee, the party’s House campaign arm. Nodding to the party’s victories in the redistricting battle, Hudson said: “If you look at the seats that are up for grabs, it’s a majority of Democrats in Trump seats. For the Democrats to pick up the majority, they would have to win a lot of Trump seats, and that’s just not going to happen.” Glossing over the collapse of peace talks and the return of fighting with Tehran, Ralph Norman, a rightwing stalwart from South Carolina who is vying to replace the late Lindsey Graham in the Senate, predicted that Trump “is at the cusp of ending this thing with Iran, and he’s doing the right thing”. “The American people’s opinion is to end it quick. I think he will do that,” he added. Nebraska’s Don Bacon, one of the few Republicans representing a district Kamala Harris won two years ago, offered muted criticism of Trump’s approach to the war, saying the president would benefit from trying to work more with the Democrats. “The go-it-alone approach fails us in the end,” said Bacon, who is not seeking re-election. “But we need their help,” he said of Democrats, “and so I think he should lean in to working across the aisle more.” However large the problems of House Republicans may be, they appear to be no solution for the Democrats’ own woes. The party’s own supporters remain sour in the wake of Harris’s defeat, and earlier this week a Washington Post-Ipsos poll found that while the most highly motivated voters are eager to back the Democrats in the midterms, they have a scant advantage over the GOP in the wider electorate. “I think a lot of people aren’t sure, depending on where you’re from, what it means to be a Democrat,” the progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said when asked about the party’s quandary. She saw hope in the party’s primary process, which this year has been defined by further showdowns between centrist and leftwing candidates and passionate debates over how to manage the US relationship with Israel. “I think that’s part of why this primary process has been so active this year, because we’re having much deeper substantive conversations than just … what is the color next to the box on your name,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

title: Meet the South Carolina Democrat looking to flip Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat
body_text: It was early Sunday morning and Dr Annie Andrews was far from the political fray, dropping her youngest daughter off at a summer camp, when she heard the news. “It was shocking and unbelievable,” she says of the death of Lindsey Graham, a Republican senator who defined South Carolina politics for a generation aged 71. “It’s a profound moment for the whole state of South Carolina.” For more than a year Andrews, a Democrat, had been building a formidable grassroots campaign designed to unseat Graham in the midterm elections. The 45-year-old paediatrician had pitched herself as the antithesis of the veteran senator she never met – an outsider running a campaign “powered by people, not Pacs [political action committees]”. Now Andrews, who had been aiming to become South Carolina’s first female senator, has seen the honour bestowed instead on Graham’s sister, Darline, who was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term and will compete in a primary next month to decide the Republican nominee in November. So everything has changed – and yet nothing has changed. “The problems that South Carolinians are facing did not change over that weekend,” Andrews says by phone from her base in Mount Pleasant. “My opponent will change but my mission remains the same and that’s what I’m staying focused on.” That mission was galvanised by the two decades that Andrews spent on the frontlines of what she describes as America’s “broken” public healthcare system, including 15 years at a children’s hospital in Charleston. The experience ultimately compelled her out of the medical ward and into the political arena. “Over those years, I started to understand that the problems my patients and their families were facing were policy problems. These were systemic problems with systemic solutions and what we needed to do was start electing people who inherently care about South Carolina’s kids and families and care about solving those problems.” Her initial foray into politics – a 2022 congressional run against Republican representative Nancy Mace – ended in a 14-point defeat. After that loss, Andrews stepped away from her practice at the Medical University of South Carolina and founded a political organisation focused on the climate crisis, gun violence and childhood poverty. But it was the darkness of Trump’s second term that pulled her back on to the ballot for the Senate, in particular the nomination of Robert F Kennedy Jr to lead the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She recalls: “In the aftermath of Trump being re-elected, the day that I decided to consider this seriously was the day RFK Jr was nominated to lead HHS because, as a paediatrician, that’s the worst-case scenario for America’s public health system.” For Andrews, the elevation of Kennedy – who spent decades amplifying baseless anti-vaccine views – is not merely a political affront but a direct threat to the lives of the children she treats. “Doctors are trained, when they take a history from a patient, to ask if their immunisations are up to date. Twenty years ago, when I started asking that question, the answer was almost universally yes. “Now when I ask that question, I brace myself for the response because bad actors like RFK Jr, grifters and conspiracy theorists have been peddling in these anti-vaccine conspiracy theories for decades and it has seeped into the consciousness of many parents in America who now don’t know who they can trust for solid evidence-based medical information about decisions for their children’s health and it’s deeply frustrating to watch as this has evolved.” The consequences are brutal. Measles cases in the US have hit a 35-year high, according to data from Johns Hopkins University, with more than 90% of reported infections occurring among the unvaccinated or those whose vaccination status is unknown. Andrews adds: “It is pervasive across sociodemographic groups now. People do not know who they can trust and sadly right now, when I talk to patients, I say: ‘You cannot necessarily trust the health information that we are receiving from the federal government.’” The Covid-19 pandemic, she believes, acted as “kerosene on the fire”, catalysing an anti-science movement that has now fully entrenched itself within the Republican party. Indeed, for Andrews, the triage urgently required in Washington is clear. She views the impending Medicaid budget cuts signed into law by Trump as a devastating threat to rural South Carolinians. She advocates for defending Medicare, lowering prescription drug costs through federal negotiating power, and gradually introducing a public option to force private insurers into offering more competitive, less profit-driven plans. And her definition of the public health emergency extends to gun violence. She speaks with the authority of a doctor who has “cared for children with bullet holes in them” and “stood at the bedside of a child who has been shot and held the parent’s hand, understanding that these are preventable injuries, these are policy choices that have been made by our lawmakers”. While acknowledging that gun control may not be the primary issue driving voters to the polls in 2026, she insists: “I will not stand on the sidelines as gun violence continues to be the leading cause of death for kids in South Carolina and kids all across this country. But the good news is the vast majority of Americans agree with me. Over 90% of Americans believe we need commonsense solutions like universal background checks.” Andrews views the broader landscape of Trump’s second term with profound alarm. She sees a state and a country buckling under the weight of “chaotic” economic and social policies. “I’m deeply concerned about the direction this country is moving in,” she says. “Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are high. There’s an affordability crisis in housing and in childcare. We don’t have jobs to meet the needs of folks who are graduating from technical colleges or from four-year universities and, on top of that, we’re witnessing unprecedented corruption in the federal government.” Her proposed remedies to break the fever include ending partisan gerrymandering, implementing term limits, banning members of Congress from trading stocks or becoming lobbyists and overturning the Citizens United supreme court ruling to purge dark money from politics. Andrews has spent a year building a statewide campaign apparatus, raising funds and recruiting more than 2,000 volunteers. This week, she gained the endorsement of Her Bold Move, a national support network for women running for political office. But even in the absence of Lindsey Graham, a close Trump ally who served four terms, she faces a monumental structural disadvantage. South Carolina is a stronghold for Republicans with state elections historically decided by double-digit margins. In 2020, the Democratic challenger Jaime Harrison shattered national fundraising records, amassing a war chest of more than $100m, yet still lost to Graham by a crushing 10 percentage points. “I’m used to fighting fights that are uphill battles,” Andrews admits. “That does not make the fight any less important and what I’ve seen over the past year is a growing sentiment that everyone on both sides of the aisle recognises that Washington DC is broken.”

title: Katy Perry ‘deeply appalled’ over White House using her song in Iran war video
body_text: Pop star Katy Perry has condemned the Trump White House after it used her hit song Firework in a TikTok video showing US military strikes on Iranian targets, saying she never approved the use of her music. The White House video, which featured Firework playing over footage of a missile striking an Iranian naval ship, has amassed more than 6 million views. The post was captioned: “Iran has been warned.” Perry responded on Saturday with a statement on X criticizing what she called the unauthorized use of the song. “I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the White House TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes,” the singer said. “I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it.” Perry continued: “I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments. To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for. My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.” The White House launched its TikTok account in August 2025, when Donald Trump threatened to ban the platform months into his second presidency. Perry is among a number of artists to criticize the Trump administration over the unauthorized use of music in government social media posts, with the president picking fights with several – mostly female – pop singers. Olivia Rodrigo previously criticized the administration after one of her songs appeared in a government video promoting deportation efforts. Beyoncé also blocked Trump from using her song Freedom after it was featured in a campaign video on social media. The track had served as the central campaign song for former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump. In March, Kesha condemned the White House’s use of her song Blow in a military-promotional TikTok video, calling it a “show of blatant disregard for human life”. Sabrina Carpenter spoke out after her hit song Juno was used in a Trump-posted video showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers making arrests. Carpenter called the video “evil and disgusting” and told the administration: “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.” In June, Ariana Grande also rebuked the White House for using her song Bye in a social media post promoting US immigration arrests, describing the video as “barbaric”. Singer Jess Glynne also objected after the White House used her song Hold My Hand in a post on X promoting ICE deportations. Glynne said she felt “sick” that her music was being used to spread “division and hate”. It was revealed in December that Perry is in a relationship with the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, who is familiar himself with Trump’s trolling. He has repeatedly been targeted by Trump, who has continually threatened to impose tariffs on Canada and has even suggested the US should annex the country, referring to Trudeau as the “governor” of the “Great State of Canada”. The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) lists the official death toll for the US-Iran conflict at 14 service members, with 420 total personnel wounded in action. Those official metrics, however, have been subject to ongoing controversy due to a sudden drop from the 18 deaths and 482 wounded recorded days earlier. The collapse of the ceasefire with Iran and the subsequent resumption of near-daily airstrikes starting on 6 July have sparked debate over how casualties are counted. Analysts and officials have questioned whether victims from the two weeks since should be tracked in a separate tally, a move that would be unprecedented. The Trump administration is attempting to have the latest resumed strikes in Iran be treated as a separate campaign from Operation Epic Fury, the US military’s official name for the Iran conflict. The separate casualty count beginning 7 July stems from that. The US House member Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, responded to the updated numbers in an X post, writing, “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.

title: Pentagon reports more than 600 Iran war casualties in quiet database update
body_text: The Pentagon updated its official war casualty database over the weekend, adding more than 140 wounded service members. The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) also introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7”. According to the updated database, the official toll for the earlier phase of the US-Iran war, known as Operation Epic Fury, now stands at 14 service members killed and more than 400 wounded in action. These figures have been a point of contention after the Pentagon previously reduced the totals from 18 deaths and 482 wounded that had been recorded just days earlier. The dispute comes after the collapse of the ceasefire with Iran and the resumption of near-daily airstrikes beginning on 6 July. Analysts and officials have questioned whether casualties from the renewed fighting should be counted separately from Operation Epic Fury, a move that would be unprecedented. The Trump administration is seeking to classify the renewed military campaign as separate from Operation Epic Fury, the US military’s official name for the Iran conflict. The change is tied to the War Powers Act of 1973, which requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. The shift became apparent earlier this week when the Pentagon’s official online list of service members killed in the ongoing Iran war did not include the four soldiers who died during renewed fighting over the weekend. Their names, however, were included in a Pentagon press release announcing the formal transfer of their remains back to the US on Wednesday. Combined with the updated Operation Epic Fury totals, the new Pentagon figures show that 18 US troops have been killed and 624 wounded since the US launched its war against Iran on 28 February. Lawmakers from both parties have challenged the administration’s interpretation of the War Powers Act timeline. Thomas Massie, a Republican House member from Kentucky, responded to the updated numbers in an X post, writing: “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.

title: Republicans have ‘nothing to run on’ in midterms after Trump failures, Jeffries says
body_text: Donald Trump’s Republican party has “nothing to run on” for the congressional midterm elections after the president broke promises to lower costs and avoid starting war overseas, the US House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, has said. The New York congressman made those comments on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, exactly 100 days from the 3 November midterms, when Jeffries and his fellow Democrats are aiming to take control of the US House and Senate from their Republican opponents. Asked to discuss the elections, Jeffries alluded to how Trump and other Republicans quickly seized on a 21 July announcement from the Democratic New Jersey governor, Mikie Sherrill, that 6,600 noncitizens in the state had registered to vote because of a software error. Fewer than 400 of them voted before the identification and correction of the error. But the president and his allies nonetheless used the disclosure to boost false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on voter rolls who could compromise the integrity of the midterms, during which Republicans are predicted to lose seats. Jeffries on Sunday argued that was because it is a more comfortable strategy to adopt rather than confront how the US and Israeli militaries began warring with Iran in February after Trump won a second presidency in 2024 having promised “not to start … endless wars in the Middle East”. The costs of the war have included the deaths of 18 US service members as of Sunday, along with injuries to hundreds more. Gas and grocery prices have also soared amid the conflict, leaving 95% of Americans believing that the US is suffering an affordability crisis, according to exclusive polling conducted for the Guardian. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, on Sunday acknowledged there was an affordability crisis in the US – but argued the blame for that fell on Democrats and Joe Biden’s presidency. “All these things will only get better if given two more years with a Republican Congress” in November, Leavitt said on Fox News. Speaking to State of the Union host Dana Bash, Jeffries said, “Republicans … have failed to actually deliver on making life more affordable for the American people.” He continued, “It was Donald Trump who promised to lower costs on day one. But we know that costs haven’t gone down in this country. Costs have gone up. “It was Donald Trump … who said that he was elected not to start wars, endless wars in the Middle East, but to stop them – and then turned around and has gotten us involved in this reckless war of choice in Iran that has skyrocketed gas prices on the American people.” Jeffries then referred to how Republicans a year earlier cut more than $1tn from Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people in the US who are low-income and disabled, adding: “They have nothing to run on. We’re going to run on fighting for an affordable America. “Too many people are working hard – they’re playing by the rules, but they can’t thrive,” Jeffries also said. “And they can barely survive, not enough food on the table, not enough gas in the tank, unable to actually regularly and consistently afford to pay the rent or pay the mortgage.” A recent analysis from Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats are likely to win a majority in the House – and that Republicans are narrowly favored to retain control of the US Senate.

title: Tariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurd
body_text: With the midterm elections less than four months away, it’s a precarious time for Donald Trump and Republicans: Trump’s war against Iran is going badly, his approval ratings are in the toilet, gas prices are soaring and pushing up inflation, and nation after nation is furious about Trump’s insults, bullying and ugly American unilateralism. So amid all this mess, what does Trump do? He turns to his favorite economic plaything: tariffs. On Monday, Trump signed orders to slap a 50% tariff on many Canadian goods, and four days later, he imposed across-the-board 10% or 12.5% tariffs on goods from more than 80 countries. Trump was no doubt thumping his chest, while millions of people overseas were dumping on him for yet another unnecessary, hostile act. Too bad for Republicans, and most Americans, though, because Trump’s fixation on tariffs will only worsen their troubles. Trump’s new tariffs will push up prices – let’s not forget that tariffs are taxes on imports, and US consumers will pay those taxes. A corollary of that: Trump’s tariffs will worsen Americans No 1 economic concern: affordability. In bad news for typical Americans, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that Trump’s tariffs will increase costs for the average US household by $1,100 each year. The tariffs are also likely to push Trump’s approval ratings deeper into the sewer. If Trump thinks these tariffs are going to distract Americans from thinking about the Epstein files or the disastrous mess he’s made with his Iran “excursion”, he’s deluding himself. The American people aren’t going to forget those things. It’s hard to tell whether Trump’s repeated use of tariffs is a fixation or an addiction. Emperor Donald I evidently loves tariffs because he can use them to clobber other countries whenever he wants. They’re a powerful cudgel he won’t let go of. Trump imposed his new tariffs on more than 80 countries on the very day that another set of tariffs he slapped on dozens of countries was due to expire. To paraphrase the actor Charlton Heston, I can imagine Trump saying: “I’ll give up tariffs when you take them from my cold, dead hands.” With these new tariffs, Trump is again engaged in his delusional, destructive tariff tomfoolery. They’ll push up prices, squeeze Americans’ wallets and anger other countries. Trump said his tariffs would boost US manufacturing, but the US has lost 75,000 factory jobs since he returned to office, with many executives complaining about all the herky-jerky uncertainty Trump has wrought. Assessing Trump’s effects on the economy, Atsi Sheth, the chief credit officer for Moody’s Ratings, told the New York Times :“Volatility and unpredictability is the new normal.” Like so much that Trump does, his new tariffs are clearly based on pique and false premises with lots of shamelessness and absurdity thrown in. After the US supreme court overturned Trump’s me-against-the-whole-world tariffs in February, Trump, refusing to let go of his tariff toy, turned to other strategies. To justify his new 50% tariffs against Canada – which are piled atop numerous other tariffs he’s imposed on a country that was long the US’s closest ally – Trump relied on a never before used provision of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a widely derided 1930 law that greatly worsened the Great Depression of a century ago. With this new tariff, placed on hockey sticks, paper, plywood, dairy products and many other Canadian goods, Trump invoked a Smoot-Hawley provision that allows retaliation against countries that engage in trade discrimination against the US. In making that case, Trump’s exhibit No 1 is something rather preposterous, or should I say rather shameless? After Trump imposed high, punitive tariffs on Canada last year, 11 of Canada’s 13 provinces and territories halted liquor imports from the US because they were so irate about those tariffs along with Trump’s outlandish and belittling statements that he wanted to make Canada the 51st state. The White House called this ban on US liquor illegal discrimination, while Canadians view it as a type of traditional trade retaliation that countries engage in when another country – here the US – slaps tariffs on them, a situation made worse by the fact that Trump’s tariffs against Canada are an egregious violation of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Trump also insists that Canada has improperly discriminated against the US because Canada imposed a 25% tariff on select US-made cars after Trump slapped a 25% tariff on Canadian-made cars. He is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US. That’s the logic of America’s leading stable genius, who also offered another far-fetched justification for his decision: “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,” he told reporters on Friday, referring to wildfire smoke that has crossed the US border. Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, isn’t happy about Trump’s painful, new 50% tariff. “We won’t back down,” he said on social media. “The fastest and only way to get US alcohol back on Ontario shelves is for the U.S. to drop its illegal tariffs on Canada.” As for the new tariffs hitting more than 80 countries, Trump, who over the years has shown next to no concern about worker exploitation, turned rather surprisingly to the issue of forced labor to slap on those tariffs. After the supreme court overturned his Liberation Day tariffs, Trump hit dozens of nations with a replacement tariff that would expire after 150 days. Eager to follow the boss’s wishes and impose a new tariff as soon as that one expired, Trump’s toadies uncovered a trade law provision that lets Washington punish countries that fail to take enough action against forced labor. No surprise here: Trump’s US trade representative issued a report that made the boss happy. That report found that dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, Australia, Norway, Japan and China, plus the European Union, were not doing enough to enforce a prohibition against forced labor. That report pointed to forced labor in producing rice in Myanmar, tobacco in Malawi, and cotton and polysilicon in China. It’s deeply perplexing that Trump is punishing some of these trading partners. Norway has pioneered laws to crack down on forced labor in overseas supply chains, while the European Union’s new ban on goods produced with forced labor will take effect in December 2027. Canada already bans imports made with forced labor, and is moving to strengthen that prohibition. It’s not as if Trump has shown much concern before about worker exploitation or forced labor. In 1998, Trump agreed to pay $1.375m to settle a lawsuit brought by undocumented Polish workers who said they were underpaid for their work demolishing a department store to make way for Trump Tower in New York. Some trade experts criticize Trump for slamming all these longtime allies about forced labor even as he is pushing vigorously to improve ties with China, which the Biden administration found to have serious forced labor problems in its Xinjiang region. Trump’s newfound concern about forced labor rings especially hollow considering that his administration chopped more than $500m from the labor department’s efforts to investigate and fight against forced labor, child labor and human trafficking. “This was a completely indiscriminate meat ax that was taken to these projects, and workers will suffer,” said Thea Lee, who served as the labor department’s deputy undersecretary for international labor affairs under Biden. Bemoaning that $500m-plus in cuts, Kelly Fay Rodriguez, who was Biden’s special representative for international labor affairs, told Equal Times. “Unfortunately, it is extremely likely that child labor and forced labor practices will increase. We know these problems are endemic but … we’ve wiped out the resources and the prioritization for fighting them.” Imagine a world where Donald Trump truly cared about worker exploitation and forced labor. He would be pushing to raise the absurdly low $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage – something he has never lifted a finger to do. He would be increasing, rather than cutting, the number of safety inspectors for mines and factories. He would be pushing to strengthen – instead of repeatedly moving to weaken – the nation’s labor unions, long the most effective voice in fighting against worker exploitation. He would be pressuring China’s President Xi Jinping to stop all the forced labor in his country. But that would be a make-believe Donald Trump – he cares far more about what’s good for billionaires than what’s good for workers. Bottom line: there remains far too much forced labor in the world – more than 27 million children, women and men are in forced labor, according to the International Labor Organization. It would be great if Donald Trump sincerely seized on that issue rather than used it as an insincere pretext to clobber other nations with tariffs. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy to arrive in Washington for Lindsey Graham funeral
body_text: Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are set to arrive in Washington simultaneously with the goal of winning the ear of Donald Trump at pivotal moments in wars affecting their respective countries. Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, and Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, will attend Tuesday’s funeral of Lindsey Graham, the former Republican senator for South Carolina, who died suddenly on 11 July and was a close ally of both leaders. Both men are scheduled to meet the president at a time when US policy towards the wars in Iran and Ukraine is in a state of flux. The meeting between Trump and Netanyahu will be the first between the two leaders since February, when they were in lockstep preparing for strikes against Iran that began on 28 February. Since then, tensions between the pair have risen as the war has drifted inconclusively, with Trump calling the Israeli premier “crazy” and declaring: “Without me, there would be no Israel.” Fueling the tensions between the pair is continuing uncertainty over Trump’s zigzagging approach to the regime in Tehran, which he once openly supported toppling – in line with the stance of Netanyahu, who has long plotted its overthrow. Last month, the US signed a memorandum of understanding that was meant to institute a 60-day ceasefire in the conflict, during which Iran would reopen the strategically vital strait of Hormuz and negotiations would begin over the country’s nuclear program. Netanyahu is not believed to have been consulted on the deal, which some analysts say took little account of Israel’s interests. Trump this month publicly repudiated the agreement as Iran continued to attack commercial ships in the strait. US forces struck Iranian targets for 13 consecutive nights as Trump threatened to escalate further by hitting civilian infrastructure. In recent days, however, the conflict has been paused once again amid reports that negotiations have resumed and Pentagon concerns that US missile stocks are running low. Axios reported that Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, had recommended stopping the bombing campaign because it had reached the limits of effectiveness. Netanyahu is also believed to be unhappy over a deal announced last week between the US and Saudi Arabia allowing for a civil Saudi nuclear program. Zelenskyy’s presence is equally significant as it coincides with signs of a dramatic change of Trump administration posture in Ukraine’s war with Russia – with the White House appearing more supportive of Kyiv’s position than at any time since Trump’s return to office. The rightwing social media influencer Laura Loomer gave the latest signal of a sea change in Washington’s position when she met Zelenskyy in the Ukrainian capital last week, before publicly recanting her previous support for Russia. Trump and Zelenskyy had a cordial meeting at this month’s Nato summit in Ankara that contrasted starkly with last year’s bitter confrontation in the White House, when Trump openly berated his Ukrainian counterpart and told him: “You don’t have the cards.” Trump has long been open in voicing his preference for Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. Zelenskyy posted on social media at the weekend that he had instructed Ukraine’s intelligence services to share information on Russia’s support for Iran in the conflict with the US. He wrote on X that Ukraine had recorded Russian satellite surveillance of US military facilities in the Gulf, and that of Washington’s allies in the region. Graham – a hawkish supporter of Israel and fierce critic of Iran’s Islamic regime – met Zelenskyy in Kyiv, the day before his death, and had been in the process of advancing a Senate bill to strengthen sanctions on Russia.

title: Mitch McConnell still not cleared to resume Senate duties, office says
body_text: US senator Mitch McConnell is still not cleared to return to work, his office confirmed on Monday, six weeks after he was hospitalized after a fall at his home. An update released alongside a new photograph of the Republican lawmaker – one of the highest-profile figures in Congress, as a former Senate majority leader – said he was undergoing “intense physical therapy” and is “working hard” to get back to his duties. “I’m still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders,” McConnell, of Kentucky, said in a statement released by his office on Monday. In the statement, he said that he wouldn’t be able to make it to Kentucky this coming weekend for an annual Fancy Farm picnic. “There’s no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton,” said McConnell, 84. “I hate that I’ll miss the fun this year, but I’m sending my best wishes to the St Jerome community for a successful picnic,” he said. “As always, I appreciate all of your continued well wishes, and I’m looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon.” McConnell has been absent from the Senate and not seen in public since mid-June, when his office said he was hospitalized and recovering, but did not elaborate on his condition. After weeks of silence, and mounting speculation about his health, McConnell’s office provided an update on 12 July, where they said that he was recovering at a rehabilitation center after having been admitted to the hospital on 14 June after suffering a fall at his home that left him “briefly unconscious”. In the 12 July statement, the senator also disclosed that he had also been dealing with “a mild case of pneumonia” and explained the long silence about his condition by saying that “folks of my generation often hesitate to share the vulnerability that comes with growing older”. McConnell has missed 38 Senate votes since he was hospitalized. He said last year that he would not seek re-election, and is set to retire from the Senate at the end of his term, in January. Along with the statement and photograph, McConnell’s office also released a statement from the office of the attending physician (OAP) in US Congress. “OAP physicians visit with the Senator every day, discussing all aspects of his rehabilitation care,” the OAP statement said. “Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls.” “His bout with childhood polio continues to be a significant factor in his mobility,” it added. “He is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.”

title: Trump administration’s revision of Iran war casualties ‘huge disrespect’, say veterans
body_text: A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead. “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families,” said Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral and the founder of National Security Leaders for America. “To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.” In a quiet weekend update to the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, the US Department of Defense – renamed the Department of War under Donald Trump – added more than 140 wounded service members. They also introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7” which splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran. Four US service members killed in action by Iranian forces fall under that category: 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, Pvt Isabella Gonzales, Sgt Angel S Rampersad and Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton. “I definitely think that this isn’t an issue just about numbers, but also about accountability,” said Tristeza Ordex, a US Marine Corps veteran and the national organizer of partnerships and engagement at VoteVets. “When I was deployed to Afghanistan, I remember attending ramp ceremonies,” she said, referring to an airfield memorial honoring a fallen service member before their casket is loaded on to an aircraft and returned home. Gonzales, 19, was from Carrollton, Texas, near Ordex’s home near Dallas. Gonzales was not yet born when Ordex first enlisted in 2004. “Thinking about it now makes me emotional, to think about how we have people coming home now … 19 years old,” she said. “I think about people like her that were excluded. Not only are Latinos being excluded from so much more and being targeted: we have this person that paid the ultimate sacrifice for this country who isn’t even being recognized as a casualty of this war, so it feels like erasure.” The War Powers Act of 1973 requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension, which it has not. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. Smith, who completed combat tours in Iraq, Bosnia and Kosovo, likened the administrative change to the manipulation of Pentagon casualty data last seen in the Vietnam war. “It’s so disrespectful to our service members who gave their lives, and the only reason they died was because Donald Trump decided to do this illegal war,” Smith said. “I mean, clearly the president is very sensitive about the deaths. You know, he is comparing it to Korea and Vietnam. “Obviously their boss doesn’t want to hear about deaths. OK, well, here’s one way we can make it look like there’s not as many deaths.” Joel Valdez, acting Pentagon press secretary, said: “The classification of Iran conflict casualties under Overseas Operations is grounded strictly in a factual basis, not commentary or narrative. We honor our fallen service members forever and always.” The department’s reclassification of Iran war casualties has faced criticism in Washington, including from Thomas Massie, a Republican House member from Kentucky, ousted in a primary earlier this year after repeatedly breaking with the president. “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire,” Massie wrote on X on Friday. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, a Democrat on the armed services committee, added: “Americans deserve the truth about the human cost of President Trump’s Iran war, and I will not stop fighting until this administration gives our military members and their families the transparency and accountability they deserve.”

title: Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed says ‘ogre’ remark not directed at rival
body_text: The Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said his comments that progressives need to put the head of an “ogre” on a pike was in reference to the Senator John Fetterman – not his opponent, Representative Haley Stevens. In a televised debate on Monday, the final head-to-head before the state’s 4 August primary, the moderator asked El-Sayed whether he regretted his comments made in a Zoom meeting, in which, according to leaked audio published by Politico, he suggested that if “you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message”. The comments drew immediate backlash from several high-profile Democrats and charges of sexism by those who believed the remark was a reference to Stevens. “Many people took offense to that,” the debate moderator, Roop Raj, noted. “Do you regret any of the comments that you’ve made?” El-Sayed did not reply directly, but said he had been speaking of supporting a primary challenge to Fetterman, the towering Pennsylvania Democrat who campaigned as a progressive but has moved to the right since taking office. “I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman, who’s a senator from Pennsylvania who has done terrible things, got elected on a set of values, and is now completely throwing those values in the mud,” El-Sayed said in the debate. Fetterman and El-Sayed have clashed mightily over the senator’s increasingly robust support for Israel, and in recent weeks Fetterman has said he would consider leaving the Democratic party if it became “anti-Israel” . During the hour-long debate, El-Sayed pushed back on criticism that he had failed to foster a spirit of political civility as candidate, noting that he recently chided his supporters for mocking Stevens’s accent. “Look, I took to Twitter last week and said that the tone in which people talk about my opponent is unkind, and I asked anybody who supported me to not talk about her that way,” he said. Before the moderator moved on, Stevens quipped: “Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre.” The expensive and increasingly bitter Democratic primary to replace retiring senator Gary Peters has evolved into a proxy fight over the party’s future, pitting the establishment-backed moderate Stevens against El-Sayed, a progressive former Detroit health director. The candidates have split sharply on the issue of Israel, with Stevens identifying as a “proud pro-Israel Democrat” and accepting substantial support from American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). By contrast, El-Sayed has called Israel’s campaign in Gaza a “genocide” and has denounced US arms support for Israel. Last week, Stevens picked up the endorsement of Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer, who El-Sayed challenged unsuccessfully in the 2018 gubernatorial primary. El-Sayed has rallied the party’s left flank, and has been endorsed by the independent senator Bernie Sanders and New York congressmember Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. The dueling coalitions have turned Michigan’s closely watched Senate contest into a clear test of whether the twin forces of anti-Washington sentiment and progressive energy can overcome broad institutional support in a presidential battleground state. Asked about whether he would call himself a progressive or a democratic socialist, El-Sayed replied: “I’m not a socialist. I’m just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works. The biggest threat to capitalism was never the idea of government regulation. It was always monopoly.” The contest – one of the few open-seat races this cycle – is widely viewed as central to the battle for Senate control. Donald Trump won Michigan in 2024, making it among Republicans’ most promising pick-up opportunities. Former congressman Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost Michigan’s 2024 Senate race to Elissa Slotkin, cleared the Republican field early and has spent months preparing for the general election. Earlier on Monday, Rogers appeared on stage with Trump at a rally in Milford, Michigan, where he promised to help the president enact his agenda, if elected.

title: Javier Milei accuses US Democrats of financing ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ at World Cup
body_text: More than a week has passed since Ferran Torres scored the extra-time goal that gave Spain its second World Cup, but – at least for Argentina’s president – the tournament is not over. Javier Milei has claimed that a coordinated “anti-Argentina campaign” was behind criticism of the country’s team, accusations of racism among its fans and conspiracy theories alleging that Lionel Messi’s side was secretly being favoured by Fifa. Now, the far-right president has taken the narrative a step further, alleging that the supposed campaign was financed by the US Democratic party and the governments of Brazil and Mexico. “It was the work of progressive minds who do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed,” claimed the self-styled libertarian in an interview with a local radio station on Sunday. He went on to claim that the “government of Brazil”, led by the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had allegedly provided the largest share of the funding. Analysts in Argentina said Milei had embraced the narrative as a distraction from his plummeting popularity, while others argued that the “real anti-Argentina campaign” was the one the president was waging “with his chainsaw” austerity plan. Yet the narrative has gained traction, even reaching people who do not support Milei. Pablo Torres, a 52-year-old bookseller from Buenos Aires who “never voted for him and never would”, said there had been a social media “bombardment” against the country that left him feeling “outrage” and “disgust”. He said some of the accusations of racism had come from “great colonial powers that enslaved people, trafficked enslaved people and decimated populations”, adding: “They denied the existence of the black population in Argentina, and ignored our idiosyncrasies and our history … We are a welcoming home for all nations.” During the tournament, incidents involving racist behaviour by some Argentine supporters drew widespread attention. Hours before the final, the US actor Samuel L Jackson posted an Instagram story that said: “Dear black people, please do not cheer or root for Argentina to win the Fifa World Cup. Argentina has historically been one of, if not the most, racist countries in the world.” The post prompted reactions even from human rights organisations such as Amnesty International Argentina, which acknowledged racism in the country but criticised “reducing the country to a stereotype”. Milei, meanwhile, posted that the criticism could be attributed to Argentina’s opposition, which had “validated the woke movement that is now accusing us of being racist”. Over the weekend, he also decided to blame Brazil – while on Brazilian soil. On Saturday, the Argentinian president attended the launch of the presidential campaign of the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro and Lula’s main challenger in October’s presidential election. In his speech, as well as calling Lula a “thief” and a “prisoner” – prompting a strong reaction from the Brazilian government – Milei said: “If you examine the data from the recent anti-Argentina campaign, the place from which the most attacks came was Brazil.” He reinforced the claim on Sunday, this time adding Mexico and the US Democratic party. The digital anthropologist Mercedes Máspero analysed more than 2m posts on social media and wrote that she had found “some undeniable patterns” of orchestration such as the repeated use of variations of “disgusting human beings” in different languages. Even so, it was “a tough call” to describe it as a coordinated campaign “because the narrative is incredibly widespread”, she wrote. Natalia Aruguete, a researcher at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council who specialises in social media and political agendas, said she had seen “no evidence of a large-scale coordinated operation”, despite the existence of “a hostile, widespread and transnational conversation centred on Argentina”. “Brazil had a significant presence [in those messages],” she added, “particularly in the conversation about racism, but … Milei’s accusation of alleged Brazilian involvement was not backed up by any public evidence.” Some critics said that the last time the idea of such a campaign was propagated by the state was during the brutal 1976–83 dictatorship, whose crimes Milei has repeatedly downplayed. During the 1978 World Cup, hosted by Argentina, the military junta claimed that criticism of the regime’s human rights violations was part of an “anti-Argentina campaign”. Aruguete said Milei had turned a “diverse online conversation” into a political conflict that fits his narrative of a “culture war” against the left, at a time when his administration is facing “internal deterioration”: inflation appears to be under control, but rising unemployment and corruption scandals have driven the president’s popularity to its lowest point since taking office. The narrative that suggests Argentinians are all victims of a supposedly orchestrated campaign by leftwing foreign governments “allows Milei to shift the focus of the debate away from his own governance issues and on to an external adversary”, said Aruguete.

Two British women went to Suffolk police in August 2019 to allege that James Loubeau and another US airman had drugged and raped them. Less than two weeks later, Suffolk police allowed the US air force to take responsibility for investigating the two alleged rapes. It has since emerged that Loubeau, 38, allegedly attacked a total of six women in East Anglia over a four-month period in 2019, in what US prosecutors described as a “frightening and dangerous” pattern of assaults. DoJ urges supreme court to allow Trump order targeting mail-in voting The Trump administration has asked the supreme court to clear the way for an executive order from Donald Trump that could dramatically change mail-in voting. The emergency appeal comes after an appeals court upheld a ruling blocking the president’s order in nearly half the country ahead of November’s midterm elections. What is the president attempting to do? Trump ordered the government in March to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters and deliver mail ballots only to those people on that list. The legal challenge says the constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. Trump promoted the proposed changes as safeguards to keep non-US citizens from voting, which has been shown to be rare. Stat of the day: Johnson & Johnson to pay $5.5bn settlement in talc cancer lawsuit Johnson & Johnson said it would pay an estimated $5.5bn to resolve tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging its baby ⁠powder and other talc products caused ⁠ovarian cancer, in a landmark deal that could end a contentious, decade-long legal battle. A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war as being killed in “overseas 0perations” is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead. Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral who completed combat tours in Iraq, Bosnia and Kosovo, said: “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families. To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.” The change came as Donald Trump once again warned that the US would return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts did not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East. “We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.” What changes did the Department of Defense make? The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7”. That splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran into effectively two different campaigns. How is the administration justifying the change? The War Powers Act of 1973 requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension, which it has not. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. The comments drew immediate backlash from several high-profile Democrats and charges of sexism by those who believed the remark was a reference to Stevens. El-Sayed claimed he had been speaking of supporting a primary challenge to Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat who campaigned as a progressive but has moved to the right since taking office. “I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman, who’s a senator from Pennsylvania who has done terrible things, got elected on a set of values, and is now completely throwing those values in the mud.” US airman accused of ‘spree’ of rapes on sleeping women in England avoided UK courts A US airman accused of a “spree” of rapes and sexual assaults in England, drugging some women and breaking into the homes of others, was able to avoid English justice after local police handed over part of the case to the American military. Two British women went to Suffolk police in August 2019 to allege that James Loubeau and another US airman had drugged and raped them. Less than two weeks later, Suffolk police allowed the US air force to take responsibility for investigating the two alleged rapes. title: How close is the Trump administration to the toxic Tate brothers? Let’s ask the president’s son Barron …
body_text: Unlike his garrulous father, Barron Trump seems to be a man of few words. The president’s youngest son has been busy flogging energy drinks and making millions from cryptocurrency schemes, but he’s not big on public speaking. Indeed, the best-known clip of him talking is probably from when he was four years old and said “I like my suitcase” in a Slovenian accent. Still, while 20-year-old Barron Trump might prefer to stay behind the scenes, he may find himself hauled in front of Congress and forced to answer some difficult questions. Last week, Yassamin Ansari, a Democratic congresswoman and a member of the House oversight committee, called for Barron to testify about his alleged connections to the toxic influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate. The Tate brothers, who have become household names by monetising misogyny, were recently arrested in Miami, just before Andrew was due to co-host a bare-knuckle boxing event. They’re now fighting extradition to the UK, and face allegations of rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”. They deny these charges. What’s Barron got to do with all this? Over the years, the Trumps and the Tates seem to have forged a mutually beneficial alliance. Donald Trump Jr has been friendly with Andrew since 2016 and, while I wouldn’t go so far as to call Barron and Andrew besties, the New York Times has reported that a teenage Barron admired the influencer and had a Zoom call with him. According to the New Yorker, Barron also spent a lot of time with Justin Waller, who has called himself the Tates’ “third brother”, and gave Barron dating advice. Barron, in turn, gave his dad a political steer: he is widely credited, including by the president himself, for pushing Trump to tap into manosphere influencers such as Tate during the 2024 election in order to mobilise young male voters. In return for their help with the election, the Tates got friends in high places. “The Tates will be free, Trump is the president,” Andrew posted after the inauguration. And that prediction was partly correct: it has been widely reported that the Trump administration intervened in 2025 to get the Romanian government to lift travel restrictions on the Tates, who were under house arrest in the country for trafficking charges. (Romania’s foreign minister has said he did not face any pressure from the US regarding the Tates. The Trump administration has said it had no insight into the matter.) Will the Trump administration help the brothers when it comes to this new extradition request? Press secretary Karoline Leavitt has said the White House won’t get involved. Secretary of state Marco Rubio has also dismissed the idea. Whether you should believe this is debatable, but it’s certainly possible the Tates have outlived their usefulness to the ever-transactional Trumps. Still, the Trump family can’t sever ties with the Tate brothers that easily. As congresswoman Ansari notes, there are plenty of questions that remain unanswered about the Tate-Trump relationship. In a letter to the House oversight committee chair, Ansari said: “The committee must investigate whether back-channel communications between the Tate brothers, presidential advisors, and members of the First Family such as Barron Trump influenced official actions or administration policy regarding criminal prosecution and investigation of the brothers or international law enforcement cooperation.” The letter specifically recommends a subpoena for Barron to see if he had “any involvement” in relation to the Tate brothers’ alleged crimes. Over the weekend, Ansari reiterated her calls for an investigation on the MeidasTouch podcast, noting that Barron “is a full-blown adult, and he is very influential in the Trump White House orbit”. Republicans have a slight majority in the House, so it’s highly unlikely that Ansari’s request will go anywhere. I don’t need to tell you that we still don’t have real answers about Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Nor do I need to tell you that Trump is an adjudicated sexual abuser. This isn’t an administration that takes violence against women seriously. That said, if the Democrats win the House in the midterms, as they are expected to do, the situation might shift and Barron might find himself with some explaining to do. And if the US government won’t demand answers from Barron, then the media should. As Ansari notes, Barron is very much an adult now. He may not have chosen to be born a Trump but he has chosen to profit from his name and connections. He’s not some little kid who needs protecting. But there are a lot of vulnerable young kids out there who do need protecting from the bigotry and hate that men like the Tates peddle. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Ex-FCC officials warn agency sending ‘chilling message’ with ABC license review
body_text: A group of prominent former Federal Communications Commission (FCC) officials, including key staffers and commissioners appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents, issued a filing on Tuesday that warns the agency is trying to send a “chilling message” to broadcasters after it received petitions to deny ABC license renewals for eight of its local television stations. The network’s licenses are up for early renewal after an extremely unusual order from the Brendan Carr-led FCC in late April, following criticism of ABC by Donald Trump and Melania Trump. The group behind the filing includes Mark S Fowler, who served as FCC chair during Ronald Reagan’s presidency; Alfred C Sikes, who served as FCC chair during George HW Bush’s presidency; Thomas E Wheeler, who served as FCC chair during Barack Obama’s presidency; and several high-ranking lawyers and advisers to past commissioners. “This early license renewal proceeding is unprecedented in the history of the Federal Communications Commission and a grave violation of both the Communications Act and the Constitution,” the coalition wrote in the filing. “Through this proceeding, the FCC seeks to censor Disney’s and ABC’s speech and send a chilling message to all broadcasters: carry speech we don’t like at your peril.” Seeking to put the ABC license challenge into context, the group called the order “the latest attack in a sustained campaign by Chairman Carr and the Trump administration of threatening legal sanctions against licensees whose speech President Trump dislikes”. The filing is a response to petitions to deny ABC’s license renewals submitted by conservative media watchdog the Media Research Center (MRC) and the Center for American Rights (CAR), a conservative legal organization that is closely aligned with Carr and has initiated several complaints against television networks premised on accusations of liberal bias. CAR’s petition to deny ABC’s license renewal accused the network of “[ignoring] long-standing Commission precedents and principles protecting the integrity of the news” and “[engaging] in explicit racial and gender discrimination”. The coalition said in its Tuesday filing that the petitions should be denied because they ask the FCC to wade into “content and viewpoint regulation” and accusations of bias by punishing a network for their editorial decision-making – “a stunning – and plainly unconstitutional – expansion of the Commission’s role”. “As former Chairs, Commissioners, Chiefs of Staff, General Counsels and Bureau Chiefs, we call on the Commission to respect the constitutional and congressional prohibitions on its ‘power of censorship’ and terminate this proceeding,” the group wrote. Interested parties have until 5 August to reply to petitions to deny ABC’s licenses. After that time, the FCC could either grant the extension requests, a prospect that seems unlikely, or schedule hearings on the matter. The process has no clear timetable, leaving ABC and its eight local television stations mired in a cloud of uncertainty about their ability to continue broadcasting long-term.

title: Lindsey Graham’s funeral ceremonies to begin with Netanyahu and Zelenskyy in attendance
body_text: Two days of funeral ceremonies for Lindsey Graham, the late South Carolina Republican senator, will begin in Washington on Tuesday, with mourners set to include the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Both leaders are also meeting Donald Trump at the White House. A longtime foreign policy hawk, Graham was working on a new Russia sanctions bill when he met Zelenskyy in Kyiv earlier this month, dying shortly after returning to Washington from a heart condition aged 71. On Sunday, the Wall Street Journal released footage shot by a documentary team in February, showing Graham’s delight over the Iran war and eager support for Netanyahu and Israel. Memorial events on Tuesday will begin on Capitol Hill, where Graham, a former US air force lawyer, was a member of the House for eight years and a senator for 23. From the Capitol Rotunda, the casket will be taken to the Washington National Cathedral for an afternoon service, with Trump – who Graham once called a “jackass” and a “race-baiting bigot” before switching to support him – among the scheduled speakers. On Wednesday, in Graham’s home state, ceremonies will begin with services and an F-16 flyover at the South Carolina state house in Columbia, followed by a procession to First Baptist church for a public service. A private family burial will take place in Pickens county, home to Central, the small town where Graham and his younger sister and Senate successor, Darline, were born. Back in Washington on Tuesday, the Israeli and Ukrainian leaders will each head for high-stakes White House meetings. The behind-the-scenes footage of Graham released by the Wall Street Journal was shot on the first day of US-Israeli strikes on Iran, a move long urged by Netanyahu and eagerly embraced by Trump. “I almost cried,” Graham said. “I mean, like, how long have we been pushing this? It’s here. I talked with Trump this morning. Holy Jack. It’s here. It’s the best thing I’ve ever done. He loves blowing stuff up.” At least 175 people, most of them schoolchildren, were killed in the Iranian city of Minab in those first strikes, in all likelihood by US missiles in a controversial “double tap” strike. Another clip released on Sunday showed Graham predicting that it would take “about three or four weeks” for attacks on Iran to cause the regime in Tehran to “start losing control of some cities” and for the US-Israeli effort to achieve “almost irreversible momentum”. That has not happened. Nor has the US joined Israeli attacks on Lebanon, as Graham was shown advocating to Netanyahu. In the footage, Graham also said: “Trump and Bibi [Netanyahu] are like Roosevelt and Churchill. They’re the right two guys to confront this evil.” As it turns out, Netanyahu and Trump’s relationship has been placed under considerable stress, with reports of angry confrontations. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, will hope for a more constructive Oval Office meeting than the now-famous occasion in February 2025, when he was upbraided by Trump and JD Vance, including for not wearing a suit. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have remained strained, even as Ukraine has gained the upper hand in its long fight against Russian invaders.
