title: The Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming together
body_text: “What if all cockroaches come together?” was the question that humbled India’s strongman prime minister, Narendra Modi. It was posted on X by Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in the US with a master’s in public relations. Enraged that India’s top judge likened unemployed youths to insects and “parasites”, and that millions saw medical exams compromised by leaks, Mr Dipke lit a fuse. For India’s nearly 400 million gen Z, public exams are often the only ladder to a secure future. When papers leak or tests are cancelled, that ladder is kicked away. By June, young people were protesting peacefully in Delhi as the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a parody of Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). They demanded the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. This weekend, Mr Pradhan became the first senior minister in Mr Modi’s 12 years in power to be forced from office by a mass-protest movement. It came after credible reports suggested police officers attacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they have accused the government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally. Mr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism and demonising Muslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage. Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that has dominated the public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historian Mukul Kesavan says the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders. A similar kind of unrest during an anti-corruption movement in 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from the ruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot argues that the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? It came after credible reports suggested police officers attacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they have accused the government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally. Mr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism and demonising Muslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage. Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that has dominated the public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historian Mukul Kesavan says the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders. A similar kind of unrest during an anti-corruption movement in 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from the ruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot argues that the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Trump reportedly pushing RFK Jr to cut vaccines more aggressively
body_text: Donald Trump is pushing the longtime vaccine opponent and current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr to be more aggressive on cutting vaccines in the US, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal. Trump has a long record of anti-vaccine statements, but the White House recently put a hold on vaccine changes after polling indicated they were a losing issue in the midterm elections. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, recently slashed the routine childhood immunization schedule in an unprecedented move. Trump reportedly asked Kennedy at his northern Virginia golf course in May if the health secretary had the “yips”, according to the Journal. Trump wasn’t talking about a sudden inability to make putts. Kennedy wasn’t making enough cuts to the US vaccination schedule, Trump reportedly said. The US president hopes to make “alleviating autism” a component of his legacy, the Journal reported – and he has taken issue with Kennedy’s less aggressive changes to vaccination recommendations in recent months. “Donald Trump has been anti-vaccine at least since 2015,” said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center and an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. At the Republican primary debate that year, Trump said that autism had gotten “totally out of control” and vaccines should be in “smaller doses over a longer period of time”. Trump regularly posted on social media about debunked links between vaccination and autism as early as 2014, and his posts on Truth Social have recently advocated for breaking up shots into individual components and delaying some childhood vaccines for more than a decade. Tony Fabrizio, a top pollster for Trump, found that anti-vaccine moves are unpopular with voters in key districts, concluding in a December memo that “skepticism toward vaccine requirements is politically risky for both parties”. Susie Wiles gave HHS the deadline of New Year’s Eve to make vaccine changes, to allow vaccines to fall into the background with the midterms looming, according to reporting by the Rolling Stone. But Trump’s priorities appear to lie elsewhere. He issued a memo, two days after Fabrizio’s poll results, directing HHS to align with “peer” nations on vaccination recommendations, even though the US was already making similar recommendations to other countries. A month later, Kennedy slashed vaccine recommendations by one-third, from 17 to 11. A federal judge ordered a halt to these changes following a lawsuit in March from the American Academy of Pediatrics. The judge also paused the work of the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP), which was illegally formed under Kennedy, he said. Kennedy has not made any significant changes to the vaccine schedule since then, though he has continued speaking about autism and its potential causes, and the US government is appealing the judge’s stay on vaccine changes. Kennedy also sought to divert $5bn in funding – more than 10% of the entire National Institutes of Health budget – toward research on vaccines and autism, according to reporting by Reuters. Decades of research into the causes of autism point overwhelmingly to genetics, and dozens of studies have indicated no link between vaccines and autism. Even so, Trump issued an executive order in May urging HHS to change vaccine recommendations. Kush Desai, a spokesperson for the White House, did not dispute the details reported by the Journal and others in a statement to the Guardian. He instead pointed to parents of autistic children – but not to autistic people themselves – with “questions and concerns” who “have long been ignored if not mocked”. The Trump administration was “committed to leaving no stone unturned” to address those concerns, Desai added. Kennedy and Trump are “aligned in their commitment” to confront the “chronic disease epidemic affecting America’s children”, said Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, in an apparent reference to autism. HHS would “continue to pursue evidence-based research to identify the root causes of autism and other chronic diseases”, she added. “I think Donald Trump has a fixed, immutable belief that vaccines cause autism,” Offit said. That makes Trump the most powerful anti-vaxxer in the world, Offit said – and it means he is unlikely to fire Kennedy, even as rumors have swirled that the health secretary is on his way out. The abrupt rise of measles and other deadly diseases are more likely to be Trump’s legacy than advances in understanding autism, Offit said. As top leaders have downplayed the safety and importance of vaccines, measles has surged to its highest rate in 30 years, and the nation has suffered a rise in deaths from whooping cough, flu and tetanus in recent years. “And our commander in chief, our vaccine guy in chief, is our president. He’s fine with this. Just as RFK Jr is fine with this,” Offit said. “Trump has become the president of Measles Land,” Offit added. “That should bother him.”

title: Lindsey Graham remembered as ‘true American original’ at Capitol memorial
body_text: Donald Trump and other political leaders convened in Washington for the memorial of the long-serving US senator Lindsey Graham on Tuesday afternoon, remembering the “swashbuckling” South Carolina Republican as “a true American original” whose embrace of “America first” never softened his advocacy for a staunch interventionist US foreign policy. Graham, a polarizing figure and one-time rival turned stalwart ally of Trump, was known for championing the US-Israel war on Iran and was a prominent voice in the anti-abortion movement and an unwavering supporter of Israel, serving as one of Capitol Hill’s most outspoken foreign policy hawks. “He died doing the work he was born to do. He was truly a great politician, serving the country he loved to serve so deeply,” Trump said of Graham in his eulogy at the National Cathedral. “He went out at the peak of his career, the top of his game as a legend that every one of us, many of us here today, blessed to know him and a friend that none of us will ever forget,” he added. Trump took the opportunity to reiterate his support for Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to the late senator’s seat for the remainder of his term. And he focused on Graham’s foreign policy record as a war hawk. “I will tell you, he never saw a war that he didn’t like. Only his true friends would understand that. But he wanted it for the good of our country,” he said. The president, who ran against Graham in the 2016 presidential election, admitted that “Lindsey and I did not exactly get off to the best of starts”. Recalling his leaking of Graham’s phone number to the public after Graham called him a “jackass” during the presidential race, Trump said: “It was Lindsey who had the last laugh because while I blew up his phone all for one day, we became great friends, and Lindsey did not stop calling me for the next 10 years. It was not easy.” Other speakers included the Fox News host Sean Hannity, who said Graham would have been honored by the presence of Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who held meetings with Trump earlier in the day. The television host also turned to flattery with Trump in the pews. “Lindsey, Mr President, I would argue in my mind probably has a heavenly version of Mar-a-Lago. It may even be a little bigger … Because he would want to obviously duplicate his dearest friend in life. You, Mr President,” he said. Speaking during a ceremony earlier on Tuesday inside the Capitol Rotunda, the US Senate majority leader, John Thune, hailed Graham as a “fierce defender of Ukraine”, following its full-scale invasion by Russia in 2022, and a “powerful voice for the [anti-abortion] movement”. “I feel his absence every day, and I know my colleagues do as well,” Thune continued, growing emotional. “I look forward to the days when you make us laugh again.” Darline Graham, who was sworn in earlier this month, attended both services. She is running in the Republican primary to permanently succeed her brother. Graham died suddenly earlier this month, aged 71, shortly after returning to Washington from a trip to Kyiv. The Ukrainian president and the Israeli prime minister are due to attend an afternoon service for Graham at Washington National Cathedral. JD Vance, the US vice-president, credited Graham with the successful confirmation of Brett Kavanaugh to the US supreme court in 2018, which helped conservatives secure a supermajority on the bench within two years. “I believe that he saved that nomination,” Vance said. “I choose to remember Lindsey Graham as a person who could fight with you on one issue, but fight for you on another issue,” the US vice-president said. “I remember Lindsey Graham as a man who loved people, and because he loved people, he was willing to reason with them, to respect them and ultimately to persuade them.” “May God rest the soul of Senator Lindsey Graham, a true American original,” he said. A former air force lawyer who served in the air force reserve while in Congress, Graham was elected to the House of Representatives in 1994 and served as a manager during Bill Clinton’s 1999 impeachment trial before winning a Senate seat in 2002. Weeks before his death, Graham defeated a field of challengers to win the Republican nomination in his bid for a fifth term. On Wednesday, in Graham’s home state, ceremonies will begin with services and an F-16 flyover at the South Carolina statehouse in Columbia, followed by a procession to First Baptist church for a public service. A private family burial will take place in Pickens county, home to Central, the small town where Graham and his younger sister and Senate successor, Darline, were born.

title: Trump pausing Iran attacks shows US military power is not enough on its own
body_text: Has Iran won a war it didn’t start against the United States? It is not a victory in any conventional military sense: about 3,500 Iranians have been reported killed and the US-led bombing has caused anywhere between $150bn and $270bn of damage. Yet Donald Trump’s decision to pause, rather than intensify, the 13-night summer bombing campaign in effect represents a degree of recognition that the US cannot achieve its stated goals by military power alone. “Iran’s initial standard for victory was simply to survive,” said HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute. “If anything, that’s been raised. The regime has demonstrated it is not going anywhere, and Tehran has changed the calculus on the strait of Hormuz”. The past five months are a clear demonstration of how an asymmetric conflict can flip the tables. All Iran, helped by its extensive and mountainous geography, has needed to do is maintain enough of a missile and drone capability to scare merchant shipping from using the strait of Hormuz. It is a low bar Iran’s military is still clearing. Two tankers were attacked sailing north of Oman last week. One of them caught fire in the engine room and had to be evacuated, before being towed to Oman, one of a handful of serious attacks on merchant shipping that took place during the nearly two-week July escalation of fighting. The US, meanwhile, has spent at least $38bn and used more than 1,000 Tomahawk and 1,100 Jassm $2.6m cruise missiles, according to estimates by the CSIS thinktank, to bomb targets in Iran, a third and a quarter of total stockpiles. The Tomahawks, which cost up to $3.6m each, might not be replaced until 2031. It is surprising that the US has allowed key munitions to be run down at such speed. On Monday, Trump tried in part to blame Ukraine, arguing that “so much was given” to Kyiv in military aid – though the reality is that Ukraine was never given long-range cruise missiles, only Patriot air defence systems. Patriot missile interceptors were more heavily depleted, by 1,000 or so, or 50% of the total US stockpile, raising questions as to how well the US can continue to defend its bases in the Gulf. More were used during the 38 days of heavy fighting in the spring than the 600 or so that Ukraine has said it had received during four years of war. A fresh escalation in the Red Sea by the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen, complicates the picture further. The rebel group kept out of the first phase of the US-Iran war in the spring but, as Saudi Arabia seeks to redirect oil traffic through the Red Sea, they have stepped up attacks, targeting a refinery in the Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday. The US’s stated central war aim, meanwhile, may have repeatedly shifted but it has always been maximalist – whether it was regime change (as demonstrated by the killing of Ali Khamenei), destroying Iran’s entire missile programme or, as most frequently stated, preventing the country from having a nuclear weapon. Yet the US has no means of enforcing this level of demand without committing ground forces in numbers to occupy Tehran – an unlikely move that the US has not shown signs of preparing for. Donald Trump’s previous threats to bomb Iranian power plants to try to force the regime’s capitulation have raised concerns they would amount to war crimes, and he dropped them in April and again last week. “I don’t think the Iranians can be bombed into accepting US terms,” said Peter Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser. “Until the US accepts it can’t get its way by bombing, Iran has effective leverage. Tehran can absorb the pain, and they know they can close the strait with the economic impact it has on the US.” The resulting situation is what Ricketts calls an “escalation dominance” that he says favours Iran. Tehran, faced with US pressure to abandon its nuclear programme, can string out peace negotiations, wait for the White House to get impatient and restart bombing, then close Hormuz until the US has to stop attacking because the oil price is tto high for too long. The question then becomes who gains as unstable equilibrium endures. Tehran may well believe it has leverage as the US heads towards midterm elections in November, given how unpopular the war is. Just a third of all Americans support the war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey out on Tuesday, though that rises to 71% of Republicans. Laurel Rapp, from the Chatham House thinktank, said that “a resumed ceasefire and promise of future talks is the least bad option for Washington” – though whether that is attractive to US ally Israel, whose prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu has his own election to fight in October, is another source of uncertainty. But if Tehran may have short or medium-term leverage, any idea that it has won the war is exaggerated. Hellyer argues that Iran, long struggling under western sanctions, cannot afford to rebuild without an agreement with the US: “Ultimately this isn’t sustainable for Iran, because its economy isn’t going to be able to survive”.

title: Senate confirms Trump ally Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence
body_text: The US Senate voted to confirm Jay Clayton as the director of national intelligence on Tuesday, giving Trump another key ally directing the nation’s intelligence apparatus. The tally, 51-47, fell along party lines, with all Republicans supporting his nomination and all Democrats opposing it. Clayton, currently the US attorney for the southern district of New York, will replace Bill Pulte, a staunch Trump loyalist who had been temporarily serving in the role since June. Trump’s first director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned earlier this year. Clayton served as the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) during Trump’s first term. During his confirmation hearing on 15 July, Clayton sidestepped several questions about the 2020 election and declined to say that Trump lost it. During an interview on CNBC in June, Clayton also suggested there was something amiss about the long period California takes to count ballots. “We had a problem, a deep problem with voting in America,” he said on the network. “On the integrity side, we’re doing an absolutely terrible job, and the American people are right to question it.” Clayton also would not say during his confirmation hearing whether voter fraud was a problem in American elections, even though several studies have shown it is exceedingly rare. His office also issued widely criticized subpoenas to New York Times journalists over their reporting on security concerns around Trump’s Air Force One airplane that was a gift from Qatar. The government abruptly withdrew those subpoenas during a court hearing in which a federal judge pressed an attorney from Clayton’s office about errors and irregularities in the subpoenas. While Democrats saw Clayton as a more preferable pick than Pulte, who has assisted in executing some of Trump’s sloppy and ugly acts of political retribution, including the criminal prosecution of Letitia James and a ham-handed effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve board of governors, Pulte was also leading the office of the director of national intelligence earlier this month when Trump declassified and released intelligence in support of false claims about the 2020 election. Pulte oversaw several rounds of layoffs at the agency. But Clayton’s contentious hearing earlier this month cost him bipartisan backing. Before the vote, the senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, spoke in opposition to the nomination, warning that Clayton was unqualified and would act as the president’s “election conspiracy win”.

While Democrats saw Clayton as a more preferable pick than Pulte, who has assisted in executing some of Trump’s sloppy and ugly acts of political retribution, including the criminal prosecution of Letitia James and a ham-handed effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve board of governors, Pulte was also leading the office of the director of national intelligence earlier this month when Trump declassified and released intelligence in support of false claims about the 2020 election. Pulte oversaw several rounds of layoffs at the agency. But Clayton’s contentious hearing earlier this month cost him bipartisan backing. Before the vote, the senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, spoke in opposition to the nomination, warning that Clayton was unqualified and would act as the president’s “election conspiracy win”.

title: Trump praises back-to-back meetings with Zelenskyy and Netanyahu
body_text: Donald Trump hosted back-to-back White House meetings with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, as Ukraine seeks more firepower for its air defenses and the Israeli prime minister tries to repair his strained relationship with the US president. Trump described both meetings in positive terms on social media on Tuesday evening, remaining vague about what was discussed. “Had a very good meeting!” Trump said of his sit-down with Netanyahu. “Obviously, many important subjects were discussed.” He posted a similar statement about his time with Zelenskyy, writing the “meeting went very well!” It was Netanyahu’s first visit to the Oval Office since he and Trump launched their joint military campaign against Iran on 28 February. Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump has been complicated in recent weeks by his push to keep fighting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon, even as Trump pursued a diplomatic opening with Tehran. Tensions between the pair have risen as the war has drifted inconclusively, with Trump calling the Israeli premier “crazy” and declaring: “Without me, there would be no Israel.” The two men are each facing pressure at home, with Netanyahu in a tough re-election fight, and Trump under pressure to end an unpopular war that has pushed up prices before November’s midterms. Trump signaled some of that friction beforehand. Asked on Fox & Friends on Tuesday morning about reports that Netanyahu planned to brief him on intelligence about Iranian activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site Trump has threatened to bomb, he said he knew “exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe”, adding that Netanyahu raises it because “he wants me to stay involved”. Far outside the White House, behind the fences, protesters chanted: “Netanyahu, you’re a tyrant” and “Bibi, you’re not welcome here” on Tuesday. The closed-door meeting, which lasted about an hour, was expected to cover Iran, a framework deal the US and Israel signed with Lebanon, and a possible expansion of the Abraham accords, according to a White House official. Netanyahu also faces the task of reassuring Trump he will not obstruct US-led diplomacy in Gaza and Lebanon, as support for Israel among the US public has slipped, with a new AP-Norc poll showing a sharp decline amid accusations, denied by Israel, that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. In a statement, Zelenskyy said he had discussed licensing arrangements to let Ukraine manufacture its own interceptors for Patriot missile systems. “We also spoke about diplomacy – it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated,” said Zelenskyy. “Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support.” He opened by offering condolences over the death of the US senator Lindsey Graham, calling the late foreign policy hawk “a true friend of Ukraine”. Graham died suddenly earlier this month, aged 71, shortly after returning to Washington from a trip to Kyiv. Later on Tuesday, with Zelenskyy watching from the Senate gallery, the chamber advanced a sweeping Russia sanctions bill in tribute to Graham. The bill, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, easily cleared a procedural hurdle, 86 to 12, hours after Graham’s funeral in Washington, where the late senator was hailed as a “fierce defender of Ukraine”.

title: Welcome to America, where you’re never quite sure if your senator is dead or not
body_text: Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends in the US. Mitch McConnell was hospitalized for a medical event on 14 June and we are now in week six of What on Earth Is Going on With Mitch? – a mystery that has riveted the nation. According to McConnell’s team there isn’t actually a mystery at all. The 84-year-old is doing great, they want us to know. So great that they have now released two photos to prove it. The first was made public on Sunday 12 July, almost a month after McConnell’s hospitalization and appears to have been prompted in part by Trump ally and far-right agent of chaos Laura Loomer’s claim that Mitch was “officially brain dead”. Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, had also just sent a letter to McConnell asking him to be transparent and put an end to the speculation about his health. Funnily enough, the day before that photo came out, I’d published a column with the headline “Is Mitch McConnell secretly deceased?” Rarely is a question answered so quickly. Perhaps, as my next offering to the mischievous headline gods, I’ll put out a piece titled: “Is Benjamin Netanyahu going to escape accountability forever?” But back to that photo, which we’ll call Proof of Life One (POL1). Mitch, I’ll be honest, looked pretty good. He was wearing a nice pink shirt and his wife was standing next to him with her mouth stretched into something resembling a human smile. I wouldn’t say she was caressing him exactly, but she had a hand under his arm. Mitch was also holding a copy of the day’s Washington Post Sports section so we could all see that he was not secretly deceased. Very normal stuff! Our tech overlords have ushered in a world where no one can be ever sure that visual evidence is real and POL1 immediately set off rabid speculation that the photo was AI. There is, I should note, no evidence whatsoever that the photo was AI. But there is also no evidence that McConnell had any idea what was going on in that photo, or that he is in a fit state to continue serving his constituents. His office put out a statement saying he’d had a fall in his home and had subsequently been treated for pneumonia, but we still haven’t actually heard directly from the senator. All of which is why POL1 did not put an end to the speculation that McConnell’s office is hiding details about the senator’s condition from the public. So, on Monday, to try and quell a new round of speculation, his office released a new photo dated 26 July, which we’ll call Proof of Life Two (POL2). This photo is pretty similar to the first one, except the senator is in a blue shirt. His office also put out a statement saying the senator is out of hospital, but still having “intense physical therapy” and wouldn’t be able to travel to the annual Fancy Farm picnic in western Kentucky. The statement did not say when he might be expected back in the Senate, which is scheduled to break for a month on 7 August. He has already missed 38 votes. Once again, this photo of an apparently living, breathing Mitch has not put an end to the questions around McConnell’s health. If the issue is his mobility rather than his mental capacity, why can’t McConnell come into the Senate in a wheelchair to do his job? That’s what happened last year, after all, after he suffered a fall and then was seen using a wheelchair at the Capitol. Demanding more transparency from a public servant who is collecting a taxpayer-funded salary to represent his constituents is not unreasonable. Indeed, if McConnell were in perfect health and a Democratic senator were in this position, McConnell would be leading the charge to ensure they resigned. The man has never been interested in empathy or civility, just power. It looks like Kentucky’s governor hasn’t been reassured by POL2 either. On Monday, Beshear renewed his calls for transparency, asking the senator to directly address Kentuckians about his health or resign. “As Governor of the state you serve, I am calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign,” Beshear wrote in a letter. “If you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve, I will insist Leader Thune fully investigate your condition, report to the American people, and begin the process [to fill your Senate seat] if warranted.” Is this letter finally going to lead to answers? I don’t know. But I do know that it’s highly likely that a situation like this is going to happen again. Regardless of where they are on the political spectrum, US lawmakers seem determined to cling to power until they die at their desks. Earlier this month, Senator Lindsey Graham became the fourth member of the US Senate since 2013 to have died while in office and the sixth member of Congress to have died while serving in the 119th Congress. Because the US is the greatest democracy in the world, Graham has now been replaced in the Senate by his sister Darline. And if lawmakers aren’t dying in office, then they’re vanishing from their responsibilities without feeling the need to be transparent with their constituents. In 2024, for example, a reporter discovered that Kay Granger, a Republican congresswoman from Texas, who hadn’t cast a vote in months, was dealing with “dementia issues” at a senior living facility. Her office hadn’t felt the need to disclose this to the public. There was also some speculation that House Republican leaders had been aware of the situation and deliberately chose to keep the information quiet to maintain their majority. And earlier this year Tom Kean Jr, a Republican, went off the radar for almost four months. He missed more than 100 votes but continued to collect his salary. Eventually he resurfaced and said he’d been to inpatient treatment for depression and hadn’t wanted to explain because he was a private person. Which is fair enough. But then may I suggest that a job in public office isn’t for you? It’s funny, isn’t it? There are millions of Americans who are never going to have the funds to retire. Who are going to be forced to work for minimum wage until they keel over on the job. Our lawmakers, however, have excellent salaries and an array of taxpayer-funded health benefits. They can retire early if they choose to do so. It’s a tragedy for our democracy that more of them don’t. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist and the author of Strong Female Lead

title: How free childcare started winning US elections: ‘Overnight, people realized how essential it was’
body_text: In a matter of weeks, Francesca Hong, an unlikely candidate for governor in one of the country’s most heated battleground states, will test a message that is at once radical and, to many, incredibly practical: the government should help pay for childcare. “When we talk about free childcare, you can connect to folks whether it’s on an economic argument or just purely that it’s the right thing to do for our kids,” said Hong, a democratic socialist running in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary on 11 August. “I always like to remind folks: if we don’t take care of our kids, who’s going to take care of us?” For 50 years, US childcare policy lived in the welfare drawer with programs such as Head Start, a free early learning initiative for low-income families, and subsidies focused on keeping poor mothers in the workforce. Anything broader was often shut down by conservatives advocating for families’ “personal choice” over government-run childcare. And while Democratic lawmakers, often women, campaigned on the need for affordable childcare – presidential hopefuls Hillary Clinton, Elizabeth Warren and Kamala Harris made it central to their platforms – they had little success. Then something shifted as the cost of care surpassed college tuition and a pandemic hangover pushed caregivers, and their wallets, to their limits: childcare became a middle-class problem that could no longer be ignored. In November, Zohran Mamdani made universal childcare a cornerstone of his New York mayoral campaign, and two centrists, Abigail Spanberger and Mikie Sherrill, won the governorships in Virginia and New Jersey, respectively, running on the same plank. In March, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare for all. In the nation’s capital, Janeese Lewis-George won the mayoral primary this summer with universal childcare among her top priorities. “We’re in an era of real affordability issues,” said Deb Haaland, former secretary of the interior who is currently running for governor of New Mexico. “Universal childcare is good for our economy – it creates jobs, it helps parents go to work without worrying about their children.” Behind these wins, though, are decades of painstaking organizing. Compounding crises, coupled with organizers’ longstanding work, have catapulted childcare from the sidelines to a kitchen-table issue as politically potent as the price of eggs or a grocery bill. Now, candidates vying for office in the midterm elections are seizing the moment to build on half a century of advocacy and win contests to give families some relief. Georgetown professor Joan Lombardi, who has advocated for early childhood policy across presidential administrations, distilled the moment into three parts: “First, for more parents today, childcare is their everyday reality. Second, affordability is driving it. And third, we have new innovations coming out of states and communities that can help inform policy decisions.” From radioactive policy to winning platform The US almost had a federally funded childcare system more than 50 years ago: Congress passed the Comprehensive Child Development Act, but Richard Nixon refused to sign it, fearing the alienation of his conservative base. At the time, one-third of women with children under age six worked. In the aftermath of the veto, the veteran civil rights activist Marian Wright Edelman founded the Children’s Defense Fund, which kept the vision of universal childcare alive, laying the groundwork for politicians’ childcare policy platforms since the 1970s and other legislative wins, such as the 1990 Child Care and Development Block Grant, which gave low-income families a voucher to pay for childcare. As more working mothers joined the halls of Congress, so did the push for federal childcare policy. Patty Murray, a senator from Washington state and former preschool teacher with two children, introduced the Child Care for Working Families Act in every Congress since 2017, but it took the pandemic to accelerate her cause: the bipartisan American Rescue Plan in 2021 infused $39bn into childcare – the first time Washington DC paid providers directly for operating costs rather than subsidizing individual slots. “Childcare facilities shut down, so our nurses couldn’t work, our essential employees couldn’t work,” she said. “And almost overnight, people realized how essential it was.” Solutions to affordability issues – the high costs of rent, groceries and childcare – have only continued to resonate with voters over the past year. In a sign of the times, the political action committee Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy is pouring $50m into races this midterm cycle. Even the Senate Democratic leadership is making childcare a pillar of their affordability agenda. “It’s not something people plan for the way they plan for buying a first home – suddenly it falls on their shoulders and they’re figuring it out alone,” Sondra Goldschein, executive director for Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, said about childcare. “This appeals to people who are older and younger, Democrats and Republicans, people in cities and in suburban and rural areas. It’s just top of mind.” Universal childcare in the midterms While there is still no federal law that supports childcare for all families who need it, organizers are pushing states – and running candidates in those states – to fill the vacuum. In Wisconsin, Hong, a leading candidate for governor, has made a payroll-funded universal childcare guarantee a key part of her platform – a message that particularly resonates after $110m in pandemic-era childcare funding ran out last month. “We have not seen childcare, paid leave, elder care as part of infrastructure,” Hong said. “It is the care economy that allows us to have communities.” Hong’s plan would provide free childcare up to 400% of the federal poverty level, a 7% cap on childcare spending for all families and loan-forgiveness programs for early educators. “We cannot have a sustainable workforce without affordable childcare for working families,” Hong said. In DC, parents and childcare providers protested after outgoing mayor Muriel Bowser cut early childhood educators’ pay and initiated an enrollment freeze in the city’s childcare-subsidy program for low-income families. “We coordinated the largest-ever day of early learning program closures in March – ‘a day without childcare’ – culminating in about 150 people rallying in subzero temperatures,” said Travis Ballie, executive director of the Under 3 DC coalition. “We did all that because this was existential – not just to preserve what we’d won, but because losing it would set us back.” Lewis George, the democratic socialist who won the Democratic primary for DC mayor in June, has heard voters’ concerns and promised to take a different tack. Her platform for “childcare for all” would build a subsidy toward universal affordable care on top of universal pre-K for all three- and four-year-olds in the district. “People don’t want to hear what government can’t do – they want to hear what government can do, how government will solve their problems,” said Lewis George. How one state won childcare for all New Mexico is perhaps the most-cited example of where the vision of universal childcare has been realized – and it took more than a decade of organizing to make happen. Before Javier Martinez was the speaker of the house in New Mexico, he was a community organizer helping immigrant families obtain driver’s licenses. “We’d look at this room full of little kids, and the parents themselves were saying: ‘It’s impossible to find childcare,’” he said. Immigration advocacy groups, such as New Mexico Voices for Children and Olé, led the charge for the state to pay for universal childcare in an innovative way: through a land grant funded by oil and gas revenue. In session after session, the legislature refused to hold a hearing on the issue, said Martinez. “I got to the point where, looking from the outside in, I thought: ‘Is this the best we can do as a legislature, as Democrats especially?’” he said. That’s when he decided to run for office in 2014. When the childcare plan remained stymied by three fiscally conservative Democratic state senators, organizers targeted their re-election in 2020. “Our coalition pushed hard and ran good people,” said Martinez. “Once those three people were out of the equation, this thing flew right by.” In 2022, organizers successfully put a state constitutional amendment on the ballot establishing a right to early childhood education funded by the land grant. A state law established universal early childcare earlier this year. Martinez said that New Mexico’s circumstances were sometimes viewed as exceptional: “Some people have pooh-poohed our idea because they say: ‘Well, not everybody has oil and gas.’ No, but everybody has poor people. You [need to] organize poor people in genuine ways.” Not all pro-universal childcare candidates are winning their races in the midterms. In Colorado and California, progressive candidates lost their primaries to incumbents and longtime local politicians. In New York, the lieutenant governor, Antonio Delgado, laid out a clear universal childcare vision for the state but lost to his competitor, incumbent Kathy Hochul, who had adopted a version of his plan after seeing Mamdani become New York City mayor on a similar platform. For organizers, affordable childcare is more than a winning platform and a goal in the current midterm cycle. “Childcare is having a moment,” said Helene Stebbins, executive director for the early childhood advocacy group Alliance for Early Success. “Let’s build it. Let’s solidify it. But let’s recognize that that’s not the solution, or the end, for building that infrastructure.”

In DC, parents and childcare providers protested after outgoing mayor Muriel Bowser cut early childhood educators’ pay and initiated an enrollment freeze in the city’s childcare-subsidy program for low-income families. “We coordinated the largest-ever day of early learning program closures in March – ‘a day without childcare’ – culminating in about 150 people rallying in subzero temperatures,” said Travis Ballie, executive director of the Under 3 DC coalition. “We did all that because this was existential – not just to preserve what we’d won, but because losing it would set us back.” Lewis George, the democratic socialist who won the Democratic primary for DC mayor in June, has heard voters’ concerns and promised to take a different tack. Her platform for “childcare for all” would build a subsidy toward universal affordable care on top of universal pre-K for all three- and four-year-olds in the district. “People don’t want to hear what government can’t do – they want to hear what government can do, how government will solve their problems,” said Lewis George. How one state won childcare for all New Mexico is perhaps the most-cited example of where the vision of universal childcare has been realized – and it took more than a decade of organizing to make happen. Before Javier Martinez was the speaker of the house in New Mexico, he was a community organizer helping immigrant families obtain driver’s licenses. “We’d look at this room full of little kids, and the parents themselves were saying: ‘It’s impossible to find childcare,’” he said. Immigration advocacy groups, such as New Mexico Voices for Children and Olé, led the charge for the state to pay for universal childcare in an innovative way: through a land grant funded by oil and gas revenue. In session after session, the legislature refused to hold a hearing on the issue, said Martinez. “I got to the point where, looking from the outside in, I thought: ‘Is this the best we can do as a legislature, as Democrats especially?’” he said. That’s when he decided to run for office in 2014. When the childcare plan remained stymied by three fiscally conservative Democratic state senators, organizers targeted their re-election in 2020. “Our coalition pushed hard and ran good people,” said Martinez. “Once those three people were out of the equation, this thing flew right by.” In 2022, organizers successfully put a state constitutional amendment on the ballot establishing a right to early childhood education funded by the land grant. A state law established universal early childcare earlier this year. Martinez said that New Mexico’s circumstances were sometimes viewed as exceptional: “Some people have pooh-poohed our idea because they say: ‘Well, not everybody has oil and gas.’ No, but everybody has poor people. You [need to] organize poor people in genuine ways.” Not all pro-universal childcare candidates are winning their races in the midterms. In Colorado and California, progressive candidates lost their primaries to incumbents and longtime local politicians. In New York, the lieutenant governor, Antonio Delgado, laid out a clear universal childcare vision for the state but lost to his competitor, incumbent Kathy Hochul, who had adopted a version of his plan after seeing Mamdani become New York City mayor on a similar platform. For organizers, affordable childcare is more than a winning platform and a goal in the current midterm cycle. “Childcare is having a moment,” said Helene Stebbins, executive director for the early childhood advocacy group Alliance for Early Success. “Let’s build it. Let’s solidify it. But let’s recognize that that’s not the solution, or the end, for building that infrastructure.”

title: Trump officials turned to AI and a mafia killer to bolster case, Comey lawyers allege
body_text: Lawyers for former FBI director James Comey alleged on Tuesday that US Secret Service agents illegally surveilled Comey, Donald Trump requested regular updates into the investigation, and law enforcement turned to ChatGPT and a known mafia killer as they scrambled to find justification for criminally charging Comey for posting a picture of seashells that spelled out “8647”. The claims were laid out in a motion to dismiss a criminal case the US Department of Justice filed against Comey in April, in which it said the post by Comey – whom Trump fired in his first term – was a threat on the US president’s life. In the motion filed on Tuesday in federal court in North Carolina, Comey’s lawyers said the case should be dismissed for vindictive and selective prosecution. “The government had initially investigated Mr Comey’s seashells post, but that investigation appeared to be going nowhere until Mr [Todd] Blanche and US attorney Ellis Boyle reinvigorated it,” Comey’s lawyers wrote. “The ensuing indictment is not based on a good-faith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a years-long campaign by the president to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the president’s deep-seated animosity.” Comey filed a separate motion earlier this week, seeking dismissal of the case on grounds that the post was protected speech and not a “true threat” against the president. Trump has long fumed over the way Comey handled the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while director of the FBI. Comey has also been an outspoken critic of Trump. The justice department indicted Comey last year in a separate case, claiming he had lied to US Congress. Those charges, which were seen as thin, were tossed out after a judge ruled the prosecutor handling them had been unlawfully appointed. Comey told investigators he came across the formation of shells while on vacation with his wife in eastern North Carolina in May 2025. The phrase “86” is often used as shorthand to get rid of something, while Trump is currently serving as the 47th US president, and Comey posted the photo to Instagram. Comey later deleted the photo, saying he didn’t know it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down.” Comey and his wife, Patrice, voluntarily spoke with Secret Service investigators after the incident. Internal Secret Service documents show that Trump was requesting updates on the investigation as it was ongoing. Even though Comey agreed to a voluntary interview in Washington, a Secret Service supervisor was asked about the possibility of tracking Comey’s phone on his drive back from Washington to North Carolina through an “exigency” request without a warrant. The supervisor said it was a “bad idea”, according to their notes that were attached to the motion. “To declare an exigency exemption, we needed to believe that there is an imminent threat to life or limb,” the supervisor wrote. “At that time we did not believe that anyone’s life was in immediate danger and legally it was a bad idea to ping the phone.” The supervisor wrote another agent agreed with him, but said the Secret Service might do it anyway. The next day, the supervisor wrote a note saying the “#3 guy at DOJ” wanted to ping the cellphone with an exigency request. The notes do not say the name of the official. Comey’s phone ultimately was tracked and the couple was also followed as they drove back from North Carolina, Patrick Fitzgerald, his attorney, said in a sworn affidavit. Documents included in the filing also lay out how law enforcement officials were unable to confirm that the term “86” was one that implied violence. Secret Service agents interviewed an unidentified person who knew the Comeys, but said they had not talked to them in several years and hoped the former FBI director went to jail. After telling agents they initially believed the term “86” meant something on a menu, they came to believe it was a violent threat after hearing Rudy Giuliani claim Comey had worked on cases where the term “86” meant kill. The FBI searched records related to the federal case against mobster John Gambino, which Comey handled when he was a federal prosecutor for references to “86”, according to the motion. There were no references to it. The FBI also conducted a broader search of all of its records going back decades for the term and the results were inconclusive. After the indictment was filed against Comey in April, Comey’s lawyers said, law enforcement officials were still hunting for evidence that Comey would have understood the term “86” to be a violent one. They interviewed two former FBI agents who worked on mafia cases, who said they were familiar with the term, but could not say definitively that it would have been used violently by the mafia. Agents also turned to ChatGPT and Google AI to search for meanings of the term “86”. Neither returned definitive results. Officials also interviewed Salvatore “Sammy The Bull” Gravano, a one-time underboss in the Gambino crime family, who confessed to nearly 20 murders, to try to build a case against Comey, the filing says. Gravano was a cooperating witness in the Gambino case Comey prosecuted. He told agents that while he believed it meant “to get rid of someone” he did not recall ever discussing the term with Comey, Comey’s lawyers said. Gravano, a podcaster who has praised Trump, told investigators that he interpreted Comey’s photo to mean “let’s kill Trump,” but he did not take it to mean Comey personally was going to kill Trump, Comey’s lawyers wrote.

title: Fauci invokes fifth amendment and declines to testify in Senate Covid hearing
body_text: Dr Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19 and accused the Republican senator leading questioning of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Fauci, the veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), served as a key adviser to Donald Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic. The hearing was called by Kentucky senator Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years. Fauci said Paul’s goal was “embarrassing and intimidating me”, and ultimately landing him “behind bars”. “Therefore, although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said in his opening statement. Paul, frustrated, later told reporters that he would hold a vote to hold Fauci in contempt of US Congress next week, and described the question of whether the fifth amendment could shield him as “a question for the courts”. Fauci, 85, served under seven US presidents and through numerous health crises, including the HIV crisis, Ebola outbreaks and the first coronavirus outbreak, called Sars-CoV-1. He became a household name overnight when the Covid-19 pandemic halted social life in 2020. Quickly after opening statements, the hearing became a back-and-forth between Paul and Fauci. Paul grew visibly agitated as Fauci refused to answer, threatened the scientists with “repercussions”, and then tossed one of Fauci’s attorneys from the hearing room. “Did the [National Institutes of Health] ever fund gain-of-function [research] on monkeypox?” Paul asked, in reference to research that manipulates viruses to make them more effective to shed light on how outbreaks happen. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” said Fauci. After another description of research Paul found unacceptable: “Dr Fauci, did the NIH ever conduct research for or in coordination with any element of the intelligence community, CIA, [Office of the Director of National Intelligence]?” Fauci responded: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.” Paul pressed on: “Dr Fauci, would you at least like to answer this one question for us today, and let us know whether or not you have changed your mind on whether or not the benefits of gain-of-function [research] outweigh the risks?” Fauci replied: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.” A visibly frustrated Paul soon scolded Fauci: “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.” Soon, an attorney for Fauci attempted to join him at the table, and Paul demanded the attorney move. “This is not a game with his lawyers,” said Paul, to the attorney who was apparently trying to speak, but could not be heard for lack of a microphone. “The attorneys were not recognized.” “There’s a row behind you, sir,” said Paul. “This is the way Anthony Fauci wants to be remembered – for a lawyer not recognizing the rules … Security please remove him from the room,” Paul said. The attorney patted Fauci on the shoulder and voluntarily left, alongside a guard. Members of the audience, which conspicuously included rightwing media figure Laura Ingraham, applauded. In part, Paul’s frustration at the hearing stemmed from a presidential pardon Fauci received from Biden, which in turn implicates the fifth amendment. There is debate among experts about how far the fifth amendment extends. Some argue that once a person accepts a presidential pardon, they cannot invoke the fifth amendment for federal crimes. Without that right, Congress could hold a witness in contempt, which can lead to fines or – in the extreme – jail time. Others have argued that the right extends as long as there is a valid threat of prosecution, particularly by states. “You don’t have any rights under the fifth amendment,” claimed Josh Hawley, a Republican senator of Missouri, in a line of accusatory questioning. “This is about contempt – contempt for this body, and contempt for the American people.” Democrats, meanwhile, defended Fauci. Paul is “single-mindedly fixated on seeing Dr Fauci prosecuted for imaginary crimes, and you are so invested in that outcome you have created a personal brand around it”, Fauci’s attorneys argued in a statement read aloud by the Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, of Connecticut. Ahead of the hearing, Republicans characterized their work as investigating “the origins of Covid-19 and risky taxpayer-funded life science research”, while scientists have characterized the investigation as “vilification and harassment” of Fauci, who led Niaid for 38 years before retiring in 2022. Indeed, Republican senator Bernie Moreno took the opportunity to demand Fauci apologize for a military policy that required service members to take the Covid-19 vaccine, to Americans who lost businesses during the pandemic and to a single Ohio mother who was arrested for not wearing a mask during an outdoor football game early in the pandemic. The senator called Fauci a “total and complete disgrace”. Ron Johnson, a Republican senator of Wisconsin, used the hearing to call the Covid-19 vaccine, credited by scientists with saving millions of lives, an “experimental gene therapy”. He also accused Fauci of “lying” to his own diary, which elicited a smirk from Fauci. The hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the “lab leak” theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, a theory many virologists contend is improbable. “For years, Americans were told a lab origin wasn’t just unlikely – it was dismissed outright by the very people funding and reviewing this research,” Paul, who chairs the Senate committee on homeland security and governmental affairs, where Fauci testified, said last week. Paul has argued that Fauci lied about the origins of the pandemic to shield his own culpability, because the NIH funded the lab in Wuhan through a sub-grant. Paul argued Fauci lied about the origins of the pandemic because, as Paul later hypothesized to reporters: “Holy you know what – if it came from the lab, If I funded the lab, I could be responsible for this entire pandemic.” The “lab leak” theory has gained significant traction in Republican circles since political opinion on the pandemic began to fracture. In just one example, the White House published a treatise on the theory in April 2025 that served as a rationale for defunding the National Institutes of Health (NIH). The theory in part impugns gain-of-function research, in which scientists seek to develop better vaccines by working with potentially dangerous pathogens. A 2024 survey of virologists from the Global Catastrophic Risk Institute found that most believed the pandemic began as a so-called spillover event, or a virus jumping from an infected animal to a human. Similarly, a group of virologists argued in the Journal of Virology that the “preponderance” of evidence points to a natural origin, that the “lab leak” theory received outsized attention and that, ultimately, the origin may never be known. Gain-of-function research, meanwhile, has split the scientific community for years. The scheduled hearing comes just days after Paul released what he described as Fauci’s “diary”, a more than 1,100-page document characterized as revealing Fauci’s inner conflicts about the lab leak theory. Scientists have said this is a normal part of scientific debate. The diary also contained entries about Trump, who he advised closely during the early days of the pandemic. He described the president as “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”. Gary Peters, a Democratic senator of Michigan, described the hearing as damaging to science and ignoring ongoing public health threats, such as the outbreak of the food-borne parasite cyclospora and measles, both at record highs. “It’s attempting to turn one person into a scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across the Biden and Trump administrations were responsible for handling,” said Peters, who did not ask Fauci any questions. “This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service.”

title: Anthony Fauci’s high-profile Senate hearing: what we learned
body_text: A US Senate committee hearing featuring Dr Anthony Fauci revealed at least one certainty: six years after the pandemic, politicizing science remains a vital political tactic. The high-profile hearing was pitched by its Republican chair, Rand Paul of Kentucky, as an investigation into the origins of the Covid pandemic. It quickly became a forum for recrimination of a once-leading US government scientist by Republican senators. Fauci, a career civil servant who spent 38 years at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (Niaid), declined throughout the hearing to answer questions. Here are five takeaways from Wednesday’s hearing. Rand Paul’s ‘unhinged obsession’ with Fauci The hearing was centered around an assertion Paul has promoted for years: that the Covid pandemic began in 2020 as a “leak” from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, even as virologists see a natural jump from animals to humans as more likely. This belief underpinned Paul’s argument for bringing Fauci before the committee. If the pandemic was indeed started by a “lab leak”, Fauci “could be responsible for this entire pandemic” because the National Institutes of Health (NIH) provided the institute with a sub-grant, he later told reporters. His only witness was Fauci, who served as a key adviser to Trump and Joe Biden during the pandemic, and has become a political punching bag on the right. Paul has interrogated Fauci in the past. Fauci appeared at Senate hearings at least a dozen times, according to his attorneys, and answered lawmakers’ questions. Fauci described Paul’s investigation as an “unhinged obsession” with seeing him “behind bars”, and one that had led to starkly different advice from his attorneys this time around. “Although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” said Fauci. Paul appeared to know Fauci would do this. The senator had a copy of a law which he claimed compelled Fauci to testify ready to hand to him. Criticism of scientists continues Scientists have not witnessed Fauci’s compelled testimony – he only appeared on Capitol Hill on Wednesday under subpoena – without dissent. A group of 155 scientists wrote an open letter calling for the government to stop the “vilification and harassment of many American scientists”. “The charges against Dr Fauci are baseless, suggesting he covered up the origins of Covid, that he bribed or persuaded other scientists to join his cover-up, that Niaid-funded research sparked the pandemic, that he personally holds patents on the virus, and that he’s working with intelligence agencies to suppress the true story of the pandemic,” the letter stated. “No credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges.” Paul’s frustration with fifth amendment Whether or not Fauci can successfully invoke the fifth amendment of the US constitution – which allows Americans to decline to answer questions that could incriminate them, without repercussions – became a part of the hearing itself. Fauci received a presidential pardon before Biden left office. Recent presidential pardons from Trump and Biden have led to renewed debate about whether the amendment can be invoked when a witness appears before federal lawmakers post-pardon. Visibly frustrated by Fauci’s assertions, Paul told him: “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.” Later, Paul told reporters he intends to call a vote for contempt of Congress next week, in the committee on homeland security and security and governmental affairs where Fauci appeared. His Republican colleague, Josh Hawley of Missouri, later joined in. “You don’t have any rights under the fifth amendment,” he said. “This is about contempt: contempt for this body and contempt for the American people.” Republican criticism of Fauci wide-ranging Republicans lined up to attack Fauci. The Wisconsin senator Ron Johnson accused him of covering up unfavorable information about Covid vaccines, which he described as “experimental gene therapy”, even after scientists credited them with saving millions of lives. The Republican senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio demanded Fauci apologize for a military policy that required service members to take the Covid vaccine, to Americans who lost businesses during the pandemic, and to a single Ohio mother who was arrested for not wearing a mask during an outdoor football game early in the pandemic. The senator called Fauci a “total and complete disgrace”. The Republican Joni Ernst of Iowa criticized use of aborted fetal tissue in research. The Democratic senator Gary Peters of Michigan argued the hearing was an attempt to “turn one person into a scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across the Biden and Trump administrations’ were responsible for handling”, warning: “This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service.” Criticizing science important for Republicans The Trump administration has invoked the “lab leak” theory to criticize past pandemic policies – even as the party has asserted that the end of the pandemic justified cutting $11.4bn state and local health department funding. Canceling grants based on political priorities, trialled at the National Institutes of Health in 2025, are now the basis of a proposed rule that would bring the $1tn entire federal grant-making apparatus under the control of political appointees. title: Trump’s pick for US attorney general Todd Blanche in jeopardy as vote postponed
body_text: Todd Blanche’s hopes of becoming US attorney general seemed to be in jeopardy on Wednesday after the Department of Justice did not provide written assurances to a key Republican senator that a $1.8bn slush fund was dead. The US Senate judiciary committee postponed a vote scheduled for Thursday on whether to advance Blanche’s nomination. “Chairman [Chuck] Grassley works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure. Senators [John] Cornyn and [Thom] Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement,” a committee spokesperson said in a Wednesday statement. “Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.” Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, is already serving as acting US attorney general. He needs the vote of every Republican on the Senate judiciary panel to advance his nomination to land the role on a permanent basis. But a swing vote on the committee, John Cornyn of Texas, told reporters on Wednesday he would not support Blanche’s nomination until he received written confirmation that the fund was not moving ahead. Cornyn also wants to clarify that a provision giving the president, his sons and related businesses blanket immunity from tax audits for all matters up until this year could not be applied to future matters, or to people who were not parties to the settlement. “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or, you know, go along, but they’re mistaken,” said Cornyn, a four-term Republican senator who lost a re-election bid earlier this year to a Trump-endorsed rival. “We actually sent them a red-line strikeout of what we need, and they just need to make a decision. And if they do, then we’ll proceed with the markup tomorrow.” The US federal government reached the agreement to resolve a $10bn lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS over the unauthorized leak of his tax returns. The deal created a $1.8bn loosely controlled fund to compensate people who say they are victims of government weaponization and gave Trump, his family and businesses blanket immunity from audits for anything filed until the agreement was reached. The agreement immediately faced bipartisan scrutiny and outrage. The justice department did not make any effort to defend itself from the lawsuit, prompting a federal judge overseeing the case to conclude the case was brought with an “improper purpose”. Under pressure, Blanche announced in June that the department was scrapping the “anti-weaponization” fund, but has repeatedly declined to say so in writing. Pressed by Cornyn during his confirmation hearing, Blanche acknowledged that Trump or the other plaintiffs in the case could try to enforce the settlement agreement. He also did not say the tax immunity provision was dead.

title: Anthony Fauci’s diaries take aim at News Corp journalist Sharri Markson’s ‘nonsense’ Covid-19 investigation
body_text: Dr Anthony Fauci, the US’s chief medical adviser at the start of the pandemic, has described a book by News Corp investigative journalist Sharri Markson backing the “lab leak” theory of Covid-19’s origins as a “bunch of nonsense” in his newly released diaries. This week, Fauci, 85, was subpoenaed by the Republican senator Rand Paul to appear at a Senate hearing into Covid-19 and his handling of the pandemic. The physician and veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, who retired in 2022, accused Paul of an “unhinged” campaign lobbying for his imprisonment and refused to answer questions at Wednesday’s hearing. The hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the lab leak theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Ahead of his appearance, Paul published 1,141 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era journal entries. In the entries, Fauci criticised reporting in The Australian newspaper and a book by Markson that claimed a facility in Wuhan was “immersed in genetically manipulating bat-coronaviruses in perilous experiments”. On 7 May 2021, Markson reported in The Australian that Chinese military scientists “discussed the weaponisation of Sars coronaviruses five years before the Covid-19 pandemic” and predicted a third world war would be fought with biological weapons. Fauci, who served under seven US presidents but became a household name overnight in 2020, wrote in his private diary that the article “does not make any sense”. “Why would someone want to make an agent that could equally infect your own population. Something is wrong with this report. I will have to follow up on it,” he wrote. Guardian Australia later found the “chilling” document produced by Chinese military scientists in the article was based on a discredited 2015 book containing conspiracy theories about biological warfare which is freely available on the internet. Markson’s story was criticised as misleading and alarmist by China analysts. A deputy editor of Foreign Policy magazine and China expert, James Palmer, said the article had links to conspiracy theories about the origins of the coronavirus which are popular with the political right. The story was published to promote Markson’s debut book, What Really Happened in Wuhan, which argued there was “no scientific consensus that Covid-19 has a natural origin” and that China had conspired to cover up the truth. Fauci also took aim at Markson’s book, writing in his diary that “the same old crap is going on with the far right continuing to attack me”. “The latest written by an Australian person who says I’m the father of gain of function research quotes from the infamous Richard Ebright saying that I’m a liar and I have misled everybody about gain of function,” he wrote. “What a bunch of nonsense! The far right continues to try and discredit me.” Ebright is an American molecular biologist and proponent of the lab leak theory. Markson told Guardian Australia “the majority of the intelligence community now concludes that Covid-19 likely originated in a Wuhan laboratory”. “I led the way internationally exposing the role of Anthony Fauci’s agency funding 65 projects at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, funnelling the money through EcoHealth Alliance,” she said on Thursday. The origins of the Covid-19 pandemic remain the subject of intense debate among scientists and the wider public. There are two competing theories – the natural-origins hypotheses, which suggests the pandemic began when a close relative of Sars-CoV-2 jumped from a wild animal to a human through the wildlife trade, and lab leak theories, which argue that the virus emerged when Chinese scientists became infected through research-associated activities. News Corp was approached for comment.

title: US economy grows sluggish 1.5% in second quarter as inflation tops Fed target
body_text: The US economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5% pace from April through June as rising imports weighed on growth. But consumer spending rose. And the Federal Reserve’s favored measure of inflation grew more slowly last month despite remaining above the central bank’s 2% target. The commerce department reported on Thursday that growth in US gross domestic product (GDP) – the nation’s output of goods and services – decelerated from 2.1% in the first three months of 2026 and came in below economists’ expectations. The commerce department also said on Thursday that its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the measure of inflation favored by the Fed, rose 3.7% last month from June 2025 , down from a 4.1% year-over-year increase in May. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, so-called core consumer prices were up 3.3% from a year earlier, little changed from a 3.4% increase in May. The latest data paints a clearer picture of the effects the war in the Middle East has had on the economy after increasing energy prices and pushing inflation higher. The first GDP reading of this year captured the effects of just a month of war, but indicated that consumer spending was starting to slow as prices started to creep up. Oil prices have come down from their wartime high, and took a sharp downturn when the US and Iran announced a peace deal. But when that deal collapsed and the two countries began trading strikes again, oil prices climbed and still remain much higher than prewar levels. The pressure is growing within the Fed to raise interest rates in order to combat heightened inflation, which Kevin Warsh, the central bank’s chair, has acknowledged has remained too high for years. Though the Fed on Wednesday chose to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the fifth straight meeting, three regional Fed presidents dissented, saying they wanted to raise rates to combat elevated inflation. It was the first time in a decade so many Fed officials had dissented in the same direction over a policy vote. Higher costs have frustrated Americans ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine whether Donald Trump’s Republicans keep full control of Congress. Two-thirds of Americans, including 49% of Republicans, say they have little faith the federal government will address the high prices they face, according to a Harris Poll survey released earlier this month. Still, the US economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of the Iran war and the spike in energy prices it caused. The job market has bounced back this year from a lackluster 2025, giving consumers the wherewithal to spend. Employers are adding an average 92,000 jobs a month this year, compared with fewer than 10,000 a month in 2025 when high interest rates and Trump’s erratic use of tariffs discouraged businesses from hiring. Thursday’s GDP report was the first of three commerce department estimates of second quarter economic growth. The Associated Press contributed reporting
