title: Three-quarters of Americans think Trump isn’t focusing on top US issues – poll
body_text: Three-quarters of Americans believe Donald Trump is not paying enough attention to the country’s most important problems, and two-thirds think he places himself above the needs of the US, according to a new poll. The CNN survey, conducted by the market research company SSRS, comes less than 100 days before November’s midterm elections in which the president’s Republican party is widely expected to lose control of one or both chambers of Congress. Trump’s overall approval rating has slumped to 34%, the poll found, matching his previous lowest immediately following the 6 January 2021 insurrection he incited trying to cling on to power after losing the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden. The figure reflects growing dismay at the ongoing war in Iran – only 28% approve of Trump’s actions there, and even fewer, 25%, say the conflict has been worth it in terms of cost and American lives lost; meanwhile, the war’s effects at home are also causing disquiet, with 74% saying rising gas prices have caused at least some hardship, up from 63% in March. In the parallel poll a year ago, 58% of respondents said Trump had not gone far enough in trying to reduce the price of everyday goods, a figure that has climbed to 71% this week. Even Trump’s hardline immigration policies, previously a bright spot for his approval ratings, are dragging the president down. Only 39% believe he is doing a good job, and 54% say he has gone too far in mass deporting undocumented immigrants. Overwhelmingly, Americans are outraged by Trump stamping his personality on the presidency. His pursuit of a taxpayer-funded White House ballroom, botched renovation of the Washington DC reflecting pool, and plans for a self-aggrandizing ceremonial arch, have left only 17% feeling positive. In direct contrast, asked if Trump was in touch with problems Americans face in their everyday lives, 73% said no. Only 38% of those polled consider him to be an effective world leader; and 57% say the 80-year-old president lacks the stamina and sharpness to serve effectively.

title: Trump says he may ‘temporarily’ drop bid to make Blanche US attorney general
body_text: Donald Trump said on Thursday he may “temporarily” pull the nomination of Todd Blanche to serve as attorney general, but would keep him in the role in an acting capacity until two Republican senators objecting to his confirmation leave office next year – an extraordinary escalation of an intra-party fight over an agreement to create a $1.8bn slush fund and give the president tax immunity. Two Republican senators – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – have refused to back Blanche’s nomination until they receive written confirmation from the justice department that it is not moving forward with a widely criticized agreement creating a $1.8bn fund to compensate people claiming they were targets of political weaponization and granting the president, his family and business entities broad immunity from past tax investigations. Blanche has already said publicly that the payout fund to compensate victims of so-called government weaponization is not moving forward amid bipartisan backlash. But Cornyn and Tillis had sought assurances in writing, something Blanche has refused to do. Cornyn also sought to clarify the terms of the tax immunity portion of the agreement. The Senate judiciary committee canceled a vote on Blanche’s confirmation scheduled for Thursday when it became clear he did not have the votes to advance. The two senators – who are both leaving Congress in January – appeared to be negotiating language with the justice department on Wednesday. On Thursday, Trump blasted Cornyn and Tillis and vowed that he would instead keep Blanche, the president’s former personal lawyer, as the acting attorney general – a role he has held since April, when Trump fired Pam Bondi. Federal law allows the deputy attorney general – Blanche’s role under Bondi – to serve indefinitely as the acting attorney general until a successor is confirmed. “John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Trump posted. Cornyn, who lost his re-election bid to a Trump-endorsed rival, responded by saying: “POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis.” The fate of Blanche’s possible confirmation remains unclear. Cornyn met with Blanche on Thursday, according to a source familiar with the matter. The Texas senator and Tillis were reportedly close to a deal to advance Blanche’s nomination. Tillis, who is not seeking re-election after repeated clashes with Trump, told reporters on Capitol Hill: “It makes no sense to me. This is not popular.” “The president’s not winning on this issue,” he continued. “It is killing some of our candidates because they can’t explain it. And now it looks like they weren’t being honest when they said it was inoperative.” Earlier on Thursday, both Cornyn and Tillis had expressed a willingness to vote for Blanche. “If this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out, but, apparently, he’s getting some pushback from higher-ups at the White House. I don’t know who, but it doesn’t need to be this hard,” Cornyn said on Capitol Hill. The agreement was reached as part of a settlement in a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS over the unauthorized leak of his tax returns. A federal judge who oversaw the lawsuit blasted the arrangement, noting that the justice department did not make a good faith effort to defend the government and that it appeared to be a collusive effort to engineer a beneficial result on behalf of the president. Blanche needs the vote of every Republican on the Senate judiciary committee, including Cornyn and Tillis, to advance his nomination to land the role on a permanent basis. Anna Betts contributed reporting

title: Fifa could draw US Congress inquiry over ‘smash-and-grab scam’, top Democrat warns
body_text: Fifa could face a sweeping US congressional investigation into its expanding financial and political ties to Donald Trump and his family if Democrats reclaim the House of Representatives in November, a senior party figure has warned. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, accused global football’s governing body of a “smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions” after it proposed a multibillion-dollar privatization of its commercial operations. Raskin, a Democratic representative of Maryland, would become the judiciary committee’s chair under a Democratic House majority, vowed to make Fifa an early target of scrutiny – and accused the organization of embedding itself in what he described as a pattern of corruption surrounding Trump’s second administration and the Kushner family. “Over the last few weeks, Fifa’s cozy relationship to Donald Trump has been floating to the top of the swamp of quid pro quo corruption in which the Trump Administration is swimming,” Raskin said in a statement to the Guardian. “But now we see where all the bribes, kickbacks and sweetheart deals have been leading.” Raskin’s comments follow plans of the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to pursue a spin-off of the organization’s commercial business into a standalone company, reportedly valued at about $20bn. JPMorgan Chase is leading the fundraising effort, with Thrive Eternal, an investment vehicle linked to the Thrive Capital founder, Joshua Kushner, among the prospective investors. Joshua Kushner is the brother of Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a high-level White House adviser. The proposal has sparked an immediate backlash across world football, and beyond. Uefa, the European football governing body, has warned that “none of us are the owners of football”, and on Thursday voted to boycott the World Cup if Fifa presses ahead. The inquiry also follows a series of similarly scandalous controversies surrounding Fifa’s relationship with the Trump administration. The organization invented its first-ever “peace prize”, which they awarded to Trump in December, weeks after he publicly complained about missing out on the Nobel peace prize. During this summer’s World Cup, Uefa accused Fifa of undermining the tournament’s integrity after officials reversed a red card issued to the US forward Folarin Balogun following a call from Trump to Infantino. Separately, the US Department of Justice dropped the long-running bribery and money-laundering cases tied to the Fifa corruption scandal after prosecutors said they no longer fit the administration’s enforcement priorities. Should Democrats – who lack the legal power to demand that witnesses appear under the current Republican House majority – win control of the chamber in November’s US midterm elections, Raskin would have the authority to compel testimony and documents from Fifa, JPMorgan and entities connected to the Kushner family’s investment vehicles. “Fifa needs to cooperate in good faith now,” he added. “If and when Democrats take the House, this Committee will have the tools we need to get answers, expose corruption, protect sports fans against exorbitant and fraudulent charges and block this attempt to turn world soccer into a global financial shakedown.” The White House has previously dismissed similar allegations as politically motivated. Fifa did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The judiciary committee minority under Raskin has already requested records from Fifa, including documents related to gifts provided to Trump, communications with the justice department, and visitor logs for Fifa’s Miami headquarters and its Trump Tower office. “Fifa appears to have struck a several hundred-billion-dollar deal orchestrated by Jared Kushner’s brother and JPMorgan to privatize Fifa’s business operations so private equity, hedge funds, autocrats, kleptocrats and large investors can come to own and control the world’s most beautiful game,” Raskin said. “The United States is set to host the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and we have a responsibility to ensure Fifa will not again bring its own brand of corrupt pay-to-play politics and exploitation onto our soil,” he added.

title: Republican congressman Max Miller faces backlash over domestic abuse allegations
body_text: The Ohio representative Max Miller is facing growing pressure to resign over a series of domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife and former girlfriend. The Republican congressman, 37, who represents Ohio’s seventh congressional district, has denied accusations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and former girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, as he campaigns for re-election. Moreno, a conservative policy adviser, shares a two-year-old daughter with Miller. The pair have been engaged in a legal battle over custody of their child since 2024. In one alleged incident, Miller “took hot water from a pan he had just cooked eggs in and threw it at me”, Moreno testified earlier this year amid a defamation lawsuit Miller filed against her. Moreno has also accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, the New York Times reported. The pair married in 2022. In addition, Moreno alleged that Miller “regularly speaks to me in an inappropriate, aggressive and demeaning manner, which is not in the best interest of our child”. A prominent anti-gun-violence group has called for Miller’s resignation after Moreno alleged he had held a gun to her head. Responding to Moreno’s allegations, Miller told Spectrum News in June: “They’re false allegations. Our divorce was finalized on December 18 in 2025. No police reports were ever filed.” In May, Miller also claimed on X that Moreno’s father, the Republican US senator for Ohio Bernie Moreno, “continues to fund and enable his daughter’s malicious campaign to ruin my life despite his knowledge of her mental health issues”, adding: “These antics harm your own grandchild.” In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson for Bernie Moreno said: “Senator Moreno’s top priority is the safety and well-being of his daughter and granddaughter … While he will not litigate these matters in the media or respond to baseless public attacks, he will do whatever it takes to ensure a just outcome for his family.” Separately, Miller’s former girlfriend Grisham, who served as White House press secretary during Donald Trump’s first administration, has also accused him of abuse, an allegation he has denied. Grisham and Miller dated from 2019 to 2020. In a 2021 Washington Post op-ed, Grisham – without naming Miller – wrote about a relationship that “turned abusive”, and of a former partner who was “physical” with her. Although she did not identify Miller in the article, he said it was widely understood that the op-ed referred to him. She later confirmed she was talking about Miller, according to the Times. Miller subsequently sued Grisham for defamation before later dropping the lawsuit as part of a confidential settlement agreement. Grisham has since filed a new lawsuit against Miller, alleging that he violated the confidential settlement through comments he made to Spectrum News. In his June interview with Spectrum News, Miller said: “What should be noted is [Grisham’s] allegation came out on the same day as somebody’s book launch. And the other part, what I would like to discuss, is my ex-wife was with me every single day during that time of my life in that election, and she, in her own words, will tell you that I never did any of those things.” The Guardian has reached out to Miller’s campaign and office for comment. Miller himself described a New York Times reporter as “disgusting” when approached for comment earlier this month. In a statement to the New York Times, Miller’s Democratic rival for Ohio’s seventh congressional district, Brian Poindexter, said: “If the allegations prove to be true … Miller should be in jail, not worried about retaining a seat in Congress.” The Guardian has reached out to Poindexter for additional comment. He trailed Miller by a single point in a June survey. Giffords, the national gun violence prevention group founded by former House representative Gabrielle Giffords, called on Wednesday for Miller’s resignation. “Congress is no place for violent abusers who attack their family and hold a gun to their wife’s head. Max Miller needs to resign now – and if he refuses, the House should expel him,” the group’s executive director, Emma Brown, said of the allegations. Brown continued: “If Republicans in Congress use their power to shield dangerous abusers from consequences, it will give voters yet another reason to take away their majority this November.”

title: US Senate rejects bid to rein in Trump’s authority over Iran war
body_text: The US Senate on Thursday rejected a largely symbolic effort to limit Donald Trump’s authority to wage war in Iran, amid rising regional tensions after the US conducted a “heavy wave” of retaliatory airstrikes. The war powers resolution failed in a 49-50 vote, marking the second time in two weeks the chamber has taken up legislation aimed at forcing Trump to end hostilities. The US military said it launched a fresh wave of airstrikes in Iran on Wednesday, in retaliation for an Iranian missile attack targeting a US base in Jordan. The exchange marked an escalation in the Iran war, following the collapse of a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran. The Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman voted with Republicans to sink the measure, the only Democrat to do so. The Republican senators Susan Collins, of Maine, Lisa Murkowski, of Alaska, and Rand Paul, of Kentucky, crossed the aisle to vote in favor of the motion, which would have directed Trump to withdraw US forces from hostilities with Iran absent explicit congressional authorization. Mitch McConnell was absent for the vote as he continues to recover from a fall in June and has not received medical clearance to return to work. The vote is the latest sign of eroding patience with a conflict that has now stretched more than five months, far beyond the “four to five weeks” Trump predicted when he co-launched the war with Israel against Iran on 28 February, killing the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. The often twisty aim has been to prevent Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and to curb its support for militant proxies across the Middle East, though under its new leadership the regime seems more inclined to pursue a bomb than ever before. Iran responded by striking US bases and allied targets across the Gulf region and by disrupting oil traffic through the strait of Hormuz, triggering a global energy shock. A ceasefire brokered in June collapsed within weeks, and fighting resumed with a nearly two-week escalation in July before a renewed pause. At least 18 US service members have so far been killed in the conflict and more than 450 wounded, according to Pentagon figures, which Democratic lawmakers have questioned over a lack of transparency. Four of those deaths came within a 48-hour span in mid-July, when service members were killed in an attack at Muwaffaq Salti air base in Jordan. Thousands of Iranian civilians and combatants are estimated to have died. The Pentagon has told Congress it needs roughly $80bn more to sustain the war effort, on top of the more than $37bn already spent. The Senate approved a war powers resolution for the first time in late June, in a 50-48 vote that saw Collins, Paul, Murkowski and Louisiana’s Bill Cassidy break with their party. Trump confronted the defecting Republicans at the Capitol the next day, and Paul and Cassidy both reversed their votes within 24 hours, allowing the Senate to kill a nearly identical measure by a similarly narrow margin. Since then, the chamber has rejected the legislation repeatedly. The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, noted after one earlier defeat that a growing number of Republicans had nonetheless broken ranks over the course of the war. The House, unlike the Senate, has twice passed its own symbolic resolution calling on Trump to end the war, most recently by 214-208 in late July, with a handful of Republicans joining Democrats. Because the House measure is a concurrent resolution rather than a joint one, it does not carry the force of law and would not go to Trump’s desk even if the Senate followed suit. The Trump administration has separately argued that the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which set out Congress’s authority to check presidential military action, is itself unconstitutional. The scale of the political problem for Trump was underscored by a new poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, released on Thursday. About two-thirds of US adults said the war has not been worthwhile, versus 33% who said it was worth fighting. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as roughly 37% of Republicans. Ahead of Thursday’s vote, the senator Kirsten Gillibrand, of New York, urged colleagues to back the resolution, arguing that the war was straining household budgets and that Congress held the constitutional authority to end it immediately. “This reckless war is driving up monthly bills and making everyday life harder for working families,” she said. “Under the constitution, we have the power to end the war today – let’s use it!”

title: Trump’s tax immunity scheme hoists president by his own petard on Blanche AG nomination
body_text: Donald Trump’s refusal to officially end a hugely controversial agreement giving him broad tax immunity and creating a $1.8bn slush fund underscored how the US president’s own self-interest takes precedence above all else in his government. For weeks, Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, has said that the slush fund portion of the agreement was dead. And for a few brief hours on Wednesday, it seemed that the president might agree to a relatively modest request from two Republican senators to put in writing that there were certain limits on an extraordinary tax immunity deal. After all, it seemed like a small price to pay in exchange for getting Blanche, a staunch Trump loyalist who previously served as his personal lawyer, confirmed permanently as the US attorney general. The agreement was part of a deal between Trump and the government to end a lawsuit seeking $10bn in damages for the unauthorized disclosure of the president’s tax records. A federal judge overseeing the case harshly criticized the government earlier this month, noting the government did not make a serious attempt to defend itself in the case and it seemed to be an effort to engineer a favorable result for the president. As negotiations wore into Thursday, the two Republican holdouts, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, signaled they were ready to support Blanche. “If this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out, but, apparently, he’s getting some pushback from higher-ups at the White House. I don’t know who, but it doesn’t need to be this hard,” Cornyn said on Capitol Hill. “I don’t know who it is – I’m just trying to get them out of the way so we can get the president his AG,” Tillis told Punchbowl News. But as reports of negotiations continued into the morning, Trump left little doubt who the one holding up the negotiations was. “John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” Trump posted on Truth Social a little before noon on Thursday. “Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.” It was not immediately clear if a confirmation vote for Blanche was off the table. Both Cornyn and Tillis met with Blanche late on Thursday afternoon and were reportedly close to reaching a resolution. In the immediate future, there is no penalty for Trump or Blanche in blowing up the negotiations. Under federal law, Blanche, who was confirmed by the Senate to be the deputy attorney general, can continue serving as the acting attorney general indefinitely. In some sense, the episode was a vindication of the power of Congress and an illustration of the immense sway even one or two Republicans can have when they push back on the president. Trump’s ultimate position also underscored how unwilling he is to concede anything to political rivals – he has openly feuded with Cornyn and Tillis – even if it means sacrificing a political achievement. The White House declined to comment. “Refer you to the TRUTH,” a spokesperson said. One does not have to look very far to understand why Trump would be unwilling to cede any ground on the agreement. One IRS audit could have cost the president $100m, according to the New York Times. So it’s easy to understand why Trump would want the tax provision in the agreement – which grants him, his family, and businesses or related entities immunity from audits for any matter until the agreement was reached. Cornyn reportedly sought to get Blanche to put in writing the agreement that clarified the exemption only applied to the named plaintiffs in the case, exclusively applied to the IRS, and was only about past tax returns. Even under those conditions, Trump still could have benefited tremendously. Under the settlement agreement, Trump and his sons were prohibited from making a claim on the slush fund. Blanche has been publicly adamant that the fund is not moving forward, though he conceded during his confirmation hearing that the plaintiffs in the case could theoretically try and push to enforce it. Trump’s refusal to formalize the end of the fund leaves open the possibility he could try to do it. Trump also seemed to be making a gamble that any resistance to confirming Blanche would disappear after the midterm elections. Cornyn suggested on Thursday that was not going to happen. “POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis,” he posted on X. Anna Betts contributed reporting

I don’t know who, but it doesn’t need to be this hard,” Cornyn said on Capitol Hill. “I don’t know who it is – I’m just trying to get them out of the way so we can get the president his AG,” Tillis told Punchbowl News. But as reports of negotiations continued into the morning, Trump left little doubt who the one holding up the negotiations was. “John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” Trump posted on Truth Social a little before noon on Thursday. “Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.” It was not immediately clear if a confirmation vote for Blanche was off the table. Both Cornyn and Tillis met with Blanche late on Thursday afternoon and were reportedly close to reaching a resolution. In the immediate future, there is no penalty for Trump or Blanche in blowing up the negotiations. Under federal law, Blanche, who was confirmed by the Senate to be the deputy attorney general, can continue serving as the acting attorney general indefinitely. In some sense, the episode was a vindication of the power of Congress and an illustration of the immense sway even one or two Republicans can have when they push back on the president. Trump’s ultimate position also underscored how unwilling he is to concede anything to political rivals – he has openly feuded with Cornyn and Tillis – even if it means sacrificing a political achievement. The White House declined to comment. “Refer you to the TRUTH,” a spokesperson said. One does not have to look very far to understand why Trump would be unwilling to cede any ground on the agreement. One IRS audit could have cost the president $100m, according to the New York Times. So it’s easy to understand why Trump would want the tax provision in the agreement – which grants him, his family, and businesses or related entities immunity from audits for any matter until the agreement was reached. Cornyn reportedly sought to get Blanche to put in writing the agreement that clarified the exemption only applied to the named plaintiffs in the case, exclusively applied to the IRS, and was only about past tax returns. Even under those conditions, Trump still could have benefited tremendously. Under the settlement agreement, Trump and his sons were prohibited from making a claim on the slush fund. Blanche has been publicly adamant that the fund is not moving forward, though he conceded during his confirmation hearing that the plaintiffs in the case could theoretically try and push to enforce it. Trump’s refusal to formalize the end of the fund leaves open the possibility he could try to do it. Trump also seemed to be making a gamble that any resistance to confirming Blanche would disappear after the midterm elections. Cornyn suggested on Thursday that was not going to happen. “POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis,” he posted on X. Anna Betts contributed reporting

title: Senators accuse Republican ‘gelatinous blobs’ of caving to Trump on Iran war
body_text: Senior Democrats accused Republicans in the US Congress of becoming “gelatinous blobs” who won’t stand up to Donald Trump and “rubber stamps” for his war on Iran. Elizabeth Warren, a US senator for Massachusetts, and Chris Van Hollen, a US senator for Maryland, argued that the Republican-controlled Congress had surrendered its constitutional authority to the president. In interviews with the Guardian, the senators urged their Republican colleagues to stand with Democrats and assert Congress’s authority as a separate branch of the federal government – with power over declaring war. “The Republicans have all had their spines surgically removed,” Warren said in Michigan, while stumping for the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “I mean, they’re just gelatinous blobs that kind of make it through the United States Senate.” The constitution sets up three separate branches of government to hold one another accountable, Warren noted – and the assumption was that each of the three branches would “jealously guard its own powers”. “But with Donald Trump in the White House, and a bunch of weak-kneed Republicans in the House [of Representatives] and the Senate, all of a sudden, we’ve lost the whole game,” she said. The US-Israel war on Iran, launched in February, has cost the US tens of billions of dollars. Hundreds of US service members have been wounded and 18 have been killed since the start of the operation. A tentative peace deal fractured in recent weeks. The latest congressional bid to rein in Trump’s attacks on the Middle East failed on Thursday, when a war powers resolution failed by 49 votes to 50 in the Senate. The controversial conflict rumbles on, as Trump faces a crucial political test with November’s US midterm elections. Democrats could win back power in the House, which is currently controlled by Republicans, and are also vying to retake control of the Senate. If there is a Democratic majority, Warren suggested that, coupled with the groundswell of opposition to the war among voters, could enable Congress to serve as a proper check on Trump. If that happens, “I think we are able to rein in Donald Trump and [defense secretary] Pete Hegseth, even if they have gallons of testosterone”, said Warren. Earlier this month, the House passed a war powers resolution for the second time that directed Trump to withdraw the US military from Iran – this time on a 214-208 vote, with four Republicans joining all Democrats in voting in favor. But in the Senate, the resolution failed 47-49. In June, a similar war powers resolution passed the Senate. The resolution directs the US military be removed from Iran without explicit approval from Congress. Van Hollen, who introduced the war powers resolution, said the situation in Iran was a “senseless war” that “should never have started”. “Ultimately, Congress will have to turn off the funding spigot for this war,” Van Hollen, also in Michigan to support El-Sayed, said. “And I will not vote for a dime for this illegal war,” adding that he wouldn’t support Hegseth’s request for more funding, delivered to the appropriations committee earlier this month. “At some point, these Republican senators are going to have to explain to their constituents why they’ve contracted out their constitutional responsibilities to Donald Trump, because that’s what they’re doing,” said Van Hollen. “So long as you have a majority of senators who are turning over their constitutional responsibilities to Donald Trump, then they’re just rubber stamps for Donald Trump’s illegal war.” Van Hollen said Democrats should continue to press for votes on the war powers resolution, to hold Republican senators accountable. The war is unpopular in the US, with 29% of Americans approving of Trump’s handling of the situation with Iran, and 69% disapproving, according to a Washington Post-Ipsos poll earlier this month. “I would rather see Republicans assert their constitutional duties and help us end the war now,” added Van Hollen. “But, you know, maybe they’ll get the message from their constituents.”

title: McCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerous
body_text: There are many parallels between the first McCarthy era, roughly 1946 to 1956, and Trump’s campaign of political repression, his own updated McCarthyism. Both regimes crafted a monster of quasi-facts and innuendo and fed it with fear: an enemy within, well-organized and financed, secretive and violent, allied with evil foreigners and bent on overthrowing capitalism, democracy and Christian morality. Both used flagrantly unconstitutional means to cleanse the nation of the spectral menace. Each time, federal employees were targeted first. President Harry S Truman’s Federal Loyalty Program screened 5 million workers for communist affiliation; 2,700 lost their jobs, 12,000 resigned. Schools, unions and Hollywood fell in line; blacklists outlasted their makers. The Trump administration purged the federal agencies of his equivalent of the cold war communist, the “woke”. Applicants for civil service jobs were asked to identify their favorite administration policies and explain how they would advance them if hired. The federal employees’ union correctly called this request a “loyalty question”. Then as now, law firms quailed, media companies capitulated, universities collaborated. Artists and performers – Zero Mostel, Jimmy Kimmel – were exiled from film and television. In the 1940s and 50s, the attorney general compiled lists of supposedly subversive organizations, which, along with communists and socialists, included groups from the National Negro League to the Nature Friends of America. Trump’s justice department is investigating progressive non-profits, including ActBlue, a chief funding source for Democratic candidates, the Southern Poverty Law Center, and the Open Society Foundations, funded by George Soros, best known for supporting democracy movements in the former Soviet Union. In both eras, the standard bearers were full of ideological passion. “Can there be anyone who fails to realize that ... this is the time for the showdown between the democratic Christian world and the communist atheistic world?” McCarthy thundered to the Senate in 1950. Trump believes in nothing but himself. But like McCarthy and his confederates, the intellectuals behind this repression are true believers. “When the leftist – who does not believe in freedom, who does not believe in civil rights, who does not believe in any ordinary notion of justice – protests that we are violating his rights, understand that he is lying to try to persuade people who are not closely following the political scene that some injustice has perpetrated against him,” Trump’s policy adviser Stephen Miller said in a speech. “We must stay the course and be completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization.” McCarthy and his more powerful and enduring co-conspirator, the FBI director J Edgar Hoover, ruined countless lives and crippled progressive movements. But the scope of this administration’s ambitions; its armies of enforcers inside a gargantuan carceral state; the technological and legal tools at its disposal; and the dearth of principled government actors to obstruct it make this McCarthyism far more dangerous. Global ambitions While McCarthy claimed that American communists were puppets of the Soviet Union, and the CIA conspired to undermine progressive organizing in Europe, today’s attempt to enlist foreign governments in a coordinated fight against “far-left terrorism” potentially extends the administration’s repressive reach around the globe. On 22 September 2025, Trump issued an executive order designating the non-organization “antifa” a “domestic terrorist organization”. Three days later it issued National Security Presidential Memo-7 on “countering domestic terrorism and organized political violence”. Invoking Charlie Kirk’s murder, the assassination attempts against Trump and the supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, and “riots in Los Angeles and Portland” – but not the January 6 insurrection or the 2019 El Paso, Texas, massacre of 23 Chicano shoppers by a young white supremacist – the memo is as much manifesto as battle plan. “This political violence,” it says, “is a culmination of sophisticated, organized campaigns of targeted intimidation, radicalization, threats, and violence designed to silence opposing speech, limit political activity, change or direct policy outcomes, and prevent the functioning of a democratic society. A new law enforcement strategy that investigates all participants in these criminal and terroristic conspiracies – including the organized structures, networks, entities, organizations, funding sources, and predicate actions behind them – is required.” But if a war on the US left inside US borders were not enough, on 16 July the White House announced a “global campaign to crush radical left terrorism”. The secretary of state, Marco Rubio, invited representatives of more than 60 countries to a “summit”, where he named four European “far-left terrorist organizations” and offered $10m for information on their financing. He promised: “There will be more [terrorist] designations soon.” At the same time, the US implemented new visa restrictions targeting people who have allegedly “supported or incited acts of terrorism”. Europe has expressed skepticism that leftwing terrorism is a big problem. Still, some countries are cooperating. The US requested the extradition from Spain of a wealthy American who has donated to humanitarian aid efforts in Palestine – which the administration views as support for Hamas. Spanish authorities are detaining him while they decide whether to send him home or release him. Unlike the US criminal code on domestic terrorism, the laws on combatting foreign terrorism offer “many more tools” to pursue not just people planning or committing violent acts, but also those within “two to three degrees of separation” from the act, Mike German, a former FBI special agent, told Democracy Now. The purpose of the 16 July summit, he said, was “to reframe the discussion around domestic terrorism to imagine that it has these foreign connections that justify the use of these much more aggressive tools”. Laws passed since 11 September 2001, make this sleight of hand easier. The 1947 National Security Act created a wall between the CIA and the FBI, between international and domestic intelligence gathering. But the USA Patriot Act, written and signed hastily after al-Qaida’s attacks on US soil, broke down that wall. Civil libertarians have long argued – and whistleblower Edward Snowden proved in 2013 – that the collection of communications to, from or about a foreign target can sweep up tons of private information about Americans. “The most acute danger” of “uncontrolled sharing of criminal investigative information with intelligence agencies”, argued the ACLU at a 2005 congressional hearing, “is that federal prosecutors and law enforcement agents … concerned with preventing and punishing criminal activities” will become “a domestic spy network directed at unpopular religious and political organizations”. In fact, after September 11, that is what happened. George W Bush’s administration maligned and shut down US Muslim and Arab charities and non-profits under the suspicion that they were supporting a vaguely defined foreign terrorist enemy. German continued, citing current investigations into progressive non-profits like the Southern Poverty Law Center: “This effort to designate left-wing groups as foreign terrorists … using these broad terms like ‘antifa’ will allow them to go after people who are not committing violence, but who are simply engaging in the political process.” Extreme policing In June, the administration circulated a press release boasting of the blows it had delivered the “violent anarchist network” antifa. It cited crackdowns from coast to coast – from Spokane, Washington, where “multiple Antifa insurgents were convicted on federal conspiracy charges for their roles in a violent attack at [an] ICE facility”, to Newark, New Jersey, where “Antifa thugs violently laid siege” to an immigrant detention center, “resulting in dozens of arrests and federal charges”. For the record, the Spokane protesters blocked an ICE van. The New Jersey public defender has filed a motion to dismiss the charges against 40 protesters, which “contain nearly identical, generalized allegations and fail to identify the specific conduct attributed to each individual”. It makes sense that an administration that criminalizes immigration and sends federal agents to detain and deport law-abiding gardeners, shopkeepers, mothers and toddlers will use the same tactics to suppress protest against that brutality. A carceral system that locks up millions and imposes extraordinarily harsh sentences functions in concert with these enforcement tactics to intimidate would-be dissenters and punish those who openly dissent. The charges often don’t stick. The New York Times reviewed hundreds of cases involving charges of assaulting or impeding federal immigration officers and found that most of them unraveled, due to federal agents’ “extensive misconduct”, from “attacking protesters” to “misrepresenting facts in court”. But when they stick, the damage can be devastating. Case in point: the trial and conviction of nine participants in a 4 July 2025, action outside ICE’s Prairieland detention facility in Alvarado, Texas. Some brought guns, which is legal in Texas. Benjamin Song fired at a police officer – he said he aimed at the ground – who was injured. Others scrawled graffiti on cars and shot off fireworks. Song was convicted of attempted murder, the other eight on charges of riot and explosives (the fireworks) and material support for terrorism; the prosecution presented a claim that their black clothing and use of Signal are antifa tactics. Daniel Sanchez-Estrada, who was not there, was convicted of conspiracy to conceal documents for moving a box of zines. The prison sentences they received were extreme by any measure: 100 years for Song, 30 for Sanchez-Estrada; 50 to 70 years for the others. The justice department proudly broadcast the total: 450 years for a “terrorist attack” on an ICE facility. The woman who attempted to assassinate supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh got eight years. By comparison, between 1941 and 1957 hundreds of communists and others were prosecuted under the Smith Act, which made it a crime to “advocate, abet, advise or teach the … desirability or propriety of overthrowing the Government of the United States or of any State by force or violence” – all constitutionally protected speech. Eleven leaders of the Communist party convicted in one major trial were sentenced to three to five years. Techno-surveillance At the counter-terrorism summit, Miller described efforts to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute these political terrorists that are operating in our country”. Aided by technology and undeterred by watchdogs, they can do it. McCarthy relied on wiretapping, spies, informants and human bureaucrats digging through paper files to identify his targets. He managed to find thousands. But late 21st-century technology, including artificial intelligence, which enables the state to conduct surveillance on millions and collate data from government agencies at all levels, makes Hoover’s witch-hunt look like a game of hide-and-seek. The examples are myriad. ICE has a new $25m-a-year contract with a subsidiary of the data broker Thomson Reuters to provide “continuous monitoring” of such things as potential government fraud and the arrival of unaccompanied immigrant minors. It also does “academic risk flagging”, whatever that is. The agriculture department has contracted with Palantir to provide an AI-empowered return-to-office tracking tool, which critics say can be used for other kinds of employee surveillance. The White House has mandated the installation of an app on federal workers’ phones that “gives all Americans direct access” to administration news alerts, social media posts and policy announcements. A “text President Trump” option pre-populates a message praising him. What happens to the worker who wants to criticize him? Those antiterrorist visa restrictions are determined through the ideological vetting of travelers by pulling social media content into government databases using AI-powered monitoring tools; the process continues after the person enters the country. Trump’s friendly relations with tech companies that amass mountains of customer data constitute an incalculable asset to the repressive regime. Submissive Washington On 2 December 1954, the Senate, led by three Republicans, censured Joe McCarthy. Its resolution described the senator’s hunt for suspected communists in the federal government as “contrary to senatorial traditions”. Quaint as that sounds, it initiated his undoing. Throughout the 1950s, Chief Justice Earl Warren’s supreme court dismantled the tools of McCarthyism piece by piece, fortifying the fifth amendment against self-incrimination and reining in Congress’s power to call witnesses when testifying would “unjustifiably” abridge their right to privacy or “liberty of speech, press, religion or assembly”. Now, cowed by their vengeful and fickle commander-in-chief, the Republican Congress has relinquished its powers – of appropriation and regulation, declaration of war or removal of a corrupt, incompetent or emotionally unstable president. While the lower federal judiciary has ruled frequently against Trump, the supreme court’s majority has upheld the president’s prerogative to reshape the federal government according to his whim. The recent ruling that allowed his no-cause dismissal of the Federal Trade commissioner Rebecca Slaughter – and overturned a 91-year-old decision limiting such executive authority – reverberates throughout the federal workforce, politicizing the public sector and reopening the door to the ruinous inquests of the McCarthy era. What will be the next frontier of political repression? Will the postal inspector be deputized to open packages in search of abortion pills bound for red states? Will Trump send ICE or the national guard to intimidate voters at the polls? A president without a moral compass and advisers whose true north is the extreme right, helming a government with unparalleled legal, technological and financial resources, can implement a regime of political repression that Joe McCarthy – or even Big Brother – could not have dreamt of. Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

The White House has mandated the installation of an app on federal workers’ phones that “gives all Americans direct access” to administration news alerts, social media posts and policy announcements. A “text President Trump” option pre-populates a message praising him. What happens to the worker who wants to criticize him? Those antiterrorist visa restrictions are determined through the ideological vetting of travelers by pulling social media content into government databases using AI-powered monitoring tools; the process continues after the person enters the country. Trump’s friendly relations with tech companies that amass mountains of customer data constitute an incalculable asset to the repressive regime. Submissive Washington On 2 December 1954, the Senate, led by three Republicans, censured Joe McCarthy. Its resolution described the senator’s hunt for suspected communists in the federal government as “contrary to senatorial traditions”. Quaint as that sounds, it initiated his undoing. Throughout the 1950s, Chief Justice Earl Warren’s supreme court dismantled the tools of McCarthyism piece by piece, fortifying the fifth amendment against self-incrimination and reining in Congress’s power to call witnesses when testifying would “unjustifiably” abridge their right to privacy or “liberty of speech, press, religion or assembly”. Now, cowed by their vengeful and fickle commander-in-chief, the Republican Congress has relinquished its powers – of appropriation and regulation, declaration of war or removal of a corrupt, incompetent or emotionally unstable president. While the lower federal judiciary has ruled frequently against Trump, the supreme court’s majority has upheld the president’s prerogative to reshape the federal government according to his whim. The recent ruling that allowed his no-cause dismissal of the Federal Trade commissioner Rebecca Slaughter – and overturned a 91-year-old decision limiting such executive authority – reverberates throughout the federal workforce, politicizing the public sector and reopening the door to the ruinous inquests of the McCarthy era. What will be the next frontier of political repression? Will the postal inspector be deputized to open packages in search of abortion pills bound for red states? Will Trump send ICE or the national guard to intimidate voters at the polls? A president without a moral compass and advisers whose true north is the extreme right, helming a government with unparalleled legal, technological and financial resources, can implement a regime of political repression that Joe McCarthy – or even Big Brother – could not have dreamt of. Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

title: Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war
body_text: Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military as Donald Trump gathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort. Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports. The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan. Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties. In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targeting Hezbollah tunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast. Lebanese officials accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents. Trump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, but increasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections. On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”. Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began. Support in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote. Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans. Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.

title: Trump defends $1.8bn slush fund that is holding up Todd Blanche confirmation
body_text: Donald Trump has defended controversial plans for a $1.8bn slush fund even as they threaten to derail the nomination of his former personal lawyer Todd Blanche for US attorney general. Blanche “should be immediately approved” by the US Senate, the president declared in a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday morning, defending the payout scheme proposed by his officials in the Department of Justice as it holds up Blanche’s confirmation. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since Trump fired Pam Bondi in April, has been lined up to take the job permanently. Under agreements to resolve a long-shot $10bn lawsuit filed by Trump against the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over the leak of his tax returns, the justice department proposed the creation of a secretive fund – to be awarded with no restrictions to allies of the president – and barred the IRS from auditing his tax returns. Democrats and some government watchdogs, however, are calling it a slush fund, and have warned it could end up paying out to defendants convicted over their role in the January 6 Capitol riot. While Blanche later said the slush fund was dead after an extraordinary backlash, two Republicans on the Senate judiciary committee – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – have demanded assurances in writing that the fund will never be activated before they back his confirmation as attorney general. Blanche has not given them that assurance, and the committee’s vote to advance his nomination was postponed this week as a result. “I felt that they should be given compensation for what has been done to them,” Trump wrote of his supporters, whom he described as “a group of people treated so badly in our Nation’s history”, adding: “I gave up any payments for myself, which would have been substantial … I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined! “John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund’ … until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent,” Trump wrote. That opponent, the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, beat Cornyn by roughly 28 points in May, ending Cornyn’s Senate career and making him the first Texas Republican senator to lose a renomination bid. Blanche was previously Trump’s personal defense lawyer, representing him in the New York hush-money case and other criminal matters, before joining the justice department as Bondi’s deputy. Responding to Trump’s post on Friday, Tillis said the president had made clear the fund was “still alive”. He said Blanche had been “forthright, thoughtful and patient” throughout the course of negotiations. “It’s a shame his confirmation has hit a snag only because an incompetent personal advisor to the President refuses to amend the bogus settlement,” Tillis wrote on X, without naming the advisor. “I will continue working in good faith to put an end this legal and political albatross and prevent any potential misallocation of taxpayer dollars.” Judiciary committee Democrats have said Blanche privately told the senator Dick Durbin that pushing for the fund had been a mistake. He has also faced questions over his firm’s past payments from a Trump-aligned political action committee and his handling of the Epstein files. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, has said he expects the nomination to come back for a vote once Cornyn and Tillis are satisfied. Trump has said he is willing to pull Blanche’s name temporarily and resubmit it later, once Cornyn and Tillis are “out of office”, while keeping Blanche on as acting attorney general in the meantime.

title: EU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challenges
body_text: Extraordinarily, given the importance of geopolitics, the office of foreign secretary has sometimes appeared a consolation prize in British politics, perhaps reflecting the transfer of responsibility to Downing Street or the Cabinet Office. That is not how Ed Miliband views the job. His allies say suggestions that he nurses resentment after he was deprived of the chance to be chancellor misunderstand his grasp of the policy challenges ahead. “Ed has an immense appetite to get things done and is relishing being in this job,” one says. “Ed will be a policy-driven foreign secretary.” To that end, he is preparing a distinct agenda on relations with the EU over the next decade, Britain’s chairing of the G20 next year and the climate crisis. Miliband is also determined to contribute to some of the big debates about shaping the international order of the future – debates that may take him into difficult territory given the volatility of the US alliance. Palestine may take longer to address, partly owing to the Israeli elections and the sudden glimmer of progress over Hamas disarmament, but his instincts are clear. In 2014, as Labour leader, he urged his MPs to vote to recognise Palestine. Acutely conscious that he is the tenth foreign secretary since William Hague stood aside in 2014, Miliband also arrives without a Foreign Office permanent secretary after the sacking of Olly Robbins, and with some staff on a rolling strike over the large job cuts that Robbins had announced he would impose. But Miliband, working with the new Europe minister based in the Foreign Office, Hamish Falconer, intends to be closely involved in talks on the UK’s relations with the EU since he regards a successful solution to that relationship as the single biggest question facing the UK. His personal involvement will give the Foreign Office greater influence in the Europe debate than under Keir Starmer’s leadership, when the Cabinet Office was the sole proprietors of negotiations with the EU. Miliband represents a Eurosceptic constituency and remains bound by Labour’s manifesto red lines not to enter the single market or customs union in this parliament. But that does not prevent him from seeking to influence Andy Burnham’s longer-term thinking about where the UK’s relationship with the EU should be in 10 or 15 years. Burnham, Miliband’s aides argue, has shown an openness to ideas on social care and the same openness may apply to issues such as European defence. “Having a closer relationship with Europe is a key foreign policy priority to protect our national security and grow our economy,” an ally said. “Ed will be working in lockstep with No 10 and Hamish Falconer to make this happen. He sees Europe as at the heart of this agenda.” Friends also said Miliband wants to find a way to revive the ailing G20, a largely economic multilateral body that has been steadily declining in influence since 2008, when the UK played a major role coordinating the response to the financial crash during Gordon Brown’s premiership. In the latter days of his own tenure at No 10, Starmer appointed Brown to act as his special envoy on global finance and cooperation in advance of the G20, and Brown will retain the role, working alongside Miliband who was one of his advisers while chancellor. Lord Wood, who acted as a foreign policy adviser during the Brown premiership, has also been appointed to the Foreign Office as a minister in the Lords, and will bring experience and intellect to the role. With the UK due to chair the postponed illicit finance summit in December in advance of taking over the G20, ideas such as a global wealth tax and greater transparency in overseas financial holdings are all being promoted. But the secrecy of Britain’s overseas territories has for a decade been a millstone in the UK’s call to combat corruption. Kirsty McNeill, the new international development minister and a former executive director at Save the Children, has been asked to wrestle with the impact of massive aid cuts. She has previously said the UK will not regain credibility on aid unless it sets out a path for returning aid spending to 0.7% of GDP. Aid will fall to 0.3% next year and Burnham’s £2 bus fare cap is being funded by a raid on the aid budget. The G20 at least provides a creative way for her to build alliances to tackle unjust debts and illicit financial flows. A global wealth tax was proposed during the Brazilian presidency of the G20 in 2024 after a study commissioned from the French economist Gabriel Zucman. “There is overwhelming public support for this idea,” Zucman said at the report’s launch. “Ten years ago, nobody believed 130 countries would support a minimum tax on multinationals. It was thought of as utopian.” The report said billionaires were paying an average of 0.3% tax on their wealth – less than the rates paid by workers. Zucman said the average wealth of the top 0.0001% of individuals had grown by 7.1% a year on average between 1987 and 2024, increasing the share of global wealth held by billionaires from 3% to 14%. Trump’s own G20 summit is due in Miami in December, by which time he could be diminished by a reverse in the midterm congressional elections. There has been a slow drop-off in world leaders attending the G20 partly owing to geopolitical rifts over Ukraine and questions over its value, but by next year the economic fallout from the war in Iran may require economic and political coordination. Miliband is not, meanwhile, expected to act quickly on Burnham’s admission that Labour needed to “do better” on Gaza. Burnham suggested action on trade with illegal Israeli settlements was on his agenda, but Foreign Office diplomats have questioned the enforceability of such a ban. A debate is under way as to whether European states would best help the political parties opposed to the Israeli prime minister in the October elections by imposing fresh sanctions, underlining Benjamin Netanyahu’s diplomatic isolation, or whether he would use international disapproval to his domestic advantage. The pressure from the Labour backbenches for a more robust policy that treats international law with the same seriousness in the Middle East as the UK does in Ukraine is intense. A letter from 80 parliamentarians coordinated by the MP Kim Johnson called on Burnham to impose comprehensive sanctions on Israel and recognise the findings of the UN commission of inquiry that Israel is committing genocide. Burnham has said it is for the international courts to make such determinations. But a consequential question will be how Miliband retains his progressive credibility and yet remains on good terms with the US state department under Trump. Wood, a sceptic about past UK foreign military interventions, strongly opposed the US military attack on Iran. But the need to retain a modicum of US support for Ukraine has, ever since Trump’s election, been seen as an essential UK foreign policy priority, one that has required compromises and often involved working with the recently deceased Republican senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine. That is unlikely to change in the short term.

title: Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’ prompts activists to turn up the volume
body_text: This summer, torrential rains have washed away Texas neighborhoods, dangerous heat has blanketed swaths of the country, and smoke from Canadian wildfires has choked communities as far south as Florida. Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe. Yet the climate crisis has largely disappeared from the political agenda, with many Democrats who once described it as an existential threat now shying away from talking about it. Now US activists are pushing back against this trend of “climate hushing”, arguing it is misguided. During the summer’s federal recess, during which lawmakers leave the nation’s capital to work directly within their home states or districts, demonstrators organized by the environmental advocacy coalition Climate Action Campaign are calling on representatives to put climate back on the political agenda. “The long history of the climate movement proves that we move fastest when there’s real pressure from the grassroots,” said Bill McKibben, the environmental author and activist who co-founded climate non-profit 350.org, “All the evidence shows those grassroots are as worried about [the] climate crisis as they ever were.” The events, set to take place over the next month in at least 20 states during the House and Senate recess periods, will mobilize members of groups including local Sierra Club chapters, the senior citizen-led climate organization Third Act, which McKibben founded, and local affiliates of the racial justice group the NAACP. “It’s the broadest brush that we are working with,” said Margie Alt, director of the Climate Action Campaign. “The message is, talk about climate, climate can’t wait, and we want to see action.” Actions began on Thursday and will take a variety of forms. In Michigan, participants will demonstrate against the Republican representative Bill Huizenga who voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which boosted planet-heating fossil fuels. In Arizona, young activists will meet with the Democratic representative Adelita Shirley Grijalva, a climate champion, and encourage her to continue talking about global warming. In other districts, organizers have circulated petitions calling on the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, to prioritize climate issues or plan to call on their representatives to connect the climate crisis to recent heatwaves. The activists’ campaign comes as new polling challenges the need for “climate hushing”, a trend that took off as some policy wonks argued that talking about global warming could alienate voters and distract from the message of affordability. July research from the University of California, Santa Barbara found that emphasizing climate change was neutral to beneficial for Democratic candidates, suggesting that talking more about the issue does not alienate voters and can even increase support in competitive races. Though the Trump administration frequently derides climate policy as a “scam” and a “hoax”, polling indicates most Americans are not onboard with that view. Another July poll from Data for Progress found that 61% of likely voters believe extreme weather has become more frequent over the past five years, including nearly half of Republicans. And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming. “Smart politicians will grab on this issue,” said McKibben. “There’s perhaps no other question where the gulf between Maga and the general public is higher.” Alt said she saw climate-hushing as “the climate denial of 2026”. “I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said. “I think that it is dropping the ball on the biggest threat the US and the world faces.”

Another July poll from Data for Progress found that 61% of likely voters believe extreme weather has become more frequent over the past five years, including nearly half of Republicans. And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming. “Smart politicians will grab on this issue,” said McKibben. “There’s perhaps no other question where the gulf between Maga and the general public is higher.” Alt said she saw climate-hushing as “the climate denial of 2026”. “I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said. “I think that it is dropping the ball on the biggest threat the US and the world faces.”

title: Trump vows to push $1.8bn slush fund as Senate committee set to reconsider AG nomination
body_text: The US Senate judiciary committee has scheduled a meeting early next week to consider Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, as Donald Trump promised to revive the controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund. The meeting, set for Tuesday, comes as Blanche’s confirmation has stalled over a dispute between the president and outgoing Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who are seeking written confirmation that the justice department would not establish the proposed fund. A spokesperson for the committee said in a statement that Chuck Grassley, committee chair and Iowa Republican, “wants Todd Blanche’s nomination to be successful”. “Grassley would like to see Blanche confirmed before the August recess as he has an excellent record restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” the statement added. Opponents of the president consider it a slush fund to compensate political allies for political lawfare; supporters say it is a vehicle to compensate individuals who claim they were wrongfully targeted by the government more broadly. “It is dead, but I wish ⁠it weren’t, to be honest with you. I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused,” Trump had said during a cabinet meeting on Friday. “I’d like to ⁠see them compensated for the pain.” At the cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump urged Republican senators to confirm Blanche and warned that they “will never get anybody like him” and repeated a claim that Cornyn was blocking Blanche because Trump had endorsed Cornyn’s Republican primary challenger Ken Paxton. “I’d be upset also,” ‌Trump said. “I fully understand it. He shouldn’t be that way. I shouldn’t be that way.“ Trump then slammed Cornyn and Tillis in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, claiming that both were upset because he had not endorsed them. Trump threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination, keep him on as acting attorney general and “push hard” for anti-weaponization bill. “Todd Blanche was a voice of reason!” Trump wrote. “It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done.” Blanche, Trump’s former personal attorney, has told senators that the fund was dead, but has so far not agreed to put that in writing. The “anti-weaponization” fund was crafted as part of a ⁠legal settlement between Trump and the justice department to resolve his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS over allegedly mishandling his tax records. Trump wrote that the fund “will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed”. Tillis has said those who attacked law enforcement during the 6 January 2021 riots should still be in prison and should not get a check from the federal government. Cornyn and Tillis also object to an IRS deal that would prevent tax audits of Trump and his associates. Tillis responded on Saturday, saying that despite Trump’s comments that the fund is dead, the president “clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against”. “It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal,” he said on X. “Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday.” The back-and-forth over Blanche’s nomination, which is vigorously opposed by victims of Jeffrey Epstein over his handling of investigative files related to the late sex trafficker, now likely lies with backroom negotiations over the weekend. The same controversy dogged Trump’s original second-term attorney general, Pam Bondi, before she resigned. Cornyn and Tillis were reported to be close to backing Blanche as recently as Thursday. But with just more than two years left in Trump’s second term, Blanche may not need formal Senate confirmation to serve so long as his nomination is pending and not formally rejected or withdrawn.
