title: Michigan votes in key Senate primary as Democrats battle over party’s future
body_text: The Democratic party faces a crucial test of its direction on Tuesday as voters in the midwestern swing state of Michigan decide whether to nominate for US Senate a progressive candidate advocating for universal healthcare or an-establishment-backed moderate. The state’s Democratic primary is the latest high-profile battle over the party’s future, as it seeks to chart a course back to power in Washington following Donald Trump’s victory in 2024. Leftwing candidates have surged in Democratic primaries in solidly blue areas across the country in recent months. Some congressional primary races in Michigan will also offer a sense of where the party is headed as it looks to take back control of US Congress from the Republicans. Progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old former public health official, has led in recent polls against his moderate rival, Haley Stevens, the 43-year-old US representative who first came to Congress after flipping a red seat. A flood of more than $40m in outside spending has come into the race to support Stevens or attack El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby. The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face Mike Rogers, a former congressman from the state who was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024 when he lost to Elissa Slotkin. The Michigan US Senate seat is critical for Democrats in their dark-horse quest to retake the upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats. Michigan is not the only state with primaries on Tuesday. In Missouri, voters will weigh whether to nominate Cori Bush, the former US representative who is running to return to the chamber against Wesley Bell, in a race punctuated by the war in Gaza and outside spending by pro-Israel groups. And in Washington state, voters will decide which two candidates to elevate in the third congressional district, where blue-dog Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is seeking re-election amid challengers from both sides of the aisle. Congressional seats, including one in Slotkin’s former district, are also in the mix in Michigan, with further tests of progressives’ rise. The progressive US senator Bernie Sanders has boosted El-Sayed and two progressive challengers in congressional races. In the Lansing-area seventh district, Sanders backed William Lawrence, a community organizer who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, over the former US ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal. Maasdam received Slotkin’s endorsement in the race for the purple district, currently held by Republican Tom Barrett. In the 13th district, Sanders boosted the state representative Donavan McKinney, who is running against the incumbent Democratic representative Shri Thanedar in the Detroit-area district. On the right, Republicans will figure out if they want to nominate John James, a US representative with Donald Trump’s endorsement, or businessman Perry Johnson to face Jocelyn Benson, the secretary of state and likely Democratic nominee for the governorship. James has led in polls, but late grassroots energy has given Johnson some momentum. Governor Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, served for eight years and faced term limits, preventing another run for the high office.

title: David Ellison claims opposition to his mega-merger stems from potential CNN control
body_text: Speaking out on the lawsuit against the big merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), Paramount’s CEO, David Ellison, said that the legal backlash against the deal is “not really about market share” but rather stems from political motivations. Noting in a New York Times guest essay published on Tuesday that the deal had “been reviewed and approved by regulators reflecting 65 countries, including the United States”, Ellison played down the competitive concerns raised by the state coalition and Writers Guild of America West and Writers Guild of America East, which also sued to block the deal, and said he believed the reaction came from a “plainer worry”. “The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions,” Ellison wrote. “Unfortunately, I can’t give anyone a view into my heart and mind, but I can share this: I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans.” Reporting has showed that Ellison and his father have made promises to the Trump administration about swaying the network in a more favorable direction, purportedly to encourage federal regulators to approve the merger, prompting backlash from Democrats such as Senator Elizabeth Warren. Backlash against Ellison, son of the tech mogul Larry Ellison, one of the wealthiest people in the world, as a media owner began last summer after after his company, Skydance Media, went through an $8.4bn merger with Paramount Global. As the deal was closing, CBS abruptly announced it was canceling The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, which aired its last episode in May. Once the merger was completed, Ellison appointed the heterodox opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News, a controversial move that has led to layoffs and editorial tensions at the network. Without directly addressing any of the controversies around CBS News, Ellison wrote that he was committed to the independence that is at the core of the “founding principles” of CNN and CBS News. “I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth,” Ellison wrote. “Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle. That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve – not to any party or cause. “These were founding principles for both CNN and CBS News,” Ellison continued. “For legends like Ted Turner and Edward R. Murrow, and it is exactly that kind of independence that has always fueled the greatness of ‘60 Minutes.’” Ellison’s essay (“The Critics Are Wrong About My Politics”) comes at a pivotal time for his $111bn merger agreement to buy WBD, which is currently held up in a California court after a 12-state coalition sued to block the deal on anti-competitive grounds. After district judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín agreed to temporarily block the deal, Paramount made the unusual decision to bypass the temporary injunction stage and hold up the merger until the case can go to trial – or until June 2027. The parties have both made proposals for when the case should reach trial, with Paramount asking for a November trial and the state coalition asking for a date in April 2027.

title: Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination will advance to full US Senate vote
body_text: The US Senate judiciary committee voted along party lines to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after he confirmed in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Experts say, however, that Trump could easily reverse the deal. His nomination will now proceed to the full Senate, where it will probably face intense skepticism from Democrats. Ahead of the vote on Tuesday, every Democrat on the committee railed against Blanche’s nomination, saying he was unfit for the role and would do the president’s bidding. They emphasized his work defending the controversial fund, his mishandling of the files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the murder of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, and prosecutions of protesters and Trump’s political rivals. “We are going to advance out of this committee probably the most discreditable person ever to seek the office of attorney general of the United States,” said Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator from Rhode Island. Blanche, one of Trump’s most trusted legal aides and formerly his personal defense lawyer, has faced questions over his suitability to lead the Department of Justice, which is supposed to operate independently of the White House. He signed an order scrapping the so-called “anti-weaponization” fund – a roughly $1.8bn pool of money created in May as part of a settlement ending Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service – in an attempt to defuse a Republican rebellion over his nomination. The lawsuit came after the leak of the US president’s confidential tax records by a former IRS contractor, who has been serving a prison sentence since 2024. Trump had cast the fund as compensation for people he claimed were unfairly targeted by politically driven investigations, and defended it as recently as this weekend. Critics said it risked becoming a taxpayer-funded payout to Trump loyalists, including some defendants from the January 6 Capitol riot. The most consequential criticism stemmed from two Republican members of the judiciary committee, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina. Blanche’s nomination required their support. But both outgoing senators have turned on Trump, recently telling party leaders they would not let Blanche’s confirmation move without firm guarantees that the fund would be shelved for good. Speaking ahead of the vote on Tuesday, both Cornyn and Tillis said their concerns had been satisfied. Tillis described the anti-weaponization fund as a “payout pot for punks”, but said he was satisfied it would not be moving forward. “I’ve never liked this 1776 fund. It made no sense to me, and I thought it was an insult to the police officers and the people that defended us on January the sixth. It’s done. It’s been rescinded, and I am satisfied,” he said. Despite saying he would vote for Blanche, Tillis lamented the politicization of the justice department under Blanche’s leadership. He criticized the department’s ongoing prosecution of the former FBI director James Comey in eastern North Carolina over a picture Comey posted with seashells arranged saying “86 47” – shorthand for getting rid of Trump. “Some bonehead in North Carolina thinks that that’s a crime. Well, they better damn sure have information to back it up because if all it is is a picture, that person should lose his job, his or her job,” Tillis said. Cornyn and Tillis faced public criticism from Trump over the weekend for pushing Blanche to put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund was dead and the scope of the tax immunity was limited. Cornyn defended the push on Tuesday. “While this may sound like nitpicking to some, it’s critically important not only to me but to other members of the Senate,” Cornyn said. “Given this agreement with Mr Blanche, I expect the department to live up to to this in future litigation.” Echoing the concerns of many other Democrats, Cory Booker, a Democratic senator from New Jersey, said the agreement with Blanche offered little assurance the justice department could not reverse itself and go ahead with the fund anyway. “I’ve been here 14 years. I have not seen something as farcical as what I’ve witnessed over the last few weeks,” Booker said. “I’m going to say it very clear: this is all hat and no cattle.” In his order, released on Sunday, Blanche stressed that the fund had never actually been operational: no board had been appointed, no money moved, and no claims filed or paid. While there was concern that the settlement also provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits, the US Department of Justice separately clarified the IRS-related order was limited to the plaintiffs in the original settlement, and did not amount to blanket protection from future audits. Both Cornyn and Tillis later confirmed they would vote to advance Blanche’s nomination. Because the underlying settlement still references the fund, a future attorney general – or Trump himself, with Congress’s help – could try to revive it. Trump added to that uncertainty over the weekend, saying that if Blanche’s confirmation stalled, he would simply keep him on in an acting capacity and push lawmakers to create the fund through legislation instead.

title: Washington state Democrat who flipped pro-Trump district faces tough primary
body_text: The two-term Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is heading into one of the country’s most closely watched contests on Tuesday after national recognition for flipping a Republican seat in 2022. Representing Washington state’s third district, Gluesenkamp Perez finds herself squeezed between the Democrat and progressive Brent Hennrich and the Republican state senator John Braun on her right. There are six other candidates on a single crowded ballot and the top two finishers will advance to the November general election regardless of party. Democrats are favored to win the House of Representatives in November’s midterm election, but highly contested seats such as Gluesenkamp Perez’s will be crucial to securing a majority, and expanding the margin. Republican Jaime Herrera Beutler won Washington’s third district in 2010 and held it for six terms, until Gluesenkamp Perez narrowly beat Trump-endorsed Joe Kent in 2022. Trump has carried the district in all three of his presidential runs, most recently by about three points, and yet in 2024 Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of her party’s presidential nominee. Logging, mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life in much of the area and Gluesenkamp Perez’s success has stemmed from her appeal to moderates and rural voters. An auto repair shop owner, she won over many in south-west Washington, including Republicans who considered Kent too extreme. “We like her a lot,” said Laura Oltmann, 41, a resident and supporter who describes herself as a conservative. Kent did not embody conservatism, Oltmann said. But through Gluesenkamp Perez’s two terms, frustration has built among her own party, growing when Democrats saw her siding with Republicans on major legislation. Hennrich, who is challenging her in the primary, ran for the same seat in 2022 before standing down, but decided to run again. “I stepped out of this race to unify Democrats to help get Marie through, so we could get rid of our six-term incumbent, Jaime Herrera Beutler,” he said. “[Gluesenkamp Perez] has turned out to be just an absolute epic failure for Democrats.” Hennrich is not alone. Several local Democratic organizations inside the district have broken with her. “She ran as a Democrat and inspired a lot of people, and she won, and we thought she was going to be what we wanted her to be. But everybody’s disappointed,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th legislative district Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. Kirkpatrick traces that disappointment to Gluesenkamp Perez’s votes for the Save Act, Trump’s effort to overhaul elections, as well as for a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity, and federal funding tied to the war in Iran. She claims the congresswoman has also stopped talking to her own party’s local officers. Thea Zahn, the chair of the 20th legislative district, agreed. “What majority are you going for?” she said. “Are you going for a majority that believes in Democratic values, or a majority that will fail over and over again when it comes down to it, when you really need people to stand up and say this is what we believe in?” Asked if she would vote for the congresswoman if she is on the ballot in November, Zahn said: “I won’t vote for Marie. I will never vote for Marie Perez again.” The congresswoman’s defenders make a different argument: that the district’s partisan lean leaves her little room, and that the seat matters more than any single vote. “The reality is we live in a Republican district. It is Republican,” said Terri Niles, who chairs the 17th legislative district Democrats and spoke in a personal capacity. “I’ve knocked on tens of thousands of doors.” Niles argues that none of Gluesenkamp Perez’s contentious votes actually resulted in legislation passing, and that the calculation for Democrats is simpler than her critics allow. “The most important thing everybody should keep in mind is that flipping the House is our goal,” she said. “That should be the most important thing for every Democrat out there.” The Democratic infighting comes at a precarious moment. An Emerson College poll conducted in mid-July for the Northwest Progressive Institute found Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican Braun tied. Braun, the Republican leader in the Washington senate, has become one of the GOP’s top congressional recruits, earning Donald Trump’s endorsement in April and the backing of the National Republican Congressional Committee. “We could hand a truly 100% Maga candidate a congressional seat for life,” said Tim Probst, a local Democratic party leader. “Because once he gets in there, he’s not getting out.”

Braun, the Republican leader in the Washington senate, has become one of the GOP’s top congressional recruits, earning Donald Trump’s endorsement in April and the backing of the National Republican Congressional Committee. “We could hand a truly 100% Maga candidate a congressional seat for life,” said Tim Probst, a local Democratic party leader. “Because once he gets in there, he’s not getting out.”

title: Jay Clayton sworn in as US director of national intelligence
body_text: Jay Clayton has been sworn in as the US’s top spy after a contentious Senate confirmation hearing during which ⁠he refused to directly ⁠acknowledge that Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election. The oath of office was administered to Clayton on Tuesday by the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in the Oval Office as the president looked on and applauded. He becomes the ninth director of national intelligence, replacing Tulsi Gabbard, who stepped down in June. Clayton, a former US attorney for the southern district of New York and chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), will oversee 18 US intelligence agencies. His appointment follows a turbulent two months in which the intelligence apparatus was temporarily led by Bill Pulte, the housing regulator whom Trump installed as acting director after Gabbard’s departure. Pulte’s appointment had unsettled some Republicans because of his lack of national security experience. During his brief tenure, however, he became involved in the administration’s increasingly prominent campaign to raise concerns about the integrity of US elections. Shortly before Clayton’s confirmation, Pulte released intelligence community documents from 2020 describing China’s capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system. The material was largely previously known but its release came as Trump has made “election security” a central political issue ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump has continued to promote false claims that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen. During Pulte’s tenure, he also released classified material that he said supported his arguments. Clayton’s own confirmation was overshadowed by the same issue. Democrats condemned his refusal to state that Biden had won the election, while Republicans ultimately confirmed him along party lines. The controversy has raised questions about how the intelligence community will operate under a president who has repeatedly accused federal agencies of being “weaponised” against him. In his first statement as director, Clayton sought to address those concerns, promising to protect the intelligence community from political interference. “The safety and security of the ‌American people will be ‌our North Star, and we will work to make sure the ‌American people have complete confidence in the [intelligence community] through proper oversight, transparency and accountability,” Clayton said in a press release from the office of the director of national intelligence. “This includes ensuring the vital work of our [intelligence community] is never weaponized for political motives,” he added, echoing language frequently used by Trump and his allies to describe their claims that previous administrations abused federal power to target the president. Clayton brings substantial experience in law enforcement and government to the job. As US attorney in Manhattan, he oversaw prosecutions involving terrorism, international drug trafficking and organised crime. Before that, he chaired the SEC from 2017 to 2020, where the administration says he oversaw more than 2,300 enforcement actions resulting in more than $10bn in penalties and disgorgement. He has also held senior positions in business and law, including at Apollo Global Management and Sullivan & Cromwell, and has taught at the University of Pennsylvania and Wharton. Republican senators have pointed to that record as evidence that Clayton is qualified to lead the intelligence community. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, has called him a “proven leader” whose record inspired confidence. Tom Cotton, the chair of the Senate intelligence committee, said Clayton had deep experience in national security threats. Other Republican supporters highlighted his previous bipartisan confirmation as SEC chair. Senator Katie Britt of Alabama added via X on Tuesday: “Congratulations to our Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton! I look forward to seeing him lead our intelligence community and keep our nation safe from threats.” Clayton now inherits an intelligence community that has already endured a succession of upheavals under Trump. Gabbard’s tenure was marked by clashes with congressional Democrats, who accused her of advancing the president’s political agenda and promoting debunked election claims. Pulte’s temporary appointment then raised fresh concerns about the politicisation of the intelligence agencies. Clayton said his aim was to create an intelligence organisation that was “streamlined, agile, team-oriented and mission-focused”. He added: “I look forward to making sure the men and women of the [intelligence community] have the resources they need to carry out our critical mission.” With just more than three months left before midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, Trump has escalated efforts ‌to make “election security” a central issue, despite established findings that voter fraud is rare.

title: Ohio Republican Max Miller faces growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations
body_text: Max Miller, the beleaguered US Republican representative from Ohio, has vowed to defy a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. In a combative interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, Miller turned the tables by attacking Moreno, accused three women – including his ex-wife – of lying by saying he had been violent towards them, and invoked Donald Trump in insisting that he would not resign. As a deadline loomed for party leaders to choose a potential replacement, Miller, a former White House aide, took an unapologetic stand a day after Trump himself brought pressure to bear by calling him and reportedly telling him “things aren’t looking good” for his re-election campaign against his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter. The congressional ethics committee launched an investigation into allegations that Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct”, it said on Tuesday. Earlier in the day, Miller said he would request an ethics investigation into himself “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family”, adding: “I have absolutely nothing to hide.” Pleas for Miller to step down intensified after Moreno – the father of Miller’s former wife, Emily Moreno – broke his silence after months of refraining from comment on allegations concerning the alleged abuse of his daughter. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno, an ally of Trump, posted on Sunday. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.” Addressing reporters on Tuesday, Moreno described the dispute between his daughter and Miller as “truly the seventh level of hell”, adding: “This has been a horrific experience for my entire family. “This has been brutal beyond comprehension, and if there’s any minimum standard for being an elected official, as I said, he fails to meet that minimum basic standard.” Moreno said he had to handle the pickup of his granddaughter at a police station this weekend because he didn’t “want my daughter interacting with this man”. “I don’t know what this guy’s capable of,” he said. Moreno’s comments came after Miller posted a livestream video defending himself against the abuse accusations and saying his former wife had “significant mental-health challenges”. The senator also accused Miller of withholding a blue bunny from his small daughter that he said helped the toddler go to sleep – an allegation that drew a belligerent response from Miller when Tapper asked on The Lead if he had been guilty of “emotionally abusive behavior”. “I would agree that if that were true, that would be incredibly disturbing, and that the senator would be right,” Miller said. “However, he has taken two years to publicly acknowledge for me to resign from my seat. Why is that?” After a prolonged back-and-forth, Miller gave an unambiguous response when asked if Emily Moreno and two other women – including Stephanie Grisham, a former White House spokesperson in Trump’s first presidency – had lied in accusing him of treating them violently. “Yes, it’s very easy … Every single time, and people have asked me, what are you going to do? Are you going to drop out of this race? Are you going to resign? Are you going to get out before the deadline? And my answer to you, Jake, is no, and I can tell you why. “In 2016, when President Donald J Trump faced the most extreme allegations in the world that hit him day after day after day, and people in the media, very much like yourself and others, said that he would have no shot at winning, that he should not be the president of the United States. But guess what? He stayed in, and he was resilient. “So for no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations, and be pushed out of the seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community.” Yet a series of public statements from Moreno’s fellow Republican senators indicate that their sympathies are with him. “[Miller] should resign. He should quit,” Roger Marshall, a senator from Kansas, told Politico. “I don’t know Mr Miller’s story, but I trust Bernie [Moreno] so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values.” The West Virginia senator Shelley Moore Capito said: “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.” Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said: “The accusations are very serious, and if there is truth to them, I am one who says that our elected officials need to be held to high standards. “And certainly, when it comes to allegations of domestic abuse, child abuse, that’s not what we want in our lawmakers.” Three other senators, Rick Scott of Florida, West Virginia’s Jim Justice and Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, also gave public backing to Moreno against Miller. “I don’t know enough about the allegations, but like Bernie said, it sounds like he thinks he needs psychological help,” said Scott. “I trust Bernie.” Miller – who married Emily Moreno at Trump’s club in Bedminster, New Jersey, in 2022 – has been accused of holding a gun to her head and scalding her with boiling water. Their toddler daughter, who was born in 2023, is also said to have suffered a broken collarbone due to his actions. Miller denies allegations of abuse and has filed a defamation case against his wife over the claims. The couple divorced in 2025. Axios reported that Trump called Miller on Monday amid concerns that the situation threatened Republican chances of holding the congressional seat in November’s midterms, when the party already faces an uphill challenge to keep its wafer-thin majority in the House of Representatives. But the president avoided taking sides when asked about the issue by reporters in the White House. “I know Max, he’s a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I’m going to let the families figure that out,” he said. Miller has resisted calls for him to withdraw from the race and told the Wall Street Journal that Trump “was supportive of me over the phone” on Monday’s call. “He said he had a poll with no detail, and I pushed back with our poll that has us winning by 9 with our message out there,” Miller told the newspaper. “He kept on reiterating it’s going to be tough, and it’s going to be a really hard one for you.” If Miller were to remove his name from the ballot before the close of business on Tuesday, a special Republican primary would be held to replace him. If he were to withdraw after that, the party would still need to replace him by 10 August, but would need to give two days’ notice beforehand to hold a meeting to choose a substitute candidate. • In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud
body_text: Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election. The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassador Daniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. “We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said. The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.” The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump. Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.” Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before the first round of the election, on 4 October. The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country. “President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.” The latest confrontation follows Brazil’s refusal last month to issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides. The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression. Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time. Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”. The row is particularly sensitive because Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election. The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region. Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met. Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family. The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government. Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.

title: Wesley Bell wins Missouri House primary as Cori Bush comeback bid fails
body_text: The Democratic congressman Wesley Bell won his primary in the St Louis area on Tuesday, ending the progressive former representative Cori Bush’s bid for a comeback and blunting the momentum pro-Palestinian candidates have shown in recent elections. Bell unseated Bush, a democratic socialist who opposes aid to the US ally and accuses it of committing a genocide in Gaza, in the Democratic congressional primary two years ago with the help of millions of dollars in spending from pro-Israel groups. Their rematch this year came amid a spate of primary defeats of Democratic incumbents at the hands of progressive outsiders. On Tuesday, according to the Associated Press, Bell prevailed in the heavily Democratic district, making him the favorite to win a second term in the November election. “St Louis is up against a president that is coming after our healthcare, our due process and the paychecks of working families,” he said, vowing to “keep standing up to this reckless and cruel administration every single day”. Amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, Bell’s victory bucks the trend, notching a win for moderate and pro-Israel Democrats. “Tonight’s result is another clear victory for Democrats who are focused on delivering results,” said the New Democrat Majority, a political action committee (Pac) that supports the centrist New Democrat Coalition, which invested $1m in the contest to defeat Bush. “Wesley Bell is focused on fighting to deliver for Missouri families, not fighting his own party.” Bush was first elected to the House in 2020 and served two terms as a member of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers of color. The former congresswoman had sought to make the race a referendum on Bell’s support for US aid to Israel, working to channel progressive fury over pro-Israel spending on her opponent’s behalf. The United Democracy Project, a Super Pac aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), poured about $3m into helping Bell’s campaign overwhelm Bush on the airwaves. In a post on X, Aipac congratulated Bell on his victory. Bell was also backed by House Democratic leadership and the Congressional Black caucus, while Bush drew support from the Democratic Socialists of America and other progressive groups. The two candidates had squared off over who would better stand up to Donald Trump and spur growth in the St Louis region, which is managing the aftermath of a deadly tornado last year. title: Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez survives Washington’s crowded primary
body_text: The Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez secured one of two spots in Washington state’s crowded all-party primary, overcoming criticism from both the left and the right to advance in one of November’s most closely watched US congressional races. The two-term Democrat – known for bucking her party on key issues – heads into the general election as she seeks to defend a district carried by Donald Trump in 2024 and a seat that remains central to the battle for control of the House of Representatives. She will face the Republican state senator John Braun in November. Gluesenkamp Perez faced competing ideological pressures in a sprawling field that included Braun, a navy veteran backed by Trump, and progressive Democrat Brent Hennrich, who mounted a challenge from the left, arguing the US congresswoman had drifted too far from the Democratic party. Six other candidates also appeared on the primary ballot. Under Washington’s primary system, the top two finishers advance regardless of party. “Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is an authentic, independent leader who is fiercely loyal to south-west Washington,” the Washington representative Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in a statement. “Marie is focused on the issues that matter most to her community, like lowering costs for families, revitalizing Washington’s timber economy, and investing in rural schools and infrastructure.” Gluesenkamp Perez, who has carved out a distinctive political profile, is viewed as one of the most vulnerable House Democrats. Since flipping the Republican-held seat in 2022, she has built support among moderates, independents and some Republican voters, often emphasizing her background as the co-owner of an auto repair shop and breaking with her party on high-profile issues such as immigration, transgender rights and Trump’s elections overhaul bill, known as the Save Act. That approach, however, increasingly alienated parts of her own party. Progressive critics argued she has too often sided with the president and Republicans, while supporters countered that her willingness to stake out opposing views reflected the realities of a district that has consistently backed Trump for president, most recently by about three points. They argue that ideological purity is less important than maintaining a foothold in Trump territory – and a seat that could ultimately help deliver Democrats the House majority in November. In 2024, Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of Kamala Harris, her party’s presidential nominee. Democrats hope Trump’s poor approval ratings, and frustration with the economy and the US-Israel war on Iran, will help propel them to power in Congress by winning control of the House and possibly even the Senate. But Republicans see the seat as one of their top pickup opportunities. “John Braun is a navy veteran and job creator, and in November south-west Washington will send Perez’s sputtering political career straight to the scrapyard,” Christian Martinez, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement.

title: El-Sayed holds narrow lead in Michigan Senate primary but race too close to call
body_text: The marquee race for the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan remained too close to call on Tuesday night, with Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, holding a narrow lead over congresswoman Haley Stevens. The battleground state is crucial to the party’s hopes of winning back control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections. The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face the Republican nominee, former representative Mike Rogers, in November, to succeed the retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters. As ballot counting continued into the early hours of Wednesday morning, hundreds of restless El-Sayed supporters remained at the election watch party at the Majestic Theater in Detroit, as his lead over Stevens remained at a few percentage points. At about 4am local time, El-Sayed had 48.7% of the vote and Stevens 47.3%, with 95% counted, according to the Associated Press. In remarks to supporters, El-Sayed turned his attention from the contentious primary against Stevens to the Republican nominee. He called for the party to unite against Rogers, who he assailed as a “corporate sellout” who “should never see the inside of the US senate”. “We’re going to have to wait a little longer to see the outcome of this race,” El-Sayed said, “but as I look in front of me, I already see the outcome.” Hasan Piker, the streamer and new Democratic kingmaker, as well as the Democratic nominee for Philadelphia’s third district, Chris Rabb, and the Democratic nominee for Colorado’s 1st district, Melat Kiros, were among the crowd listening to El-Sayed speak at length about his American story as the son of Egyptian immigrants. With 13 weeks left before November, El-Sayed argued that however much his supporters may disagree with his Democratic opponent, there was more uniting the left than dividing it. “However we might feel about the campaign we’ve just come through, I want you to understand that it pales in comparison to the cynicism, in comparison to the corporatism, in comparison to the lies that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump are going to tell,” he said. Nearby, at the Hotel Saint Regis, an upbeat Stevens told supporters at her election night event that results may not come until later Wednesday morning. “We knew that this was going to be a close race, and that’s exactly what we’ve got,” she said. “But friends,” she said to loud cheers from the room, “I am feeling good about this race.” El-Sayed, 41, built a grassroots campaign statewide on a message of universal healthcare and getting money out of politics. Stevens, 43, cast herself as a pragmatic problem-solver, and saw her campaign boosted by tens of millions of dollars in outside spending, including from groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), the pro-Israel lobbying organization. Rogers, a former Michigan congressman who was also the Republican nominee for Senate in 2024 when he lost to Elissa Slotkin, ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Mallory McMorrow, a Democrat who dropped out of Michigan’s Democratic primary race in July, said it was vital for the party to come together after a bruising campaign to help the ticket win in November. “I voted for great Democrats up and down the ballot, and I made a commitment that whoever wins the Senate race tonight, I will be endorsing as soon as that race is called,” she told CNN. “I will be headed to their election night party to show we all come together after whatever happens tonight, so that we can be a team as we head in November.” McMorrow later endorsed El-Sayed. “Abdul has my full endorsement and support,” she wrote on social media. “This was a brutal primary (believe me, I know). And Trump and Mike Rogers are counting on us staying divided. Let’s prove them wrong by beating Mike Rogers and taking our country back.” With ballots still being counted, the results in Michigan – and in four other states holding elections, including Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington state – were coming into focus. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic secretary of state, will face John James, a Donald Trump-endorsed congressman, in the state’s open governor’s race after Gretchen Whitmer faced term limits. James has denied the results of the 2020 election where Joe Biden won; most recently, alongside Trump at a rally, James claimed Trump had won Michigan “three times”. In Michigan’s seventh congressional district, progressive organizer William Lawrence beat out two more moderate candidates, former US ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal. Lawrence secured an endorsement from Bernie Sanders, the progressive Vermont senator. A challenge to the incumbent representative Shri Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th district by Detroit state representative Donavan McKinney remained too close to call. In Missouri and Washington state, the Democratic establishment struck back, blunting a string of progressive victories. In Missouri’s first congressional district, the Democratic congressman Wesley Bell defeated the progressive former representative Cori Bush in a rematch for the St Louis-based seat. Bush had sought to make the contest a referendum on pro-Israel spending and the war in Gaza. “When we think about all of the division that we hear, I think it is important that we focus on what this place can be,” Bell said after his race was called. Meanwhile, in Washington’s third congressional district, blue dog representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fended off a progressive challenger in her battleground district, prevailing in a crowded all-party primary. She will face Republican John Braun in November. Missouri voters also rejected an amendment that would have required citizens’ initiatives to pass in all congressional districts rather than by a simple statewide majority. In Kansas, state senator Cindy Holscher won the Democratic nomination in the gubernatorial race, beating two other politicians to advance to the general election. And in Virginia, Shannon Taylor won in the first congressional district and Elaine Luria won in the second congressional district, in wins for moderate Democrats.

title: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy
body_text: On Thursday, 23 July, after weeks of escalating attacks between the US and Iran, Donald Trump told a reporter that Iran hadn’t received “enough pain yet”, and he leveled a threat. “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before,” he warned. “I am close to making a decision.” Then, on Monday 27 July, he called it off. A few days later, on Friday 31 July, Trump said: “We’ll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they’re going to say: ‘We just can’t take it any more.’” This time, it took him just one day to back down. Here we go again. Ever since the US and Israel launched their latest war on Iran on 28 February, the people of the planet have been subjected to Donald Trump’s on-again off-again relationship with raining down catastrophic destruction on the nation. It started on 21 March, when Trump promised to hit Iranian power plants (a war crime, incidentally) unless Iran opened the strait of Hormuz. He delayed that plan for five days, and then another 10 days, before issuing his next threat. That was on 7 April, when he wrote: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.” A mere 10 hours later, he walked back that (genocidal) threat. On 17 May, he wrote: “For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won’t be anything left of them. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE!” On 18 May, he wrote that he had been asked by Gulf leaders to “hold off on our planned Military attack of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which was scheduled for tomorrow”. The approach seems as tedious as it does childish, constantly threatening one thing only to back down in a cringey, face-saving effort shortly thereafter. Let’s call it what it is: kindergarten diplomacy. From appearances, it would seem that Trump considers this a strategy. One can only assume he holds out hope that it will achieve an end to this catastrophic conflagration he and Benjamin Netanyahu began. The war is a massive failure, plunging his popularity along with American regional dominance in the Middle East. What’s clear is that Trump hasn’t a clue about how to exit a war he never should have started in the first place. Leadership is needed when difficult decisions must be made, but Trump is not capable of such resolve. Instead, he seems primarily driven to make pronouncements based on the last person he talked to. When Netanyahu visited him in the Oval Office on 21 July, the Israeli prime minister discussed three options for the war with Trump, according to reports: “a (negotiated) deal, continuing the blockade and economic pressures, and a massive strike”, is how a senior Israeli official described the meeting to Reuters. (Let’s not forget that Netanyahu helped convince Trump to start this war back in February.) Two days later, Trump threatened a massive strike (then called it off, then threatened it again). When the president’s threat reappeared, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on 1 August to argue for de-escalation. Guess what? To no one’s surprise, Trump backed down again. Nixon had his madman theory, in which he sought to project an image of himself as unhinged and irrational to frighten the Soviet Union into concessions. Trump, whether he knows it or not, is turning indecision into his own presidential doctrine. Such indecision is probably in part a reflection of Trump’s unflagging desire to please influential people around him. Trump’s deep-seated need to be liked by those he perceives to be powerful or popular (see: Trump’s meeting with Zohran Mamdani) is, I think, often underappreciated. But there is more behind Trump’s indecision as well. This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split, as if by a lightning bolt, by the question. Vice-President JD Vance has been the most skeptical in the president’s inner circle of the war. Ever aware of the political winds, the vice-president is said to be carefully watching the rising rightwing criticism of Israel, due in part to this war. Vance went on the popular podcast The Joe Rogan Experience in mid-July and claimed that there was an Israeli government campaign to shape popular opinion in the US about the war. “There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” he said. “Not toward any objective, but just indefinitely.” Ever the faithful lieutenant to Trump, Marco Rubio, on the other hand, told Lara Trump on Fox News that the Iranian regime “has never faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action”. Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner (along with Vance and their fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff) favors reducing the conflict, thereby lowering gas prices and limiting the danger to US armed forces, but just until after the midterm elections, when the war could potentially be ramped up again, according to Israel Hayom. The chairperson of the joint chiefs of staff, Gen Dan Caine, who counseled the president against the war in the first place, is now warning that stockpiles for air defense interceptors are dangerously low due to the war in Iran, putting the men and women in the US military at greater risk. Meanwhile, the Memorandum of Understanding that the US signed with Iran in June has been the subject of fierce Republican opposition, with the Louisiana Republican senator Bill Cassidy calling it “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades”. Even Trump loyalists such as the Texas senator Ted Cruz criticized the memorandum, saying: “The president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal.” And the Maga faithful have grown cold on the war, with only about a third of its voters believing the war is worth the economic cost, according to a Politico poll. Add to this the fact that CNN is now reporting that US military leadership is basically out of ideas about how to proceed with Iran at this point and is soliciting, via a crowdsourcing-type email sent to a group of military analysts, “new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. The report also explains that Trump “has been considering strikes akin to a ‘fireworks’ display’”, which would suggest “a symbolic victory that would allow him to exit the war without actually accomplishing one of his initial aims: ridding Iran of its nuclear program”. Charting a course through the stormy winds of political decision making is what presidents must do all the time. A debacle like the war in Iran, begun with a terrible decision and bringing much unnecessary harm to the people of the region, must eventually be followed by a brave one, however painful it is to this nation or its leadership. A responsible president would make such a choice, even when difficult, and explain the reasoning to the nation. We, unfortunately, do not have serious leaders. And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

title: First Thing: Michigan Democratic race in the balance with El-Sayed holding narrow lead
body_text: Good morning. A Democratic Senate primary in Michigan remains too close to call, with Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, holding a narrow lead over the establishment-backed congresswoman Haley Stevens. The battleground state is crucial to the party’s hopes of winning back control of the Senate in November. At about 4am local time, El-Sayed had 48.7% of the vote and Stevens 47.3%, with 95% of votes counted, according to the Associated Press. In remarks to supporters, El-Sayed said: “We’re going to have to wait a little longer to see the outcome of this race, but as I look in front of me, I already see [it].” In Missouri, the Democratic congressman Wesley Bell won his primary, ending the progressive former representative Cori Bush’s comeback attempt and blunting the momentum that pro-Palestinian candidates have shown in recent elections. Who won in the crowded primary in Washington state? The Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez secured one of two spots in the all-party primary, overcoming criticism from both the left and the right. She will face the Republican state senator John Braun in November. Why are citizens being denied a voice in Missouri? The state’s top election official has rejected a petition seeking a statewide referendum on redistricting. Hundreds of thousands of petition signatures had been submitted in an effort to force a vote on whether to use a new US House map approved by the Republican-led state legislature. The Republican secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, said the number submitted did not matter because challenging a congressional map was unconstitutional under Missouri law. US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US, in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The administration stopped short of expelling Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti. The confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, with their governments sharply diverging over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region. Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. What is the dispute about? The US Department of State said Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brasília’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Brazil and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats. Brasília swiftly condemned the decision, calling it part of a deliberate campaign to influence the outcome of the presidential election in Brazil this October. Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Flávio Bolsonaro, the senator son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro and a close political ally of Trump. OpenAI pays $3.2m to settle claims it discriminated against US workers OpenAI and a subsidiary will pay $3.2m to settle US government claims they ⁠favored foreign workers with temporary employment visas and discriminated against US job applicants in recruiting and hiring, the justice department has said. The assistant attorney general Harmeet Dhillon said: “This substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so US workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions.” OpenAI did ‌not immediately respond to ‌a request for comment. The company denied wrongdoing in the settlement agreement. El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of 2027 About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting. This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices caused by the Iran war. Even if the forecasted El Niño is less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme said on Wednesday. In other news … A Russian attack on Kyiv has killed at least 17 people after Ukraine was unable to shoot down any incoming missiles. The intensifying attacks have prompted Kyiv to plead for more US-made Patriot interceptors. The celebrity blogger Perez Hilton has been hospitalised after apparently livestreaming acts of self-harm on TikTok. The Trump ally Mike Lindell is leaving his role with the MyPillow company to focus on his campaign to become the next governor of Minnesota. Lindell has spent millions of dollars trying to prove the 2020 election was rife with fraud. An armed man has been arrested at Trump’s California golf course. Jeanine John Taele allegedly took photos and videos of the property days before the president’s visit. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the scope of the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak in the US to 15 states. Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina are now said to be affected. title: Republican Chuck Edwards drops bid for re-election after report finding sexual harassment of staffers
body_text: Chuck Edwards announced he would not run for re-election after the US House of Representatives ethics committee determined the US congressman “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. Edwards, a Republican for North Carolina, said he would complete his current term, which is due to end in January. In a statement posted on social media early on Wednesday morning, Edwards said: “After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term. Serving western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support.” The bipartisan congressional ethics panel recommended on Monday that Edwards face censure over its findings. Should the House agree, he will have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The ethics committee launched an investigation into Edwards earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, it said there was “substantial reason to believe” that Edwards had broken House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior probably violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. Edwards was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week the election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up”, in a sign of improving Democratic chances.

title: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary in defining race for Democrats
body_text: Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan, becoming the latest leftwing candidate to capture the party’s nomination ahead of November’s midterm elections. El-Sayed, a progressive, beat Haley Stevens, a moderate US representative backed by the party’s establishment. He will now face Republican Mike Rogers in the race to represent the midwestern purple state in the Senate. The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday morning, moments after Stevens’s campaign said she had called El-Sayed to concede. El-Sayed succeeded by a relatively close margin, in a sign that battleground state voters are still grappling over the direction of the Democratic party. Michigan voters also delivered victories for other progressive candidates, nominating climate activist William Lawrence and Donavan McKinney, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, both of whom are backed by Bernie Sanders in their bids for seats in the House of Representatives. Donald Trump won Michigan in 2016 and 2024, though Joe Biden won it in 2020. Both the state’s current senators are Democrats and retaining the seat remains critical to Democrats’ hopes of winning back the US Senate this year, and a crucial part of the map for the 2028 presidential election. El-Sayed, 41, is a former public health official who centered his run on the Medicare for All model of universal healthcare, while confronting heavy outside spending against him, which became another theme of the race. Stevens, meanwhile, touted her work on the US auto rescue taskforce, where she served as chief of staff. Rogers, a former congressman from the state, was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024, when he lost to the senator Elissa Slotkin. Should he win in November, and beat Rogers in the general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator. While he is not a democratic socialist, his primary win came amid a wave of wins by democratic socialist candidates elsewhere in the country. He has said he is a “capitalist who understands how capitalism works”, and who wants to regulate monopolies. “They spent an unprecedented amount of money to beat us,” El-Sayed said at a press conference on Wednesday, referring to the tens of millions of dollars in spending against him. “But it turns out the commercials are the part of the television show most people don’t want to watch. “We took on a machine. You’re not supposed to be able to beat $70m of outside spending, a record amount of money spent in a campaign against a Democrat in a primary, in any campaign. You’re not supposed to be able to beat that. And what we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.” Stevens saw the backing of establishment Democrats, including Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, while El-Sayed received endorsements from prominent progressives such as Sanders. In a statement on Wednesday, Stevens said: “I love Michigan and am so proud to have put up my hand to serve. I spoke with Abdul a few moments ago to offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November.” Until earlier this summer, the race was a three-way race with Mallory McMorrow, a state senator who eventually dropped out. Early Wednesday, McMorrow threw her support behind El-Sayed. “I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party,” she said in a statement. The role of Black voters in the Democratic primary came into focus in the final weeks of campaigning, with both candidates seeking to turn out the vote in Black communities, which make up about one-fifth of the Democratic primary electorate, via events at churches and festivals. More than $40m poured into the race from outside groups supporting Stevens or attacking El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby. Some ads elevated Stevens’s connection to Barack Obama on the auto rescue, which voters have seen as a quasi-endorsement, despite Obama not formally endorsing in the race. Trump celebrated El-Sayed’s victory on Tuesday, claiming it was “great news” for Republicans in a post on his Truth Social platform. The president went on to call El-Sayed a “communist loser who hates Jews and Israel”, despite the Democratic nominee’s frequent denunciations of antisemitism. “Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Trump wrote. Shortly after 1am, when the race remained too close to call, El-Sayed took the stage at Detroit’s Majestic Theater to Tupac Shakur’s Changes, telling hundreds of supporters to stay patient as the votes were being counted. Instead, he cast his contest with Stevens as proof that a grassroots campaign could compete against unprecedented outside spending. “We’re still standing,” he told the raucous crowd, arguing Michigan voters were motivated less by ideological divides than by the rising cost of rent, groceries and healthcare. The political streamer Hasan Piker, the democratic nominee for Philadelphia’s third district, Chris Rabb, and Colorado Democratic nominee, Melat Kiros, were in the room. Rabb said he believed El-Sayed’s campaign reflected a broader shift inside the Democratic party, pointing to recent victories by progressive candidates including Zohran Mamdani in New York and Adam Hamawy in New Jersey. “This is not just among coastal elites,” Rabb said. “That’s something that could benefit Democrats if they have the collective wisdom to move us forward, not left or right. Because if they don’t learn this lesson, it’ll be through all of our defeats.” More than 1.2 million Michiganders cast ballots before election day, including nearly 139,000 who voted during the state’s nine-day early in-person voting period, a number that doubles 2024’s primary, according to the Michigan department of state. Rabb argued that unusually strong early turnout suggested the campaign was expanding the Democratic coalition rather than simply energizing existing voters. He said voters were turning out “because they believe in this brother”, adding that Democrats should see the result as evidence that “our base is radically expanding to folks who have not been seen, heard, or respected”. During his speech in the early hours of Wednesday, El-Sayed sought to lower the temperature of the bitter primary, calling on his supporters to unite behind the eventual Democratic nominee against Rogers. “Tomorrow we begin to mend fences,” he said. “There is so much more that unites us than divides us.”

title: Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their future
body_text: In the final stretch of the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate, Abdul El-Sayed challenged voters at a small event in rural Michigan to think about the message they could send the rest of the country when they cast their ballots. “Who are we? Who do we want to be?” El-Sayed said. “Do we want a state that’s defined by how much money corporations brought in to tell us what we couldn’t have? Or do we want to be a state where we demonstrate to the rest of the country what’s possible when you build a movement of, by and for the people?” On Tuesday, El-Sayed’s vision cleared its first hurdle: he won the primary over moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by the party’s establishment, and tens of millions of dollars in outside spending. His rise, and victory, could serve as a revision to how the political establishment views swing-state politics – not requiring candidates to run from the center, but articulating how you will materially improve people’s lives as the working and middle classes struggle with affordability and rising healthcare costs. A contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits. El-Sayed led by 48.5% to 47.5% over Stevens when the race was called. The narrow margin, in addition to more than 60,000 votes for a candidate who dropped out altogether, suggest he will have to unite the party, and convince more independent and even right-leaning voters in a swing state, to beat Republican Mike Rogers. But the race solidified a growing anti-establishment sentiment on the party’s left, where activists and supporters have sought a proactive vision that doesn’t rely on the pre-Trump status quo, apparent in a string of wins for insurgent candidates. There’s a sense that systems were already broken before Trump’s rise, and a return to those norms won’t serve everyday Americans. They’re looking for politicians who can call out their own party’s orthodoxies, and challenge the big money that haunts US politics. Michigan voters found it in El-Sayed, who centered his campaign around universal healthcare, and wasn’t shy about calling the war in Gaza a genocide. “It doesn’t limit us to just what we think is possible, but it changes what we think is possible,” said David Sernick, a voter in Detroit who supported El-Sayed. El-Sayed first ran for office in 2018, losing to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor of Michigan, in a Democratic primary. This time, he built a grassroots machine, barnstorming the state with in-person rallies while delivering clippable moments for social media feeds. His campaign knocked on more than 200,000 doors and made more than 1m phone calls, aided by leftwing groups such as the Working Families party and Indivisible chapters. El-Sayed held more than 500 campaign events and visited 150 churches. People like Racquel Garcia, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, Michigan, said his willingness to show up underpinned their vote. El-Sayed worked as a public health official in Detroit and in Wayne county, and would show up at permit hearings and represent the people, she said. “Every time we meet with the city of Detroit officials, we’re like, ‘we need you to be like him’,” said Garcia. “You’re here to protect us, not to protect industry. So we’ve been wanting him in office. We were happy that he’s real.” Andy Levin, a former congressman from Michigan who lost to Stevens in 2022 after their districts were redrawn, said the moment rejected a “static notion of electability” that stems from a politics of anxiety and fear. “They want authenticity, they want truth telling and they want brave policy, not just proposals but action, so they can breathe in their lives,” Levin told Democracy Now. “This is a movement of Americans who are saying, enough of politics as usual.” Roy Harris, who voted in Detroit on Tuesday but wouldn’t say for whom, detailed how it was time for a change. “First-time homebuyers can’t buy a house – $400,000, first time you going out, nobody can afford that,” he said. “I’m tired of paying $4 for gas, and I am looking for a change. And I hope the new regime coming in brings that to us.” In Washington, El-Sayed’s effort to win the US Senate race in Michigan is critical for Democrats’ ambitious hopes of retaking control of the upper chamber, and will be closely watched by all factions of the left as a bellwether for the party’s future. Michigan voted for Trump, then Biden, and then Trump, in presidential elections. It is firmly a swing state. If El-Sayed, an unabashed progressive who frequently notes he has a “funny name”, can win a statewide general election, it could remake the contours of the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment and pundit class will call him, and his ideas, too extreme – a cautionary tale for play-it-safe politics. In other parts of the country, moderates won their Democratic primaries, including blue-dog Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in a purple district in Washington state, who staved off a progressive challenge, and Wesley Bell, who saw off a challenge from Cori Bush, a former representative. Chris Rabb, a progressive who won a contested primary for a US congressional seat in Pennsylvania, recently noted the high bar people from his branch of the party face as they seek to challenge moderates. “Nobody asks ‘centrist’ Dems to explain their losses,” Rabb wrote on X. “They lose purple districts every cycle & Beltway pundits call it ‘a tough map’. Progressives lose one major race & Dem operatives call us electoral pariahs. It’s a specious double standard.” Meanwhile, the attack lines from the right have already been drawn. Rogers posted an AI-generated video of El-Sayed, depicting him as Odysseus among other prominent Democrats inside a Trojan horse, and saying “don’t let communism into Michigan”. A Republican has not won a US Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. The Republican National Committee called El-Sayed “Michigan’s Mamdani” and said the race “pits common sense against crazy”. El-Sayed himself remains confident. In November, he is counting on turning out people who normally turn off from politics because they’re cynical, or believe the system cannot change in a way that would make their lives better. “The goal now is not to dunk on anybody, the goal now is to come together so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said.

title: Progressive climate organizer William Lawrence wins Michigan Democratic House primary
body_text: William Lawrence, a prominent environmental organizer who foregrounded his support for a datacenter moratorium, has won the Democratic primary in Michigan’s seventh congressional district in a victory for progressives. Lawrence was a co-founder of the youth-led climate justice organization the Sunrise Movement, the group that in 2018 mainstreamed calls for a Green New Deal to battle economic injustice while rapidly phasing out planet-warming fossil fuels. The 36-year-old defeated Bridget Brink, a former US ambassador to Ukraine and Slovakia, and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal and military aide to Barack Obama. In the November general election, Lawrence will face off with incumbent Republican Tom Barrett. Lawrence secured endorsements from Senator Bernie Sanders, as well as Representative Rashida Tlaib and progressive US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed,. On the campaign trail, he highlighted his support for universal healthcare, boosting taxes on billionaires and ending the war in Iran and arms sales to Israel. But his biggest focus may have been his opposition to the unchecked build-out of AI datacenters; he focused on the issue in his first television ad. “Will made opposing datacenter development a core part of this campaign and it helped power him to victory all across the district, including massive margins in small towns where DC insiders didn’t expect him to compete,” Stevie O’Hanlon, Lawrence’s campaign manager, said. “In Mason, where one datacenter is being proposed, Will won with 49% of the vote in a three-way race.” In May, Lawrence said “datacenters put a tremendous, unprecedented and unexpected burden on the grid to increase overall demand” and that there is “no plan to do that in a clean way”. Survey research conducted by the left-learning polling firm Data for Progress found that 63% of US voters, including 66% of independents and 47% of Republicans, were more likely to support a candidate calling for pausing datacenter construction. “Tonight the people of Michigan’s 7th district sent a clear message: They are tired of Silicon Valley billionaires and D.C. insiders determining the future of our towns and our country,” he said in a Tuesday night statement. “They want an unbought representative who isn’t afraid to stand up to leaders of both parties and fight for working people.” Lawrence’s district in central Michigan is one of just 18 House seats that the Cook Political Report called “toss-ups”. Barrett has often voted with Trump. “Tom Barrett may have the high-powered DC consultants and corporate CEOs in his corner, but our movement is made up of real Michiganders, coming together across political differences,” Lawrence said in his election night statement.
