title: What we learned from midterm primary elections in five key states
body_text: Tuesday’s primary elections in five states will be looked back on as a marquee moment ahead of November’s midterm elections, as voters in Michigan, Washington, Virginia, Kansas and Missouri selected candidates for races that could decide which party wins control of Congress. Here’s a rundown of what we learned from the results: Progressives thought their Michigan Senate candidate would be a shoo-in – but his victory was narrow Michigan was the site of a bitterly contested Democratic Senate primary in which the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens faced former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, in a state that Donald Trump won two years ago. Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, polls showed El-Sayed with a firm lead over Stevens, who had the backing of Governor Gretchen Whitmer as well as the top Senate Democrat, Chuck Schumer, and his campaign projected confidence accordingly. But the election turned out to be a squeaker, with El-Sayed winning 48.5% of the vote to Stevens’s 47.5%, the Associated Press reports, far from the blowout polling appeared to show. Republicans nominated former congressman Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost the race for the state’s other Senate seat two years ago. The left’s momentum remains strong … El-Sayed’s victory underscored the continued momentum of progressive candidates, who have been on a roll in primaries in New York and Colorado as they harnessed discontent among Democrats with party leadership and their traditional support for Israel. Adding to the movement’s trophies was William Lawrence, the co-founder of the climate change activist group the Sunrise Movement, who clinched the Democratic nomination for the battleground seventh congressional district in central Michigan. In Detroit, progressive Donavan McKinney succeeded in ousting Congressman Shri Thanedar, who had been backed by groups aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). … but not unstoppable Leftwing challengers did not triumph everywhere. In Missouri, voters in the St Louis area rejected former congresswoman Cori Bush’s attempt at a political comeback and renominated the incumbent Wesley Bell, who unseated her two years ago with the help of spending from pro-Israel groups. Bush, a progressive who believes the US ally committed a genocide in Gaza, attempted to harness dislike of Israel among primary voters to her advantage against Bell, who received heavy backing from an Aipac-linked Super Pac. But she lost badly, receiving not even 40% of the vote. In Washington, Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the few Democrats holding on to a district that Trump won two years ago, clinched her primary against a crowded field that included a challenger to her left. Republicans asked too much of their own voters Missouri’s Republican leaders had backed a ballot initiative that would have made it more difficult for state constitutional amendments to pass, after their voters in recent years approved abortion protections, paid sick leave and cannabis legalization at the ballot box. That measure was rejected by a whopping 80% vote, as was an attempt to phase out the state income tax, by a similarly huge margin. And four years after voters in heavily Republican Kansas approved abortion protections in the state constitution, they turned back a GOP-backed attempt to have state supreme court judges popularly elected rather than appointed by the governor. The current bench had attracted Republican ire for issuing rulings against the party’s interests, including on abortion rights. Democrats in battleground Michigan are split all kinds of ways Michigan’s Democratic voters chose their fighters in Tuesday’s primary for a Senate race that could determine whether the party returns to the majority in the chamber, as well as for vital House races. But the primaries also underscored sharp divides among their backers over which brand of the Democratic party works best for them. Stevens’s strong primary performance shows El-Sayed has work to do to win over the centrist voters she courted, as well as those who preferred her views on Israel. The task is much the same for Lawrence, who triumphed over a divided field of moderate Democrats but now must convince voters to get on board with his progressive politics in a district that’s one of the most narrowly divided in the country.

title: Michigan nominates first trans woman for state legislature
body_text: A former megachurch pastor who endured 15 years of conversion practices is set to become the first transgender member of Michigan’s state legislature after winning a Democratic primary election on Tuesday. Joanna Whaley comfortably defeated Frank Liberati, a former state representative, and Gary Schlack in the primary for the second district of the Michigan statehouse, a Democratic stronghold. Earlier this year Liberati sought to have Whaley disqualified from the ballot over her name change but the Wayne county clerk’s office dismissed the challenge, finding that Whaley’s candidate affidavit was legal and proper. Sarah McBride, the first openly transgender member of the US Congress, posted on X on Wednesday: “So proud of my friend, Joanna Whaley! She faced indignities from her opponent, channeled the energy into knocking on doors, doubled down on her economic agenda, and she defeated that former Dem legislator (who took the low road against her) by 30+%! Way to go, Joanna!” Whaley, 38, who grew up in a Catholic family, previously spent nearly two decades working as a pastor at an evangelical megachurch. As she wrestled with her gender identity, the church forced her to undergo Christian conversion therapy with four different therapists over 15 years. In 2022 she was forced to quit when the church’s leaders discovered she was contemplating a gender transition. Whaley went to work for a more progressive church, shared her story on social media and launched a podcast. She also found work as a hospital chaplain in emergency rooms, intensive care units and hospice. Since deciding to run for state office, she has had some unusual meetings with potential campaign donors. She told the LGBTQ Nation website in April: “Some of those conversations go weird. We have a semi-pro hockey team in the area, and I was sitting down with one of the directors. In the middle of the conversation, he says, ‘So do you have a brother? I went to high school with someone named blah blah blah,’ and they said my dead name. I’m like, ‘That’s me.’ And they’re like, ‘Whoa, what?’” Whaley added: “It happens all the time. I’m honored by it, but at the same time, it does turn into some really weird and uncomfortable conversations, especially with some of my old Christian friends who then try to save my soul and tell me that I’m living in sin.” But in a separate interview with the Detroit Free Press newspaper, Whaley noted that some voters appreciate her historic candidacy: “It hits me when I’m talking to trans folks across the state. I’ll get in that conversation with someone across the state who just comes up and says, ‘Thank you,’ and I’m, ‘What are you thanking me for?’ “I understand in this moment in politics what it would mean to elect a trans woman could be monumental. I don’t take that responsibility lightly at all. I take it very seriously.” Whaley has earned endorsements from groups including the LGBTQ Victory Fund, Run for Something, Her Bold Move and Families United for Trans Rights. She will run against Republican Ronald Kokinda to replace Liberati’s brother, Tullio Liberati, in the statehouse in the 3 November general election.

title: Republican who withdrew last month beats Trump-backed rival in Michigan
body_text: Thomas Smith withdrew from the Republican primary contest for Michigan’s eighth district last month. On Tuesday, he won the nomination. Unofficial results show Smith with more than 50% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, defeating the man he endorsed, anti-abortion activist Al Lemmo, and the man Donald Trump endorsed, former federal law enforcement officer Amir Hassan. In a statement on Wednesday, Smith said he was “humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet”, the Democratic incumbent in the battleground House district. “I look forward to working with Speaker [Mike] Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s ‘America first’ agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again,” he added. In June, Trump endorsed Hassan, an African American navy veteran who worked for the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and Transportation. The president also appeared with Hassan at a campaign event in Michigan. Hassan said during his campaign that he had recently converted to Christianity from Islam. Nonetheless, social media commentary suggests Republican voters did not view Hassan’s conversion as authentic and were apprehensive about nominating a Muslim candidate. “It was a tough race, but over the last year I’ve had some incredible dealings with people across the entire district,” Hassan said in a video posted to X and Facebook. “The biggest conservative value is that we don’t make excuses.” In a statement, Joe Gruters, the chair of the Republican National Committee, congratulated Smith on a “hard-fought, well-earned primary victory”. Smith, who did little campaigning, posted on social media in July to endorse Lemmo, describing Hassan as a crypto-Republican. In Michigan, a US House candidate must withdraw their candidacy before 24 April for election officials to have enough time to remove their name from ballots. The Federal Election Commission has no electronic campaign finance filings from Smith. It does have a handwritten letter dated 12 July declaring $1,850 in fundraising. “I could not file this electronically because I have had no success logging in and have not been able to get a response from the helpdesk,” Smith wrote in a postscript on the letter. The Flint native and retired General Motors engineer made a brief appearance at a Republican unity event hosted in Macomb county by Mike Rogers, the party’s newly minted Senate candidate. Smith said he intended to “unseat communist comrade Rivet”. Though the victory on Tuesday of Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary has drawn national attention to progressive politics in Michigan, Rivet has signaled her relative moderation as one of 10 House Democrats to join Promise to America, a congressional initiative led by US representatives Tom Suozzi of New York and Adam Gray of California explicitly embracing capitalism and rejecting socialism. The congressional district along Michigan’s Saginaw River, connecting Flint to the Saginaw Bay, was one of 13 districts nationwide that voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election while also electing a Democratic representative to Congress.

Though the victory on Tuesday of Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary has drawn national attention to progressive politics in Michigan, Rivet has signaled her relative moderation as one of 10 House Democrats to join Promise to America, a congressional initiative led by US representatives Tom Suozzi of New York and Adam Gray of California explicitly embracing capitalism and rejecting socialism. The congressional district along Michigan’s Saginaw River, connecting Flint to the Saginaw Bay, was one of 13 districts nationwide that voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election while also electing a Democratic representative to Congress.

title: Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director
body_text: Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts. Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination. Donald Trump’s third pick to run the CDC, Schwartz is set to take the reins of the agency after a tumultuous period of leadership turnover, and amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines. At her confirmation hearing last month, senators pressed Schwartz on whether she would stand firm against any attempts by the health secretary to erode the scientific consensus around vaccines. She replied that she “will never betray the science” but generally deflected questions about how she would manage the relationship with Kennedy. “We need a CDC director that will ⁠actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization,” said Bill Cassidy, the committee’s Republican chair and a physician. Schwartz replied that Kennedy “will absolutely allow me to be CDC director”, and Cassidy later announced his support for her nomination. “There are challenges facing Americans’ health today. I will work with her to face those challenges and regain trust in the CDC,” Cassidy said after the Senate confirmed her. A navy veteran, Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, after positions in the United States Public Health Service where she was detailed to the Coast Guard, eventually becoming the force’s chief medical officer. Trump’s first nominee to lead the CDC, David Weldon, a former Florida congressman, was withdrawn by the White House in March 2025 just before his confirmation hearing. Schwartz will be the first permanent CDC director since Susan Monarez, Trump’s second pick, who was fired by Kennedy last year after less than a month over a clash on vaccine policy.

title: Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-Sayed
body_text: Leading Democrats quickly papered over whatever qualms they had about progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed after his win in the Michigan Senate primary was confirmed on Wednesday, instead welcoming the former public health official as their champion against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers. The state is now key to Democrats’s hopes of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. Winning in Michigan would put them on the path to snarling Donald Trump’s legislative agenda and blocking his judicial nominees for the final two years of his presidency, while defeat could undermine their prospects of gaining a majority in the chamber for years to come. Rogers lost a Senate race in Michigan two years ago by a slim margin to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. Schumer was among a long list of Democratic establishment figures who had rallied behind Stevens in the weeks before the vote, as polls showed her trailing El-Sayed. He ultimately prevailed but by a far slimmer margin than data indicated, winning by 48.5% to Stevens’s 47.5%. “There’s a lot of passion and energy in these primaries, and that’s a good thing. Democrats are ready to beat Republicans across the state,” said Governor Gretchen Whitmer, who had endorsed Stevens. “We’re all united by our shared goal of getting things done for the people in Michigan.” The easiest path for Democrats to win back the Senate – which Republicans control with 53 lawmakers to their 47 – requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Democratic leaders believe they have the right candidates to pull that off in North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska, but it will nonetheless be a tall order, given that all three states backed Trump in 2024, and the latter two by double-digit margins. Michigan’s Democratic senator Gary Peters, whose decision not to seek re-election had sparked the primary for his seat, backed Stevens as his replacement but quickly endorsed El-Sayed after his primary. “Both candidates ran strong campaigns focused on improving the lives of all Michiganders. But now it’s time to come together as a party and rally around our nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, to make sure Mike Rogers never sees the floor of the US Senate,” Peters said. In a statement released following her loss, Stevens congratulated El-Sayed but did not outright endorse him, instead indicating she was ready to campaign for him as well as Democrats vying to win swing districts in Michigan. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic party – and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan,” Stevens said. Republicans meanwhile pounced on El-Sayed’s views to paint him as too far left for voters in Michigan, a state that backed Trump in 2016 and again in 2024. “The choice this November is simple: common sense or complete insanity,” Rogers said. The former congressman blamed Democrats – who have held both of Michigan’s Senate seats since 2001 – for job losses in manufacturing, while saying El-Sayed “doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism.” The question of aid to Israel animated the primary, with Stevens arguing Democrats should continue backing the US’s top ally in the Middle East and El-Sayed calling for an end to military support in response to its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. The United Democracy Project, a Super Pac connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), spent more than $30m in the race to support Stevens and oppose El-Sayed, to no avail, and he now joins others in Denver, New York City, New Jersey and Philadelphia in having wooed Democratic voters in part by vowing to stand up for Palestinian rights. “Abdul’s victory is a win for everyone who supports equality, justice, and a thriving future for all,” said the IfNotNow Movement, a Jewish organization opposed to Israel’s policy towards Palestinians. “We urge those who see Abdul’s support for Palestinian human rights and blocking weapons to Israel as a threat to our community to reconsider. It is incredibly dangerous to conflate Jewish safety with support for Aipac or Israel’s military.” Brian Romick, president of the Democratic Majority for Israel Pac, called El-Sayed’s victory an indicator that “there is clearly strong anti-establishment energy this cycle, but no one should count pro-Israel Democrats out”. “While El-Sayed’s razor-thin victory in Michigan is disappointing, it was hardly the sweeping triumph he predicted or a mandate for his views,” Romick said, noting that Stevens lost only narrowly.

title: Why making Anthony Fauci the enemy will harm US public health for years
body_text: Katie Miller, an erstwhile Trump administration official and wife of Stephen Miller, once relied on Dr Anthony Fauci to get through Covid. Now, she’s calling for his imprisonment – a reversal that illuminates the politicization of Fauci and of public health writ large, a trend that could have major repercussions for America’s preparedness for future crises. A US Senate committee will vote on Thursday morning over whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after the physician and former public health official invoked his fifth amendment rights during a Senate hearing last week focused on Fauci’s actions during the Covid pandemic. The invocation of the worst days of the Covid pandemic comes as midterms loom and the administration struggles to address several infectious outbreaks, including cyclosporiasis and Ebola. Rand Paul, a senator, released contemporaneous notes that Fauci took during his time in public office, which Paul called Fauci’s diary, that reveal the confusion and fear of the time and illuminate the private episodes of a man who became known as America’s doctor. “By focusing entirely on one human being and by calling him all sorts of names, including ‘evil’, and by calling for him to be jailed, it abdicates Republicans’ own responsibility in the US response to the pandemic, which was under President Trump,” said Gavin Yamey, director of the Center for Policy Impact in Global Health at Duke University. “I think that this is all aimed at riling up the base ahead of the midterms and at washing their hands of any culpability themselves in the mass death event of Covid.” And it comes after substantial cuts to the public health infrastructure; misinformation has spread at the highest levels of the government, and growing outbreaks of measles, whooping cough, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and more. “This is an extraordinarily good way to distract people from the very deliberate destruction of the US public health system,” Yamey said. Like most Americans, Miller turned to Fauci for advice during the pandemic. As communications director for then-vice president Mike Pence, she was involved in the White House Covid-19 response. Fauci, who served as the director of the National Institute for Allergies and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), was also the chief medical adviser to seven presidents over three decades. Fauci described Miller warmly, writing that she was “great (tough, smart, but great)” on 25 March 2020, and that they “laugh at each other” in the Situation Room on 6 May 2020. When Miller tested positive for Covid, Fauci called to check on her several times a day. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote on 9 May 2020. Later, Fauci wrote that he had directly contacted Miller’s pediatricians to discuss the baby’s care. It is perhaps not surprising that Miller would turn to Fauci, as many others in the country also relied on his advice and insight during a deeply uncertain and terrifying time. But her actions contrast with the intensity and speed at which Covid was politicized – and the extent to which Fauci would draw conservatives’ ire, even years later. In February and March 2020, Miller was reassessing communications from the Covid taskforce, and Fauci was told to stand down on media appearances until he received clearance again. “That’s the episode that got tagged ‘muzzling Fauci’,” said Céline Gounder, editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News and a member of the Covid transition team under Biden. Soon after “deciding how much of Dr Fauci the public gets”, Miller was getting regular check-ins from Fauci on her own health, Gounder pointed out. “The same expertise: she’s rationing public access, but it’s available to her in private.” By April 2020, the pandemic was already being heavily politicized. The administration released plans for states to reopen, and President Trump posted a series of tweets encouraging supporters to “LIBERATE” blue states such as Minnesota, Michigan and Virginia. In late April, nearly half of Republicans (47%) surveyed by Pew Research Center said the pandemic was “made a bigger deal than it really is”. By June, that figure was 63%, and it rose to 66% in September. Republican attention to pandemic coverage went from 48% in March to 43% in late April to 35% by early June, while Democrats did not see any such changes. Spring 2020 looked similar across America; schools, for instance, were closed at about the same rate in red and blue states. But that changed by the fall, when “local partisanship predicted which districts would remain remote better than local Covid incidence did”, Gounder said. Those decisions were made not by Fauci, as he has been accused, but by about 13,349 public school districts, she pointed out in her newsletter, Underlying Conditions. “The more interesting story to me is who had private access to federal scientific expertise, what that access was worth in 2020, and what those same people have said about that expertise since,” Gounder said. She also pointed to early access to experimental treatments for Covid for Trump and his inner circle, nearly two months before they were available to the public. “A president publicly minimized a virus he was privately treated for with a drug the public couldn’t get,” Gounder said. Even after conservatives began publicly opposing his recommendations, the Millers still turned to Fauci for support. Fauci recounted speaking with Miller multiple times in October 2020, after her husband tested positive for Covid and she was traveling. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote on 6 October 2020. “Am on phone frequently with Katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on 31 December 2020. Katie Miller has since come out forcefully against Fauci. On the Covid taskforce, “Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Miller wrote in September 2025 in an apparent reference to wearing a face mask. In June, she said “he should be in jail”. After Fauci’s notes were made public, Miller claimed Fauci used the pandemic to “maximize his popularity”, and she endorsed calls to prosecute him. She told Notus she kept Fauci close so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”, though she didn’t specify what Fauci might leak. “Dr. Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponized my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandize himself,” Miller posted on Thursday, adding that “this man should be in prison”. Fauci has led the US through epidemics and pandemics over the decades: anthrax attacks in 2001, HIV, Sars, Ebola, Covid-19 and more, and he co-authored one of the most esteemed internal medicine textbooks. “We lose a lot when we see Republicans vilify Tony Fauci,” Yamey said. The US wasn’t unsafe because of Fauci’s leadership, Gounder said. “It wasn’t safe to leave home because a novel airborne virus was circulating in a population with no immunity, no vaccine, and no treatment.” And the Trump administration’s politicization and mismanagement “raised the toll”, she added. The trials facing Fauci make it less likely that others will step forward to guide public health, now or during a crisis. There were 1,499 harassment events across 583 local health departments between March 2020 and January 2021, and 222 officials left the field because of the targeting, Gounder pointed out. About 71% of the public health workforce reported at least one symptom of burnout and 20% reported near-constant symptoms in a 2024 survey. Three senior CDC leaders resigned last August over politicization of the agency, and one was fired for refusing to “rubber-stamp” Robert F Kennedy Jr’s anti-vaccine policies. The same month, a man fired more than 180 rounds into the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) campus because of misinformation about the Covid vaccine. He killed a police officer, David Rose. “If you’re 40 and choosing between US government service and industry, that’s now part of the math, not just the vast differences in compensation,” Gounder said. Yamey said he worried “that’s going to put future public health leaders off”. And there is an overwhelming amount of work to be done in addressing current public health crises and decades of repair to come. “But we will get there,” Yamey said. “We will all roll up our sleeves and build back, and hopefully build back better.”

title: The real meaning of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan
body_text: With the victory of progressive Abdul El-Sayed over representative Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic primary, prepare yourself to hear enormous quantities of bullshit about the Democratic party now being “taken over” by the “left” or by “democratic socialists”. Or as the reliably establishment New York Times put it: “Can an insurgent candidate, with unabashedly liberal positions, win a general election in a moderate state?” Oh, p-l-e-a-s-e. Michigan Democrats didn’t choose El-Sayed because he’s “unabashedly liberal”. Or because he’s a democratic socialist (in fact, he’s not). They chose him because he’s a fighter – at a time when America needs fighters willing to stand up to the worst tyrant who has ever occupied the Oval Office. Corporate Democrats – such as Haley Stevens, along with Rahm Emanuel, Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries – aren’t up to the task because they won’t bite the corporate hands that feed them campaign money. They won’t criticize the billionaire class. They refuse to talk about how big money has corrupted America. Yet it’s big corporations and the billionaire class that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism. They’ve sucked up to Trump for corporate welfare, giant tax cuts, tariff exemptions, antitrust acquiescence and war contracts. They’ve given Trump hundreds of millions for his inauguration, his ballroom, his 250th birthday, his Super Pac. Jamie Dimon and his cronies on Wall Street; Elon Musk and his billionaire bros; Brad Carp and his corporate lawyers; Peter Thiel, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and the Ellisons – all have sold their integrity for huge profits. They’ve created media empires that won’t criticize Trump, financial empires that feed Trump’s crypto, energy empires that feed off Trump’s war, and legal empires that allow Trump to ride roughshod over the rule of law. Which is why the US desperately needs people in Congress who will fight against Trump and his sycophants. The Democratic party isn’t being taken over by “the left” or by democratic socialists. There’s no civil war between progressives and moderates. We aren’t witnessing an ideological battle between the “left” and the “center”. We’re seeing the US wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us, and to a crisis of affordability that’s causing most Americans to struggle financially while fueling the biggest stock market rally in history. Trump’s tyranny and America’s affordability crisis are related. When corporate America and Wall Street are unleashed – when the president of the United States has made an implicit deal with the moneyed interests to back him and his authoritarian regime in exchange for tax cuts, deregulation, monopolization and pay-to-play corruption – of course prices soar and wages stagnate. Tyranny is the handmaiden of the moneyed interests. The Democratic party’s mega-donor class may be horrified by the rising tide of progressive populism overtaking more than a few primaries this cycle. After all, it spent tens of million of dollars on Stevens – making the Michigan primary one of the most expensive in US history. Too bad. It’s time that the Democratic party’s mega-donor class recognizes that its real choice is between democracy and tyranny, between an economy that works for all or one that works for a small sliver at the top. If the mega-donor class chooses the latter, it may be acting in its narrow self-interest, but it will also be acting against the future of this nation. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK
cleaned_body_text: With the victory of progressive Abdul El-Sayed over representative Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic primary, prepare yourself to hear enormous quantities of bullshit about the Democratic party now being “taken over” by the “left” or by “democratic socialists”. Or as the reliably establishment New York Times put it: “Can an insurgent candidate, with unabashedly liberal positions, win a general election in a moderate state?” Oh, p-l-e-a-s-e. Michigan Democrats didn’t choose El-Sayed because he’s “unabashedly liberal”. Or because he’s a democratic socialist (in fact, he’s not). They chose him because he’s a fighter – at a time when America needs fighters willing to stand up to the worst tyrant who has ever occupied the Oval Office. Corporate Democrats – such as Haley Stevens, along with Rahm Emanuel, Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries – aren’t up to the task because they won’t bite the corporate hands that feed them campaign money. They won’t criticize the billionaire class. They refuse to talk about how big money has corrupted America. Yet it’s big corporations and the billionaire class that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism. They’ve sucked up to Trump for corporate welfare, giant tax cuts, tariff exemptions, antitrust acquiescence and war contracts. They’ve given Trump hundreds of millions for his inauguration, his ballroom, his 250th birthday, his Super Pac. Jamie Dimon and his cronies on Wall Street; Elon Musk and his billionaire bros; Brad Carp and his corporate lawyers; Peter Thiel, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and the Ellisons – all have sold their integrity for huge profits. They’ve created media empires that won’t criticize Trump, financial empires that feed Trump’s crypto, energy empires that feed off Trump’s war, and legal empires that allow Trump to ride roughshod over the rule of law. Which is why the US desperately needs people in Congress who will fight against Trump and his sycophants. The Democratic party isn’t being taken over by “the left” or by democratic socialists. There’s no civil war between progressives and moderates. We aren’t witnessing an ideological battle between the “left” and the “center”. We’re seeing the US wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us, and to a crisis of affordability that’s causing most Americans to struggle financially while fueling the biggest stock market rally in history. Trump’s tyranny and America’s affordability crisis are related. When corporate America and Wall Street are unleashed – when the president of the United States has made an implicit deal with the moneyed interests to back him and his authoritarian regime in exchange for tax cuts, deregulation, monopolization and pay-to-play corruption – of course prices soar and wages stagnate. Tyranny is the handmaiden of the moneyed interests. The Democratic party’s mega-donor class may be horrified by the rising tide of progressive populism overtaking more than a few primaries this cycle. After all, it spent tens of million of dollars on Stevens – making the Michigan primary one of the most expensive in US history. Too bad. It’s time that the Democratic party’s mega-donor class recognizes that its real choice is between democracy and tyranny, between an economy that works for all or one that works for a small sliver at the top. If the mega-donor class chooses the latter, it may be acting in its narrow self-interest, but it will also be acting against the future of this nation. title: The American left is making strides. But can they win in November?
body_text: The ideological struggle within the Democratic party continued on Tuesday night with primaries in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. The results showed an increasingly intense conflict within the party, with high Democratic primary turnout and bruising ideological battles up and down the ballot. The Democratic electorate is shifting, becoming more progressive and more willing to challenge party leadership, but not as quickly or uniformly as many assumed. Progressives and socialists scored another round of victories, most notably Abdul El-Sayed for Senate, but also downballot with Donavan McKinney and Will Lawrence in congressional races, and in state legislative seats such as Chris Gilmer-Hill in Detroit. But the scale and breadth of those victories fell short of the expectations created by polling and media coverage. A few key lessons have emerged. First, building a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisans. Second, the left is nonetheless growing rapidly, able to win beyond young, deep-blue urban areas where concerns about general-election viability against Republicans are relatively limited, and across an entire statewide Democratic primary electorate in a swing state. This is a major step in the left’s development as an electoral force. Third, the left’s next and most important challenge is winning swing states and competitive seats against Republicans. The left has enjoyed a string of notable electoral victories during the second Trump administration, beginning with Zohran Mamdani’s primary win in New York City, and continuing up through the 2026 primaries. The Democratic electorate’s attitudes are changing: party leadership has grown less popular, while democratic socialism has gained support. The left has quickly gone from an extremely marginal force, with just a handful of members of Congress, largely confined to deep-blue urban districts and a small number of favorable constituencies, to a driving force in the party. Much of the media coverage has portrayed the party as being overtaken by an ascendant left. That broader narrative, reinforced by favorable polling, created an expectation that El-Sayed would win resoundingly. In practice, the recent wave means that a meaningful additional share of Democratic primary voters, perhaps 10-15%, is now willing to consistently support left candidates, on top of the existing leftwing base. It does not mean that every candidate backed by the DSA or the broader progressive movement will automatically win, or every Democrat backed by Aipac will lose. The actual campaign still matters tremendously; a large share of Democratic voters remain moderate, cross-pressured or primarily candidate-driven. Politics just doesn’t move that fast. The project of building a leftwing base and turning it into a durable majority, even within the Democratic party, is still a long-term one. El-Sayed’s narrow victory has been described as disappointing, because of favorable polling and the expectations created by the recent wave of leftwing victories. It is anything but. The polling miss has distorted how the result is being interpreted. Viewed against Michigan’s demographics, the left’s previous statewide performance, spending disparities, endorsements and comparable results elsewhere in the country, the victory was historically significant. The left has not previously won a genuinely competitive statewide Democratic primary of this kind, nor has a left candidate previously assembled a winning primary coalition extending this far beyond the movement’s urban base, especially in a swing state where voters are likely to weigh general-election viability. The left’s strategy over the past decade has been one of patience, winning seats in friendly areas, knocking doors and slowly building a base. It began by winning city council and state legislative victories and expanded more recently into successful mayoral and congressional races, all in deep blue areas. This is the first time the left has real proof of concept that beyond urban cores with friendly demographics, it can win over a majority of Democratic voters. It also offers early evidence that a left candidate could compete seriously in a Democratic presidential primary in 2028. The next test is November. The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates, party institutions and well-funded outside groups such as Aipac and the crypto lobby. But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain. El-Sayed, along with Francesca Hong if she advances in Wisconsin, needs to demonstrate the left can win not only a winning Democratic primary coalition, but a broad enough general-election coalition to prevail outside deep-blue territory. This matters in the near term, for Democrats to win the Senate and retain governorships; in the medium term, because presidential primary voters in 2028 will want evidence that left candidates can win competitive general elections; and in the long term, because the leftwing political project rests on being able to twin and govern with durable electoral majorities. On Tuesday, the left continued its string of victories, activating young voters and bringing Arab and Muslim voters back into the Democratic fold. But these victories do not resolve the movement’s central challenges. Every primary remains a brutal fight, highly contingent on candidates, organization, spending and local conditions. And the movement must now prepare for the more difficult terrain of November. The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party, but it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of defeating Republicans. Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of America

title: Exclusive: Major Republican fundraiser winning contracts from Trump administration, emails reveal
body_text: Wealthy Republicans on the west coast received an emailed invitation in July to an upcoming fundraiser titled “Keep the Senate”. The email, obtained by the Guardian, described the event as a “private roundtable and dinner with the National Republican Senatorial Committee” where donors can pledge $50,000 for seats at the head table, and mingle with legislative heavy hitters from Capitol Hill including the Senator majority leader, John Thune, and Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in Michigan with Donald Trump’s endorsement. One of the organizers listed on the invite was the defense industry tycoon Palmer Luckey, the 33-year-old co-founder of sprawling weapons manufacturer Anduril Industries. The invitation is one of dozens of emails obtained by the Guardian that unravel Luckey’s vast Maga political fundraising over the last seven years. A longtime GOP donor and activist who spoke on condition he not be identified in order to preserve his political relationships said Luckey was now the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. “If you’re raising campaign money in California, you have to go to Palmer Luckey,” he said. “Luckey is the top tier. There are others who are important below him but no one at his level.” Anduril, launched just nine years ago, has emerged as a major military contractor for the Trump administration, working on contracts for everything from drones to autonomous jet fighters to space-based interceptors. In March, the US army awarded a $20bn sole-source contract to Anduril for a variety of drones it sells, though it is not clear which of its weapons systems are operational or have been deployed for combat in US operations. Anduril, though it is not widely known as a space contractor, announced in May it would work, with a team of other companies, on what may be the mother of all contracting opportunities offered by the Trump administration, the so-called “Golden Dome” anti-missile space-based interceptor effort. Estimates for the Golden Dome range between $185bn and $1.2tn. Much of Anduril’s PR sparkle comes from Luckey. He’s a media darling, profiled on 60 Minutes and in the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, which called him the “It Guy of the booming defense-technology industry”. His offbeat, relaxed attire – colorful Hawaiian shirts, a chin puff goatee, cargo shorts and flip-flops – counterintuitively makes him seem more credible. Luckey is treated by many in the defense industry as a technology prophet and futurist who often holds forth on what he believes to be the true nature of warfare. For example, he told Axios that future wars will be fought in a “subterranean domain”, under the earth’s crust, in underground conflicts. Anduril’s success in winning huge contracts has blossomed with little attention paid to the central role Luckey plays as a donor and fundraising “bundler” for the Republican party. Bundlers hold large fundraisers for candidates or campaign committees and political action groups, and curate high-dollar invitation lists for those events. The emails obtained by the Guardian shed light on Palmer Luckey’s vast GOP political fundraising efforts and activism over the last 10 years. Palmer declined an interview for this piece, writing, “I am not going to help you guys make money,” and did not respond to a detailed list of questions. Rising influence OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, says Federal Election Commission (FEC) records show that Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans since 2017. While that is a tremendous amount of money for one person to give to politicians, it does not put him in the order of, say, Miriam Adelson, the widow of Sheldon Adelson, who has forked over $100m to Trump’s campaign in 2024. Luckey doesn’t have her wealth. His real value to GOP politicians exceeds his own donations. He hosts and organizes fundraising events and campaigns for Republicans from the president all the way down to state races. “If you become a bundler, it just multiplies your influence,” said Brendan Glavin of OpenSecrets. “It makes you a more important person. You’re bringing in not just your money. You’re bringing other people’s money. It integrates you in the campaign and makes you more important to the candidate than just a donor.” Behind the scenes, Luckey has reached a position in campaign finance and politics that rivals his influence in military contracting, according to two GOP fundraising figures. The emails, which are a partial list of invitations, show that Luckey has held fundraisers over the last seven years for at least 20 Republican politicians, ranging from Trump to a California attorney general candidate. Just as Luckey has emerged as a major fundraiser on the right, his co-founder, Anduril’s CEO, Palantir veteran Brian Schimpf, became a major donor to Democratic causes, albeit on a far smaller scale. So, in time-honored tradition, Anduril’s management ends up donating to both sides of the political aisle, though the vast majority goes towards the GOP. FEC records show Schimpf’s donations at $1.16m over the same period that Luckey gave $5.9m. An Anduril official emailed the Guardian: “It shouldn’t surprise anyone that two executives at the same company have different political views. Like millions of Americans, Brian and Palmer don’t share identical political views.” A fundraising dam breaks Luckey first became famous in tech before he could legally drink. At 20, in 2012, he launched a Kickstarter that raised more than $2m for a virtual reality gaming headset he said he was building first in his parents’ garage. It was a Silicon Valley Cinderella narrative. Two years later, Facebook became the prince at the ball and paid him $2bn for the company. In 2016, after four years of hype, the first Oculus Rift headset started getting shipped to consumers. And then, quickly, Luckey seemed to flame out in scandal. The Daily Beast revealed he’d been secretly funding a group dedicated to “shitposting” negative memes about Hillary Clinton. “We know Hillary Clinton is corrupt, a warmonger, a freedom-stripper. Not the good kind you see dancing in bikinis on Independence Day, the bad kind that strips freedom from citizens and grants it to donors,” Luckey had written, under the pseudonym Nimblerichman, on Reddit. The disclosure had an immense impact, at least for a time. Eight months later Luckey left Facebook, and he later portrayed himself in interviews as simply being canceled for giving money to Republicans, ignoring the main criticisms over the group’s crude and underhanded tactics. Luckey left Facebook with immense wealth, and in April 2017, just four months after Trump’s first inauguration, he founded Anduril. His partners in the venture came from the Peter Thiel-backed Palantir, a company that had long had success in federal contracting through major lobbying and PR battles. In June of 2017, his company just two months old, Luckey gave his first ever actual campaign finance donation, to Ted Cruz, the senator from Texas. Looking at his subsequent donations, it appears that the dam broke for him. Palmer gave 25 more times to political committees and legislators that year alone, FEC records show, and he has donated on more than a thousand occasions, or, on average, about 100 times every year. In the emails shared with the Guardian, the very first fundraising event Luckey co-hosted took place in August of 2017, two months after his donation to Ted Cruz. It was a major effort, and would include GOP House members such as Ken Calvert, Duncan Hunter, Darrell Issa, Devin Nunes, Dana Rohrabacher and Kevin McCarthy. Then in November, in a separate email chain, Palmer’s name came up again, for the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC). A congressional aide named Jason Pitkin wrote to a party official: “we are going to be asking people for $33,900 for the NRCC and then after the first of the year we can ask them for $101,700.” Pitkin noted that congressman Rohrabacher had introduced Luckey to Kevin McCarthy, then the powerful House majority leader, “at a Private meeting”. “As you can see by the attached invitation,” Pitkin said, “Palmer is hosting an event for Dana [Rohrabacher] On December 15th. Our understanding is that Palmer was going to contribute $100,000 for the CA Victory event. Please let us know how much more Palmer can give to the NRCC.” Pitkin did not respond to emailed questions. In July of 2020, just three years after its creation, Anduril won its first mammoth contract from the first Trump administration. Customs and Border Protection awarded the young company a contract estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars for surveillance towers on the border. And in that period it was clear that Luckey had hit the most senior levels of political access. On 6 October, the emails show, Luckey and his wife hosted Trump himself at a lunch at their waterfront mansion. The stakes were high and so were the tickets. Donors were told that $150,000 would get access to the round table, a VIP reception and event, and a photo op with the president. During the Biden years, Anduril still maintained its business efforts targeting US national security, and still won contracts. It went on a major acquisition binge, buying up drone companies across the country. And Luckey’s fundraising for the GOP continued. The records obtained by the Guardian show that after 2021, Luckey hosted fundraisers for key figures including Tom Cotton, the head of the Senate intelligence committee; Rick Scott, the Republican senator from Florida; Ken Calvert, then the influential ranking member of the House’s defense appropriations subcommittee; and Mike Waltz, now Trump’s UN ambassador and briefly his national security adviser. Luckey also hosted another event for a future Trump official: a $50,000-a-plate fundraiser in June 2022 for Mehmet Oz, who would later join the Trump administration. That event became scandalous when Jezebel reported the fundraiser incorporated a speech by Oz in front of a car that once belonged to Adolf Hitler. Jezebel pointed out that Luckey’s sister is married to Maga firebrand Matt Gaetz, then a congressman from Florida. Now that Trump is president, Anduril appears to be taking its turn at the table of the major contractors, amid Lockheed Martin, Raytheon and General Dynamics. Certainly it has raised extraordinary money. In the latest round, led by Thrive Capital, controlled by Jared Kushner’s brother Joshua, it raised $5bn in venture capital. Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%, but still only reached $2.2bn for 2025, which is barely a blip in the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget. Still, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has twice toured Anduril factories. “Palmer and everyone, thank you so much,” he said last December as he visited Anduril’s factory in Costa Mesa, California, at a giant former industrial site where the Los Angeles Times was once printed. The Anduril factory was “foundational” to the new Pentagon, Hegseth said. On that tour, Hegseth donned a special helmet designed by Anduril. A soldier wearing the helmet would be able to see the outside world not through his eyes but through sensors, as a kind of virtual or “augmented” reality, just like the old Oculus Rift headset Palmer Luckey made his fortune on. In his speech, Hegseth referred to “that cool helmet I just saw that the army might be wearing eventually”.

It went on a major acquisition binge, buying up drone companies across the country. And Luckey’s fundraising for the GOP continued. The records obtained by the Guardian show that after 2021, Luckey hosted fundraisers for key figures including Tom Cotton, the head of the Senate intelligence committee; Rick Scott, the Republican senator from Florida; Ken Calvert, then the influential ranking member of the House’s defense appropriations subcommittee; and Mike Waltz, now Trump’s UN ambassador and briefly his national security adviser. Luckey also hosted another event for a future Trump official: a $50,000-a-plate fundraiser in June 2022 for Mehmet Oz, who would later join the Trump administration. That event became scandalous when Jezebel reported the fundraiser incorporated a speech by Oz in front of a car that once belonged to Adolf Hitler. Jezebel pointed out that Luckey’s sister is married to Maga firebrand Matt Gaetz, then a congressman from Florida. Now that Trump is president, Anduril appears to be taking its turn at the table of the major contractors, amid Lockheed Martin, Raytheon and General Dynamics. Certainly it has raised extraordinary money. In the latest round, led by Thrive Capital, controlled by Jared Kushner’s brother Joshua, it raised $5bn in venture capital. Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%, but still only reached $2.2bn for 2025, which is barely a blip in the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget. Still, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has twice toured Anduril factories. “Palmer and everyone, thank you so much,” he said last December as he visited Anduril’s factory in Costa Mesa, California, at a giant former industrial site where the Los Angeles Times was once printed. The Anduril factory was “foundational” to the new Pentagon, Hegseth said. On that tour, Hegseth donned a special helmet designed by Anduril. A soldier wearing the helmet would be able to see the outside world not through his eyes but through sensors, as a kind of virtual or “augmented” reality, just like the old Oculus Rift headset Palmer Luckey made his fortune on. In his speech, Hegseth referred to “that cool helmet I just saw that the army might be wearing eventually”.

title: First Thing: Democrats look forward after progressive El-Sayed victory in Michigan
body_text: Good morning. The progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic primary for the US Senate in Michigan. Despite many backing his opponent, Haley Stevens, in the race, leading Democrats are now uniting behind the former public health official with the goal of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. What does El-Sayed’s victory mean for the Democratic party? Though a contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits, his rise could serve as a revision to the political establishment’s prior playbook of requiring candidates to run from the center in swing-state politics. What do the Democrats need to retake the Senate? Republicans currently control the chamber with 53 lawmakers. The easiest path for Democrats to take back the Senate requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director In a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts, Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). As Donald Trump’s third pick to run the CDC, Schwartz will take the reins of the agency amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines. What was the vote? Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination. Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups Investigations from Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Legal Agenda have determined that Israel deliberately and directly attacked the Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. Deliberate attacks on civilians is a war crime. Khalil, 42, was killed while Faraj, 21, was injured. What has Israel said about the attack? Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. How many journalists have been killed in this conflict? Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office. In other news … Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank with policies that began with Trump rescinding sanctions on his first day in office. Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday. Donald Trump’s legal team is pushing to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster. The Cambridge professor Jason Arday, accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career. Stat of the day: 90% of US adults listed groceries and food costs as their top cost-of-living concern A new survey found that a majority of Americans agree that the rising cost of living is a significant barrier to achieving a better life. According to a new survey of more than 30,000 adults from across the country spanning generations and economic classes, 60% of respondents said they wanted greater financial security but 40% described themselves as either “getting by but financially vulnerable” or “struggling to meet basic needs”. The Filter recommends: 32 things worth buying from Nordstrom’s anniversary sale Nordstrom’s annual sale, which runs until 9 August, includes more than 22,000 items across home, fashion, beauty, travel and more. The Filter crew has sifted through all of them to find the 32 deals they endorse, on top brands ranging from Le Creuset to Ray-Ban. Don’t miss this: Black college gymnasts in a divided South Gymnast Nyla Aquino is one of the University of Georgia’s brightest stars, leading her team to a resurgent sixth-place finish at the 2026 NCAA championships. But she and other Black athletes competing in the Southeastern Conference are striving to make their mark in a region of historical anti-Black prejudices, in a time when diversity, equity and inclusion programs and voting rights are under attack. “No matter how well I do, someone’s going to be racist,” she said. …or this: Achieving gender parity in Latin America’s city of cycling While Bogotá records nearly 900,000 bicycle trips each day – more than any other city in Latin America – less than a third of cycling journeys are taken by women. City officials are looking to change that. “Many older women come here because they were never allowed to ride a bicycle as girls,” said Sergio Prieto, who helps to oversee Bogotá’s Bike School. “They were told bikes were for men, that women shouldn’t be riding them. Here, those barriers and stereotypes are left behind.” Climate check: How the human-driven climate crisis fuels Canada’s deadly wildfires A new study conducted by World Weather Attribution found that the human-driven climate crisis amplified the conditions that led to fires blazing across Canada. Burning coal, oil and gas has overheated the planet and caused climate-influenced conditions to occur every two to six years in the Northwest Territories and every six to 15 years in Ontario. There are 700 fires burning in Canada at present. Last Thing: How well do you know the latest dating terms? Fresh dating trends seem to emerge every week in this age of app-based romance. Some terms such as “ghosting” or “catfishing” have become part of the modern parlance. But how familiar are you with other dating trends? Take this quiz and find out. title: ‘He should resign’: unease in Republican Max Miller’s Ohio district amid domestic abuse allegations
body_text: David Griffith was a registered Republican for years. But on Sunday evening, he watched the Ohio congressman Max Miller stumble through an 18-minute statement in which the lawmaker attempted to defend himself against allegations of domestic abuse against his ex-wife and infant child. What Griffith saw and heard, he said, was a person that bore no resemblance to the Republican party he once supported. “What I saw was a person who needs help,” said Griffith, seated at a bench in a community park in Wooster, a quiet town of 26,000 people situated at the southern end of the beleaguered Miller’s congressional district. Though he has been critical of Donald Trump for years, last May Griffith ended his formal affiliation with the Republican party. “At this [midterm] election, I’m voting a straight Democratic ticket,” he said. “I’ve never done that before.” Across Miller’s largely red district, Republicans are deeply concerned with their representative’s alleged behavior and political future. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of the Republican Ohio senator Bernie Moreno, has accused Miller of pointing a gun at her head, pouring hot water on her and potentially breaking their two-year-old daughter’s collarbone. Emily Moreno has also alleged Miller physically attacked her attorney and another legal representative, and filed for a restraining order on her lawyer’s behalf. Emily Moreno and Miller are now locked in a bitter custody battle. On Sunday, Bernie Moreno called for Miller to resign in an X post after years of silence on the issue: “He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.” Miller, who faces an election this November, has denied any allegations of domestic abuse. In his statement on Sunday, he blamed the so-called leftwing media and his former wife for initiating a campaign to sully his name. On Tuesday, he attempted to defend himself further on Jake Tapper’s evening show on CNN, likening his fight to that of Trump’s when the president also faced sexual assault allegations. “The police are not investigating it; ask yourself, why aren’t they investigating these things?” he said. Before specific details of the allegations against Miller were recently made public and before Senator Moreno’s calls, Miller was expected to easily retain his seat, with pollsters suggesting in June the district leans Republican by five points. Miller, 37, who had previously served as a presidential aide during Trump’s first administration, was endorsed by Trump in 2021 during his first campaign. But this week, reports emerged that the president’s support for Miller may be waning. The final day the Ohio Republican party could replace Miller with another candidate, if it decides to do so, is 12 August. Bill Heck, vice-chair of the Republican party of Medina county, which lies inside Miller’s district, wouldn’t say if he thinks the congressman should resign. “There is so much stuff flying around that we have not been able to decipher what’s real and what’s not. What we’re trying to determine right now is how much of this is credible and how much he can refute and recover from,” he said. But he did concede that Republican voters in Miller’s district are worried. “I think a lot of our members and our steadfast Republicans are concerned,” he said. “I’m sure the president does not want to lose that seat. With 92 days left [to the election] it’s going to be really difficult for anybody to come in and take over the position – if appointed.” A host of other Republican party county organizations and groups across Miller’s district, including the women’s branch of the Republican party of Cuyahoga county, asking if they thought the congressman should resign, did not respond to requests for comment on the situation. While Miller as the incumbent won his 2024 congressional election by a 15% margin, a Democrat and an independent candidate split the vote between them. In November, Miller faces Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker from Brook Park, a Cleveland suburb. “The district leans Republican, but it is not so overwhelmingly Republican that a Democrat could never win,” says Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. “If you combine a midterm election moving everything nationwide towards the Democrats with a weak Republican candidate, that could be enough for the seventh district to flip. Miller is weakened at the moment, so if he tries to stay in the race, that helps Poindexter, and if Miller withdraws, then without a strong replacement, that still helps Poindexter.” ‘He hasn’t engaged with our community’ A former Marine Corps reserve, Miller, who is seeking a third congressional term, has a long history of allegations of violence towards women, including from the former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, who accused him of pushing her against a wall and slapping her when the two were dating. (Miller has denied the allegation.) In north-eastern Ohio, the Miller family is known as one of the most powerful and respected in the region. Max’s grandfather, Sam, who died in 2019, was an esteemed Cleveland real estate mogul and philanthropist. Sixty miles south of Cleveland, Wooster, the county seat of largely rural Wayne county, was once a heartbeat of the industrial midwest. The collapse of the local jobs market in the early 2000s and accompanying economic decline that followed over the past two decades has fueled resentment locally that Trump has long since tapped into. In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won 70% of the vote in Wayne county. Wooster hasn’t elected a Democratic mayor for decades. “If the [Republican] party followed the standards we did, then I’d say he should resign,” says Bill Bailey, a former judge and the chair of the Wayne county Democratic party. “In my view, the Republican party is more concerned about retaining votes than they are about enforcing any kind of standards.” He says he doesn’t believe Miller’s claims of innocence, nor do many typically Republican voters. In Wayne county’s primary elections held last May, Bailey says about 1,600 registered Republican voters chose independent candidates and another 500 Republicans picked Democrats. “He hasn’t engaged with our community,” says Bailey of Miller. “I doubt that the average person would recognize him on the street.” For Griffith, who runs a local Facebook group called Defending Democracy and believes that the Republican party should support the US’s allies overseas, Miller represents everything that’s gone wrong with the party. “I have to believe that people get involved in public service because they want to do good, regardless of party,” he says. “Max Miller is not one of those people.”

title: US Senate panel votes to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress over Covid hearing
body_text: A Republican-controlled US Senate committee voted to hold Dr Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after the veteran public health official repeatedly pleaded the fifth amendment to parry a hostile inquisition into his stewardship of the response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Fauci, the former director of National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), who led the agency for 38 years before retiring in 2022, gave the same response to dozens of questions while refusing to give clarifying answers during a tense hearing last week, citing his constitutional protections. The Senate homeland security and government affairs committee voted in favor of referring a potential criminal case against Fauci to the US Department of Justice. The vote was condemned as “shameful” and a “crude political stunt” by Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, who was forcibly ejected from last week’s hearing when he tried to speak on behalf of his client. The committee is chaired by the Republican Kentucky senator Rand Paul, whom Fauci last week accused of having an “unhinged obsession” with him as he refused to answer questions at the hearing. Paul insisted on Thursday that he wasn’t trying to entrap Fauci. “He had no liability if he told the truth,” Paul said. “The chair directed Anthony Fauci to answer. He refused,” Paul said in his opening statement. “That is what we are voting on today – not his opinions, not his policies, not anything he said from the podium six years ago. “We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a sweeping federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence.” But top Democrats criticized the Republican-led process. The Michigan senator Gary Peters, the ranking Democrat on the Senate panel, argued that the drive to subpoena Fauci, and now to hold him in contempt, accomplished nothing to advance public health. Paul’s work amounted to “a one-sided investigation and a rushed process … that could harm our ability to conduct future investigations”, said Peters. While a contempt referral must typically be approved by the full Senate after a congressional committee, this would probably require a 60-vote majority – requiring Democratic support. Paul acknowledged this standard path on Wednesday, but said he did not “want to waste time” moving the matter to a vote of the full Senate. He previously suggested during a Fox News interview that he could send the referral directly to the justice department, with a legal brief. Peters warned that bypassing a full Senate vote might not be legally valid and said punishing Fauci for exercising his fifth amendment rights could deter future witnesses from giving congressional testimony. “Future witnesses will argue that appearing before Congress exposes them to punishment regardless of whether they comply with a subpoena and invoke a constitutional protection,” he said. The fifth amendment is enshrined in the US constitution as a protective measure intended to save individuals from being forced to incriminate themselves when under investigation or asked to provide testimony. The evening before the vote, it emerged that the US Department of Health and Human Services had provided a copy of Fauci’s phone to a Senate subcommittee. “Hopefully, this device will address many of the questions he refused to answer at last week’s hearing,” Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, the subcommittee’s Republican chair, wrote on social media. Fauci, 85, who was pardoned by Joe Biden at the end of his presidency, declined to answer questions after accusing Paul of harboring a goal of “embarrassing and intimidating me” and of putting him “behind bars” because of his leading role in urging widespread restrictions, including masking and social distancing, to combat the pandemic. The senator has long accused Fauci of deliberately downplaying the possibility that the virus originated from a research laboratory in the Chinese city of Wuhan, rather than jumping from an animal to humans in a wet market, as most scientists believe. “Although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said during the hearing. Thereafter, he warded off all subsequent questions with identical answers that invoked the fifth amendment, enraging his Republican critics. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” he said, in an undeviating answer to different questions. Paul – who had subpoenaed Fauci to appear – warned him during the hearing that his stance would have “repercussions”. Later, he told him: “Because you refuse to answer, citing a privilege that is unsupported because of your pardon, and after being denied to do so, this committee has scheduled a vote next week on a resolution certifying your contempt.” It is unclear whether a vote in favor of contempt will have legal force. According to the constitution, the fifth amendment guarantees that no individual “shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself, nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law”. The US supreme court has confirmed in several decisions since 1955 that witnesses can invoke it in congressional investigations, according to the Library of Congress. “Although the [Fifth] amendment’s protection expressly refers to criminal cases[s], the Court has nevertheless found the privilege against self-incrimination to be available to a witness appearing before a congressional committee,” the library’s annotated interpretation of the constitution states. Paul has insisted Fauci is precluded from pleading the fifth, however, on the grounds that the pre-emptive pardon Biden granted him means he cannot be prosecuted for any of the matters senators were asking him about. Paul argued that Fauci’s refusal to answer could lead to criminal prosecution for contempt of Congress or obstructing a congressional proceeding. Federal law makes it a crime for witnesses to “willfully” refuse to answer questions when called to give congressional testimony. A separate law makes it illegal to obstruct an investigation by a congressional committee. Fauci’s lawyers have argued that he is on unassailable legal grounds by pleading the amendment. “For years, Senator Paul has proclaimed to anyone who would listen that Dr Fauci should be prosecuted and put in prison,” Schertler, Fauci’s legal counsel, said on Thursday. “Dr Fauci has committed no crime – and Senator Paul knows it. “Today’s resolution is a continuation of Senator Paul’s personal vendetta against Dr Fauci, who spent 50 years in public health and has saved countless lives. It is shameful and wrong that Senator Paul is abusing his power by trying to weaponize the justice department against an honorable public servant.” Robert Mackey contributed reporting
