The committee is chaired by the Republican Kentucky senator Rand Paul, whom Fauci last week accused of having an “unhinged obsession” with him as he refused to answer questions at the hearing. Paul insisted on Thursday that he wasn’t trying to entrap Fauci. “He had no liability if he told the truth,” Paul said. “The chair directed Anthony Fauci to answer. He refused,” Paul said in his opening statement. “That is what we are voting on today – not his opinions, not his policies, not anything he said from the podium six years ago. “We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a sweeping federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence.” But top Democrats criticized the Republican-led process. The Michigan senator Gary Peters, the ranking Democrat on the Senate panel, argued that the drive to subpoena Fauci, and now to hold him in contempt, accomplished nothing to advance public health. Paul’s work amounted to “a one-sided investigation and a rushed process … that could harm our ability to conduct future investigations”, said Peters. While a contempt referral must typically be approved by the full Senate after a congressional committee, this would probably require a 60-vote majority – requiring Democratic support. Paul acknowledged this standard path on Wednesday, but said he did not “want to waste time” moving the matter to a vote of the full Senate. He previously suggested during a Fox News interview that he could send the referral directly to the justice department, with a legal brief. Peters warned that bypassing a full Senate vote might not be legally valid and said punishing Fauci for exercising his fifth amendment rights could deter future witnesses from giving congressional testimony. “Future witnesses will argue that appearing before Congress exposes them to punishment regardless of whether they comply with a subpoena and invoke a constitutional protection,” he said. The fifth amendment is enshrined in the US constitution as a protective measure intended to save individuals from being forced to incriminate themselves when under investigation or asked to provide testimony. The evening before the vote, it emerged that the US Department of Health and Human Services had provided a copy of Fauci’s phone to a Senate subcommittee. “Hopefully, this device will address many of the questions he refused to answer at last week’s hearing,” Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, the subcommittee’s Republican chair, wrote on social media. Fauci, 85, who was pardoned by Joe Biden at the end of his presidency, declined to answer questions after accusing Paul of harboring a goal of “embarrassing and intimidating me” and of putting him “behind bars” because of his leading role in urging widespread restrictions, including masking and social distancing, to combat the pandemic. The senator has long accused Fauci of deliberately downplaying the possibility that the virus originated from a research laboratory in the Chinese city of Wuhan, rather than jumping from an animal to humans in a wet market, as most scientists believe. “Although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said during the hearing. Thereafter, he warded off all subsequent questions with identical answers that invoked the fifth amendment, enraging his Republican critics. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” he said, in an undeviating answer to different questions. Paul – who had subpoenaed Fauci to appear – warned him during the hearing that his stance would have “repercussions”. Later, he told him: “Because you refuse to answer, citing a privilege that is unsupported because of your pardon, and after being denied to do so, this committee has scheduled a vote next week on a resolution certifying your contempt.” It is unclear whether a vote in favor of contempt will have legal force. According to the constitution, the fifth amendment guarantees that no individual “shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself, nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law”. The US supreme court has confirmed in several decisions since 1955 that witnesses can invoke it in congressional investigations, according to the Library of Congress. “Although the [Fifth] amendment’s protection expressly refers to criminal cases[s], the Court has nevertheless found the privilege against self-incrimination to be available to a witness appearing before a congressional committee,” the library’s annotated interpretation of the constitution states. Paul has insisted Fauci is precluded from pleading the fifth, however, on the grounds that the pre-emptive pardon Biden granted him means he cannot be prosecuted for any of the matters senators were asking him about. Paul argued that Fauci’s refusal to answer could lead to criminal prosecution for contempt of Congress or obstructing a congressional proceeding. Federal law makes it a crime for witnesses to “willfully” refuse to answer questions when called to give congressional testimony. A separate law makes it illegal to obstruct an investigation by a congressional committee. Fauci’s lawyers have argued that he is on unassailable legal grounds by pleading the amendment. “For years, Senator Paul has proclaimed to anyone who would listen that Dr Fauci should be prosecuted and put in prison,” Schertler, Fauci’s legal counsel, said on Thursday. “Dr Fauci has committed no crime – and Senator Paul knows it. “Today’s resolution is a continuation of Senator Paul’s personal vendetta against Dr Fauci, who spent 50 years in public health and has saved countless lives. It is shameful and wrong that Senator Paul is abusing his power by trying to weaponize the justice department against an honorable public servant.” Robert Mackey contributed reporting

title: Aipac-linked Super Pacs spend millions in California to thwart progressive candidate
body_text: Super Pacs tied to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) have spent millions in a California congressional race to keep a progressive Democrat from winning Eric Swalwell’s former seat. Aisha Wahab, a state senator who has been endorsed by the California Democratic party, is widely considered the frontrunner in the special election for the district covering a swathe of the East Bay. Swalwell had been in office for more than a decade when he resigned earlier this year following multiple allegations of sexual assault. Wahab, who was the first Muslim woman and Afghan American elected to the state legislature, has had a significant lead in the contest to represent one of California’s most diverse congressional districts. Wahab outpaced her closest competitor, Melissa Hernandez, the president of the board of directors for the Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) agency and a former Dublin mayor, in a June primary as well as a special election to complete the remainder of Swalwell’s term, by more than 20 points. They are set to face off against each other in a runoff election later this month, and then again in November. Super Pacs are pouring money into the race, dropping more than $5m in recent weeks and supporting pro-Hernandez ads and Wahab attack ads, Politico reported on Thursday. The spending includes $1.2m from United Democracy Project, which is backed by Aipac, and $2.1m from Bold America Pac, which has received significant financial backing from the United Democracy Project, according to the outlet. Track Aipac, which tracks the group’s funding of US politicians, reported that the lobby had spent more than $4.4m to support Hernandez in the race. Wahab said there had been a barrage of attack ads against her in the last month that had misrepresented her record, particularly as it relates to public safety issues. She described the Super Pacs’ involvement as election interference. “You have to ask yourself, why? Aipac is clearly not interested in having diverse voices at the table, they are not interested in supporting the Jewish community and a peaceful dialogue,” she argued. “They want a puppet they can control.” The ads had generated outrage among her constituents, she said, adding that her campaign fields calls and emails daily from people “disgusted by the ads”. People were familiar with her record, Wahab added, and her personal history. Her father was murdered when she was a child, and Wahab grew up in the foster care system. As a state lawmaker, she has prioritized victims, she said, and supported legislation to make human trafficking a serious felony and a bill of rights for sexual assault survivors. Aipac, which is one of the largest Super Pacs and the most powerful pro-Israel lobby organization in the US, has significantly expanded its political spending in recent years. The New York Times reported earlier this week that Aipac had doubled its spending, largely in Democratic primaries, to $67.2m. The organization spent millions to support moderate Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. The progressive Abdul El-Sayed ultimately won the primary race in what has been described as a defining contest for the party. Wahab pointed to her record and wide-ranging support, including endorsements from the organization Our Revolution to state and local officials including the attorney general, Rob Bonta, and the Alameda county sheriff, Yesenia Sanchez. In a statement to the Guardian, Ajay Mohan, campaign manager for Hernandez, said: “Melissa does not control independent expenditures. No candidate does. That is the law, and she sees those ads when you see them. “Melissa remains laser focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, and supporting strong public safety - just as she did as Mayor,” Mohan added. The Guardian has contacted Aipac for comment.

title: Mitch McConnell announces discharge from rehabilitation center
body_text: The Republican US senator Mitch McConnell has been discharged from a rehabilitation center following the fall that left him hospitalized, he announced on Thursday. McConnell, 84, whose weeks‑long absence from Capitol Hill fueled mounting speculation about his health, said he will continue his recovery at home. While the Senate is set to wrap up legislative business this week, before a five‑week recess, several agenda items remain – including a vote to confirm Todd Blanche as US attorney general. McConnell’s absence further narrows Republicans’ already tight path to approving Donald Trump’s former personal attorney as head of the Department of Justice. McConnell is one of the highest-profile figures in Congress, as a former Senate majority leader. He has been absent from the Senate and not seen in public since mid-June, although his office has released several photos of him. “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period,” McConnell said in a Thursday statement. “And I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.” His 53‑day absence has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties. Last month, Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, publicly urged McConnell to release more information about his health, writing: “Kentuckians have grown increasingly concerned about the current state of your health and wellbeing, and ability to hold office.” McConnell was admitted to hospital on 14 June. His office initially offered few details, saying only that he was “continuing to improve”. A month later, McConnell disclosed that a fall at his home and a “mild case of pneumonia” had prompted the hospitalization and his extended time away. In late July, his office said he still had not been cleared to return to work.

title: Trump’s birthright citizenship attack the latest effort in obsessive campaign
body_text: With a pair of executive orders on Thursday, Donald Trump has tried – once again – to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship, a right enshrined in the US constitution and reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago. The orders attempt to broaden the categories of children who would be ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”, which the president claimed is practiced by “hundreds of thousands” of people. That estimate appears to be wildly inflated. According to the non-partisan Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024”. It was the latest attack in a quixotic campaign that the US president has waged for more than a decade. At a Republican presidential primary campaign event in Orlando, Florida, in November 2015, Trump hinted that he had a plan to end what he called the scourge of “anchor babies”, a derogatory term for the US-citizen children of undocumented immigrants. “You can’t come into the country – you’re illegal, you come down, you sit down, you have your baby, and we take care of the baby for the next 85 years!” Trump said. “Everybody says, ‘Well, you need a constitutional amendment, it’ll take 15 years, it’ll never happen’. You don’t, you don’t. You need a simple act of Congress. You might not even need that.” If elected, Trump promised the crowd at a resort near Disney World, “the anchor baby, birthright citizenship, it’s over.” Three years later, as president, Trump said in a televised interview just before the 2018 midterms that he planned to issue an executive order to instruct federal agencies that children born in the United States to non-citizens were not entitled to US citizenship at birth. “It was always told to me that you needed a constitutional amendment. Guess what? You don’t,” Trump told the interviewer Jonathan Swan. “You can definitely do it with an act of Congress,” Trump added, incorrectly, “but now they’re saying I can do it just with an executive order.” As Swan reported at the time, Trump’s claim that he could undo the birthright citizenship guaranteed by the 14th amendment to the constitution was a minority view among legal scholars, but was supported by a then-obscure figure: John Eastman, a former law clerk to the supreme court justice Clarence Thomas who had argued for decades that the amendment granting citizenship to “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” should be read to exclude the children of people who are not US citizens when their child is born. Eastman later claimed in a 2020 Newsweek op-ed that Kamala Harris was ineligible for the vice-presidency because she had no right to US citizenship at birth, since she was born in Oakland, California, in 1964 to non-citizen parents who were, “subject to the jurisdiction” of their native lands of India and Jamaica. In the 2018 interview, Trump called birthright citizenship “ridiculous”, and falsely asserted that the US is “the only country in the world where a person comes in and has a baby, and the baby is essentially a citizen.” In fact, 32 other nations grant citizenship this way. He also claimed then that an executive order was in the process of being drafted. Although that order did not materialize until the start of Trump’s second term, and was struck down in June by the supreme court, his obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had an overtly political element from the start. Trump’s original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claim that Barack Obama, born to an American mother and a Kenyan father in Honolulu, just two years after Hawaii became a state, might have been born outside the US. Then, after Joe Biden picked Harris as his running mate in 2020, Trump repeatedly refused to confirm that she was eligible for an elected office open only to “a natural-born citizen”. Instead, Trump called the question Eastman raised about Harris’s citizenship at birth in his Newsweek op-ed “very serious” and a potential “problem” for her. He also praised Eastman as “a very highly qualified, very talented lawyer” and called him “brilliant”. Eastman, who went on to devise the fake electors scheme designed to keep Trump in office after he lost the 2020 election, and gave an inflammatory speech before the Capitol riot on 6 January 2021, was finally disbarred by the California supreme court in April, based on “clear and convincing evidence that he advanced false claims about the 2020 presidential election to mislead courts, public officials, and the American public”. While asserting the right to deny citizenship to some children of non-citizens is clearly still a priority for Trump, it remains to be seen if his latest attempts to curtail the right will succeed. The two new orders are likely to face legal challenges, and come just weeks after the US supreme court struck down Trump’s previous order denying citizenship to the children of non-citizens, issued on the first day of his second term. In the court’s June decision, Chief Justice John Roberts said Trump’s first order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” he wrote. “The framers of the 14th amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land’. We keep that promise today.”

title: Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war
body_text: Tehran has set out a protracted negotiating timetable designed to keep Donald Trump embroiled in the Iran conflict until the midterm elections, in the hope of inflicting the same ruinous blow on his presidency as Jimmy Carter suffered over the 1979-81 US embassy hostage crisis. For many inside Iran, inflicting meaningful revenge on Trump is a legitimate and self-standing war aim, reflected in the mood of those attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei where demands for retribution were ubiquitous. While Iranian officials since the 1979 Islamic revolution have never trusted the US, that animus is now also directed personally towards Trump. He not only tore up the painfully negotiated nuclear deal in 2018, but he sanctioned the assassination of the military leader Qassem Suleimani and twice involved Iran in negotiations on its nuclear programme only to launch wars against it. He shows no remorse for the killing of the country’s supreme leader, or for the attempt on the life of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian. As the countdown to November’s midterms begins, what could be Trump’s political demise has become a subject of obsessive speculation in Tehran. Iranian media track the US president’s waning ratings, attributing the decline to the war’s unpopularity and high oil prices. The changing politics of the Democrats is minutely examined. But the focus on the midterms became more obvious this week when the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told the official IRNA news agency that after agreeing a route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz, it would take two to four months to reach the second phase of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. The original plan – to commence the nuclear phase of the talks within 30 days of signing June’s memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US – had been jettisoned by the Trump administration, Gharibabadi said. To get to that second stage, he laid out an obstacle course including the lifting of sanctions, the end of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and new commitments on non-belligerence in a process that could last well beyond the midterms. If Tehran gets its way on this timetable, Trump will be going to the polls with no Iranian commitment on nuclear weapons, only a hefty economic bill for a failed war. “This raises the very likely scenario of continued cycles of conflict between the US and Tehran over the strait,” said Jason Brodsky from United against a Nuclear Iran, an advocate of the war. “There won’t be any true quiet before the midterm elections – Tehran has no interest in giving this to the Trump administration … It will continue to play games.” Mehr News, an agency close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, published a piece saying Iran had given Trump a major dilemma. “Continuing the war could increase political and economic pressure on the government and exacerbate the decline in his popularity. On the other hand, backing down, or moving towards reducing tensions, could also be interpreted by some of Trump’s supporters as a retreat from his campaign slogans,” it said. From this perspective, the outcome of this war will not be played out on the battlefield, but at the ballot box. The agency suggested the outcome could affect the course of American domestic and foreign policy for years to come. Few in Iran take Trump’s statements at face value. But his denials that the midterms affect his Iran strategy are treated with special scepticism. Iranian media point to comments from Marc Zell, chair of Republicans Overseas Israel, who has said: “It’s all about the midterms … the American public simply is tired of war and the administration is navigating the pre-election waters adroitly in order to avoid a Democratic takeover of Congress.” Such remarks fuel the debate inside Iran about how much the midterms should be part of Iran’s calculus. Some believe the loss of Congress will inhibit Trump or lead to his impeachment; at the very least, it may mark the end of the war’s funding. Mostafa Zahrani, a former Iranian diplomat, argued electoral defeat “will make it inevitable that Trump will not be able to go back to war and will take the negotiations seriously”. Others such as Nasser Hadian, a professor of international relations at Tehran University, disagree, advocating cashing in on Iran’s victories now rather than waiting for Trump to become weaker. “If he loses, he’ll have less incentive to reach an agreement with Iran, because in that case he’ll be weakened, and Israel and others will find it much easier to attack him – something they don’t dare do now,” he said. “Those who say we should wait for the midterm elections have no understanding of politics in America.” Iran’s pleasure in seeing Trump defeated would indeed be reduced if he felt he had nothing left to lose, but its diplomats overall believe the US president’s freedom to act will be constrained by the unpopularity of more conflict and by Republican presidential candidates’ anxiety to wrap this up. Trump would also be at risk of seeing his whole second term consumed by a disastrous war. The bigger question is what Iran itself wants to achieve. Agreeing to keep the dispute simmering until November is not an answer to that question – one that Iranians are better at debating than resolving. Pezeshkian, working in alliance with Mohammad Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, repeatedly says he does not want endless war, and insists that almost all the supreme national security council concur. He still has faith in the MoU, saying it should be the cornerstone of Iran’s foreign policy. But the conservative newspaper Kayhan describes the memorandum as worthless since the US always breaks its commitments. “Accordingly, officials should know that the strait of Hormuz is not a bargaining chip and should not be opened as a passage for America,” it said. Both hardliners and moderates envision the war leading to a new regional security architecture. But the hardliners put the emphasis on America’s expulsion and see this as something less to be negotiated and more to be enforced using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz as a lever to close US bases. Pezeshkian says he sees a place for legitimate US investment in Iran, while the former foreign minister Javad Zarif, in an essay this week, argued Iran in “a post-polar era would benefit from not depending solely on Russia and China in future”. If Iran developed “a balanced and multifaceted foreign policy”, Tehran would not be forced into relationships based on necessity, he wrote. “Continuing uncontrolled tensions with the United States not only imposes direct costs on Iran, but also makes it more difficult for other countries, even close partners such as China and Russia, to cooperate with Iran.” Just as Trump cannot resolve from one sentence to the next what he thinks of Iran, nor can Iran agree what it thinks it can get from America.

Iranian media track the US president’s waning ratings, attributing the decline to the war’s unpopularity and high oil prices. The changing politics of the Democrats is minutely examined. But the focus on the midterms became more obvious this week when the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told the official IRNA news agency that after agreeing a route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz, it would take two to four months to reach the second phase of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. The original plan – to commence the nuclear phase of the talks within 30 days of signing June’s memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US – had been jettisoned by the Trump administration, Gharibabadi said. To get to that second stage, he laid out an obstacle course including the lifting of sanctions, the end of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and new commitments on non-belligerence in a process that could last well beyond the midterms. If Tehran gets its way on this timetable, Trump will be going to the polls with no Iranian commitment on nuclear weapons, only a hefty economic bill for a failed war. “This raises the very likely scenario of continued cycles of conflict between the US and Tehran over the strait,” said Jason Brodsky from United against a Nuclear Iran, an advocate of the war. “There won’t be any true quiet before the midterm elections – Tehran has no interest in giving this to the Trump administration … It will continue to play games.” Mehr News, an agency close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, published a piece saying Iran had given Trump a major dilemma. “Continuing the war could increase political and economic pressure on the government and exacerbate the decline in his popularity. On the other hand, backing down, or moving towards reducing tensions, could also be interpreted by some of Trump’s supporters as a retreat from his campaign slogans,” it said. From this perspective, the outcome of this war will not be played out on the battlefield, but at the ballot box. The agency suggested the outcome could affect the course of American domestic and foreign policy for years to come. Few in Iran take Trump’s statements at face value. But his denials that the midterms affect his Iran strategy are treated with special scepticism. Iranian media point to comments from Marc Zell, chair of Republicans Overseas Israel, who has said: “It’s all about the midterms … the American public simply is tired of war and the administration is navigating the pre-election waters adroitly in order to avoid a Democratic takeover of Congress.” Such remarks fuel the debate inside Iran about how much the midterms should be part of Iran’s calculus. Some believe the loss of Congress will inhibit Trump or lead to his impeachment; at the very least, it may mark the end of the war’s funding. Mostafa Zahrani, a former Iranian diplomat, argued electoral defeat “will make it inevitable that Trump will not be able to go back to war and will take the negotiations seriously”. Others such as Nasser Hadian, a professor of international relations at Tehran University, disagree, advocating cashing in on Iran’s victories now rather than waiting for Trump to become weaker. “If he loses, he’ll have less incentive to reach an agreement with Iran, because in that case he’ll be weakened, and Israel and others will find it much easier to attack him – something they don’t dare do now,” he said. “Those who say we should wait for the midterm elections have no understanding of politics in America.” Iran’s pleasure in seeing Trump defeated would indeed be reduced if he felt he had nothing left to lose, but its diplomats overall believe the US president’s freedom to act will be constrained by the unpopularity of more conflict and by Republican presidential candidates’ anxiety to wrap this up. Trump would also be at risk of seeing his whole second term consumed by a disastrous war. The bigger question is what Iran itself wants to achieve. Agreeing to keep the dispute simmering until November is not an answer to that question – one that Iranians are better at debating than resolving. Pezeshkian, working in alliance with Mohammad Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, repeatedly says he does not want endless war, and insists that almost all the supreme national security council concur. He still has faith in the MoU, saying it should be the cornerstone of Iran’s foreign policy. But the conservative newspaper Kayhan describes the memorandum as worthless since the US always breaks its commitments. “Accordingly, officials should know that the strait of Hormuz is not a bargaining chip and should not be opened as a passage for America,” it said. Both hardliners and moderates envision the war leading to a new regional security architecture. But the hardliners put the emphasis on America’s expulsion and see this as something less to be negotiated and more to be enforced using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz as a lever to close US bases. Pezeshkian says he sees a place for legitimate US investment in Iran, while the former foreign minister Javad Zarif, in an essay this week, argued Iran in “a post-polar era would benefit from not depending solely on Russia and China in future”. If Iran developed “a balanced and multifaceted foreign policy”, Tehran would not be forced into relationships based on necessity, he wrote. “Continuing uncontrolled tensions with the United States not only imposes direct costs on Iran, but also makes it more difficult for other countries, even close partners such as China and Russia, to cooperate with Iran.” Just as Trump cannot resolve from one sentence to the next what he thinks of Iran, nor can Iran agree what it thinks it can get from America.

title: Trump is laying waste to the agency that keeps hospital patients safe
body_text: When I started my training in 1980, we accepted an arithmetic that would now be indefensible. Central lines, the catheters we threaded into the great veins of the critically ill, became infected, and some of those patients died. We recorded the deaths as complications. Almost no one thought of them as preventable, because no one had yet done the slow work of proving they were. That work got done, and federal money paid for it. Beginning in 2008, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, a small arm of the health department, funded a national effort in more than a thousand adult intensive care units: a checklist, a sterile insertion protocol, and a unit culture in which a nurse could stop a surgeon. Central-line bloodstream infections fell by 41%, from 1.915 to 1.133 per 1,000 catheter days. The agency estimates that effort alone averted between 290 and 605 deaths. Across its wider work on hospital-acquired harm, AHRQ’s own accounting credits 20,500 deaths prevented and $7.7bn saved in the four years from 2014 to 2017. Hardly any of my patients have heard of the agency. That was always rather the point. On 15 July, AHRQ sent researchers around the country nearly identical letters ending at least 104 grants, most of them aimed at making care safer. Congress appropriated $345m for the agency this fiscal year. It has spent under $15m on grants and has not issued a new one in more than a year. About three-quarters of the staff have been fired or have quit since Donald Trump took office, and the office that ran grant review was eliminated last summer. An agency with no grant managers cannot make grants, which tells you how long the closure is meant to last. Senator Tammy Baldwin, the ranking Democrat on the appropriations subcommittee that funds AHRQ, counts 150 awards cut off, worth $94m. If you have spent a night in a US hospital in the past 20 years, this agency was working on your behalf whether you knew it or not. It built the patient-experience surveys Medicare uses to help set what hospitals are paid. The quality indicators regulators rely on to spot a hospital that is harming people are its work. With the defense department, it produced the team-communication training now standard in operating rooms and emergency departments. The scientist who spent three decades building those Medicare surveys learned her funding was gone from an email that arrived around 5pm. Among the other grants killed this month: training for physicians, nurses and paramedics managing high-risk pregnancies, in a country where rural women die of pregnancy-related causes at two to three times the rate of women elsewhere; a study of how to spare children in community emergency rooms from unnecessary CT scans and the radiation dose that comes with them; work on catching lung cancer earlier; and telehealth projects serving rural patients. The stated rationale does not hold. AHRQ’s director, Roger Klein, told grantees the agency was redirecting resources toward patient safety, antibiotic resistance, overmedication of children and measurable health outcomes. When KFF Health News examined about 20 of the cancelled grants, nearly all of them pursued those objectives. One of the cancelled grants studied antibiotic resistance. The Michigan pediatrician who lost the last two years of her award said none of it makes any sense, and her field studies exactly what Robert F Kennedy Jr’s “Make America healthy again” agenda claims to champion. Klein has held no agency-wide meetings and published no plan. He has said little in public since January, when he co-wrote an essay in Newsweek arguing that “scientific neutrality” had given way to “moral signaling”. He has reportedly told staff that artificial intelligence can replace much of what his scientists do. A White House science report released on 22 July urged the government to back individual scientists over legacy institutions, to move past slow consensus peer review and to build the future on AI. I use AI tools daily. They are gifted assistants, and they have never placed a central line. I wrote this week in the Annals of Internal Medicine about patients who arrive holding a chatbot’s answer. The models are fluent and often correct, but they have no way of knowing what they were never told. That limit scales. A language model can summarize everything ever published about catheter infections. Someone still had to stand in the unit at three in the morning and notice that the nurses were quietly working around the protocol. Someone still had to design the study that found out why. None of that knowledge existed until people went and got it. Then there is the money. Congress decides how public funds are spent, a principle written into statute after Richard Nixon tried withholding appropriations he disliked. The Society of General Internal Medicine and the North American Primary Care Research Group sued Kennedy and Klein last August over the frozen grant-making, and the case is pending in Maryland. The Government Accountability Office is examining whether the agency’s conduct amounts to an unlawful impoundment. On 17 July a federal judge in Boston held that agencies may not cancel awards over priorities they adopted after making them. Now consider what the health department says about the AHRQ letters: nothing was terminated, and the grants were merely “not awarded continued funding”. That phrasing is doing work. It is an attempt to walk through the one door the court left open. After 45 years in medicine, I know this much about safety. When it works, no one notices. No patient wakes up grateful for the bloodstream infection she did not get, or for the dose a pharmacist’s protocol caught before it reached her line. AHRQ costs each American about a dollar a year, roughly 0.3% of the health department’s discretionary spending, and it is being dismantled in the confidence that the people it protects will never learn what they were spared. The deaths will arrive one at a time, in different hospitals, unlabeled. No letter from Washington will claim them. In 1980 we did not know how to prevent those deaths. We know now. That knowledge took 30 years and public money to build, and it is being discarded by people who have not said why. Robert B Shpiner is an internist and clinical professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. He has practiced and taught intensive care medicine for more than 40 years

title: Trump’s attorney general pick Todd Blanche appears to clear last hurdle for confirmation
body_text: Bill Cassidy, the US Republican senator seen as the decisive holdout on Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, announced on Friday that he will support the pick, setting the stage for a major win for Donald Trump. Confirmation that Cassidy, of Louisiana, is prepared to back Blanche – Trump’s former personal lawyer, and a loyal ally of the president – appeared to clear the last hurdle of his confirmation process, which had been challenged by the defections of the Republican senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins. Blanche is already serving as acting attorney general. “I will vote for Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said in a US Senate floor speech on Friday morning. “Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche; it is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump, and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.” With Cassidy now on board, Blanche is expected to be confirmed by a narrow margin, probably along party lines, as the Senate works through a final vote series before senators leave for the five-week August recess that starts this weekend. Cassidy, who lost his Louisiana primary in May after facing two challengers, including one backed by Trump, had faced weeks of pressure from the White House and had voiced concerns about “lawfare” at the justice department before announcing his decision. Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, had announced earlier on Friday that she would not vote for Blanche’s confirmation, leaving his path to the job down to a single Republican vote. Murkowski’s announcement came a day after Trump, speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, was asked about his fraying relationships with Republican critics including Murkowski and Cassidy and whether the president would reach out to either Republican senator to save the vote. “I’ll reach out to whoever I have to, but anybody voting against [Blanche] would be doing a great disservice to the country,” Trump told reporters. “People have such unbelievable respect” for Blanche, he claimed, expressing hope that reaching out to those lawmakers “won’t be necessary”. Maine’s Susan Collins had already said she will oppose Blanche’s confirmation over concerns about the independence of the US Department of Justice, and with Murkowski’s opposition now confirmed, Cassidy had been the last undecided Republican vote standing between Blanche and confirmation. Murkowski and Cassidy were among the handful of Republicans who voted to convict Trump after his 2021 impeachment over the January 6 Capitol riot. After the Oval Office meeting, Trump acknowledged the political toll his feuds with GOP holdouts have taken. “Look, I don’t regret it. You do what you have to do,” Trump told Punchbowl News. “And just so you understand, they voted to impeach me … In all fairness, you think that I’m going to support somebody that voted to impeach me?” She took her stance even though Blanche confirmed in writing the controversial fund was dead. Experts say Trump could easily reverse it. Murkowski said the Senate only currently has leverage over the fund because Blanche’s nomination to head the Department of Justice is pending necessary confirmation by the upper congressional chamber. Blanche had persuaded the Senate judiciary committee in a 12-10 vote in his favor earlier this week only because he promised Republican holdouts that he would not pursue the payout fund. Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” slush fund designed to compensate political allies who had been “targeted” by the justice department, including prosecutions of January 6 insurrectionists. That move followed weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general – Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, who were eventually swayed by Blanche. Murkowski posted on X on Friday, praising Blanche but then saying “ultimately” she would oppose his nomination, a position she took on Tuesday and is now sticking with. “The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she wrote, as part of a much longer post on the topic. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who was just released from the hospital, is not attending sessions because of his health.

title: Mike Lindell faces legal complaint over pillow giveaway amid run for Minnesota governor
body_text: An administrative law judge in Minnesota has found probable cause to believe Mike Lindell, candidate for Minnesota governor and the MyPillow founder, violated campaign finance law by handing out free pillows at a public event last month. In a four-page ruling issued on Thursday, Judge Nicholas Lienesch found that a complaint against Lindell had enough to move on to an evidentiary hearing in front of a three-judge administrative panel. “There is probable cause to believe that the pillows in this case were a thing of monetary value and were not explicitly exempted by any provision of the statute,” Lienesch wrote. “There is probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election.” Lindell, one of Donald Trump’s most reliable political allies and a US pillow advertising fixture, is running for Minnesota governor against six Republican rivals, including Minnesota’s house speaker, Lisa Demuth, and state GOP-endorsed candidate Kendall Qualls, and seven Democrats, including the Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar. The candidates face a primary election next week to tease out who will go head-to-head in November. Reached for comment on Friday, Lindell argued the pillow giveaway complaint was “complete nonsense”. “It’s been a nonstop campaign since President Trump endorsed me three weeks ago,” he said, claiming that he had checked out the pillow giveaway ahead of time with Minnesota’s campaign finance board. “We got everything completely OKed. This a just a catch-up right before the primary to put doubt in people’s heads. We did everything right. There was no law broken, period. “It’s just an attack,”Lindell added. “It’s disgusting.” On Tuesday, Lindell said he was stepping down as MyPillow CEO to focus his “time and energy” on his run for governor, calling it “one of the biggest decisions” of his life. The complaint against Lindell was brought by Dan Fiskum, a Democrat running for state senate, saying that Lindell threw free pillows from the company he started at an event at a Fourth of July parade in Delano, Minnesota. Under Minnesota law, it is impermissible to give away or promise something of monetary value to induce a voter to vote in a particular way or refrain from voting. Food and beverages valued at less than $5 are exempted. Lindell has said that the pillows he threw were bought wholesale for $4.90 each. Thursday’s ruling does not say Lindell broke the law with the pillow distribution, but Lienesch wrote that he was determining whether “sufficient facts exist in the record to believe that a violation of the law has occurred”. Lindell’s MyPillow fortune, once valued at $300m, has diminished in recent years and he has faced defamation lawsuits and financial judgments over his claims that the 2020 US presidential election was rigged. The candidate said at a hearing on Monday that he could not see a difference between the pillows, which came with campaign literature, and typical campaign trinkets like buttons and keychains. Lindell compared the pillow giveaway to his campaign purchasing his memoir – titled What Are the Odds? From Crack Addict to CEO – and handing it out free at campaign events. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that he was asked what the pillow was worth to people who got one. Lindell responded that most of the pillows went to kids and “those little kids, they like a good night’s sleep and hug that pillow”, but acknowledged that sleep patterns “would be subjective between each individual”. For the adults who received a pillow, Lindell said: “The gift of sleep, I don’t know, it’s all subjective. I don’t think any one of them said: ‘Oh I’m getting a value of $10 and I’m getting it for free.’”

title: US Senate passes Russia sanctions bill championed by Lindsey Graham
body_text: By a large, bipartisan margin, the US Senate on Friday approved a bill intended to punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports over the invasion of Ukraine, capping a legislative push that was spurred by the death of its champion, the Republican senator Lindsey Graham. The measure, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act in honor of the late senator’s work on the issue, was approved by an 86-11 vote. Rand Paul of Kentucky was the sole Republican to oppose the legislation, together with 10 Democrats. The bill would impose new sanctions and visa bans on Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and top military commanders, as well as put tariffs of up to 500% on the country’s exports. It would also allow Donald Trump to impose levies of up to 100% on goods from countries that are the top five importers of Russian oil and gas. The proposal was a top priority for Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina who spent the final days of his life working to advance it. But the effort had became mired in months of negotiations between the White House and Senate leadership. After Graham’s sudden death last month at the age of 71 following a trip to Kyiv, party leaders announced an agreement to get the bill through the chamber and honor his legacy as an ally of Ukraine. The Senate took the first step toward advancing it last month, on the day of Graham’s funeral, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, watching from the chamber. “This bill forces those primary countries keeping Russia’s economy afloat to make a simple yet critical choice – a choice between doing business with America or buying cheap Russian energy,” said Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to his seat after his death. Graham, who presided over the Senate and announced the bill’s passage, added: “This legislation tells Russia’s customers that the United States of America will not sit by while they fund Putin’s assault.” The measure was a relatively rare bipartisan accomplishment ahead of November’s midterm elections, where Democrats hope to channel voter sentiment against Trump to regain control of Congress. “By imposing steep sanctions that will further drain the Kremlin’s war chest, Congress is delivering an important reminder to Putin and his allies that this is a losing war and authoritarianism will never go unchallenged,” said Chuck Schumer, the minority leader. “I urge Trump to use these sanctions to hit Putin where it hurts. Continuing to appease Putin won’t work.” After the vote, Zelenskyy thanked the US Senate, writing on X that the bill’s advancement “certainly helps increase pressure ⁠on the aggressor to bring this insane Russian war against our ‌independence and our people to an end”. Ursula ⁠von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, also cheered the Senate’s action. “Together, let us drain Russia’s means to continue a war it cannot win,” she wrote on X. “With hard-hitting, complementary ⁠sanctions, Europe and the United States can once again show what historic partners can ‌achieve when we act together.” The measure now heads to the House of Representatives, which may consider once it returns from recess at the end of August. Some Democrats have warned that the bill would give Trump new tariff powers at a time when he has put such levies at the center of his trade policy. Paul and Democratic senator Ron Wyden had offered an amendment that would have stripped some of the new tariff authority from the text, but the Senate rejected it by a 32-64 vote. “This bill gives him so much discretion that Trump can ultimately decide what countries to tariff, or what countries to exempt. And he can modify tariffs at his will,” said Wyden, who voted against the bill. “Trump can pick and choose even more countries to tariff every 180 days, but there is no mechanism in this bill for Congress to roll back these tariffs,” he continued. “If Congress passes this bill, members will be condoning the tariff chaos of the last year and a half – and inviting more.” Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, and Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the joint economic committee, criticized the legislation for creating “sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon, as he has repeatedly done in the past”. Noting that Trump just weeks ago imposed new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, the two Democrats said: “We welcome our Senate colleagues’ urgent effort to support Ukraine and punish Russia for its continued illegal war, but this bill would not achieve those goals. Instead, it would allow President Trump to dodge holding Russia accountable and impose yet more tariffs in his destructive trade wars, leaving Americans to foot the bill.”

title: David Brat bound for Australia as diplomat confirmed as next US ambassador
body_text: Former Virginia congressman David Brat has been confirmed by the US Senate to be the next US ambassador to Australia, after the role had been left vacant for 18 months. Brat’s confirmation was among more than 70 votes pushed through the Senate by Republicans on Friday, Washington time, before the summer recess. Brat was nominated by Donald Trump in April. The 61-year-old served two terms in Congress until 2018, when he was defeated by a Democrat, and was vice-president of business relations at Virginia’s Liberty University. The ambassador role had been vacant since November 2024, when Joe Biden’s ambassador, Caroline Kennedy, left the post. Anthony Albanese in April said he would work with anyone Trump nominated, when asked to respond to Brat’s earlier claims that US intelligence agencies conspired to remove Trump from office. “We respect the sovereignty of countries to put forward ambassadors just like we expect our choices to be endorsed,” he said at the time. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, welcomed Brat’s appointment in a statement on Saturday. “He will find Australia to be a warm host and a good friend,” she said. “We share his priorities of critical minerals, defence cooperation and partnership in the Indo-Pacific. Together we will strengthen the alliance in the interests of both our countries.” The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, told reporters on Saturday it was important to have the position now filled. “The bilateral relationship is of course a deeply important one and we welcome the appointment of the new ambassador.” Brat was described by Time magazine in 2010 as a “Tea Party professor” and an enthusiast of the author Ayn Rand. In a 2011 paper, he argued that capitalism and Christianity should merge, writing: “If we all did the right thing and had the guts to spread the word, we would not need the government to backstop every action we take.” Brat was swept into Congress in 2014 when he defeated the then House of Representatives majority leader, Eric Cantor, in a primary. He lost his seat in 2018 to Democrat Abigail Spanberger, who is now the governor of Virginia. The confirmation comes amid tense US-Australia relations, with Trump levelling 12.5% tariffs on many Australian exports in July. Australia was on a list of 54 economies hit with the tariffs due to what the US claimed was a failure “to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”. At the time, the trade minister, Don Farrell, called for the tariffs to be removed, saying they were inconsistent with Australia’s free-trade agreement with the US. Brat’s arrival in Australia will coincide with the 75th anniversary of the Anzus treaty, a security pact over defence of the Pacific, and comes after the Albanese government announced in May it would instead buy three second-hand American nuclear submarines as part of the $370bn Aukus deal, instead of two second-hand and one new as originally intended. While the Albanese government has remained supportive of Aukus, there has been growing disquiet from some within Labor about the plan. Former cabinet minister Ed Husic said in June that the change meant “we are not going to get the deal that was promised to us”. The former defence secretary Greg Moriarty has been Australia’s representative in Washington since taking over from former prime minister Kevin Rudd in April. • This article was amended on 9 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly stated David Brat entered the US Senate in 2014; he was elected to the House of Representatives.

title: US promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdown
body_text: The Trump administration plans to provide $1bn in security assistance to the ⁠government of Colombia’s new rightwing ‌president, the US state department announced, soon after Abelardo De La ‌Espriella was sworn in and used his inaugural speech to pledge a vigorous fight against drug trafficking, as well as austerity measures to restore confidence in the economy. De La Espriella, 48, won June’s runoff election with ⁠promises to crack down on armed groups, shrink ⁠the state by as much as 40% and revive the oil and gas sector. “I have come to close a long chapter of national resignation and, together with the people, embark on the most profound transformation ⁠of our destiny,” De La Espriella said at the Pichincha Battalion military base in Cali after being sworn in on Friday. “I send a firm message to the Colombian people: the time has come to restore order, authority and freedom,” said De La Espriella, who received the endorsement of Donald Trump before his runoff election. “Members of criminal gangs and narco-terrorist groups have two choices: submit to the ⁠rule of law or face the determined response of the Colombian state and its security forces,” the new president told assembled troops at the base during a 75-minute speech, adding the option of peace talks with armed groups had been “completely exhausted”. The US ⁠state department said in a statement on Friday: ⁠“As a cornerstone of this renewed partnership, the United States, working with Congress, ‌intends to announce $1 billion in assistance as part of a security package to support ⁠President de la Espriella’s Administration in achieving our shared goals.” De La Espriella’s election is part of a rightward shift rippling across Latin America. In Peru, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama, weak ‌economies and rising crime have reshaped voter priorities, allowing once-fringe ‌hard-right candidates to gain traction by promising crackdowns amid a global rise of rightwing nationalism. De La Espriella could push through some of his policies via decree, but analysts say many of his proposals will require backing from a divided congress and could ‌be watered down in negotiations. The new president vowed to “definitively eradicate the scourge of illicit crops”, saying he would use aerial herbicides that did not harm human health or the environment to destroy coca, the plant used to make cocaine. In one of his first acts as president, Colombia would join the Shield of the Americas program founded by Trump, he said. Before his inauguration, he held bilateral meetings with the king of Spain and the presidents of Argentina, Ecuador, Chile, Paraguay and Panama. Also attending was Gianni Infantino, the embattled head of Fifa, football’s world governing body, while the US sent a delegation headed by the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche. De La Espriella has blamed former president Gustavo Petro, who has not recognised the new president’s victory, for an expansion of armed groups, and narrowly defeated leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda – a Petro ally – in the runoff. Cepeda led a morning march on Friday in Barranquilla, where he told demonstrators that the country’s opposition would work to defend democracy and called for peaceful civil disobedience. With Reuters

title: Senate passes funding bill to prevent shutdown through US midterms
body_text: The US Senate on Friday passed a government funding bill that will prevent a shutdown through the midterm elections, though it still must be approved by the House of Representatives. The continuing resolution (CR) passed by a 90-6 vote will keep the government running at its current funding levels until 11 December, more than a month past the midterms in which Democrats are hoping to regain control of Congress and block Donald Trump’s legislative agenda for the final two years of his presidency. The measure’s passage signals a recognition by both parties that they would prefer to avoid a messy battle over federal spending in the weeks leading up to the 3 November vote. The government will shut down after 30 September if new funding is not approved, and the Republican Senate appropriations committee chair, Susan Collins, called the CR “a major step toward averting a damaging shutdown that only harms vital programs and federal workers”, and noted it makes no major changes to funding levels. The House had last month approved a different CR that would continue funding until 4 December. It is unclear which bill will ultimately be adopted – the House is on recess until the end of the month, and senators were expected to leave Washington DC for their break following the vote. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate appropriations committee, said the House’s bill had “several major issues” that the Senate’s version addressed. It would block until 11 December a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats fear would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. The Senate CR also closes what Murray called a “loophole” in the House bill that would have allowed the White House to take money meant for other purposes and give it to the border patrol. “Today’s CR gives us the breathing room necessary to work out a budget that helps make life more affordable to working families and reins in Trump’s rampant chaos, his rampant corruption,” the Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said ahead of the vote. Democrats instigated a government shutdown last year when they refused to approve funding bills without an agreement to extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive. While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations. A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push, then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.

title: Trump loyalist Todd Blanche confirmed by Senate as US attorney general
body_text: The US Senate voted to narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a major win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana cast the deciding vote in Blanche’s favor after two other Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska – voted against him. Every Democrat rejected Blanche’s nomination as the Republican-led Senate voted 50-49. Blanche had already been leading the department in an acting capacity, and the vote came after his nomination had been in limbo for weeks. He faced pushback from Republican senators over the department’s deal to create a $1.8bn so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and to give the president, his sons and his businesses tax immunity. “Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said Friday on the Senate floor announcing his decision. “It is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.” The Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said Senate Republicans have “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general. “If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,” he wrote in a post on X. “Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.” Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me”, adding that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him. Concern around the “anti-weaponization fund” appears to have cost Blanche among at least some GOP senators who opposed his nomination, including Murkowski. “I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund – which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters – is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage. Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds,” Murkowski said in a post on X on Friday, announcing she was voting against Blanche. But John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina successfully pushed Blanche to put in writing that the fund was not moving forward and to clarify the scope of the IRS deal. Even though experts said the assurances were far from ironclad, Cornyn and Tillis wound up supporting Blanche, allowing his nomination to narrowly clear the Senate judiciary committee. Blanche also faced heavy criticism for the department’s sloppy rollout of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, which redacted information that should not have been redacted and left unredacted the names of victims that should have been kept private. During his confirmation hearing, Blanche refused to personally meet with Epstein victims, then agreed to do so. The survivors said they received few answers from Blanche during the meeting. Blanche, who left a lucrative partnership to represent Trump in 2023, has been at the center of the president’s attempt to bend the federal government to his will. Scores of career justice department attorneys have left the agency under his leadership. Department lawyers have been rebuked by judges across the US for making misrepresentations to the court. Blanche has also been at the center of Trump’s efforts to use the justice department to punish political rivals. During his tenure as both the deputy attorney general and acting attorney general, the department has indicted former FBI director James Comey twice; the New York attorney general, Letitia James; and the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center – all in cases that exerts see as thin. It has also tried to bring criminal charges against two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and used its investigative powers to try and get leverage over Jerome Powell, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve. “The Attorney General should serve the American people, not the president’s wish list,” Kelly said in a statement on Saturday in which he also noted that Blanche “met with Ghislane Maxwell in secret” before the convicted Epstein accomplice was transferred to a minimum-security prison camp. Blanche, Kelly added “is defined by his loyalty to Trump”. As his nomination was pending, Blanche also promised anti-abortion advocates the department would make the Dobbs decision permanent in every state, according to Politico. “While I believe Mr Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political,” Collins, who is running for re-election in Maine, said earlier this week. “Mr Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation.” Earlier this year, Blanche spoke about how he would feel if someone else was named attorney general. “As to whether or not I want this job, I did not ask for this job. I love working for President Trump, it’s the greatest honor of a lifetime,” he said in April, shortly after being named the acting attorney general. “If he chooses to nominate somebody else and asks me to go do something else, I will say, ‘Thank you very much. I love you, sir.’ I don’t have any goals or aspirations beyond that.”

Blanche also faced heavy criticism for the department’s sloppy rollout of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, which redacted information that should not have been redacted and left unredacted the names of victims that should have been kept private. During his confirmation hearing, Blanche refused to personally meet with Epstein victims, then agreed to do so. The survivors said they received few answers from Blanche during the meeting. Blanche, who left a lucrative partnership to represent Trump in 2023, has been at the center of the president’s attempt to bend the federal government to his will. Scores of career justice department attorneys have left the agency under his leadership. Department lawyers have been rebuked by judges across the US for making misrepresentations to the court. Blanche has also been at the center of Trump’s efforts to use the justice department to punish political rivals. During his tenure as both the deputy attorney general and acting attorney general, the department has indicted former FBI director James Comey twice; the New York attorney general, Letitia James; and the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center – all in cases that exerts see as thin. It has also tried to bring criminal charges against two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and used its investigative powers to try and get leverage over Jerome Powell, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve. “The Attorney General should serve the American people, not the president’s wish list,” Kelly said in a statement on Saturday in which he also noted that Blanche “met with Ghislane Maxwell in secret” before the convicted Epstein accomplice was transferred to a minimum-security prison camp. Blanche, Kelly added “is defined by his loyalty to Trump”. As his nomination was pending, Blanche also promised anti-abortion advocates the department would make the Dobbs decision permanent in every state, according to Politico. “While I believe Mr Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political,” Collins, who is running for re-election in Maine, said earlier this week. “Mr Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation.” Earlier this year, Blanche spoke about how he would feel if someone else was named attorney general. “As to whether or not I want this job, I did not ask for this job. I love working for President Trump, it’s the greatest honor of a lifetime,” he said in April, shortly after being named the acting attorney general. “If he chooses to nominate somebody else and asks me to go do something else, I will say, ‘Thank you very much. I love you, sir.’ I don’t have any goals or aspirations beyond that.”

title: Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on voting
body_text: In a Washington DC conference room last month, some of the most senior Democrats in the US Senate gathered to plan for a prospect that only recently would have felt more akin to science fiction: they started to wargame democracy. Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios. The first: realistic deepfake videos, created with artificial intelligence, showing “evidence” of widespread election fraud, spreading through social media a few weeks before voting begins. Forensic experts discredit the videos quickly as synthetic in the given scenario, but rightwing media – and the US president – amplify the claims, nonetheless. Election workers begin receiving death threats. Armed men start appearing at polls. If you’re a Democratic senator, what would you do? “These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen,” said Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy. “But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.” Senate Democrats have held two election disruption exercises this year. Voting rights and legal groups like Protect Democracy have also participated, along with election attorney Marc Elias, former attorney general Eric Holder, election law expert Norman Eisen and members of the left-leaning non-profit Democracy Forward. Skye Perryman, CEO of Democracy Forward, expressed confidence in the resilience of the foundations of US democracy, pointing to the legal system and the distributed nature of American elections, which she said builds a defense against crass political interference, even from the US president. “The president can try to imagine whatever he may wish to imagine,” Perryman said. “He can’t imagine a new constitution, and the constitution, frankly, is quite clear in no uncertain terms; there’s not a role for the president in election administration in this country.” Nonetheless, Donald Trump’s continuous false claims about a stolen election in 2020, and his increasingly strident demand for the US Congress to pass a package of federalized oversights of elections, have raised concerns among progressive voters that the administration may mar November’s midterms with misinformation, or worse. The administration billed Trump’s primetime TV address last month as a presentation of new evidence that the 2020 election was illegitimate, and that his administration had uncovered new findings about vulnerabilities in the US election system. Instead, Trump claimed China had illicitly acquired voter information on 220 million Americans, and that China had undermined his 2020 campaign in other unspecified ways, arguing that intelligence officials had suppressed this information. Trump’s claims fell apart under scrutiny. His own intelligence officials had already concluded that China refrained from interfering in the US election out of concern for potential political blowback if caught. Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry the address live. In his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls. Republican senators refuse to dispense with the 60-vote filibuster threshold to pass the law. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, representing a swing state that is a favored rhetorical target of the president, described Trump’s address as “signaling his unmistakable intent to attack these elections and our voting rights, just as he tried to throw out our votes and seize the presidency in 2020”. Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference. Trump’s public commentary, and the actions of agencies under his supervision, shaped the scenario building as Democratic leaders plan their possible responses. Senators were asked at their recent session to contemplate how to react to a threat to withhold Office of Management and Budget (OMB) funding for states that don’t submit their voter rolls for federal oversight. They also considered a threat of Federal Communications Commission (FCC) action against news outlets covering deepfakes. “The development of AI will only add to the complexity and could create confusion among voters in our fragmented media landscape,” said Vail. “Unfortunately, that confusion can be to the benefit of the administration’s strategy.” FCC enforcement actions seem relatively mild compared to more extreme scenarios, like planning a response to armed vigilantes in tactical gear at ballot drop boxes – which was not a hypothetical problem in Arizona during the 2022 midterms. Senators were asked to plan responses for online license-plate doxxing, a midnight firebombing of an early voting site and a last-minute unilateral deployment of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents and the national guard to polling stations. The main lesson of the exercise “is that this is an all-hands-on-deck moment, and it is an all-hands-on-deck response”, said Perryman. “And so what that means is that, we’re not looking at any one silver bullet to be able to fully protect elections. It’s going to take all of us.”

title: Moderate Democrat Ed Case defies progressive challenge in Hawaii primary
body_text: The moderate Democratic representative Ed Case has seen off a progressive challenge to retain his party’s nomination for the US House of Representatives election in Hawaii’s first congressional district. Case, who has represented the district in Washington DC since 2019, prevailed in Saturday’s primary over Jarrett Keohokalole, the state senator. A wave of leftwing candidates has swept through a series of high-profile Democratic primaries in recent months, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan this week. Focus will turn next week to Wisconsin, where the democratic socialist Francesca Hong is leading the party’s chaotic gubernatorial primary. Keohokalole, 43, had argued during the campaign in Hawaii that the time had come for a new generation of political leadership in the state. With 91% of votes counted, Case had won 60% of the vote, according to the Associated Press. Keohokalole, in second place, had 36.1%. “I feel very grateful that the voters want me to continue in office,” Case, 73, told Hawaii Public Radio on Saturday. He will now face Adriel Lam, the Republican who ran unopposed in the party’s primary, in the general election. “The voters decided, and we respect the results,” Keohokalole told KHON2. “The seats don’t belong to any individual. You have to earn them, and so the voters spoke.” Case had faced criticism from Democrats including Keohokalole after voting last year for Donald Trump’s Save Act, which would require US voters to prove their citizenship when registering for federal elections. More recently, Case stressed that he no longer supported the legislation, after an option for voters to attest in writing that they are a citizen was removed. But he used his former vote as an example of his independence. “I’m not 100% voter with my party,” Case told HawaiiNewsNow. “Never have been, never will be.” Case holds a senior position on a key spending committee and had argued that Hawaii would attract fewer federal dollars if he was not re-elected. Keohokalole highlighted Case’s campaign donations from businesses to argue he has lost touch with voters. Hawaii is divided into two US congressional districts. The first, represented by Case, covers the urban center of Honolulu. The second, represented by Jill Tokuda, covers the rest of the state. Tokuda also won the Democratic primary for the second congressional district. According to AP, with 90% of votes counted, she had won 91.6%. Josh Green, the Hawaii governor who has led the state since 2022, also defeated several challengers for the Democratic nomination. Reuters contributed reporting
