title: Taylor Swift songs removed from Trump and White House’s social media posts
body_text: Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House, silencing efforts to mock the pop star. A video posted on 3 August featuring the US president and the first lady, Melania Trump, watching fireworks was posted this month on TikTok with Swift’s song August. “I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august,” the accompanying text states. Trump’s campaign later published another post, needling Swift over the title of her 2012 album, Red. “Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican party?” it said, suggesting parody track titles. Both videos are now silent. Trump-related social media accounts have used Swift’s music in other campaign videos, too, but several of those also no longer have sound. As the text with the August video suggests, Trump’s social media accounts have used pop stars’ songs as rage bait. They have featured music from artists including Ariana Grande, Katy Perry, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo and Kenny Loggins, all of whom publicly objected to the use of their music. “Please do not use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense,” Grande posted after the White House posted her music over a montage of ICE agents handcuffing and detaining people. When Trump’s White House used one of Carpenter’s songs to soundtrack a video of immigration raids in 2025, the singer wrote: “This video is evil and disgusting. Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.” In this latest case, Swift has not commented. Trump had previously attacked Swift, who endorsed then Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris during the 2024 election. “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” Trump declared at the time. Last year he wrote: “Has anyone noticed that, since I said ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,’ she’s no longer ‘HOT?’” Swift’s Eras tour was the the highest-grossing tour of all time, according to Pollstar, generating about $2.2bn worldwide. Her album The Life of a Showgirl became the most pre-saved album ever on Spotify ahead of its October 2025 release.

title: Abdul El-Sayed embraces Trump claim he represents ‘very different’ America
body_text: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”. In a Saturday night post on his Truth Social platform, Trump shared an image of himself and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab. “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s [sic],” read the caption. “Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN, when asked about the post on Sunday. “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things. “Yes, you’ve got two different visions of America,” said El-Sayed. “Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?” El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan this week, setting up a bruising general election campaign against former US representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in the swing state. Victory for him is widely seen as crucial to the Democrats’ hopes of retaking control of the Senate from Republicans. During a speech on Thursday, Trump called El-Sayed a communist and said he was “full of shit”, which was met with loud cheers. Asked about the president’s expletive remark, El-Sayed told Sky News: “At least I don’t let mine go in the middle of the Oval Office.” Unlike some other new Democratic candidates, El-Sayed, who ran to the left of his primary opponent, is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and has said he is a capitalist who wants capitalism to work better. Former US president Barack Obama spoke with El-Sayed after his primary win, in what is deemed an early sign of support for his campaign. “It was a really good conversation about what we need to do to be able to win, and obviously this is somebody who knows a lot about winning Michigan,” El-Sayed told NBC News. Michigan backed both of Obama’s runs for the presidency, in 2008 and 2012, before voting for Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020, and turning back to Trump in 2024. Obama also called Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat whom El-Sayed defeated in the primary, Politico reported. Stevens urged the former president to “come to Michigan and campaign for the Democrats”, she told the outlet. Should he beat Rogers in November’s general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator. Republicans have described him as “the most radical Senate candidate in America”, and Trump has repeatedly used his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. El-Sayed noted the party – and Trump – did the same to Obama, regularly including his middle name “Hussein” when referencing the former president. “At the end of the day it’s not radical to believe that people should be able to afford their groceries,” he told NBC’s Meet The Press. “It’s not radical to believe that you should have healthcare in this country. “It’s not radical … that you don’t think the president should be able to deny elections, or make $2.2bn out of his role in office. It’s not radical to believe all of us should be able to breathe clean air and drink clean water. Those are the things that I’ve been fighting for.” El-Sayed said: “They are going to try to paint me as a certain thing, given my name, but I also think it’s important to recognize that America has a long history of embracing, “America is a lot bigger than very small people like Donald Trump or [Vice President] JD Vance or Mike Rogers want to make it out to be. And so I’m grateful for all that America has given me.”

title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump
body_text: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.” Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal. The Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts in Gaza and Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home. Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month, Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory – strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.” But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.” Netanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With US midterm elections due in November, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices. But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel. Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?” More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause. In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel. Yet more broadly, support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who is publicly sceptical of Israel and the war in Gaza. title: Trump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counsel
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure approval for the $400m White House ballroom project from a key official body, will become ⁠White House counsel and assistant to the president. Effective 1 September, Scharf will replace David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Warrington formerly served as a personal counsel and a lawyer ‌for Trump’s 2024 campaign. Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the supreme court. Scharf also led the National ‌Capital Planning Commission, which approved the president’s construction of the White House ballroom. “Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!” The shake-up in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, in which Trump’s Republican party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November. The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the justice department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity. Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region. Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled on Friday that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the supreme court. The project is already well under way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Will democratic socialist Francesca Hong shake up the establishment – or help Republicans win Wisconsin?
body_text: As Francesca Hong surged ahead in the final weeks of the chaotic Democratic primary to be Wisconsin’s next governor, the democratic socialist has become the internet’s main character. Donald Trump has mocked her old tweets, while major figures in her own party publicly questioned her ability to win a general election. The man she is vying to succeed even launched a late blitz in support of one of her rivals. But on the ground in Wisconsin, the enthusiasm for her shines through. Riding through a 24-hour bike race in Milwaukee’s Riverwest neighborhood in late July, residents passed Hong coloring books on a table of campaign merch; a scrolling sign saying “We love Fran”; and a DJ calling Hong “so fresh and so clean” as he played OutKast. After the sun went down, Hong hopped on a bike herself after a line of supporters grabbed photos with her. She danced with other racers in a tame mosh pit at one of the race’s side quests, and later that night got a tattoo to commemorate the race, Riverwest 24, on her leg, alongside her Milwaukee Bucks tattoo. In hundreds of events across Wisconsin – from karaoke nights to ramen pop-ups – Hong, 37, built a grassroots army that pushed her to the verge of clinching the Democratic nomination for governor in a marquee battleground state. Her status as frontrunner put Hong on national shows in recent days, summoning a wave of headlines about her past tweets, including one – seized on by Republicans, including Trump – in which she called for cancelling Thanksgiving. After the progressive Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in nextdoor Michigan last week, scrutiny of Hong intensified. In Wisconsin, Democrats face another test of whether voters in a swing state will side with leftwing candidates in primaries – and what that could mean for the party’s chances in a typically close general election in November. Hong – a chef and former restaurant owner, a single mom and a state lawmaker from Madison – is running on a progressive platform that includes universal childcare and fully funding the state’s public schools. She is also calling for a moratorium on datacenters, a centerpiece that differentiates her from the other Democratic candidates. “I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.” Four candidates are vying for the open governor’s seat on Tuesday, with most polls showing Hong in the lead. Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, a former head of the state administration department, are still in the race. A previous contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July. David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, exited the race and then re-entered it – receiving the endorsement of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers. A memo from the Crowley campaign on 5 August suggested polling may be off, pointing to Michigan polls showing El-Sayed with a much broader lead than he actually achieved. Evers recently claimed Hong’s campaign was “in a tough place”, because she had to spend time dealing with “what’s on the Twitter”. Hong has pointed to Crowley’s change of heart as evidence of panic by the Democratic establishment. There is a “reluctance to change, and a fear of change” among “a lot of our candidates and some of their consultants”, she suggested after he re-entered the race. A really good chance Whoever wins the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin will face Tom Tiffany, an ardent Trump supporter running unopposed in the Republican primary. He voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost. Tiffany has more cash than any of the Democratic candidates so far, and Republicans are sure to flood the market to boost him. “The Wisconsin governor certifies the presidential election results, and Tom Tiffany was part of a plot to overturn the 2020 results,” said Ben Wikler, the former chair of the Wisconsin Democratic party. “This is a very high-stakes seat that will affect not just the lives of every Wisconsinite, but also potentially the future of American democracy.” Five of the last seven presidential elections in Wisconsin had come down to less than one percentage point, Wikler noted. Most states have trended red or blue over time, but Wisconsin stays “consistently right on the knife’s edge”, he said. The stakes are greater than Wisconsin’s role in the national elections. Democrats are angling for a governing trifecta in Wisconsin, trying to win back control of both chambers of the state assembly and keep the governor’s office so they can enact a full agenda. Some want a perceived “safe” candidate, and have expressed doubt that Hong could win a general election, even in a predicted wave year for Democrats. David Axelrod, the Democratic strategist who helped Barack Obama win, has repeatedly panned Hong, whom he has described as “a font of zany liberal, faculty lounge exotica”. Michael Wagner, the director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s journalism school who researches political communication, said that while Republicans have increasingly run more extreme candidates in the past decade, Democrats have instead believed the only way to win statewide in swing states is with moderate candidates. But there’s evidence that’s not true, he said: Wisconsin’s two US senators fall on either edge of their parties, with the progressive Tammy Baldwin, and Ron Johnson rising from the Tea party. “Sometimes the party establishment can get too cute with what they worry about,” said Wagner. “But it’s not unreasonable that they’re worried, because in an election in Wisconsin, any one of 20 things could shift 10,000 votes, and that could be it.” Wagner said Hong’s strongest coalition was among young voters, so she needs to make sure they show up and vote for her, while calming any fears from moderates and independents. But in a place like Wisconsin, where voters are willing to take chances on people who speak directly to the issues they are about, Hong had a good shot at winning both the primary and the general, he added. “That doesn’t mean she’ll win either of them, but she’s got a really good chance.” Hong often counters the electability question with: “The person who wins the most votes is the most electable. And we are fighting harder than any other campaign to win the most votes.” On the trail In one recent conversation on the campaign trail, a voter asked Hong point blank: what are you going to do for me? “I was like, I’m going to work harder for you than anyone else and make sure that we’re raising wages, taxing the billionaires and we’re stopping datacenters,” she recounted, sitting outside at the University of Wisconsin-Superior in northern Wisconsin after an education forum with other gubernatorial candidates. She thinks voters appreciate her firm, bold stances. She doesn’t shy away from the democratic socialist label, but noted that the DSA hadn’t endorsed her, and stressed that she doesn’t agree with the full DSA platform. She previously said she wanted to defund the police but now says she does not. “The urgency of this moment requires actually meeting the scale and speed in which these different things have become a problem,” she said. “You see the mass income disparities. You have to meet that with a policy that’s going to fix it permanently. And that’s changing a rigged system.” She wears a stack of beaded bracelets picked up while campaigning – one from a datacenter organizing meeting, another with the ICE watch hotline. Born in Madison, she cut her teeth in restaurants, and was elected to the state assembly in 2020, becoming the first Asian American member. As a lawmaker, she authored a bill that would provide healthy school meals for all kids and a package of bills that would fight back against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) overreach. Chris Larson, a state senator who recently endorsed Hong, cited her ability to form coalitions at the capitol, including by bringing in outside groups affected by policy ideas. He is friends with multiple people running for governor, but saw the maneuvering against Hong over electability concerns “lacking in imagination”. “This is where we build hope. This is how we get shit done,” he said during Riverwest 24. “And that for me is what Francesca Hong brings. And if there are folks who are saying that that is too much, I want to be part of the pushback against that.” On datacenters, Hong’s call for a one-year moratorium on their construction opens the door for voters to wonder why no one else is trying to stop this, Larson said. Hong said the datacenters piece resonates because people feel the most threat to their own control. The unregulated boom of AI has people feeling a need for quick action, she said. “Just because I’m team human doesn’t mean I’m anti-AI. I just don’t want it to control us. I think that we get to regulate it.” Riding through the Riverwest neighborhood with bright green Hong signs strapped to his bike, people stopped Larson to ask if Hong would be there. One man, Chris Montezon, asked if he could snag a sign. Larson handed one off as they biked through city streets. Montezon said he appreciated Hong’s policies, but also that she had gone all over the state, including rural Wisconsin, to engage with people. He thinks she can win a statewide general election. “I think there’s a lot of disaffected voters in the state.” At the education forum in Superior, four gubernatorial candidates went deep on funding formulas and spending. They didn’t attack each other; for the most part, the race has remained friendly, with veiled references to electability aimed indirectly at Hong. Terrence Dahmen, a 73-year-old independent who said he ends up voting for Democrats most of the time, watched the candidates at the forum and found them all “young, enthusiastic, well-read and well-spoken”. He didn’t think the state could go wrong with any of them, but was leaning toward Hong because of her datacenter moratorium. She was “a little more of a socialist, which doesn’t bother me at all”, he said, adding that Evers’ intervention in the race “doesn’t smell good”. “I know she could probably get elected in Madison pretty easily and probably in Milwaukee, but I’m a little leery about northern Wisconsin,” Dahmen said. “I live in northern Wisconsin and there’s a lot of racism up here, so that might weigh against her.” But Robert Edelstein, a 62-year-old who described himself as progressive but isn’t registered with a political party, was concerned that Republicans were boosting Hong. He wants a a Democratic candidate who will prevail in November. “I’m troubled that it could be someone who can’t win.” Enter the establishment Crowley, 40, told the Guardian his decision to re-enter the governor’s race and make a last-minute, all-out bid to topple Hong did not have anything to do with the so-called Democratic establishment. While he’s happy to have Evers’ endorsement, he has insisted his re-entry didn’t hinge on the governor’s support. Instead, after Rodriguez, Wisconsin’s lieutenant governor, unexpectedly left the race, Crowley and his wife prayed over whether he should get back in, and the answer was at first a solid no. They had booked a trip to Jamaica. He knew it could be confusing to voters. His wife asked the Lord to send a sign – a red bird – if they should get back in the race. Crowley continued to field calls from supporters. His wife saw a red cardinal on a Friday morning, just minutes before Rodriguez announced she would drop out. “We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate – not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done,” Crowley said. “And that’s what voters want. They want someone that they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.” Crowley said voters had raised concerns about electability in a general election as he had traveled throughout the state, and he said polls showed him beating Tiffany in a head-to-head matchup. “We need to make sure that we build a winning coalition to bring not just Democrats, but those independents and even Republicans who are exhausted by Maga on to this campaign to make sure that we reach our ultimate goal.” “I know that it has been a little chaotic,” he acknowledged. “It’s a little messy in this primary, but so is our democracy.” He is “far from” the establishment, he said: he grew up with parents who struggled with mental health and drug addiction. He was evicted three times. He worked hard to get to where he is. “I don’t want folks to get me being established because of what I’ve worked extremely hard for, for me being a part of any type of establishment,” he said. Some voters have struggled with his re-entry, and Evers’ involvement. William Norman, a Hong supporter who biked in the Riverwest 24 alongside his parents, said the race got hectic in the last few weeks “for all the wrong reasons”. “I think it’s kind of loser behavior to think that one of your candidates can’t beat somebody who’s running on such a nasty platform across the aisle,” Norman said. “I just feel like you should have faith in your candidate. Whoever the people want should be the person to be sent into battle.” Others, including Crowley and Evers, point to the haranguing over Hong’s old tweets, most of which have not been deleted, that journalists and Republicans have elevated. Her campaign told the New York Times that a lot of those tweets were written during “peak woke” in the 2020s. When initially asked by CNN about the since-deleted “cancel Thanksgiving” tweet from November 2020, Hong said “views can evolve” and that Thanksgiving can be “incredibly painful for many people in our communities”. She later joked to Politico that Thanksgiving was her favorite. Becky Cooper, Hong’s campaign manager, said digging up tweets from more than five years ago was an attempt to distract from voters’ needs, including affordable healthcare and property tax relief, as well as a “huge waste” of time and energy. “But,” she added, “we’re always working to sharpen language and deliver the message.” Hong told the Guardian she welcomed national interest in her campaign, but did feel the pressure. For a Democratic socialist running on a broad agenda that disrupts the political status quo, winning in a place like Wisconsin could change politics – not just in the state, but across the country, she said. “We can’t have a more representative democracy unless we have more folks who are willing to fight the way things have been done,” she said. “Because that’s what’s gotten us here.”

He wants a a Democratic candidate who will prevail in November. “I’m troubled that it could be someone who can’t win.” Enter the establishment Crowley, 40, told the Guardian his decision to re-enter the governor’s race and make a last-minute, all-out bid to topple Hong did not have anything to do with the so-called Democratic establishment. While he’s happy to have Evers’ endorsement, he has insisted his re-entry didn’t hinge on the governor’s support. Instead, after Rodriguez, Wisconsin’s lieutenant governor, unexpectedly left the race, Crowley and his wife prayed over whether he should get back in, and the answer was at first a solid no. They had booked a trip to Jamaica. He knew it could be confusing to voters. His wife asked the Lord to send a sign – a red bird – if they should get back in the race. Crowley continued to field calls from supporters. His wife saw a red cardinal on a Friday morning, just minutes before Rodriguez announced she would drop out. “We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate – not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done,” Crowley said. “And that’s what voters want. They want someone that they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.” Crowley said voters had raised concerns about electability in a general election as he had traveled throughout the state, and he said polls showed him beating Tiffany in a head-to-head matchup. “We need to make sure that we build a winning coalition to bring not just Democrats, but those independents and even Republicans who are exhausted by Maga on to this campaign to make sure that we reach our ultimate goal.” “I know that it has been a little chaotic,” he acknowledged. “It’s a little messy in this primary, but so is our democracy.” He is “far from” the establishment, he said: he grew up with parents who struggled with mental health and drug addiction. He was evicted three times. He worked hard to get to where he is. “I don’t want folks to get me being established because of what I’ve worked extremely hard for, for me being a part of any type of establishment,” he said. Some voters have struggled with his re-entry, and Evers’ involvement. William Norman, a Hong supporter who biked in the Riverwest 24 alongside his parents, said the race got hectic in the last few weeks “for all the wrong reasons”. “I think it’s kind of loser behavior to think that one of your candidates can’t beat somebody who’s running on such a nasty platform across the aisle,” Norman said. “I just feel like you should have faith in your candidate. Whoever the people want should be the person to be sent into battle.” Others, including Crowley and Evers, point to the haranguing over Hong’s old tweets, most of which have not been deleted, that journalists and Republicans have elevated. Her campaign told the New York Times that a lot of those tweets were written during “peak woke” in the 2020s. When initially asked by CNN about the since-deleted “cancel Thanksgiving” tweet from November 2020, Hong said “views can evolve” and that Thanksgiving can be “incredibly painful for many people in our communities”. She later joked to Politico that Thanksgiving was her favorite. Becky Cooper, Hong’s campaign manager, said digging up tweets from more than five years ago was an attempt to distract from voters’ needs, including affordable healthcare and property tax relief, as well as a “huge waste” of time and energy. “But,” she added, “we’re always working to sharpen language and deliver the message.” Hong told the Guardian she welcomed national interest in her campaign, but did feel the pressure. For a Democratic socialist running on a broad agenda that disrupts the political status quo, winning in a place like Wisconsin could change politics – not just in the state, but across the country, she said. “We can’t have a more representative democracy unless we have more folks who are willing to fight the way things have been done,” she said. “Because that’s what’s gotten us here.”

title: The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem
body_text: At the end of July, Donald Trump announced that a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it was reported that another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe. Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitly rejected the sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.” In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazen violation of the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle. Formal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largely destroyed and the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first building contract issued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievous miscalculation in which Israel’s prime minister also played his part. In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue a scorched earth project of revenge following the Hamas massacre of October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruption charges first laid more than five years ago. Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point. Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recent polling suggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza. title: Todd Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, sworn in as US attorney general
body_text: Todd Blanche has been sworn as the US attorney general, cementing Donald Trump’s installation of his former personal attorney as head of the Department of Justice. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was confirmed in his new position during a ceremony at the White House on Monday. The 52-year-old is the second Senate-confirmed attorney general of Trump’s second term, after Pam Bondi, who was ousted earlier this year. He previously served as Trump’s personal criminal defense lawyer, representing him in the New York hush-money case and other criminal matters, before joining the administration as deputy attorney general in early 2025. “Congratulations to a great lawyer and an even better man!!!” the press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, posted on social media following his closed-door confirmation. Since taking over, Blanche has presided over the departure of more than 200 prosecutors and agents who worked on Trump-related investigations, pushed expansive theories of presidential power and suffered a string of courtroom setbacks, including a stinging ruling in which a federal judge sent her findings to bar authorities considering disciplinary action against him. He now officially takes over the department after Trump ousted his predecessor, Pam Bondi, whom the president had become frustrated with over insufficient action from the Department of Justice against his political foes. Bondi’s tenure had also been dogged by controversy over the botched handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, which still shadows the department, with lawmakers continuing to press for the full release of records and Democrats accusing Blanche of following Bondi’s playbook of stonewalling survivors and Congress alike. The Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation in the role, with the Republican-led upper chamber voting 50-49 in the early hours of Saturday morning. Every Democrat rejected his nomination, as well as the Republican senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

title: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths
body_text: Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse. The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy. “Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.” The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised. The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls. On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza. Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace. Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”. Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region. “Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote.

title: Republicans name candidate to replace Chuck Edwards after sexual harassment investigation
body_text: North Carolina Republicans on Monday chose the state lawmaker Jennifer Balkcom to replace Chuck Edwards, the incumbent congressman who earlier this month dropped his re-election bid after a US House investigation determined his conduct towards young female staffers probably amounted to sexual harassment. Balkcom will face off against the Democratic nominee, Jamie Ager, in the November midterm elections to represent the 11th congressional district in western North Carolina. Though Donald Trump won the district by 10 percentage points two years ago, Democrats believe Ager may have a shot at winning amid the president’s low approval ratings and frustration over the pace of recovery from Hurricane Helene, which devastated the region in 2024. “I’m blessed to receive the Republican nomination for the 11th Congressional District. Western North Carolina is where I was born, raised, and chose to raise my own family,” Ager said in a statement following her nomination. “Rest assured, I will work every single day between now and Election Day to earn the votes of our friends and neighbors. Our region is incredibly strong and resilient, and I plan to be the fighter everyone who calls Western North Carolina home deserves.” Edwards was first elected in 2022 after defeating the scandal-plagued congressman Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary. Last week, the US House ethics committee found he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” towards two female employees in his Washington DC office. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior probably violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances, and the ethics committee recommended he be censured. Even before Edwards dropped out, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the House Democratic campaign arm, had added his district to its list of targets to regain the majority in the House of Representatives in November’s midterms. No House Democrat has won election to the region since 2010, and the race between Ager and Balkcom is likely to see concerted spending from both parties and outside groups. Edwards had won the Republican nomination for his district in last March’s primary, and the North Carolina Republican party had convened in Asheville a meeting of officials from the region to select a replacement. Zach Almond, the state party’s executive director, said Balkcom beat five other candidates on the first round of balloting.

title: Minnesota primaries could mark change of path for Democrats and Republicans
body_text: Minnesota voters on both sides of the aisle are weighing the direction of their parties – and their chances of winning over the general electorate – in marquee statewide races on Tuesday. On the left, Peggy Flanagan, the state lieutenant governor and a progressive, faces off against Angie Craig, a US representative, for the Democratic bid for US Senate in a race punctuated by the role of immigration enforcement in the state that saw two residents killed by immigration agents in a winter surge. On the right, Mike Lindell, an election denier and pillow salesman, carries Donald Trump’s endorsement in a three-way race for the Republican nomination for governor, where Republicans face an uphill battle to challenge Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic contender and a US senator, now seeking the governor’s office. After Tuesday, the general election for the open governor and US Senate seats will shape up, signaling a change for top roles in the state. Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat, initially sought a third term, but dropped his bid after ongoing fraud scandals threatened to distract from the race. Tina Smith, the Democratic US senator, decided not to run again, saying she wanted to spend time with her grandkids and make way for new faces in the chamber. She has endorsed Flanagan. The state leans Democratic. It has not elected a Republican statewide since 2006, when Tim Pawlenty won a second term as governor. A Republican presidential candidate has not won the state since 1972. Still, Republicans hope to seize on fraud problems in state programs, including criminal cases against a sprawling group accused of organized theft of meals for children, services for kids with autism and housing programs. US Senate race While Republicans have a primary for US Senate on Tuesday as well, Michele Tafoya, a former National Football League sideline reporter, is likely to be the GOP nominee. On the Democratic side, polls of the race have been mixed. Flanagan has attacked Craig for supporting the Laken Riley Act, a federal law that requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes, named after a woman murdered in Georgia by an undocumented immigrant. Craig has since expressed regret for her vote, writing in March that it has “become clear that supporting any bill that gives ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] new authority in this administration was the wrong decision”. Flanagan told the Guardian she appreciated that Craig has said she regrets the vote, but that she thinks Craig owes Minnesotans an apology and that the vote showed “a real lack of judgment”. “I also think it shows a pretty big disconnect from Minnesotans and the communities here,” Flanagan said. “I think it demonstrates that she doesn’t have a lot of relationships with the people who are most impacted. I think that matters.” Craig has gone after Flanagan on the fraud issue, saying Flanagan has not taken accountability for any role that allowed fraud to perpetuate. “State fraud is the No 1 issue as Minnesota voters go to the polls in November,” Craig told the New York Times. “Fairly or not, the lieutenant governor has a unique vulnerability as our statewide Senate candidate because she’s been helping run the state for the last eight years.” Craig was not available for an interview with the Guardian. The 54-year-old was first elected to Congress in 2018, flipping a seat from a Republican to become the first out lesbian to be elected to US Congress from the state. She represents a purple district south of the Twin Cities, which she has pointed to as a sign of electability statewide. Flanagan, 46, served in the state house of representatives before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019. She is a citizen of the White Earth Nation and began her political career as an organizer, a vocation she says would help her build power for progressives in the Senate if she wins. “My job, as soon as I get to Washington DC, is to have 99 cups of coffee with people, to build those relationships, to find opportunities for common ground with folks on the other side of the aisle,” she said. “We may find some unexpected places to work together.” Her platform now includes support for the proposed Medicare for All system of universal healthcare, an issue that she didn’t start off her campaign supporting, but embraced after talking to people across the state who had healthcare horror stories. “They want folks who aren’t going to govern by sternly worded letter,” Flanagan said. “And I think that people are ready for big, bold change.” Tafoya, a Republican who is pro-choice, is counting on winning over independent voters. She has centered her campaign on the fraud scandals. Republican delegates at the state convention endorsed Adam Schwarze, a marine and Navy Seal. Governor’s race Lindell, the pillow salesman, is hoping to ride Trump’s endorsement to a victory over Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker, and Kendall Qualls, a businessman. Qualls won the endorsement of Republican activists at the state party convention earlier this year. Lindell has faced opposition from the state Republican party, which has questioned his eligibility to hold office in the state, saying it wanted clarity on whether Lindell has lived in Minnesota long enough to qualify. Lindell, who is from Minnesota, has also lived in Texas. He has said he moved back to Minnesota in August 2025, though only registered to vote in the state in July 2026. Lindell, who has been sued for defamation by voting machine companies and others, has not relented in his claims that the 2020 election was stolen and that Trump had actually won. He currently faces allegations of a potential campaign finance law violation over handing out free pillows at a parade. An administrative law judge in the state recently said there was “probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election”. Lindell called the complaint “complete nonsense”. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, saying he needed to focus on his campaign for governor. He also faces millions in creditor claims over unpaid bills from the company. Alex Plechash, the Minnesota Republican party chair, said Trump’s endorsement of Lindell was a “surprise” and noted that Lindell has “significant electability concerns”. Klobuchar faces several Democratic contenders in a primary, though is likely to easily win on Tuesday. Klobuchar, who ran for president in 2020, has handily won her US Senate campaigns since she was first elected in 2006. Congressional races Multiple congressional districts in Minnesota have contested Democratic primaries on Tuesday as well. In Craig’s congressional district, the second district south of Minneapolis-St Paul, three people with experience in the statehouse are running. Matt Little, a former state senator, Kaela Berg, a state representative, and Matt Klein, a state senator, are vying for the seat. Both Little and Berg spent time during Operation Metro Surge patrolling ICE activity. Outside spending has flooded the race in recent days. While the district is seen as purple, Cook Political Report rated it as a likely Democratic seat this cycle. In southern Minnesota’s first congressional district, previously represented by Walz, Jake Johnson, a high school math teacher, is hoping he can flip a seat now held by Brad Finstad, a Republican, though he first needs to beat Alex Eaton in the Democratic primary. In the eighth congressional district in northern Minnesota’s Iron Range, Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, faces Luke Gulbranson, who has been on the reality TV show Summer House. The winner will face Pete Stauber, the Republican representative for the area, in a solidly red district.

Flanagan told the Guardian she appreciated that Craig has said she regrets the vote, but that she thinks Craig owes Minnesotans an apology and that the vote showed “a real lack of judgment”. “I also think it shows a pretty big disconnect from Minnesotans and the communities here,” Flanagan said. “I think it demonstrates that she doesn’t have a lot of relationships with the people who are most impacted. I think that matters.” Craig has gone after Flanagan on the fraud issue, saying Flanagan has not taken accountability for any role that allowed fraud to perpetuate. “State fraud is the No 1 issue as Minnesota voters go to the polls in November,” Craig told the New York Times. “Fairly or not, the lieutenant governor has a unique vulnerability as our statewide Senate candidate because she’s been helping run the state for the last eight years.” Craig was not available for an interview with the Guardian. The 54-year-old was first elected to Congress in 2018, flipping a seat from a Republican to become the first out lesbian to be elected to US Congress from the state. She represents a purple district south of the Twin Cities, which she has pointed to as a sign of electability statewide. Flanagan, 46, served in the state house of representatives before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019. She is a citizen of the White Earth Nation and began her political career as an organizer, a vocation she says would help her build power for progressives in the Senate if she wins. “My job, as soon as I get to Washington DC, is to have 99 cups of coffee with people, to build those relationships, to find opportunities for common ground with folks on the other side of the aisle,” she said. “We may find some unexpected places to work together.” Her platform now includes support for the proposed Medicare for All system of universal healthcare, an issue that she didn’t start off her campaign supporting, but embraced after talking to people across the state who had healthcare horror stories. “They want folks who aren’t going to govern by sternly worded letter,” Flanagan said. “And I think that people are ready for big, bold change.” Tafoya, a Republican who is pro-choice, is counting on winning over independent voters. She has centered her campaign on the fraud scandals. Republican delegates at the state convention endorsed Adam Schwarze, a marine and Navy Seal. Governor’s race Lindell, the pillow salesman, is hoping to ride Trump’s endorsement to a victory over Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker, and Kendall Qualls, a businessman. Qualls won the endorsement of Republican activists at the state party convention earlier this year. Lindell has faced opposition from the state Republican party, which has questioned his eligibility to hold office in the state, saying it wanted clarity on whether Lindell has lived in Minnesota long enough to qualify. Lindell, who is from Minnesota, has also lived in Texas. He has said he moved back to Minnesota in August 2025, though only registered to vote in the state in July 2026. Lindell, who has been sued for defamation by voting machine companies and others, has not relented in his claims that the 2020 election was stolen and that Trump had actually won. He currently faces allegations of a potential campaign finance law violation over handing out free pillows at a parade. An administrative law judge in the state recently said there was “probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election”. Lindell called the complaint “complete nonsense”. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, saying he needed to focus on his campaign for governor. He also faces millions in creditor claims over unpaid bills from the company. Alex Plechash, the Minnesota Republican party chair, said Trump’s endorsement of Lindell was a “surprise” and noted that Lindell has “significant electability concerns”. Klobuchar faces several Democratic contenders in a primary, though is likely to easily win on Tuesday. Klobuchar, who ran for president in 2020, has handily won her US Senate campaigns since she was first elected in 2006. Congressional races Multiple congressional districts in Minnesota have contested Democratic primaries on Tuesday as well. In Craig’s congressional district, the second district south of Minneapolis-St Paul, three people with experience in the statehouse are running. Matt Little, a former state senator, Kaela Berg, a state representative, and Matt Klein, a state senator, are vying for the seat. Both Little and Berg spent time during Operation Metro Surge patrolling ICE activity. Outside spending has flooded the race in recent days. While the district is seen as purple, Cook Political Report rated it as a likely Democratic seat this cycle. In southern Minnesota’s first congressional district, previously represented by Walz, Jake Johnson, a high school math teacher, is hoping he can flip a seat now held by Brad Finstad, a Republican, though he first needs to beat Alex Eaton in the Democratic primary. In the eighth congressional district in northern Minnesota’s Iron Range, Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, faces Luke Gulbranson, who has been on the reality TV show Summer House. The winner will face Pete Stauber, the Republican representative for the area, in a solidly red district.

title: ‘Fiercely independent’ South Carolina votes on Lindsey Graham’s Senate successor
body_text: In the race to replace the late US senator Lindsey Graham, 10 candidates have been barnstorming South Carolina diners, church halls and recreation centers, compressing a normal year of campaigning into about a fortnight. The Republican party is staging a special primary election in the state on Tuesday to choose Graham’s replacement. His sister, Darline, who has been serving as interim senator following his sudden death last month, is on the ballot. If no candidate wins an overall majority of votes, the top two will advance to a runoff on 25 August. Polling suggests that this is the most likely outcome. “You know, South Carolina politics is very local,” said Eaddy Roe Willard, a longtime Republican activist in South Carolina’s Richland county. “Something one of our former chairmen used to say about presidential candidates: we don’t decide whether or not we’re gonna vote for you until we’ve had a chance to shake your hand at least three times.” On Friday Russell Fry, a Republican representative, pressed the flesh at Savage Craft Ale Works in West Columbia. On Monday morning, Darline Graham shook hands at Lizard’s Thicket breakfast restaurant, 2 miles away. Mark Sanford, the former South Carolina governor, and the US representative Ralph Norman were also just a few miles down the road in Aiken on Friday, Willard said. After Lindsey Graham’s death on 11 July, Henry McMaster, South Carolina’s governor, appointed Darline Graham to fill the vacancy in the US Senate. Lindsey Graham had already won the Republican primary election for his seat, so the Republican party must hold a special election to replace him on the ballot in November’s general election. The timeline is brutal by American political standards, holding an election within a few weeks of the vacancy. The winner will face Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, in the November general election. ‘South Carolina politics is different’ Darline Graham had the recommendation of Donald Trump to serve as McMaster’s Senate appointee, and has the president’s endorsement in the primary as well. She has spent decades as a public administrator and disability advocate, serving as the commissioner of the South Carolina commission for the blind from 2019 to 2026. She also has her brother’s considerable state political apparatus behind her. Trump’s endorsement is important, but it is not decisive, according to Frank Tiller, the chair of the Spartanburg county Republican party. “It’s very important, but a lot of people are saying Donald Trump does not know South Carolina politics,” Tiller said. “South Carolina politics is different from a lot of places. Everybody here is fiercely independent.” The compressed election cycle complicates the retail politics South Carolina voters have grown accustomed to, Tiller said. “There are not enough people that know the candidates. Everybody’s calling around trying to find out who to vote for, because they don’t know the candidates.” Aside from Graham, two of the most able Republican competitors for the seat boast substantial campaign infrastructure of their own. Norman has served in the US House of Representatives since 2017, in a district covering the southern suburbs of Charlotte, North Carolina. He is a wealthy real estate developer and a prominent member of the House Freedom caucus. Norman ran unsuccessfully for South Carolina governor earlier this year, and while he did not advance to the runoff, the infrastructure of his campaign was still largely intact when Graham died. Fry represents Myrtle Beach and South Carolina’s conservative eastern border. Fry, an attorney, rose from the ranks of South Carolina’s state legislature after successfully challenging then US representative Tom Rice in the GOP primary in 2022. Rice was one of 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump after the January 6 insurrection. Trump paid him back by endorsing Fry and campaigning to replace Rice. Both Fry and Norman have campaigned as fiscal hawks, highlighting culture war issues. Sanford is a household name in South Carolina politics as a former governor with two separate stints in the US House. Sanford briefly challenged Trump in the 2020 Republican presidential primaries, and made headlines as governor after disappearing from the state for a week, ostensibly on an Appalachian Trail hiking trip, when he was instead having an extramarital affair in Argentina. Lindsey Graham had faced a handful of primary challengers on 9 June, the most successful of which – businessman Mark Lynch – is campaigning for a second time this year, as a conservative outsider with a populist platform.

title: Trump put a wrecking-ball through the East Wing – and through democratic norms
body_text: History has shown us how much dictators and aspiring dictators love building monuments to themselves. They enjoy reminding the world that they can do anything, no matter who is responsible for the physical labor or who will be paying the financial and human cost. They prefer outsized structures, heroic arches, towers and columns designed to prove that their signature and their esthetic will be with us forever, even after they’re dead, though dictators often seem to believe they are too powerful to die. There’s a chilling photograph of Hitler in the bunker beneath Berlin, not long before his suicide, contemplating an architectural model of the Austrian city of Linz which he had intended (and perhaps still intended) to rebuild to his specifications. In Tirana, Albania, is a bizarre glass pyramid that the tyrant Enver Hoxha constructed as a museum about his life, and in which he is now buried. In Rome’s EUR, Mussolini and his city planners designed a neighborhood scaled for the race of Fascist giants to which they imagined they belonged. So it comes as no surprise that Donald Trump has invested so much energy, sacrificed so much popular goodwill, and already spent a fortune on the East Wing ballroom, a project that will occupy an astonishing 90,000 square feet. I can’t have been the only person who was shocked and saddened by photos of the jagged, gaping hole in the White House’s east facade, ripped apart by a wrecking crew, and by pictures of the historic rose garden remade to resemble an outdoor food court at a mall. Also unsurprisingly, estimates of the building’s costs have varied widely, though it’s clear that the price tag will be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. ($400m is the most recent figure to have been mentioned.) Though the president has promised that the American tax payer will not be stuck with all or part of the bill, some of the money has already been diverted from publicly funded agencies such as the Secret Service. And there’s been precious little reporting about who is getting contracts for all this expensive work and about the nature of the contractors’ relationships (financial and personal) with the president. We were supposed to have been relieved and mollified to learn that the ballroom – a pleasure palace for the president and his most loyal and generous supporters – would occupy a mere 22,000 of those square feet. The remaining 68,000 would provide, as the president wrote in a post, “one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations!” Beneath the ballroom, a six-story underground bunker, designed to protect our leaders in the event of an attack, will make Hitler’s roomy 3,000 square feet look, by comparison, like a studio apartment. Most recently, Trump discussed using the new building’s roof as a launching pad for killer drones and other lethal weapons. This clever use of the air space seems to have occurred to the president even after the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled, in a 2-1 decision, that he could not continue renovating the East Wing without congressional approval. According to Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia, “each president is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence”. Brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the reasoning behind the suit seems obvious: a temporary tenant cannot change a rental cottage into a skyscraper without the landlord’s permission. The legal requirement to ask permission from Congress has already been ignored by a president who has levied tariffs, attacked Venezuela, gutted government institutions and started a war with Iran – all without bothering to consult the elected senators and representatives. Now Trump has vowed to take the case before the US supreme court which, as we have seen, is inclined to support him, though there have been a few happy surprises when the majority of chief justices decided to uphold the constitution. Much of what Trump does seems pointless, illogical, a response to some passing whim. But let’s not forget that he has the instincts of an autocrat, that he is the heir to a playbook, a series of actions designed to attain and consolidate increasing power and control. This story has always been about more than a building, more than about the intentional desecration of a national symbol, of a handsome structure with a history and a meaning. We’ve seen how Trump feels about history when he accused the Smithsonian Institution of being anti-American for telling the truth about our past. Though the case was initially brought by Alison Hoagland, an architectural historian and a board member of the National Trust, who claimed that the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront, it was never as simple as asking a town board to rule that a neighbor can’t build a view-blocking three-story vertical addition on to his house. We know, as the judges must have known, that the whole thing is about control, about the reckless grab for absolute power and about the necessity to resist it. It might seem like a distraction – a relatively trivial concern – to worry about a building when our government agents are shooting and kidnapping innocent people on our streets. But it’s part of the same story, a narrative about the subversion – at once reckless and calculated – of our ethical and democratic norms. Like our response to the ruined reflecting pool and the proposed Trump triumphal arch, our reaction to the proposed ballroom is partly about our wanting our grandchildren and great-grandchildren to be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface it. Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences

title: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate
body_text: As the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writing thinkpieces on what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this week published 6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future. Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of his essay – which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity. Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”. Vast amounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means. Earlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign. Countervailing forces are emerging. Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where the power of money already holds far too much sway. In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump to cancel the signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square. If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.

title: Darline Graham to face Ralph Norman in South Carolina Republican primary runoff
body_text: Senator Darline Graham, appointed to complete the Senate term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham of South Carolina will face congressman Ralph Norman in a runoff election for the Republican nomination. Graham held a narrow lead in the polls going into the abbreviated special primary on Tuesday, which predicted a close contest for second place. Norman, Russell Fry, a congressman, and Mark Sanford, a former governor, had polled within a point of each other in the most recent survey from the Trafalgar Group. The winner of the runoff on 25 August will face Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, in November. Graham has loudly trumpeted her endorsement from Donald Trump, but also enjoys the support of South Carolina’s governor, Henry McMaster, and John Thune, the Senate majority leader. In recent interviews the political outsider sought to convince people that her experience, and focus on affordability, made her the right candidate. “I ran a state agency. I turned it from a struggling agency into a national model. I think that’s great experience to bring to the table,” Graham said, addressing reporters after casting her ballot on Tuesday. She highlighted the passage of a sanctions bill targeting Russia during her short tenure in Washington. “I was the deciding vote on Todd Blanche as attorney general. So I think I’ve accomplished a whole lot in three weeks.” Norman represents a congressional district in the suburbs of Charlotte that is vote-rich for Republicans, contributing disproportionately to statewide primary results. The real estate developer has served in Congress since 2017, and is most notable for his role as vice-chair of the far-right Freedom caucus. His broad support from state legislators and a statewide campaign apparatus largely remained intact after his failed primary bid for the governor’s office in June. Norman’’s campaign highlighted support for the Save America Act, a Trump-backed bill to impose federal requirements on states to mandate proof of citizenship at voter registration and to submit state voter rolls to federal oversight. He also has promoted a bill to strip housing funding from cities that do not cooperate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The last-minute squabble for the Republican nomination saw a spectrum of conservative approaches to the seat, with candidates quickly turning on each other in debate, social media and political advertising. Sanford, who served as governor between two stints in Congress, had campaigned on fiscal stewardship, noting the dramatic increase in the federal debt. “I got into this race because I believe our nation is at a financial tipping point.” Sanford wrote on social media on Tuesday. “I held the line on spending as Governor unlike any Governor before or since and ask for your vote today so that I might fight for our grandkids’ ability to afford the American Dream.” Fry’s political attack advertising amplified a comment Graham made in a debate that was favorable to datacenter development, and has likened her appointment to an act of “DEI” – the practice of diversity, equity and inclusion that has become anathema to the right. Fry has come under fire from Graham and others for running simultaneously for the US Senate and to retain his congressional seat. Statewide special elections in South Carolina are rare events. The resignation of Senator Jim DeMint, a Republican who left office in 2013 to lead the Heritage Foundation, triggered the most recent example. Governor Nikki Haley named then congressman Tim Scott as DeMint’s successor. Scott won both the nomination and special election to complete the term handily, becoming only the second Black Republican senator since Reconstruction and the first Black senator in the southern United States elected directly by voters.
