title: Progressive Peggy Flanagan sweeps Minnesota Senate primary in race defined by anti-ICE anger
body_text: Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in a race centered on immigration enforcement after the Trump administration crackdown turned deadly and destructive earlier this year. Flanagan ousted congresswoman Angie Craig in yet another example of progressive campaigns toppling moderates amid an anti-establishment wave among Democrats. “It’s time to fight for what people actually need,” Flanagan recently told the Guardian. “And so often I think Democrats are like: ‘What do we think we can win?’ Instead of: ‘What are the fights that we should be picking?’” Flanagan will now face Michele Tafoya, a Republican former National Football League sideline reporter, in November. If she wins, Flanagan will become the first Native American woman in the Senate. Meanwhile, the state’s gubernatorial race proved a rebuke of Donald Trump’s endorsement power as Mike Lindell, an election denier and pillow salesman, lost to Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota house speaker. Demuth will face Amy Klobuchar, a Democratic US senator, in November, with Klobuchar favored to win. Lindell’s significant liabilities had led his own party to speak out against his campaign. He is contending with ongoing defamation cases because of his election denialism, as well as a potential campaign finance violation for handing out free pillows at a parade. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, which faces legal claims for unpaid bills. Minnesota leans Democratic. It has not elected a Republican statewide since 2006, when Tim Pawlenty won a second term as governor and a Republican presidential candidate has not won the state since 1972. Both the governorship and US Senate seat are fully open, with no incumbents seeking to stay in office. Tim Walz, the Democratic governor, initially sought a third term, but dropped his bid after ongoing fraud scandals threatened to distract from the race. Tina Smith, the Democratic US senator, decided not to run again, saying she wanted to spend time with her grandchildren and make way for new faces in the chamber. She endorsed Flanagan. *** The role of immigration enforcement served as a major issue in Minnesota’s US Senate primary after the state experienced devastation, including the deaths of two residents and hundreds of deportations, when the Trump administration sent in thousands of immigration officers in early 2026 as part of Operation Metro Surge. The lingering impacts of the crackdown had dogged Craig, who as a congresswoman voted for the Laken Riley Act, a federal law that requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes. In March, Craig said she regretted her vote on the act, but it has followed her campaign throughout her run for Senate. Craig, meanwhile, attacked Flanagan on fraud scandals that have rocked state social services, saying the lieutenant governor had not faced accountability for any role in the scandals. Craig, 54, was first elected to Congress in 2018, flipping a seat from a Republican to become the first out lesbian to be elected to Congress from the state. She represents a purple district south of the Twin Cities, which she has pointed to as a sign of electability statewide. Flanagan, 46, served in the state house of representatives before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019. She is a citizen of the White Earth Nation who began her political career as an organizer, a vocation she says would help her build power for progressives in the Senate if she wins in November. Flanagan said she expected to be part of the US Senate “fight club” of progressive senators in the chamber. She was boosted by its members, Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders. “Peggy Flanagan’s win is further proof that the many can beat the money,” Warren said in a statement. “Voters want leaders with backbones who will stand up to dark money Super Pacs and fight to make life more affordable. I was the very first senator to endorse Peggy because she’s the fighter we need in Washington.” In congressional races, Matt Little edged out Matt Klein and Kaela Berg to win the Democratic nod in the purple district now represented by Craig, the second congressional district made up of suburbs and exurbs south of the Twin Cities. Little had patrolled immigration agents during the surge. In the first congressional district in southern Minnesota, Jake Johnson, a high school teacher, secured the nomination to take on Brad Finstad in a potential Democratic pickup. And in the eighth congressional district in northern Minnesota, the reality TV star Luke Gulbranson lost his bid to Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, who will face the Republican Pete Stauber in November.

title: Francesca Hong aims to ride progressive wave in Wisconsin primary for governor
body_text: Wisconsin voters will decide on Tuesday whether to nominate a democratic socialist for the state’s highest office in the latest test of an anti-establishment wave among Democratic primary voters. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist state lawmaker, emerged as the frontrunner in a four-way race to succeed Tony Evers, the Democratic governor who is not seeking another term. Evers threw his support behind David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive. Crowley previously left the race, before re-entering it on 18 July. Crowley and Evers toured the state in the last two weeks, centering his campaign around electability, saying Crowley was more poised to win a general election in a swing state like Wisconsin than Hong. Eyes turned to the Wisconsin governor’s race after Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan last week in the most recent example of a progressive beating out a moderate. Nextdoor, Minnesota voters have also been weighing a US Senate primary between a moderate and a progressive. After a wave of wins of progressives and democratic socialists in solidly blue parts of the country, the midwest primaries centered more on electability concerns given the close nature of statewide races there. While some saw Crowley’s re-entry as evidence that the establishment was working to derail Hong’s campaign, Crowley balked at the idea that he was part of the establishment. Hong, meanwhile, saw her past comments – including a tweet that suggested cancelling Thanksgiving, and previous support for defunding the police – scrutinized by journalists and attacked by Republicans, led by Donald Trump, as more national attention turned to Wisconsin’s primary. Marquette University Law School surveyed the Democratic primary in late July, after Crowley re-entered, and found Hong leading the pack, though a sizable chunk of voters were still undecided at that time. The race had rearranged itself multiple times in the weeks leading up to 11 August, landing at four candidates: Hong, Crowley, the state senator Kelda Roys, and the former state administration department head Joel Brennan. A previous top contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race following campaign finance irregularities, after which Crowley re-entered the race. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July. Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, was first elected to the state assembly in 2020. She ran on a platform that included childcare for all, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on new datacenter construction. She said voters throughout the state have pushed back against the political establishment and want candidates who will advocate for changes that materially improve their lives. “I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she previously told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.” The winner will face Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. He voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost. Tiffany’s role in the 2020 election highlighted the importance of keeping the governor’s office for Democrats. Democrats also hope to win both chambers of the state legislature to install a governing trifecta and enact their agenda. Elsewhere in Wisconsin, voters in the western part of the state will decide which Democratic contender will face the Republican Derrick Van Orden in the third congressional district, a key pickup opportunity for Democrats. Rebecca Cooke, a “blue dog” Democrat who previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, has seen national support for her campaign against Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is most poised to win the district.

title: ‘Unrig the economy for working people’: the California candidate who wrote updated labor laws
body_text: Legislation that would modernize federal labor law began with a handful of lawyers meeting, of all places, in an ice-cream shop. “We wrote for hours what we would do to amend the National Labor Relations Act,” said Marni von Wilpert, a member of the San Diego city council who was then an attorney for the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). Bringing together “our collective experience as labor lawyers over the years, really trying to unrig the rules so that working people could have a fair shot”. Though that meeting in Washington DC took place over a decade ago, the plan to reform labor law that came from it still has not passed Congress. Von Wilpert is vying to see the job through. In the fall, she launched her bid to replace Darrell Issa, a longtime Republican US representative who represents a district in San Diego. After a bitter primary against a fellow Democrat, Wilpert is now part of the party’s effort to win back the US House through a focus on affordability and empowering workers. “One of my biggest priorities for running for Congress myself is to finish this work, to come back as a member of Congress and finally get labor law reform across the finish line,” Von Wilpert said. After beginning her legal career as a legal fellow at the Mississippi Center for Justice then as a federal law clerk, Von Wilpert joined the NLRB as an attorney in 2014, serving until 2017. During that time, she saw how the rules were rigged against workers fighting labor violations, who often faced long delays and backlogs. “A worker would either be fired for organizing or an election would be overturned, and it would take three to four years to get to me in Washington DC,” she said. “I saw how hard it was for working people to try and navigate our current labor law system.” The legislation would update labor laws, including the 1935 National Labor Relations Act, and strengthen protection for organizing workers, including allowing the NLRB to assess monetary penalties for labor violation and impose liability on corporate executives. Von Wilpert worked with Bobby Scott, a Democratic congressman, and Patty Murray, a senator, to draft the legislation that would eventually become the Protecting the Right to Organize (Pro) act. Though the bill has been introduced in Congress annually since 2019 and passed the House in 2021, it has long been stalled in the Senate. When Von Wilpert first ran for her seat on the city council, she ended up flipping one of the most conservative districts in the city. In November, she will face Jim Desmond, a Trump-endorsed San Diego county supervisor, in a newly redrawn district that now slightly leans in favor of Democrats, though polls show a clean split between Desmond and von Wilpert. Von Wilpert has been trying to emphasize her labor background to appeal to voters, noting that Desmond is aligned with the Trump administration that has set back workers’ rights by, among other things, decreasing workplace safety standards and firing hundreds of thousands of federal workers, including at the NLRB. As a county supervisor, Desmond has opposed pro-labor policies, including minimum wage increases for contracted county workers, a contract for county janitorial workers who made several allegations of abuse on the job and the creation of a country office for labor standards, Von Wilpert said. “There is a big difference in this race about which candidate is going to stand up for workers and who is not,” von Wilpert said. “I am running to actually stand up for workers, level the playing field again and really unrig the economy for working people, not just the wealthy few,” she said. “This is what government, to me, should be about.” Desmond’s campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

title: In Ohio, Haitians’ American dream shatters as ICE prepares to deport them
body_text: When Monsanto Maler walked out of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Blue Ash, Ohio, at 9.15am on Sunday with an ankle monitor freshly attached to his left leg, he put his hand over his face, burst into tears and fell to the ground. He had come to the US in June 2023, fleeing gangs in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, where he had been hit over the right side of his head, leaving a large, visible scar. Grief-stricken and unable to hold himself up, he collapsed on the ground, his dozens of immigration documents, which a moment before had been carefully packed under his arm, strewn across the concrete. His face was full of confusion, his eyes bewildered. His American dream had ended in humiliation and despondency, with a metal box tied around his ankle. “I feel depressed, physically, mentally. I feel dizzy,” he said through an interpreter. Four hours earlier, 75 miles (120km) to the north in Springfield, Viles Dorsainvil, who heads the Haitian Support Center, and Pastor Carl Ruby loaded into a sedan on a humid, foggy morning at 5.30am. They were about to embark on the drive south to the Blue Ash facility to help Haitians such as Maler in any way they could. On the drive, the pair talked about their efforts to help a family from Ruby’s church in Springfield emigrate to Quebec City, one of the thousands of Haitians forced to leave the US due to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies. “I was helping them pack. The dad had all this patriotic stuff with him,” said Ruby, who knows at least two Haitians from his congregation who have been called to Blue Ash to be fitted with ankle monitors. “It makes me sad that what he’s going to remember from the United States is that he had to leave.” Dorsainvil talked about a Haitian man who worked at a local Amazon warehouse, had temporary protected status (TPS) until 2029 and had come to his center last Friday seeking help. “When he got that letter [requiring him the come to the Blue Ash facility], he was terrified, he got sick,” Dorsainvil said. Dorsainvil, himself a TPS holder, and Ruby chatted about what was happening in Haiti right now – that a burger there cost $16 and how the absence of opportunity was pushing people into gangs or to flee the country for their lives. On 5 August, the Washington DC district judge Ana Reyes, whose ruling had previously prevented the Trump administration from lifting TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians, was forced to remove her stay, following a decision from the supreme court backing the Trump administration’s efforts. It means that for about 350,000 Haitians in the US on TPS, it’s an end for their lives in the US. Over the last decade, more than 12,000 Haitians moved to the Rust belt town of Springfield, where they worked in labor-intensive jobs in manufacturing and food packaging, jobs that local companies struggled to fill. But in September 2024, then presidential candidate Donald Trump falsely claimed that immigrants in Springfield were eating pets, setting off a firestorm of unrest that fueled neo-Nazi marches, bomb threats and school closures in Springfield, and the national immigration debate centered on the town of 60,000 people. In recent weeks, dozens of Haitian nationals living in Springfield – some who had applied for asylum, others who had TPS – have begun receiving emails from the Department of Homeland Security ordering them to show up at the Blue Ash facility, often early on a Sunday morning. The letter, a photo of which was seen by the Guardian, contained no stated reason for the requirement or an indication that a monitoring device would be attached to their bodies. According to advocates and lawyers representing the Haitian nationals, those who received the ankle monitors will not be allowed to travel more than 75 miles from their home without the consent of an immigration judge. The Blue Ash Ice office is at least 71 miles from Springfield. By 7am outside the Ice facility, streams of protesters – nuns and priestesses, children, and men wearing USA hockey jerseys – had positioned themselves along the road in front of the building. Aside from one marked DHS police vehicle parked outside, the ICE building, a single-story, red-brick office, had no obvious marking to indicate its use as a federal government facility. “Life there is extremely difficult. Haiti is the poorest country in the western hemisphere; [it’s a country] exploited for all of its resources,” said Lorne Hlad, a pastor from Cincinnati attending the protest, who has worked in Haiti and visited six times. “[TPS] should be renewed. Gangs control Port-au-Prince; there’s no active government. Sending people back to a country that has no infrastructure to protect them is inhumane.” At 7.40am, the first Haitian national, a man dressed all in black, arrived for his appointment. By 8am three people, including Maler, had arrived. Thirty minutes later, a Haitian man and woman arrived and were given communion by Ruby, who had brought a vat of wine, bread and a large gold cross. “We want to give them the message that Jesus is with them,” said Ruby. “The Bible isn’t policy, but the Bible is very clear that God loves immigrants. It teaches that they are to have access to justice.” Dorsainvil and immigration lawyers said they were assisting Haitians to file a motion for amelioration that could remove or replace the ankle monitors with monitoring devices worn on the wrist. “The wrist monitors may be slightly less stigmatizing,” said Heather Campbell, an immigration lawyer representing several of the Haitian immigrants. “But anything that differentiates you from somebody else, especially if you are part of a community that people know this is happening to, it’s going to make you uncomfortable.” Questions sent by the Guardian to Ice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asking, among other things, the stated objective of attaching ankle bracelets to Haitian nationals, were not directly responded to. Instead, Ice shared a statement that read: “Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations.” Organizers of Sunday’s protest estimate that about 700 people showed up to support the Haitian immigrants. “It’s reminiscent of the shackles used during slavery, something the Haitian people are very familiar with, after liberating themselves from slavery in the late 18th century,” said Samantha Searl of Ignite Peace, the non-profit leading the protest action outside the Ice facility. “The ankle monitors send a message to all immigrants that they will always continue to be subjected to the violence of our punitive immigration system.” Facing midterm elections in November, recent polls show American public opinion is souring on the Trump administration’s Ice enforcement activity. A YouGov poll released on 21 July found that just 30% of those surveyed believe Ice has been using necessary and justified force in its activities. Having gotten back to his feet and walking a short distance from the Ice facility, Maler, still visibly reeling from what happened to him, was driven away by a friend in a small sedan car, his hopes and dreams of a better life in America shattered. On the drive back to Springfield, Ruby and Dorsainvil stopped at a McDonald’s. Ruby ordered an iced tea, Dorsainvil some ice water. Dorsainvil was clearly exhausted – he said he stayed up late the previous night working on his university thesis. “It’s a study of the economic impact of Haitian immigrants on Springfield,” he said.
cleaned_body_text: When Monsanto Maler walked out of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Blue Ash, Ohio, at 9.15am on Sunday with an ankle monitor freshly attached to his left leg, he put his hand over his face, burst into tears and fell to the ground. He had come to the US in June 2023, fleeing gangs in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, where he had been hit over the right side of his head, leaving a large, visible scar. Grief-stricken and unable to hold himself up, he collapsed on the ground, his dozens of immigration documents, which a moment before had been carefully packed under his arm, strewn across the concrete. His face was full of confusion, his eyes bewildered. His American dream had ended in humiliation and despondency, with a metal box tied around his ankle. “I feel depressed, physically, mentally. I feel dizzy,” he said through an interpreter. Four hours earlier, 75 miles (120km) to the north in Springfield, Viles Dorsainvil, who heads the Haitian Support Center, and Pastor Carl Ruby loaded into a sedan on a humid, foggy morning at 5.30am. They were about to embark on the drive south to the Blue Ash facility to help Haitians such as Maler in any way they could. On the drive, the pair talked about their efforts to help a family from Ruby’s church in Springfield emigrate to Quebec City, one of the thousands of Haitians forced to leave the US due to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies. “I was helping them pack. The dad had all this patriotic stuff with him,” said Ruby, who knows at least two Haitians from his congregation who have been called to Blue Ash to be fitted with ankle monitors. “It makes me sad that what he’s going to remember from the United States is that he had to leave.” Dorsainvil talked about a Haitian man who worked at a local Amazon warehouse, had temporary protected status (TPS) until 2029 and had come to his center last Friday seeking help. “When he got that letter [requiring him the come to the Blue Ash facility], he was terrified, he got sick,” Dorsainvil said. Dorsainvil, himself a TPS holder, and Ruby chatted about what was happening in Haiti right now – that a burger there cost $16 and how the absence of opportunity was pushing people into gangs or to flee the country for their lives. On 5 August, the Washington DC district judge Ana Reyes, whose ruling had previously prevented the Trump administration from lifting TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians, was forced to remove her stay, following a decision from the supreme court backing the Trump administration’s efforts. It means that for about 350,000 Haitians in the US on TPS, it’s an end for their lives in the US. Over the last decade, more than 12,000 Haitians moved to the Rust belt town of Springfield, where they worked in labor-intensive jobs in manufacturing and food packaging, jobs that local companies struggled to fill. But in September 2024, then presidential candidate Donald Trump falsely claimed that immigrants in Springfield were eating pets, setting off a firestorm of unrest that fueled neo-Nazi marches, bomb threats and school closures in Springfield, and the national immigration debate centered on the town of 60,000 people. In recent weeks, dozens of Haitian nationals living in Springfield – some who had applied for asylum, others who had TPS – have begun receiving emails from the Department of Homeland Security ordering them to show up at the Blue Ash facility, often early on a Sunday morning. The letter, a photo of which was seen by the Guardian, contained no stated reason for the requirement or an indication that a monitoring device would be attached to their bodies. According to advocates and lawyers representing the Haitian nationals, those who received the ankle monitors will not be allowed to travel more than 75 miles from their home without the consent of an immigration judge. The Blue Ash Ice office is at least 71 miles from Springfield. By 7am outside the Ice facility, streams of protesters – nuns and priestesses, children, and men wearing USA hockey jerseys – had positioned themselves along the road in front of the building. Aside from one marked DHS police vehicle parked outside, the ICE building, a single-story, red-brick office, had no obvious marking to indicate its use as a federal government facility. “Life there is extremely difficult. Haiti is the poorest country in the western hemisphere; [it’s a country] exploited for all of its resources,” said Lorne Hlad, a pastor from Cincinnati attending the protest, who has worked in Haiti and visited six times. “[TPS] should be renewed. Gangs control Port-au-Prince; there’s no active government. Sending people back to a country that has no infrastructure to protect them is inhumane.” At 7.40am, the first Haitian national, a man dressed all in black, arrived for his appointment. By 8am three people, including Maler, had arrived. Thirty minutes later, a Haitian man and woman arrived and were given communion by Ruby, who had brought a vat of wine, bread and a large gold cross. “We want to give them the message that Jesus is with them,” said Ruby. “The Bible isn’t policy, but the Bible is very clear that God loves immigrants. It teaches that they are to have access to justice.” Dorsainvil and immigration lawyers said they were assisting Haitians to file a motion for amelioration that could remove or replace the ankle monitors with monitoring devices worn on the wrist. “The wrist monitors may be slightly less stigmatizing,” said Heather Campbell, an immigration lawyer representing several of the Haitian immigrants. “But anything that differentiates you from somebody else, especially if you are part of a community that people know this is happening to, it’s going to make you uncomfortable.” Questions sent by the Guardian to Ice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asking, among other things, the stated objective of attaching ankle bracelets to Haitian nationals, were not directly responded to. Instead, Ice shared a statement that read: “Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations.” Organizers of Sunday’s protest estimate that about 700 people showed up to support the Haitian immigrants. “It’s reminiscent of the shackles used during slavery, something the Haitian people are very familiar with, after liberating themselves from slavery in the late 18th century,” said Samantha Searl of Ignite Peace, the non-profit leading the protest action outside the Ice facility. “The ankle monitors send a message to all immigrants that they will always continue to be subjected to the violence of our punitive immigration system.” Facing midterm elections in November, recent polls show American public opinion is souring on the Trump administration’s Ice enforcement activity. A YouGov poll released on 21 July found that just 30% of those surveyed believe Ice has been using necessary and justified force in its activities. Having gotten back to his feet and walking a short distance from the Ice facility, Maler, still visibly reeling from what happened to him, was driven away by a friend in a small sedan car, his hopes and dreams of a better life in America shattered. On the drive back to Springfield, Ruby and Dorsainvil stopped at a McDonald’s. Ruby ordered an iced tea, Dorsainvil some ice water. Dorsainvil was clearly exhausted – he said he stayed up late the previous night working on his university thesis. “It’s a study of the economic impact of Haitian immigrants on Springfield,” he said.

title: Trump ally loses, mixed results for progressives: takeaways from primaries in Minnesota, Wisconsin and beyond
body_text: A series of primary elections on Tuesday shaped the future of both the Democratic and Republican parties, pitting newcomers against established candidates and testing name recognition. Wisconsin, Minnesota, Alabama, South Carolina, Vermont and Connecticut held elections, with a gubernatorial race in Wisconsin capturing nationwide attention. That election, in which progressive challenger Francesca Hong faced David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, was seen as another key test of the left wing of the Democratic party in a swing state. Democratic socialist falls short in Wisconsin Despite polls suggesting she was on course for victory, the progressive state lawmaker Francesca Hong was narrowly beaten in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor by David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive. The result amounts to a stunning upset after a messy campaign, during which Crowley exited the race, only to re-enter it – and promptly received the endorsement of Tony Evers, the outgoing Democratic governor. It comes after a wave of leftwing candidates won prominent Democratic primaries in recent months, including Abdul El-Sayed, running for US Senate in Michigan, last week. Hong had pointed to Crowley’s return in the campaign as evidence of panic by the Democratic establishment, although Crowley insisted he was “far from” the establishment. The fight for a new generation of Democrats prevails in Connecticut Luke Bronin, the former mayor of Hartford, ousted the incumbent congressman John Larson in Connecticut’s first congressional district, the AP projects. Larson, 78, has represented the district since 1999. Bronin, 47, talked to the Guardian last year about Democrats challenging older members of Congress in the aftermath of Joe Biden’s 2024 exit from the presidential race over age and mental fitness concerns. At the time, Bronin said Democrats needed to be “relentless and clear” about the ways Donald Trump is making life worse for Americans, and “equally relentless and clear” about the Democratic party’s vision for improving their daily lives. In a statement on Tuesday, Bronin said: “Tonight, voters sent a message that if we are going to fix this mess we’re in, we need to build a Democratic Party that’s bringing a whole new energy to this fight. It’s time to be courageous, bold, and clear about who we’re fighting for and what we’re fighting for.” Alabama voters cast ballots again in redrawn district that dilutes Black voting power Some Alabama voters took to the polls for the second time this primary season after the state’s Republican-controlled legislature reconfigured four of the seven districts. The redrawn district map came after the US supreme court dismantled a key section of the 1965 Voting Rights Act and several southern states moved to redistrict and consolidate Republican power. In June, the supreme court ruled that Alabama could use a redrawn congressional map that eliminates one of the state’s two majority-Black districts in this year’s midterm elections. The new map poses steep challenges for Shomari Figures, the Democratic representative who was first elected in 2024 after the creation of a new district that included the mostly Black cities of Mobile and Montgomery. But the district no longer includes Mobile, Figures’s home town. Rhett Marques, a Republican state representative and small-business owner who became part of the new district, won the primary to challenge Figures in November. Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, advances to runoff in South Carolina Republican primary Interim US senator Darline Graham advanced to a runoff in South Carolina’s special Republican primary to replace her brother, Lindsey Graham, in the Senate one month after his sudden death. She will face Congressman Ralph Norman, an ultraconservative Freedom Caucus member, on 25 August. The winner of that contest will run against Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, in the November general election. Trump-backed Graham was appointed to the Senate after Lindsey Graham died one month ago. A political outsider, she has sought to cast herself as focused on affordability, not national security like her brother. Trump ally Mike Lindell loses significantly in Minnesota governor primary Mike Lindell, the CEO of MyPillow and a staunch Trump ally lost decisively to Lisa Demuth, the Republican speaker of the Minnesota house of representatives. Minnesota has not elected a Republican governor in decades, but the primary was still a test of Trump’s strength among his party in the state. Lindell’s loss could be attributed to the weakness of his campaign, but also a sign of Trump’s waning support amid low approval ratings. The known election denier did not concede when the race was called for his opponent. Demuth became speaker last year in an evenly divided house, becoming the first Black person in the role. The impact of Trump’s immigration agenda weighed heavily over Minnesota Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won decisively on Tuesday after a campaign that attacked Angie Craig, a US representative, on her immigration record. At the center of the attack was Craig’s vote for the Laken Riley Act, which requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes, and Craig has since expressed regret for voting for it. The role of immigration enforcement served as a major issue in the primary after the state experienced devastation, including the deaths of two residents and hundreds of deportations, when the Trump administration sent in thousands of immigration officers in early 2026 as part of Operation Metro Surge.

title: Mike Lindell refuses to concede in Minnesota primary despite getting far fewer votes
body_text: Mike Lindell, the pillow salesman, Trump supporter and election denier, has refused to concede defeat in Minnesota’s Republican gubernatorial primary, despite trailing by a double-digit margin the morning after polls closed. The Associated Press called the race for Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker, late on Tuesday night. With almost all votes counted, Demuth was more than 45,000 votes ahead of Lindell, who had the backing of Donald Trump, beating him by 43.4% to 32.5%. Businessman Kendall Qualls, backed by the Republican state party, was trailing in third. Told by a reporter on his own streaming channel, LindellTV, that the AP had declared the race over, Lindell dismissed the wire service outright. Asked why he wouldn’t accept the call, he questioned the AP’s authority to determine the outcome and insisted hundreds of thousands of votes remained uncounted. “I’m not going to give up this race until the votes are counted,” Lindell said. “That’s nonsense.” Lindell did not return a request for comment on what steps he will take next to contest the election, as he waits for the votes to come in. Lindell built his political career on the claim that Trump’s 2020 defeat was the product of a rigged and stolen election, spending what he has said were tens of millions of dollars pursuing that conspiracy theory through lawsuits, documentaries and conferences, even as courts repeatedly threw it out. Last month he settled a $1.3bn defamation suit brought by voting technology company Liberty Vote, formerly known as Dominion Voting Systems, regarding the stolen election lies. Lindell’s campaign was also dogged by questions over his own eligibility to run. He was, for weeks, not registered to vote in the state whose governorship he was seeking – his registration remained active in Texas, tied to a property owned by a company in Lufkin, even as he told reporters he had re-established Minnesota residency. Minnesota’s same-day registration rules meant he could still cast a ballot, and run, regardless. Trump, who has failed to carry Minnesota in three consecutive presidential elections, made a late, personal push for Lindell on Tuesday, urging Minnesota Republicans on social media to hand him a decisive win and praising his commitment to “free and fair” elections. Lindell’s defeat extended a run of losses for Trump-endorsed candidates, including House races for Andy Ogles, a representative in Tennessee, and Amir Hassan, a navy veteran in Michigan who lost to a candidate who had dropped out. Demuth, who becomes the first woman to win a Minnesota Republican gubernatorial nomination, called the result a milestone but said her campaign’s work was “not done yet”. She will face Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic senator who easily won her own primary, in November’s general election to succeed the retiring governor, Tim Walz.

title: David Crowley wins Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s governor in upset over progressive Francesca Hong
body_text: David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, won the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor after beating the democratic socialist Francesca Hong in a tight contest. Crowley pulled off a last-minute victory in the critical swing state after re-entering the campaign and snagging an endorsement from Tony Evers, the outgoing governor. With most votes counted, Crowley had 39.8% of the vote, ahead of Hong’s 39.4%, according to the Associated Press: a lead of just more than 3,000 votes. The race came down to the wire, with Hong and Crowley running close to each other as each batch of results came in. Polls had shown Hong as a clear frontrunner during the campaign, but with large chunks of voters still undecided and an ever-changing field of candidates, polling was difficult. Polls in Michigan had similarly shown the progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed with a more sizable lead than he ended up with in his victory in the Democratic primary for US Senate. Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, ran on a platform that included childcare for all, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on the construction of new datacenters, which differentiated her from her Democratic colleagues in the governor’s race. Crowley welcomed those who voted for Hong in Tuesday’s primary to join him in the lead-up to November’s general election. “I look forward to earning their support,” he told reporters. While the messy Democratic primary has been branded as a “battle between the left and the center”, Crowley argued this was an inaccurate characterization. “We may not agree on every policy,” he said. “We may not use the same labels, but we all want safe communities, strong schools, affordable healthcare, good-paying jobs, and a brighter future for all of our children. “Every one of us has something much bigger to unite around, and that is keeping Maga extremism from bringing the chaos we see in Washington into our neighborhoods right here in the state of Wisconsin,” said Crowley. Evers, a Democrat who has served as Wisconsin’s governor since 2019, did not seek re-election. He endorsed Crowley, who re-entered the race after leaving it earlier in the cycle. Evers hailed Crowley as “the future of our Party” in a social media post overnight. “For now, we polka,” he said. “Tomorrow, we’re back at work to win.” In a statement on Wednesday morning, Hong congratulated Crowley and said she would support him in the general election. “The last 11 months have been one of the greatest joys of my life. Traveling the state, meeting people in churches and dive bars and bike races and dance parties and in their homes, and hearing about what matters most to them informed every decision we made on the trail,” she said. “It will continue to inform the work we do – and ask our supporters to do – moving forward. “This campaign was not about getting one person into office. It is about a building movement for permanent affordability and a government that puts working people first. Our movement is strong and the work isn’t done. I am overwhelmingly proud of our team and the work they have done to achieve that goal.” Crowley’s pitch to voters in the waning weeks of the campaign was electability: he felt he was more poised to win against Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Tiffany voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost. Crowley previously told the Guardian: “We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate, not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done. And that’s what voters want. They want someone they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.” Hong’s previous statements had dragged her down in recent days, including past support for defunding the police and a tweet calling to cancel Thanksgiving, which she had since retracted. She had previously vowed to use her grassroots network built during the primary to aid whoever won. Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, who previously led the Wisconsin department of administration, rounded out the Democratic field. There were entries and exits from the chaotic race in recent weeks. A previous top contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities, after which Crowley re-entered the race, with Evers’ backing. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July. The Wisconsin governor’s race became the latest test of the progressive wing of the party’s durability with Democratic voters in the midwest, after Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan last week. Next door, Minnesota voters were also weighing a US Senate primary between a moderate and a progressive. Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic primary for Senate over Congresswoman Angie Craig. The midwest primaries came after a wave of wins of progressives and Democratic socialists in solidly blue parts of the country. Democrats in Wisconsin are angling for a governing trifecta, trying to win back control of both chambers of the state assembly and keep the governor’s office so they can enact a full agenda. The governor’s race is expected to draw huge money and attention – Wisconsin is a close state for most statewide elections, and its voters are known to swing in either direction depending on the candidate or platform. Elsewhere in Wisconsin, voters in the western part of the state chose Rebecca Cooke, a blue dog Democrat, to advance and face the Republican Derrick Van Orden in the third congressional district, a key pickup opportunity for Democrats. Cooke previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, coming close to Van Orden. Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president, ran against Cooke. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is better placed to win the district.

Cooke previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, coming close to Van Orden. Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president, ran against Cooke. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is better placed to win the district.

title: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump says
body_text: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced. The US president revealed her departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving “so she can spend more time” with her family. The 28-year-old gave birth to a daughter, Viviana, in May, and returned from maternity leave last month. The departure of Trump’s most prominent spokesperson comes with his approval rating at a historic low as voters express discontent over rising prices and a war in Iran that has no end in sight. Trump said Leavitt, who became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary on his return to office in January 2025, “will now be one of my top outside advisors” in a post on his Truth Social platform. Leavitt wrote on X: “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary – and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.” Leavitt served Trump as a press aide during his first term in the White House. She ran for Congress in 2022 as the Republican nominee for New Hampshire’s first congressional district but lost the race. She joined Trump’s 2024 campaign and was transition spokeswoman before Trump selected her to ‌be White House press secretary. At 27 she was younger than Ronald Ziegler, who was 29 when he was Richard Nixon’s spokesperson. A devout Christian, Leavitt, wearing a cross necklace, and her team would hold a short group prayer before she walked into the briefing room to face reporters. The briefings rarely strayed off message or made headlines but did keep factcheckers occupied. For example, her claim that “tariffs are a tax cut for the American people,” was rated false by Politifact. In a smooth delivery with few verbal stumbles, Leavitt zealously defended the president while berating Democrats and the “fake news” media. In her first appearance on the podium, she described Trump as “the hardest-working man in politics” with “wildly popular” policies responsible for a new “golden age”. Leavitt was cordial with reporters behind the scenes but could be combative in front of the camera. In January this year, when a journalist raised the killing of Renee Good by an ICE agent in Minneapolis, Leavitt demanded to know why Good had been killed. The reporter answered: “Because an ICE agent acted recklessly and killed her unjustifiably.” Leavitt, jabbing her finger, snapped: “You’re a leftwing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in the room as a journalist … You shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.” Trump often praised Leavitt as an effective communicator and drawing attention to her appearance. He once told the Newsmax network: “She’s become a star. It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.” On Wednesday the president’s allies joined the acclaim. Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, tweeted: “Karoline Leavitt has served President Trump and the American people with courage and conviction. She’s a great colleague, a fearless voice for the President’s agenda and a true professional.” Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, added: “Karoline Leavitt has been the most successful Press Secretary in history. Always strong, clear and right to the point … We are all Karoline Leavitt fans!” Democrats, however, took a different view. Adam Schiff, a senator for California, posted: “Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House to spend a little more time … with the truth.” Trump did not outline plans for who might succeed her. He had four press secretaries during his first term. Sean Spicer is now a political commentator and podcaster; Sarah Huckabee Sanders is now the governor of Arkansas; Stephanie Grisham is now a fierce critic of Trump who spoke at the 2024 Democratic national convention; Kayleigh McEnany is a host on Fox News.

title: AOC and Mamdani wanted to defund the police. Their backtracking puts organizers at risk
body_text: The north may not remember, but 9 August this year marked the 12th anniversary of the police killing of Michael Brown Jr in Ferguson, Missouri. That day, the US representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reassured an ABC news anchor that she, like other progressive politicians and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates, had “moved away” from statements they made during the pandemic, particularly on police and prison abolition. Questioned further, she explained: “I have a local city councilman that has this saying: ‘Woke 1 was crazy’… especially during Covid, I think that the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful. I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime in bringing crime down. And I think that we all share in the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible. I think that, you know, during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today. And I’m grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they’re campaigning on in this moment.” A few days later, on Wednesday, Zohran Mamdani, the progressive New York mayor, who has previously stated that his pandemic-era tweets supporting the defund movement were “out of step” with where he is now, chimed in on Ocasio-Cortez’s comments, saying: “Sometimes what you believe in can change. I know there are some for whom they still believe in that. I’ve made very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police and that to me, delivering critical public safety also looks like working with our police department alongside many other partners.” The New York City councilman to whom Ocasio-Cortez was referring, Chi Ossé, was actually inspired by the abolition movement to run for office. But earlier this week, he was quick to proudly claim coinage of the term “woke 1”, which has been used by people who seek to minimize statements they made in the aftermath of George Floyd’s murder by police in May 2020. In one sense, these politicians are absolutely correct. If “woke 1” represents a political baptism in shallow waters, then I have met many who were swept up in an emotional online conversion toward the radical, romantic rhetoric of “defund the police”. I know the power of the feeling of being connected to an idea that can offer relief and salvation. Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani and Ossé appeared at an altar of abolition during a global movement that condemned policing. It was a vibe. Sure, they may have even been earnest at the time. But as the abolitionist Mariame Kaba has said about centuries of organizing: abolition is not about your feelings or how you identify. It’s what you do. During the pandemic, I was a couple of years off from an ongoing campaign to close a jail and about to enter a campaign to prevent another one from opening. I wrote my book, Becoming Abolitionists, in that time partially because of how quickly some conversions happened – through charismatic check-marked profiles and inspirational protests, rather than through an organization or collective. Many people were just beginning to understand how abolition was connected to other movements, including those against capitalism, imperialism, racism and ableism. I wanted to focus on centuries of abolitionist resistance that gave rise to contemporary abolitionist demands. “Defund” wasn’t simply a new idea about removing dollars from a budget (though we’d take it!) and leaving everything in society the same. Rather, it was and is a personal and political commitment and strategy to eliminate carceral, communal, colonial, capitalist and climate-based violence while building the people, practices and institutions to help us thrive. This fact is what makes Ocasio-Cortez’s comments additionally troublesome. Even by her own logic, “crime” is largely a product of exploitative, unequal social relations, such as economic inequality, and democratic socialism would produce more equal social relationships and reduce crime. So if democratic socialism is effective, then why keep funding the New York police department at $11bn? And why dismiss taking money away as “rhetoric”? Because: the police were not created for public safety. They were created to keep property owners and slaveowners safe. The abolitionist geographer Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes in Geographies of Global Change that “the best estimate for crime as a driving force of prison expansion shows it to account for little more than 10 percent of the increase. Rather, it is a greater propensity to lock people up, as opposed to people’s greater propensity to do old or new illegal things, that accounts for about 90 percent of US prison and jail growth since 1980.” The rhetoric of public safety obscures this history and protects the institution as a heavily unionized, violent jobs program. This does not mean the police never show up when someone needs help, or that people become cops because they only want to hurt others. What it does mean is that historically, cities are willing to rely on the poverty that capitalism creates to fill its carceral ranks with people looking to enter the middle class. Seeing progressive politicians move away from their earlier feelings poses a question about what they’re moving toward. Ossé and AOC did not introduce any “woke 1” legislation or resolutions that they now have to retract. Mamdani actually attempted the opposite: the racial justice working group of DSA, among others, successfully pressured him to reverse his commitment to add almost 600 more officers and $70m to the NYPD, against his campaign promise to maintain the headcount of the force. He was positioning this move while boasting historic lows for crime in the city. So unlike the students, artists, congregants and organizers I met and know, the politicians prioritized political office over political homes. Because these figures represent more than their political ideas, I understand. But the dismissal is the problem. The ideas rooted in the defund movement that got them the spotlight were not polling well by the time their volunteers were canvassing for their political campaigns. As a result, they dismissed those ideas as something to grow and learn from, not to publicly explore and explain. By contrast, for example, upon receiving pushback from the “defund” framing, activists in North Carolina chose “refund Raleigh” instead as an organizing campaign strategy to explain abolition to the community, develop a public services investment strategy and secure policies that decouple public safety and police. Even decades before abolition entered a mainstream branding debate, Wilson Gilmore said that she and others organizing through Californians United for a Responsible Budget chose a “deliberately bland name” to attract community members to the campaign. Still, other organizers chose more explicit “defund” campaign names as clear sites of struggle, sacrificing public palatability for political clarity. These efforts are equally important: people, politicians and corporations weaponized the ambiguity of “Black lives matter” toward everything, including more police funding and hires. So whether explicit in naming “defund” or not, abolitionist organizers across the country have been spearheading electoral campaigns, mutual aid efforts, disaster recovery, anti-immigrant detention networks, stopping jails and more. It is not always successful and apparent, but the commitment remains because the struggle continues. Right now, DSA members like AOC, Ossé and Mamdani feel refreshing because electoral politics have been captured for so long by Democrats and Republicans. And the state has done such a horribly impressive job at exhausting, shackling, killing and exiling actual revolutionaries that politicians who repeat the slightest radical rhetoric can start to feel like revolutionaries. What remains, though, is that the very movements producing that rhetoric, from abolition to Free Palestine, also produced the possibilities of their elections. And downplaying those movements puts organizers who continue this work at risk, especially right now. What time is it when politicians across the political spectrum, from AOC and Ossé to Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, suggest that progressive and left organizers are “woke” and “crazy”? It is the time when those who have not yet realized that the demonization of people, organizations and ideas about justice – regardless of where they come from – leads to targeting, surveillance, deportation, imprisonment and death. If leaders of DSA, an organization of which I am also a member, want to continue to grow as an electoral political home for people who believe these ideas are not only possible, but also worth pursuing, they must know that they are subject to the same lessons they are teaching establishment Democrats right now: do not laugh off the political demands of those who put you in office. For all of what their constituents, canvassers and staffers did as part of a fight on our behalf, is it worth treating years-long radical, Black and multiracial pursuits of freedom as mere pandemic pandemonium? No, it’s not. But more than what we are called by any of them is what we continue to call ourselves. Our own histories, convictions and clarity, not politicians, lead the way.

title: Max Miller’s ex-wife sues him for sharing image of daughter as part of custody battle
body_text: Emily Moreno, the ex-wife of Max Miller, has sued the embattled Republican congressman and his lawyer for uploading a picture of their infant daughter to a publicly accessible Dropbox folder as part of their custody battle. The complaint argues that Miller “recklessly published and disclosed to the world a nude image” of their daughter. The photos in the lawsuit were part of a tranche of evidence that Miller’s team compiled in response to the domestic abuse allegations the lawmaker is facing following his divorce. Those allegations include holding a gun to Moreno’s head, pouring boiling water on her, and actions that resulted in his two-year-old daughter’s collarbone being broken, all of which Miller denies. Miller, who is seeking re-election in Ohio, has faced a wave of calls to resign, including from members of his own party and his father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a Republican senator. However, Donald Trump has remained largely supportive of the congressman, who represents a conservative district, and there are reports that the White House squashed efforts to replace him on the ballot in November’s midterm election. The suit alleges that Miller “so desperately wanted to salvage his political job” that he “recklessly and intentionally” provided his lawyer (Aaron Minc) with “a trove of documents and photos, indifferent about what they contained or how they were used”. Miller then shared the link to the files online after he went live on social media to deny the allegations against him on 2 August. Moreno’s lawyers note that “more than 400,000 people saw or interacted with” Miller’s posts containing the Dropbox folder. The lawsuit – filed in US district court for the northern district of Ohio – demands the court award $150,000 in damages for “every time someone accessed, transferred, distributed, published, or downloaded the image” of their daughter. At the time, Minc had accepted sole responsibility for inadvertently releasing the unredacted image of Moreno and Miller’s daughter in the files. The Guardian has approached both Miller and Minc for their response to the latest lawsuit. Brian Poindexter, the Democrat running against Miller in November, has ramped up attacks on his opponent. “No one credibly accused of holding a gun to his wife’s head and breaking their two-year-old daughter’s collarbone belongs in the halls of power,” he said recently on X. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has also seized on the moment to add Poindexter to the “Red to Blue” program, which identifies districts the party thinks can be flipped from Republicans to the party for congressional control. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

title: Is Florida ready for a democratic socialist?
body_text: Doors don’t get knocked on much in this stretch of south Florida, where yard signs for Republican and Democratic candidates alternate from home to home. Oliver Larkin, the 34-year-old democratic socialist running for Congress here, knows this. With a clipboard in hand five weeks before the state’s primary, Larkin and two canvassing volunteers walked down palm tree-lined streets with single-family homes to pitch residents on his plan for a better way of life. Surprisingly, many wanted to chat with the strangers at their door. “You’ve got my vote!” said George, a longtime Fort Lauderdale resident who listened as Larkin explained his plan to lower the cost of living with a reduced property insurance rate amid a climate crisis that flooded his street just three years prior. A few doors down, a resident who immigrated from Haiti was eager to chat, too. “I don’t see what [politicians have] done for Fort Lauderdale, and I’ve been in this city for 39 years,” he said. “But I don’t know who I’m going to vote for.” Larkin talked to the resident for roughly five minutes. He didn’t mention socialism by name, but discussed policies that describe what socialism is: government-funded universal healthcare, free tuition at public universities and the construction of millions of new affordable housing units. He also explained his desire to protect and expand temporary protected status and abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “All right,” the resident said. “I’ll vote for you.” When one resident asked why, on a 95F day, Larkin was wearing a dark suit, he replied: “I’m dressed for the job I want!” That weekend, about 75 volunteers for Larkin, some of whom traveled from counties on the other side of the state, knocked on thousands of doors across the district. It’s the engine – replicated by Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapters across the country – behind a campaign that establishment Democrats are watching warily and DSA leaders are treating as their next proof of concept. While DSA-backed candidates won primaries in New York City, Philadelphia, Colorado and Michigan this year, the organization is now asking whether that momentum could power an upset in a state Donald Trump carried in 2024 and where Larkin’s opponent in the Democratic primary, Jared Moskowitz, is a two-term congressman who calls himself a “DeSantis Democrat”. But Florida is not New York or Denver. Unlike the solidly blue turf DSA candidates have claimed so far, Florida’s 25th district is a brand-new, highly competitive district that boasts a diverse electorate and an almost even split between Democratic, Republican and independent voters – meaning independents will decide the election. Beyond the two men on the ballot, the race is a proxy fight over what kind of Democrat can win in a Florida remade by Republican redistricting and rightward drift. Larkin’s candidacy tests whether the DSA’s recent wins in New York and Colorado translate to a district Republicans specifically redrew to be less competitive. Moskowitz’s candidacy tests whether distancing from the national party is still the surer path to survival here. Whoever wins the primary on 18 August will shape how both parties read Florida heading into the general election, and how much room the DSA has to expand beyond the areas where it has won so far. “The anti-socialism card has been played for so long that it’s ingrained in our politics here,” said Sean D Foreman, a political scientist at Barry University. “But when you get past the name ‘democratic socialist’, and you start talking about policies like raising the minimum wage and affordable housing, they’re ideas that many voters agree with. He grew up in Fort Lauderdale, the son of a retired army officer, and was working a minimum-wage line-cook job after college when he became consumed by Bernie Sanders’ 2016 campaign. He quit, drove to New Hampshire and went from unpaid volunteer to running the campaign’s Portsmouth field office, later organizing in Nevada, Kansas, Utah, New York and Rhode Island. After the campaign ended, Larkin spent the next few years in Washington unionizing his workplace and organizing for progressive campaigns and unions before moving back to south Florida in 2022. He announced his run for Congress at a protest against “Alligator Alcatraz”, the now-shuttered Florida immigration detention camp where civil rights groups reported severe human rights violations. In late July, Larkin stood before a packed room at a contemporary art museum in Dania Beach and fielded questions from voters for two hours. He didn’t dodge and he didn’t summarize. When asked about a specific line in the federal budget or the mechanics of a housing proposal, he answered with the kind of granular detail that comes from having given the same stump speech and having absorbed the same pushback hundreds of times over the past year. Moskowitz, on the other hand, has largely avoided any public events with voters. The two-term congressman has not agreed to any debates. Larkin’s campaign has seized on the contrast. “Congressman Moskowitz doesn’t want to be accountable to voters in this district,” Larkin said. (Moskowitz declined to comment on Larkin’s claim that he does not have a field strategy to reach voters.) A self-described “cat dad” and drag show enthusiast who says he wants south Florida to be a safe and welcoming place for everyone, Larkin has turned Moskowitz’s affiliation with DeSantis into a line of attack, pointing to his being chosen by the governor to lead the state’s division of emergency management. Larkin said he was especially divergent with Moskowitz on his decision to become the first congressional Democrat to join Trump’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge) initiative and his vote for the Laken Riley Act, which expanded ICE’s detention authority. Moskowitz’s version of that record looks different. He has cast himself as a pragmatist willing to work across the aisle in a state where Republicans control every lever of government, and allies note that his emergency-management background, including his time leading the state’s disaster response to numerous hurricanes, has given him a profile distinct from the national Democratic brand. He is widely seen as more socially conservative than most of the House Democratic caucus and has drawn criticism from the left for his unwavering support of Israel and his vote against a resolution to limit US military involvement in the conflict with Iran. While Moskowitz started with a wide financial and polling advantage, that has shifted some in recent weeks. Moskowitz has raised nearly $3m to Larkin’s more than $1m, coming from nearly 20,000 unique donors, as part of his mission to reject corporate donations. Larkin has also leaned into his connection to the wider DSA wave, appearing alongside the Twitch streamer Hasan Piker at a virtual fundraiser that pulled in roughly $60,000 in one night, and citing a nearly $120,000 fundraising surge in the week after the New York City primary wins. Polls have shown the race getting tighter, too. A Beacon Insights poll in June had Moskowitz leading Larkin 51% to 19%; a poll last week from the Center for Strategic Politics found Larkin and Moskowitz in a statistical tie. Larkin’s internal polling, meanwhile, showed a wide head-to-head deficit that narrowed sharply once voters were given information about both candidates’ records, including Moskowitz’s Doge affiliation and Larkin’s status as a first-time candidate and democratic socialist. However, experts remain wary of giving too much weight to polls. “Given [that] polls way overestimated [Abdul] El-Sayed in Michigan and then [Francesca] Hong in Wisconsin, [it] underscores how difficult election polling is in general,” said David Macdonald, a political scientist at Florida State University. “And then it gets really difficult when you’re trying to poll primary races where it’s much lower turnout, much lower salience and with probably a lot more undecided voters.” The DSA’s gamble in Florida The national DSA’s push behind Larkin comes as the organization tries to expand beyond its traditional base of younger white college-educated progressives in large urban centers. Megan Romer, the DSA’s national co-chair, argues the group’s growth in rural and Republican-leaning areas – from mobile-home-park tenant unions in Idaho and North Carolina to organizing against new datacenters in her own upstate New York county – shows the model can travel beyond deep-blue cities. “The current moment is being framed as ‘economic anxiety’ and that’s such a 2016 term,” said Romer. “It’s not economic anxiety to have to pick between rent and food – it’s economic violence. So we’re fighting against this system that keeps people from living dignified, safe and healthy lives.” The seat that Larkin and Moskowitz are vying for exists because of a recent US supreme court ruling that gutted the Voting Rights Act. Shortly after, DeSantis pushed through a new congressional map designed to give Republicans an edge in as many as four Florida seats. The overhaul dismantled the 25th district long held by Democrat Debbie Wasserman Schultz and replaced it with a new coastal seat running from Delray Beach to Miami Beach. Moskowitz, whose old 23rd district had also been redrawn to lean more Republican, opted to run in the new 25th rather than face a tougher Republican-leaning seat elsewhere. The district is majority white (65%), with a sizable Hispanic population (20%) and Black voters making up just 5%. People ages 50 and older make up more than 60% of the voters in the district – all demographics similar to the district that Moskowitz has represented since 2023. That backdrop is central to why even Larkin’s allies describe this as a harder test than Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral race in New York or Melat Kiros’s in the Colorado congressional primary. “In this particular district, which is a coastal and relatively wealthy area, the economic conditions are not there to bring a critical mass of support for the democratic socialists,” said Foreman. “It’s an area where you have people who have moved in from different parts of the country, and they’re probably more conservative.” Steven Schale, a longtime Florida Democratic strategist who has worked on Barack Obama’s campaigns and is a friend of Moskowitz’s, pointed to two other considerations that make the district an uphill battle for Larkin: the 25th has one of the largest Jewish Democratic electorates in the country and the state has a history of being unfriendly terrain for the party’s most progressive flank, from Hillary Clinton’s 40-point presidential primary win over Sanders in the state in 2016 to Andrew Gillum’s narrow 2018 loss in the governor’s race. “If Oliver Larkin wins that primary, he will lose the general election, and he will probably lose it pretty badly,” Schale said, arguing that DSA positions on abolishing prisons and curtailing ICE, however popular within the primary electorate, are liabilities in a general election where affordability, not ideology, is the dominant concern. However, those distinctions are not so cut and dried; polls show that a majority of Latino voters in Florida oppose ICE. Florida also has a surprising history of voting for progressive issues. In 2018, nearly 65% of Florida voters approved restoring voting rights to most Floridians with prior convictions. Then in 2020, a $15 minimum wage amendment passed with roughly 61% of the vote even as Donald Trump carried the state. Schale doesn’t view the race as morally simple, though. The DSA, he said, “provides real opportunities for young people” to lead campaigns in a way the Democratic establishment often does not, and part of the movement’s appeal is a legitimate frustration with incumbents who “should have gone home 15 years ago”. Larkin rejects the idea that his politics are a general-election liability, pointing to his own polling, which shows him running close to a generic Democrat’s advantage in the district and ahead of the leading Republican fundraiser in early general-election matchups. He argues that Democrats’ losses in 2024, when roughly 7 million fewer voters turned out for Kamala Harris than for Joe Biden four years earlier, reflect a failure to offer working-class voters anything concrete, not an overcorrection to the left. “The label of democratic socialism just frankly is not scary,” he said, “when under capitalism people have barely enough to survive.” Canvassers who have been knocking on doors for Larkin since April say they have grown more hopeful with each passing week. Days away from the election, the campaign said it had knocked on more than 35,000 doors and made more than 170,000 calls to voters. “The democratic socialists have already won this round in Florida, even if none of their candidates win, because they’ve gotten a lot more attention than you would have expected otherwise,” said Foreman. “Even Oliver Larkin, to some extent, realizes he’s planting seeds for the future of the movement.”
