title: Karoline Leavitt leaves behind a legacy of lies. What’s next for the Trump aide?
body_text: Karoline Leavitt, 28, is leaving her demanding job as Donald Trump’s press secretary to spend more time with her two young children and her 60-year-old husband. According to a post by Trump On Truth Social, Leavitt will be departing her role at the end of the month and will serve as one of Trump’s “top outside advisors”. In other words: the official version of events is that Leavitt is resigning on her own terms for family reasons and not because Trump’s approval ratings are at record lows and she’s a rat fleeing a sinking ship. But is the official version of events the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Don’t bother asking Leavitt – I’m not sure she knows much about the T-word. She may have been the youngest White House press secretary in history, but there’s no denying her communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in the Trump administration. I won’t muck about with euphemisms such as misrepresented or stated without evidence or made false claims. Leavitt’s legacy in government was attacking Trump’s enemies and spouting lie after lie after lie. Being a lowly writer means I am held to far higher standards about what I can say than the departing press secretary or her boss, the president of the United States. Unlike Leavitt or Trump, I actually have to provide facts and evidence to back up my assertions. So here we go: here are a few fun facts about Leavitt’s tenure in public office. First, there’s her role in promoting lies about the economy. One of the most significant economic policies of Trump’s second term has been his global tariffs, which were initially extended even to volcanic islands inhabited only by penguins. During a press briefing in March 2025, Leavitt told reporters that tariffs were a “tax cut for the American people”. Economists have said this is nonsense. “Economists don’t agree on much, but we agree tariffs are taxes on consumers,” Tara Sinclair, a George Washington University economist told the fact-checking website Politifact. The non-partisan Tax Foundation has also run the numbers and said that in 2025, the Trump tariffs “amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000” per US household. But what’s $1,000, eh? It’s nothing to Trump, who made a staggering $2.2bn during the first year of his second term in various questionable ways. One imagines it’s also not much to Leavitt, who earns just under $200,000 in her role and whose husband, Nicholas Riccio, manages what has been described as a multimillion-dollar real estate business. And if you feel aggrieved about tariffs increasing the already sky-high cost of living, according to Leavitt, you should just work harder (or marry a real estate tycoon). “Some of these kids, and I call them kids because they are in their 20s and have never had real jobs, and they’re complaining things are expensive,” Fox News’ Jesse Watters told Leavitt last month during a conversation about young Democratic party voters. “Yes, things are expensive when you don’t have a real job.” Leavitt agreed, adding that her generation had been raised with “silver spoons in their mouths, just getting everything handed to them”. That was un-American, she suggested, because this country “was built on meritocracy and hard work, pulling up your sleeves, pulling yourself up from your bootstraps”. It’s not just tariffs where Leavitt’s math seems to be off. In January 2025, the press secretary justified Trump’s order to freeze federal funding to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) by claiming it was wasting money. “[T]here was about to be 50m taxpayer dollars that went out the door to fund condoms in Gaza,” Leavitt said. “That is a preposterous waste of taxpayer money. So that’s what this pause is focused on: being good stewards of tax dollars.” To be very clear: that condom claim was a lie. Documents shows that no condoms were sent anywhere in the Middle East, let alone to a place undergoing what many experts have termed a genocide. The US did, however, provide billions of taxpayer dollars to help Israel destroy Gaza, which has arguably reduced births a lot faster than condoms would have. The dismantling of USAID, justified by Leavitt, has also increased pregnancy complications and maternal death in poor countries. A study published in the Lancet journal last year estimated that US funding cuts could result in more than 14 million deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under age five, by 2030. I guess, if you’re Leavitt, being “good stewards of tax dollars” means contributing to mass death and immiseration. Money well spent! As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure. Last October, for example, SV Dáte, Huffington Post’s senior White House correspondent, asked Leavitt via text message who had suggested Budapest for a meeting between Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss Ukraine. Her response? “Your mom did.” When Dáte then asked if Leavitt thought that was funny, she replied: “It’s funny to me that you actually consider yourself a journal [sic]. You are a far left hack who nobody takes seriously, including your colleagues in the media, they just don’t tell you that to your face. Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bullshit questions.” That was a brief look at Leavitt’s past. What’s in store for her future? Despite her comments about her family, don’t expect her to go full tradwife. None of the ambitious women advancing the Trump administration’s anti-woman agenda want to devote their own lives to the domestic drudgery they extoll for others. They’ve got less privileged women to do the childcare and the cooking and the cleaning for them. No, rather than being a tradwife, one imagines Leavitt might end up with a nice little gig on Fox News or Bari Weiss’s CBS. Or perhaps, like Sean Spicer, her predecessor under Trump 1.0, she might go the reality TV route and regale us all on Dancing With the Stars. No doubt there will also be a “tell-all” book in her future in which, depending on which way the political winds are blowing, she’ll tell us all the things she thinks will rehabilitate her reputation. And, of course, for now there’s her new role as an “outside advisor”. I can’t tell you exactly what that entails but I can tell you that, going forward, communications with Trump and his outside advisers can apparently be considered privileged. On Monday, after Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general, the justice department’s office of legal counsel issued a 21-page opinion about the president’s “executive privilege” which protects communication between Trump and advisers who don’t work for his administration. This makes a future Democrat-led investigation into the Trump administration a lot harder as his advisers – who will now include Leavitt – will not be able to be comprehensively questioned by Congress. Exactly the sort of move you’d expect from a president that Leavitt has called the “most transparent” in history. Best of luck, then, to Leavitt in her future endeavors. I’m sure she’ll roll up her designer sleeves, pull herself up by her bootstraps and find a way to make huge amounts of money. And best of luck to all of us. If there’s one thing that you can be sure about when it comes to the revolving door that is the White House, it’s that no matter how bad the person leaving is, the replacement is always worse. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

In January 2025, the press secretary justified Trump’s order to freeze federal funding to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) by claiming it was wasting money. “[T]here was about to be 50m taxpayer dollars that went out the door to fund condoms in Gaza,” Leavitt said. “That is a preposterous waste of taxpayer money. So that’s what this pause is focused on: being good stewards of tax dollars.” To be very clear: that condom claim was a lie. Documents shows that no condoms were sent anywhere in the Middle East, let alone to a place undergoing what many experts have termed a genocide. The US did, however, provide billions of taxpayer dollars to help Israel destroy Gaza, which has arguably reduced births a lot faster than condoms would have. The dismantling of USAID, justified by Leavitt, has also increased pregnancy complications and maternal death in poor countries. A study published in the Lancet journal last year estimated that US funding cuts could result in more than 14 million deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under age five, by 2030. I guess, if you’re Leavitt, being “good stewards of tax dollars” means contributing to mass death and immiseration. Money well spent! As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure. Last October, for example, SV Dáte, Huffington Post’s senior White House correspondent, asked Leavitt via text message who had suggested Budapest for a meeting between Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss Ukraine. Her response? “Your mom did.” When Dáte then asked if Leavitt thought that was funny, she replied: “It’s funny to me that you actually consider yourself a journal [sic]. You are a far left hack who nobody takes seriously, including your colleagues in the media, they just don’t tell you that to your face. Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bullshit questions.” That was a brief look at Leavitt’s past. What’s in store for her future? Despite her comments about her family, don’t expect her to go full tradwife. None of the ambitious women advancing the Trump administration’s anti-woman agenda want to devote their own lives to the domestic drudgery they extoll for others. They’ve got less privileged women to do the childcare and the cooking and the cleaning for them. No, rather than being a tradwife, one imagines Leavitt might end up with a nice little gig on Fox News or Bari Weiss’s CBS. Or perhaps, like Sean Spicer, her predecessor under Trump 1.0, she might go the reality TV route and regale us all on Dancing With the Stars. No doubt there will also be a “tell-all” book in her future in which, depending on which way the political winds are blowing, she’ll tell us all the things she thinks will rehabilitate her reputation. And, of course, for now there’s her new role as an “outside advisor”. I can’t tell you exactly what that entails but I can tell you that, going forward, communications with Trump and his outside advisers can apparently be considered privileged. On Monday, after Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general, the justice department’s office of legal counsel issued a 21-page opinion about the president’s “executive privilege” which protects communication between Trump and advisers who don’t work for his administration. This makes a future Democrat-led investigation into the Trump administration a lot harder as his advisers – who will now include Leavitt – will not be able to be comprehensively questioned by Congress. Exactly the sort of move you’d expect from a president that Leavitt has called the “most transparent” in history. Best of luck, then, to Leavitt in her future endeavors. I’m sure she’ll roll up her designer sleeves, pull herself up by her bootstraps and find a way to make huge amounts of money. And best of luck to all of us. If there’s one thing that you can be sure about when it comes to the revolving door that is the White House, it’s that no matter how bad the person leaving is, the replacement is always worse. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Tennessee’s Justin Pearson takes on America’s most contentious issues
body_text: Justin Pearson made national headlines as one of the “Tennessee Three” – the state lawmakers expelled from the capitol protesting for gun control after a deadly school shooting. Three years later, the state representative won a Democratic congressional primary after boldly staking positions on some of America’s most contentious fault lines: voting rights, datacenters and the American war machine. “Republicans are responding to elected officials who stand up to billion-dollar datacenters, and the billionaires who own them. Democrats are responding to a vision of Medicare for All, ending genocide,” said Pearson. “The confluence that is happening between those issues, is [that] who profits off of war are the same people who are profiting off of polluting our communities and stealing our drinking water for their datacenters that replace our jobs.” That effort towards uniting disparate perspectives will be key in November’s midterm election, as Tennessee’s ninth district, once the state’s sole majority Black district, was split into pieces after the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act’s second provision. The redistricting was part of a larger Trump administration effort to retain control of Congress and dilute the Black vote, especially in the south. At 31, Pearson has spent most of his life fighting for his community. In school, that meant fighting for new textbooks; then he launched a campaign to stop a crude oil pipeline from running through Black neighborhoods in his native Memphis. That was all before he was elected to represent the area in the state legislature – and then, a few months later, expelled over the protest. In the years since, Pearson has been at the forefront of a local movement against Elon Musk’s xAI, which has built two datacenters powered by soot-producing turbines concentrated in a Black neighborhood in south Memphis already suffering from environmental damage. That pollution was exposed in part through Memphis Community Against Pollution, an organization Pearson co-founded with his brother. Though the NAACP and environmental advocacy groups have fought in court to halt the usage of the turbines, the justice department got in the way, arguing the datacenter was needed during Operation Epic Fury. The effects of the Trump administration in Memphis continue to be acute: last September, Trump established a Memphis “taskforce” including 13 federal agencies and sent hundreds of federal agents into the city, with agents killing four Black men in the last 10 months. Trump claimed in his announcement that the city was “suffering from tremendous levels of violent crime” – but the week before, local police celebrated overall crime hitting a “historic” 25-year low. In July, over 1,000 people attended a rally for Pearson in response to the killings, where he was joined by congresswomen Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Summer Lee and Ayanna Pressley. “I’ve been adamant about prioritizing proximity to people who are poor, communities that are disenfranchised, who have been pushed to the bottom by systems of injustice, for years. That’s how I got my start in community organizing, that’s what I believe now as an elected official, and that is part of the reason that we are seeing a momentous amount of energy in our campaign,” Pearson said. “There’s also no denying of the zeitgeist of this moment: that people are thirsting for elected officials who are bold enough … willing, and strong enough to stand up to the status quo that has been rigged against everyday working-class people for a long time. And I think people are responding to that.” With his win, Pearson has joined the ranks of Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez as young progressive-populist upstarts sweeping primaries across the country. These candidates are running robust organizing-first campaigns in a model largely credited to Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 win as New York mayor, built on small individual donations (Pearson’s average donation was $31). The strategy echoes the 2016 Bernie Sanders presidential campaign and the rise of “the Squad” to Congress in 2018; unsurprisingly, Pearson was endorsed by both Sanders and Justice Democrats, the group that propelled Squad members Pressley, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib to office. “These primaries have shown voters of all ages are ready for next-generation leadership, and are more than willing to challenge the ageing Democratic establishment,” said David Hogg, co-founder of progressive Pac Leaders We Deserve, which endorsed Pearson on day one. “From stopping a $2bn oil pipeline to taking on the richest man in the world before most Americans even knew what a data center was to his historic protest for gun safety, he’s consistently out-organized money, power and corrupt politics.” Pearson said the numbers he brings out – including 150 people at a rally in Pulaski, the birthplace of the Ku Klux Klan – and his longtime engagement with his local community could make the change he’s calling for a reality. “It’s concerning to me that our party would try and put a box around who can be a Democrat when we are literally living in a moment in time where people are trying to put a box around what it means to be an American, what it means to be a citizen,” Pearson said. “It’s the politicos in Washington DC thinking they know what’s happening in the south or what’s happening in our communities better than we do – and they’re wrong.”

title: Progressives back substitute teacher over Wasserman Schultz in Florida
body_text: A progressive group has endorsed a 27-year-old substitute teacher who overcame childhood homelessness in his bid to unseat the veteran Democrat Debbie Wasserman Schultz in Florida. The Progressive Change Campaign Committee (PCCC) said it was backing Elijah Manley in next week’s primary election in Florida’s newly drawn 20th congressional district, casting the race as a contest between a young economic populist and a stalwart of the Democratic party establishment. Wasserman Schultz, 59, an 11-term congresswoman and former chair of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), has faced criticism from African American leaders over her decision to run as the sole white candidate in a majority-minority district where she is not a resident. This followed the creation of gerrymandered congressional maps by Florida Republicans that broke Wasserman Schultz’s current seat into five shards. She decided against running in the 22nd district, where she lives, and chose instead to compete in the deep blue 20th, which has been represented by Black Democrats for more than 30 years. Yvette Clarke, chair of the Congressional Black caucus, told the Politico website on Friday: “It’s a painful situation. To have a beloved colleague who made a decision basically to run in a district where historically there’s been CBC representation, and I know that the community has been really disrupted by it.” Other candidates in the primary include former congresswoman Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who resigned in April over allegations of misusing $5m in federal funds, which she denies; former Broward County mayor Dale Holness; and community activist Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell, a rapper best known for his role in 2 Live Crew. Manley, who is Black, grew up homeless in Fort Lauderdale’s historic Sistrunk neighbourhood. He is campaigning on universal healthcare, a federal jobs guarantee and a pledge to build “an economy where workers have rights, working families can thrive, and the wealthy pay their fair share”. Stephanie Taylor, a co-founder of the PCCC, said: “Elijah Manley isn’t just talking about the fight for working people – he’s lived it. He’s running a campaign built on Medicare for All, good jobs, and an economy that finally works for the people, not just the wealthy and well-connected. Debbie Wasserman Schultz represents the Democratic establishment. Voters are ready for young new fighters like Elijah.” A May poll by the Listener Group suggested that Manley could pose a serious challenge to Wasserman Schultz. In an initial head-to-head matchup, she led 39% to 21%. But after voters were given basic biographical information about the candidates, Manley moved ahead, 36% to 27%, according to the poll cited by the PCCC. Manley welcomed the endorsement, saying the group had been “on the frontlines of every major fight for working people” for more than a decade. “I’m honoured to earn their endorsement,” he said. “Together, we’re going to fight for the working families of South Florida and build an economy that works for everyone.” Wasserman Schultz, who has been a member of Congress since 2005, has long been a divisive figure for Democrats. She was forced to resign as DNC chair after criticism from supporters of the progressive senator Bernie Sanders when leaked emails suggested a bias in favour of Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential primary election. Manley tweeted in May: “Debbie Wasserman Schultz is carpetbagging to FL-20, a black opportunity district instead of running in her own. DWS is everything that’s wrong with the Democratic establishment. From insider trading to payday lenders. I look forward to retiring her from public office permanently.” The PCCC is also backing Oliver Larkin, a democratic socialist organiser and union strategist challenging the Democrat Jared Moskowitz in Florida’s newly drawn 25th congressional district. The PCCC said its endorsed candidates who have already won primaries this cycle include Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota’s Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate contest, James Talarico in Texas’s Senate election and Brad Lander in New York’s 10th congressional district.

title: Trump asks ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of White House ballroom
body_text: The Trump administration has asked ⁠the ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of the president’s controversial $400m ⁠White House ballroom to proceed after an ‌appeals ‌court ordered work to halt. In a case testing Donald Trump’s presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled last week that the controversial ‌project lacked the necessary approval from US Congress. The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for the planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people. He and his aides have repeatedly cited national security as a benefit of its construction, too. In a filing, Trump’s administration ‌asked the supreme court justices to keep the decision by the US court of appeals for ⁠the District of Columbia circuit on hold while it prepares ‌a full appeal. “This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” D John Sauer, the solicitor general, wrote in the filing. Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for the plaintiffs challenging the project to respond. The appeals court upheld a lower court’s order blocking aboveground work on the ballroom until Congress grants its approval, but allowed construction on the underground security structure to continue. It also paused its own ruling for two weeks, until 21 August, to give the administration time to lodge its appeal to the supreme court. The government argues that “every part” of the project is “an integrated whole geared toward remedying security deficiencies and bringing critical improvements to the White House”. “The entire ballroom structure is designed to shield the military installation beneath it,” Sauer added. Trump’s administration has appealed a number of lower court decisions to the supreme court this week, in the wake of temporary injunctions over the president’s attempts to curb mail-in voting. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued to block the ballroom’s construction, said on Friday: “The administration brazenly asserted to the DC Circuit Court of Appeals that even if Ballroom construction were unlawful, not even the supreme court had authority to stop it. “The administration’s transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here. The supreme court should deny the administration’s demand that it be allowed to continue ballroom construction while it appeals.”

title: Donald Trump doesn’t just love billionaires, he loves multimillionaires too
body_text: After the House passed its version of Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) last year – the one that paired a $5tn-plus tax cut with $1tn-plus of cuts from food stamps and Medicaid – the House speaker, Mike Johnson, explained that “this is not giving tax cuts to the millionaires”. The beneficiaries, he said, were “small business owners” that “provide the jobs in every community in America”. Johnson was playing to the myth of the modest, sturdy Main Street job creator. It is an appealing story. It’s also the most consequential piece of BS distorting American policy that deprives the government of tax revenue, stunts American capitalism, twists regulations, thwarts competition and overwhelmingly serves millionaires’ interests. The speaker was specifically talking about “pass through” businesses. About 95% of businesses in the country take this form. They employ half of all workers and generate more than half the nation’s business income. These creatures of the tax code are freed from paying the corporate income tax rate. Instead, their untaxed profits are distributed to their owners, who generally face lower individual tax rates, saving them billions. Republicans have consistently gone to bat for pass throughs. In 2017 Ron Johnson, the Republican senator from Wisconsin, threatened not to vote for Trump’s Tax Cut and Jobs Act, relenting only after the Senate increased a tax deduction for pass-through business income from 17% to 20%. “I just have it in my heart a real affinity for these owner-operated pass-throughs,” Johnson said at the time. That deduction, made permanent in the ”big beautiful bill” last year, will cost the budget $820bn over a 10-year period, almost as much as was cut from the Medicaid budget. About 57% of the $1.3tn in pass-through income in 2022 went to 890,000 people in the richest 1% of the population, according to the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center. A study by economists at the Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis and Dartmouth University found that 35% of the total deductions in the year after the 2017 tax cut, a cold $54bn, flowed to taxpayers with income of at least $1m. Johnson and Johnson know this. Senator Ron owned a stake in a pass-through, a plastics maker in Oshkosh, which he sold in 2020 for between $5 and $25m and upon which he built a fortune worth about $40m in 2018, making him the sixth-richest senator at the time. Speaker Mike, a man of “modest means”, lives in a $3.7m townhouse steps from the US Capitol owned by the millionaire Republican donor Lee Beaman, who made his fortune from a string of car dealerships. Next month, economists Owen Zidar from Princeton and Eric Zwick from the University of Chicago will publish a panoramic profile of these “everywhere millionaires”. They are your dentist and doctor, the car dealer and the insurance salesman, the lawyer and the real estate developer, the accountant, the consultant and the building equipment contractor. They have largely organized themselves as pass-throughs. Many are amazingly rich. Zidar and Zwick estimate that for every billionaire in the Forbes 400 list, there are more than 4,000 Main Street millionaires worth at least $10m. Their net worth adds up to $46.7tn, nearly 12 times as much as that of the Forbes plutocrats. The political system is at their mercy. Consider Trump’s ”big beautiful” tax cut last year. The 20% deduction granted to pass-through profits means that the top income tax rate for their rich owners is only 29.6%. For people who earn wages, the top marginal rate is 37%. Concern over the political power of the plutocracy has focused on billionaires. But Main Street millionaires flying under the radar might be more influential. Political action committees (Pacs) run by the National Association of Realtors, the National Beer Wholesalers Association and the National Automobile Dealers Association were among the top 10 by donations in the 2023-24 cycle. And Main Street millionaires play in politics themselves, at the federal, state and local level. Car dealership millionaires Don Beyer from Virginia, Vern Buchanan from Florida and Mike Kelly from Pennsylvania sit on the House ways and means committee. They are probably not unhappy about the pass-through deduction, nor about the deduction for new auto loan interest that also made it into the OBBBA, which Zidar and Zwick estimate will cost the budget $5bn to $10bn a year for four years. Though tax breaks may be their top concern, the damage to the republic runs deeper. In 1997, doctors got the federal government to freeze the number of residency positions funded by Medicare, a neat way to limit the availability of new doctors. That helps explain why there are only 2.7 doctors per 1,000 people in the US, compared with 3.7 across the other OECD countries, and why 26% of American doctors fit in the richest 1% of the population, compared with only 5% in Sweden, despite Americans’ comparatively tenuous hold on life. Let’s not just pour hate on the doctors, though. Car dealers in 50 states benefit from franchise laws that prevent automakers from closing them down and stop new dealers from entering their turf. In 17 states they also benefit from a ban on direct sales by automakers. The income of real estate brokers is protected by privileged access to listing information and exorbitant, monopolistic fees of dubious legality that they extract from homeowners. Beer distributors have lobbied hard to prevent breweries from selling directly to retailers and to get ironclad territorial rights. This is not the page to pity billionaires. But it’s worth pointing to the privileges of the rich below that status. Trump may love Elon Musk. But his signature bill – which stripped the EV subsidies turbocharging Tesla’s sales – shows much more love for the car dealers and the doctors and the real estate developers living a few floors below Elon but well within the 1%. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

In 2017 Ron Johnson, the Republican senator from Wisconsin, threatened not to vote for Trump’s Tax Cut and Jobs Act, relenting only after the Senate increased a tax deduction for pass-through business income from 17% to 20%. “I just have it in my heart a real affinity for these owner-operated pass-throughs,” Johnson said at the time. That deduction, made permanent in the ”big beautiful bill” last year, will cost the budget $820bn over a 10-year period, almost as much as was cut from the Medicaid budget. About 57% of the $1.3tn in pass-through income in 2022 went to 890,000 people in the richest 1% of the population, according to the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center. A study by economists at the Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis and Dartmouth University found that 35% of the total deductions in the year after the 2017 tax cut, a cold $54bn, flowed to taxpayers with income of at least $1m. Johnson and Johnson know this. Senator Ron owned a stake in a pass-through, a plastics maker in Oshkosh, which he sold in 2020 for between $5 and $25m and upon which he built a fortune worth about $40m in 2018, making him the sixth-richest senator at the time. Speaker Mike, a man of “modest means”, lives in a $3.7m townhouse steps from the US Capitol owned by the millionaire Republican donor Lee Beaman, who made his fortune from a string of car dealerships. Next month, economists Owen Zidar from Princeton and Eric Zwick from the University of Chicago will publish a panoramic profile of these “everywhere millionaires”. They are your dentist and doctor, the car dealer and the insurance salesman, the lawyer and the real estate developer, the accountant, the consultant and the building equipment contractor. They have largely organized themselves as pass-throughs. Many are amazingly rich. Zidar and Zwick estimate that for every billionaire in the Forbes 400 list, there are more than 4,000 Main Street millionaires worth at least $10m. Their net worth adds up to $46.7tn, nearly 12 times as much as that of the Forbes plutocrats. The political system is at their mercy. Consider Trump’s ”big beautiful” tax cut last year. The 20% deduction granted to pass-through profits means that the top income tax rate for their rich owners is only 29.6%. For people who earn wages, the top marginal rate is 37%. Concern over the political power of the plutocracy has focused on billionaires. But Main Street millionaires flying under the radar might be more influential. Political action committees (Pacs) run by the National Association of Realtors, the National Beer Wholesalers Association and the National Automobile Dealers Association were among the top 10 by donations in the 2023-24 cycle. And Main Street millionaires play in politics themselves, at the federal, state and local level. Car dealership millionaires Don Beyer from Virginia, Vern Buchanan from Florida and Mike Kelly from Pennsylvania sit on the House ways and means committee. They are probably not unhappy about the pass-through deduction, nor about the deduction for new auto loan interest that also made it into the OBBBA, which Zidar and Zwick estimate will cost the budget $5bn to $10bn a year for four years. Though tax breaks may be their top concern, the damage to the republic runs deeper. In 1997, doctors got the federal government to freeze the number of residency positions funded by Medicare, a neat way to limit the availability of new doctors. That helps explain why there are only 2.7 doctors per 1,000 people in the US, compared with 3.7 across the other OECD countries, and why 26% of American doctors fit in the richest 1% of the population, compared with only 5% in Sweden, despite Americans’ comparatively tenuous hold on life. Let’s not just pour hate on the doctors, though. Car dealers in 50 states benefit from franchise laws that prevent automakers from closing them down and stop new dealers from entering their turf. In 17 states they also benefit from a ban on direct sales by automakers. The income of real estate brokers is protected by privileged access to listing information and exorbitant, monopolistic fees of dubious legality that they extract from homeowners. Beer distributors have lobbied hard to prevent breweries from selling directly to retailers and to get ironclad territorial rights. This is not the page to pity billionaires. But it’s worth pointing to the privileges of the rich below that status. Trump may love Elon Musk. But his signature bill – which stripped the EV subsidies turbocharging Tesla’s sales – shows much more love for the car dealers and the doctors and the real estate developers living a few floors below Elon but well within the 1%. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Where healthcare could sway voters, organizers ramp up an old tactic: talking to people
body_text: Going door to door in western Wisconsin multiple times per week, Bill Hogseth tells strangers about his seizure. Hogseth, the co-executive director and lead organizer of the nonpartisan group GrassRoots Organizing Western Wisconsin (Groww), tells them about waking up in an ambulance, and the impact of the seizure on his ability to drive and work. Usually standing on their doorsteps, he asks to hear their stories too – about ambulance rides, hospital bills, broken bones. Hogseth’s vulnerability encourages others to share. It’s a concept called “deep canvassing”, a long discussion, usually about 15-20 minutes, with a neighbor at their door about a political issue not tied to a specific candidate. It’s designed to assess a person’s support for a policy at the start of the conversation, then see if it changes by the end of it. Open minds are key to Hogseth’s work in western Wisconsin’s third congressional district, where a heated season is ramping up as Democrats are trying to unseat Republican representative Derrick Van Orden. A host of national Republican figures have visited the area in recent months, including Trump himself, who came to Chippewa Falls in June to talk about farming, a sign of the area’s prominence on the electoral map. Healthcare has become a critical issue in the state, and system failures have become a political liability. Democrats are reminding voters that Van Orden voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which will deliver $1tn in healthcare cuts over the next decade, starting in January. Two hospitals in western Wisconsin closed permanently in 2024, and researchers have identified others at risk of closure or service reductions. Rebecca Cooke, who won the Democratic primary to face Van Orden in November, lists “healing our healthcare system” first on her website’s priorities list. Cooke told the Guardian earlier this summer that she not only frequently heard about healthcare concerns from voters, but shared them herself. “I’ve actually canceled my own insurance through the ACA because it’s increased so much and I can’t afford it,” Cooke said in June. “There’s a lot of people that I know that are doing the same.” The people who open their doors to Hogseth and his colleagues often share stories of how the US healthcare system has failed them. There’s the man who drove himself to the hospital while passing a kidney stone to avoid a costly ambulance ride and the mom who wants to stay home with her kids but needs her job to cover health insurance. There’s the cancer care, the surgeries, the peculiarities of medical billing, the lapses in insurance coverage, the people who see the state’s Medicaid program as a lifeline for their family members. Groww is conducting these deep canvasses throughout western Wisconsin on healthcare, specifically on potentially expanding access to BadgerCare. That’s the state’s Medicaid program, which provides insurance for low-income families. The group wants to have 4,000 conversations in the northern part of the third congressional district from May to November, Hogseth said. About 40 trained deep canvassers are out in the field three times a week throughout the region. In addition to the congressional race, Wisconsin voters in November will also decide on key state legislative races and an open governor’s race that could make expanding BadgerCare a reality. Estimates show more than 276,000 Wisconsinites could lose healthcare coverage as the cuts roll out. Wisconsin is also one of 10 states that did not expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act (ACA). “Regardless of who people vote for, [the issue of healthcare] is cutting into people’s anger,” Hogseth said. At the doors in western Wisconsin’s small towns, people show a willingness to slow down and talk, even to a stranger. Most say they don’t think anyone in Washington understands their struggles with healthcare. By the end of the conversations, many people move up in support of expanding access to BadgerCare. In some instances, they say they don’t support the issue at all, then fully support it and want to get involved by the end. Studies have shown these deep canvasses can lead to reduced prejudice and decreased exclusionary attitudes. One study, commissioned by a group called People’s Action in 2020, showed that the method can change voting behavior. At a July protest in Taylor county, one of the reddest areas of the state, a decommissioned ambulance and gurney sat outside a picnic shelter right next to a Republican picnic where Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman who is the state’s gubernatorial nominee, was set to speak. The Medford, Wisconsin, protest, led by Taylor county’s Indivisible chapter and attended by allies from other parts of western Wisconsin, was so close to the Republican picnic that attendees of both could look each other in the eyes. When protesters chanted against Tiffany’s support for Trump’s budget bill and its healthcare cuts, they were a few dozen feet away from Tiffany himself. When someone at the protest mentioned Tiffany’s support for healthcare cuts, some at the Republican picnic cheered. The county is outside the competitive third district, but similar protests have plagued Van Orden’s events and Wisconsin visits from prominent Republicans, including JD Vance. Van Orden has countered the protests by claiming the upcoming cuts, which leave people uninsured partly through work requirements and other barriers, are not cuts at all. “There has been no cuts to Medicare and Medicaid. There’s not going to be cuts to Medicare and Medicaid,” Van Orden said. “What’s going to end, though, is the rampant waste, fraud and abuse present.” Sally Rasmussen, part of the Taylor county group, said participants came together during this year’s winter mostly in response to the immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis, a few hours away. The group holds a weekly protest. They sometimes get middle fingers and obscenities, she said, but the balance has felt tipped since the start of the war with Iran. “Now we get more positives than negatives,” she said. “And I think that a lot of people that want to be Republican just say, I can’t. It was a step too far for them.” At these ambulance protests, people share their experiences of getting cut off from Medicaid or seeing their premiums rise, and healthcare providers talk about the crises they’re seeing at work. “People also are not realizing that the cuts to Medicare and Medicaid are going to eventually affect them, even if they’re not on Medicare and Medicaid,” said Teresa Kriese, a voter who lives in the third congressional district and who has spoken about her experience with a cancer clinical trial. “Because hospitals and clinics do a lot of treatments that are funded by those coverages, and if they lose that money, they’re not going to be able to survive and they’re going to close.” Kriese, 61, has lung cancer that’s spread to her brain, and there’s no approved treatment option. But she has stayed alive beyond her doctor’s initial predictions due to a clinical trial in Chicago, which was defunded in January 2024. The drug she takes is still available, so she’s still able to take it – for now. “It’s the only thing that’s kept me alive for the past three years,” she said of the trial. If she loses access to the drug, she will have to seek out another trial in a scarcer environment as Trump administration cuts to scientific research have disrupted clinical trials. Kriese felt a responsibility to share the plight of people in clinical trials, so she spoke at the Eau Claire rally against the healthcare cuts. “Clinical trials are there for everybody,” she said. “It’s not just cancer that clinical trials work for. Every single drug that you take, over-the-counter or prescription, at some point was in a clinical trial. You don’t get drugs for any other condition without clinical trials. So if we’re not funding them, that to me says this entire administration doesn’t care if we live or die.” Mark Steigerwald, a 54-year-old colon cancer survivor from Eau Claire, saw his monthly health insurance premiums nearly triple this year after Congress allowed Covid-era subsidies to run out. For the small-business owner and his wife, the monthly cost is now more than $2,700. Steigerwald recently spoke publicly about his experience at a similar Eau Claire rally against the healthcare cuts. He felt it was time to speak up because he felt “we’re crossing some lines here that we shouldn’t be”. He’s started working more hours to cover the price hike. He called private insurers to see if he could get a better price, but none would cover him due to his pre-existing condition, leaving him with the ACA marketplace. His current plan has a $13,000 deductible for him and his wife. “If you’ve ever had an illness like cancer, you’ll never be without health insurance,” he said. “That illness cost over $1m to deal with, and that was a good outcome.” A political independent, Steigerwald ranks healthcare among his top three issues when casting his vote this year. Van Orden voted to extend the subsidies, he acknowledged, but the US Senate has not taken up a vote on the extension. While the Democrats fit more with his values now, he thinks they’re struggling to come up with a platform. He’d love to see a groundswell of independents challenge the two-party system. “They’ve both been around for all this time,” he said of the Democrats and Republicans. “And all these problems are still around, and they won’t face them. Almost everybody’s responsible who’s ever been in power before. “I just want to see better responsibility for humanity.” Elsewhere in the third congressional district, deep canvassers hit the doors in Menomonie, a politically mixed town of about 17,000, where most people readily agreed to talk. One older woman said people in Washington don’t know what life is like for everyday people like her. “They don’t shop for their own groceries,” she said. A man at a different house pointed out that he sees health insurance company logos on Nascar racecars. Groww filtered out strong Democrats and strong Republicans, seeking to talk to people in the political middle, Hogseth said. The script helps show why decisions made by Congress are personally relevant to the people at the doors. Canvassers also invite locals to a summit on the topic, hoping to find people interested in organizing together long term. People don’t always move up in support for expanding BadgerCare; canvassers said they sometimes talk to people who start with zero support for expanding BadgerCare and stay there at the end. Some mention concerns over fraud in the system or believe people are taking advantage of it. Even in those tough conversations, canvassers feel they’ve planted a seed or found some places for common ground. One canvasser said the conversations renewed her hope in humanity. Another said the conversations show that people have contradictions in their views, a sign they can change their minds. “There’s a lot of people who are with us on the issue, who are either hopeless or cynical,” Hogseth said. “And they’re like, the only way things will change is if there’s a major crisis or if I move to another country. Part of what I think we need to break through with people on is their cynicism and hopelessness.”

title: Alaska candidate for US Senate rejects Kamala Harris’s unsolicited support
body_text: Alaska US Senate candidate Mary Peltola has rejected the support of Kamala Harris, her fellow Democrat, after the 2024 presidential candidate sent out a seemingly unsolicited fundraising appeal on Peltola’s behalf. Harris, who lost Alaska – typically a Republican-voting state – by 13 points during her unsuccessful White House run, on Wednesday sent an email from her political organization to supporters of Peltola, a former US House member. “If there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats – it’s Mary,” the email, which was signed “Kamala Harris”, said. “But she cannot do it alone.” It asked recipients to donate to Fight for the People Pac, which Harris set up last year. Donations would be split between Harris’s organization and Peltola, the email said. It was a fairly innocuous message and didn’t explicitly endorse Peltola. But the unwanted help was swiftly batted away by the Alaskan’s campaign. “Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 – her focus is and always will be Alaska,” a Peltola spokesperson said in a statement to KTUU that invoked a term for the contiguous US. “That’s why she’s proud to have the endorsement of [the American Federation of Government Employees], the Alaska [American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations], the Alaska [International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers] Local 1547 and more than 10,000 Alaskans who have signed up to volunteer with the campaign.” The campaign was right to be concerned because Peltola’s Republican opponent almost immediately used the email to try to tie Peltola – a moderate Democrat whose campaign has focused on Alaskan issues rather than party politics – to Harris. “Kamala Harris supported the Biden administration’s disastrous anti-Alaska agenda, which is why Alaskans rejected her by double digits,” Nate Adams, a spokesperson for the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, said in a statement. “Alaskans can see exactly whose team Mary Peltola and Kamala Harris are on, and it isn’t Alaska’s.” The episode suggests Harris remains a divisive figure within the Democratic party, even as the former vice-president weighs another run for president. Earlier this year, Harris, who also ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020, left the door open when asked about her future ambitions. “Listen, I might, I might. I’m thinking about it, I’m thinking about it,” Harris said, when US civil rights leader Al Sharpton asked if she was planning to run again. Harris replaced Joe Biden as the Democratic 2024 presidential candidate after questions and concerns about Biden’s fitness as he initially ran for re-election became inescapable. With only 107 days to run her campaign, she lost the electoral college and the popular vote to Donald Trump to hand him a second presidency.

title: Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as Trump
body_text: Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more. Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner. Or maybe not. Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps. Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next. Rubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding. This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer, Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now he toes Trump’s ingratiating line on Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, has gutted USAID and seeks to dismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, he travelled to Rome and set the pope straight. The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losing on the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy is short of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu – faces defeat in October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions. Rubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. He knows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out. The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becoming Trump’s chosen successor and heir to the Maga brand. Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump. Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

title: Trump’s midterm malaise: endless war and high prices could spell doom for Republicans in November
body_text: He was always one step ahead. Donald Trump won the US presidency as a wildly unlikely outsider in 2016 and staged an astonishing comeback to win it again in 2024. Even his foes grudgingly called him a political savant with an intuition for exploiting grievances that left so-called experts floundering. But now they are asking if the dark genius has lost his touch. Trump is trapped in the quagmire of an unpopular war, obsessing over monuments in Washington and looking for a new spokesperson after his White House press secretary quit. If the 80-year-old was deliberately trying to sabotage his Republican party in November’s midterm elections, it is not clear what he would do differently. “He’s always had a reptilian political instinct for public opinion that has served him well,” said Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster. “You’re not seeing that much any more. You’re not seeing his ability to read the room. He seems tone-deaf on issues like the cost of living, the war, and the optics of gilding everything in sight and enshittifying Washington and he doesn’t care.” Trump campaigned on promises to lower prices and keep the US out of foreign entanglements and forever wars. The opposite has happened. Voters say they are suffering a cost of living crisis, exacerbated by Trump’s sweeping tariffs. Buying food to eat at home has become 33% more expensive in US cities since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures. Gas prices are at a record high for this time of year, in part thanks to the US war in Iran, which drags on with no end in sight. While Trump claims to have destroyed Iran’s military capabilities, it emerged this week that he was forced to hide in a catering truck and secretly swap planes after a Nato summit in Turkey because of a possible Iranian assassination plot. The administration’s entanglement has metastasised into a gruelling, daily haemorrhage of resources, currently costing the taxpayer an estimated $1bn a day. Critics argue the administration has strengthened Iran’s resolve and provided it with global leverage, specifically over the strait of Hormuz. They see it as betrayal of the noninterventionist posture that fuelled Trump’s rise to power and attracted a generation of disaffected voters. Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “What we’re watching right now is the complete unraveling of everything that Donald Trump, Maga and Republicans said they were about. They were against endless conflicts in the Middle East and they started a conflict in the Middle East without an exit strategy. They were supposed to be about no more spending American dollars abroad; we’re spending a billion dollars a day on this war without an end.” Yet the president appears to have other, more aesthetic concerns. Since returning to power last year, the longtime property developer has invested much time and energy in construction projects across Washington, including a White House ballroom and helipad, a triumphal arch and an ill-fated makeover of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. Bardella added: “As he continues this misadventure in the Middle East that has resulted in the cost of living going up, and continues to pour resources into putting his name on shit and building ballrooms and monuments to himself, the American people are going: what the fuck? That’s the only realistic reaction you could have when you objectively look at the circumstances.” Trump’s second term has been defined by thinking big – Greenland, Venezuela, Iran – and thinking small. The board he appointed to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts added his name to the complex, only for a judge to order that it be removed; this week the board voted to add “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump” beneath the main sign. According to Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, written by New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, the president has been seen with a tube of super glue trying to stick golden decorations to the marble fireplace in the Oval Office. Haberman estimates that Trump now devotes 70% of his mental space to renovation projects and “monuments to self”. She told Axios’s Behind the Curtain video series that she and Swan visited Trump in the Oval Office in March. “You would think that on the 17th day of the war that he would have maps of the Middle East or maps of troop deployments – who knows,” she said. “He picks up these pictures, and [they’re] of maple trees, and he says: ‘I am choosing maple trees for the White House. I am good at picking trees.’ I’m paraphrasing here, but that is pretty much what he said.” The president’s preoccupation with whether columns for his ballroom are more evocative of Athens or Rome, and with other efforts to preserve his legacy in marble, come as little surprise to Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill and longtime Trump critic. She said: “Donald Trump has been an egomaniac, a narcissist his entire life. Even in the private sector he has slapped his name on buildings and a multitude of failed branding businesses from Trump steaks to Trump airline to Trump University to Trump water to Trump wine. Why is anyone surprised that he would take that same type of narcissism and bring it over to his role in his second-term as president when he’s spending other people’s money to do it? “The problem has been that the Republican party has enabled him to get away with this and to their own detriment, which is why more and more people in his inner circle are concerned about how this is going to impact the midterms and control of Congress.” Indeed, Republicans are said to be quietly panicking about Trump costing them the House of Representatives and putting even the Senate in jeopardy. A national Quinnipiac University Poll released late last month showed his job approval rating dropping to an all-time low of 32%, with 58% disapproval. It found six in 10 Americans oppose the US military action in Iran. Past presidents such as George W Bush in 2006 and Barack Obama in 2010 have faced challenging midterms but worked with their parties in an effort to at least stem the losses. Rick Wilson, co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, said: “In both those cases their efforts were not successful, but it’s nightmarish to think what that would have been if Barack Obama had been saying, ‘I’m going to build a basketball arena at the White House,’ or George Bush had said, ‘I’m gonna build a golf course.’ “Instead you’ve got a very different visual from this White House and that visual is 'we don’t care about anything else except for the ballroom and the arch and all the throw-away ephemera that he wants to focus on. It’s a terrible political look and it’s quite dangerous for the party because they have nothing to run on right now.” The sense of malaise deepened this week when Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary, announced that she will be stepping down at the end of the month. The official explanation was that the 28-year-old wants to spend more time with her young family but the timing was unfortunate for an administration struggling to spin its way out of one crisis after another. For a president whose entire self-image is built on winning, the realisation that he is facing electoral defeat at home and humiliation abroad could be cause for an existential crisis. Sykes observed that, while Trump’s historical literacy is notoriously thin, he has begun to obsess over the ghosts of presidencies ruined by foreign blunders. “It’s awfully interesting that in the Maggie Haberman book he’s comparing himself to Napoleon and Alexander the Great and Caesar but his deepest fear right now is that he’s going to be Herbert Hoover or Jimmy Carter,” he said. Trump’s cloud does have a golden lining, however. He made an estimated $2.2bn during the first year of his second term thanks to cryptocurrency holdings, foreign interests and his Truth Social business. Sykes added: “He hasn’t lowered the cost of living, he hasn’t made America more respected, he hasn’t won the war but he has succeeded in making himself a billionaire many times over by abusing his office.”

title: Why cancer, not cost of living, may be the biggest issue in Iowa’s midterm elections
body_text: In Iowa, one of the key battleground states in November’s midterm elections, just about every political candidate agrees on one thing: something must be done about the state’s rising rates of cancer. The midwestern state has the second-highest rate of cancer nationwide and, together with Utah and West Virginia, is one of only three states where the incidence of the disease is rising, according to cancer rate monitoring from the National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities. Promises to address the issue are now top of mind for candidates ahead of the 3 November elections, in which Iowa may play an important role in deciding control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. Republicans hoping to preserve their party’s dominance of the state and Democrats who believe conditions are right for them to win key races have pledged to make fighting the disease a priority. Where they differ is in their views over the degree to which the state’s powerhouse farm economy has contributed to making Iowans sick, and what to do about it. “I think state leadership and industrial agriculture are very hesitant to have those conversations, but I think the Iowa public is calling and demanding action and conversation and answers in a way that both parties are needing to respond, and [that’s] why it has become the campaign issue of this upcoming election,” said Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council, a non-partisan group whose research into the disease’s prevalence has helped fuel public awareness of the crisis. Iowa’s cancer rates followed national trends until 2012, when they began climbing upwards for reasons that Green said remain unclear. Cancer includes a broad group of diseases, and many aspects of life, from stress to food to environment, can modify someone’s risk. What’s plain is the importance to voters – one survey has cancer ranked as the top issue facing the state, eclipsing even the cost of living. In the race for the state’s open US Senate seat, Democrat Josh Turek whose spina bifida he attributes to his father’s exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam war, has brought up his sister’s struggle with breast cancer, while his opponent, the Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson, has emphasized her attempts to reform health policy in Washington. Candidates of both parties vying for the state’s four Republican-held US House districts have battled over who would be better suited to channel federal resources to the state’s needs. In the race to replace the incumbent governor, Kim Reynolds, Zach Lahn won an upset victory in the Republican primary with the support of a Pac connected to the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, and both he and his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, have unveiled lengthy plans to curb rates of the disease. “The road I live on, I think there’s only one family that has not dealt with some kind of cancer,” said Seth Watkins, a longtime farmer in south-west Iowa who sees the emphasis on fighting the disease – and potentially changing the state’s approach to agriculture – as long overdue. “We have a farm policy that has resulted in less soil, less biodiversity in wild species, more cancer, fewer farmers and fewer opportunities. I mean, at some point, wouldn’t people just look at that data and say, you know, maybe we should do something different?” ‘Taboo’ conversations Iowa is the top producer of corn and pork in the US and one of the largest growers of soy, and agriculture generates a third of the state’s economic output and a fifth of its jobs. But that immense productivity comes at a cost: Iowa’s farmers use more fertilizer than those of any other state, and it also leads in the number of concentrated animal feeding operations (Cafos), which are part of the meat processing supply chain and generate runoff. Green pointed out that Iowa also had relatively few regulations intended to keep pesticides and farm runoff, which can be heavy with cancer-linked nitrates, away from people and out of water supplies. In 2022, Iowa’s overall rate of cancer was approximately 506 cases per 100,000 people, higher than the national average of 442 per 100,000 people, according to National Institutes of Health data. It also has elevated rates of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and acute myeloid leukemia, two cancers that some studies have found may be linked to glyphosate, the herbicide marketed as Roundup that is the most used in the state. Agriculture’s impact on Iowans has recently become pronounced, even for people that have nothing to do with farming. Some Iowa waterways are among the most polluted by nitrates in the US, and last year the water utility serving Des Moines, the state’s capital and largest city, announced its first-ever lawn watering ban because levels of the compounds in the rivers from which it draws its water supply had hit near-record levels. The utility ordered water rationed again this summer. When the Iowa Environmental Council last year dispatched researchers across the midwestern state to learn more about how cancer was affecting its residents, Green said talking about the link with agriculture was often regarded as a “taboo”. “Iowans knew there were issues, but felt like they were not supported by their state and by elected officials in, one, hearing their stories, and then two, addressing and recognizing real challenges that Iowans are experiencing a health crisis,” said Green, whose group convened the 16 listening sessions together with the Iowa Farmers Union and Drake University’s Harkin Institute, a public policy thinktank. There are other factors connected to cancer diagnoses in Iowa – its residents face a higher risk of exposure to naturally occurring radon, and this year the state legislature approved a law mandating that mitigation systems be installed in new homes. Under Reynolds, the state has also sought to curb alcohol and tobacco use, and in June the GOP-dominated legislature approved a $320m investment in water quality. But Green said that measure offered relatively little new funding and “doesn’t address pollution at the source”. The gubernatorial candidates Lahn and Sand came out against a June supreme court ruling making it more difficult for people who believe they contracted cancer from exposure to Roundup to sue its manufacturer. The Republican Lahn’s campaign platform has largely focused on incentivizing farmers to change their ways to prevent water pollution, while accusing major chemical manufacturers of misleading Iowans about their products’ safety. “We all know something is terribly wrong, but too many politicians from Washington DC to Des Moines have had their heads stuck in the sand while big ag and big pharma printed money. This will not go on when I’m governor,” Lahn said after winning the nomination in June. His Democratic opponent, Sand, has called cancer “the top issue on everyone’s mind no matter what part of the state I’m in, and rightfully so”, and proposed measures to better manage farmers’ use of manure, test for radon and help farms enroll in conservation programs. Neither has as aggressive a platform as Chris Jones, the Democratic candidate for state agriculture secretary. A former University of Iowa researcher, he wrote a popular blog that explored the state’s water quality issues, but stopped writing it after, he told the Iowa Capital Dispatch, two Republican state senators threatened the university’s funding over his writings. One of the lawmakers denied the allegations, and Jones later left the school. Jones is proposing a wholesale transformation of the state’s approach to farming to reduce its impact on water quality. His platform includes zoning changes to address the environmental effects of Cafos and a “strategic retreat” from growing corn for ethanol, a top cash crop for the state’s farmers. “We know radon is a driver of lung cancer here. Well, guess what? We have policies to help reduce exposure to radon,” Jone said. “The same could be said for nitrate and drinking water. Let’s develop policies that reduce that risk.” The incumbent agriculture secretary, Mike Naig, a Republican and former lobbyist for Monsanto, the manufacturer of Roundup that’s now part of Bayer, did not respond to an interview request sent to his campaign. ‘The Lobe Rangers’ Some farmers aren’t waiting for the election results to change their agricultural practices. Last March, three farmers in north-central Iowa announced themselves as “the Lobe Rangers”, unveiling a website complete with a logo of a masked man standing amid the corn in which they made their case for how it is possible to farm profitably without harming themselves or the environment.. “This has been boiling underneath the surface for me for 15 years, and the reason I think we launched is that we just kind of had enough. We saw the inaction of the political class and the ag lobbying leadership class of putting up the same nonsense,” said Zack Smith, a corn and soybean farmer who is one of the rangers. The group – which took its name from a particularly fertile part of the state called the Des Moines lobe – follows the state’s nutrient-reduction strategy, a blueprint to keep nitrates out of the state’s waterways and the far-off Gulf of Mexico that’s only voluntary, but which the rangers insist works. Watkins, who works land his great-grandfather first cultivated in 1848, has in recent years downsized what was once a 4,000-acre (1,600-hectare) farm, helping younger farmers grow diversified crops on smaller plots of land. The change in tack follows more than three decades of Watkins farming at scale and growing more disillusioned by an industry that depends heavily on federal subsidies while exacting a worsening toll on the environment. “I feel like we’re mining instead of practicing agriculture. And, you know, show me an area, whether it’s the oil industry or mining or any of that, where when the resources are gone, the people are better off,” Watkins said. Watching the state’s political class focus on cancer, and by extension, water quality, had been a curious experience, since it had been a concern of theirs for more than a decade, said Smith. title: Todd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White House
body_text: US attorney general Todd Blanche on Sunday declined to assure that the federal justice department he helms would always act independently of the White House and Donald Trump. “No, I’m not going to pledge that,” he said when asked about the topic by NBC’s Meet the Press host, Kristen Welker. “And no attorney general should ever pledge that.” Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crosses an ethical or legal line – after the president dismissed his predecessor, Pam Bondi, having become frustrated over insufficient action from the justice department against Trump’s political foes. “The president will never ask me to do something unethical or legal or illegal,” Blanche told Welker. “He never has. He never will. And no, I have – I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done. “And so, this narrative that’s mostly pushed by the left and pushed by the media that the president’s going to pull me aside and ask me to do something illegal is completely a false narrative, not true, will not happen and hasn’t happened.” In response to his demurring on the questions of always acting independently of the White House, Barb McQuade, a University of Michigan law professor, wrote on social media that Blanche’s stated position was “an appalling departure” from the justice department’s mission after the Watergate scandal that prompted Richard Nixon to resign from the presidency in 1974. The justice department, “as we once knew it, is no more”, McQuade wrote. “Blanche has turned it into Trump’s private law firm. What a complete disgrace.” Blanche’s comments to Welker on Sunday came days after he was only narrowly confirmed by the US Senate in a 50-49 vote to succeed Bondi, with all Democrats voting against him. He previously served as Trump’s criminal defense lawyer when a New York state jury convicted Trump between his two presidencies of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in connection with payments to adult film star Stormy Daniels. In April, Blanche said he would tell Trump, “I love you, sir,” if the president decided to fire him and nominate someone else to replace Bondi. Blanche, meanwhile, in December defended moving Ghislaine Maxwell, the convicted child sexual trafficker and Jeffrey Epstein associate, to a minimum-security prison. And Blanche has also continued facing scrutiny over his handling of the so-called Epstein files and his treatment of those victimized by the sex-trafficking network built by Epstein. While speaking with Welker on Sunday, Blanche also defended Trump’s pardoning of 1,500 supporters who were convicted of attacking the US Capitol toward the end of his first presidency in early 2021. “I’m not opining or in any way saying what President Trump did was wrong,” Blanche said when asked about the pardons, which included more than 170 people who pleaded guilty to assaulting police officers. “That is the president’s right.” Blanche declined to say whether any of the pardoned attackers might still receive settlements from the federal government – though they attorney general also claimed a $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund for allies whom Trump considered to be unfairly prosecuted was dead. “Well, anybody can file a claim against the federal government, not just anybody associated with [the Capitol attack],” Blanche said. “I’m not going to sit here and say on a news program whether a litigation that may or may not happen will result in money. I can’t do that.” He also affirmed the justice department would not drop “election integrity” efforts despite more than 20 consecutive court defeats connected to efforts to try to force states to turn over voter rolls ahead of the midterm elections in November, when the president’s Republican party is projected to lose seats in Congress and favored to lose the majority in the US House.
