title: Republican senator denounces Trump’s ‘crazy, stupid’ claims about MMR vaccine safety
body_text: The Republican senator Bill Cassidy – a medical doctor who voted to confirm anti-vaccine activist Robert F Kennedy as federal health secretary in early 2025 – on Sunday denounced Donald Trump’s “crazy, stupid” claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine for undermining faith in immunization. When Trump recently ordered changes to the recommended childhood vaccination schedule, with Kennedy by his side, the president called for two shots of the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to be scrapped in favor of two doses of three separate vaccines, claiming that the MMR shots are “sort of like a nuclear weapon” that could be “quite lethal”. Cassidy, whose re-election bid ended in defeat to a Trump-backed challenger in a Republican primary in Louisiana, has been on the president’s enemies list since 2021, when the senator voted to convict him of “incitement of insurrection” in connection with the US Capitol attack carried out by Trump supporters toward the end of his first presidency. Asked about Trump’s comment that “nothing bad can happen” from advising parents to get six separate shots for their children, instead of two, Cassidy told CNN on Sunday: “If it wasn’t so potentially tragic, you would break out laughing at a comment like that. “Let’s just take it from the perspective of the parent: now instead of going to the doctor twice to get their child vaccinated, they have to go six times. Instead of the child getting two jabs, they get six jabs,” he continued. “Instead of the insurance company paying for two doctor’s visits, they’re paying for six, which is going to ultimately drive up premiums … “So the president is wrong; there’s a lot of bad things that will come out of this.” Cassidy’s critics have lambasted the outgoing senator for expressing misgivings about Trump’s actions, including a recent shouting match over the ongoing Iran war – but continuing to cast crucial votes to confirm the president’s nominees. He cast the decisive vote on 8 August that allowed Todd Blanche – a former criminal defense lawyer for Trump – to secure Senate confirmation as US attorney general. When Cassidy, the chair of the Senate health committee, previously announced that he would vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, he acknowledged that “the most notable opponents of Mr Kennedy were pediatricians on the frontlines of our children’s health who regularly have to combat misinformation; combating vaccine skepticism with correct information – correct information that comes from their education, training and experience as physicians.” Cassidy also revealed that he had extracted a promise from Kennedy, who has pushed the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism for decades, that “CDC will not remove statements on their website pointing out that vaccines do not cause autism”. After Kennedy became health secretary, however, the “Autism and Vaccines” page on the CDC website was altered to undermine that scientific consensus. An asterisk was added to the headline “Vaccines do not cause Autism”, which leads to a footnote pointing out that “the root causes of autism” remain unknown. Text was also added to the top of the same page, so that anyone who searches for CDC guidance on autism and vaccines is now presented with two “key points” that further appease vaccine skeptics and conspiracy theorists. “The claim ‘vaccines do not cause autism’ is not an evidence-based claim because studies have not ruled out the possibility that infant vaccines cause autism,” the first key point reads. The second addition, since one of the nation’s leading anti-vaccine activists took charge, suggests that the lack of evidence for a link between vaccines and autism could be the result of a conspiracy. “Studies supporting a link have been ignored by health authorities,” the CDC site now claims. Cassidy on Sunday told CNN that Trump’s MMR commentary “will do nothing” to address the discredited link between vaccine and autism stemming from a single paper that was ultimately retracted.

title: Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions
body_text: For decades, Donald Trump cultivated a public image based on strength and dominance. He was a brash New York real estate mogul; a reality TV star who deployed his signature phrase: “You’re fired!” to eliminate contestants from The Apprentice; and eventually US president and undisputed leader of the Republican party. In recent months, Trump has taken his boastfulness to an extreme, reportedly telling confidants that he’s “the most powerful person to ever live” and comparing himself with some of history’s most feared leaders, including Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin and Mao. But recent revelations have threatened to shatter Trump’s image as a strongman: the US president departed on a secret military flight out of Turkey after attending a Nato summit, while the White House told the public he was flying onboard Air Force One. The operation involved an elaborate ruse in which Trump boarded his jumbo jet in view of TV cameras, and then was hustled out by the Secret Service through an airport catering truck. Trump was taken to an alternate military aircraft, which flew him to Britain – all unbeknown to journalists and several White House staff members who stayed on Air Force One and thought they were on the same plane as the president. The embarrassing necessity was a result of Trump’s unnecessary war against Iran. US officials used such levels of subterfuge because they were worried about an Iranian assassination attempt against Trump, according to reports in the Washington Post and New York Times. On 11 August, Trump confirmed that he had secretly switched planes in Turkey, and attributed the decision to his protective detail and military advisers. “I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump told reporters who asked why US officials had used such an intricate ploy and kept the public in the dark about it until the story was leaked. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane. Equal safety. But they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say.” Trump tried to evade criticism that the decision left several cabinet members and senior White House officials – including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary; Stephen Miller, Trump’s top domestic adviser; and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director – on Air Force One to serve as decoys, along with other Trump staffers and journalists. To deflect more questions, Trump claimed, without providing evidence, that the secret military plane he flew on was actually at “greater risk” than the Air Force One jet that the world saw him board after the Nato summit. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he said. It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse after the danger had passed, as past presidents had done when they used subterfuge to visit war zones and other hazardous locations. The image of Trump hiding in an airport catering container to avoid a potential Iranian assassination attempt is a stark contrast to the tough guy brand he spent years cultivating. It’s also an antithesis to the image Trump projected after he survived an assassination attempt at a presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In a series of photos captured by news photographers at the scene, Trump raised his fist in the air and mouthed the words: “Fight, fight, fight” to supporters as he was rushed off stage by Secret Service agents, bleeding from his ear. One image in particular, showing a bloodied Trump pumping his fist with a US flag in the background, became iconic – and his campaign quickly tried to monetize it by using the photo on the cover of a book and to sell $299 Trump-branded sneakers. Beyond the dueling imagery, the fact that Trump took refuge in a catering truck has deeper political implications. It encapsulates Trump’s failure in his war on Iran: a president who constantly boasts about US military prowess and tries to project personal strength instead appears weak in front of the world as he hides from the consequences of his own actions. Nearly six months ago, Trump launched his reckless war against Iran as an act of imperial hubris – and a culmination of a series of lawless acts since he returned to office in 2025. With little resistance from the Republican-controlled Congress or the US supreme court, Trump was able to gut government agencies, use federal law enforcement to target his political enemies, appoint his loyalists as top prosecutors, deploy national guard troops into US cities, and weaken decades-old anti-corruption laws designed to constrain presidential power after the Watergate scandal. He also steamrolled over Congress and its authority to declare war. In late February, when the US and Israel launched a series of devastating airstrikes against Iran, Trump had expansive goals: to destroy Tehran’s military capabilities and nuclear program, and to topple Iran’s theocratic regime by decimating its leadership and instigating a popular uprising. In the war’s early days, the US and Israel assassinated more than 30 senior Iranian military and political officials, including the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. But the Iranian system proved resilient and it quickly replaced those officials, partly by appointing Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader, to ensure continuity. Iran also turned its proximity to the strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which more than a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed each day, into an effective economic weapon. Tehran closed the passageway at the start of the war, increasing energy prices and disrupting the global economy. Since then, Trump has struggled to reach a deal with Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz and prevent the war from spiraling into a regional conflict that could cause severe economic damage. For months, Trump has tried to negotiate a face-saving agreement that would allow him to declare victory and shift US public attention away from the war before midterm elections in November that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. Iran’s leaders and Trump both say they don’t trust the other side to abide by any agreement – and a memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, which included reopening the strait of Hormuz and lifting a US naval blockade against Iranian ships in the region, has collapsed. Since then, tit-for-tat attacks by Iran and the US have rekindled fears of another all-out war. Not surprisingly, Iranian officials and state media are reveling in the extensive media attention over Trump secretly switching planes in Turkey – and especially the detail about him being ushered into an airport catering truck. A presenter on Iranian state TV called it a “scandal stemming from fear of Iran’s military power”, and described the incident as a source of “humiliation” for the US president. It will take time for Trump to undo the damage this ruse has done to his self-proclaimed image as a strong and dominant world leader. More importantly, his disastrous decision to launch a war against Iran will shape his legacy long after he leaves office. Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University
cleaned_body_text: For decades, Donald Trump cultivated a public image based on strength and dominance. He was a brash New York real estate mogul; a reality TV star who deployed his signature phrase: “You’re fired!” to eliminate contestants from The Apprentice; and eventually US president and undisputed leader of the Republican party. In recent months, Trump has taken his boastfulness to an extreme, reportedly telling confidants that he’s “the most powerful person to ever live” and comparing himself with some of history’s most feared leaders, including Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin and Mao. But recent revelations have threatened to shatter Trump’s image as a strongman: the US president departed on a secret military flight out of Turkey after attending a Nato summit, while the White House told the public he was flying onboard Air Force One. The operation involved an elaborate ruse in which Trump boarded his jumbo jet in view of TV cameras, and then was hustled out by the Secret Service through an airport catering truck. Trump was taken to an alternate military aircraft, which flew him to Britain – all unbeknown to journalists and several White House staff members who stayed on Air Force One and thought they were on the same plane as the president. The embarrassing necessity was a result of Trump’s unnecessary war against Iran. US officials used such levels of subterfuge because they were worried about an Iranian assassination attempt against Trump, according to reports in the Washington Post and New York Times. On 11 August, Trump confirmed that he had secretly switched planes in Turkey, and attributed the decision to his protective detail and military advisers. “I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump told reporters who asked why US officials had used such an intricate ploy and kept the public in the dark about it until the story was leaked. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane. Equal safety. But they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say.” Trump tried to evade criticism that the decision left several cabinet members and senior White House officials – including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary; Stephen Miller, Trump’s top domestic adviser; and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director – on Air Force One to serve as decoys, along with other Trump staffers and journalists. To deflect more questions, Trump claimed, without providing evidence, that the secret military plane he flew on was actually at “greater risk” than the Air Force One jet that the world saw him board after the Nato summit. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he said. It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse after the danger had passed, as past presidents had done when they used subterfuge to visit war zones and other hazardous locations. The image of Trump hiding in an airport catering container to avoid a potential Iranian assassination attempt is a stark contrast to the tough guy brand he spent years cultivating. It’s also an antithesis to the image Trump projected after he survived an assassination attempt at a presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In a series of photos captured by news photographers at the scene, Trump raised his fist in the air and mouthed the words: “Fight, fight, fight” to supporters as he was rushed off stage by Secret Service agents, bleeding from his ear. One image in particular, showing a bloodied Trump pumping his fist with a US flag in the background, became iconic – and his campaign quickly tried to monetize it by using the photo on the cover of a book and to sell $299 Trump-branded sneakers. Beyond the dueling imagery, the fact that Trump took refuge in a catering truck has deeper political implications. It encapsulates Trump’s failure in his war on Iran: a president who constantly boasts about US military prowess and tries to project personal strength instead appears weak in front of the world as he hides from the consequences of his own actions. Nearly six months ago, Trump launched his reckless war against Iran as an act of imperial hubris – and a culmination of a series of lawless acts since he returned to office in 2025. With little resistance from the Republican-controlled Congress or the US supreme court, Trump was able to gut government agencies, use federal law enforcement to target his political enemies, appoint his loyalists as top prosecutors, deploy national guard troops into US cities, and weaken decades-old anti-corruption laws designed to constrain presidential power after the Watergate scandal. He also steamrolled over Congress and its authority to declare war. In late February, when the US and Israel launched a series of devastating airstrikes against Iran, Trump had expansive goals: to destroy Tehran’s military capabilities and nuclear program, and to topple Iran’s theocratic regime by decimating its leadership and instigating a popular uprising. In the war’s early days, the US and Israel assassinated more than 30 senior Iranian military and political officials, including the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. But the Iranian system proved resilient and it quickly replaced those officials, partly by appointing Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader, to ensure continuity. Iran also turned its proximity to the strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which more than a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed each day, into an effective economic weapon. Tehran closed the passageway at the start of the war, increasing energy prices and disrupting the global economy. Since then, Trump has struggled to reach a deal with Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz and prevent the war from spiraling into a regional conflict that could cause severe economic damage. For months, Trump has tried to negotiate a face-saving agreement that would allow him to declare victory and shift US public attention away from the war before midterm elections in November that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. Iran’s leaders and Trump both say they don’t trust the other side to abide by any agreement – and a memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, which included reopening the strait of Hormuz and lifting a US naval blockade against Iranian ships in the region, has collapsed. Since then, tit-for-tat attacks by Iran and the US have rekindled fears of another all-out war. Not surprisingly, Iranian officials and state media are reveling in the extensive media attention over Trump secretly switching planes in Turkey – and especially the detail about him being ushered into an airport catering truck. A presenter on Iranian state TV called it a “scandal stemming from fear of Iran’s military power”, and described the incident as a source of “humiliation” for the US president. It will take time for Trump to undo the damage this ruse has done to his self-proclaimed image as a strong and dominant world leader. More importantly, his disastrous decision to launch a war against Iran will shape his legacy long after he leaves office. Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

title: A tale of two Dan Sullivans: Republicans with same name contest Alaska primary
body_text: Dan J Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee living in the town of Petersburg in south-eastern Alaska, who is running as a Republican for the US Senate. Dan S Sullivan is a Republican US senator, who has represented Alaska since 2015. Both candidates will appear on the ballot, one name after the other, when Alaskans vote in primary elections this week – a complicated quirk of the contest that has drawn howls from Republicans. But the incumbent senator’s real threat, Alaska politics watchers say, is Mary Peltola, a Democrat who managed to twice win election to the state’s seat in the US House of Representatives, and is now vying tobeat him in November’s midterm elections in the US Senate. The Tuesday vote in the non-partisan primary will see four candidates advance to the general election for the seat in November. Though no Democrat has been elected to the US Senate from Alaska since 2008, the party believes Peltola is the right candidate to flip the seat, and her victory would put Democrats well on their way to retaking control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. “The reason Mary Peltola has a chance is not because, necessarily, Democrats are surging in Alaska,” said Scott Kendall, an election law attorney who has worked for candidates of both parties, including the senator Sullivan. “It’s that Mary Peltola, you know, she’s very pro-oil and gas development. She’s good on issues that matter to Alaskans’ pocketbooks, and that makes her just a bit of a unicorn.” The largest state in the union but physically separated from the lower 48, Alaska has unique politics. With an economy heavily reliant on oil and gas production, the state’s Democrats tend to advocate for expanded production, in contrast with their counterparts elsewhere, who are concerned about fossil fuels’ role in driving the climate crisis. While Alaska has only once voted for a Democrat in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson, in 1964 – power has oscillated between the two parties at the state level, and bipartisan coalitions today control both the state house and senate. Independents make up two-thirds of registered voters and Republicans about 23%, while fewer than 12% of Alaskans are Democrats. Sullivan won election in 2014 after beating the first-term Democratic senator Mark Begich, and has been a reliable Republican vote in his two terms, hewing much closer to his party’s agenda than the state’s senior Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, who has grown prominent nationwide for repeatedly bucking Trump. Peltola cracked the GOP’s dominance of the state’s federal delegation in 2022 when Don Young, the Republican who had represented the state’s at-large US House district since 1973, died suddenly. She triumphed in the special election to finish his term, becoming the first Alaska Native ever to serve in Congress, and won a full term later that year. In 2024, Republican Nick Begich III narrowly defeated her bid for re-election. Alaska voted for Trump by more than 13 percentage points that year, but Peltola is viewed as Democrats’ best bet for the Senate race in one of a handful of red states the party is targeting to win back a majority in the upper chamber. Seeking to prove that she can better advocate for the state’s specific interests and needs in Washington, Peltola has put her moderate brand of politics at the center of her campaign. Her slogan “fish, family, freedom” is a nod both to the cultural importance of fishing in Alaska – and especially to its native communities, which form a potent political bloc – and to the issue of bycatch, whereby trawlers pick up valuable catches like crab and salmon in their nets, harming sport and commercial fishers alike. “Fish has always been, really, a passion issue in Alaska,” said Joelle Hall, president of the Alaska AFL-CIO, which has endorsed Peltola. Hall credited the former congresswoman with making the issue of bycatch and the health of the fishing industry in general more prominent in the state’s politics. During her time in the House of Representatives, Peltola advocated for Joe Biden to approve Willow, one of the biggest oil and gas developments in decades. The decision raised the hackles of environmentalists for its potential to drive global heating, but Hall describes it as huge for unionized workers. “We are also in the middle of a little bit of an oil and gas boom in Alaska,” said Hall. “That’s because Mary Peltola brought us the Willow project with the Biden administration.” Peltola may be further boosted by national trends breaking in Democrats’ favor. Trump’s approval ratings are low in the state as they are nationwide, while gas prices in Alaska have shot up since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, and are now among the highest nationwide. Polls have recently found the two candidates neck-and-neck before the November election, and major election forecasters view Sullivan’s re-election bid as a toss-up. A former marine who served as the state’s attorney general and natural resources commissioner, Dan S Sullivan has emphasized his focus on military affairs in a state with a large number of bases and veterans, as well as his own efforts to preserve the state’s fisheries. Steve Frank, a Republican former state senator, said that despite Peltola’s efforts to see Willow approved, he believed Sullivan would be a more reliable advocate for the state’s economically vital oil industry, especially with the presidential administration set to change in another two years. “The federal government views us kind of like a colony, and they forget that we’re American citizens trying to earn a living up here,” said Frank, referencing moves by the Biden administration to protect tracts of Alaska land and water from oil drilling. “And so they tend to want to lock us up, keep us from developing our resources, and so he’s pushing back against that.” The race has seen major spending, with the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund announcing it will put $17m towards helping Sullivan, while the Democrats’ Senate Majority Pac invested $12m into backing Peltola. Federal Election Commission filings until the end of July show Peltola has outraised Sullivan, bringing in $18.5m to his $11.7m, with $4.6m on hand compared with the Republican’s $7.3m. Meanwhile, OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, reported that two Super Pacs (political action committees) have spent a combined nearly $2m in Alaska recently to back other candidates who could syphon votes from both Peltola and Sullivan. Also on the ballot in Tuesday’s election will be Nick Begich III, who is vying for a second term against independent Bill Hill, the main challenger for the House seat after Democrat Matt Schultz dropped out and endorsed him. Alaskans will also select candidates to replace governor Mike Dunleavy, the Republican incumbent who is barred by term limits from seeking re-election. Dan J Sullivan of Petersburg, Alaska, who did not respond to a request for comment, is listed just above the senator among the 16 names running for Senate, though Dan S Sullivan has “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name. The GOP went to court to boot Dan J Sullivan from the race, arguing that he was a “sham” contender propped up by Democrats to confuse voters and undermine Senator Sullivan, but were unsuccessful. Though it’s a marquee race of this year’s US Senate elections, when it comes to Alaska-specific issues, Kendall predicted there may wind up being less daylight than would be expected between Peltola and Sullivan on Alaska-specific issues. “I think she would probably frustrate a lot of Democrats, if I’m being honest. I think she would be, to national Democrats, what Lisa Murkowski is to national Republicans,” said Kendall. “There’ll be a moment where a Democratic president says something like: ‘Well, I want to turn this huge swath of Alaska into a wilderness preserve, no hunting, no fishing, no development,’” he suggested. “She’s going to balk at that.”

title: Jon Ossoff calls Trump’s handling of Iran war ‘uniquely despicable’ in excoriating speech
body_text: Democratic senator Jon Ossoff has attacked Donald Trump’s “uniquely despicable” handling of the US-Israel war on Iran, accusing the US president of “re-rigging” a corrupt system for himself in an excoriating speech. Ossoff, who is running for re-election in Georgia in November, has repeatedly stoked speculation that he is laying the ground for a bid for the US presidency in 2028 by delivering a series of stinging attacks on Trump and his administration. “They made you pay more for everything, and took us to war on lies, and spent most of last year trying to cover up for the world’s most famous pedophile while the crook president and his crook family raked in billions while your tax dollars were put to work backing Trump’s businesses,” Ossoff said at a rally in midtown Atlanta on Sunday afternoon. He pointed to the US sailors enduring a record-setting deployment of nearly nine months onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, amid mounting concern over conditions and mental health issues onboard the aircraft carrier, whom Trump suggested last week had not been deployed “nearly long enough”. “While the sailors on the Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings,” Ossoff said. “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the amir of Qatar.” Ossoff appears to have been referring to Natalie Harp, Trump’s executive assistant, who has drawn scrutiny on social media for her perceived closeness to the US president. It emerged last week that Harp accompanied the president when he left Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent and other key officials on a decoy plane as they left Turkey under threat of Iranian attack in July. Stump speeches like the one he delivered on Sunday, with plain, sharp language well-tailored for social media, have become a staple of Ossoff’s campaign. “They’ve lied non-stop about this war like they lie about everything. And they know they’re lying, but they lie and they keep lying anyway because in this White House, they view persistence in deceit as a virtue,” the senator said. “And there’s something uniquely despicable about lying a nation into war, treating citizens as fools and those who serve as pawns.” Early voting begins in eight weeks in Georgia, and Ossoff has maintained a lead well above the margins for error in polling above the Republican nominee, US representative Mike Collins. But Ossoff has framed his campaign as something more than a referendum on his term in office, raising broader questions about Americans’ tolerance for corruption. “Corruption in American politics runs a lot deeper than Donald Trump,” Ossoff said, pointing to what he called the “coin-operated” politics of political action committees. “Trump promised to attack a broken system. I get it. Right target. Yes, the system is really rigged. But he’s not unrigging it. He’s re-rigging it for himself.” Ossoff’s personal wealth is held in a blind trust. He has pursued a ban on stock trading by members of US Congress and their families as a signature political issue. The Ending Trading and Holdings In Congressional Stocks Act passed out of the preliminary committee stage in July 2024, but has not been put to a vote in the Republican-controlled US Senate. Ossoff also highlighted the vast increase in Trump’s personal wealth since he returned to office in January 2025. “When he first announced the tariffs, you remember that? He called it liberation day and it crashed the markets because it was clown policy,” Ossoff said, noting how the president then purchased stock a week after the markets fell. “And then the very next morning, April 9th, he posts on Truth Social. ‘This is a great time to buy.’ Three exclamation marks. “OK, now listen to this. Three hours and 41 minutes after that post, one day after he bought millions in stock, he cancelled the tariffs and triggered one of the biggest same day rebound rallies in market history. He’s trying to get money.” Trump launched a subscription service on 1 August charging up to $100,000 a month for early access to his posts on his Truth Social platform. The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation have launched a suit against Trump, two of his aides and the executive office of the president over the service. Ossoff attacked the president over the offering. “Just understand what’s for sale here,” he said. “The sitting president’s pronouncements on war and peace and economic policy delivered first to paying customers. What an absolute crook.”

title: Election denier Tina Peters to be hired as elections consultant in conservative California county
body_text: A northern California county that has become a hotbed of activism for those who sow doubts about the reliability of voting machines plans to hire Tina Peters, the prominent Colorado election denier recently released from prison, to work on elections. Clint Curtis, the top election official in Shasta county, told the Guardian he plans to hire Peters as a consultant to replace Brent Turner, his top deputy, who has been on medical leave. He said Peters would not have access to the county’s voting system and did not directly respond when asked what her responsibilities would be. Plans to hire Peters, who is still on parole and must receive permission to travel outside Colorado, were first reported by Action News Now. Shasta county, a conservative region home to 182,000 people, has emerged as a center of the US election denialism movement in recent years. In 2023, the county’s governing body unsuccessfully sought to remake the voting process by cutting ties with the voting machine company Dominion Voting Systems and implementing a hand-count system that experts warned would be costly and far less accurate. The former MyPillow CEO, Mike Lindell, one of the leading promoters of falsehoods about election fraud in the US, said he would support the county’s effort. The state ultimately blocked Shasta’s plans. In addition, several candidates who lost their race for local office have embraced baseless conspiracy theories about election fraud and sued to overturn results. Last year, the Shasta county board of supervisors appointed Curtis, a Florida-based attorney who had never before overseen an elections office, to serve as the county clerk and registrar of voters. Curtis, who opposes the use of voting machines and has long argued US elections are being manipulated, vowed to overhaul the elections and set an example for the rest of the US. But his tenure has been controversial. Earlier this year investigative reports conducted by the county and an outside body concluded that he had created a hostile work environment and made violent threats against workers. Curtis has denied those claims. Last week, the same board that appointed Curtis censured him, and denounced what it described as his “ongoing and flagrant violations” of county personnel rules, pointing to policies preventing elected officials from “making unfounded allegations that have not been investigated”. Curtis accused staff of “sabotaging elections” and said he planned to sue the county, telling the Guardian: “Everything the old staff accused me of is a lie, and we will be able to prove it in court.” Peters, the former top election official in Mesa county, Colorado, was convicted of four felonies and three misdemeanors in 2024 after she allowed an activist affiliated with Lindell to impersonate a county employee and attend an upgrade of the county’s Dominion voting software. The Gateway Pundit, the far-right news website, subsequently published screenshots of sensitive county information after that breach. Peters was released from prison in June after Colorado’s governor, Jared Polis, a Democrat, commuted her nine-year prison sentence. The hiring of Peters was alarming, said Matt Crane, the executive director of the Colorado county clerk’s association. “Tina Peters and others in the election-denial movement appear to have found another weak link in the chain in California,” he said. “The idea that anyone would bring Tina Peters in as an election expert is almost beyond parody. Maybe she’s an expert on leaving ballots sitting in a ballot box for months after an election. Maybe she’s an expert on committing crimes in the process of trying, and completely failing, to prove election fraud. “When it comes to actually administering secure, lawful elections, Tina Peters is the last person anyone should be looking to for expertise,” he added. Jena Griswold, Colorado’s secretary of state, said in a statement: “Peters was convicted of four felonies and three misdemeanors related to breaching her own voting equipment while county clerk. It is troubling that she would be in a position to have direct influence on election administration.” Securing the release of Peters from prison was a celebrated cause on the right. Even as Donald Trump pardoned those involved with the January 6 attack on the US Capitol and the fake elector scheme in 2020, he could not help Peters because she was only convicted of a state crime. Polis, facing mounting pressure from the federal government to free Peters, eventually commuted her sentence in May, saying it was unfairly harsh. Polis overrode recommendations from his own clemency board in doing so, according to the New York Times, and has been rebuked by the Colorado Democratic party. The California senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat, also criticized the plan to hire Peters. “This should be stopped immediately: Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis is trying to hire election-denier Tina Peters to collude with the Trump Administration’s election mischief,” he posted on X. “Americans – and Californians – deserve nothing but safe, secure, and free elections – without political interference and partisan loyalists beholden to Trump.” Since being released from prison, Peters has hit the Maga media circuit and continued to try to undermine faith in American elections. She continues to assert, falsely, that votes were flipped in 2020, and has urged Trump to declare a national emergency ahead of the 2026 midterms, according to the Atlantic. The state quickly sued the county and a judge has temporarily blocked the implementation of the measure.

title: Trump reportedly casts mail-in ballot in Florida Republican primary
body_text: Donald Trump voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary, Politico reports, citing Palm Beach county voting records. The White House has confirmed the president’s mail-in vote, according to the New York Times, which added that this was at least the third time the president has mailed his ballot. In March, the president signed an executive ⁠order restricting the use of mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections that will decide control of US Congress. Trump has repeatedly criticized mail-in voting, calling for restrictions on the policy for years and falsely claiming that his 2020 election defeat was the result of widespread voter fraud. In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump continued his years-long false claims of election fraud in the United States – including by implying that mail-in voting is insecure. “Earlier this month, India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, asked our Administration – How can you have Elections in the U.S. without a valid Photo ID? India’s last Election had 646,000,000 Voters! Less than 1% voted by mail, and every single Voter had to have a VALID Photo Identity Document. We need to pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT, now!” Trump wrote. A federal judge has blocked ⁠the US Postal ⁠Service from implementing part of the executive order, although Trump’s administration has asked the supreme court to intervene. After Politico reported on the president’s ballot on Monday afternoon, citing local voting records, the New York Times reported that it “could not access these records through the Palm Beach county supervisor of elections website, which said that Mr Trump’s voting record was ‘protected from public disclosure’”. However, a White House spokeswoman later confirmed to the newspaper that Trump voted by mail, saying: “As everyone knows, the president is a resident of Palm Beach and participates in Florida elections, but he obviously primarily lives at the White House in Washington DC.” Trump first registered to vote in Palm Beach county in 2019. Since then, he has voted by mail in 2020, during a special election for statehouse earlier this year and last week, when he mailed his ballot on 13 August.

title: Top Democrats tussle in Florida primary but progressive liberalism not on menu
body_text: If primary elections elsewhere this summer were tussles between progressives and moderates for the direction of the Democratic party’s political future, Tuesday’s contests in Florida could not be more different. In a former swing state that has in recent years become reliably red, moderate Democratic candidates Alex Vindman and David Jolly are heavily favored to become the party’s nominees for November’s Senate and governor’s race, respectively. Analysts say the brand of progressive liberalism that worked so well for Democratic candidates in Minnesota, Michigan and New York, won’t cut it with voters in conservative Florida, and neither are Vindman, frontrunner for the Senate nomination to challenge Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, or Jolly, vying to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor, trying to sell it. “There is a lot of curiosity about me from more traditional, pre-Trump-era Republicans that feel homeless,” Vindman said in March as he weighed the broad coalition of voters he will need to topple Moody, appointed by Republican DeSantis in January 2025 to replace Marco Rubio after his elevation to secretary of state. “I’m running here as a kind of a different kind of Democrat, I’ve got my handguns, a concealed carry permit, not the standard fare.” Florida has closed primaries, meaning only those voters who have declared party affiliation can choose its nominees. But Vindman and Jolly are already looking to court independents and disgruntled Republicans beyond Tuesday. Vindman, a retired army lt col, and an impeachment witness against Trump during the president’s first term of office, is polling clear of state representative Angie Nixon in the Democratic primary. He has run a “Florida First” campaign that leans heavily on establishment values – the economy, social security stability for seniors, and tackling corruption in Washington. “My race is entirely focused on my opponent, I’m not focused on anything besides Ashley Moody,” he said. “I feel a huge amount of support and kind of a new hope for a balanced politics in this state.” Jolly, a former Republican congressman who became a Democrat last year, and is the most prominent name in a crowded field for the party’s governor’s nomination, also believes his moderate credentials are an asset. In an interview with the Associated Press last week, Jolly stated he had no plans to try to reverse DeSantis’s ban on transgender girls and women athletes playing on female teams at public schools and universities. “I don’t think we should have biologically born men playing in competitive sports,” he said in comments starkly at odds with pro-diversity positions taken by progressive victors elsewhere, such as Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, who promised to be “a lion” for LGBTQ+ rights if elected to the Senate. Even so, the likely Republican candidate for governor has been declared to be a “radical liberal” by Byron Donalds, the Trump-aligned congressman who is the clear favorite for the Republican nomination. In attack ads prevalent on Florida’s television screens in recent days, Donalds has painted Jolly as a fervent supporter of the transgender community, attempted insults Jolly has shrugged off by challenging Donalds on issues he said matter more to “regular” Floridians, such as soaring costs for property, insurance, gas and groceries, instead of focusing on culture war issues. The man of the people approach is also a theme for Jay Collins, DeSantis’s lieutenant governor, and one of three Republicans challenging Donalds for the nomination. “I mow my own yard. I gas up my own truck. I live the same Florida life that working families live,” Collins, a former Green Beret, told reporters in a press conference Thursday that portrayed Donalds, a congressman since 2021, as an absentee Washington elite. “We won’t win with vibes. We’re certainly not going to win with celebrity.” Other Republicans in the governor’s race are James Fishback, a far-right extremist who has endured a bumpy primary campaign, and Paul Renner, the former speaker of the Florida house and legislative ally of DeSantis, who has declined to make a primary endorsement. Polling shows Donalds close to 50%, with his rivals at 15% or below. Political analysts see voter dissatisfaction in Florida with Trump, and the soon-to-be termed-out DeSantis to a degree, but nothing likely to spark a wholesale ideological swing. “Going back many decades, if you look at Florida’s political culture, it’s moderate to conservative,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida. “Roughly 40% of Floridians say they’re moderate, 40% say they’re conservative, and only about 20% say they’re liberal. It’s been steady for decades, and one way of saying there’s just not as many progressives, or liberals, or socialists, in Florida as apparently there are in some other places currently. “Unlike some of the big battles we’ve seen nationwide between the progressive socialist wing of the Democratic party and the moderate wing, I don’t think that’s going to be the case in Florida. The voters will sort it out but from a Democratic perspective it would be good for them if they got the more moderate candidates, and I think that’s what most Democrats feel.” Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic party, and its most recent winner of statewide election when she became agriculture commissioner in 2018, largely sees the middle ground as the key to reversing years of disappointment. “The coalition that makes up Florida is different. Every demographic inside the Democratic party is more conservative than the demographics outside of our state,” she said. “And a coalition here that has to be built is very unique to Florida, candidates running up and down the ticket from first responders to veterans, Teach for America alumni, and just everyday Floridians who are frustrated with the state affairs here. “All of them have been at the doors, on the phones, talking to voters for the better part of the last year and a half, and really listening, listening to concerns from Floridians. And it’s a pretty consistent drumbeat.” Fried said she expected a voter backlash to DeSantis’s partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts, which was intended to reduce Democrats’ share of the state’s 28 seats from eight to four. It forced some candidates to switch districts mid-campaign, and set up rancorous primary races elsewhere between leftist hopefuls and established Congress members. Fried said DeSantis’s move could backfire. “Right now, the Republicans have a nasty primary for governor that is going to decrease their motivation to turn out in November,” she said. “You have a president who is significantly underwater, and a state where for 30 years one party has had control and people can’t afford to live here. So the enthusiasm on the Republican side to turn out is going to be significantly diminished. “One-third of our state is independent and what we have seen since the last 18 months since President Trump took a second term is that that independent block has been breaking for Democrats in record numbers. An energized Democratic base, independents breaking with us 60, 70%, and a diminished Republican turnout in energy … that’s a winning equation.” Jewett, meanwhile, said DeSantis’s eight years as a hardline governor might prompt chunks of the electorate to seek something different. “When you talk about some very specific policies, sometimes Floridians actually have more progressive views than you might think, it’s just that most of them don’t want to call themselves progressive or socialists, even if they agreed,” he said. “You know, we voted to increase the minimum wage to $15 an hour over time. We voted for medical marijuana. So there are some particular issues that Floridians may be a little bit more progressive on, but most don’t think of it like that. “That label still has a negative connotation to a lot of voters.”

title: US senator Jon Ossoff condemns Trump as ‘draft-dodging, crook president’
body_text: The Democratic senator Jon Ossoff called Donald Trump a “draft-dodging, crook president” while defending the senator Mark Kelly as a hero during a Tuesday campaign appearance in Georgia, escalating his public feud with the US president. “I don’t think anything illustrates the times more aptly than that the draft-dodging, crook president, who has plunged our nation recklessly into a war he knows not how to end or to win, tried to imprison this man, who embodies American heroism,” Ossoff said while appearing alongside Kelly and his wife, the former Arizona congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. Kelly, a former navy captain, and five other Democratic lawmakers were attacked by Trump last year after they released a social media video saying troops are not required to carry out illegal commands. Trump called for the lawmakers’ arrests, accusing them of “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!” Ossoff, who is currently running for re-election to his Senate seat in Georgia and is widely speculated to be eyeing a 2028 presidential run, has received viral attention on social media for his sharp criticism of Trump. On Sunday, during a campaign appearance in Atlanta, Ossoff similarly attacked Trump’s handling of the US-Israel war on Iran. “While the sailors on the Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings,” Ossoff said. “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the amir of Qatar.” Ossoff appears to have been referring to Natalie Harp, Trump’s executive assistant, who has drawn scrutiny for her closeness to the US president. The White House quickly criticized Ossoff on Monday, with the president calling him “Pee-wee Herman” and the White House communications director, Steven Cheung, writing on social media that Ossoff is “a radical, extremist Dumocrat”.

title: Trump-backed Byron Donalds to face Democrat David Jolly in race to succeed Florida governor DeSantis
body_text: Byron Donalds, a congressman backed by Donald Trump, won the Republican nomination for governor on Tuesday in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis. Donalds, who has represented south-west Florida since 2021, trounced three reasonably prominent Republican rivals, including Jay Collins, DeSantis’s handpicked lieutenant governor. If he wins the November election, as he is expected to do in the conservative stronghold, Donalds would become only the second elected Black governor in any southern US state. So confident was Donalds of victory that his television advertisements in the weeks leading to the primary ignored his Republican challengers and focused on former Republican congressman David Jolly, who secured the Democratic party’s nomination on Tuesday. He continued that message on Tuesday evening. “I am grateful to my family, my team, my volunteers, and every Floridian who powered us to this victory,” he wrote on X. “My Democrat opponent would raise taxes, make life more expensive, and bring the Democrats’ radical left agenda to the Sunshine State – Florida cannot afford Liberal David Jolly. David Jolly has lost before, and he will lose again on November 3. United, we will win the Governor’s mansion in 77 days and ensure that Florida remains the best state in this great country.” In his victory speech, Jolly addressed political division and the economy before placing blame on Donalds for the state’s rising costs. “To my Democratic friends, thank you for welcoming me into the party. We have built friendships, we have found common ground,” he said. He added: “Byron Donalds has sold the governor’s mansion to the highest bidder and the special interests across the state have been happy to play ball.” DeSantis did not make an endorsement in the race, but Trump did, backing Donalds and his conservative credentials, with support that could prove decisive in Florida, arguably the heart of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, and home to his Mar-a-Lago Palm Beach estate. DeSantis was largely considered dead in the water in his own campaign to become governor in 2018, before Trump’s endorsement turned things around. Republican voters roundly rejected the credentials of Collins, an army special forces veteran who called Donalds part of a Washington elite; Paul Renner, the former Florida house speaker; and extremist James Fishback. Instead, they favored Donalds, who at times polled close to 50% and is, according to his campaign website, “committed to implementing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Great Again”. A vocal Trump ally who was reportedly considered for the 2024 vice-president pick that ultimately went to JD Vance, Donalds made affordability and reducing property taxes and insurance costs a central plank of his campaign, which some have seen as a dig at DeSantis’s obsession with culture war issues during his eight-year tenure. Jolly, a former Republican congressman and lawyer, became an independent, then switched parties last year. He ran a much more moderate campaign than the ones that worked well for progressive Democrats in other states’ primaries this summer, although that did not stop Donalds assailing him as “a radical liberal” who he claimed was an advocate for gender-reassignment surgery who supports transgender males in girls’ and women’s sports. David Jolly has lost before, and he will lose again on November 3. United, we will win the Governor’s mansion in 77 days and ensure that Florida remains the best state in this great country.” In his victory speech, Jolly addressed political division and the economy before placing blame on Donalds for the state’s rising costs. “To my Democratic friends, thank you for welcoming me into the party. We have built friendships, we have found common ground,” he said. He added: “Byron Donalds has sold the governor’s mansion to the highest bidder and the special interests across the state have been happy to play ball.” DeSantis did not make an endorsement in the race, but Trump did, backing Donalds and his conservative credentials, with support that could prove decisive in Florida, arguably the heart of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, and home to his Mar-a-Lago Palm Beach estate. title: Who is Natalie Harp? Trump’s closest and most devoted aide is in the spotlight
body_text: Wearing shoulder-length blond hair, gold earrings and a red dress, cancer survivor Natalie Harp introduced herself to the 2020 Republican national convention as “a formerly forgotten American from California” and compared Donald Trump to George Bailey, the everyman hero played by James Stewart in the classic film It’s a Wonderful Life. “George Bailey’s father was right,” smiled Harp, her voice echoing in the Andrew W Mellon auditorium in pandemic-hit Washington. “All you can take with you is that which you’ve given away. Mr President, that makes you the richest man in the world.” Six years later, Harp is now one of Trump’s closest and most devoted aides. Her official job title is special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president on an annual salary of $150,000. Her unofficial job title is the “human printer” for supplying him with print-outs of information. And for years she has only been a minor character in the Trump Cinematic Universe. But all that changed this week when Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator and possible 2028 presidential contender, accused Trump in a campaign speech of wanting to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie” instead of doing his job. The remark triggered a tsunami of online speculation about the precise nature of the relationship and a furious backlash. On Monday Trump lashed out at the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes after she asked a question about Ossoff’s comments, while the White House’s anonymous “Rapid Response” team posted at Holmes: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question.” Far from dousing the flames, the White House had in fact poured kerosene on them, inadvertently enhancing Ossoff’s national standing among Democrats and inviting millions of people to ask the same question. Who is Natalie Harp? The 35-year-old Californian graduated from Point Loma Nazarene University, a Christian liberal arts college in San Diego, in 2012. Three years later, she earned an MBA from Liberty University, an evangelical college founded by Jerry Falwell in Lynchburg, Virginia. Four years later, as Trump was mounting a bid for re-election, Harp wrote a post on LinkedIn entitled: “I’m Living Proof – the Party of Healthcare is Trump’s.” Recalling her experience with bone cancer, it explained: “On November 9, 2015 – a year to the day Donald Trump would win the presidency – a nurse mixed up my IV with the deadly substance of sterile water leaving me housebound and searching for care. “Instead of studying my symptoms to diagnose my condition, my Democrat-controlled state and country offered me opioids, barbiturates, medical marijuana, disability, Do-Not-Resuscitate orders, and yes, Death With Dignity. Before one appointment, I was even instructed in the voluntary stopping of eating and drinking (VSED).” Harp praised Trump’s signing of the 2018 Right to Try Act for giving her the opportunity to access experimental treatments that proved successful. “My oncologist didn’t tell me I had other options,” she said. “Donald Trump did … Now my numbers are stabilizing and so is my pain.” The LinkedIn post caught the eye of Rupert Murdoch’s conservative Fox News network, which invited Harp on air to talk about it. Trump responded on social media: “Natalie Harp, fighting Stage 2 Cancer and doing really well, was a GREAT guest on @foxandfriends. Right To Try is producing some truly spectacular results. Proud of Natalie!” That led to Harp’s speech in praise of Trump at the Republican national convention, a month after the death of her father. She managed to take a swipe at Britain’s National Health Service (NHS) after offering a message to Trump: “I wouldn’t be alive today if it wasn’t for you.” But a Washington Post article cast doubt on the claim, noting that experts point out that “Harp’s description of the treatment she received and her timeline for receiving it make it unlikely Trump had any effect on her case.” ‘Human printer’ Still, Harp and her mother quit California and moved into an 18th-floor apartment in West Palm Beach, Florida, three miles from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate. In 2020 Harp joined the far-right One America News Network (OANN), where as a presenter she amplified Trump’s “big lie” that the presidential election had been stolen by Joe Biden. Harp left OANN in 2022 and began working for Trump, then a former president facing criminal cases and mounting a seemingly unlikely bid to return to the White House. She fed him a diet of good news on the election campaign trail. The New York Times reported in 2024: “She has no official title, but during the campaign, colleagues referred to her as the ‘human printer’ because she followed Mr Trump around with a portable printer and a battery pack to charge it, so she could hand him information in hard copy, as he prefers.” Now that Trump has returned to the Oval Office, Harp is frequently seen at his side and has become an indispensable aide. Last month, when the president was forced to secretly swap planes in Turkey because of an alleged Iranian assassination threat, she was one of the few people to join him on a military plane while other staff and journalists remained on a decoy Air Force One. One acquaintance of Harp, who did not wish to be named, said on Tuesday: “Nobody questioned [deputy chief of staff] Dan Scavino being on the military plane but frankly Natalie is a lot more capable than Dan Scavino in a lot of areas. She is beautiful by any definition and because of that people don’t understand how intelligent, articulate, loyal, trustworthy and engaged she is with politics.” ‘Guardian and Protector’ Harp also plays an outsized role in shaping both Trump’s worldview and his output. She reportedly shows him proposed Truth Social posts – often containing recycled content – then logs into his account to publish them. These have included a racist video depicting Barack and Michelle Obama as apes and an AI-generated image portraying Trump as Jesus Christ, according to the Wall Street Journal. In the book Regime Change published this year, New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan wrote that Harp’s loyalty extended to writing Trump “adoring letters” including one that read: “You are all that matters to me.” In one she wrote: “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work.’” In another she said, “I don’t ever want to let you down” and described Trump as her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. Haberman and Swan also described a typical scene: “Harp was generally on a chair off to the side, her laptop open, head cocked, listening but never contributing unless ordered to by Trump. She fulfilled, in a flash, any request, whether a ‘Trump 2028’ that needed to be fetched from the merchandise room, a quick Google search, or producing the latest story from rightwing websites like Breitbart or Gateway Pundit.” Harp’s devotion to Trump does not sit well with her estranged brother, Preston Harp, who lives in Nicaragua’s capital, Managua. He told the Daily Beast website last month: “I think that she does see Trump as a kind of father figure because he embodies the doctrine of American exceptionalism.” Meanwhile the administration’s furious response to Ossoff’s speech implies that he touched a raw nerve and looks set to invite further scrutiny of Harp and her role in Trump’s life. Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “It does invoke the famous line, ‘Methinks he doth protest too much’. You made this a bigger thing. “There’s something in life called a proportional response and what we saw from the White House was a massive response, which only further encourages questions and intrigue. It’s like, ‘Oh, there must be a there there for you to react so violently.’ If their thought process was this will tamp down speculation and gossip, whoever thought that is a moron.”

title: Why are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicated
body_text: The media pundits have written article after article desperately trying to understand why progressive candidates, despite being heavily outspent, keep defeating establishment Democrats in primaries around the country. Well, the answer is not complicated. Whether it is a corrupt campaign finance system, unprecedented income and wealth inequality, a broken and wildly expensive healthcare system, the enormous threats posed by AI or an immoral and destructive foreign policy, progressives are talking about the real issues facing working families. And they are providing real solutions. Establishment Democrats are not. Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged. The very rich get richer, while working families struggle. Today, while 60% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good. We now have more income and wealth inequality than at any time in American history. The top 1% now own more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 50% of US households. Not surprisingly, working families are tired of status quo politics and the same old, same old establishment policies that have failed them for years. They want change, real change – and are supporting progressive candidates who are fighting for that change. In the richest country in the history of the world, Americans do not want to have to struggle every single day just to pay the bills. Working-class people do not want to die years younger than they should because of illnesses caused by the never-ending stress they experience just to survive. And, like past generations, they do not want their kids to have a lower standard of living than they do. Establishment politicians and the establishment media have described the agenda that progressive candidates are winning elections on as “radical”, “far left”, “extremist” or, in the words of Donald Trump, “communist” . All that is nonsense. On major issue after major issue, the progressive agenda is reflecting exactly what a strong majority of the American people need and want. Let me take this opportunity to share with you some of the major proposals that most progressives support. And you tell me how “extreme” they are. Campaign finance reform Progressives believe that our current campaign finance system is corrupt and is undermining democracy. It is absurd that one man, Mr Musk, can spend $290m to help elect Donald Trump as president and that billionaires in both parties can spend unlimited amounts of money in campaigns through their Super Pacs. We believe that we must end the disastrous US supreme court decision on Citizens United, ban Super Pacs and move to the public funding of elections. We believe that democracy means one person one vote, not billionaires buying elections. Healthcare Progressives believe that our current healthcare system is broken, dysfunctional and wildly expensive. We believe that it is immoral and fiscally irresponsible for us to spend roughly twice as much per capita on healthcare as do the people of other major countries, while 85 million Americans remain uninsured or underinsured. At the same time, we pay, by far, the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Progressives believe that healthcare is a human right and that we should do what all other major countries on Earth do, guarantee healthcare to all people. We agree with the 64% of Americans who want a Medicare for all single payer system. Protecting American workers Progressives believe that all Americans are entitled to a decent standard of living. We regard it as outrageous that in the year 2026 millions of workers continue to earn starvation wages and that the federal minimum wage remains at a disgraceful $7.25 an hour. We believe that the federal minimum wage should be raised to a living wage of at least $20 per hour. We also believe that employers should no longer be able to deny workers their constitutional right to join unions through illegal actions. Progressives support the passage of the Pro Act which will make it easier for workers to join unions and negotiate contracts that will provide them with better wages, benefits and working conditions. Tax the rich Progressives believe that, at a time of unprecedented income and wealth inequality, the wealthiest people in this country must start paying their fair share of taxes. At a time when we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country on Earth and when one-third of our senior citizens are struggling economically, it is absurd that billionaires have an effective tax rate lower than truck drivers or nurses. The wealthiest people in this country and large profitable corporations must start paying their fair share of taxes so that we can adequately fund the needs of working families, the children and the elderly. Regulation of AI Progressives believe that AI and robotics, developed and pushed by the wealthiest people on Earth, are the most transformational technologies in the history of humanity and that they will impact every man, woman and child in our country. At a time when AI is threatening to displace millions of workers, eviscerate our privacy, harm our environment, undermine our democracy and negatively impact the mental health of our children, we believe that the government must play a decisive role in making sure that these revolutionary technologies are used to benefit all Americans, and not just make the big tech oligarchs even richer. Climate change Progressives believe that Trump’s assertion that climate change is a “hoax” is not only extraordinarily ignorant, but is a real danger to the planet. The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record and the last three years have been the hottest three years on record. This past year the United States and countries throughout the world have seen major heatwaves, flash floods, increased drought and horrific forest fires – and scientists tell us the worst is yet to come. Progressives believe that we must forcefully take on the greed of the fossil fuel industry. The truth is that we can create millions of good-paying union jobs by transforming our energy systems away from fossil fuels and into energy efficiency and sustainable energy. For the sake of our kids, future generations and the habitability of the planet that is what we must do. Foreign policy Progressives believe that we need to fundamentally reform our foreign and military policies. The war in Vietnam was based on a lie. The war in Iraq was based on a lie. The current war in Iran is based on a lie. We do not need to spend $1.5tn a year on the Pentagon fighting endless wars and propping up dictatorships around the world. We certainly do not have to invest tens of billions supporting the extremist Netanyahu government in Israel, which has killed 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 173,000 more – the vast majority of them women, children and the elderly. Despite what the media will have you believe, progressives are winning across this country for a simple reason: the ideas they are running on are extremely popular. It’s time for the political establishment to stop telling the American people what they should believe and start listening to what they actually want. Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

title: Democratic socialist Angie Nixon scores surprise win in Florida US Senate primary
body_text: In an upset for the Democratic establishment, progressive Angie Nixon won the party’s US Senate primary in Florida, beating former army intelligence officer Alexander Vindman. Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, had significantly less funding going into the primary – with $975,000 to Vindman’s $16.3m at the end of July, according to Florida Politics. But she won by a clear margin. Nixon received 56.1% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, ahead of Vindman’s 43.9%. Vindman served on the national security council in Donald Trump’s first term and became a well-known whistleblower and witness in the US president’s first impeachment, centered on Trump pressuring Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, to investigate Joe Biden. Democrats have their sights set on upsetting Republican Ashley Moody in the US Senate general election. Moody, picked by DeSantis to replace Marco Rubio when he became secretary of state last year, won what was almost a token primary election to run in November to serve the remaining two years of Rubio’s term. Nixon, who was born in Jacksonville, has aggressively opposed DeSantis’s policies, including with a sit-in at the governor’s office this spring to protest against Republican redistricting, the Miami Herald reported. That demonstration resulted in her facing misdemeanor charges of trespassing and resisting, which she is fighting in court. Vindman’s campaign had been focused on Moody, not his primary opponent, and he did not agree to debate Nixon, despite her public calls for him to take the stage with her. “Floridians don’t want the establishment in Washington DC deciding who their Democratic nominee and US senator is going to be,” Nixon told the Tampa Bay Times in an earlier interview. “I’m someone who’s willing to debate. He’s not. I’m someone who doesn’t have to be briefed on the issues Floridians are facing because I’ve been fighting the attacks alongside them for nearly two decades.” Vindman praised Nixon in a post on Tuesday night after the race was called, saying she “ran a strong campaign”. “I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me,” he wrote, adding: “Who would’ve ever thought that a Jewish refugee would make it to the US Army, to the White House, and to becoming a candidate for the US Senate. Only in America is that possible.” Vindman had been expected to win the primary given his huge fundraising advantage. Nixon’s supporters had pointed to one poll suggesting that she would perform better against Moody in November than Vindman, though that poll projected the Republican incumbent would win against either Democrat. “We did it ya’ll,” Nixon posted on Tuesday night. “Thank you to every person that put their heart into this campaign.” National Democratic leaders praised Nixon’s victory, with Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, and Kirsten Gillibrand, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, releasing a statement noting her background as a former union organizer, saying she had “dedicated her career to fighting for Florida”. Nixon’s victory follows a series of primary wins for Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates across the country, including in primaries in Philadelphia, Colorado, Michigan and New York City. But establishment Democrats prevailed in other Florida races this week, in the first election in the state after redistricting. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, an 11-term congresswoman and former chair of the Democratic National Committee, defeated Elijah Manley, a 27-year-old substitute teacher who was endorsed by a progressive group. Wasserman Schultz had faced criticisms for running in a district that has a plurality of Black voters and has long been represented by a Black Democrat. Wasserman Schultz’s previous district was broken up by Republicans’ gerrymandered congressional maps, and she chose not to run in the district where she lives, but in a newly drawn one that was solidly blue. Jared Moskowitz, a two-term congressman and centrist Democrat, defeated a democratic socialist challenger, running in a new coastal seat extending from Delray Beach to Miami Beach. Moskowitz was up against Oliver Larkin, a 34-year-old who called for universal healthcare and free tuition at public universities and has supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Moskowitz was the first congressional Democrat to back Trump’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge) initiative, which dismantled the US Agency for International Development. Moskowitz also faced criticism from Larkin over his support for a Republican-backed law that expanded ICE’s detention authority. The centrist congressman has also been a staunch supporter of Israel and voted against a resolution to restrict US military involvement in Iran.
