title: Trump is full speed ahead in making money off being the US president
body_text: Donald Trump is essentially unrestrained when it comes to enriching himself during his second term, with no sign of stopping. If anything, he’s ramping things up. The numbers so far are astonishing. He amassed $2.2bn in 2025 revenues, the Guardian and other news outlets have reported. And despite widespread criticism of this astonishing fact, very little is standing in the way of his reaping even more. “The Congress has decided not to commit oversight to this topic, and that’s just the fact of the matter at this point,” Eric Lipton, an investigative reporter for the New York Times, told National Public Radio recently. While his actions appall historians, academics and millions of ordinary Americans, they may be within legal boundaries. Moral or ethical boundaries? Not so much. “While Trump’s second term is less than half over, it already looks like the most openly corrupt administration in our history,” Larry Noble, a law professor and former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission, told the Guardian’s Peter Stone. Despite his loyal base of followers, much of the American public isn’t happy about it. Two-thirds of Americans polled by CNN said that this president doesn’t put the good of the United States over his personal gain. His overall approval ratings have tanked to 33% – the lowest level of his presidency – with a disapproval rating at 64%, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll. Startling as the details of his enrichment may be, his mindset – full speed ahead, don’t bother me with past practices – reflects his behavior in other realms. He glories in knowing no restraints or boundaries, and shrugs off criticism. His power is held back only by his “own morality”, he told the New York Times in January. “It’s the only thing that can stop me.” He was speaking specifically about being restrained on the international stage – his freedom to use any military, economic or political power for what he sees as American supremacy. But it’s a mentality he apparently brings into feathering his and his family’s own nest. As Lipton told NPR, queries about apparent conflicts of interest are brushed off, and the party line is that the Trump family’s extracurricular businesses are building the US economy. In earlier presidencies, his actions surely would have political consequences, perhaps impeachment. (He was impeached twice, but not convicted, first in 2019 for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, then for incitement of the violent insurrection at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.) Trump has amassed at least $1.4bn last year from his cryptocurrency ventures alone, the Guardian reported, noting that others fared less well; about a million investors in one of his crypto projects suffered nearly $4bn in losses as the value of their holdings cratered. Then there are the wealthy foreigners who have invested in the Trump family’s hotel and golf-resort projects, creating potential conflicts of interest. His media company, Truth Social, has been another major source of wealth. Now there’s a new plan to offer early access to his posts for a fee of $100,000. Those posts, of course, have the power to move markets. It’s come under heavy criticism – and prompted lawsuits from media organizations and advocacy groups such as the Freedom of the Press Foundation that argue it’s unconstitutional. But, to date, as with so much of what Trump does, it’s proceeding brazenly. Every once in a while, the courts step in to provide some restraints. Trump tried to use his already weaponized federal justice department to settle his $10bn lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. The initial result was to provide him and his family immunity from earlier audits of their tax returns, which might save the Trumps about $100m. But in a rare bit of accountability, a federal judge – one appointed by Barack Obama – nullified major parts of the agreement. The legal status is still being contested, and the stakes are high. All of this has the power to shock those paying attention to news reports. But there, too, Trump has given himself a form of protection by constantly playing on citizens’ mistrust of legacy media and to brand such investigations as “fake news”. The result, as author and journalist Craig Unger put it recently on Substack, is that nothing “moves the needle”. Not that long ago, he wrote, the press could “root out corruption, topple presidents, and end wars”. But now, even the biggest scoops and the most dramatic revelations seem to have little impact, Unger argues; that’s because the national citizenry doesn’t share an agreed-upon set of facts as it used to do. Trump’s low approval ratings do seem to tell a different story, however, and voters will get a chance to make their voices heard soon. At the very least, some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power with a majority in one or both chambers of Congress. Many forecasters think the Democrats may well regain the House of Representatives but that their getting a majority of Senate seats is quite a bit less likely. For now, Trump continues to take full advantage of a situation that has so greatly benefited his personal wealth, if not his reputation or legacy. Like a greedy toddler, he keeps sticking his hand in the presidential cookie jar. And no one, so far, seems able to yank it out. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: US justice department defends prosecution of James Comey over ‘8647’ seashell post
body_text: The US Department of Justice has defended its prosecution of former FBI director James Comey, claiming in new court documents there is “no serious dispute” that his social media post last year featuring a photo of seashells arranged to read “8647” could be interpreted as a threat against Donald Trump. “There is no serious dispute that an objective viewer of Comey’s post could read it to mean ‘Kill President Trump’,” prosecutors wrote in a document filed on Tuesday in response to Comey’s efforts to have the case dismissed. Comey was indicted in April after a grand jury in North Carolina charged him with making a threat against the US president and transmitting that threat, via social media, across state lines, over an image he posted on Instagram while vacationing in North Carolina last May. In the photo, the seashells were arranged to read “8647”, which the president’s allies and supporters quickly denounced as a threat against Trump. The number “86” is often used as shorthand to mean to get rid of or remove something, while Trump is the 47th US president. Comey deleted the photo after the uproar, saying he didn’t know that it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down,” he said. In the court documents filed earlier this week, prosecutors with the eastern district of North Carolina continued to argue the post was a “coded message to his followers meaning ‘kill’ or ‘get rid of’ President Trump”. Comey has denied the charges against him and his lawyers have asked the judge to dismiss the case, arguing that the post was protected speech and did not amount to a “true threat” against the president. “The indictment alleges that Mr Comey’s ‘86 47’ post constitutes a ‘true threat; on the President’s life,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in a filing last month. “That claim is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.” Comey’s lawyers have argued that “in this context, no reasonable observer would understand the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence at all – let alone to threaten that Mr Comey personally would commit violence against the President”. Comey’s lawyers have also said the case should be dismissed for “vindictive and selective prosecution” and have said the indictment is “not based on a goodfaith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity”. Trump has long feuded with Comey since his handling of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while he was FBI director. Last year, the justice department also indicted Comey in a separate case, alleging that he had lied to Congress. But those charges were later thrown out after a judge ruled the prosecutor handling the case was unlawfully appointed.

title: Lindsey Graham’s sister and fill-in senator says she’s ‘not that informed on national security’
body_text: Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea threaten US national security, Republican fill-in senator Darline Graham hesitated. “I’m just going to be honest here,” she told Tuesday night’s debate audience. “I’m – not that informed on national security, so – but I do support the military.” Gasps, and boos, rolled through the opera house hosting the only debate before next week’s Republican runoff – a race to succeed her brother, Lindsey Graham, who was one of the Senate’s most committed rightwing foreign policy hawks before his sudden passing in July. She did not retreat. “I’m not a polished politician up here,” she added. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.” Her opponent, the ultra-conservative representative Ralph Norman, who once advocated for martial law to keep Joe Biden from the presidency after his election win in 2020, needed no such disclaimer. He walked through Taiwan’s economic ties to the US and made the case that it was worth protecting from Chinese aggression. Graham, endorsed by Donald Trump and leaning on her outsider credentials, recovered later in the evening, describing her family’s reliance on social security survivor benefits after her parents died, and accusing Norman of being unable to decide whether he wants to work in South Carolina or Washington, citing his gubernatorial loss just this year. Norman, who backed his state’s former governor Nikki Haley over Trump in 2024, used the debate to distance himself from the president over the war with Iran, saying Trump “is going to have to tell the American people what it’s going to take” if the strait of Hormuz remains under the control of a country the administration has claimed to have decimated. Since 1979, the US has stuck to what’s called “strategic ambiguity” on Taiwan: refusing to say whether it would actually send troops if China invaded, on the theory that being vague keeps the peace. Trump has largely kept up that dodge, but with his own twist. At his May summit with Xi Jinping in Beijing, the US president said he wasn’t looking to fight a war “9,500 miles” away and wanted “China to cool down”, and put a pending $14bn Taiwan arms package on hold, calling it a “very good negotiating chip”. Xi, meanwhile, told him mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to “clashes and even conflicts”. Last August, Trump said Xi had personally told him China wouldn’t invade Taiwan while he’s in office – a claim Beijing brushed off, reaffirming its commitment to “reunification”. In South Carolina, early voting begins on Wednesday, ahead of the 25 August primary.

title: A democratic socialist win and losses for Trump allies: takeaways from primaries in three key states
body_text: Primaries in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming held on Tuesday provided the latest view into how voters are feeling ahead of November’s US midterm elections. One candidate aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) netted an extraordinary win while another was defeated handily. Donald Trump’s handpicked candidates received a mixed reception from voters. In Alaska, voters chose their fighters for one of the year’s marquee US Senate races, and in Florida, extremism remained alive and well among Republicans. Here’s what we learned from the results: Democratic socialists win their first statewide victory In a shocking upset, state representative Angie Nixon beat Alexander Vindman for the Democratic nomination in Florida’s US Senate race, becoming the first member of the DSA to win a statewide primary, although the group did not endorse her. Her odds of victory in November against Republican Ashley Moody appear long, but Nixon’s win was the latest sign that Democratic voters are willing to buck the preferences of their party’s establishment in favor of candidates whose policies and personalities they prefer. Vindman, known for his role as a whistleblower during Trump’s first term, had a significant cash advantage and backing from leading Democrats, yet lost by a wide margin. The US Senate battle is set in Alaska As expected, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan won his primary in Alaska, and former congresswoman Mary Peltola won the Democratic nomination to take him on in what will be one of the top US Senate contests of the year. The state conducts non-partisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance, and while counting is not complete, the Associated Press reports that another Republican candidate named Dan Sullivan and Democrat David B Leslie are in the lead to appear on the November ballot. In what may be a troubling sign for Sullivan in the midterms, Peltola led him in the primary, winning 48% of the vote to the Republican senator’s 42.8%. No clear answers for progressives Progressives did not win everywhere. In south Florida, the Democratic congressman Jared Moskowitz won his primary, easily beating DSA-endorsed challenger Oliver Larkin. In the hours that followed, the congressman harshly criticized the DSA and the popular streamer Hasan Piker for campaigning against his renomination, arguing that because his district has been gerrymandered by Florida’s legislature to be more easily winnable for Republicans, he’s the best candidate to keep it in Democrats’ hands in the US midterm elections. Democrats continue to show strength down the ballot A handful of local and special elections offered further evidence that Democratic voters were fired up this year. Pennsylvania statehouse candidate Brandon Dukes won a special election against his Republican opponent Scott Timko, in a seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024. And though Florida has become increasingly conservative and Republican in the past decade, Democrats ousted a Moms for Liberty board member in Sarasota and won an at-large city council seat in Jacksonville. Extremism in the Republican party was on display The primary elections included several extremist candidates. Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, backed by neo-Nazi influencer Nick Fuentes, lost badly in the Republican primary, but still picked up support in precincts around college campuses. Election denier Chuck Gray won his bid for the at-large US House seat in Wyoming. Congressman Randy Fine, who has been criticized for Islamophobic and homophobic statements, survived a primary challenge from antisemitic and transphobic influencer and businessman Dan Bilzerian. Trump endorsees lose Several candidates Trump had endorsed were not to voters’ tastes. The president had backed state superintendent of public instruction Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming’s Republican gubernatorial primary, but she lost to state senator Eric Barlow. Congressman Cory Mills lost his primary in Florida to former TV reporter Ryan Elijah, while a former official from Trump’s first term, Catalina Lauf, failed in a bid for a nomination to the US House. House GOP solves a problem named Cory Mills Mills’s primary loss is notable also because it solves a problem for House Republicans without dealing further damage to their razor-thin majority. The second-term congressman had been under investigation by the House ethics committee for a range of misconduct, and has faced allegations of domestic assault and fraud. While some House lawmakers had hinted that he should resign, as three other lawmakers facing similar allegations did earlier this year, Mills’s departure could have jeopardized the GOP’s control of the chamber. Instead, two of his Republican colleagues endorsed his successful primary challenger, and Mills’s time in the House will end at the start of next year.

In Alaska, voters chose their fighters for one of the year’s marquee US Senate races, and in Florida, extremism remained alive and well among Republicans. Here’s what we learned from the results: Democratic socialists win their first statewide victory In a shocking upset, state representative Angie Nixon beat Alexander Vindman for the Democratic nomination in Florida’s US Senate race, becoming the first member of the DSA to win a statewide primary, although the group did not endorse her. Her odds of victory in November against Republican Ashley Moody appear long, but Nixon’s win was the latest sign that Democratic voters are willing to buck the preferences of their party’s establishment in favor of candidates whose policies and personalities they prefer. Vindman, known for his role as a whistleblower during Trump’s first term, had a significant cash advantage and backing from leading Democrats, yet lost by a wide margin. The US Senate battle is set in Alaska As expected, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan won his primary in Alaska, and former congresswoman Mary Peltola won the Democratic nomination to take him on in what will be one of the top US Senate contests of the year. The state conducts non-partisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance, and while counting is not complete, the Associated Press reports that another Republican candidate named Dan Sullivan and Democrat David B Leslie are in the lead to appear on the November ballot. In what may be a troubling sign for Sullivan in the midterms, Peltola led him in the primary, winning 48% of the vote to the Republican senator’s 42.8%. No clear answers for progressives Progressives did not win everywhere. In south Florida, the Democratic congressman Jared Moskowitz won his primary, easily beating DSA-endorsed challenger Oliver Larkin. In the hours that followed, the congressman harshly criticized the DSA and the popular streamer Hasan Piker for campaigning against his renomination, arguing that because his district has been gerrymandered by Florida’s legislature to be more easily winnable for Republicans, he’s the best candidate to keep it in Democrats’ hands in the US midterm elections. Democrats continue to show strength down the ballot A handful of local and special elections offered further evidence that Democratic voters were fired up this year. Pennsylvania statehouse candidate Brandon Dukes won a special election against his Republican opponent Scott Timko, in a seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024. And though Florida has become increasingly conservative and Republican in the past decade, Democrats ousted a Moms for Liberty board member in Sarasota and won an at-large city council seat in Jacksonville. Extremism in the Republican party was on display The primary elections included several extremist candidates. Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, backed by neo-Nazi influencer Nick Fuentes, lost badly in the Republican primary, but still picked up support in precincts around college campuses. Election denier Chuck Gray won his bid for the at-large US House seat in Wyoming. Congressman Randy Fine, who has been criticized for Islamophobic and homophobic statements, survived a primary challenge from antisemitic and transphobic influencer and businessman Dan Bilzerian. Trump endorsees lose Several candidates Trump had endorsed were not to voters’ tastes. The president had backed state superintendent of public instruction Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming’s Republican gubernatorial primary, but she lost to state senator Eric Barlow. Congressman Cory Mills lost his primary in Florida to former TV reporter Ryan Elijah, while a former official from Trump’s first term, Catalina Lauf, failed in a bid for a nomination to the US House. House GOP solves a problem named Cory Mills Mills’s primary loss is notable also because it solves a problem for House Republicans without dealing further damage to their razor-thin majority. The second-term congressman had been under investigation by the House ethics committee for a range of misconduct, and has faced allegations of domestic assault and fraud. While some House lawmakers had hinted that he should resign, as three other lawmakers facing similar allegations did earlier this year, Mills’s departure could have jeopardized the GOP’s control of the chamber. Instead, two of his Republican colleagues endorsed his successful primary challenger, and Mills’s time in the House will end at the start of next year.

title: Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerve
body_text: Jon Ossoff really struck a nerve. That much is clear. The US senator for Georgia, running for re-election in November, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections campaign so far when discussing Donald Trump at a rally on Sunday. “While the sailors on the [USS Abraham] Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks,” said Ossoff. “See, he doesn’t want to do the job. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.” Not only did the remark enter into national consciousness the existence of “Natalie” – Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old aide to Trump who rarely leaves the president’s side – Ossoff’s riff also succeeded in upsetting Steven Cheung, Trump’s director of communications. “Jon Jackoff,” Cheung wrote on X on Monday, misspelling, perhaps deliberately, the name “Ossoff”, “has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he’s a miserable person who hates this country. It’s because he’s a radical, extremist Dumocrat.” Even for someone in Trump’s orbit, where outbursts against political opponents are commonplace, this plumbed new lows. What could possibly have triggered Trump’s stoutly built, middle-aged communications guru into attacking Ossoff, the handsome, athletic, 39-year-old senator? It’s hard to be sure. But, apropos of nothing, this essay by Dana Schwartz, from 2016, examined why rightwing men are obsessed with calling people “cucks”: “‘Cuck’ is a concept borne [sic] out of insecurity: a fear that one is inadequate, sexually or otherwise, and that inadequacy will lead to the loss of the things that are important to him,” Schwartz wrote. In any case, Trump wasn’t far behind Cheung, calling Ossoff a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” – a reference to a TV and film character whose popularity peaked 40 years ago. (Trump has also called Ossoff “Pinky Herman”, which is neither a character nor a thing.) The anonymous White House Rapid Response X account joined in too, branding a CNN reporter who had asked Trump about Ossoff a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession”, and later posting: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.” It’s hard to really be shocked by any of this any more, with daily attacks on the media from the president and his most senior aides, but an official White House account, with 2.2 million followers, invoking a reporter’s children prompted widespread criticism. In truth the rhetoric from Trump and his acolytes, always bellicose, has been getting worse for a while – and people who dare to publicly question Trump’s narrative that he is a successful, popular president, seem to particularly trigger those on the right. Take James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Texas, who is running neck and neck against Ken Paxton, whom Trump picked for the Republican side. Talarico’s popularity in a traditionally red state has seen Republicans come out swinging. Trump dubbed the Democrat “Talafreako” in July; earlier US senator Bernie Moreno had called Talarico, “a far left freak”, while a Texas congressman falsely claiming Talarico “daydreams about trans kids”. (There was also Trump branding a reporter “piggy” after she asked him a question onboard Air Force One.) Perhaps the fury is prompted whenever something, or someone, succeeds in puncturing the alternate reality that Republicans have created for themselves: a reality where the GOP is not predicted to suffer heavy losses in November’s midterms, and one where Trump is a spry, capable president. When someone points out that Trump is an 80-year-old, easily distracted man who is overseeing an ill-defined, meandering war in Iran, while doing little as prices soar at home, it appears to bring out the particularly vulgar insults. Ossoff did all this on Sunday – and sparked fresh speculation about the president’s relationship with a close aide. With Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, stepping down, there is some jostling taking place in Trump’s circle to replace her, perhaps explaining the amped up language as each potential successor seeks to be more pugnacious than the last. And given Democrats in Congress will be running on Trump’s unpopularity this November, there’ll be plenty of opportunity for bellicose responses from the White House. We should brace ourselves for plenty more of this sort of thing.

title: Republican senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola advance in Alaska Senate primary
body_text: Incumbent Dan S Sullivan, the US senator, advanced in Alaska’s non-partisan primary race for his seat on Tuesday alongside Mary Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman. With the top four candidates moving forward from Alaska’s open primaries to the general election, the Associated Press reported that Sullivan and Peltola had qualified for November’s general election. Another Dan Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee who infuriated his namesake senator by running as a long-shot Republican candidate, was in a distant third place, although his qualification had yet to be confirmed. David B Leslie, a Democrat from Fairbanks, Alaska, is currently in fourth place. He appears to have raised no money for his campaign, and has reportedly said he has no idea why a Super Pac (political action committee) named the American Democracy Project spent about $300,000 supporting his candidacy. After 80% of votes were counted, Peltola led the primary, at 48%, while Sullivan, the senator, had 42.8%. The result tees up one of the marquee races of this year’s US midterm elections, which could determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the Senate for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. First elected in 2014, Sullivan easily won re-election in 2020, but this year faces what is expected to be a stiff challenge from Peltola. She is the first Alaska Native ever to serve in the US House of Representatives, and won a special election for the state’s at-large congressional district in 2022, then a full term later that year. In 2024, Peltola lost her re-election bid to Republican Nick Begich III, but is nonetheless viewed as a top-tier Democratic recruit to take on Sullivan in the Senate race. Both candidates are champions of Alaska’s oil and gas industry – a major employer and economic driver – but Peltola has sought to distinguish herself through her advocacy for the state’s fisheries and opposition to Trump’s economic policies. Sullivan has meanwhile described himself as a reliable advocate both for the state’s oil needs and its military installations, while championing more popular aspects of the president’s agenda such as the tax cut extensions included in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But Sullivan’s path to retaining his seat in the US Senate has been complicated by the emergence of Dan J Sullivan, his namesake rival, who is also running as a Republican. Alaska Republicans have condemned him as a “sham” candidate who is backed by Democrats and running solely to confuse voters, but their efforts to disqualify him from the race were unsuccessful. Alaska figures prominently in Democrats’ ambitious plans to retake the US Senate, which would require flipping at least three Republican-held seats in states that voted for Trump in 2024. The party is hoping to see its candidates elected in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio and elsewhere, but is also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire. Peltola, who recently replaced her longtime campaign manager, has raised more than $18.5m this election cycle, with upwards of $4.6m on hand. Sullivan has brought in more than $11.7m, with nearly $7.3m on hand. In the primary for Alaska’s sole US House district, Begich advanced to the general election, alongside his main challenger, independent Bill Hill. Alaskans in November will also elect a successor to the incumbent Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, who is barred by term limits from seeking re-election. In a crowded field of 17 candidates, Democrats Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich advanced to the November election. Two more nominations remain open, with 80% of votes counted.

title: Another democratic socialist victory – Angie Nixon in Florida – sends shock waves through party establishment
body_text: It wasn’t supposed to be this way. In conservative Florida, Alex Vindman – a retired army intelligence officer who blew this whistle on Donald Trump in his first term – appeared set to carry the Democratic establishment banner as the party staged a long-shot bid to topple a Republican US senator. Florida’s Democratic voters had other ideas. Democratic socialist Angie Nixon emerged a surprise victor in the US Senate primary on Tuesday, after a campaign in which she was outfunded and outspent by Vindman at a ratio of more than 10 to one. Her triumph sent shock waves through the Democratic party machine as it prepares to mount a challenge to the incumbent Republican senator, Ashley Moody, in November’s US midterm elections. Nixon, a tenacious leftwing fighter and former union organizer who has represented Jacksonville in the Florida house since 2020, raised $975,000 in her campaign, as against Vindman’s $16.3m, but garnered more than 750,000 votes to her opponent’s 550,000 – an overwhelming victory that left his campaign scratching its head as to where it all went wrong. “The reason that we all collectively thought that he was the favorite was because he had that national name recognition, and especially because he was able to raise so much money,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida. She noted, however, that polling largely focused on how Nixon and Vindman would respectively fare against Moody in a general election, rather than whether Democratic voters preferred Nixon or Vindman as their party’s candidate. “Is Florida ready for a democratic socialist candidate in a general election? I still don’t know the answer,” added Jewett. “But what this primary showed was that, within the Democratic party base, there is a strong majority of progressive social Democrats in Florida – just like there apparently is across the country.” Nixon’s victory followed a series of primary wins for progressive candidates this summer, including in Philadelphia, Colorado, Michigan and New York City. She only recently joined the Democratic Socialists of America, and was not endorsed by them. She is also set to face trial next month – charged with trespassing and resisting an officer without violence – after a sit-in protest at the office of the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, in May. It remains to be seen how attractive Nixon will be to Florida’s wider electorate in November. As Jewett notes, Florida is heavily populated by Hispanic communities, and Moody is certain to try to affix the “socialist” label to Nixon’s campaign that has long proven toxic at the ballot box for such voter groups. The conservative commentator Noah Rothman, writing in National Review on Wednesday, went one step further, characterizing Nixon as “communist-curious”. “Even if the race for Senate in Florida is now a foregone conclusion, this race will still feature prominently in the national conversation,” he argued. “Why? Because it demonstrates that Republicans are right when they warn that the socialist phenomenon is coming to a town near you.” Pollsters already appear to have concluded that Nixon’s primary victory has limited Democrats’ chances of taking the seat. Within hours of her fiery victory speech on Tuesday night, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, the respected analytical wing of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, moved the Florida Senate race from “likely Republican” to “safe Republican”. It also leaves Democratic leaders in the US Senate, who publicly warmly welcomed Nixon’s win, in something of a quandary. While their path to reclaiming control of the upper chamber from Republicans was never predicated on success in Florida, Vindman, as a moderate, was considered to have at least an outside shot of an upset. Accordingly, the party’s hierarchy was preparing to send dollars and resources to bolster his campaign. Now, with Nixon on the ticket, analysts expect a rethink. “The Democratic establishment was more comfortable with Vindman,” Jewett said. “He had a demonstrated track record of being able to raise money, and Nixon does not.” Florida has about 1.5 million more registered Republican voters than Democrats, she noted. “Nixon is really going to have her work cut out for her to show that she can raise money, or if she can’t, to show that somehow they can recreate the success of the grassroots campaign that brought her victory here,” Jewett added. Her supporters are certain that will be possible. Among a flood of tributes to her on Tuesday night and through Wednesday were calls for unity, including from Vindman himself, who said: “I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me.” Some of the messages were also critical of Vindman, and those in Democratic circles who bet on the wrong horse. “Angie Nixon’s win sent shock waves through the Democratic establishment who got too comfortable behind corporate donors and moderate candidates,” said Hayley Margolis, an organizer with Jewish Voice for Peace South Florida. “Her votes were hard earned through heartfelt grassroots conversations with the working class across the state of Florida.” Nixon, who was reprimanded for using a bullhorn on the Florida house floor earlier this year, does not care for internal party wrangling. And she made one thing clear: she is unlikely to change tack as she presents herself to the wider statewide electorate before November. “They look at this movement and they call us extreme, they call us radical, but I think people see through that. I won’t let them define me and I know you will always know where I stand,” she told supporters on Tuesday night. “If believing a mom shouldn’t have to work three jobs to keep a roof over her head is extreme, call me extreme. Ashley Moody can call me whatever she wants, but in November she’ll be calling me senator.”

title: Trump shows off White House renovations and ornate new helipad
body_text: As the US national debt climbed past $40tn for the first time on Wednesday, and the war with Iran that Donald Trump started nearly six months ago dragged on, forcing Americans already struggling to pay the bills to spend more on fuel, the US president led the press corps on a tour of the extensive remodeling of the White House grounds he is personally overseeing in his role as the self-styled “builder-in-chief”. The tour, during which Trump showed off upgrades such as a new granite driveway and refurbished columns, and expounded at length on newly laid grass, culminated in Trump autographing the back of a stone, inscribed with his name, to go in the center of the ornate new helipad he insists he needs. All in all, the 40-minute diversion from the work of being US president, which seemed at times like a lost episode of the 1980s TV show Lifestyles of the Rich and Famous, did little to help Trump beat the charge laid against him by senator Jon Ossoff, the Georgia Democrat who said earlier this week that the former real estate developer is not really that interested in the work of leading the nation. While US service members “fight his war” on Iran, Ossoff said, “the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom” and travel with his close aide Natalie Harp on the luxury jet gifted to him by the emir of Qatar. At one point in the tour, after Trump boasted about the “flawless granite” he replaced the asphalt driveway with, he told his captive audience of reporters: “We get the best stuff; one thing I know how to do is build.” “It’s ridiculous the way this place was taken care of,” he said. “Nobody, including other presidents, they didn’t see it. But I see it because I was very good at real estate, like maybe the best in a lot of ways.” Drawing attention to the newly laid sod around the helipad, golf course owner Trump repeated one of his favorite lines. “You know, grass has a life like humans have a life,” he said, for at least the 10th time in public remarks in the past year. “It’s all been top-soiled. In other words, we put top soil, brand new earth on top. Very, you know, very – a lot of good ingredients in that earth for grass. If you’re grass, you’re very happy,” the president said. He then pivoted to something like a product placement. “This grass is the highest quality. It was given free of charge by Scotts Miracle-Gro. Scotts. And Scotts is a great a great company. title: Trump threatens Iran’s trade partners, as military strikes make way for economic pressure
body_text: Donald Trump has announced a new campaign to isolate Iran’s economy, threatening “tremendous economic consequences” on any country that helps or does business with Tehran, a move that could set up a fresh confrontation with China if implemented. “Today, I am announcing the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face tremendous economic consequences.” His announcement however contained no detail on what actions would be taken or which countries could be affected, and comes as the war nears its six-month mark, with the president facing pressure over the cost of the conflict as the US midterm elections approach. Last month the US president paused attacks on Iran, after a fortnight of nightly strikes that had failed to bring officials in Tehran back to the negotiating table and reports that the war has run down US stockpiles of key munitions. Pentagon advisers reportedly told Trump last month that the US had nearly exhausted its list of targets in Iran and the military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness. The White House has signalled in recent weeks a shift in strategy to tightening pressure on Iran economically. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said last week the US would begin ramping up efforts to isolating Iran economically. The US treasury has for months been carrying out an effort, called Operation Economic Fury, aiming to cut off Iran’s funding with targeted sanctions, while a naval blockade in the strait of Hormuz has sought to block Iranian ports from exporting oil vital to keeping the country’s economy afloat. Iran’s economy already faces a punishing array of US and western sanctions that have ground down the economy over years and curtailed its ability to sell oil. But experts say the country’s leaders have learned to adapt to the measures, including by exporting oil through a sophisticated network of shadow tankers. In his announcement on Wednesday, Trump listed several activities that he said needed to stop immediately, including “oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies”. The wording of the president’s announcement suggested that he could be threatening secondary sanctions on countries that buy Iranian oil, but experts say such a move could lead to direct confrontation with China – Iran’s biggest trading partner – at a time when the US is trying to establish a new trading relationship with Beijing. “Whatever new economic measures the US can use will need to be directed at Iran’s trading partners,” said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst at theEurasia Group, adding that it will be “hard for the US to direct such actions at China, the country that matters most to Iran’s economic future.” Chinese leader Xi Jinping is also expected to visit the US next month, further complicating any efforts to target Beijing’s imports of Iranian oil. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said on Tuesday that military pressure and sanctions would not break Iran’s resolve. He added that Iran remained open to dialogue ⁠with the US, but would not confuse negotiations with surrender, according to the semi-official Fars news agency. On Tuesday, the United Arab Emirates, announced it would suspend all trade activities, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran, after it said it had detected two missiles launched from the country. Tehran dismissed the reports as baseless. Prior to the war, the UAE was one of Iran’s biggest trade partners, providing more than 30% of its imports. Earlier on Wednesday, Trump also claimed that vessels from Gulf countries allied with the US were continuing to move through the strait of Hormuz, despite the Iranian threat to shipping in the waterway. The president said the US military was aiding ships in the strait, saying “right now, a lot of boats are coming through.” Axios reported that US forces were facilitating the transit of 15 to 20 ships in and out of the Hormuz each night in recent weeks – carrying “roughly half the prewar volume” of daily oil shipments – while also continuing to blockade Iranian exports. Those volumes were disputed by some, with ship tracking data ‌from Kpler showing transits remained low. Referring to the Axios report, Danny Citrinowicz, the former head of the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, said it was an important operational development, but questioned how long the US government would be able to sustain such an operation. “More importantly, this will not force Iran to surrender or fundamentally change its negotiating position,” said Citrinowicz.

title: Michele Tafoya: from unassuming NFL sideline reporter to rightwing firebrand
body_text: As the third leg of NBC’s Sunday Night Football crew alongside play-by-play man Al Michaels and the tart-tongued analyst Cris Collinsworth, Michele Tafoya was a paragon of deference and neutrality for 11 years as an NFL sideline reporter, dutifully relating boilerplate tactics, talking points and injury updates when she wasn’t nodding along to softball interviews or fumbling through hammy production gimmicks for viewers who might have been too offline to get the bit. She was almost pathologically committed to not doing anything to draw attention to herself or her gender in an era when sideline reporting was a fast track to national celebrity. Even her football takes hewed to the middle. (“New Orleans doesn’t want to lose to Atlanta twice in a season …”) Anyone who says they saw the 61-year-old emerging as a rightwing firebrand was watching a different game. And yet here we are. Last week, Tafoya was the decisive winner of Minnesota’s US Senate Republican primary, earning the party’s nomination for November’s general election. Even more striking: she beat back eight challengers, not least Adam Schwarze, the party-endorsed pro-gun, pro-military ex-Navy SEAL, and Royce White, the anti-leftist, anti-trans NBA flameout currently testing WNBA gender norms. Next, Tafoya will face off against Minnesota lieutenant governor Peggy Flanagan – a Native American trailblazer, progressive champion and convenient stand-in for governor Tim Walz, Tafoya’s favorite political punching bag. (She’s been going after Walz since Kamala Harris tapped him for the 2024 Democratic presidential ticket, alleging wanton corruption.) And even though Schwarze has so far refused to back Tafoya, Minnesota Republicans are starting to like their chances with her in the race, particularly as her fundraising surge gives her the resources to compete with Flanagan. Recent polling gives the lieutenant governor a seven-point lead over Tafoya, a healthy advantage but by no means insurmountable. With her midwest mom vibes and broadcast polish, Tafoya presents as a conservative correction to Maga that may play well in a state that hasn’t sent a Republican senator to Washington in 24 years. But the difference is mostly packaging. On the issues that define today’s Republican Party – cops, immigration and the culture wars – Tafoya is every bit as committed as the chorus. In a recent Fox News appearance, she claimed there is a sense of fatigue among Minnesotans around progressive causes. “Minnesotans are exhausted,” said Tafoya, a Southern California transplant who put down roots in the 1990s. “I have talked to hundreds of voters in Minnesota who have told me, ‘Gosh, I went on vacation this summer. I didn’t want to tell people where I was from because it’s embarrassing.’ And it’s true.” It was a curious read on a famously left-leaning electorate, especially for an Emmy-winning reporter. But Tafoya gets away with it because her bland TV reputation trained audiences to hear her as harmless. So the bombshells don’t always register on arrival; especially to people who already agree with her, they sound less like provocations than conversation, another injury update perhaps. That’s not accidental. As her time on SNF was winding down in 2021, Tafoya appeared as a guest host on The View, an audition for the conservative seat on the panel that had been opened after Meghan McCain’s departure. On her first day, Tafoya sparred with Joy Behar over vaccinations, saying “the flu kills people too” in response to mounting Covid fatalities; she pushed back when Whoopi Goldberg suggested white people need to take more accountability for institutional racism. “[White people have] been doing that since the Civil War,” Tafoya said. “I’m not saying they’re perfect.” On day two, Tafoya bickered with Sunny Hostin about Colin Kaepernick, arguing the Pro Bowl quarterback turned social justice activist had been cut loose from the NFL because he couldn’t hack it any more. “I think all of us can agree that there is probably a lot to this story we still don’t know,” Tafoya, ostensibly an insider, said to audience jeers. “Oh, you’re going to groan at me?” she shot back. There was no day three. After that, Tafoya beat a hasty retreat to cable TV news, podcasting and social media, letting fly with some bracingly barbed takes – by her standards, at least. “This whole thing is insanity,” she said in a 2024 OutKick riff on trans athletes. “Thank God for voices like JK Rowling and Riley Gaines and others. I don’t care if the male is intact or was born a male – they don’t belong in a women’s locker room, they don’t belong on a women’s team.” In a recent OutKick appearance, Tafoya called the WNBA veteran turned Maga pick-me Sophie Cunningham “a hero” for opposing a supposed trans-athlete encroachment that is – checks notes – almost entirely theoretical. Critically, she has positioned herself as a grounded Maga alternative. In 2022, she published an open letter urging Donald Trump not to seek reelection, bemoaning his “messy” politics – but has since come around to toe the party line. “I had my own little Trump protest,” she said in a 2025 Fox News appearance. “I didn’t think he should run again because I thought we needed a more conventional kind of candidate. Clearly, I was wrong.” On her campaign site, she is less extreme on some subjects than Maga Republicans, making a case for abortion access in the first 12 weeks, connecting her position to her personal struggles to become a mother of two children. “I believe my position – aligned with Trump, respectful of the Dobbs decision, and firmly opposed to taxpayer funding – helps broaden the coalition of support, particularly with independents and others who seek middle ground,” she writes. “It reflects both principle and pragmatism as well as the political reality of this issue.” The day after Tafoya’s broadcast signoff from Super Bowl LVI, she was named co-chair of the 2022 Minnesota gubernatorial campaign mounted by Kendall Qualls, a Black ex-Army vet who shills a sadly familiar strain of raceless conservative politics. After failing to receive the party endorsement, Qualls withdrew from the race three months before the primary. But Walz’s resounding reelection victory as Minnesota governor, vice-presidential nomination and a rightwing-driven scandal cycle that has helped undo his progressive record, culminating in his retreat from elected office, would prove enough for Tafoya to hang a villainous origin story on, recasting herself as the lone figure who can fix what the left has broken. In another timeline, one could easily see her rushing through a soft-focus aside on Walz’s early football coaching career before swiftly tossing it back to Al and Cris. That Tafoya became the first Sunday Night Football personality to jump into politics is undoubtedly the biggest twist in America’s most-watched television show since Odell Beckham Jr’s one-handed grab. If anyone was going to be the GOP’s best chance of flipping a Senate seat in decidedly blue Minnesota, it was Tony Dungy – the Focus on the Family-coded, history-making Super Bowl coach who was a pioneering quarterback at the University of Minnesota and a visionary defensive coordinator with the Vikings. Tafoya has negotiated a political landscape that has been tough for sports candidates recently. The past four years alone have seen White (the WNBA troll), Herschel Walker (the Heisman Trophy winner), Steve Garvey (the decorated first baseman), Colin Allred (the ex-NFL linebacker) and Derek Dooley (the journeyman football coach) fail in their election bids. Only Walker landed softly, as Trump’s handpicked US ambassador to the Bahamas. Tommy Tuberville’s shambolic term as Alabama’s US senator has only served to underscore the fact that sporting greatness doesn’t necessarily translate to political skill. For all its talk of the collective, high-level athletics remains, at its core, a fundamentally individualistic endeavor pursued by inveterate glory hounds. It’s just their good fortune that the electorate takes to sports like catnip. The polls have Tuberville up 10 points in his Alabama governor bid. Once an Auburn fan, always an Auburn fan, after all. That’s what makes Tafoya’s candidacy so compelling: her long sports career placed her firmly in the spotlight, and yet she always understood her place on the sideline and deflected the attention anytime it lingered too long. She was there to illuminate, to facilitate and then quickly step out of the way so viewers could enjoy the game. That’s a formidable reservoir of residual trust to carry into politics. But will it still hold sway with Minnesota’s general election voters? No state rejects the Trumpian agenda as forcefully as the Land of 10,000 Lakes – hub of the corporate DEI rollback backlash, bulwark against the ICE incursion, laboratory of populist governance. But Tafoya’s name recognition certainly gives her a fighting chance with an electorate that, for all its stolid pretensions, has a surprising record of falling hard for celebrity candidates. Early in her broadcast career, Tafoya went by “Mickey Conley” because her radio co-host found her paternal surname too “ethnic” and not catchy enough. (Conley comes from her Irish-American mother’s side.) It’s the kind of assimilation story that could resonate in an immigration-friendly state if she didn’t also staunchly oppose federal amnesty programs. If she wins in November, Tafoya would become the first Latina Republican ever elected to the US Senate. Ultimately, though, what could hold Tafoya back is the very thing that once made her distinctive – being the standout woman in a man’s game. Maga world tends to prefer its telegenic female surrogates in front of the camera, as adornments to the movement rather than viable leaders – lest the tradwives start getting ideas. You could see how that impulse may be even stronger as Marjorie Taylor Greene, Nancy Mace and Lauren Boebert – all once fiercely loyal to Trump – broke ranks with him over the handling of the Epstein files. But in finally making herself the story, Tafoya has shown that slightly less extreme conservatism can be made more palatable through the veneer of fastidiously rehearsed professionalism. And if she pulls off an upset? Well, that’ll write the new rightwing political playbook.

Maga world tends to prefer its telegenic female surrogates in front of the camera, as adornments to the movement rather than viable leaders – lest the tradwives start getting ideas. You could see how that impulse may be even stronger as Marjorie Taylor Greene, Nancy Mace and Lauren Boebert – all once fiercely loyal to Trump – broke ranks with him over the handling of the Epstein files. But in finally making herself the story, Tafoya has shown that slightly less extreme conservatism can be made more palatable through the veneer of fastidiously rehearsed professionalism. And if she pulls off an upset? Well, that’ll write the new rightwing political playbook.

title: From McDonald’s to Congress: can a former fry cook flip a key district for Democrats?
body_text: During his presidential campaign in October 2024, Donald Trump staged a photo op at a McDonald’s franchise in Pennsylvania, where he was briefly taught how to work the fryer and drive-thru window at the closed restaurant, while making several unsubstantiated claims about Kamala Harris’s past summer job at McDonald’s. The posturing around McDonald’s garnered significant publicity, as Trump and Republicans capitalized on an affordability crisis triggered by high inflation that occurred globally due to the Covid pandemic. Now, as Trump’s promises to “end inflation” and bring down prices have fallen flat, a real former fry cook is hoping affordability will help him flip Colorado’s eighth congressional district, a swing district narrowly won by the Republican Gabe Evans in 2024. The district is rated a toss-up by the Cook Partisan Index, and affordability is front and center in Democratic nominee Manny Rutinel’s congressional campaign. Rutinel was raised by a single mother, an immigrant, and his family was one of millions who lost their homes to foreclosure in the 2008 economic recession. When Rutinel graduated high school, he was also finishing his second year working at McDonald’s. He worked multiple jobs through college, taking community college courses, having to sell his own blood plasma so frequently it has left a scar on his arm. “I’m the son of a single mom who came to America in search of that American dream, and we worked hard every single day for this country, but we still struggled,” Rutinel told the Guardian. “I remember being 10 years old the first time I started filling out food stamp and Medicaid forms, and those are the same programs that Donald Trump and my congressman Gabe Evans are destroying right now to get tax breaks to their billionaire buddies.” He worked through his associate’s degree to a bachelor’s degree, then worked as an economist for the US army corps of engineers and obtained a master’s degree from Johns Hopkins University before attending Yale Law School. He currently serves as a representative in Colorado’s state legislature, where he has “co-sponsored over 400 laws to fight for an affordable economy, make sure that folks have good-paying jobs”. Those bills include expanding the earned income tax credit, and establishing a family affordability tax credit and child tax credit in Colorado, which collectively reduced child poverty in Colorado by nearly 40%, making Colorado the state with the lowest childhood poverty rate in the US. “I think that’s the kind of leadership that we need right now in Congress, folks that understand the struggles of working people deep in their bones,” added Rutinel. “Sometimes you hear politicians talk about the affordability crisis, like they just read it in a memo somewhere. But for me, it’s deeply personal.” His opponent has faced scrutiny over whether he received an endorsement from Trump in 2024 after claiming that questions on whether the 2020 election was stolen “aren’t yes-no questions”. Earlier this year, the UFCW local 7 president, Kim Cordova, accused Evans of privately claiming he would stand by meatpacking workers in the district, only to renege on the promise when they went out on strike and remain silent. He has also not held any in-person town halls in his district since winning his election by roughly 2,500 votes in 2024. Rutinel has consistently held in-person town halls throughout the district, where he says he hears from constituents who feel as though they have been lied to by Trump and Evans over promises to address affordability. “I think folks feel like they’ve been lied to, and what they’re looking for are leaders who have the lived experience of working people, understand their struggles, and have a track record of fighting for them,” said Rutinel. He cited a family of four that is now faced with health insurance premiums of $2,000 a month compared to $500 a month in 2025 for the exact same plan, and the hundreds of thousands of Americans who are going to lose Medicaid coverage due to cuts in Trump’s “big, beautiful” bill, plus several hospitals in Colorado that are at risk of service cuts or closures due to the cuts. “We’re real grassroots campaign, and we have never accepted a single penny from corporate Pacs,” said Rutinel. “Meanwhile, Gabe Evans has accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars from the same corporate Pacs that are now driving up the costs of our groceries, our healthcare, our gas, and so there’s a big difference in our approaches, our policies, and the sort of things that we’ll be doing for this district when we get to Congress.” The Evans campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

title: ‘Starve the beast’? The $40tn cost of Republicans’ false promises to cut spending
body_text: You could pin the US’s staggering $40tn in government debt to Donald Trump’s Keystone Cops-style governance. Tariffs he sold as a new source of revenue were struck down by the supreme court, forcing the government to return tens of billions of dollars to importers. Elon Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge), ostensibly created to stop wasteful government spending, decimated federal programs and probably killed millions of children, but did nothing to close the budget deficit. The burst of inflation following Trump’s misguided adventure in Iran sharply raised the cost of serving the government’s obligations. Yet as the federal debt hits an all-time high, up from about $35tn when Trump took office less than two years ago, it is worth noting that the US’s gargantuan indebtedness is in fact the product of a longstanding Republican strategy that took shape well before Trump could even dream about gold-plating the White House. It was called “starve the beast”. One might recall Ronald Reagan’s address to the nation on 5 February 1981, just two weeks after he had taken office, when he delivered the sad news that “we’re in the worst economic mess since the Great Depression”. Government spending was out of control, he said. The budget deficit the year before had hit 2.6% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Federal debt added up to a mind-boggling trillion dollars, a third of gross domestic product (GDP) – the broadest measure of the national economy. To end the government’s profligacy, Reagan argued, required depriving it of revenue. “There were always those who told us that taxes couldn’t be cut until spending was reduced,” Reagan said. “Well, you know, we can lecture our children about extravagance until we run out of voice and breath. Or we can cure their extravagance by simply reducing their allowance.” And starving the government beast of tax revenue became the goal of Republican economic policy. The staggering budget deficit left behind by Reagan forced his successor, George H. W. Bush, to raise taxes, which cost him re-election. Every Republican administration since that speech has taken a machete to the tax schedule, slashing income tax rates for businesses and individuals, cutting estate taxes, and carving out broad tax deductions for preferred constituencies. What remained unsaid, over nearly half a century worth of tax cuts, was that the ultimate goal of the plan was not really to cure the “extravagance” and fix the government’s finances. It was, instead, to cement the Republicans’ hold on power. Despite Republicans’ sloganeering, their tax cuts never “paid for themselves” by generating a burst of economic growth. Instead, they borrowed the money to keep up spending. That invariably left Democrats in a budgetary mess to clean up every time they came into office. Bruce Bartlett, a former Republican policy adviser who worked on a precursor to Reagan’s 1981 tax cut plan, explained the strategy thus: “It’s all part of Republican plan going on for quite a long time to tie the hands of Democratic presidents.” The huge tax cuts in Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”. History may come to see Trump’s “beautiful bill” as an unprecedented attack on the nation’s public finances. The federal deficit (the annual shortfall when the government spends more money than it takes in) is now running at about 6% of GDP. The federal debt (the total owed) is running at about 123% of GDP, higher than during its peak in the second world war. Last year, paying interest on that debt cost 3.2% of GDP, about a trillion dollars, more than was spent on national defense or Medicare. Destructive though it appears, the OBBBA was just one big step along a path set 45 years ago. Federal government revenues declined as a share of GDP in every Republican administration since Reagan’s. Budget deficits widened every time. The precedent bodes ill for the Democratic administration that seems likely to succeed Trump’s unhinged four years in power. Bill Clinton’s administration offers the starkest example. Boxed in by a budget deficit equal to 4.5% of GDP that he inherited from George HW Bush, Clinton was forced to focus on deficit reduction. “Clinton comes with all these plans and ideas but they all get stomped on,” Bartlett recalled. Rather than shore up the US’s threadbare safety net, Clinton ended “welfare as we know it”, putting a stop to Democrats’ longstanding commitment to poverty alleviation. He raised taxes, despite their unpopularity, raising federal revenues over his eight years in the White House from 17% to 20% of GDP. At the end of his term, he bequeathed a budget surplus of 2.3% of GDP. His successor, George W Bush, happily spent the inheritance on huge tax cuts that largely benefited the rich. To be fair, the OBBBA, the latest chapter in the Republican’s fiscal path of destruction, did cut spending – $1tn-plus from Medicaid and food assistance programs for the poor. But that was no match for $5tn-plus worth of tax cuts doled out largely to the most affluent Americans. And this leaves Democrats, again, in a budgetary pickle. If the optimistic predictions come to pass and they win control of both houses of Congress in November and the presidency in 2028, they will arrive into the seat of power with at least one hand tied behind their back. Ambitious, expensive ideas like Medicare for All or allowances for families with children will struggle, given the ballooning deficits and debt Trump left in their way. Even undoing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, food stamps and subsidies for health insurance under Obamacare will seem forbidding. Republicans have never been punished politically for their dismal stewardship of the budget. Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden didn’t gain much from efforts towards deficit reduction. But it won’t be easy for Democrats to simply take a page from the GOP’s playbook. Financial markets are jittery. Rising bond yields alone will raise the government’s cost of servicing the debt, crowding out Democratic spending priorities. That’s hardly the end of it. Once Democrats are in the White House, Republicans will surely rediscover their long-lost concerns about the government’s lack of fiscal restraint, and do their standard budget hawk cosplay thing to force Democrats to fix the budget. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Why is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets?
body_text: Government borrowing costs around the world have surged to the highest levels in decades amid growing fears over US bond market turmoil. Anxiety about Donald Trump’s handling of the US economy, and concern that the US president’s war with Iran is driving up inflation, are causing a sell-off in the US bond market. Highlighting the world economy’s dependence on US stability, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on UK, French, German and Japanese government debt has been dragged higher. Here we look at the factors driving the bond market, and the likely consequences. What is happening in the bond market sell-off? Long-term US government borrowing costs have risen to the highest level since 2007, with the 30-year Treasury bond yield trading above 5%. A bond is a form of loan that investors make to a borrower, or bond issuer. The yield represents the money an investor receives for owning the debt as a percentage of its current price. Prices fall when investor demand wobbles, which pushes up yields. Against this backdrop, the US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said this week that Washington would at least double its purchases of long-term US bonds in an attempt to assuage investor concerns. Washington also staged a joint intervention this month with Tokyo to prop up the value of the Japanese yen. Bessent’s intervention on Wednesday helped to push down yields, but the impact was only temporary: they were rising again on Thursday, reversing most of that early move. With US Treasury bonds a lynchpin in global financial markets, the rise in US borrowing costs has dragged yields higher for other countries. G7 nations have faced among the sharpest increases: UK 10-year bond rates are close to the highest since 2008 and 30-year rates are near 1998 levels; Germany’s are at 2011 levels and France at a 16-year peak. Japanese borrowing costs have also hit the highest level since 1996. Why are bond investors rushing for the exits? The breakdown of negotiations in the US-Israel war on Iran is the main source of investor unease. The US national debt hitting $40tn (£29.3tn) for the first time – after having doubled over the past decade – is also stoking fear that Trump’s tax and spending plans are unsustainable. The stop-start fighting in the Middle East has pumped up the oil price, adding to worries over inflation and the hit to economic growth worldwide. Inflation is bad news for bond investors. This is because it undercuts the future value of money received for owning the debt, so investors demand a higher yield to compensate for the risk. In response to the inflation shock, the world’s most powerful central banks are also increasingly expected to raise interest rates. However, the unpredictable nature of the Iran war, and of the Trump administration, are making the challenge tougher. Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at Société Générale, said: “Many also believe US bonds are having a tantrum because new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, refuses to spoon-feed investors with the forward guidance they had become accustomed to.” Investors are also worried by political risk: in the US, the fear is that Trump has little appetite to curtail soaring borrowing and debt levels. Investors have asked similar questions of Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, and France is preparing for an election year in 2027 amid mounting political schisms. Japan also faces challenges as it pumps up government spending despite elevated debt levels and with its currency under pressure. Some analysts have also suggested Washington’s yen intervention was driven by worries about falling Japanese demand for US treasuries. Before the joint action, Tokyo had been attempting to prop up the currency by selling holdings of US treasuries to free up money to buy yen, which pushed down bond prices and lifted yields. The AI boom is another factor. Silicon Valley companies are borrowing heavily to fund their rollout of datacentres, which means bond investors are being asked to swallow sizeable amounts of debt. What are the consequences? The impact is far-reaching. Higher yields will push up the costs for consumers and businesses for their mortgages, loans and corporate bonds – hitting their capacity to spend elsewhere, and weighing on the economy more broadly. Governments worldwide, already awash with debt after the economic shocks of recent decades, are being squeezed. The rise in interest costs will not only add to Washington’s debt pile, complicating Trump’s tax and spending plans, but also make life harder elsewhere – including the UK and France ahead of tough budgets. Some experts predict a doom loop whereby higher debt costs crowd out room for governments to spend on growth-enhancing measures, locking in weak economic growth and tax revenues and making budget deficits and rising debt levels more likely. For the UK chancellor, John Healey, analysts at Société Générale expect the rise in borrowing costs could erase about half of the £23.6bn headroom left in reserve in the spring against the government’s self-imposed fiscal rules. What happens next? Much will depend on how the Iran war unfolds; and on whether the Trump administration changes course on tax and spending, or intervenes again in markets to support bond prices. The response from the world’s most powerful central banks will also be key. The US has historically held an “exorbitant privilege” given the US dollar’s status as the global reserve currency, ensuring demand for dollar assets and enabling it to run persistently high trade and budget deficits. However, some analysts warn that the Trump administration is putting this at risk through the president’s trade policies and eye-wateringly expansive tax and spending plans. The uncertainty comes as pressure is likely to mount on Trump in the run-up to the midterm elections in November. Most investors will be looking for an easing in geopolitical tensions, further market intervention, or a shift in tax and spending policy from Washington. Central banks offering reassurance could also help. However, some analysts warn that the ingredients are there for a market accident. Société Générale’s Edwards, who is famous for his gloomy predictions, said the conditions could be coming together for a US financial crisis. Highlighting parallels to the conditions preceding the 2008 global stock market crash, started by the US sub-prime debt crisis, and the 1997 Asian financial crisis, Edwards said: “Just as well I have a long memory, for I can remember exactly what was happening in financial markets the last time French and US long bond yields were at these levels – c2007 and even further back to c1997 for Japanese and UK yields.”

title: FBI raids Eric Swalwell’s home amid sexual assault claims inquiry – report
body_text: Authorities are said to have searched the Washington DC home of disgraced former California Democratic representative Eric Swalwell on Sunday amid an ongoing law enforcement investigation into sexual assault allegations. CNN reported that federal agents on Saturday also “seized electronic devices” from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport, citing unnamed sources familiar with the investigation. Multiple other outlets have confirmed the federal search; the Daily Mail was the first to report this law enforcement activity. Attorneys who have represented Swalwell could not immediately be reached for comment. Swalwell has denied allegations of sexual assault. Swalwell resigned from Congress following multiple allegations of sexual assault and misconduct that thwarted his campaign for governor. Before stepping down, he faced extensive bipartisan demands for him to resign or face an expulsion vote. “I am deeply sorry to my family, staff, and constituents for mistakes in judgment I’ve made in my past,” Swalwell said in a statement posted to social media in April. “I will fight the serious false allegation made against me. However, I must take responsibility and ownership for the mistakes I did make.” “Expelling anyone in Congress without due process, within days of an allegation being made, is wrong,” Swalwell had said, in reference to potential removal from office. “But it’s also wrong for my constituents to have me distracted from my duties. Therefore, I plan to resign my seat in Congress.” Swalwell’s resignation came after the US House ethics committee said it had launched an investigation into him. This bipartisan committee announced it would investigate “allegations that [Swalwell] may have engaged in sexual misconduct, including towards an employee working under his supervision”. CBS noted this investigation ended when Swalwell resigned, as the ethics committee “only has jurisdiction over current members and staff”. The US Department of Justice opened an investigation into the disgraced legislator following his resignation, a source previously told the Guardian. Swalwell’s descent from gubernatorial frontrunner to investigative target started in April. The San Francisco Chronicle published an account from an unnamed ex-staffer, who alleged that he sexually assaulted her. CNN also had a similar report which featured allegations from three other women who claimed that Swalwell had sent them unwanted explicit text messages or photos. Asked about the search, the FBI declined to comment. The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The White House on Monday disclosed declassified documents on an FBI investigation into Swalwell’s purported relationship with a possible spy more than 10 years ago. The FBI director, Kash Patel, had been reportedly pushing for the disclosure of files in this investigation, CBS News also reported.
