On 31 July, DHS released a public notice arguing that New Jersey’s administrative errors demonstrated a need for standardized federal oversight. The taskforce also declassified documents in a Michigan case where the FBI investigated suspected fraudulent voter registrations by a get-out-the-vote organization, in which no criminal charges were filed, and investigative material related to a data scrape of voter information in Maricopa county, Arizona. The pace of releases has been accelerating. On Monday, the taskforce declassified and released investigative files related to an investigation into Chinese intelligence, which disclosed how disgraced former Democratic US representative Eric Swalwell had told FBI agents how he had “occasionally hooked up” with Christine Fang, a Chinese national allegedly engaged in a political influence campaign. On Tuesday, the US Census Bureau released a brief claiming it had identified 24,000 noncitizens voting in the 2020 election in a preliminary match of 128m records. It did not reveal its methodology and was sharply criticized by democracy advocates. “This alleged analysis based on census data fails the laugh test,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “The administration does not provide a sufficient explanation of how it arrived at these numbers – and for good reason.” Branch, of Elias Law Group, suggested the Trump administration is “searching for” the legal basis for an executive order. “I think they believe there may be one. I think such a document just doesn’t exist, because the fact is our elections are secure,” she said. “Noncitizen voting in our elections is just not a widespread problem … All of the fear and narrative around that issue is just completely unfounded, and it’s really just to stoke fear and lay the groundwork for future action.” In July, DHS also released an analysis arguing that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections. It did not reveal its methodology for identifying the noncitizens, either, or disclose how confident its officials were in their assessment. The tool it used to flag noncitizens on voter rolls is known to be inaccurate. ‘The founders recognized the risk of centralizing power’ Asked about the possibility of an executive order declaring a national emergency on elections, the White House did not rule it out, refusing to comment on hypotheticals. “Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the Save America Act,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, referring to legislation that would enforce a crackdown on voting. “The American people overwhelmingly support this commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections. President Trump is absolutely right: we fix this now, or we lose our country.” The Save America Act would require states to submit their voter rolls to federal inspection, effectively give DHS the power to de-register anyone it deemed ineligible to vote. The act would also sharply curtail mail-in voting – a practice Trump repeatedly criticized, but has reportedly done himself as recently as in this week’s Florida Republican primary – and require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and a narrow set of photo IDs to cast a ballot. “I mean, we’ve been closely monitoring what the administration is saying,” said Branch, who sees the rhetoric itself as an act of intimidation. “The constitution is extremely clear on this, and the founders recognized the risk of centralizing power over elections in the executive branch,” she added. “Very helpful, in terms of litigation to push back on these types of efforts.”

title: Tim Scott defends Darline Graham’s ‘national security is not my thing’ comment
body_text: Tim Scott defended fellow US South Carolina Republican senator Darline Graham’s knowledge of national security issues ahead of their state’s runoff election on Tuesday. Graham, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat held by her brother Lindsey Graham after his sudden death in July, is in a Republican primary runoff against South Carolina congressman Ralph Norman. During a debate between the two on Tuesday night, Graham struggled to answer a question about US national security interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,” she said during the debate. She added: “National security is not my thing.” Scott tried to assuage concerns about her experience on Sunday when he was asked about Graham’s qualifications – and whether a US senator should have an understanding of national security issues. “Well, the answer is yes. And she does,” he said during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press. He went on to give an answer that did not detail any of her national security experience. “The question we’re asking ourselves today is whether or not she is prepared to serve in the United States Senate and represent the people of South Carolina on the issues that are germane to the moment, with all the issues of the moment,” he said. “And is she prepared to hit those issues? She hits those issues spot-on.” Graham held various public policy jobs in South Carolina – but never had run for or held public office before she was appointed to the Senate. Beside Scott, Donald Trump has endorsed Graham – and he traveled to South Carolina on Friday to rally for her. The president also brushed off Graham’s answer on Friday. “I watched that,” he said. “I thought it was a very honest answer, actually.”

title: Democrats incredulous over Hakeem Jeffries and Jared Kushner meeting
body_text: Democrats and other Donald Trump critics reacted incredulously to a New York Times report on Sunday that House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries met with Jared Kushner, the president’s influential son-in-law, to discuss possible areas of collaboration. The reported meeting comes months ahead of the November midterm elections in which Democrats are favored to retake the US House, a development that would make Jeffries speaker. If they are in the majority, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively investigate the Trump administration, including self-enrichment by the president and his family. There are longstanding conflict-of-interest concerns about the way Kushner has continued to make money from foreign nations as he works on foreign affairs, including conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza. Asked about the reported meeting, Jeffries said in a statement: “Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people. To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition. “The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver. In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us.” Nonetheless, among some who lamented the reported gathering was Tommy Vietor, previously an aide to former president Barack Obama and now a co-host of the left-leaning podcast Pod Save America. “Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas,” Vietor posted. In April, Democrats on the House judiciary committee opened an investigation into Kushner’s financial conflict of interest. The investigation is focused on the way Kushner’s private business has raised money from Gulf nations while Kushner served as a special envoy for peace for the government. “You cannot both be a diplomat and a financial pawn of the Saudi monarchy at the same time; you cannot faithfully represent the United States with billions of dollars in Saudi and Emirati cash burning a hole in every pocket of every suit you own,” Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, wrote in an April letter to Kushner. The reaction to the meeting underscores the appetite that Democrats have to bring a no-holds barred approach to investigating Trump during the final two years of his second presidency, should they have the opportunity. Not all Democrats have taken such a pugilistic approach to Trump. The Michigan governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, for example, has taken a more collaborative approach to working with Trump in his second term. Asked whether he supported the meeting during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Senator Chris van Hollen – a Maryland Democrat – said: “I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas. But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.” Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican congressman from Illinois who is an outspoken Trump critic and served on a House committee that investigated the Capitol attack, posted in reference to the meeting, “Make this make sense,” while tagging Jeffries. Appearing on Sunday on Fox News, Mike Johnson, the US House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, asserted Kushner was “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House”. “I don’t know what that’s about,” Johnson said of Kushner’s reported meeting with Jeffries. “I know Jared has interests and lots of other things going on.”

title: Start your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar race
body_text: He got the wrong end of the stick. Donald Trump couldn’t figure out how to hold the green flag until his wife, Melania Trump, and Command Sgt Maj Matt Williams set him right. Then the US president waved the flag fast and furious like an excited schoolboy. The race was under way – and his conquest of Washington DC was complete. Since returning to Washington, Trump has deployed the national guard, wrecked the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, demolished the East Wing of the White House and run the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts into the ground. His face adorns the Department of Justice, and he still has grand plans for a triumphal arch worthy of a Roman emperor. On Sunday he made the nation’s capital tremble with fast, flashy cars brazenly roaring around a 1.7-mile (2.7km) street circuit in IndyCar’s Freedom ⁠250 Grand Prix, the capstone of his Maga-flavoured celebration of the 250th anniversary of US independence. Washington was not built for a Trump rally on wheels and had to make accommodations, like a party host bracing for a noisy and obnoxious guest. More than 200 manhole covers were welded down around the course so they would not be sucked up by cars thundering over them. The National Gallery of Art studied how vibrations from the vehicles might affect its exhibits and shielded some outdoor sculptures. Indeed, as the vehicles whizzed by the National Archives, home to the US’s desperately fragile founding documents, and the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, where Neil Armstrong’s spacesuit requires constant vigilance, it was not hard to imagine anxious curators twitching at every rattle of crockery or spillage of tea. Not that the president seemed to be sweating it. While officially the Grand Prix was open to everyone – and DC’s Democratic mayor, Muriel Bowser, declared, “Drivers, to your cars!” – the event had a distinctly Trumpian flavour reminiscent of June’s Ultimate Fighting Championship bouts on the White House South Lawn. The UFC impresario Dana White, testosterone avenger Pete Hegseth and “human printer” Natalie Harp, who would wait for Trump as ardently as Penelope did for Odysseus, were among the guests. Democratic socialists were less in evidence. IndyCar is neither Woke 1 nor Woke 2. Wearing a dark blue suit, white shirt and red tie, Trump gave fist pumps and shook hands with the IndyCar drivers. They posed for photographers, Trump giving his signature thumbs-up, as the sun gleamed off the US Capitol dome beyond. The president gave a perfunctory TV interview to the Fox network. Why was it important for him to bring IndyCars to the streets of DC? The reply was very Trumpian: “Well, Roger [Penske, a billionaire who owns the IndyCar series] told me they’ve been trying to do it for 20 years, and he’d come down; I think he said he was down 211 times to try and get it done. And when he came to see Trump, it got done in about 15 minutes, and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible.” Translation: every previous administration and mayor thought this plan was madness, and told Penske where to go. Note also the characteristic reference to “Trump” in the third person, and the boast that only he could fix it, and in 15 minutes. (If only ending the Ukraine war were so easy.) A ceremonial trundle True to form, the president also bragged about the crowd size and, as he has done since UFC night, insisted that he knows better than the meteorologists. “You know, I was hearing about rain all week long. ‘It’s gonna rain, it’s gonna rain.’ I said: ‘No, it’s not.’ And this is as nice today as I’ve seen in Washington in a long time.” Trump climbed into his armoured limousine, the Beast, mounted with flags and flashing blue and red lights, and trundled a ceremonial lap of the track. Was that Harp sprinting after him? Or hiding in the trunk? No, but we did get the Qatari-gifted plane that Trump has used as Air Force One flying overhead, escorted by four fighter jets. Then Christopher Macchio, one of Trump’s favourite singers, performed The Star-Spangled Banner as Trump saluted and Melania, wearing a white blouse, stood with hand on heart in the presidential box, a temporary white, air-conditioned structure with a clear front. A trained bald eagle was released near the start line, swooping and flying overhead before returning to its handler. There were flyovers of military aircraft including a B-2 stealth bomber. Officials paused air traffic at Washington’s Ronald Reagan National airport for three hours to accommodate them. It fell to another stalwart ally, interior secretary Doug Burgum, sporting sunglasses, to bellow: “Gentlemen, start your engines!” The race began, with drivers completing 147 laps covering roughly 250 miles (400km), and produced an American winner in Kyle Kirkwood. It was the latest chapter of a sporting summer in which Trump inserted himself into the UFC fights, the football World Cup final and the Patriot Games, a cross between a game show and athletics meet for high schoolers. Never slow to demonstrate his fealty to Trump, Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, told Fox News that he wants to bring the IndyCar Grand Prix back next year and make it an annual event. By then, one hopes, Trump will have figured out how to hold and wave a green flag. Or as they say in Iran, a white flag.

title: Ex-mayor Dan Sullivan supports incumbent Dan Sullivan’s Senate bid against third Dan Sullivan
body_text: Dan Sullivan supports Dan Sullivan against Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s US Senate election, says a former Alaskan mayor who recently backed the race’s Republican incumbent over a challenger sharing their name. That development provided another of multiple absurd elements to Dan S Sullivan’s campaign for a third term in the US Senate, which – beside Mary Peltola, a former Alaska Democratic congresswoman – has drawn opposition from Dan J Sullivan. Dan J Sullivan emerged from an 18 August primary to join a four-candidate field rounded out by Dan S Sullivan, Peltola and one other contender. His presence in the field for the general election during the 3 November midterms has prompted accusations that he is a Democratic plant aiming to draw enough votes away from Dan J Sullivan – whose name was positioned consecutively to him on the primary ballot – so that Peltola can win. Donald Trump’s Republican party is projected to lose congressional seats during the midterms, and the president wrote on social media on the day of the primary, “ALASKA: Be careful. VOTE FOR THE REAL DAN SULLIVAN TODAY. “The Dumocrats know how good he is and have put up an imposter of the same name.” Trump, though, was not the only Republican politico to come out swinging for Dan S Sullivan’s re-election bid on the day of the primary, in which Peltola finished first. Another who came out in favor of the incumbent was Dan A Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, Alaska, for six years beginning in 2009. “As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for [Senator] Daniel S Sullivan,” he also wrote. “He’s been great for Alaska.” Dan A Sullivan’s statement of support for Dan S Sullivan, the senator, at the expense of Dan J Sullivan invoked a colloquial term meaning original. It was unclear if he staked the claim of being the original because, at 75, he was older than Dan S Sullivan, 61, and Dan J Sullivan, 70, a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee with no prior political experience. He also entered his first elected office before Dan S Sullivan – on Anchorage’s governing assembly, where he served from 1999 to 2008. The Republican party unsuccessfully went to court to try to prevent Dan J Sullivan from running in the primary, maintaining that his campaign was a Democratic-engineered sham trying to confuse voters into selecting him rather than Alaska’s junior US senator since 2015. Dan J Sullivan – who appeared on the primary ballot with no party affiliation – has denied running at the behest of the Democratic party, which has not held a Senate seat in Alaska since 2008. “This is my choice,” he said to the Associated Press in June. Adding that he was displeased with the state of affairs in the US, he told the outlet: “I have every right to run.”

title: From Arizona to Wisconsin, election deniers are vying for office nationwide
body_text: Election deniers are back on the ballot. In most swing states, at least one major Republican candidate has questioned or outright denied the results of the 2020 US presidential election, which Donald Trump lost to Joe Biden. While voters in swing states have previously largely rejected candidates who denied election results, Republicans running for statewide offices across much of the country are trying again. In Arizona, gubernatorial candidate and US representative Andy Biggs voted against certifying his own state’s election results. In Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial hopeful Tom Tiffany similarly voted against certifying the 2020 results as a US representative for his state. Candidates for governor in Pennsylvania and Michigan have cast doubt on the validity of the 2020 results. And some swing state Republican candidates for secretary of state have questioned or denied election results. Governors sign off on state election results, issuing certificates to the presidential electors of whichever candidate wins. They can call for investigations or special sessions, and use their bully pulpit to cast doubt on election results. Secretaries of state are meanwhile the chief election officials in most US states, overseeing voting systems and advising the local jurisdictions that run elections. They usually play a role in certifying election results, too. In 2020, Trump pressured governors and secretaries of state, alongside a host of state and local officials in several swing states, to withhold their signatures in a broad campaign to overturn his loss. Swing state governors and secretaries of state refused to stall or impede their states’ results. But if election deniers or skeptics are elected to these key statewide roles, they would be in office in 2028, raising apprehension that they may refuse to sign off on results, or succumb to pressure from Trump and his allies, should Republicans lose. None of the candidates mentioned below responded to inquiries from the Guardian about who they currently believe won the 2020 election, or whether they would certify the 2028 results. Arizona Governor candidate: Andy Biggs Biggs, a former state lawmaker elected to the US Congress in 2016, still has not straightforwardly acknowledged Biden’s 2020 victory. That year, he pressured Arizona Republicans, including the speaker of the statehouse, not to certify the valid election results. He has repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that there is widespread voter fraud and cast doubt on voting machines. On 6 January 2021, Biggs voted against accepting the electoral votes in his home state of Arizona, and in Pennsylvania. In prepared remarks, he called for an audit of the results in Arizona. The eventual audit by the Arizona senate affirmed Biden’s win. The Arizona senate president who launched the audit, Warren Petersen, is the Republican nominee for attorney general this year. “The debate as to the legitimacy of the 2020 presidential election has been suppressed by the left and its propogandists [sic] in the media….until today,” Biggs said in his prepared remarks. He reportedly sought a presidential pardon for his role in seeking to overturn the election results. He faces incumbent Democratic governor Katie Hobbs in November. Secretary of state candidate: Alex Kolodin Kolodin, a state representative and attorney, served as legal counsel on lawsuits seeking to overturn the 2020 results in Arizona. He has also represented some of the fake electors in the state, who were charged for their roles by attorney general Kris Mayes, though the case was dismissed earlier this year. Kolodin was disciplined by the state bar of Arizona, including a period of probation and required ethics courses. Kolodin dismissed the complaints as made by “radical left-wing activists”. Kolodin faces Democratic incumbent Adrian Fontes in November. Georgia Governor candidate: Rick Jackson Jackson, a rich healthcare executive, attacked Georgia’s current Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, calling him a “Judas” in his campaign ads. Raffensperger refused to give in to pressure from Trump to question and overturn the state’s results. Raffensperger lost in the primary, where Jackson and Burt Jones, who was one of Georgia’s fake electors, made it to a runoff. Jackson won the runoff. title: US supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in voting
body_text: The US supreme court sided with Donald Trump on Monday in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it remains unclear if his administration can take action ahead of the midterm elections in November. Justices on the court voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction from June that a judge in Massachusetts placed on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful,” the majority wrote in an unsigned order. “On that score, time will tell.” The three liberal justices dissented. In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”. Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections. Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued over Trump’s March order, saying the US constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. They argued that imposing sweeping changes so close to the election risked disenfranchising voters and disrupting preparations already under way. A judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, sided with the plaintiff states – nearly half the country – and ruled that Trump lacked authority to dictate how states administer federal elections. She also questioned whether federal agencies could compile accurate citizenship lists. An appeals court upheld her decision. Talwani later issued a second injunction with nationwide effect. The justice department had argued that the states’ lawsuit was premature because the administration had not yet taken concrete actions that harmed them and they therefore lacked legal standing to sue. The administration said the Massachusetts injunction prevented it from finalising and implementing policies intended to promote “election integrity” before November. Republican-led states backed the administration before the supreme court, arguing that states would have an opportunity to provide input on the final lists of eligible voters. The supreme court’s conservative majority has now lifted the first injunction, allowing the administration to move forward while litigation continues. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the House of Representatives, said: “The sycophantic Supreme Court majority’s decision in the vote-by-mail case is sowing chaos in service to Donald Trump’s effort to undermine our free and fair elections. The Trump-aligned justices on the supreme court did not and cannot give the President the power to decide how states run elections or who gets to vote by mail.” Jeffries added: “The legal fight against Donald Trump’s unlawful executive order is not over, the order does not override the Constitution and the power to regulate elections remains with states and the Congress.” Letitia James, New York’s attorney general, called the court’s decision a “painful setback” but said her office was exploring all legal options. “It won’t be the final word,” she said. Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said his state is also planning a legal challenge. “The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country,” Newsom said in a statement. “California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented.” Voting right activists condemned the ruling. Derrick Johnson, the president of the NAACP, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever, guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it, and we have to protect the rights we do have within it. “Those in power know full well that they are unpopular and will lose in a free and fair election, and so they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote. Trump’s order has nothing to do with election integrity. It has everything to do with maintaining power at all costs.” The wrangling over how US voters can cast their ballots comes less than 100 days until November’s midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in the US Senate and House of Representatives. Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024, according to the States United Democracy Center, alongside one in five registered Republicans. About 30% of all ballots were cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found roughly four cases of fraud for every 10m mail ballots cast. Trump’s executive order forms part of a wider effort to reshape the electoral system. He has repeatedly made false claims of widespread fraud in American elections, including his defeat by Joe Biden in 2020, and has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass the Save America Act, a contentious package of voting restrictions.

title: Darline Graham and Ralph Norman head to South Carolina’s Senate runoff
body_text: Reese Boyd, the chair of the Horry county Republican party marveled on Monday afternoon at how little time Senator Darline Graham and Representative Ralph Norman have had to campaign for the Senate primary: “This is not the normal way of things.” “This is something that usually lasts at least, you know, the better part of a year,” he said. “People normally spend the better part of 18 months getting ready for it. Who knows? This may be the right way to do it? Who knows.” On Tuesday, Graham and Norman will conclude a 45-day campaign sprint that began with the unexpected death of Lindsey Graham in July. Henry McMaster, the state’s Republican governor, appointed Graham’s sister, Darline, to serve out the remainder of his term. Because Lindsey Graham had won the Republican primary, state law required a fresh election to replace him on the ballot in November. The winner will face Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and the Democratic candidate, in a state where Democrats haven’t won statewide in two decades. Many observers had expected Darline Graham to serve in a caretaker role while South Carolina’s political leadership staged a political knife fight for a rare shot at a US Senate seat. Instead, the political newcomer – a career civil servant who led the state’s commission for the blind – surprised the political establishment and announced her decision to stand for a full term – with the encouragement and backing of Donald Trump. Graham overcame concerns about her lack of legislative experience earlier this month, claiming the top spot to advance to the 25 August runoff, from a sprawling, 10-candidate Republican field. “I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” Graham said recently, referring to a well-publicized gaffe in a debate last week with Norman, where she responded to a question about defense policy by saying that military stuff “is not my thing”. Norman has pounced on her comment, highlighting it as an example of her unreadiness for the role. “Imagine if I went to [head football coach] Dabo Swinney at Clemson and any of the coaches and said: ‘Look, I got a prospect I want you to look at, and I want them to,” Norman said to the Associated Press. “‘They can start. I want you to sign them up. They can start for the next six years.’ ‘What’s the qualifications?’ ‘They’re kin to Tom Brady.’ Tell me how that analogy doesn’t work here.” Lindsey Graham had built a reputation as a foreign policy hawk, who championed the US war against Iran and rallied support for Ukraine in its defense against the Russian invasion. Darline Graham has framed her candidacy as a way to “carry my brother Lindsey’s legacy”. Since being sworn in as his successor last month, she has voted along party lines, but little else is known about her politics. Norman, who has been called the most conservative member of the US House, is running billboard advertisements on South Carolina highways that say “Voting for Ralph Norman is MAGA” as an answer to Trump’s endorsement of Graham. Trump framed his support for Darline Graham as the repayment of a favor to his late friend, Lindsey Graham. “I asked her to do this,” Trump said on Friday in a campaign stop in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. “I said, ‘Darline, you gotta do it.’ ‘Cause everyone loves her, everyone respects her. I’ve known her, through Lindsey … I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows, including me. That does not make me happy. I’m not happy about that.” But by elevating a relative political unknown whose primary appeal to voters is her promise to follow the president’s lead, Trump has offered one more high-profile test of his influence over Republican voters before the midterm elections in 10 weeks, a point he made explicit at the rally on Friday. “The problem that we have is, they say that Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come and they don’t vote for senators, congressmen and other Republicans,” the president said. “And that these people, they’re running, they’re great. But Trump isn’t actually on the ballot. So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote.”

title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?
body_text: In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting “tariffs and war”. If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate. “When it comes to tariffs, healthcare, immigration, when it comes to the war in Iran, these are all things that are having a negative impact on people in Kansas,” Hamilton, 62, said in an interview. “That makes this a particularly vulnerable time for Roger Marshall. Then, I think I’m a particularly strong candidate. I wouldn’t have got in the race if I didn’t.” The founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary earlier this month. His campaign recently announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party’s primary, though Marshall is still favored to win. For national Democratic leaders, the possibility of a close Senate race in Kansas is enticing. Their path to retaking Congress’s upper chamber involves winning at least three seats in states that Donald Trump carried two years ago, and they’ve named Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa as among their best bets to do so. The US president’s slumping approval ratings and the Iran war’s impact on prices for gasoline and other staples are seen as boosting Democrats’ chances in those states, but Kansas is a bit redder. Trump carried it two years ago by a 16 percentage point margin. This week, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told Punchbowl News that if the November elections wind up producing a “blue wave” of Democratic victories, Hamilton may well win. Asked what he thought of Schumer’s prediction, Hamilton said: “I don’t agree with that. I think there will be a blue wave, but I’m telling you, here in Kansas, we have a real chance to win. I don’t care what else happens across the country.” No Kansas Democrat has won a full term in the US Senate since attorney George McGill in 1932, the longest streak of any state. In 1974, Senator Bob Dole, who would go on to become the chamber’s Republican leader and run unsuccessfully against President Bill Clinton in 1996, nearly lost his bid for a second term, but Republicans have wiped out their opponents ever since. Democrats and their causes have had better luck at the state level. The governor’s mansion has seesawed between the two parties since the late 1950s, and the race this year to replace outgoing Democratic governor Laura Kelly is viewed as a toss-up. After the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, Kansans have on two occasions rejected Republican-backed attempts to curb abortion access in the state. “Kansas voters, the majority anyway, there’s something about the Senate where, especially those moderate Republicans, still won’t pull the trigger in terms of enough of them voting for a Democrat, where they will for governor,” said Bob Beatty, a longtime state politics watcher who chairs the political science department at Washburn University in Topeka. But Hamilton’s experience in leading a church gives him a unique skill set that Beatty predicts will make for “a very competitive race” against Marshall. “What Hamilton has going for him is the communication side. He’s been giving sermons, AKA speeches, to crowds of thousands for years,” he said. Marshall is an OB/GYN who represented western Kansas in the US House of Representatives, then won election to the Senate in 2020 and embraced Trump’s debunked claims of fraud in that year’s presidential vote. He has been an ally of Trump in Congress, and last year left a town hall early after attendees pressed him about the Trump administration’s funding cuts and layoffs of federal employees. A spokesperson for the senator did not respond to a request for comment. Hamilton said he decided to jump into the Senate race ahead of Easter, as he prepared to preach the sermon on the mount at his Church of the Resurrection outside Kansas City, which boasts around 24,000 congregants. Hamilton has criticized Marshall for being “a spokesperson for Washington and Donald Trump instead of representing the people of Kansas”, and accused the senator of spending most of his time in Florida. Marshall has acknowledged owning a property in that state, but recently told reporters it was destroyed by a hurricane. Earlier this month, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported he’d put the Sarasota property on the market for $1.45m. The senator recently called his opponent a “megachurch pastor that’s too woke for Kansas”, the Capital-Journal reported. Main Street Fund, a Massachusetts-based Super Pac that lists its treasurer a consultant who has worked for Republican campaigns, spent more than $600,000 this month to air ads in Kansas, making a similar accusation against Hamilton that the Kansas City Star found relied on snippets from his sermons that were taken out of context. Like so much in his career, Hamilton’s chances may come down to faith. Jim Slattery, a Democratic former congressman from the state who supports Hamilton, described him as “a known quantity in the Methodist world in Kansas” and among Christians in the Kansas City area who may win if he gains the support of right-leaning Catholic voters opposed to the war with Iran. “The reason Hamilton is a compelling candidate is because he can, and he has the ability to, dramatically expand the audience for a Democrat candidate in Kansas,” Slattery said. “It’s the bottom line.” • This article was amended on 26 August 2026. title: First Thing: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan
body_text: Good morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges. Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections. What did the dissenting judges say? In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”. How have rights organisations reacted? The president of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Derrick Johnson, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it and we have to protect the rights we do have within it … they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote.” Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steel Donald Trump has announced a new 50% tariff on automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbours with traditionally strong economic ties. The US president said Canada had been “ripping off” the US for years and that it was “among the worst Nations in the World to deal with”. How has Canada reacted? The country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters that Trump’s announcement was largely expected. “It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff,” he said. Carney has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”, and said Canada could not accept any proposed trade deal that would weaken French language protections. US strikes vessel in eastern Pacific, killing two people in first attack in months The US military has struck a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking. US Southern Command (SouthCom) said it had “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”. SouthCom did not provide evidence of the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking. Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series since the Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US. Numerous reports, however, indicate the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country. US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do. It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally. Iran vowed retaliation against any country that takes part in the US-led isolation campaign. Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war. In other news … Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants. The country continues to deal with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes. US healthcare officials said a food-poisoning outbreak tied to alfalfa sprouts had sickened people in at least 15 states. Target has pulled a controversial Halloween costume off its shelves after criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature. A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said. An independent arbitrator has ordered the Washington Post to rehire the high-profile opinion columnist Karen Attiah, who was fired abruptly last September over social media comments about Charlie Kirk. Stat of the day: Trump administration plans to revoke 200,000 asylum seekers’ visas A Department of State spokesperson said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security “to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”. Associated Press put the number of people potentially involved at as many as 200,000, which would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history. Culture pick: Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover The creators of Strange New Worlds talk about boldly sewing where no one has sewn before. Don’t miss this: Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold Everybody loves seals and sea lions – the dogs of the ocean – but in Australia there are fears that bird flu has jumped species and could endanger them. Lisa Cox investigates. … or this: Why we’re still so fascinated by Meg White Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer who did things her own way. Climate check: Nevada files lawsuit challenging federal plan for Colorado River revival Nevada has filed a federal lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s plan for the imperilled Colorado River, which threatens to cut roughly 20% of the water supplied to lower basin states – Nevada, Arizona and California – over the next two years. It could become the first of many court battles over the waterway that supplies 40 million people, dozens of tribes and 5.5m acres of farmland across the American west. Last Thing: Toddler invades pitch during Minnesota’s MLS win over San Jose A toddler interrupted a Major League Soccer match between Minnesota United and San Jose Earthquakes at the weekend by invading the pitch – a bizarre scene punctuated by an on-air analyst saying: “There’s a baby on the field.” There’s an adorable video of it to enjoy. title: Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it
body_text: Despite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking about Abdul El-Sayed’s biceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot of fitness content in his campaign. I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has a serious image problem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal. “Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News website Axios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed ‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”. Fox News would appear to reluctantly agree with the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.” Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewole proclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.” Sex sells too: it’s well established that voters around the world prefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016 study found that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study by the Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.) Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960, 70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedy in the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup. You can quibble with the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In his memoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.” In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’
body_text: Ken Paxton, a Republican candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has unveiled plans to tackle the “negative impact” of datacenters amid a growing backlash across the political spectrum. Paxton, endorsed by Donald Trump but facing a close contest against Democrat James Talarico, posted a “Texas first” datacenter plan on X with a graphic that the social media network flagged as “Made with AI”. Republicans have been struggling to keep up with a shift in public opinion fueled by concerns that power- and water-hungry datacenters will push up energy costs and harm the environment. Some fear the issue could prove costly in November’s US midterm elections. An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey last month found that 61% of Americans now oppose the building of a new datacenter in their area, an increase from 49% in March. This includes 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents. Last year Greg Abbott, the governor of Texas, dubbed his state the “epicenter of AI development”, but on Sunday he told ABC’s This Week program that tech companies “basically dug their own grave for the problem that’s been caused for them and that’s why they got the backlash they deserve”. On Monday his ally Paxton, currently the state attorney general in Texas, outlined a four-point plan that includes banning Chinese technology to power US datacenters, holding companies criminally liable if AI chatbots undermine children’s safety and cutting red tape to ensure datacenters do not raise Texans’ electricity bills. He also pledged to support Abbott’s state plan to ban new datacenters from rural neighborhoods, repeal sales tax exemptions and ensure they are adding to Texas’s electricity capacity rather than taking from it. Paxton said in a statement: “Texans deserve a fighter to lead and represent them as we address the growing presence of datacenters in Texas and stop their negative impact on our neighborhoods. “This plan will ensure that happens while putting Texas first, protecting our culture and land, and safeguarding our families and communities. My plan will also work to ensure that datacenters are not utilized to power Al platforms that endanger our children.” The move signals an effort by Paxton, a rightwing populist who defeated the incumbent US senator John Cornyn in a Republican primary runoff, to blunt attacks on what could be a potential electoral issue. His rival Talarico has urged tighter regulations on datacenter development and an end to sweetheart tax deals for big tech companies. Talarico accused Paxton of trying to erase his history giving datacenter tax handouts. He said in a statement: “Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million dollars from the datacenter industry, voted to flood Texas with datacenters by giving them billions in tax handouts, and has refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans’ requests to block datacenter development in their communities. “Now he’s scared his ties to big datacenter companies will lose him the election, so he’s making a sad attempt to reverse course by releasing a plan he literally used AI to make.” The race is tight in what is traditionally a Republican stronghold. A Fox News poll in late July showed Talarico leading 51% to 48%. The Cook Political Report describes the election as a toss-up. Paxton is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement. Last year his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Politicians are scrambling to adjust to the backlash against AI datacenters, which consume huge quantities of electricity and water, threaten to alter the landscape of local communities, and create relatively few jobs. Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, last year championed a $20bn investment by Amazon but last week signed an executive order he said imposes the “strictest guardrails in the nation”. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator for Vermont, has urged big tech leaders to pause AI development. The Axios website reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter discontent with the centers is endangering the party’s chances of defending a Senate seat in Ohio. Trump, however, remains supportive of the industry. He told Punchbowl News recently: “I saw Texas the other day sort of is against datacenters. I think it’s a mistake. And I’m not taking positions, I just think it’s a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

title: Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared Kushner
body_text: Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the US House of Representatives, has defended his meeting with Jared Kushner and claimed it was arranged at the request of Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Jeffries, who has come under attack from Democrats since the New York Times reported on Sunday that the two met privately to discuss common ground on issues like housing, immigration and the high cost of living, said he agreed to the meeting “to discuss the affordability crisis” in the US. In an X post on Monday, Jeffries insisted: “No one from the Trump cartel is getting a pass.” “I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass,” he said. “We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.” Jeffries appeared to be referring to actions planned by Democrats should they retake control of US Congress in November’s midterm elections. But in meeting with Kushner – who serves as an envoy for the Trump administration, working on conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran – Jeffries provoked a response from Democrats and Republicans alike. Tommy Vietor, a former Obama aide and co-host of Pod Save America, criticized Kushner, noting that he had “no actual government job” and claiming he “just uses his family connections to get money from Gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals”. Former Clinton strategist James Carville said in an “urgent message to Hakeem Jeffries” that the House minority leader had no business meeting with Kushner. A more appropriate response than meeting to discuss affordability, Carville suggested, would be to “drag his ass” before a congressional committee and grill him on his “backdoor-dealing” with other figures in Trump’s orbit. The Trump administration, family members and cronies “have no idea what they’re doing”, Carville added. “They’re making every backdoor bullshit deal they can. And we don’t meet with them. Don’t meet with them.” New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who opposed a primary challenge to Jeffries’ Brooklyn seat by the city councilman Chi Ossé, was asked if he would still support the representative as House majority leader if Democrats take back the House in November. “I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader,” Mamdani said. Republicans have mostly been more circumspect about the meeting. “I don’t know what that’s about,” the House speaker, Mike Johnson, told Fox News’s Peter Doocy on Sunday. “I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on.” “He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House,” Johnson added. In an earlier response to news of the meeting, Jeffries said that he was looking “to stop the madness”, adding that Democrats “have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition”.

title: Trump faces backlash from Republicans over plan to lift tariffs on beef imports
body_text: Donald Trump is facing growing criticism from within his own party over his decision to temporarily pause US tariffs on foreign beef in a bid to bring down grocery prices. The president’s announcement that the US will import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs has alarmed some senior Republicans, who warn that “flooding” stores with imports will hit US ranchers. This comes as the US faces a 75-year low in cattle inventory. Trump claimed his administration had secured a commitment that the imported would be sold at 25% below “current market prices” on Friday, adding: “This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.” But many GOP members are apprehensive and issued rare rebukes of the new policy. “Americans want US beef on the table – not foreign imports,” John Barrasso, a Republican senator from Wyoming and the majority whip, wrote in a post on X. “Wyoming ranchers produce the highest quality beef in the world. Our ranchers don’t ask for special treatment. They simply want a fair marketplace. It needs to be easier – not harder – for Wyoming ranchers to feed America.” On Tuesday, Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, defended the president’s move as an attempt to mitigate prices for consumers. “This is a very short-term fix from the president’s perspective, that he believed necessary to get lower cost beef on to American plates,” Rollins said in an interview with Spectrum News. However, the agriculture secretary said that she did not yet know where the beef would be imported from, noting that it was part of US trade representative Jamieson Greer’s remit. “I am actually not part of any of those conversations, so I am not sure what that looks like. I think we’ll know very soon,” Rollins said. This comes after a cascade of criticism from Republican lawmakers last week. “I absolutely want to see those prices come down,” said congresswoman Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee in a competitive race for a US Senate seat in Iowa. “But I think this isn’t the way to do that.” In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Hinson added: “I think we need to focus on letting our cattle men grow their herd … it takes some time and it takes some resources, and so I think we should be letting market conditions to do what they do – demand for beef is still really high.” Other Republicans in states with sizeable cattle farming industries also criticized the president’s recent decision. “Short term policy shifts do not equal long term solutions,” said Pete Ricketts, a Republican senator from Nebraska and prominent ally of Trump. “Flooding the market with lower quality beef compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers. They should be enabled to grow herd sizes and meet consumer demand.” Another Trump loyalist, Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana, said that he had advised the president “against this course of action for a year”. Sheehy added that while Trump’s “heart is in the right place on wanting lower prices for the American people”, the action would actually make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild their herd. Most of whom, he said, are “Maga Republicans”.

title: From Hasan Piker to Jesse Watters, El-Sayed seeks to focus on affordability amid scrutiny from both sides
body_text: The Democratic candidate for Senate in the swing state of Michigan has spent the week trying to keep his affordability message front and center as scrutiny mounts from both ends of the political spectrum. In the span of two days, Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, spoke out against rightwing hate directed at the Muslim community, and debated Fox News host Jesse Watters on taxing billionaires. The clip circulating most from the Fox interview, though, focused on circumcision - specifically, El-Sayed asking Watters whether he circumcised, in a retort to Watters’ question about gender-affirming care. In each instance, El-Sayed tried relentlessly to stay on message. On Fox, he called opponent Mike Rogers a “beta” and took a jab at Pete Hegseth in a response to a question about the federal deficit, saying Watters didn’t seem concerned that the defense secretary, “the guy who used to work on your channel”, wanted to increase the military budget to $1.5tn. “Why, so we could fight a war we don’t know how to get out of, to raise our gas prices $5 a gallon?” El-Sayed said. At a press conference condemning Islamaphobic agitator and January 6 rioter Jake Lang on Tuesday morning, El-Sayed emphasized a religious unity message in Michigan, then brought it back to Rogers and the cost of groceries. Perhaps the most heated dialogue this week has been between centrist Democrats and the left wing of the party about controversial political streamer Piker. In the most recent dustup, Piker called out Jeremy Moss, who is Jewish and running for Congress in Michigan’s 11th district, for not endorsing El-Sayed. Moss has said he’s not ready to endorse El-Sayed because of their differing views on Israel. “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” Piker said in a stream. “I don’t know how people don’t recognize how dangerous this predicament is, how dangerous this is for Jews.” The comments were met with online anger from some prominent Democrats, including the House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who didn’t mention Piker by name but called the comments “dangerous and antisemitic”. Politico reported that Representative Hillary Scholten, a Democrat, does not want to put her name on campaign literature with El-Sayed due to his association with Piker. Others defended Piker, saying he did not call for violence, but that Israel’s actions had dangerous effects on the safety of Jews. El-Sayed campaigned with Piker during the Democratic primary, which his Democratic opponents at the time took issue with because of the Twitch streamer’s comments on Israel. “If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all. We’re waiting, Abdul …,” Rogers said, calling Piker the candidate’s “running mate”. El-Sayed did put out a statement, saying his “commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters” and calling antisemitism a “scourge”, though he did not say Piker was antisemitic. It was a rare step for El-Sayed to distance himself from the Twitch streamer and drew condemnation from some who said it was playing into efforts to conflate Israel and Jewish people. The move came at a time when El-Sayed works to win over Jewish voters, some of whom have expressed concerns over his comments or positions on Israel. “I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk,” El-Sayed said. “But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.” But like all of his responses to attacks in recent days, he brought it back to the same note: the cost of living. “While politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare,” he said. “Because that’s what Michiganders keep asking about. It’s why I’m fighting to get money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All.” Piker said on a stream in response to El-Sayed’s statement: “There are going to be a lot of people who are already questioning Abdul El-Sayed’s sincerity on these issues that will then turn around and say, ‘he’s moderating his position on Israel!’ I don’t think he is. I will say this: I am literally the person that is being dangled and I’m going to tell you once again; he’s not moderating on his perspective on Israel or anything like that.” In the anti-hate press conference on Tuesday, El-Sayed told reporters he has had ongoing conversations with Moss “about what it looks like to come together agreeably across our disagreements”. He said he was grateful to Judaism and the Jewish community, who he called “a light unto the world, and said the Jewish faith was a “beautiful faith that rhymes with so much of my own”. “I think all of us agree that the things that divide us are so much smaller than the things that unite us against somebody like Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. According to Semafor, Moss was in talks to endorse El-Sayed before the Piker comments. Moss said in a statement late Monday that he has been in “continual dialogue” with El-Sayed over their disagreements, which he said he was grateful for. “But provocateurs are exploiting this moment to create further divisions,” he said. “I will not be lectured by a California podcaster about what Oakland County, Michigan’s Jewish community should and shouldn’t believe.”

title: South Carolina chooses Darline Graham as Republican nominee for US Senate
body_text: South Carolina voters have chosen Darline Graham as the Republican nominee for US Senate, the seat formerly held by her late brother, Lindsey, on November’s ballot. Darline Graham, with Donald Trump’s full-throated support, overcame concern about her lack of legislative experience to beat the five-term congressman Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s Republican special primary runoff. With nearly all of the ballots counted, Graham had received 52.5% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, ahead of Norman’s 47.6%. Lindsey Graham, a US senator for more than two decades, won the party’s primary in June, but died the next month. Days later, Darline Graham was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother’s Senate term. “The critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate,” she told a rally audience on Friday. “They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged.” Graham will face Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a Charleston-area pediatrician, in November. Andrews faces steep historical odds; the last Democrat to win a statewide race in South Carolina was state superintendent Jim Rex in 2006. Trump recommended the appointment of Darline Graham, a career civil servant who was head of South Carolina’s Commission for the Blind, then encouraged her to run for a full term – upending a Republican scramble to select a new Senate nominee. She advanced to the runoff election after emerging as the top vote-getter in a 10-candidate field that included two congressmen and a former South Carolina governor. “What I really want you to do is pretend – please – that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said at a rally in Myrtle Beach on Friday. “Just come and vote.” Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac spent more than $800,000 in support of Graham during the campaign. Graham spent the last week of the unusually short campaign digging out from a gaffe made at a debate. Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues, she replied that she was “not that informed on national security … but I do support the military”. Some Republican voters saw that as evidence that she was not prepared for the role. Others dismissed the perceived effect as media spin. “Who is going to back Trump?” said Bill Bullard of Conway who, along with his wife, Linda, voted for Graham on Tuesday. “Who is going to support Trump? It’s just that simple.” Horry county, home to Myrtle Beach, proved decisive in the race. Though Norman won the northernmost counties of South Carolina – his political base – he did not win them by enough to counter the strength of Myrtle Beach and the coastal communities that have been surging in population and have less political loyalty to the state’s political apparatus than they have to Trump. Norman, a member of the far-right House Freedom caucus, is ranked by Heritage Action and other conservative organizations as one of Congress’s most conservative members. In the days following the January 6 riot at the US Capitol, Norman texted Trump’s chief of staff, urging Trump to declare martial law to prevent Joe Biden from taking office. In the whirlwind campaign to replace Graham, Norman leaned into hard-right themes on the Senate campaign trail, calling for Anthony Fauci, the former National Institutes of Health director, to be jailed. His campaign sought to cast Graham as a creation of the Washington elite and himself as the true heir to South Carolina’s Maga legacy. But many of Trump’s most ardent supporters in South Carolina remember that in 2023, Norman endorsed Nikki Haley, the former South Carolina governor, over Trump in her candidacy for the Republican presidential nomination. A deluge – by South Carolinian standards – of negative advertising suggested that Norman had bucked Trump on border security votes, a charge he says mischaracterized his long holdout on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to strip subsidies for electric cars and renewable energy. “I would do that over again,” he said in a debate. “I don’t apologize.”

She advanced to the runoff election after emerging as the top vote-getter in a 10-candidate field that included two congressmen and a former South Carolina governor. “What I really want you to do is pretend – please – that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said at a rally in Myrtle Beach on Friday. “Just come and vote.” Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac spent more than $800,000 in support of Graham during the campaign. Graham spent the last week of the unusually short campaign digging out from a gaffe made at a debate. Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues, she replied that she was “not that informed on national security … but I do support the military”. Some Republican voters saw that as evidence that she was not prepared for the role. Others dismissed the perceived effect as media spin. “Who is going to back Trump?” said Bill Bullard of Conway who, along with his wife, Linda, voted for Graham on Tuesday. “Who is going to support Trump? It’s just that simple.” Horry county, home to Myrtle Beach, proved decisive in the race. Though Norman won the northernmost counties of South Carolina – his political base – he did not win them by enough to counter the strength of Myrtle Beach and the coastal communities that have been surging in population and have less political loyalty to the state’s political apparatus than they have to Trump. Norman, a member of the far-right House Freedom caucus, is ranked by Heritage Action and other conservative organizations as one of Congress’s most conservative members. In the days following the January 6 riot at the US Capitol, Norman texted Trump’s chief of staff, urging Trump to declare martial law to prevent Joe Biden from taking office. In the whirlwind campaign to replace Graham, Norman leaned into hard-right themes on the Senate campaign trail, calling for Anthony Fauci, the former National Institutes of Health director, to be jailed. His campaign sought to cast Graham as a creation of the Washington elite and himself as the true heir to South Carolina’s Maga legacy. But many of Trump’s most ardent supporters in South Carolina remember that in 2023, Norman endorsed Nikki Haley, the former South Carolina governor, over Trump in her candidacy for the Republican presidential nomination. A deluge – by South Carolinian standards – of negative advertising suggested that Norman had bucked Trump on border security votes, a charge he says mischaracterized his long holdout on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to strip subsidies for electric cars and renewable energy. “I would do that over again,” he said in a debate. “I don’t apologize.”

title: Dan Sullivan v Dan Sullivan: officials confirm challenger will join senator on Alaska midterms ballot
body_text: Dan S Sullivan, the Republican senator, will be joined on the November ballot in Alaska by a challenger with a nearly identical name from the same party, election officials confirmed on Tuesday, adding a twist to what is expected to be one of the most hotly contested races of the midterms. The Republican senator is running for a third term against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former US House representative whom polls show is neck-and-neck with him in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 2008. Alaska holds nonpartisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance to the general election. The Associated Press reported that with 85% of the ballots counted, Dan J Sullivan, a retired school teacher and US Forest Service employee running as a Republican, would appear on the ballot alongside incumbent Dan S Sullivan and Peltola, with a fourth candidate yet to be announced. The other Sullivan entered the race earlier this year, with the incumbent senator condemning him as a “sham” candidate who is running at the behest of Democrats to confuse his supporters and split their votes. In June, Alaska election officials disqualified the other Sullivan from the election, but the state supreme court ordered him restored. The two were listed next to each other among the 16 candidates on primary ballots, but the senator had “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name, while his similarly named challenger was unadorned. It’s unclear how much of a threat the other Sullivan may pose to the senator’s chances of winning re-election. His 2.5% of the vote is much less than the more than 48% received by Peltola and almost 43% senator Sullivan won in last week’s primary. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for general elections for congressional offices, raising the possibility that residents who want to vote for the senator but are confused by the similar names can rank both, with their votes likely to wind up going to the incumbent. In addition to Alaska, Democratic leaders are seeking to win Senate seats from Republicans in North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa, all of which voted for Donald Trump in 2024. They also hope to pick up a seat in blue state Maine, while defending Democratic-held seats in Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire.
