title: A conservative strategist called for ‘getting rid of Trump’ three years ago. Could he be his next press secretary?
body_text: In 2016, a month before the presidential election that Donald Trump would win, the longtime Republican strategist Scott Jennings described him as “a vulgar, crude, braggadocious, desperate-to-impress playboy who tends to view most everything through a sexual lens”. After Trump’s loss in the 2020 election, Jennings excoriated Trump’s conduct during the January 6 Capitol insurrection, saying he “clearly violated his oath of office to preserve, protect and defend the constitution to the best of [his] ability”. When Trump was in the political wilderness in 2022, Jennings said the party “[needs] a new nominee”, later encouraging the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, to launch a primary challenge. “There’s only one strategy for getting rid of Trump: it’s to beat his ass,” he said the following year. So why exactly is the 48-year-old conservative TV pundit being considered “an early favorite” to serve as Trump’s top spokesperson, replacing the departing Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary? The answer can be traced to Jennings’s virtuosic ability to pivot (or shape-shift, as some critics might suggest) to land on the right political side. As soon as it became clear that Trump would in fact win the Republican nomination, in early 2024, Jennings became a bigger supporter than ever. And over the last few years, Jennings has emerged as a star in his own right: CNN’s in-house Maga gladiator who is always game to appear on television and beat up any liberals that challenge him. Highlighting his transformation, Jennings appeared onstage with Trump in 2025, telling a rally crowd: “Michigan, we were flying in here today and I said: ‘Look at these farms. I got to get a farm in Michigan, because when you own as many libs as I do, you gotta [get] a place to put them all.” Jennings’s bombastic performances have made him a target of hatred for Democrats but won him praise – and, most importantly, attention – from conservatives, including those in Trump’s circles, even as the president still reportedly holds some reservations about picking him as press secretary. ‘It’s an important job,’ Jennings says Ben Ferguson, who served as a conservative contributor on CNN for many years and still occasionally appears as a guest, said Jennings was uniquely talented as an on-air pugilist – and that he could use that experience to serve him well as Trump’s press secretary. “The more reps you get, the more fights you have, then the better you are, and the better you can serve the president,” he said in an interview. It would also help that Jennings is already well-acquainted with the CNN journalists who cover the administration, he added. Some longtime politics reporters have vouched for Jennings, who became a known quantity to beltway journalists as a staffer in George W Bush’s administration and a longtime adviser to Senator Mitch McConnell from his home state of Kentucky. “Not that my opinion matters here, but Jennings would be great in this role,” Rachael Bade, a former Washington Post and Politico journalist, wrote on X last week. “Most reporters in this town have known him for years from his time in McConnell Land – WELL before he was a CNN celeb. He’s also just a nice & fair guy – tho maybe not so nice if you’re on the other end of his slap-down.” But Jennings has plenty of detractors. During a May 2024 segment on CNN, Jennings clashed with George Conway, the conservative attorney who had been married to the Trump counselor Kellyanne Conway, after a New York jury found the then ex-president guilty on 34 felony counts. “You’re lying. You’re lying, Scott. You’re lying about the law,” Conway told Jennings, drawing the objection of a CNN anchor when he asked “why this network is paying Scott to say those lies.” Conway, who later claimed that he was temporarily “shadow-banned” by CNN after the segment, wrote on X last week that Jennings would be perfect for the job as press secretary. Asked by the Guardian to explain why he was seemingly endorsing his former sparring partner, Conway responded: “Because it’s a terrible job for a terrible boss and he’s a terrible guy! All around, a great fit.” Mark Feldstein, a former CNN and ABC News journalist who teaches broadcast journalism at the University of Maryland, noted that Jennings’s background “is mostly as an establishment Republican rather than Maga fanatic, so in that sense he may seem a bit more credible than one of the more obsequious Trump toadies from the rightwing mediasphere”. “But,” he added, “I don’t think he, or any press secretary for the Trump White House, will carry much credibility with the mainstream Washington press corps because anyone appointed to that position will be expected to defend the indefensible and convey Trump’s habitual lies to the news media. It’s an inherently credibility-diminishing job.” Jennings’s reputation for embodying a certain kind of folksy charm faced scrutiny this spring, when he told Adam Mockler, a 23-year-old progressive commentator, to “get your fucking hand out of my face” during a contentious segment about Trump’s war on Iran. Despite calls for CNN to punish what former network contributor Keith Boykin called a fireable offense, there is no evidence that he faced any punishment from the network, which has struggled in the past to find credible Trump defenders. While he’s never expressed interest in working for the Trump administration, he has also never said no – though he told a McClatchy reporter for a 2024 profile that he was not auditioning for the job by taking on the president’s critics on CNN. “It would be a major life upheaval,” he said for the story, which was headlined: “KY’s Scott Jennings is CNN’s breakout pundit. Could he be Trump’s White House press secretary?” Jennings has continued playing coy in the days since his name was first floated as Leavitt’s potential successor, even when asked directly about it on CNN. (The White House did not respond to a request for comment.) “I don’t have any comment about that, but it’s an important job, because that person has to represent the most powerful person in the world, and the entire US government,” Jennings told the CNN anchor Abby Phillip, who hosts the evening show that he most regularly appears on. “And what they say matters … whoever gets it, it’s a big responsibility.” (When asked if he would take the job, Jennings replied: “I’m not going to answer that.”) When asked about the rumors by the CNN anchor and chief White House correspondent, Kaitlan Collins, Jennings said: “I don’t really have anything to say about it, other than, I would get to see you every day, and I would think you’d be happy about this.” (“I already see you every day. … We already work together, Scott,” Collins responded.) Highlighting the irony of a CNN contributor being the subject of CNN reporting, a recent story about Jennings’s prospects noted that “CNN has reached out to Jennings” for comment. Some have accused Jennings of using his perch on CNN to lobby for the job, particularly in his recent vociferous defenses of the Trump aide Natalie Harp. A CNN spokesperson declined to comment on Jennings’s potential appointment, but noted that he had been asked about it on air several times. Were Jennings to take the job, it would leave CNN without its most high-profile and prolific conservative commentator, and it would take a reliable Trump defender off one of the president’s most-hated networks. But, Ferguson, the conservative former CNN contributor, said: “I think Scott can serve the president in an even better way being his press secretary than he does being at CNN.”

title: ‘It’s all you can hear’: New Jersey lawsuit takes on datacenter’s noise pollution
body_text: It’s a sound Steve Brown, a 63-year-old Vineland, New Jersey resident, literally hears in his sleep: BGRRRRRRRRRRR. It drones, oscillates, growls – these are machines at industrial scale. Are they generators? Pumps? Fans? Brown does not know what equipment causes the sound or why. He only knows two things: he’s tired of it, and it’s coming from DataOne – a 350MW datacenter under construction a little more than a mile from his home of 25 years. “It woke me up probably around, I don’t know, somewhere around 2 o’clock in the morning,” said Brown, who was weary by mid-afternoon. “I couldn’t get back to sleep, because once you hear it, it’s all you can hear.” Of all the concerns Americans have raised about datacenters – including mind-boggling electricity demands, water use and emissions – sound pollution ranks high among them, according to attorneys, experts and the people whose homes are nearby. Now, Brown and two of his neighbors are the named plaintiffs in a lawsuit that alleges the sound is a nuisance for up to one mile around the datacenter, which is seeking class-action status. They are represented by a seasoned environmental pollution law firm in Michigan: Liddle Sheets PC. “We have four cases that are being litigated in court against datacenters for noise, and we’re gearing up to file quite a few more,” said Laura Sheets, attorney for the class. “This is one of several.” Opposition to datacenters across the country has led to raucous town halls, protests and now potential election consequences. Republicans recently told AI companies they were concerned backlash could swing elections. Democrats appear to have also smelled blood in the water: a challenger for Vineland’s very red congressional seat hired a truck outfitted with digital billboards reading: “No datacenter here.” The Vineland datacenter, at 2.4m sq ft, represents both the scale and speed with which many facilities are coming to American communities. As recently as October 2024, the site was a brand new nine-hole public golf course. By March 2025, Amsterdam-based Nebius, a spin-off of Russian search-engine Yandex, had contracted with DataOne. Since spring, permit meetings and town halls about the datacenter have packed the Landis Theater, a music venue in town. DataOne executives have sought to quell the backlash with a town hall of their own and a “microsite” dedicated to questions about the datacenter. The company even promised, “weekly baskets of organic, non-GMO fruits and vegetables” to “underprivileged residents of Vineland”. “What I say is that there’s really four problems here: three are given a great deal of attention – energy consumption, water use and contamination,” said Jamie Banks, president of Quiet Communities Inc, a non-profit advocacy group. “The forgotten stepchild is noise.” The dangers of noise to public health have been recognized since at least 1968, when then US surgeon general, William H Stewart, attended the first meeting of the American Speech and Hearing Association in Washington DC. “Aside from hearing, it has been demonstrated that noise can cause physiological changes,” Stewart said in a keynote address. “These include cardiovascular, glandular and respiratory effects reflective of the generalized stress reaction,” which can occur “under sustained high level, or even moderately high noise conditions”. Congress tasked the EPA in 1972 with regulating sound and funded regional noise centers. They got to work regulating consumer goods such as motorcycles – and people can still appreciate the relics of this work on EPA-stamped-and-approved mufflers. However, when the Reagan administration defunded noise pollution offices in 1982, regional centers closed, and the EPA has done no appreciable research or enforcement since. Noise pollution, as a priority for federal government enforcement, was all but forgotten. Except by people like Bank. As class actions scrutinizing the sound of datacenters ramp up, Quiet Communities won an important legal victory – they sued the EPA for failing to regulate sound. In July, they won. Now, there is just one EPA regional noise center still in operation: the Rutgers University Noise Technical Assistance Center in New Jersey. Eric Zwerling, its director, kept the center alive by turning it into the training center for every noise control officer in the state. “It’s 50 years since then – there’s been a lot more research on the impacts of low frequency,” said Zwerling. “My personal opinion – not that of Rutgers and the center, [is] the permissible sound levels for sources such as this need to be re-evaluated according to the correct state of knowledge on the impact.” He continued: “If [datacenters] are designed and properly built, they can be relatively quiet. On the other hand, if there is no consideration to the sound emissions from the facility, the facility can have impacts that are virtually catastrophic to the people nearby.” Volume is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale based on human hearing. It begins at the edge of auditory perception – zero. If a whisper is 30 decibels and a normal conversation is 60 decibels, it means the typical conversation is 1,000 times louder than the whisper. A rock band, at 100 decibels, is 1,000 times louder than the conversation. A second dynamic of sound is its disruption of atmospheric pressure as it moves in waves. The frequency with which those waves cycle through the atmosphere per second is measured in hertz. Experts describe this as important for people living with the thrum of a nearby industrial facility, because low frequencies are known to travel long distances and can be experienced as vibration. “Effects like hum, whooshing, whistling,” occur in “very narrow frequency bands in the low frequency range”, said Banks. “That noise … is coming right into people’s homes.” Another plaintiff in the Vineland suit, Michael Gentile, 63, said he “found out it was a datacenter after I began to hear the noise”. He estimates he has called the county health department, responsible for enforcing noise ordinances, about “20 times”. “I said, ‘I know you guys are testing for sound, but what about vibration?’ I said, ‘Can you feel that?’ I could feel it on my porch,” he said. “They don’t have any tools to do that. I said, ‘Well that doesn’t help me now.’” In a statement to the Guardian, a DataOne spokesperson, Naomi Race, said the company was working to mitigate sound. The company, built “a northerly wall … as an additional layer to mitigate any sound from the construction site”; adjusted construction timing, said it would be using “quiet fuel cells to power the facility” and that it “retained the services of a sound mitigation specialist to assess the project site”. Race said the company was unable to comment on litigation, but that it was “committed to constructive dialogue, regulatory compliance, and being a valuable and responsible long-term member of the community”. Nebius echoed DataOne. “In Vineland, we are working with DataOne to minimize impact, including measures to minimize noise and water use and ensure local residents don’t pay more for electricity … We remain committed to engaging openly with the Vineland community and being a responsible long-term partner,” the vice-president of public affairs, John Sutter, said in a statement. title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city
body_text: Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry. News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”. “We don’t need Canada, they need us,” Trump declared. But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped. Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program. By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices. Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump. “I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said. Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada. The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group. “Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added. This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation. The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery. “El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.” In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis. “Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.” El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation. “If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those. “Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added. Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025. The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster. “This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said. The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade. But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster. The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state. “Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added. Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”. The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.” The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef. “What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.” Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words. “Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most. “Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.” • This article was amended on 28 August 2026. An earlier version gave incorrect commencement dates for the US and Canadian tariffs.

title: Vaccine misinformation spreads as RFK Jr suggests two measles deaths were ‘fabricated’
body_text: Anti-vaccine activists are trying to track down the families of two people, including at least one newborn, who died after contracting measles in Pennsylvania, as Governor Josh Shapiro tangles with Robert F Kennedy Jr over his “inaccurate and misleading claims”. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), suggested late on Wednesday that the deaths in the state may have been “fabricated” after a Republican coroner – an elected political office in Lancaster county – claimed one of the measles-associated deaths was unrelated to the virus, although the given cause would be consistent with measles. Brian Hooker at Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization that until recently was led by Kennedy, said in a recent video that the organization is “trying to get boots on the ground” and “do outreach” in Pennsylvania. Kennedy is “an anti-vaccine activist in the role of the most powerful public health person in this country”, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s like the world’s turned upside down.” It would be helpful to know the deceased patients’ ages and more information about their deaths, he added. “By not having that information, it allows fertile ground for the kind of conspiracy theory that RFK Jr puts out there, where he said in some posts that these weren’t measles deaths.” The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a Thursday post on X that it was “working to determine what actually occurred”, including “whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles”. The HHS did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about whether Kennedy recommends the vaccine or whether the newly confirmed CDC director, Erica Schwartz, would make a statement about the outbreak and the need for vaccination. About 424 Pennsylvanians have confirmed measles cases, and 73 have been hospitalized. None of the sickened people are fully vaccinated. The two deaths were in unvaccinated patients in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, which is home to large Amish and Mennonite communities. While these communities do not have religious objections to vaccines, they eschew many parts of modern life, and thus are relatively disconnected from modern healthcare. Few other details have been released about the patients, fueling a firestorm of misinformation from anti-vaccine activists spreading conspiracy theories about vaccines, which are 97% effective at preventing measles. The anti-vaccine activists are attempting to figure out who died so they can reach the families, as they did in Texas when a six-year-old girl died last year, Hooker said. They filmed a misinformation-filled interview with the Mennonite parents in a rare media appearance after their daughter’s death. Hooker also speculated that the Pennsylvania announcement was a political ploy in advance of the US midterm elections, claiming it was “a strategic move” to “get measles deaths on the tip of everybody’s tongue, to get in the forefront”. The Trump administration has at times attempted to downplay its anti-vaccine moves because they are not popular with voters, according to internal polling. When Shapiro first announced the deaths, he pointed to the inaccurate claims from the highest levels of the US government, saying at a press conference: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” Kennedy responded on X with debunked myths about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Shapiro called those claims “inaccurate and misleading” in his own X post. When Kennedy offered to help after the announcement of the two deaths, Shapiro asked him to encourage vaccination and stop spreading misinformation, the governor said in the post. The health secretary responded by repeating vaccine misinformation and saying “it would be better if we went back to ‘natural measles’,” Shapiro wrote. “Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others – and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases,” Shapiro added. In 2021, for instance, Kennedy gave a speech praising Amish parents in Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he said. There is no cure for measles, only supportive care. A few hours after Shapiro’s response, Kennedy posted to X wondering whether the deaths had been “fabricated” and alleging that Pennsylvania was refusing to share information with the CDC. But Pennsylvania notified the CDC of the deaths early on Tuesday morning, before making the public announcement, Dr Debra Bogen, the state’s secretary of health, said in a statement. “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County,” she said. The cases were also thoroughly investigated by the state’s epidemiology team, and both individuals tested positive for measles, she added. One of the deaths was in a newborn who tested positive for measles, the department of health said on Facebook. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner for Lancaster county, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that a test on the baby’s lung tissue after death indicated a measles infection acquired before birth. He believes the baby died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. Spleen issues are a known complication of measles infection. Having an enlarged spleen from measles “was not uncommon actually in the pre-vaccine era”, Offit said. The scientific literature includes doctors’ observations of enlarged spleens, which can lead to rupture. “If you have an enlarged spleen and you’re infected with measles virus, the measles virus caused your enlarged spleen. If you then have a splenic rupture which kills you, you die from measles,” Offit said. Anti-vaccine activists have been successful in driving down vaccination rates, Offit said. The ensuing outbreak “isn’t a good look” for them, he said. Children’s Health Defense appeared to want to downplay its role and put out “the same kind of bad information” after the children died in Texas, Offit said. “It’s very easy to convince those parents – very easy – that this wasn’t their fault, because otherwise, they would have to take on the responsibility or the notion that they could have prevented their child’s death.” Hooker complained on Wednesday that the scant details released about the patients made it difficult to reach them. He also noted that his organization was unable to contact the family of a measles-positive adult who died in New Mexico last year, because the state did not release more public information. “The more information that they release regarding these particular deaths, the more that we would be able to dig in and contact family members, get access to medical records and see exactly what happened,” said Hooker. Children’s Health Defense has claimed that one of the child deaths in Texas last year was due to medical error, not measles, despite findings from officials on measles. Measles deaths have become rare in the US because of vaccination, but between one and three people usually die with every 1,000 infections. The US is now experiencing its worst outbreak of measles in three decades. It is unusual for measles to spread in summer months like this – and now children are heading back to school, potentially amplifying transmission, Offit said. “You’re just going to see, I think, an explosion of measles.” Infants under the age of six months are too young to be vaccinated against measles, which is a large reason why it is important to vaccinate pregnant parents and others in the community, Offit said. More than 35,000 Pennsylvanians got vaccinated against measles last month – an increase of 10,000 compared to typical months.

Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), suggested late on Wednesday that the deaths in the state may have been “fabricated” after a Republican coroner – an elected political office in Lancaster county – claimed one of the measles-associated deaths was unrelated to the virus, although the given cause would be consistent with measles. Brian Hooker at Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization that until recently was led by Kennedy, said in a recent video that the organization is “trying to get boots on the ground” and “do outreach” in Pennsylvania. Kennedy is “an anti-vaccine activist in the role of the most powerful public health person in this country”, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s like the world’s turned upside down.” It would be helpful to know the deceased patients’ ages and more information about their deaths, he added. “By not having that information, it allows fertile ground for the kind of conspiracy theory that RFK Jr puts out there, where he said in some posts that these weren’t measles deaths.” The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a Thursday post on X that it was “working to determine what actually occurred”, including “whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles”. The HHS did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about whether Kennedy recommends the vaccine or whether the newly confirmed CDC director, Erica Schwartz, would make a statement about the outbreak and the need for vaccination. About 424 Pennsylvanians have confirmed measles cases, and 73 have been hospitalized. None of the sickened people are fully vaccinated. The two deaths were in unvaccinated patients in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, which is home to large Amish and Mennonite communities. While these communities do not have religious objections to vaccines, they eschew many parts of modern life, and thus are relatively disconnected from modern healthcare. Few other details have been released about the patients, fueling a firestorm of misinformation from anti-vaccine activists spreading conspiracy theories about vaccines, which are 97% effective at preventing measles. The anti-vaccine activists are attempting to figure out who died so they can reach the families, as they did in Texas when a six-year-old girl died last year, Hooker said. They filmed a misinformation-filled interview with the Mennonite parents in a rare media appearance after their daughter’s death. Hooker also speculated that the Pennsylvania announcement was a political ploy in advance of the US midterm elections, claiming it was “a strategic move” to “get measles deaths on the tip of everybody’s tongue, to get in the forefront”. The Trump administration has at times attempted to downplay its anti-vaccine moves because they are not popular with voters, according to internal polling. When Shapiro first announced the deaths, he pointed to the inaccurate claims from the highest levels of the US government, saying at a press conference: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” Kennedy responded on X with debunked myths about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Shapiro called those claims “inaccurate and misleading” in his own X post. When Kennedy offered to help after the announcement of the two deaths, Shapiro asked him to encourage vaccination and stop spreading misinformation, the governor said in the post. The health secretary responded by repeating vaccine misinformation and saying “it would be better if we went back to ‘natural measles’,” Shapiro wrote. “Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others – and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases,” Shapiro added. In 2021, for instance, Kennedy gave a speech praising Amish parents in Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he said. There is no cure for measles, only supportive care. A few hours after Shapiro’s response, Kennedy posted to X wondering whether the deaths had been “fabricated” and alleging that Pennsylvania was refusing to share information with the CDC. But Pennsylvania notified the CDC of the deaths early on Tuesday morning, before making the public announcement, Dr Debra Bogen, the state’s secretary of health, said in a statement. “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County,” she said. The cases were also thoroughly investigated by the state’s epidemiology team, and both individuals tested positive for measles, she added. One of the deaths was in a newborn who tested positive for measles, the department of health said on Facebook. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner for Lancaster county, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that a test on the baby’s lung tissue after death indicated a measles infection acquired before birth. He believes the baby died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. Spleen issues are a known complication of measles infection. Having an enlarged spleen from measles “was not uncommon actually in the pre-vaccine era”, Offit said. The scientific literature includes doctors’ observations of enlarged spleens, which can lead to rupture. “If you have an enlarged spleen and you’re infected with measles virus, the measles virus caused your enlarged spleen. If you then have a splenic rupture which kills you, you die from measles,” Offit said. Anti-vaccine activists have been successful in driving down vaccination rates, Offit said. The ensuing outbreak “isn’t a good look” for them, he said. He also noted that his organization was unable to contact the family of a measles-positive adult who died in New Mexico last year, because the state did not release more public information. “The more information that they release regarding these particular deaths, the more that we would be able to dig in and contact family members, get access to medical records and see exactly what happened,” said Hooker. title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela
body_text: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves. The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”. Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves. “This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media. Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves. Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest. Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude. Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, which could be eased through cheaper oil supplies and expanded output. The US also has ‌been looking for solutions to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers. Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”. The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves. The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro. “It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.” The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal. Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Democrats ignored the uncommitted movement for Gaza in 2024. Now, it’s winning elections
body_text: Abbas Alawieh initially thought the uncommitted movement of 2024 had failed. The insurgent group, which he helped co-found, had gotten more than 700,000 Democrats to vote “uncommitted” on their 2024 presidential primary ballots to pressure the US government to call for a ceasefire in Gaza. But when the group pushed for the Democratic party to add an embargo on arms to Israel in its platform, it didn’t happen. And when they asked to have a Palestinian American speaker address the Democratic national convention, it was also a no-go. Those failures, said Alawieh, prompted a new solution – one, observers say, that has been shaping Democratic primaries across the country. “I decided: ‘Oh, actually, the only fix here is we have to take power away from those leaders who are misusing it,” said Alawieh over Yemeni coffee in Dearborn, a city neighboring Detroit that has the highest share of Arab immigrants in the country. In August, Alawieh won the Democratic nomination for Dearborn’s state senate seat, which is safely Democratic. He is expected to win in November. Alawieh is one example of a larger trend that’s emerged across multiple Democratic primaries, including the marquee victory of progressive Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Democratic nomination for Michigan’s open US Senate seat: by linking nominally Arab American concerns, like the war in Gaza, to progressive politics, organizers and campaigns are building winning coalitions. “We’ve seen a lot of leadership from the Arab American community [and] Muslim American community,” said Amirah Sequeira, director of federal affairs for the Working Families Party, which organizes for progressive change within and outside of the Democratic party. It has been “extraordinarily important” to the progressive victories across the 2026 primaries, she said. Arab American votes became ‘up for grabs’ Organizing Michigan’s Arab American voters has taken on increasing importance in recent years, as the longstanding community has grown and election margins have tightened. The number of Arab residents grew by 75% from 2010 to 2020, and the group now represents roughly 4% of the state’s electorate, mostly concentrated in metropolitan Detroit, according to data from the Arab American Institute (AAI), a research, policy and civic engagement group. Until the genocide in Gaza, the Arab community’s growth had primarily benefited Democratic presidential candidates, which had drawn the majority of Arab votes since the mid-2000s, according to AAI data. But in 2024, as the Democratic party refused to change course on the genocide in Gaza, Arab voters shifted away from the Democratic ticket. This shift was especially pronounced in Michigan. The high concentration of Arab voters in certain pockets of the state made it easy for campaigns to target ads and candidate visits, said Maya Berry, executive director of the AAI. While this was something Democrats failed to do, Trump and third-party candidate Jill Stein made campaign stops in Dearborn in 2024, and Republicans blasted mailboxes with literature opposing the war, she said. “It was a lack of leadership from the [Democratic] campaign to not engage at the level of the candidate when the other guy was showing up to have meals with people,” Berry said. It “was a night-and-day difference”. The Democratic party’s absence in Arab communities was exactly what uncommitted had hoped to change, said Andy Levin, a former congressman and mentor to Alawieh. Anti-genocide Democratic party activists launched “Listen to Michigan” in the lead-up to that state’s late February primary. They organized primary voters to use the ballot’s “uncommitted” option to indicate support for a ceasefire in hopes that it could get the White House to change course – a tactic that quickly spread to other states. Beyond the moral issue, said Levin, there was a real political issue as well. “Our point was, President Biden, wake up. We need you to win re-election. We can’t have Donald Trump anywhere near the White House ever again,” said Levin. “And we just can’t see how you can win Michigan if you don’t change course on Gaza.” On election day, Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris took just 31% of the vote across Michigan precincts with majority Arab voters, compared with 47% of Arab voters nationally in the 2024 presidential election, according to AAI. Much of the Arab vote shifted to third-party candidates, who took 20% of the vote in the same Michigan precincts, significantly more than the 8% nationally. The 2024 presidential election showed that Arab American votes “are up for grabs”, said Branden Snyder, Michigan state director for the Working Families Party. The war in Gaza, and Democrats’ reluctance to oppose it, galvanized not just Arab American voters, but young and progressive voters across backgrounds. Uncommitted’s organizers, who had feet in both worlds, saw themselves fighting a moral battle that had a pragmatic angle: money spent on war meant less for social programs at home. In the process, the genocide became politically entwined with the broader progressive movement. ‘Muslim issues are American issues’ Uncommitted’s strategy of linking what were traditionally considered Arab American issues to broader progressive politics has turned into electoral work and support across many of this year’s primary upsets. “The genocide in Gaza has obviously exponentially increased involvement in politics” for Arab voters, as well as for progressives and young people, said WFP’s Sequeira. But “issues of affordability, housing, healthcare are central to those communities as well”, she said. Two other uncommitted co-founders, Layla Elabed and Lexis Zeidan, have since founded Arab Americans for Progress in metropolitan Detroit. The group runs a fellowship program to train Arab Americans for leadership and helps organize grassroots efforts like door-knocking and mailers for candidates, which it did for Alawieh, said Elabed. The group has also prioritized building relationships with Black residents through a recurring discussion group and events like an iftar solidarity dinner during Ramadan. Other organizations have also bridged a common cause between progressive groups and Arab voters. This includes the work of Emgage Action, which lobbies Congress and endorses candidates addressing concerns for Arab Muslim voters. In 2026, their endorsements stretched across 14 states, including Michigan, Texas, Florida, New York and New Jersey. Although the group is bipartisan, the Islamophobia pushed by Republican officials has led Emgage to endorse progressive Democratic candidates, said Nada Al-Hanooti, the group’s national deputy organizing director. That has been especially pronounced since December, said Al-Hanooti, after Republican representatives from Texas launched the anti-Muslim “Sharia-Free America” congressional caucus in the US House of Representatives. Emgage has organized canvassers to knock on doors, coordinated mailers and sent text messages for some of the year’s most notable progressive wins across the country. In Michigan, that included Arab Muslim candidates Alawieh and El-Sayed, as well as white progressive Will Lawrence and the Michigan state representative Donavan McKinney, a Black Detroiter who bested the incumbent US representative Shri Thanedar in a safely Democratic district. In Florida, Emgage backed upset candidate Angie Nixon, who bested a former national security official to win the Democratic nomination for Senate by 12 points. As a state lawmaker, Nixon had been the lone backer of a ceasefire resolution in Florida’s house in November 2023. In New Jersey, Emgage turned out canvassers, developed mailings and reached out to Muslim voters by text to increase support for Adam Hamawy, a Palestinian American doctor. In a field of 13 candidates, Hamawy won the Democratic nomination for the state’s 12th congressional district. Emgage’s strategy has been to endorse candidates aligned with the group on policy, not identity alone, said Al-Hanooti. “Muslim issues are American issues,” she said. “We’re here to prove that you need our vote in order to win, and you need to start visiting our communities.” All of it is a sign that Arab and Muslim Americans are building real power, said Razi Jafri, a journalist who covered the uncommitted movement in a documentary of the same name. “What’s fascinating about Abbas [Alawieh] is that his trajectory embodies this evolution,” from representation alone to shaping politics and coalitions, said Jafri. Alawieh and El-Sayed have even fielded calls and meetings with Kamala Harris recently. “That transition from protest to power building is really incredible,” Jafri said.

title: ‘Inept, incompetent, craven’: Scott Bessent struggles to clean up the president’s mess
body_text: History remembers Gen Dwight Eisenhower, the supreme commander of the allied forces in Europe during the second world war, for his role in the D-day invasion of Normandy. Whether Scott Bessent will achieve similar posterity as the face of the “economic D-day” in Iran remains to be seen. The US treasury secretary, already trying to manage a $40tn national debt pile, this week took charge of Donald Trump’s effort to reverse-engineer his war of choice. Whereas the US would typically take on an adversary with diplomacy, sanctions and military force, in that order, the US president started with a six-month bombing campaign and now hopes that economic isolation can finish the job. The effort shines a harsh spotlight on Bessent, a billionaire hedge fund manager and former Democratic donor who the president likes to say is “central casting” but critics warn is dangerously out of his depth. The coming months could reveal whether Bessent serves as a constraint on Trump’s worst impulses – or, in fact, enables them beneath a veneer of respectability. “He is, bar none, the worst treasury secretary in the history of the United States,” said Steve Schmidt, a former political strategist for President George W Bush and the John McCain presidential campaign. “Because the first treasury secretary was a true genius, the distance between Alexander Hamilton and Bessent in evolutionary scale is the difference between a flea and a human being. He is inept, he is incompetent, he is dishonest, he is smug, he is craven.” Scott Kenneth Homer Bessent is an unlikely avatar of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. Born in South Carolina, he made his way to Yale and graduated in 1984. Openly gay, in 2015 he told the Yale Alumni magazine: “If you had told me in 1984, when we graduated, and people were dying of Aids, that 30 years later I’d be legally married and we would have two children via surrogacy, I wouldn’t have believed you.” Bessent went on to play an influential role in the liberal philanthropist George Soros’s London investment operations, including his famous 1992 bet against the pound, which generated huge profits on “Black Wednesday”, when the pound was delinked from European currencies. He also donated to various Democratic causes in the early 2000s, notably Al Gore’s presidential run, but eventually drifted toward the Republican fold, transforming into an adviser and intellectual defender of Trump’s economic nationalism. He championed spending cuts while vigorously advocating for the extension of the tax cuts approved by Congress in Trump’s first term. Still, in a cabinet of questionable qualifications, there were hopes that Bessent – an advocate for deficit reduction and deregulation – would prove a moderating influence on Trump. Last year the Senate confirmed him as treasury secretary by a vote of 68 to 29, with those in favour including some Democrats and independents. Bessent was hailed as the first openly gay treasury secretary in US history. It has been far from smooth sailing. With the national debt ticking past $40tn, the bond markets have begun to rebel. Yields on long-dated treasury bonds have soared to heights not seen in nearly 20 years, dramatically escalating the cost of servicing the nation’s debt. Earlier this month, Bessent carried out the first joint intervention in the Japanese yen in 15 years to support currency stability. Then, last week, he surprised global investors by announcing that the treasury would double the size of its quarterly buybacks of longer-dated bonds – boosting the repurchases of 10-to-30-year securities to at least $4bn per operation. Bessent claimed that his objective was to support liquidity in a thinly traded August market. The market intervention achieved its goal, but only fleetingly. Yields dropped briefly before retracing nearly all of those losses by the end of the week. The core problem remained: Bessent has not identified the funding source for the buybacks, leading analysts to assume he will tap the Treasury General Account (TGA) at the Federal Reserve. Perceptions of Bessent’s competence were shaken by the move. Charlie McElligott, a cross-asset strategist at Nomura, told the Financial Times newspaper that it was a “band-aid on a bullet hole” and would “not be enough to placate market forces”. Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, summed it up: “The long bond buyback was perceived as somewhat farcical by the financial community, and when he went on to opine that we could grow our way out of the debt, I’m sure he knows better than that. I don’t think he’s thrown away his reputation but as headlines in the past 24 hours have been indicating, Wall Street, like Queen Victoria, is not amused.” Then there was Iran. With a six month-bombing campaign having failed to break Tehran’s will, and the US running low on the defensive weapons it would need to repel a counterattack, Trump handed Bessent the unenviable task of finding another way. The upshot was “Operation Economic Outcast”, designed to isolate Iran from the global financial system. Galston observed: “The president has decided on a strategy of maximum economic pressure. Bessent has no choice but to devise the best plan possible. Now, it does matter what he’s telling the president behind the scenes.” At a press conference on Monday, Bessent’s rhetoric about “economic asphyxiation” was sweeping, but the reality was far more tentative: a series of warnings rather than the immediate imposition of secondary sanctions on Iran’s major trading partners. If Bessent were to enforce secondary sanctions fully, he would have to target major Chinese state-owned banks. This could spark a catastrophic trade war between the world’s two biggest economies, shattering the fragile trade truce that Trump has spent the last year trying to maintain. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” the secretary reasoned. The president has been right.” He has also described tariffs as “a useful tool for achieving the president’s foreign policy objectives”, claiming that Hamilton was their original proponent. Such remarks suggest that the former Democratic supporter now feels the zeal of the convert, and has become a true believer in Trump. But now that he is into the thick of a job you can see how ill prepared he is for a complicated situation with an out-of-control president.” The price to pay, however, could be Bessent’s reputation. title: Is Donald Trump’s bid to brand Democrats as ‘radical’ communists working?
body_text: After casting his vote in South Carolina, a man who introduced himself as Chestnut was unwilling to give his full name. “You don’t have a need to know,” the air force veteran declared. He was, however, happy to share his views. “I’m a true American. I believe in the USA,” said the man, outside Christ the Servant Lutheran church in Conway. “And I don’t believe in communism or socialism.” Several hundred thousand South Carolinians took part in a Republican special runoff on Tuesday, selecting the party’s nominee for US Senate after the sudden death of the veteran lawmaker Lindsey Graham. Darline, his sister, prevailed – in a victory for Donald Trump. The US president had traveled down to South Carolina days before the vote, reaching for a familiar theme as he rallied supporters to get behind his handpicked candidate. Also on the ballot was a message that Trump has been ramping up in recent months. “So the Democrats hate our country. They’re communists,” Trump declared at a rally in Myrtle Beach. During the speech, he mentioned communists or communism no fewer than 13 times. “They’re radical left lunatics.” As Democrats have looked left in some primaries, nominating socialists to represent the party in November’s US midterm elections, Trump has increasingly – erroneously – claimed the party has been overrun by communists. “You can be a communist or you can be a patriot,” he said in the shadow of Mount Rushmore during the US 250th birthday celebrations this summer. “You cannot be both.” As Trump seeks to galvanize his base ahead of November’s US midterm elections, the thoughts of voters in South Carolina, and fears of an ascendant “Communist party” on the left, offer a window into how his efforts are faring. Chestnut was not the only voter with whom such warnings appeared to resonate. In deep red South Carolina, where no Democrat has won statewide in 20 years, there is apprehension of a deeper red surge in US politics. “I don’t like the DSA,” Charles Rogers said, referring to the Democratic Socialists of America, as he left a polling station at Marion intermediate school. “I don’t like how the Democrats want to back them. Democrats used to be for the working man, but something’s changed … I do not agree with the DSA, and more Democrats are backing them with crazy ideas.” While DSA members would adamantly describe themselves as standing for working people, fears of communism coming for America – fanned by Trump – were on the mind of Republican voters contemplating their choices on Tuesday, and in November. Lee and Donna Criswell voted on Tuesday afternoon at the Lamar library in Darlington county, South Carolina. Asked what issues they viewed as politically important, Lee replied: “We’re concerned about the socialism thing going on in some parts of the country. I don’t think we have an issue regardless of whether you’re Republican or Democrat here in South Carolina, but I don’t know where it’s going, you know, in other areas.” “We want to maintain our freedoms,” Donna added. As Trump continues to level allegations of political “extremism” at the feet of the Democrats, his own extreme actions – from persistent election denial to the pursuit of his political enemies – continue to cause alarm in much of the country. Such concerns were not raised by Republicans in South Carolina who spoke to the Guardian this week. Zachary Cogan, a retired army engineer voting in Lamar, called himself a transplant from the “communist state” of New York. He said he was looking for responsiveness and accountability from conservative political leaders, saying: “We’re not importing [New York City mayor Zohran] Mamdani voters into South Carolina. South Carolina has no danger of turning purple.” Cogan thought about the political environment he left behind, and laughed. “I mean, when you have to say [US Senate minority leader] Chuck Schumer is the more moderate of the Democrats, that’s going the wrong way. OK? But why – why are the Democrats … well, you’ve got the Communist party now that is so pro-intifada.” The victories of Mamdani in New York City, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s US Senate primary and now Angie Nixon in Florida’s US Senate primary have been heralded by American progressives as a sign of renewed vigor for the left in Democratic politics amid the provocations of Trump’s administration. But they have also become daily fodder for conservative cable news channels like Newsmax or Fox News, and social media accounts on Facebook and X. The fear of communism has become a driving rhetorical force on the right. Fox and other media outlets catering to a conservative audience have been amplifying the anticommunist rhetoric of Trump, according to Brian Leiter, a law professor and director of the Center for Law, Philosophy & Human Values at the University of Chicago. Leiter co-authored a book on Karl Marx and is a keen observer of America’s history with red-baiting politics. “Trump and Fox News work in tandem on these things. They’re mutually reinforcing,” Leiter said. “Trump understands red-baiting better than anyone, because who was his mentor? Roy Cohn. And Roy Cohn was, of course, legal counsel to Joseph McCarthy in the original purge and political persecution.” The words “socialist” or “socialism” have been mentioned almost 6,000 times in Fox News programming since 1 January, according to a search of the Internet Archive’s database of show transcripts. The word “communist” appeared more than 1,700 times. In each case, mentions spiked sharply in May and have steadily increased, occurring about five times as often in August as they did in April. Often, Leiter said, Fox invites on its shows members of the DSA who – unlike media-savvy Democrats like Mamdani or congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez – look and sound like progressive caricatures, espousing fringe views within the Democratic party, unwilling or unable to articulate the difference between the beliefs of a democratic socialist and a committed communist. “I gather they have been doing a lot on democratic socialism on the theory that it’ll help the Republican party,” Leiter said. “Communism has always been a bogeyman in American politics in a way it’s not in Europe, say, and it’s not helped by the fact that every self-proclaimed communist government was a disaster … None of these people – Zohran Mamdani, Bernie Sanders, AOC – none of them are communists. They’re not even close.” But those distinctions do not seem to have generally filtered down to rank-and-file Republican voters of South Carolina. Trump’s rhetoric has landed.

title: Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers says he saw Bin Laden’s body with his ‘own eyes’. He did not
body_text: In a recent fundraising email, the Republican candidate for Michigan’s open US Senate seat, former congressman Mike Rogers, appeared to mislead supporters about his past by suggesting that he had played an active role in the killing of Osama bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaida who was shot and killed in an American military raid on his compound in Pakistan in 2011. “When I served as a US army officer and an FBI special agent, I swore a sacred oath to defend the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic,” Rogers wrote, according to a screenshot of the email shared online by Azi Paybarah, a former Washington Post reporter now with Straight Arrow News. “I dedicated my life to keeping our families safe – working in the shadows, hunting down terrorists, and standing on the frontlines of our national security.” He then added, in a section of the email highlighted in bold type: “I saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.” Rogers, however, was not in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on 1 May 2011, when Bin Laden was shot and killed – nor was he in the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama and senior administration officials at the time, including Joe Biden and Hillary Clinton, followed the raid in real time. Instead, as Rogers told reporters the next day, and recounts in a campaign video, he was at home in Washington DC – where, as the chair of the House intelligence committee at the time, he was informed about the raid in a phone call from Obama’s CIA director, Leon Panetta. While the Rogers campaign did not respond to requests to explain what the former congressman meant by his claim, Paybarah, who first reported the fundraising email sent by Rogers on Sunday, suggested that Rogers must have been referring to the fact that he was one of a select few US officials to have seen a photograph of Bin Laden’s dead body. Rogers said – days after the raid – that the photograph he’d seen made it clear that Bin Laden was dead. But he said he supported Obama’s decision to not make the graphic images of the raid public. “The risks of release outweigh the benefits,” Rogers said in a statement at the time. “Conspiracy theorists around the world will just claim the photos are doctored anyway, and there is a real risk that releasing the photos will only serve to inflame public opinion in the Middle East.” In the years since, though, Rogers has frequently referred to his role as a congressman who helped provide funds for US intelligence agencies in vague terms that seemed to exaggerate his role. Since Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim doctor and former public health official, became his opponent in the Senate race, Rogers has repeatedly cited his own role in the US war on Islamist terrorism in his campaign statements. “Abdul doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism,” Rogers said the night that El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” A New York Times factcheck pointed out that the second part of Rogers’s “incendiary statement” was false: it was not El-Sayed, but one of his supporters, the Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once said that the US deserved 9/11, before retracting and apologizing for that statement seven years before he endorsed El-Sayed. For his part, El-Sayed has clearly denounced the 9/11 attacks for years. In a recollection of that day written in 2021, El-Sayed wrote: “I watched terrorists with names like mine attack my country in the name of my faith. Three thousand of my fellow Americans were killed in the craven terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania. The attack devastated me.”

title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher
body_text: Donald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran. There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship. Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too. Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms. This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received. Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz. These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it. That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions. There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted. Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day”. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation. That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not. Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.
