title: In 2016, Trump pledged to erase the federal debt. It just hit $40tn
body_text: Dear reader, I recognize that your eyes might glaze over at any mention of the nation’s $40tn federal debt. But your reaction to this mind-boggling number shouldn’t be ennui; it should be outrage and dismay. Outrage is in order because the nation’s debt has climbed to more than $40tn under Donald Trump, even though back in 2016, when the debt was less than half what it is today, candidate Trump insisted that he’d totally eliminate the debt within eight years. That was yet another example of the Demagogue-in-Chief’s willingness to say anything, no matter how insincere or untrue, to woo voters. Not only has Trump failed to reduce the debt, he has spectacularly increased it. Take Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” and the huge tax cuts it lavished upon the very rich and corporations. That legislation is expected to increase the nation’s debt by a whopping $3.4tn over the next decade. Worse, during Trump’s time as president, including his first term, the federal debt has climbed by a colossal $11.6tn. Outrage is also in order because the trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis that is squeezing so many Americans. Those trillions could have gone to creating more affordable childcare for every family or increasing subsidies to hold down soaring healthcare premiums or expanding government aid to make college more affordable. Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and the $40tn debt have worsened the affordability crisis in one important and painful way. They have helped push up long-term interest rates to their highest level in nearly two decades, and that has pushed up mortgage rates, too. The unhappy result: housing has become less affordable, when housing affordability has already been a big problem for young Americans. Higher mortgage rates often mean that homebuyers have to pay several hundred dollars more in interest each month. Interest rates have climbed not only because investors are dismayed that the national debt has hit a record, but also because Trump’s tariffs and war against Iran have fueled inflation and because investors are unsettled by all the chaos Trump has created at home and abroad. Outrage is also called for because of the way Trump and his Republican yes-men in Congress jumped to enact giant tax cuts when their super-wealthy donors and friends said jump. In a move that shows how rigged the system is, Trump and the GOP legislated these tax cuts for the rich and corporations even though the wealthy and corporations were already doing perfectly well and would continue doing just fine, with their mansions, yachts and private jets, even without those tax cuts. Of the $4.4tn in tax cuts in the “big, beautiful bill”, nearly half go to the richest 5% of Americans. If any further evidence is needed to show that Republicans in Congress have sold their souls to billionaires, millionaires and corporations, the increased debt caused by the big, unbeautiful bill’s tax cuts will be a burden on our children and grandchildren for decades to come. By the mid-2030s, the nation will have to pay more than $2tn in interest payments each year to finance the federal debt. That’s double the $1tn a year we are paying now – $1tn is slightly less than what the government spends on Medicare, is higher than this year’s Pentagon budget and is more than five times what the federal government spends on education each year. All this is maddening for another reason. In recent decades, Republicans held themselves out as the party of “fiscal responsibility”. But they’ve really become the party of fiscal irresponsibility. During George W Bush’s two terms, with his tax cuts tilted toward the wealthy and his expensive, ill-fated war against Iraq, the federal debt ballooned by 85% (by $4.9tn). In Trump’s first term, the debt soared by $7.8tn (a 39% increase), stemming from his initial big tax cuts for the rich as well as increased Pentagon spending – and then there was more than $2tn in emergency spending to stabilize the economy during the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic. During Trump’s second term, the debt is likely to soar by nearly $8tn once again. Trump is pushing for a record $1.5tn annual defense budget, far higher than any previous year, even though it will send our country’s debt further into the stratosphere. Some of that money will go to redesigning aircraft carriers merely because Trump dislikes how the current ones look. Bill Clinton was the last president to have an annual budget surplus, but Democratic presidents have also pushed up the federal debt. During Biden’s four years as president, the debt rose $8.4tn, partly because of the annual budget deficits he inherited from Trump and partly because of his $2tn-plus pandemic-era emergency spending package to stabilize families’ finances and ensure the US didn’t sink into a deep economic downturn. The federal debt has grown even larger than the country’s overall gross domestic product. Indeed, the ratio of the debt to GDP will soon be higher than the record 106% where it stood when the second world war ended. Franklin D Roosevelt ran up huge debts for an urgent reason: to defeat Nazi Germany and its allies. In sharp contrast, under Trump, the US is running big deficits, of approximately $2tn a year, for the opposite of urgent reasons: to finance a disastrous war in Iran and to give big tax giveaways to two powerful groups that were already prospering, eg the ultra-wealthy and corporations. It would be a very different thing if Trump were borrowing money to build a better future, as people do to build a new house or pay for college. But Trump is not jacking up the country’s debt to improve our future; he’s not spending to improve education, childcare or our country’s infrastructure or to fix the housing crisis. I am not a fiscal conservative and nor are many Democrats, but it is a real concern that for the first time in US history, other countries and many investors seem truly worried about the record size of the federal debt. Those worries have spooked financial markets and pushed up interest rates. As the midterm elections heat up, the Democrats should attack Trump and the Republicans over the huge, fast-growing federal debt. Democrats need to make clear that Republicans have become the party of fiscal irresponsibility. We can agree that the $40tn debt isn’t a sexy issue, but the Democrats can and should turn it into a hard-hitting and winning campaign issue that they can use to hammer Trump and the Republicans, along with the affordability crisis and Trump’s calamitous war against Iran. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’
body_text: Iran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”. As Iran’s military targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”. “This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait with missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television. The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added. In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”. The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday. Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this week after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. The latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic. Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes. Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes. The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems. Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down. Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them. “Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said. “However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified. The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures. “We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees. The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months. “An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”

title: US House passes bill penalizing universities that participate in boycott of Israel
body_text: The US House of Representatives on Thursday passed a Republican-backed bill that would penalize universities that participate in boycotts of Israel, or attempt to prevent students from taking part in exchange programs with the country. The Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act passed by a 237-169 vote, with 33 Democrats breaking with the rest of their party to vote in favor, and only two Republicans opposed. It now goes to the Senate for consideration. The measure would require that colleges and universities who participate in federal student aid programs not participate in boycotts of Israel and also mandates that institutions receiving federal funding for international study and foreign language programs certify annually that they do not impose restrictions on their students participating in programs in Israel, or on students from Israel participating in programs on their campuses. House Republican leaders had brought the measure to the floor as they attempt to exploit divisions among Democrats over hot-button issues ahead of the midterm elections, in which voters will decide control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. “This legislation is about a simple principle: our colleges and universities should not discriminate against Israel, Israeli institutions or Israeli students, and federal taxpayer dollars should never support institutions that engage in such discrimination,” said Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House education committee. After the 7 October attack and Israel’s invasion of Gaza, student and faculty groups at some universities intensified calls for administrators to participate in the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against the country, but were largely unsuccessful. Bobby Scott, the top Democrat on the education committee, criticized the bill as unnecessary and potentially in conflict with first amendment protections of protest. “No college or university has embraced the BDS movement anyway. So, we should combat antisemitism wherever it occurs, but we should not do so by punishing protected speech or conflating a student’s view with university policies,” he said. Democrats who voted for the bill typically face tough re-election contests in November, or are supporters of Israel. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey congressman who co-sponsored the legislation with Republican Virginia Foxx, described the proposal as “narrow and tailored” and necessary to combat antisemitism. “No student, no professor should be shut out of research, study abroad opportunities, or academic partnerships or feel unwelcome in the classroom because of where they are from or what religion they practice. Yet that’s exactly what the boycott-divest-sanction movement seeks to do – targeting one country and one religion: Israel and Judaism,” he said. The question of support for Israel has divided House Democrats in recent months. In July, more than 100 House Democrats supported a bill cutting off some military aid to the US ally amid accusations its military’s actions in Gaza constituted a genocide.

title: North Carolina becomes first state to send out mail-in ballots for US midterms
body_text: North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for November’s US midterm elections on Friday, as Donald Trump’s administration fights to impose sweeping restrictions on the practice before millions of Americans cast their votes. The state’s decision to proceed – hours after Trump’s officials asked the supreme court to let the administration press ahead with its proposed crackdown – comes amid deep uncertainty over whether new federal rules governing mail ballots will be allowed to take effect, and whether the US Postal Service can implement the changes in time. North Carolina is first out of the gate because its state statute requires county boards to begin sending absentee ballots 60 days before a general election – one of the earliest start dates in the country. Other states set their own timelines, ranging from a few weeks before election day to, in a handful of cases, similarly early starts, meaning most will follow in the coming days and weeks. The Trump administration asked the supreme court on Thursday to let it revive a rule barring the postal service from delivering ballots in states that don’t share voter data with the federal government, and requiring ballot envelopes to be screened against new standards before delivery. D John Sauer, the US solicitor general, told the justices that a lower court’s freeze on the plan was causing “serious irreparable harm” to the government, states and voters. It is the second time in weeks the administration has turned to the court over the plan, part of an executive order Trump signed in March directing agencies to compile citizen lists for use in screening mail ballots. A federal judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, blocked the plan in June, ruling that it encroached on states’ constitutional authority over elections. The supreme court’s conservative majority sided with Trump in August but called the challenge premature, leaving the door open for further litigation once the plan was finalized. Talwani froze key parts of it again on 27 August. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who oversees emergency applications from the region, has not granted the administration’s request for an immediate stay. Instead, she has given challengers until Tuesday to respond, a timeline that leaves little room for the postal service to act before ballots need to be in voters’ hands nationwide. Underscoring how tight the window has become with barely two months left before polls open, a postal service official told the Massachusetts court this week that the agency was still refining its screening system and expected to make it available to states on a voluntary basis “sometime next week”.

title: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all
body_text: What is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’s controlled by a secret cabal of its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for which the first postal ballots were sent out today. That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage. At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoff back to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain. The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look at the graph measuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began, hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East. And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, by Apple and Google in their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects. For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’s Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy. What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot. Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, with seven in 10 Americans saying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans, there is deep concern over their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters. So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too. It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whether demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly. And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas was impeached by his fellow Republicans on a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even that red-state stronghold is shaky. Put it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance? One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime. But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new book Regime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot. Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, with seven in 10 Americans saying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans, there is deep concern over their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters. So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too. It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whether demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly. And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas was impeached by his fellow Republicans on a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even that red-state stronghold is shaky. Put it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance? One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime. But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new book Regime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

title: US judge extends block on Trump order to restrict mail-in voting
body_text: A federal judge on Friday again blocked Donald Trump’s executive order to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting, the latest in a legal back-and-forth playing out less than two months before election day. US district court judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking the president’s mandate and has now extended that prohibition with a stronger preliminary injunction. The ruling comes hours after North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for the 3 November midterm elections. Talwani referred to the tight timeline in her ruling. “Plaintiff States are required under state law to mail millions of ballots to voters on a prescribed timeframe. As detailed below, they are unable to pivot this late in the election cycle, nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters,” the judge wrote in her ruling. Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters, compelling the US Postal Service (USPS) to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. The result would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists. The Trump administration had already appealed against her temporary block to the supreme court, and it appeared the justices were likely to have a final say on the matter. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the administration quickly appealed Friday’s ruling. The USPS has said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the order isn’t even available. Earlier this week, a USPS whistleblower came forward and warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order. After Trump signed the order, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general sued the USPS to challenge the rule. They also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction as litigation was ongoing. Oral argument on the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction was held on Thursday. “We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” said Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, who co-led the state coalition. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.” The order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. To date, not a single state has announced that it will do so. A coalition of voter service and civic groups, plaintiffs represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in the lawsuit, issued a statement: “Today’s ruling makes it crystal clear: The US Postal Service must deliver all election mail. USPS has no authority in the Constitution or federal law over how states administer mail voting. And the President cannot order the Postal Service to create a disruptive new bureaucracy that will throw the election into chaos and disenfranchise untold numbers of voters.” Trump has long sought to limit mail voting, even though he himself often uses that method to cast his own ballot. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss, spreading baseless claims of fraud, but has so far been unable to change the longstanding voting procedure. An initial executive order Trump issued last year to change election rules, including a requirement for people to show documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, was halted by federal judges. They ruled that the constitution gives states and, in some cases, Congress the power to set voting procedures, not the president. After Trump issued his mail voting executive order in March, Democrats and voting rights groups filed several lawsuits. Two ended up before Talwani, who placed an initial hold on the order in June, prohibiting its implementation until after November. But the supreme court late last month overturned that order. Its conservative majority pointedly did not say Trump’s move was legal but found the lawsuits were filed prematurely before the US Postal Service issued its rule on how it would implement the order. The rule came out just before the supreme court released its ruling, and the plaintiffs refiled their suits.

title: Leftist insurgents are storming the midterms – just don’t call them all democratic socialists
body_text: Days before he won the Democratic primary for a US Senate seat in Michigan, insurgent newcomer Abdul El-Sayed was asked whether he was concerned about being labeled a “socialist”. “I’d rather think of myself as a capitalist who has actually read about capitalism,” El-Sayed told CBS News anchor Ed O’Keefe. “I’m not a socialist.” While El-Sayed might take pains to distance himself from the label in the swing state of Michigan, O’Keefe noted that the candidate has been linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the ascendant leftist group whose meteoric rise has captured the enthusiasm of voters desperate for bold change and whose recent wins have stoked the anxieties of both conservatives and the party’s establishment. “I’m not DSA,” El-Sayed stressed in the interview, though he made clear there is room for the DSA in the “big tent” he said he’s seeking to build. El-Sayed is just one of a number of progressive candidates and elected officials across the country who are navigating their relationship and differences with the DSA, which has come under increasing pressure as its candidates have won one race after the other in Democratic primaries mostly in blue states. But as other progressive candidates to the left of the Democratic establishment have mounted bids for office, there has at times been confusion about who is a “DSA candidate” – a confusion some Republicans have been eager to exploit. Some, like El-Sayed, espouse many of the group’s political priorities – fighting fascism, instating universal healthcare, getting money out of politics and boosting labor rights, to name a few – but are not members, nor have they been endorsed by the DSA. Others, like New York’s Claire Valdez, have been organizing with the group for years. Then there are those like Colorado’s Melat Kiros and Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb who have long identified as socialists but only recently joined the organization. (All three are DSA-endorsed.) Brad Lander was once a member but left the group over its response to the 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the national figure most often associated with the DSA, rejoined the New York City chapter last month after letting her membership lapse for seven years, as speculation mounts about her intention to run for president. But DSA membership doesn’t guarantee endorsement, and intense debates have roiled the organization in recent months about which candidates to endorse and how to best ride the current momentum. In Los Angeles, for example, the local DSA chapter voted to endorse mayoral candidate Nithya Raman this week after weeks of discussions on whether she was too centrist to earn their backing. Pragmatism v purism A decade into Trumpism and the Democrats’ failure to stop it, and buoyed up by the popularity of longtime member Zohran Mamdani, the DSA has helped popularize positions once viewed as radical – from taxing the rich to ending support for Israel. The DSA has become a “shorthand for this rebellion against Democratic party leadership”, said Peter Sterne, an editor at City & State New York who has extensively covered the DSA and a former member of the group. In recent months, the group has seen its membership soar to 120,000, its leaders are getting prime time on cable news and a recent poll found that one-third of Democrats now openly identify as “socialist”, a term not long ago viewed as a slur. The backlash has been swift. After DSA candidates won nine out of 10 races in which the group had fielded candidates in New York City in June, party establishment figures issued a string of hostile statements. Third Way, a centrist Democratic group, announced a $15m effort to go to “war” against them. DSA leaders and members have become tabloid fodder. And this week, House Republicans – joined by eight Democrats – adopted a resolution condemning “socialism” and specifically naming the DSA. The organization’s critics point to some of its more radical stances, from eliminating the Senate to abolishing borders and defunding the police, as a sign of its unseriousness. But many DSA members view those as aspirational and consistent with the group’s fundamental values, while calling for a more realistic approach. Even some more moderate Democrats recognize that the DSA’s message is resonating because the rest of the party has failed to present a satisfying vision of its own. “You can’t beat something with nothing,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington. “The more moderate wing of the Democratic party is going to have to raise its game substantially.” The DSA’s popularity and campaigning capacity on the one hand, and the animosity from more conservative corners on the other, has left some candidates, particularly in swing states, navigating a balancing act. In Florida, Angie Nixon, who recently won the Democratic Senate primary in one of the biggest upsets of the primary season, joined the DSA only in June but has not been endorsed by the group. When asked whether she identified as a democratic socialist, she equivocated. “I don’t agree with everything that they agree with, but they’re fighting hard to ensure we have access to universal healthcare, access to free college and fully funded public schools,” she said in an interview with the Guardian. “I’ve always been a lifelong Democrat but I’m more of [a] social democrat who believes in strong safety nets.” Some of the most popular politicians associated with the DSA have broken with the group on some issues. The group has for months been debating how to respond to a possible presidential run by Ocasio-Cortez. Some factions, and particularly many NYC-DSA members, have openly encouraged it, while others are suspicious of what they view as her willingness to compromise on DSA priorities. Mamdani has also broken with the group over policing. Ultimately, the decision will be made democratically – DSA members report often excruciatingly deliberative processes and stress that the “democratic” element of the group’s identity is just as fundamental as its socialist one. Endorsements, Sterne noted, can power a campaign with an “army” of canvassers and phone bank volunteers – the DSA’s New York City chapter says that its 50,000 volunteers knocked on doors 1.6m times in support of Mamdani’s candidacy. But the “DSA doesn’t just want to help get people into office and then let them do whatever they want”, he added, noting that there was some concern within the organization that candidates may opportunistically hitch their wagon to the group but not work with it after getting elected. The tension between the pragmatists and the purists, he argued, is healthy, and a sign of the organization’s strength. “More people are joining,” he said. “More people are identifying as socialists, which was once seen as a taboo term.”

title: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
body_text: In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile. But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary. Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy. The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more. Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East. While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents. “The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.” Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.” After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple. The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party. Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation. The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year. The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long. The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post. The Pentagon reached out to the Guardian after publication of this story. Hegseth “has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength”, press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all time highs. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” ‘The past six months has failed’ “I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after? “We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability. “We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.” Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade. “It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength. As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions. The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets. The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”. Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts. A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank. In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN. Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis. The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain. Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.” Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said. ‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war. Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the World Bank. During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein. But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth. “Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now. “But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat. “If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.” Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced. He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa. “We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.” Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.” • This article was amended on 5 September 2026. But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary. Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy. The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more. Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East. The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party. Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation. The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year. title: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
body_text: More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup. Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican. That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times. The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash. Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times. But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times. Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic. A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

title: The world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter future
body_text: Don’t look up! The world is a mess. The sky could fall in any day. Unending wars, expanding humanitarian crises, rising authoritarianism, dysfunctional democracies, rampant racial and religious extremism, and unchecked lawlessness cast a dark cloud as the west’s new political year begins. Set all that against a backdrop of staggering global economic inequality, corporate and individual greed, irresponsible government indebtedness, dangerous AI gambles, climate breakdown and proliferating nuclear weapons, and a truly apocalyptic global outlook begins to take shape. It’s enough to make anyone shut their eyes, cover their ears and utter a Munch-like scream. And it’s only getting worse. Democratic leaders who promise a better, safer, more optimistic future – what Britain’s freshly arrived prime minister, Andy Burnham, calls a “new era of possibility” – cannot escape this wider international context. Last week’s global bond market upheaval, sparked by external factors, left Burnham’s cash-strapped government struggling with sharply increased borrowing costs before he barely got started. The fact he chose Ukraine for his first overseas trip, while symbolically important, highlighted another grim reality. As a lead opponent of Vladimir Putin’s invasion, Britain now finds itself in a de facto state of war with Russia – and facing attack. Argentina, too, is eyeing UK defence vulnerabilities. These are not the sort of possibilities Burnham envisaged. Little wonder some analysts believe a third world war has already begun. Those who say this is over-dramatic should consider the following snapshots of the state of the world in 2026. From Kyiv to Khorramshahr, Kordofan and Kachin, conflicts flare and subside but never seem to end. All-out Russian aggression in Ukraine, now mostly comprising daily attempts to murder and terrorise civilians, is into its fifth year. Trump has lost his Iran bet, but keeps killing and bombing with no end in sight. In southern Sudan, appalling atrocities go unchecked. In Myanmar, a people’s war against a brutal junta rages on. Israel’s response to the 2023 massacres has triggered an ongoing regional war embroiling Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Iran and the Gulf states. Worldwide, record numbers of people are displaced by conflict. Increasingly interconnected, these wars threaten to merge into one uncontrollable global conflagration. The alliance system, key pillar of the post-1945 order, is eating itself. Donald Trump taunts Europe and Nato with tariffs, troop withdrawals, barbs and insults at a time of acute vulnerability. Canada and the US are at daggers drawn as the White House bully fatuously threatens Venezuela – or Greenland-style annexation. China aids North Korea, which also aids Russia, which aids Iran, which aids Hezbollah and the Houthis. In Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia, China looms menacingly as partnerships with Washington fray. In Taiwan, fears of invasion grow, aggravated by Trump’s obsequious appeasing of Xi Jinping. Everywhere you look, humanitarian crises caused by war, the climate crisis or natural disasters are producing chaotic mass migrations, malnutrition and disease. Increasingly, the suffering overwhelms a UN-led aid system crippled by US and UK funding cuts. In the fertile West Bank, 900,000 Palestinians, their homes and farms besieged by settler extremists, are now food insecure, the World Food Programme says. In Somalia, millions go hungry amid record drought and predicted El Niño-related flooding. Colombia and Afghanistan face similar perils. Humanitarian and human rights outrages take individual form, too. In Hong Kong, for example, an ailing Jimmy Lai, brave champion of free speech, languishes in 23-hour-a-day solitary confinement, a tortured casualty of Chinese communism’s hatred of democracy and civil rights. Skittish bond markets may be the least of the world’s economic and financial problems. Is a crash coming, reminiscent of 2008, only worse? The signs are ominous. The US just notched up a record $40tn in national debt. France, the UK, Japan and others are deep in the red, too. Unmanageable current-account deficits, rising inflation and the huge, draining diversion of investment into bloated AI tech companies all point to what market analysts cutely call a “disorderly correction”. By some estimates, the Nvidia chip-maker, plus Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, are “worth” about 23% of the entire US stock market. Meanwhile, unaffordable northern-hemisphere energy and food prices loom this winter, exacerbated by Trump’s Middle East forever folly. In the worst case, all this could translate into global recession and yet more political instability. It’s a gigantic bubble waiting to burst. The existential hazards posed by the climate crisis and global heating should require scant elaboration after the terrifying Nepal-Tibet flood disaster. Similarly inimical to life on Earth, in an avoidable, human-made way, is the rapid proliferation of nuclear weapons, including so-called “battlefield” or tactical nukes that are more likely to be used in war zones such as Ukraine or Iran. All nine nuclear weapons states are expanding or modernising their arsenals, with China in the lead. Countries such as South Korea and Saudi Arabia weigh their nuclear options. And now this atomic arms race is expanding into space. There really seems no limit to humanity’s relentless, doom-laden drive towards self-destruction. The fundamental values of post-Enlightenment liberal societies are everywhere under siege. The rule of law is routinely flouted. While Putin and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu ignore war-crimes arrest warrants, Trump and his unctuous lickspittle, Marco Rubio, actively work to destroy the international criminal court. Across Europe, far-right racists, loons and bigots make political advances, seen again this weekend in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt. Next year, France will approach its own fateful national reckoning. In the US, Trump, enabled by a supine majority in Congress and dishonourable supreme court justices, is constructing a “constitutional dictatorship” to subvert future elections, symbolised by a gross, 250ft-tall “Arc de Trump”. Let alarm bells ring: US democracy and the entire western democratic tradition are in dire peril. What is to be done? Is any consolation to be had? First, key pillars of the post-1945 order, though badly battered, are still just about intact. The UN and most of its agencies, the international court of justice and collaborative, multinational western democratic alliances such as the EU, Nato and the G7 have so far survived the current tumult. Second, the age of tyrants is nearing an end. These angry old men are mostly headed for nursing homes, jail or the grave. May their legacies of fear and hate die with them. Last, younger generations in many “middle power” and developing countries, exemplified by India’s Cockroach youth protest movement, are making plain their revulsion and rejection of the way the world is now. Like Burnham, they believe passionately in the power of possibility and change. The future lies not in the hands of political thugs and killers, of dictators and megalomaniacs, but in the hands of ordinary people everywhere. It depends on millions upon millions of individual daily acts of kindness, selflessness, faith and courage. So don’t lose heart. Keep your eyes open. Unblock your ears. And don’t look down! Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Game on: November elections kick into high gear with control of Congress in the balance
body_text: When voters went to the polls in the 2022 midterm elections, all the ingredients were there for Joe Biden’s allies to suffer a wipeout. The president was unpopular, inflation was high and historical trends predicted voters would take out their frustrations by ending the Democratic party’s control of Congress. But when the ballots were tallied, the gains Republicans expected to make did not quite materialize. They had won the House of Representatives, but only by a slim margin, while Democrats had expanded their majority in the Senate and built up their strength in state legislatures. Four years later, those very same factors are present once again as Republicans prepare in the 3 November midterms to defend the Senate and House majorities they won two years ago, when voters elected Donald Trump president. Like Biden before him, the president is unpopular and inflation is still high, though not as high as it was under his predecessor. And though he and his allies insist otherwise, there are few reasons to believe Trump can beat the historical trend of voters using midterm elections as an opportunity punish the party holding power in Washington. “The out party, typically speaking, is frustrated or even angry at what has happened during the previous two years, and they’re itching to register their disagreements and discontent, and 2026 is going to be no exception,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington who previously advised Democratic presidents. Campaigning is set to intensify following Monday’s Labor Day holiday, a milestone in election years that marks roughly two months until voters head to the polls. Recent public opinion surveys have shown Democratic candidates for House and Senate seats are either ahead of their opponents or in close contention, and major election forecasters have moved their ratings of key races in the party’s favor. But Republicans appear to have an advantage in one important realm, and that’s cash. Though some Democratic candidates like the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff and James Talarico, who is running for a Senate seat in Texas, have posted strong fundraising figures, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has $400m that could be deployed to help his allies, while his erstwhile ally Elon Musk has $50m in another Super Pac, which began spending in favor of some Republican candidates last week. Republican-led states have likely limited to some degree the party’s losses in the House by redrawing congressional maps, with the help of a recent supreme court ruling, despite efforts by Democratic-led states to retaliate. “I’ve been saying this over and over, but Republicans are going to defy history in 63 days and we’re going to hold this House majority,” the House speaker, Mike Johnson, recently told reporters. *** A little over a year after the September 11 attacks, George W Bush’s Republican allies were able to expand their majorities in the House and Senate in the 2002 midterms, but most other elections have been unpleasant to terrible for the party in power. Bill Clinton lost both chambers in 1994, and Bush suffered the same fate in 2006. In 2010, Barack Obama famously described the major losses suffered by Democrats in his first midterm election as a “shellacking”. Democrats lost control of the Senate four years later. In 2018, Trump’s Republicans lost the House, even as they built up their Senate majority. Biden’s first and only midterm – 2022 – stands out for the deus ex machina that appeared in the form of the supreme court’s decision in Dobbs v Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v Wade and ended the constitutional right to abortion. “It was very clear that women were more energized than usual, and that young people were more energized than usual because of one thing: the Dobbs decision. But without actually being on the ballot, congressional Republicans weren’t able to benefit from his popularity, as they would in the 2024 elections. It’s a tall order – with a majority no bigger than three seats, many things would have to go right for the GOP to hold the House. Winning the Senate is expected to be tougher for Democrats, because the party must capture at least three seats in states Trump won two years ago, including several that elected him by double digits. *** Control of either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s legislative agenda and give their lawmakers subpoena powers they can use to investigate his administration. Party leaders have centered their pitch to voters on the issue of affordability, arguing that the president’s attack on Iran, imposition of tariffs on trading partners, refusal to extend tax credits for Affordable Care Act health plans and cuts to the social safety net have all driven prices higher. “Life has gotten far too expensive in this country, and Republicans don’t give a damn about it,” the Democratic House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, told reporters last week. Recent polls of the generic ballot – an important indicator of sentiment in congressional elections – have shown that Democrats have an edge of between three and eight percentage points. But the trend isn’t unanimous. This week, a Harvard CAPS-Harris Poll taken in August showed Republicans with a slight advantage among likely voters. In Washington, the House reconvened last week after a five-week recess, but Johnson opted to cut its schedule for September short by two weeks, which will give representatives the opportunity to return home to campaign. But though it is typical for electioneering to intensify in the 60-some days before the election, Galston believes voters’ perceptions are “baked in”, with the only lingering question being which party can get more of their supporters out to vote. “A lot of people have already made up their minds,” he said. “Especially for Republicans, the question is not so much whether they’re going to cross party lines and vote for Democrats, although I think some will, but whether they’ll get out of bed on election morning.” There, the Democrats appear to be ahead. An Economist/YouGov survey from the final weeks of August showed Democratic voters with a six percentage point lead in enthusiasm, higher than it was earlier in the summer. “It’s hard to get excited about a presidency that has been defined by a complete failure to get prices under control, coupled with a war that is looking increasingly like a fiasco,” Galston said.

title: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
body_text: Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict. Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight. “It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”. “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added. Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings. US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.” He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries. “And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.” In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership. “The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.” The White House was also contacted for comment. In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure. Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said. Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing. The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender. That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East. The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint. “So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said. Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.” He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open. “So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.” Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And when asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.” Panetta said he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it. He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health onboard. “Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said. “So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”
