title: Trump-backed John Sununu wins New Hampshire Republican Senate primary
body_text: Former senator John E Sununu triumphed on Tuesday in the New Hampshire Republican Senate primary over Scott Brown, earning the GOP nod in what will probably be a must-win race if Democrats hope to seize the upper chamber. Sununu, 61, was the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary. He served one term in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. Brown represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term. The US president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year, despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of Trump, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary. On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power, and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. He told New Hampshire Public Radio it was “a tactical mistake” to go to war “without having a plan for protecting the strait of Hormuz”. That posture may matter in a state where Trump’s approval rating sits at 38%. Sununu and Brown did not respond to the Guardian’s interview requests. Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said Sununu was a “strong candidate” who was “well positioned to beat out Pappas” in a general election. “While Democrats have been consumed by infighting, Republicans have been laser-focused on real issues like affordability and security,” she added in a statement. Sununu will face congressman Chris Pappas, who beat back a progressive challenger in the Democratic primary, advancing as most observers expected to what will be a closely watched general election that is critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the upper chamber. Some Democrats, however, worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, now the governor, captured a seat.

title: First Thing: Conflicting court rulings on Missouri map threaten November’s midterm election
body_text: Good morning. Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty less than two months before the November midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress. Conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Donald Trump’s support to give Republicans an edge in the midterms, but a ruling by a federal judge in Missouri temporarily prevented the state from using its old congressional maps. Why is there legal action over the maps? The Missouri supreme court has previously ruled that the new map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in time for the November election. The president and Republicans had fumed over the decision, with Trump calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unconstitutional”. What are the significant changes to the map intended to favor Republicans? The revised map targeted the fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas. Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after UK imposes sanctions on West Bank settlements The UK government has entered a diplomatic row with Israel after it announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements. In the country’s starkest condemnation since the founding of the Israeli state, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband – whose mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – said settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, claimed the ruling UK Labour party Miliband belongs to was gripped by “Jew hatred”. What has the British prime minister said? Writing in the Guardian, Andy Burnham said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, and that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”. “The measures we are taking,” he said, “are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole.” How has Israel reacted? Israel has ordered the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem among retaliatory measures including entry bans on several UK lawmakers. The Israeli government added that longstanding British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces on the West Bank would be terminated. Britain will also be excluded from the US-led Gaza coordination mission. US says Iranian tankers ‘destroyed’ as Houthis strike Saudi Arabian cities The US military on Tuesday said it had “destroyed” several Iranian tankers after Iran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles, as violence once again surged across the region, pushing the price of oil past $100 a barrel. Centom said the strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The IRGC said it had struck a US military base in Jordan in retaliation. What have been the other developments in the region? Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the overnight strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south. US bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war escalates The US is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, the White House said on Tuesday, as the trade war between the two neighbors and longtime allies escalates. The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US imports earlier on Tuesday. Donald Trump also moved Tuesday to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts. Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of US alcoholic products – a move that prompted the retaliatory US ban on Tuesday. Canadian tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment. In other news … The pilots of an Amazon cargo plane tried to abort landing in Miami seconds before the crash that killed five employees of an aircraft cleaning company who were in a van it struck. Ex-60 Minutes managing editor Guy Campanile says fired staffers “refused to be accomplices” in the show’s “destruction” under new editorial leadership. The Trump administration plans to confront Australia’s government over its decision that US tech companies must allow users to opt out of social media algorithms. Television programme South Park is to change its name to South America “inspired by bravery and patriotism” of Apple and Google, who capitulated to Donald Trump’s requests to change Lake Ontario to Lake America. Stat of the day: Ukraine books in 1,000 Patriot missiles as UK and EU open up aid Ukraine is ⁠contracting a supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles over the coming years with the help of allies and ⁠through an E⁠U loan, the country’s defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has said. The development comes as Kyiv faces food shortages after Moscow’s forces continually bomb warehouses supporting civilian life. Well actually: the truth behind ‘old person smell’ No you aren’t imagining it, people do smell different as they get old. Jillian Pretzel gets into the science of why, and whether you can do anything about it. Don’t miss this: Grief, fury, conspiracy – inside Turning Point USA after Charlie Kirk’s killing A year since his assassination, the movement Kirk started is reckoning with the void he left behind - and a revolution that eats its own. … or this: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss Rafael Behr has a warning that far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism on the continent for another generation. Climate check:the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spaces The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of the climate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens. Last Thing: Tame Impala frontman announces he will no longer sign autographs due to ‘aggressive’ collectors The Australian musician Kevin Parker has announced he will no longer sign autographs, citing “aggressive” professional collectors who he claimed had used children in order to get his signature. The Tame Impala singer also said he would no longer meet with fans in the parking lot after shows “for the time being” after being warned of “the obvious security risk”. title: ‘They’re ready to come home’: the movement to bring young voters back to Democrats
body_text: On the first day of the fall semester at California State University, Northridge, student organizers holding “Hot People Vote” signs wheeled a bright pink wagon outside the student union. They offered “no strings attached” donuts, heart-shaped sunglasses and voting information for the November general election. Even though it was 105F outside, dozens of people stopped by to chat with the Donuts + Democracy volunteers and register to vote. One student told organizer Dzian Tran that she didn’t plan to vote because she was disillusioned with politics. Tran chatted with her about how civic engagement is important to democracy and how some elections are won by a margin of only 400 votes. As she thanked Tran, the student held her phone up to a QR code to get more information about voting. About 50 million young people are eligible to vote in 2026, but nearly half are either not registered or civically engaged, according to US Census Bureau data. After Donald Trump made significant gains among young men in the 2024 election, Democratic-aligned groups have been eager to capture gen Z voters who may be disaffected by politics. From bringing politicians, celebrities and donuts to campuses to hosting tailgating events, happy hours and street parties, a crop of youth-led and youth-focused organizations are employing fresh tactics to meet gen Z where they are – and luring them in with fun. Heather Haggarty, who runs Donuts + Democracy with her daughter, said traditional voter engagement strategies such as postcards, clipboards and phone-banking fail with young voters. When her two gen Z children suggested taking donuts to a university voter registration event a few years ago, she ended up speaking to more than 100 kids in 90 minutes. Haggarty said the deep-fried snack is akin to “breaking bread”, making zoomers more willing to talk and connect. “Young kids aren’t apathetic,” she said. “They care. But voting isn’t easy and traditional voter engagement can feel transactional and alienating.” ‘From a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly’ While Republicans invested more than $1bn to target young voters from 2020 to 2025, Democrats haven’t historically backed campus organizing and young organizers, said Haggarty. It’s often left up to young people to inspire and educate their peers. Since 2021, the Keep Arizona Blue Student Coalition, or Keep AZ Blue, has registered about 15,000 students at high schools and colleges. “We engage people online where young people are most, on campus and at community events and coffee shops and other hangout spots,” said Jacob Marson, the group’s 22-year-old executive director. “As football starts up, we’re going to bring elected officials to tailgates along with energy drinks and donuts – these are conversation starters.” Marson’s team has found that community colleges have been largely ignored by organizers in the past. When they show up on those campuses, whether in rural areas or Maricopa county (the fourth-most populous US county), they have “amazing conversations”, Marson said. Last year, Keep AZ Blue brought the Arizona representative Lorena Austin to Mesa Community College, and earlier this year they introduced Arizona’s attorney general, Kris Mayes, to students at Arizona State University. “I think some young voters took a chance on Trump, but it’s clear they’re ready to come home and support our Democratic candidates,” Marson said. “They’ve seen the policies of a Republican-controlled House, Senate and presidency. I am fully confident that young voters are ready to elect Democrats across the state.” Although research has shown that 43% of zoomers do not identify with a political party, they are twice as likely to move left in recent years. And while young people face the most obstacles to voting of any age group, once gen Z is registered to vote, they vote at close to the turnout rates of those over age 30. Youth-focused organizations understand that gen Z voters swing elections. The non-partisan voter organization When We All Vote, founded by Michelle Obama, hosted more than 500 Party at the Polls events throughout the US in 2024. This year, they are scaling up to 5,000 events with a goal of reaching an estimated 20 million gen Z voters. They are particularly focusing on Black and brown communities in the aftermath of the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and other suppression efforts. “It could be anything from a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly to smaller cookouts and barbecues,” said senior adviser Kalisha Dessources Figures. “We’re meeting communities where they are with what looks like joy and celebration to them.” The organization recently brought Love Island USA winner Serena Page to the University of Houston for a conversation on college, dating and civic engagement that was attended by hundreds of students who received free giveaways such as tooth gems and custom merch. HeadCount is another organization mixing voter registration efforts with joy. This year, they have teamed up with celebrities such as Ilana Glazer, Harry Styles and Bob the Drag Queen to encourage gen Z to take action for chances to win tickets and VIP experiences at concerts, sporting events and music festivals. All of this outreach might be helping: some primaries this year have already seen increased turnout among zoomers. In El Paso’s primary, the youth turnout nearly tripled compared to 2022. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed received almost 60% of the vote in key counties where college-aged voters live, and some experts believe the youth vote was likely responsible for his close primary win. California, meanwhile, has added nearly 2 million more gen Z-aged registered voters since 2022, and more than two-thirds of 18- to 29-year-olds say they are inclined to support progressive candidates in the state. Harnessing anger and frustration Some youth-led organizations are also rallying young people to get more involved in activism, organizing their peers and building political power for their generation. At the recent Voters of Tomorrow summit in Raleigh, North Carolina, hundreds of young people turned out to hear from progressive politicians such as the Tennessee representative Justin Pearson and North Carolina representative Jordan Lopez. Attenders also participated in trainings and workshops on peer-to-peer organizing and building political power online. “We’re working to make sure young people know what’s at stake, but we’re also working with candidates to make sure they are making promises that they can actually deliver on,” said Santiago Mayer, the founder and executive director of Voters of Tomorrow (VOT). “We’ve seen in New York and New Jersey and Virginia and Michigan – young people are looking for candidates who are talking about the issues they need addressed.” The gen Z-led organization has more than 11,000 members and chapters in more than 25 states. In addition to campus events, they have hosted happy hours in Iowa and a film festival in North Carolina to engage new voters. “We’re trying to host events where young people can make new friends and come back not just because they agree with the politics, but because they feel it’s a third space where people can find community and have fun,” said Mayer, who founded VOT in 2019 at age 17. While he said the left was outspent when it came to targeting young voters in 2024, he believes Democrats can win gen Z in the midterms. “Trump lied to them when he said no new wars and that prices would come down,” he said. “Young people do not like being lied to or used, and that’s what Republicans did. They immediately threw us under the bus.”

They are particularly focusing on Black and brown communities in the aftermath of the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and other suppression efforts. “It could be anything from a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly to smaller cookouts and barbecues,” said senior adviser Kalisha Dessources Figures. “We’re meeting communities where they are with what looks like joy and celebration to them.” The organization recently brought Love Island USA winner Serena Page to the University of Houston for a conversation on college, dating and civic engagement that was attended by hundreds of students who received free giveaways such as tooth gems and custom merch. HeadCount is another organization mixing voter registration efforts with joy. This year, they have teamed up with celebrities such as Ilana Glazer, Harry Styles and Bob the Drag Queen to encourage gen Z to take action for chances to win tickets and VIP experiences at concerts, sporting events and music festivals. All of this outreach might be helping: some primaries this year have already seen increased turnout among zoomers. In El Paso’s primary, the youth turnout nearly tripled compared to 2022. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed received almost 60% of the vote in key counties where college-aged voters live, and some experts believe the youth vote was likely responsible for his close primary win. California, meanwhile, has added nearly 2 million more gen Z-aged registered voters since 2022, and more than two-thirds of 18- to 29-year-olds say they are inclined to support progressive candidates in the state. Harnessing anger and frustration Some youth-led organizations are also rallying young people to get more involved in activism, organizing their peers and building political power for their generation. At the recent Voters of Tomorrow summit in Raleigh, North Carolina, hundreds of young people turned out to hear from progressive politicians such as the Tennessee representative Justin Pearson and North Carolina representative Jordan Lopez. Attenders also participated in trainings and workshops on peer-to-peer organizing and building political power online. “We’re working to make sure young people know what’s at stake, but we’re also working with candidates to make sure they are making promises that they can actually deliver on,” said Santiago Mayer, the founder and executive director of Voters of Tomorrow (VOT). “We’ve seen in New York and New Jersey and Virginia and Michigan – young people are looking for candidates who are talking about the issues they need addressed.” The gen Z-led organization has more than 11,000 members and chapters in more than 25 states. In addition to campus events, they have hosted happy hours in Iowa and a film festival in North Carolina to engage new voters. “We’re trying to host events where young people can make new friends and come back not just because they agree with the politics, but because they feel it’s a third space where people can find community and have fun,” said Mayer, who founded VOT in 2019 at age 17. While he said the left was outspent when it came to targeting young voters in 2024, he believes Democrats can win gen Z in the midterms. “Trump lied to them when he said no new wars and that prices would come down,” he said. “Young people do not like being lied to or used, and that’s what Republicans did. They immediately threw us under the bus.”

title: New Mexicans meet Trump’s threat to change state’s name with ridicule and outrage
body_text: When scrolling through social media over the Labor Day weekend, Steven Michael Quezada, an actor, comedian and native New Mexican, was stopped cold by a post about Donald Trump’s recent call to rename New Mexico as “New America”. “At first I thought, nah, that’s got to be a joke,” said Quezada, who played the drug enforcement agent Steven Gomez in the legendary TV series Breaking Bad. But it’s not drawing a lot of laughs in the state with the largest percentage of Latinos and 23 federally recognized Native American tribes. “In his mind, the word ‘Mexico’ has some kind of connotation of people of color and it just feels like the whitewashing of our state,” said Sarah Noss, a native New Mexican and non-profit executive, one of many residents expressing outrage at Trump’s social media posts in interviews with the Guardian. The president’s calls to rename New Mexico have reopened deep wounds for a state with a racial and ethnic composition that has made it a target for bigoted attacks dating back to 1848, when the US acquired the Mexican territory as part of the treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Later, the former civil war general William T Sherman said the US should “declare war on Mexico and make it take back New Mexico”. An AI-generated video of the president changing a “Welcome to New Mexico” sign to “Welcome to New America” comes 10 days after the Trump administration sued the state for providing in-state tuition and state-funded financial assistance to undocumented immigrant students – the majority of whom are Latino – another example of what some residents said were policies targeting people of color. “We were New Mexico even before we were the United States,” said Antoinette Armijo-Rougemont, a multigenerational New Mexican and army national guard veteran. “Every day is a new illogical idea. He should be focusing on ending the war and improving the economy.” The messages have tapped into longstanding anger in the state over racist government policies. US lawmakers resisted statehood for New Mexico for more than 60 years – until 1912 – because of its large Spanish-speaking and Native populations. “We were denied statehood because we were considered mixed-blood Mexicans, fanatical Catholics and savage Indians,” said Rob Martinez, the New Mexico state historian. “We went to bed Mexicans and woke up supposedly American citizens, but we weren’t treated like Mexican American citizens, we were treated like foreigners in our own land.” Martinez said the state’s name traces back to the 1560s, when Spanish settlers called it Nueva Mexico, in a reference to Mexico City. The name evolved to Nuevo Mexico, then New Mexico. By the 1920s, various civic groups launched campaigns to rename New Mexico, including a push to call the state Coolidge, in honor of the sitting president Calvin Coolidge. Republicans in the state, including gubernatorial candidate Gregg Hull, have dismissed the president’s suggestion out of hand, and congressional candidate Greg Cunningham, who is running in a swing district, called the president’s posts “satire” and an attempt by Democrats to “distract voters from their awful record by focusing on what the president is posting on social media”. Quezada, who called his 2022 comedy special The New Mexican, said Trump is like a comic on stage who knows he is losing the room. “Everything’s a mess right now, and I guess the best entertainer knows to distract you from what’s really going on,” he said. But the last laugh will be for New Mexicans, who would have to approve an amendment to the state’s constitution for a name change, an unlikelihood in a state in which every major statewide office is held by a Democrat. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly said that New Mexico has the most federally recognized Native American tribes in the United States.

title: Texas Republican in race for key House seat under fire for derogatory comments
body_text: A Republican candidate for a key congressional district in Texas has come under scrutiny over a series of derogatory comments made about women in his social media posts and videos. Brandon Herrera, who is the GOP candidate for Texas’s 23rd congressional district, has made a string of insults while fashioning a rightwing online persona as the “AK Guy”, and hosts a YouTube channel with more than 4 million subscribers that tests and reviews firearms. The comments, first reported by CNN, include Herrera taking aim at people he opposes politically, and women. In a 2023 video, he said that a gun range dummy’s empty head was “full of mush – much like the average Austin feminist”, and in a separate 2024 video, he likened the weight of “angry blue-haired” feminists to that of orca whales and elephants. In 2020, Herrera filmed himself firing a gun at bottles of ranch dressing and, after they exploded, rubbing the condiment on to himself and declaring that this would “make me irresistible to the fat bitches”. While discussing the merits of a car on X in 2023, Herrera opined that “4 doors means more whores”. Other groups have also been the focus of Herrera’s online content. In 2020, while firing a gun at a ham, Herrera said that while purchasing a ham for target practice was expensive, it was “still cheaper than a homeless person”. This isn’t the first time that Herrera has come under scrutiny. In 2024, during a run for Congress, Herrera said: “I am not, nor have I never [sic] been, a neo-Nazi” after describing a Nazi-era gun as “the original ghetto blaster”. The Republican Jewish Coalition condemned him at the time as “a goose-stepping extremist”. Herrera said that all these comments were jokes, and took aim at his opponent in this November’s midterm election, Democrat Katy Padilla Stout. “It’s disappointing that CNN would allow someone to allege that jokes about feminism lead to violence when Stout is fighting to return children to the parent convicted of abusing them,” Herrera said in a statement to CNN, referring to a case in which Stout was appointed as a defense attorney for a father seeking to restore parental rights after a domestic abuse allegation. Asked to comment on his previous statements made online, Herrera said via his campaign that it was “disappointing” that “alleged journalists” would “ignore” the Stout case. He did not reference his own past statements. The past comments could add to Republicans’ challenge of holding on to the US House of Representatives seat. Herrera is attempting to replace Tony Gonzales, a Republican lawmaker who resigned in April amid a House ethics committee investigation into his relationship with a former aide. While Democrats havenot prevailed in this district since 2015, the party has recently added it to its target list and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has sent funding to Stout, a former teacher and attorney, in what is expected to be a strong year for Democrats amid rising voter dissatisfaction with Donald Trump.

title: Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband
body_text: British intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has said. The disclosure counters predictions that his decision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies. The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments. Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House. Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. “I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday. Trump, now locked in fighting midterm elections, appears reluctant to leap to the aid of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who persuaded him to go to war against Iran. That decision has pushed oil prices beyond $100 a barrel, helping to swell a threatened “blue wave” that could leave the Democrats in charge of both the House and the Senate. There is also cross-party concern in the US at the violent tactics adopted by some Israeli settlers. Miliband said on Sky News on Wednesday: “We obviously talked to the Americans in advance of our announcement. I think the whole international community, let me say this, has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government. “I think there is real concern about what is happening … underlying so much of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine. “It’s in our interest to act not just because it’s standing up for our values, but because it’s in our interests to have this two-state solution as a rock of stability in the Middle East.” The US decision not to oppose the UK over its sanctions and ban on trade with the Israeli settlements follows conversations between Trump and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday, as well as previous diplomatic exchanges at lower levels. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, was careful not to endorse the UK sanctions, but affirmed he shared the objective of securing greater stability. Miliband can also claim credit for persuading Canada and France to join the trade ban, the surprise element in the package announced on Tuesday. The agreement came together late in the process. Eight other European countries have announced their intention to introduce such measures or to support the measures within the EU, a statement of solidarity that represents probably less of a shift than headlines might suggest. Some of the signatory countries had already taken steps independent of the EU, or had long been advocating for measures such as suspension of the Israel-EU trade agreement. For France, the decision to join the British initiative was formalised relatively late during Emmanuel Macron’s trip to London, when he met Burnham on 3 September and celebrated the display of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum. France acted after a Franco-Swedish proposal made to the EU27 in April appeared to be making little progress. The French plan aimed to establish an embargo or tariff on products from the occupied territories, but resistance from a constellation of countries including Germany, Italy and Bulgaria blocked progress. The commission also appeared to raise objections. Paris last year had led the push to recognise the state of Palestine as critical to the two-state solution, but much of the French diplomatic energy had subsequently drifted. The UK, along with Jordan, will hold a meeting concerning improving humanitarian supplies into Gaza at the UN general assembly later this month. In advance of Miliband’s statement, Trump had been hinting that he might support the Argentinian claim to sovereignty over the Falklands, a proposal mooted by Netanyahu’s son. But in a little-noticed move likely to please Washington, Miliband this week supplemented the action against Israel by announcing fresh nuclear-related sanctions against Iran, including targeting Iranian ships involved in “malign behaviour”. The UK also said it was backing a motion to be put to the UN stating Iran was in breach of its obligations on nuclear proliferation. The new sanctions are extended to cover energy, software, metals, gold and related activities such as shipping, insurance and banking. Most Iranian aircraft will be prohibited from landing in the UK. In response to the UK ban on goods, not due to come into force for at least six months, Israel has said it will: close the British consulate in in occupied East Jerusalem; remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel; terminate the UK’s role in training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank; and deny 12 mainly leftwing MPs entry to Israel.

title: Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes
body_text: Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July. The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports. The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods. Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis. Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday. The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing. The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”. A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks. Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas. The US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days. Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data. The back-and-forth strikes signalled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told reporters. Iran said it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time. The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia. The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh. Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea. The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil.

title: Republicans kick off ‘midterm convention’ to overcome Trump unpopularity
body_text: Republicans are gathering in Texas on Wednesday for a rare “midterm convention”, as they attempt to convince Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has overseen inflation and led the US into an increasingly unpopular war. Donald Trump will dominate the two-day convention, appearing both nights as the GOP works to cling to control of the House of Representatives in November. Republicans plan to put the president at the center of the event, a bold strategy given his approval rating is hovering at about 38%, while accusing the Democratic party of being socialist and out of touch with Americans. However, in a sign of Trump’s toxicity, some vulnerable Republicans have said they will not attend the Dallas event: risking the potential ire of the president, but avoiding a public association with a deeply unpopular leader. Less than two months out from the midterm elections, the Republican party faces a serious battle to retain its slender control of the House, while Democrats are increasingly hopeful they could pick up Senate seats. Winning either would put the Democratic party in position to stymie Trump’s aims during his final two years in office. The convention represents perhaps Republicans’ final opportunity to make a large-scale, high-profile pitch to Americans. Joe Gruters, the chair of the Republican National Committee (RNC), which is organizing the convention, said the program would attempt to demonstrate how Republicans are “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Whether voters buy that is a different matter, given costs, including gas prices, have risen during Trump’s presidency. Forecasters give Republicans a slim chance of holding on to the House, in particular, and some members of Congress have been keen to distance themselves from the event. Several Republican members of Congress said they will skip it entirely. Some Democrats are congregating in Dallas to counter the convention’s narrative. On Wednesday, JB Pritzker, the Illinois governor, joined a Texas Democratic party event and accused Republicans stumping for Trump of “bootlicking”. He also alleged that Trump’s efforts to enact restriction on mail-in voting amount to a promise to end fair elections in the future. “If Democrats don’t win, if they don’t win in this election, we may not have other elections,” Pritzker said. “Or certainly we’re going to have future elections, every single one of which will be rigged.” Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, said a contingent of Democrats on Thursday will “counter the falsehoods and extremism” on display in American Airlines Center. Tom Barrett, facing a close re-election fight in Michigan, and Zach Nunn, locked in a tight race in Iowa, are among those who have said they won’t be in Texas, and on Thursday Axios reported that “only about 100 lawmakers and candidates are expected to attend”. As well as risking association with Trump, there was the issue of cost. Multiple reports have suggested that House Republicans were being asked to donate at least $25,000 to the party to get a ticket. Among the few who are confirmed to be attending are JD Vance and the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, along with Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas who is polling neck-and-neck with Democrat James Talarico in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. There are signs too, that enthusiasm is low among the rank and file. The RNC announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery, and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Friday, days before the event was due to begin, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page, suggesting the event was not yet at capacity. Should the attendance be lacklustre, it will be a clear indictment of Trump himself, given RNC marketing materials in the buildup had made it clear it was the president’s show. Indeed, some messages billed the event as “Trump’s midterm convention” – ditching the term ‘Republican’ altogether – while every press release has been at pains to stress Trump will be there both nights. Trump himself was bullish about the convention in a podcast interview last week, telling the Texas lieutenant governor, Dan Patrick: “It’s going to be big stuff.” Chris Hippensteel contributed reporting

title: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity
body_text: Imperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing a fifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession. This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bring online might bring down oil prices eventually, but not anytime soon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American voters are struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates. The US president also promotes the idea that he is transforming the US’s industrial landscape through fossil fuels. Although the Venezuela oil grab might be highly profitable for a few selected companies, the windfall is dwarfed by the size of the US economy. Mr Trump is not getting cheap energy but a spectacle of American power. That may be enough for him. Before Mr Maduro was captured, Mr Trump had decided that Venezuela’s oil belonged to the US. The Venezuelan strongman was offered exile if he gave Washington want it wanted. When he dithered, a US armada assembled off Venezuela’s coast. Yet Mr Trump did not replace Mr Maduro with María Corina Machado from the democratic opposition. He instead backed the authoritarian regime that could secure the oilfields from ambitious army generals and spare the costs of occupation. The US doesn’t rule Venezuela directly, but it is exercising power through a lifelong socialist, Ms Rodríguez. She is remaking Chavismo, the revolutionary movement launched by Hugo Chávez, in her image – enraging some leftists. Ms Rodríguez has granted North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep) concessions to 17 oilfields in Venezuela for decades to come. Nabep’s boss, Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial Venezuelan oil billionaire, popped up in Caracas for this week’s visit by the US energy secretary, Chris Wright. Nabep has in turn granted the Pentagon a 35% equity stake at no cost to the US taxpayer. The charge of “Yankee imperialism” was often dismissed as kneejerk anti-Americanism. Mr Trump has turned it into an American boast. Ms Rodríguez argues that she is no puppet. Cooperation with Mr Trump, she says, will bring Venezuela investment and could generate $200bn in oil revenues. Unequal bargains have often benefited local rulers and intermediaries. The question is: what kind of economy and social order will that revenue produce? Oil cash is not the same as sovereign development. Mr Trump is a playground bully handed the world’s most powerful military. He mistakes coercion for greatness and sovereign nations for toys. He uses US power to feed his bottomless ego – recently claiming himself to be a bigger historical figure than Caesar, Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Stalin and Mao. When he departs the stage, others will have to rebuild what he has squandered: the US’s authority, its alliances and its reputation. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Bond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debt
body_text: The US treasury moved to cut the cost of borrowing on Wednesday only to be swiftly rebuffed by the bond market. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, announced the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a selloff in the US bond market that has put pressure on interest rates. But the size of the deal failed to appease bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high. Rising inflation and uncertainty from the war in Iran have spooked investors from US bonds, historically known to be one of the safest investment vehicles. Treasury yields have been rising, with the yield for the 30-year treasury bond hitting about 5.2% – the highest yield since the 2008 financial crisis. In an attempt to alleviate the bond market, Bessent on 19 August announced the treasury would at least double its typical buyback operation. The move is meant to stabilize the market: fewer bonds on the market should mean that yields go down. But in the weeks since the announcement, treasury yields have continued to rise. Even after Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise. In August, US government debt for the first time in the country’s history reached $40tn – double the amount of debt from just 10 years ago. Higher yields could ultimately mean higher interest rates on loans, including mortgages, student debt and car loans, as these loans are often tied to the bond market. The move puts more pressure on the US Federal Reserve to deal with inflation, which has been pushed up by the war in Iran. The annualized inflation rate hit a three-year high in May before going down to 3.4% in July – 0.7% higher than the same time last year – largely because of higher energy prices. Donald Trump on Wednesday warned that oil prices were unlikely to come down before the midterm election. Though Iran “can’t hold out any longer”, its leaders are “desperate to try and affect the election”, he said. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump predicted. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday as conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate. The Fed could raise interest rates to mitigate higher prices, at the risk of upsetting the White House. Last week, Trump said the Fed “must get smart” and lower interest rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he wrote on social media. The pressure puts the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, who stepped into the role in May, in a bind: manage inflation or face the president’s wrath. In a closely watched speech at the Fed’s Jackson Hole symposium in August, Warsh affirmed that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”, but held off on whether the the central bank would raise rates anytime soon.

title: Trump officials push to exclude undocumented immigrants from US census
body_text: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed changes to the US census intended to exclude immigrants without legal status in addition to other groups, with potentially significant effects on the allocation of federal resources and drawing of districts in the US House of Representatives. In a proposed rule published in the Federal Register, the Census Bureau also announced it was considering changes to the data it collects about race and ethnicity, amid the Trump administration’s push to rid the government of diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Conducted decennially, the census historically counts the “whole number of persons” in the United States specified in the 14th amendment, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. The data is used by states to draw congressional maps that are crucial in determining which party controls the House. Donald Trump and his rightwing allies have long insisted that undocumented immigrants could skew the data, and the president called last year for the 2020 census to be redone in favor of a new survey based on “results and information gained from the Presidential Election of 2024”. “People who are in our country illegally will not be counted,” he wrote on Truth Social. The new rule proposed by the Census Bureau would continue counting lawful permanent residents, while excluding undocumented immigrants “due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States”. It also proposes excluding “aliens whose legal status is less durable and indefinite in length than lawful permanent resident status”. The bureau, which is under the commerce department, notes that it is considering using “its enormously broad access to administrative records” to determine the legal status of respondents. That could include data collected by the US departments of the treasury, health and human services, defense, and homeland security, as well as the postal service, the proposal says. The changes reprise a campaign Trump waged during his first term, when he tried unsuccessfully to add to a question about respondents’ citizenship to the 2020 survey. The bureau determined the citizenship question would have reduced the numbers of people willing to participate, and the supreme court ultimately ruled against the effort, which was abandoned when Joe Biden took over as president in 2021. The bureau is also reconsidering questions it asks regarding “race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation”. The rule points to the “(potentially) sensitive nature” of such inquiries and “the reduced need for or usefulness of this information”, which could conflict with the public’s obligations under federal law to respond truthfully to census questions. “Substantial doubts about the meaning, significance, and impact of attempting to categorize persons by race and ethnicity, in particular, have featured prominently in our national discourse and have been reflected in shifts in the law,” the proposal reads. Should the Census Bureau move forward with the changes, it will likely face legal challenges from Democrats and allied advocacy groups. Democrats on the House oversight committee accused the president of trying to “rig” the survey, and said: “The 14th amendment is clear: the census is meant to count ALL people living in the United States. We will fight this.”

title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
body_text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday. Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists. “We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said. The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US. Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country. In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region. During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America. On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence. Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”. Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations. During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government. During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy. Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

title: Missouri’s voting maps saga reaches supreme court after conflicting rulings
body_text: A high-stakes legal battle over Missouri’s congressional map returned on Wednesday to the US supreme court, after a series of conflicting decisions threw the state’s elections into turmoil less than two months before the November midterm elections. On Wednesday, a federal appeals court panel declined to block a ruling ordering Missouri to use the newly drawn congressional lines backed by Donald Trump to give Republicans an edge in the midterms elections. Opponents of the state’s redistricted map immediately filed an appeal to the US supreme court. The appeal is the latest move in an extraordinary legal back-and-forth spanning four courts. The rulings have left voters and local election officials in the state confused and uncertain about what the November ballot will look like. And there’s little time left before the pivotal elections that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress – and will affect the fate of Trump’s agenda for the rest of his term. On Tuesday, the conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh had denied a request from Missouri officials to use the House map favored by Republicans. His refusal left in place a unanimous ruling from the Missouri supreme court, which blocked the newer maps, drawn to carve an additional Republican-friendly House seat. But not long after, a federal district judge in St Louis issued a contradictory decision, temporarily preventing the state from using its old congressional maps in the November elections. The temporary restraining order, or TRO, ordered Missouri to use the newly drawn districts that favor Republicans, which the state used in its August primary elections. That ruling, issued by Stephen Clark of the eastern district of Missouri, was then appealed to the eighth US circuit court of appeals. “Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries. Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark, who was appointed by the president, wrote. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor of a TRO.” People Not Politicians, the group leading the challenge to the Republican-drawn map in Missouri, said in a statement on Wednesday that the eighth circuit court’s decision to deny their stay request had left state election officials with “no legal map to use”. title: Democrat John Fetterman makes surprise appearance at Republican convention
body_text: The Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing. The video message will do little to dampen speculation that the renegade senator, who is now more popular among Republican voters in Pennsylvania than the Democrats who helped elect him, is preparing to switch political parties. Fetterman has repeatedly said that is not his plan, though he recently suggested he would be forced to formally break with the Democratic party if it ever became “the anti-Israel party”. Democrats currently hold 47 seats in the US Senate. Despite the long odds, Democrats believe discontent with the economy and Trump’s low approval ratings have given them a rare opportunity to retake control of the upper chamber. A defection would jeopardize their already narrow path to a majority. Yet if Fetterman remains a Democrat, he would hold outsized influence, effectively wielding veto power in a 51-49 majority. In the roughly one-minute video, Fetterman, wearing his trademark black hoodie, stood outside the Mon Valley Works – a processing plant operated by US Steel in Pittsburgh. In a stunning display of support for a Republican colleague in the Senate, Fetterman called McCormick his “great friend”, and said that he would work with him and Donald Trump “to fight and defend the steel way of life”. “Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat. I’m always going to stand with America,” the Pennsylvania lawmaker said in the pre-recorded message. “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life. Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done, and he’s going to fight for Pennsylvania.” At the convention center in Dallas, attenders welcomed the senator’s rightward march. “I actually think it’s really awesome that he’s come around,” Tracy Smith, an attender from Maryland, said. “He’s more commonsense, and even though he’s a Democrat, he can see both sides. You have to get along. It’s like a seesaw. You know, not right or left, but in the middle. And I think he realized that, and it’s actually amazing.” Asked if she thought Fetterman could switch to the Republican party, Smith said: “I actually do. I think he’s leaning that way right here. It would be great. I think it would be awesome.” Eric Torrison, who traveled from Arizona to attend the convention, was also laudatory. “There is no way on God’s green Earth that I would have supported Fetterman when he ran for the Senate, and [was] aghast when he got elected,” said Eric Torrison, who lives in Arizona. “But it’s really interesting. He seems to have held to his beliefs, and not run to the left, and he seems to be, from a conservative standpoint, from a Republican standpoint, the only sensible Democrat there.” Fetterman’s fellow Democrats were far less charitable. “John Fetterman is the laziest Benedict Arnold America has ever seen. He didn’t even have it in him to get off his couch in his million-dollar penthouse to kiss Donald Trump’s ring in person. He phoned it in, just as he has every day as our senator. John should do his job or resign,” the Pennsylvania state representative Malcolm Kenyatta said in a statement. Fetterman has been in the limelight after reports from current and former staff that he was avoiding constituent events, behaving erratically and cozying up to conservative media. In the past week, the senator has attempted to defend himself after an account on X, which claims to be run by former staffers, gained traction.

title: Rhode Island’s Democratic governor loses primary amid anger over bridge
body_text: Rhode Island’s Dan McKee became the first sitting governor to lose a primary in nearly a decade, bested not by a more progressive challenger or a more youthful upset but by frustration over a bridge. McKee lost his Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes, a former longtime executive with the Rhode Island-based retail pharmacy CVS, the Associated Press said on Wednesday. “Tonight, we may have won the Democratic primary for governor, but let me be clear about what happens next: you will have a governor for everyone,” Foulkes said during her victory speech in the state’s capital, Providence. “Because there is so much work that needs to be done, and we need to do this together.” It is rare for a sitting governor to lose a primary election. It hasn’t happened in Rhode Island since 1994. In his concession speech, also in Providence, McKee promised to work with Foulkes to ensure she is elected in November. “This is something that I think is difficult to deal with,” McKee said, “but we just got to hold our heads high.” Several Democratic incumbents have been toppled this cycle, in a wave of anti-establishment anger that has elevated young and progressive insurgents. But this contest was different. On the campaign trail, Foulkes criticized McKee’s handling of repair work on Providence’s Washington bridge, a major east-west traffic artery that carries roughly 100,000 vehicles a day. She accused him of bungling those repairs, which have dragged on longer than originally planned. McKee closed the bridge in December 2023, after inspectors uncovered serious structural problems. By March 2024, officials had concluded that repairing the structure was not feasible and that it would have to be rebuilt. State officials initially estimated that the bridge would be reopened to traffic this year, but the project’s completion date has since been delayed to November 2028. The primary contest was something of a rematch from four years ago, when Foulkes, who is the niece of former Democratic Senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut, came in a close second behind McKee in a five-way contest. McKee went on to easily win the general election in 2022, after having assumed the role from then-governor Gina Raimondo, who stepped down to become Joe Biden’s US commerce secretary in 2021. Election prognosticators rate the seat as strongly Democratic, and therefore the winner of Wednesday’s primary is seen as having a major advantage in the November general election. McKee’s defeat was not the only electoral upset on Wednesday. In Providence, David Morales, a 27-year-old Democratic socialist defeated Mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary, ending the incumbent’s bid for a second term. Morales’s campaign was backed by progressive stalwarts, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and several labor unions.

title: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech
body_text: Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which the president assailed Democrats as “radical” and defended his unpopular war in Iran. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. But it laid bare the extent of the Republicans’ concern about their prospects in the pivotal November elections. “If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour speech in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” – despite his historic unpopularity causing many vulnerable Republican politicians to avoid the event. Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency. “There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.” The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely. Even so, Trump’s speech made it clear he thinks he will be the deciding factor in November. Noting that the party which holds the White House traditionally struggles in the midterm elections, Trump said: “We’ve got to change that, because we have something going that’s so good. “If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago,” he said. The buildup to the midterm convention had somewhat of a chaotic air. Trump was initially scheduled to speak on the second night, before the Republican National Committee announced that he would deliver the keynote on Wednesday, and instead give closing remarks on Thursday after his vice-president, JD Vance, speaks. Trump made several references to the war in Iran, warning Tehran “not to get cute” or the US “will have to hit them very hard”. But he also appeared to acknowledge the economic pain caused by the soaring price of oil. Trump re-enacted the way he told his economic advisers that the US needed to start the conflict because Iran was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. “I hate to do this to you,” he said he told them, noting the economy had been doing well. At the convention center, there were signs of middling enthusiasm among the rank and file. Compared with the four-day traditional convention in Milwaukee two years ago, the first day felt muted. There were no long queues to enter, no eternal waits for food or bathrooms. Swathes of empty seats were visible throughout Trump’s speech. Visible, except to Trump, who claimed, wrongly, that the arena was full. “Not only is this packed but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump declared. This was not observed by Guardian reporters. The RNC had announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Wednesday, with the convention under way, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page. Trump himself, however, appeared energized in his call to action on the first night, cracking jokes, including at the expense of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate in Texas who won a primary against the incumbent John Cornyn earlier this year. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.” Trump spent several minutes attacking Democrats, including Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, who Trump mocked as a “weird-looking dude”; the former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper, who is now running for Senate; and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. The Republicans’ unusual midterm convention features 12 hours of programming across two nights. On Wednesday, the speaker lineup featured Trump loyalists and candidates, but showmanship remained at the center of the agenda. Byron Donalds, a rising star in the party who is running for governor of Florida, and Mehmet Oz and Scott Bessent, two of Trump’s cabinet secretaries, were among those to take the stage, yet the president, a UFC fan, decided he would be introduced by two fighters, the middleweight Bo Nickal and Justin “The Highlight” Gaethje, a lightweight. Most speakers only got five minutes. Nickal and Gaethje, who both fought at the UFC 250 event on the White House Lawn in June, got 10. Gaethje told the crowd he had earned his “Highlight” nickname when he knocked out his first opponent very quickly in 2016, before linking himself to the 80-year-old Trump. “One mistake I’ve made in my career was becoming complacent while I was on a winning streak and forgetting how unforgiving my sport would be,” Gaethje said. “If we are not just as passionate about voting and winning in these midterms as we were in the last presidential election, then we risk being knocked out and losing all the momentum we have been fighting for.” Earlier, Republicans said the focus would be on “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Yet speaker after speaker instead attacked Democrats on alleged support for transgender rights, in particular, suggesting the Republican party intends to put culture wars towards the front as November approaches. Trump will speak again on Thursday, but said his address would be much briefer. “I gave you a lot of material,” he said, capping his remarks on Wednesday, before pleading one more time with voters to “please pretend that I’m running”. • This article was amended on 10 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Roy Cooper as a Republican.

title: As the midterms loom, Trump returns to his happy place: on stage in the theatre of the absurd
body_text: Kim Il-sung of North Korea reportedly sought transfusions of blood from young men; Mao Zedong of China believed sex with young women could prolong his life; Muammar Gaddafi underwent fat injections and hair transplantation to make himself look younger. But for Donald Trump, the secret of eternal youth lies in nights like this. The occasion of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas was enough to get the 80-year-old US president’s juices flowing. An arena with thousands of fanatical supporters indulging his lies, laughing at his jokes and burnishing his fantasies of greatness is Trump’s happy place. It certainly beats stuffy Washington. “State of the Union, you have to be very staid,” he said, feigning stiffness and a dreary voice: “Ladies and gentlemen, it’s an honour to be your president.” The crowd laughed. Trump continued: “You do that for about an hour and then everybody’s falling asleep. This is a much harder routine, let me tell you. We’re also out here to have a little bit of fun.” The crowd roared. Trump’s second term has been a quest in self-mythology. It is there in the dramatic foreign policy aimed at reshaping the world. It is there in the monuments and renovations in the capital, Washington DC. It is there in the barrage of social media posts and AI slop in which Trump appears as a young and virile all-conquering hero. It was also there on Wednesday night as Trump milked the adulation of his fanbase, the Make America Great Again diehards who, in some cases, have followed him for more than a decade. He was visibly gratified to see the “front row Joes” from his rallies, including Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit resembling his brick wall. The president spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, surpassing his own record length convention speech set in Milwaukee two years ago. He never stopped to sip water, though the adrenaline shot of this crowd, as devoted as his aide Natalie Harp, likely could have kept him going much longer. Anyone who suspected that this unconventional convention would be a “Trump-a-palooza” had the view reinforced when Lee Greenwood sang (somewhat shakily) “God Bless the USA”, the familiar intro to Trump campaign rallies. A giant video screen with the US flag slowly rose to reveal dozens of mainly female Trump fans, waving little flags and smiling exuberantly. Trump, wearing a navy blue suit, white shirt and blue tie, walked slowly across the shiny black stage, trimmed with gold. Chants of “USA! USA!” erupted as the song finished. “Welcome to the first ever midterm convention of any party,” Trump said, conveniently ignoring three that the Democrats held in the 1970s and 1980s. He soon told another lie. “Not only is this packed, but you have an equal number of people standing outside. If anybody would like to give up their seat!” In fact there were dozens of empty seats in the stadium, with the “nosebleeds” in the upper tier mostly unfilled. Making the dubious boast that no one had left the arena after 80 minutes, the president said: “It’s a great tribute to Trump … Everybody loves me and I love everybody!” But the most grievous lie came when he falsely claimed to have won three presidential elections, and declared, also falsely, that “people on the other side are actually admitting it”. The crowd cheered and shouted: “Four more years!” This was political theatre of the absurd with many bizarre Trumpian riffs, ranging from bad sporting trades involving the Dallas Mavericks and Babe Ruth to how Trump had to sacrifice hygiene for his political career so he could shake hands (“I’m a very clean person”). In trying to champion Texas attorney general Ken Paxton for the US Senate, he said: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly and he may not be the best looking guy I’ve ever seen but you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator. I’m sorry, Ken. Where the hell is he? He’ll never speak to me again but that’s OK.” There were language games. He spoke as if his big idea of changing “Democrats” to “Dumocrats” was a piece of marketing genius or political artistry worthy of Lee Atwater. USA!” He said, “Lake Ontario, you know we’re going to call that Lake America” – more cheers. “We did come up with one the other day which we think is appropriate. You have a neighbouring state, New Mexico. But Trump, true to form, bulldozed straight ahead. He also advised Iran “not to get cute” and asked the crowd: “Does anybody here think that Iran should have a nuclear weapon?” There was a huge shout of, “No!” Trump even speculated what would have happened if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon and subjugated the US. “If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ – as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.” Somewhere in all this mess, Trump talked about the midterms. He asked voters to “pretend” that he is on the ballot and promised $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. It was the old Trumpian trick: flaunt your bribery in public so blatantly that enough people assume it can’t be corrupt. He railed against Democratic “communists” and declared: “They have more bullshit than any human beings on the planet.” His supporters went wild. Such a witty putdown, sir! Trump castigated James Talarico, the Democrats’ candidate for the Senate in Texas, as “Talafreako” and claimed: “He ran a campaign to ‘beat meat.’ He called it ‘beat meat.’ I don’t know what the hell he meant by that … he wants to ‘beat meat?” … I’m getting myself in trouble. He was recently seen having a barbecue and eating a lot of meat.” All this and so much more. It went on and on, looping back on itself, zigzagging across the map, bamboozling any outside observer but somehow here, in the arena of Maga, making a warped kind of sense. “I love the weave,” Trump mused, gesticulating wildly. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom, or you bring in an aeroplane, or you bring in Air Force One – but you notice I always get right back to the same topic. Some day there’ll be a time when I do the weave, weave, weave; some day there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject.” Pointing his finger in the air, Trump said: “And then you can say: he’s had it.”
