title: Trump personality cult alive and well in Dallas – will it power Republican midterm success?
body_text: “We’re going to have a good time listening to music,” Donald Trump told thousands of supporters in downtown Dallas before handing the mic to an opera singer, “because I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.” Millions of Americans seem tired of politics after a decade dominated by Trump. So the US president’s decision to close out this week’s first ever Republican midterm convention with a plea – treat November’s congressional elections as a referendum on Trump himself – was received by his Democratic opponents with glee. They saw the president’s core pitch as a combination of begging and bribery. First he urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Then he promised $5,000 payouts to every US adult if Republicans retain control of the House of Representatives and Senate in November. Andy Beshear, the Democratic governor of Kentucky, told reporters on Thursday: “If Donald Trump wants to hold a convention saying this election is about him, I fully support his decision. He’s telling me to pretend that he is on the ballot – I want people to pretend that he is on the ballot.” But with hundreds of members of Congress and candidates staying away from the convention, most seats in the upper tier remained empty both nights. Trump’s keynote speech drew a modest 2.5 million viewers on Fox News, ⁠according to ⁠Nielsen data. Some attendees expressed discontent over the cost of living and Iran war while starting to look beyond the president to potential successors in 2028. With Trump’s approval rating at a historic low, it was far from certain that the two-day “Trump-a-palooza” will have the desired effect of galvanising the party’s base and recreating the turnout that powered his 2016 and 2024 presidential election victories. Holding a convention in a midterm year was an attempt to make history in order to defy history. The party that holds the White House typically suffers midterm losses: George W Bush’s Republicans took a “thumping” in 2006, while Barack Obama’s Democrats endured a “shellacking” in 2010. The omens this year are no less foreboding: the Decision Desk HQ website projects that Democrats are poised to capture the House of Representatives 229-206, with the Senate hanging on a knife-edge at 50-50. The spectacle in Dallas was rapidly pulled together at Trump’s behest after the host committee raised $45m in three weeks. It had some familiar trappings, including tall state delegations on the convention floor, fiery speeches and a celebratory balloon drop at the end, but no nominations or formal business. And there was no doubt who was the star of the show. Trump’s image was everywhere in the corridors of the American Airlines Center. Attendees wore clothes with phrases such as “Trump tribe”, “Trump has our back” and “Proud deplorable”. Speaker after speaker lavished him with effusive praise. Among them was Robert Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, who recalled their meeting soon after Trump survived a shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania: “I discovered a self-effacing man of superior intelligence, of empathy and compassion, with an encyclopedic grasp of the issues in molecular detail. And most of all, a near reckless courage to challenge vested interests and official orthodoxies.” But while the Trump personality cult was alive and well, another theme was just as prominent. Unable to point to falling grocery bills or peace in the Middle East, the convention leaned heavily into fear, painting a nightmarish portrait of what the US would look like with the Democrats back in charge. Images of the influencer Hasan Piker and other leftwing figures loomed ominously on giant video screens. A narrator’s voice boomed: “Today’s extreme left hasn’t simply moved away from Republicans. It has moved away from Democrats in its own party. Far beyond the common sense of the American people. This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat or conservative versus liberal. Today, the choice is unmistakable. Extreme versus mainstream.” Numerous speeches sought to whip up a new red scare. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent warned that Democrats wanted to transform the US into a “socialist hellscape” while House Speaker Mike Johnson framed the midterms as a simple choice between “common sense and crazy”. Many speakers emphasised their own Christian faith while stressing the godlessness of communism and conflating it with threats from outside America’s borders, at times invoking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said: “We are witnessing a new and dangerous red-green alliance – communists and Islamists coming together and sweeping over the Democrat party. They are united because they share the same enemies. They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the constitution, and they hate America!” There were shouts in the arena of “He should be shot!” as Cruz singled out some leading progressives by name: “When people tell you who they are, believe them. When Hasan Piker says, America deserved 9/11, believe him. When Mamdani says he wants to seize the means of production, he means it. When Abdul El-Sayed says he has an ‘obligation’ to comply with Sharia law, he means it. And when James Talarico says he wants to dismantle capitalism, he means this.” On the convention floor, Republicans echoed Cruz’s apocalyptic framing. Pavel Sokolov, 33, vice-chair of the New Jersey Republican party, drew on his personal background to reinforce the point. “I was born in the former Soviet Union; my parents and I fled that exact rhetoric,” Sokolov said. “It always starts nice and friendly, saying everyone must pay their fair share. But it inevitably ends up the same. In the Soviet Union, ostensibly everyone was equal, yet somehow the party bosses ate caviar every day.” Conversely, most speakers swerved past voters’ everyday concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s war of choice in Iran. Trump himself claimed that concerns about ‌inflation were exaggerated and the word “affordable” was “fake”. Interviews with more than a dozen attendees found staunch support for him – but with some reservations beneath the surface. Gregorio Heise, 59, a disabled army veteran from Texas, described Trump’s second term as “friggin’ awesome”, explaining: “I prefer to pay $5 a gallon [of gas] and put my head on a pillow and wake up knowing this country is still here than watching it go boom with a nuke. No, thank you. I’m a vet and I didn’t serve this country to watch it go to crap.” Joseph Ditto, a 50-year-old statistician from suburban Minneapolis wearing an elephant-patterned Republican tie, admitted his frustration with the administration’s foreign policy. “I’m not a fan of the war in Iran. I hope it’s over quickly,” he said. “I voted for the anti-war Trump, so that’s frustrating.” Democrats, who held three midterm conventions in 1974, 1978 and 1982 with mixed results, have no plans for a rival event this time. But some travelled to Dallas to counter the Republican messaging. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a congresswoman from California, highlighted what she saw as the fundamental disconnect of Trump’s second term. “Last night, Donald Trump was talking about how he wanted to build a big ballroom like they have in China,” she said. “The average American family can’t afford groceries or gas, and he’s fantasising about a ballroom in the people’s house. This entire event is built around one man who likes to hear himself talk.” To many political strategists, turning a midterm election into a direct referendum on an incumbent president whose national approval rating languishes in the low-to-mid 30s looks like a huge own goal. But Trump’s energetic performance on Wednesday night buoyed Republicans who believe he retains a unique ability to galvanise people who might not otherwise vote at all. David Hopkins, a professor of political science at Boston College, said: “There’s been a lot of journalistic dunking on Trump saying that making the election more about him is an ego trip winning out over smart strategy. That’s not an unreasonable take but there’s another way to look at it. The worst-case scenario for Republicans is that Republican voters stay home.” Hopkins pointed out that Trump commands a unique, low-propensity “Make America great again” (Maga) electorate that turns out passionately for him but frequently ignores down-ballot congressional races when his name is absent. “If they can’t get those people out, it looks like a real national wipeout.” The midterm convention also offered an intriguing subplot: the question of who inherits the Maga movement when Trump, the 45th and 47th president, is gone. Vice-President JD Vance was greeted by chants of “JD 48!” as he delivered Thursday night’s keynote address. He spoke at length about his family while describing Democrats as “the party that despises America and the people who built it”. When a protester waving a Mexican flag briefly interrupted his speech, Vance drew thunderous applause with a sharp put-down: “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.” In the concourses, delegates were actively sizing up the potential 2028 field. While Vance commands a substantial lead in early polling among Republican primary voters, several other names – most notably secretary of state Marco Rubio and Florida governor Ron DeSantis – were frequently cited. Heise said: “Marco Rubio is doing everything. He’s building on the foundations this country was created on in 1776.” Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, who has been a delegate at every Republican convention since 2004, echoed that sentiment. “I prefer Marco Rubio over Vance if I had to pick one today. He has proven his ability to lead in any capacity.” Rusat Ramgopal, 26, executive director of the Queens county Republican party in New York, envisioned a pragmatic resolution to avoid a damaging primary battle. “Instead of a divisive primary between Vance and Rubio, I think the two of them and the president will sit down in a room and decide the ticket,” he predicted. “It just depends on who is top of the ticket and who is vice president.” Republicans declared the convention a triumph. Outside the arena, the verdict was rather less enthusiastic. Veteran pollster John Zogby described the two-day gathering as an “act of desperation” that highlighted internal vulnerabilities rather than strength. “The president promised that the war in Iran would end by August, inflation would be down by August, fuel prices would be low again by August,” Zogby noted. “None of those have been achieved. We have moved from the politics of anger into the politics of disappointment.”

He has proven his ability to lead in any capacity.” Rusat Ramgopal, 26, executive director of the Queens county Republican party in New York, envisioned a pragmatic resolution to avoid a damaging primary battle. “Instead of a divisive primary between Vance and Rubio, I think the two of them and the president will sit down in a room and decide the ticket,” he predicted. “It just depends on who is top of the ticket and who is vice president.” Republicans declared the convention a triumph. Outside the arena, the verdict was rather less enthusiastic. Veteran pollster John Zogby described the two-day gathering as an “act of desperation” that highlighted internal vulnerabilities rather than strength. “The president promised that the war in Iran would end by August, inflation would be down by August, fuel prices would be low again by August,” Zogby noted. “None of those have been achieved. We have moved from the politics of anger into the politics of disappointment.”

title: Why is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox News
body_text: I think I finally understand why Fox News pays Jesse Watters the big bucks. The network star, famous for hot takes like men shouldn’t “eat soup in public”, has an incredible talent for inserting misogyny into absolutely any news story. Take, for example, Donald Trump’s ludicrous announcement on Wednesday night that he will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm election. That’s a story about apparent bribery, right? A story about fiscal recklessness and empty promises. A story about how the president, whose popularity is plummeting, is so out of ideas that he’s resorted (yet again) to dangling cash in front of voters. Actually, says Watters, it’s none of the above; it’s just Trump behaving like a woman. “That $5,000 check, Dana, that’s not a bribe,” Watters told Fox anchor Dana Perino on Thursday. “We’re calling it an enticement … It’s like a woman. Sometimes a woman can entice you, OK? Maybe – it doesn’t mean you’re going home with her, but it keeps you interested. It keeps you intrigued and wanting more. That’s what this is about.” Perhaps the Fox News host isn’t completely wrong. After all, I am a woman and I am about to entice you to look up the story about how Watters courted his much younger second wife. It’s very intriguing. But back to this definitely-not-a-bribe $5,000 payment which the president calls a Trump “dividend”. I wouldn’t start spending it now, if I were you. The president, like his right-hand man Elon Musk, has a habit of making grandiose promises he doesn’t keep. Remember the Doge dividends floated last February? Those haven’t materialized. Nor have the tariff dividends that Trump made so much noise about. “People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump said in a Truth Social post last year. “We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and … A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” Almost a year after that post, nobody has received a tariff dividend. However, it has been estimated by the Joint Economic Committee – Minority that the average American family will pay more than $2,500 in tariff costs this year. I feel pretty confident saying there is a 0.00001% chance that anyone is going to get a $5,000 Republican celebration check. But let’s just play along for a minute and pretend that Trump isn’t a fabulist. Let’s pretend that the president is a serious man who makes thoughtful policy proposals, rather than an opportunist who says whatever inane thing happens to pop into his brain in the moment. Isn’t it a bit reckless to be giving all this money away, a total that exceeds $1tn, when the US national debt recently surpassed $40tn for the first time? As Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement, that debt “doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers”, it is shouldered by everyone. “The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad.” Don’t worry about all that, says the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick told NBC News on Thursday. The Trump administration is going to earn that money from various moneymaking endeavours like the Trump Platinum Card, which allows wealthy people to pay up to $5m to extend their US visas. JD Vance, meanwhile, has suggested that the money might come from US tariff revenues, even though economists have pointed out the $125bn in tariff revenues wouldn’t come close to covering the costs. The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters. When the ABC reporter Rachel Scott asked him about the rationale behind the $5,000 checks on Thursday night, he said it was a reward to Americans for putting up with Joe Biden. After Scott tried to ask a follow-up question, Trump lunged at her and said: “Your network … you’re the worst.” Which is very on-brand for the president. He can’t seem to handle being asked tough questions by anyone, but gets particularly nasty when those questions are posed by a woman. While Trump doesn’t want to get into the details of his dividend, the proposal reflects how the president is looking at some very unconventional ways to sway the midterms. He may not end up issuing people celebration checks, but he has already gutted election security programs and attempted to limit voting access. The real story here isn’t $5,000 cheques, it’s the fact that America’s self-styled king seems intent on meddling with the election, and no meaningful checks and balances are stopping him. Ectopic pregnancy deaths in the US have nearly doubled A ProPublica analysis found almost 200 women died after an ectopic pregnancy from 2020 to 2025. That’s compared to about 100 in the previous six years. To nobody’s surprise, mortality is worse in states with strict abortion bans. “While they cautioned that abortion bans alone can’t explain the national rise, maternal health experts said any examination of the spike should include the documented delays in care caused by the laws, including for ectopic pregnancies,” ProPublica notes. Sudanese refugees are being forced into sex work Sudan’s civil war, which started in 2023, has created the world’s worst displacement crisis. Now, many of the women who fled to Egypt are being sexually exploited. What’s happened to Pete Hegseth’s testosterone screening guidance? The Pentagon published a guidance document on 2 September outlining a new mandatory testosterone screening process to create a “High-T military”. However, the very next day it was withdrawn from the public domain for reasons that remain unclear. Maybe someone in the Pentagon came to their senses. Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed Naza, a highly-feted new film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, reveals the secret systems used in mass killings of civilians in Gaza. “Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,” the Guardian writes. “[O]ne said their mission was to ‘thwart peace’.” Why does the hard right shrug off domestic abusers in their midst? The short answer is because they are misogynists who cynically weaponize women’s rights to advance their agenda. But do read Zoe Williams, who has a longer and more eloquent answer, following on from the attack on a female protester at the Reform UK conference. The Republican convention showed an image of Hasan Piker in his underwear They seem to think showing photos of a buff podcaster in his underwear demonstrates that the left are scary “radicals”. The rise of hairy young women Phoebe Bridgers’ unshaven legs at her Venice film festival debut sparked a flurry of headlines. But, says Leah Harper, Bridgers’ “au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations”. Emma Bonino, feminist Italian politician, dies aged 78 Bonino got involved in politics after she had an abortion (then illegal) at age 26 and said she decided that “never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation”. She handed herself in to the police as an act of protest, leading a campaign to eventually legalize abortion in 1978. Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ is going up for auction Diana famously wore the fitted black dress on the same night that Charles admitted to his infidelity on TV in 1994. It will be auctioned off in December. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Calls for Democrats to be shot go unchallenged at Republican convention
body_text: On the night Republicans gathered to mourn the killing of Charlie Kirk and warn against the dangers of violent rhetoric, a crowd at the party’s irregular midterm convention in Dallas repeatedly called for a sitting Senate candidate to be shot, while the Republican senator at the podium never denounced or even noted the outbursts. The outbursts came repeatedly during Ted Cruz’s Thursday night address at the American Airlines center, when he named a Democrat he accused of holding radical views. After the senator mentioned the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, video footage depicts at least one audience member shouting: “He should be shot!” The same cry followed when Cruz named Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and again after he named Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. Cruz did not pause or respond to the shouting, and it remains unclear whether he heard it from the stage. Cruz did not respond to a request for comment. Cruz had accused Mamdani of wanting to seize the means of production, said El-Sayed felt an “obligation” to follow Sharia law and claimed Talarico wanted to dismantle capitalism. Each characterization stretched past remarks the three men had actually made in other contexts. Asked about the moment on CNN’s The Source With Kaitlan Collins, El-Sayed said such rhetoric had become dangerously normalized and that it should unsettle anyone who heard it. He called on Republicans to name the chant for what it was: incitement that both parties ought to reject, and appealed for a return to a politics centered on people’s basic needs and dignity. “Look, I’m a dad with two daughters, and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad. This is what has become the norm in our politics … literally calls to violence and the inability for anybody to actually call it out,” El-Sayed said. “We can learn to disagree agreeably, and when you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us,” he added. A spokesperson for Mike Rogers, the Republican former congressman challenging El-Sayed for Michigan’s open Senate seat who was in Dallas for the convention, said Rogers condemned the remarks and “all political violence”. The convention fell on the first anniversary of the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, an occasion Republican speakers repeatedly invoked, including the vice-president, JD Vance, who spoke of his friendship with Kirk during a headlining address. El-Sayed is locked in one of the cycle’s most closely watched Senate races. A CNN poll released on Wednesday showed him leading Rogers 47% to 44% in the contest to succeed the retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters, as both parties fight for control of the chamber.

title: Taxes wouldn’t fund $5,000 Trump ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms, says commerce secretary
body_text: Donald Trump’s controversial proposal to give a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections would not be paid out from US tax revenues, according to the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick said in an interview with NBC News, adding that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers”. In a speech at the Republican midterm convention rally in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday, Trump said he would issue the dividends “because of our tremendous strength and success economically” and likened the payment to a one-time, tax-free $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” approved for about 1.45 million US military service members last year. Trump suggested the dividend, which could cost as much as $1tn if paid out to all Americans, could come in part from tariff revenue. “If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” he said, adding that it would be called “the Trump dividend”. But the proposal has been widely criticized, in part because the US national debt recently surpassed $40tn, up from $10tn in 2008, marking a near 300% increase over 18 years. Lutnick told NBC that some of the dividend money could come from a planned commerce department program to charge wealthy visitors to the US to pay up to $5m to extend their visas. “We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come,” he said, and calculated that this could raise $500bn. He also cited the government’s $8.9bn investment in chipmaker Intel, which has since appreciated in market value, from $20 per share to $100. In his comments, Lutnick joined with other administration officials in floating ideas on where the $5,000 checks might come from. Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, told Bloomberg TV that the White House is considering a “reconciliation process” in Congress to fund the program. “We can do it in a fiscally responsible way,” Hassett said. “The bottom line is there are multiple paths to getting it done – don’t underestimate President Trump.” JD Vance has also suggested tariff revenues would cover the cost and that the payments would not go to wealthy Americans. However, the supreme court has ruled that revenue raised by Trump’s “liberation day” 2025 import tariffs must be returned, and an earlier proposal to return $2,000 to US taxpayers from tariff receipts was more than the revenue that had been raised, according to the nonpartisan Tax Foundation. Trump’s $5,000 dividend proposal comes as a recent Associated Press poll found that only about three in 10 US adults, or 32%, approve of how the president is handling the economy, down from 40% at the start of his second term.

title: ‘Trump accounts’ promise to mint child millionaires. Experts have their doubts
body_text: Since returning to the White House, Donald Trump has scrapped rules that made childcare more affordable and pushed to cut funding for the nation’s public schools. But with midterm elections fast approaching and his approval ratings very low, the US president has repeatedly trumpeted a two-month-old program designed to help the nation’s children. That program, unhumbly named “Trump accounts”, calls for the federal government to give a one-time $1,000 seed deposit to every newborn whose family applies. In campaign speeches this summer, Trump has sought to milk these accounts for maximum political advantage, making big promises about how much these accounts will help the nation’s children. In a speech in Las Vegas last month, Trump hailed the program, saying: “It’s really giving [children] a head start on the American dream… They start off with $1,000 … and they can end up with $100,000, $200,000, $300,000” and if the stock market booms, “you’d end up with $1m”. With these accounts, Trump seems to want to come across as a Santa Claus stuffing $1,000 into every newborn’s stocking (although that money comes from the federal government). He and other Republicans boast that these accounts will significantly lift up all children, including children from low-income families, and also narrow the wealth gap between rich and poor. When Trump kicked off these accounts in early July, the treasury department said: “Trump Accounts level the playing field by allowing every parent to invest in their children’s future, not just wealthy families with trust funds.” A big problem, however, is that many economists say Trump’s claims about these accounts are vastly exaggerated or false. As Trump seeks to excite voters about these accounts, he has hyped how much they will grow, especially with regard to non-affluent families who don’t have the wherewithal to deposit money into these tax-deferred accounts to help their children. In his speeches, Trump sometimes gives the inaccurate impression that a newborn’s account with a $1,000 seed deposit will mushroom to $200,000 or $300,000 by the time the child turns 18, even when that child’s family doesn’t have money to make subsequent deposits. What’s more, “Trump accounts” are likely to increase, not decrease, the wealth gap between rich and poor. These accounts have definite tax advantages for wealthier families, who, unlike most low-income or working-class families, are able to make the maximum $5,000 deposit allowed each year into these tax-deferred accounts. It’s the families rich enough to contribute $5,000 a year who could see their children’s accounts grow to $200,000 or $300,000, far outstripping the accounts of children from poorer families. “This policy is not about giving poor kids a leg up. It’s more likely to widen the gap between rich and poor,” said Justin Wolfers, an economics professor at the University of Michigan, in a video. Kush Desai, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “Trump Accounts are already shaping up to make a generational difference for working-class children who have not historically benefitted from traditional tax advantaged accounts.” He noted that the billionaires Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, as well as multinational corporations, have “pledged to donate billions of dollars of their wealth to the Trump Accounts of working-class children”. Desai rejected any assertions that the program would increase inequality, saying: “High income parents have always had an array of tools to grow wealth for their kids, but Trump Accounts are giving middle class parents the same opportunity – with billionaires chipping in to help. Only a moron would argue billionaires giving money away to working-class kids will worsen inequality.” The Trump administration has hyped the accounts with extremely optimistic claims. A White House website forecasts that many children with “Trump accounts” will have $271,000 in their account by age 18 and $13m by age 55. That sounds fabulous, but according to Wolfers, those big numbers are based on an impressive 10% annual rate of return for decades – a rate of return that is extraordinarily hard to achieve year after year. Moreover, those higher numbers are for children whose parents put in $5,000 annually until age 18, and then $7,000 a year when their children are in their 20s. Wolfers derided these White House estimates, saying in his video: “They’re ridiculous, they’re dishonest and they’re misleading.” Administration officials defended their estimates of how much the accounts would grow, saying those estimates are “not dissimilar to similar projections issued by retirement account providers”. In his speeches, Trump omits something important: he fails to note that for families unable to contribute beyond the initial $1,000 seed deposit, that amount would, according to White House estimates, grow to $6,000 by age 18. (That too is also based an optimistic 10% annual return.) No one should pooh-pooh a government-given deposit of $1,000 or a possible $6,000 at age 18. But Darrick Hamilton, a New School economics professor and one of the inventors of the baby bonds idea, said those amounts are too small to change the life of a child in need – too small to make college affordable or to buy a house. “It’s really an income transfer, not a wealth-building tool,” Hamilton said. He said it is the wealthiest 20%, especially the top 10%, who save money, while “people in the bottom 80% are usually dis-savers, they’re usually borrowers.” In other words, he said, the richest 20% will benefit from the tax breaks by depositing $5,000 a year into Trump accounts for their children. “The main mechanism for these accounts is active savings by parents, and that’s by nature regressive,” Hamilton said. “These accounts will actually increase wealth inequality because they favor people wealthy enough to have money to put into savings.” As part of the program, employers can contribute $2,500 a year to the account of an employee’s child. That $2,500 becomes a nice tax break for well-paid employees – the $2,500 contribution won’t be counted as taxable income. As a result, high-income workers in higher tax brackets will receive bigger tax breaks than lower-paid workers. The $1,000 seed deposits for newborns – the main part of the program helping the non-affluent – are to expire when Trump’s second term ends. But the parts of the program that help the wealthy most – the tax deferrals and tax breaks – are to continue indefinitely. Many Republicans and business executives have hailed “Trump accounts” as a way to make American children participants in the capitalist system. Senator Ted Cruz said: “Trump accounts are, in many ways, Donald Trump’s New Deal – but instead of having government taking care of everyone, Trump accounts are about making every child and every American a capitalist.” Hamilton sees things differently. Noting that Trump accounts are invested in the stock market, he said: “This is part of their larger plan to privatize our social safety net. This is in line with Republican plans to dismantle social security.” Senator Cory Booker and Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced a never-enacted baby bonds bill in 2019 under which children would receive $1,000 in their birth year and up to $2,000 more every year to age 18. Under their proposal, based on ideas from Hamilton and the Duke professor William Darity, lower-income families would receive larger government contributions than affluent ones. Children from families at the poverty level would see their accounts rise to an estimated $46,000 by age 18, about three times as much as children from families making twice the poverty line and more than 20 times as much as children from wealthy families. But with midterm elections fast approaching and his approval ratings very low, the US president has repeatedly trumpeted a two-month-old program designed to help the nation’s children. That program, unhumbly named “Trump accounts”, calls for the federal government to give a one-time $1,000 seed deposit to every newborn whose family applies. In campaign speeches this summer, Trump has sought to milk these accounts for maximum political advantage, making big promises about how much these accounts will help the nation’s children. In a speech in Las Vegas last month, Trump hailed the program, saying: “It’s really giving [children] a head start on the American dream… They start off with $1,000 … and they can end up with $100,000, $200,000, $300,000” and if the stock market booms, “you’d end up with $1m”. With these accounts, Trump seems to want to come across as a Santa Claus stuffing $1,000 into every newborn’s stocking (although that money comes from the federal government). He and other Republicans boast that these accounts will significantly lift up all children, including children from low-income families, and also narrow the wealth gap between rich and poor. When Trump kicked off these accounts in early July, the treasury department said: “Trump Accounts level the playing field by allowing every parent to invest in their children’s future, not just wealthy families with trust funds.” A big problem, however, is that many economists say Trump’s claims about these accounts are vastly exaggerated or false. As Trump seeks to excite voters about these accounts, he has hyped how much they will grow, especially with regard to non-affluent families who don’t have the wherewithal to deposit money into these tax-deferred accounts to help their children. In his speeches, Trump sometimes gives the inaccurate impression that a newborn’s account with a $1,000 seed deposit will mushroom to $200,000 or $300,000 by the time the child turns 18, even when that child’s family doesn’t have money to make subsequent deposits. What’s more, “Trump accounts” are likely to increase, not decrease, the wealth gap between rich and poor. These accounts have definite tax advantages for wealthier families, who, unlike most low-income or working-class families, are able to make the maximum $5,000 deposit allowed each year into these tax-deferred accounts. It’s the families rich enough to contribute $5,000 a year who could see their children’s accounts grow to $200,000 or $300,000, far outstripping the accounts of children from poorer families. “This policy is not about giving poor kids a leg up. It’s more likely to widen the gap between rich and poor,” said Justin Wolfers, an economics professor at the University of Michigan, in a video. title: Trump reiterates $5,000 ‘dividend’ pledge if Republicans win midterms
body_text: Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if his Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections. The plan has been greeted with expressions of incredulity across the US political spectrum as well as outraged accusations of seeking to bribe voters. The proposal – which would cost more than a trillion dollars – also comes amid huge concern over the US national debt, which topped $40tn for the first time in August. “I don’t ‌know but ‌it’s easy if the ‌Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we’re taking in ‌so much money,” Trump told reporters in Ireland, where he is on a visit to his golf course in Doonbeg. Trump had been asked if Congress would need to approve the $5,000 pledge. He said: “The Democrats can’t make that pledge ⁠because it would all go to hell right away, we’d go into a depression … ‌I made that pledge, I always keep my pledge.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting a cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. When the plan was first touted by Trump last week at a rally in Texas, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X: “The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” Democratic political leaders also reacted with a mix of outrage, disbelief and condemnation to the remarkable suggestion, which comes at a time when Trump is struggling with low poll numbers and a disastrous conflict in Iran, which is having an impact on the health of the US economy. “After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” said California governor Gavin Newsom. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.” Some Republicans have backed the idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” said US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, in a social media post on X. Any such payment would have ‌to be approved by Congress. On Sunday Mike Johnson, the House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, told CNN: “Of course, the devil’s in the ‌details. We have to figure all that out.” But Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talkshows in the US dismissed the idea. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, told ABC’s This Week that the plan was not a “serious proposal”. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

title: ‘It’s just straight bigotry’: wave of Islamophobic rhetoric looms over US midterm elections
body_text: Within hours of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic US Senate primary, Republican senator Tommy Tuberville of Alabama declared that the party had “just voted to send a TERRORIST” to Washington. El-Sayed – or “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed”, as Tuberville called him on X – was a “RADICAL ISLAMIST” who would “do everything he can to destroy America”, he claimed. It was the opening shot in what researchers who track anti-Muslim sentiment describe as the most concentrated wave of Islamophobic rhetoric in US electoral politics since the 9/11 attacks, arriving at the exact moment Muslim candidates are winning office in unprecedented numbers. “It’s probably the worst of what we’ve seen,” said Saher Selod, director of research at the non-partisan Institute for Social Policy and Understanding (ISPU), which has tracked anti-Muslim sentiment nationally for a decade. “We’re certainly seeing in 2025 and 2026, ahead of these midterms, really very Islamophobic ads – more so than what we saw after 9/11.” ISPU’s 2025 Islamophobia Index, a 100-point scale built using common anti-Muslim stereotypes, rose from 25 in 2022 to 33 among the general public in 2025, with the sharpest increases among white and Hispanic Americans. The Pew Research Center found in a survey this spring that 51% of US adults now say Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence, up from just 25% six months after the 2001 attacks. The partisan gap on that question has widened sharply. Back in 2002, 32% of likely Republican voters and 23% of Democrats said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence, according to the Pew survey. Today, 76% of Republicans say the same, and 29% of Democrats. Anti-Muslim hate crimes reported to the FBI, which spiked to 481 in 2001 from 28 the year before, have never returned to pre-2001 levels, according to Pew’s research. The ISPU separately found that 63% of Muslims reported experiencing religious discrimination in the past year, the highest share of any faith group it measures. Set against that backdrop is a wave of Muslim electoral success. There are four Muslim members of US Congress, with a fifth likely on the way, compared with zero in 2001. Ghazala Hashmi became Virginia’s first Muslim woman elected to statewide office this year, as lieutenant governor. Zohran Mamdani was inaugurated as New York’s first Muslim mayor in January 2025, and El-Sayed’s primary win put him on track to potentially become the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. The reaction to El-Sayed’s victory showed how quickly the rhetoric escalates. The Center for the Study of Organized Hate found Islamophobic posts naming El-Sayed rose by nearly 1,900% in the week after his win, from an average of 155 to more than 3,000 a day. The attacks are also coming from the very top of the Republican party. Donald Trump infamously called in 2015 for a “total and complete shutdown” on Muslims entering the US when he was running for president, and attempted to enact one via executive order in early 2017. After years of legal wrangling, the supreme court did allow Trump to implement a limited version of his travel restrictions for majority Muslim countries. This year, Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist” from the Oval Office, and separately claimed – without naming anyone – that “jihadists” were being elected to office “all over the place”. Vice-president JD Vance, meanwhile, called El-Sayed “very, very evil” at a Michigan rally and, separately, invoked his own late grandfather to attack comments El-Sayed made in 2022 defending a legal challenge to an Oklahoma anti-Sharia ballot measure. The attacks go beyond one candidate, however. Senator Ted Cruz told Fox News that El-Sayed and Mamdani were “Islamists” who “want Sharia law” and “hate Jews, they hate Christians, they hate capitalism, they hate America”. Representative Nancy Mace posted that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic”, and followed up by writing that Islam “must be removed from civil society in the US”. In March, Representative Randy Fine of Florida wrote on X, “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational,” while Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee posted that “Muslims don’t belong in American society”. Republican leadership has been mostly silent. For Mobashra Tazamal, associate director of Georgetown University’s Bridge Initiative, which studies Islamophobia globally, the shift is shockingly noticeable. “It is almost as if the veil has been lifted,” she said. “It is so bigoted, and it’s so crude, and there is no red line. It’s just straight bigotry.” *** The rhetoric has also extended beyond individual candidates into policy fights. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott has spent much of the summer campaigning against what he calls the imposition of Islamic law, ordering a review of state grants to two major airports and referring both to federal regulators over privately funded wudu stations, ritual washing facilities Muslims use before prayer, which he called illegal religious favoritism. Abbott has separately fought a proposed mosque-anchored housing development outside Dallas. Nationally, the Center for the Study of Organized Hate documented a coordinated campaign among 89 elected officials over 13 months, including 1,111 social media posts and eight bills, tied to a “Sharia Free America Caucus” that has grown to 65 members. The anti-Sharia campaigns are not new: close to two dozen states passed largely symbolic anti-Sharia laws in the early 2010s. “This isn’t an issue. It’s not something that’s real,” said Tazamal. “It’s constructed, and then these politicians claim to be tackling this constructed problem that they create.” The picture is complicated, though. Researchers caution against treating every attack on El-Sayed or Mamdani as bigotry. El-Sayed drew criticism – including from Vance – after he responded to a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue by saying “hurt people hurt people”, noting that relatives of the attacker in Lebanon had recently been killed in an Israeli airstrike. El-Sayed eventually apologized, and said the remarks may have been misconstrued. He has also faced scrutiny over his public association with the hyper-popular leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, who mainstream Democrats and Republicans have attacked for past comments minimizing the 11 September attacks. Mamdani has faced sustained criticism, including from rivals in his own mayoral race, over his refusal to unequivocally condemn the phrase “globalize the intifada”, a phrase Jewish groups say amounts to a call for violence against Jews, but one that he has never personally used. Mamdani subsequently said he would discourage the term after a rabbi told him it evokes memories of bus bombings and restaurant attacks for many Jewish New Yorkers. The controversy among Jewish organizations, rival campaigns and national Democrats, was not, in the end, disqualifying in the eyes of voters who ultimately decided the race. The devastation in Gaza, mass settler violence in the West Bank and the suppression of pro-Palestine speech in the US has brought an additional dimension to this discourse. US opinion on Israel has soured immensely in recent years, especially among Democrats, and criticism of Israeli policy by the likes of El-Sayed and Mamdani is cited by those describing Muslim politicians “jihadists”. Mahmoud Khalil, Rümeysa Öztürk and other Muslim residents in the US were among the first swept up for pro-Palestinian campus advocacy, even though most of the students protesting were not Muslim. That pattern, criticism aimed at religious identity rather than positions or votes, is consistent with what researchers have documented since well before this election cycle. And the point, Selod and Tazamal say, is whether that criticism is being used as cover for a broader claim – that Muslim identity itself, not any specific position on issue or another, is disqualifying from US public life. “With Abdul El-Sayed, we’re seeing these kinds of intense Islamophobic attacks against him, as opposed to attacking his platform or critiquing his policies,” Selod said. “It’s a playbook. They’re going to attack him for his religious identity to see if this will help pull voters away from him.” That playbook resurfaced this week in New York, where Mamdani attended the ceremony marking Friday’s 25th anniversary of 9/11 at Ground Zero, as his predecessors have every year. A petition with more than 100,000 signatures, riddled with attacks, unashamedly asked him not to. Rudy Giuliani, mayor of New York City at the time of the attacks, who is now closely aligned to Trump, claimed from thin air that Mamdani “doesn’t agree that September 11 was an Islamic terrorist attack”, and that his attendance “offends” him, adding even more venom against Muslims generally: “They have every desire to take us over … they want to dominate us. Mamdani is a clear supporter of that.” Giuliani offered no evidence for either claim. Cheri Sparacio, one of the petition’s organizers, whose husband died in the attacks, has said her objection is “not about the mayor’s background or faith, but his public actions”. Mamdani attended anyway, and on Friday morning, Mamdani and Giuliani shook hands at the ceremony. *** Yet the current moment cannot be separated from the infrastructure built after 9/11, Selod said. “All of the surveillance programs that were put into place, your no-fly list, ICE – these are a product of 9/11,” she said. “We didn’t have Immigration and Customs Enforcement. We didn’t have the TSA, the Transportation Security Administration. These were all put into place to protect the nation against threats of terrorism.” That architecture has since been extended well past its original target, Selod argued, pointing to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, a post-9/11 “fusion center” built to detect terrorist plots. Local reporting and ACLU of Massachusetts records show the center has also been used to monitor Black Lives Matter demonstrators. “It’s expanding beyond a Muslim population to target others,” she said. “Muslims are one to two percent of the US population. My hope is when people start to see how it’s expanding beyond that population, maybe they’ll start really critiquing these programs.” ISPU polling suggests the sentiment tracks politics rather than faith. Americans who identify as somewhat or very conservative are 13 percentage points more likely than others to endorse anti-Muslim stereotypes, the ISPU found, while religiosity shows no correlation. Tazamal ties the current spike partly to political calculation. “Polling for Trump is low, and the GOP is the sitting party, and they haven’t delivered on their promises,” she said. “So instead of focusing on institutional failures and policies they haven’t been able to put into place, they’re stirring up hate and bigotry towards a certain group, which is a routine tactic that they do.” Caleb Elfenbein, a Grinnell College professor who has mapped Islamophobic rhetoric for years, sees a small, organized network reactivating on a predictable schedule. “It really looks, and feels, like a very cynical effort to take advantage of a general sense of fear that can be activated at any given time,” he said. Whether it works for a GOP that polling indicates is likely to face heavy losses in November’s midterm elections is the open question hanging over this campaign. Republicans are simultaneously contending with an unpopular war with Iran and rising costs that have squeezed their approval ratings. Whatever happens, amid growing political mobilization among Muslim Americans and other groups, Tazamal does not expect the party to abandon this effort, or the Islamophobic rhetoric at the center of it. “I don’t think the GOP is going to do away with it,” she said. • This article was amended on 15 September 2026 to clarify the date of polling carried out by the Pew Research Center.

These were all put into place to protect the nation against threats of terrorism.” That architecture has since been extended well past its original target, Selod argued, pointing to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, a post-9/11 “fusion center” built to detect terrorist plots. Local reporting and ACLU of Massachusetts records show the center has also been used to monitor Black Lives Matter demonstrators. “It’s expanding beyond a Muslim population to target others,” she said. “Muslims are one to two percent of the US population. My hope is when people start to see how it’s expanding beyond that population, maybe they’ll start really critiquing these programs.” ISPU polling suggests the sentiment tracks politics rather than faith. Americans who identify as somewhat or very conservative are 13 percentage points more likely than others to endorse anti-Muslim stereotypes, the ISPU found, while religiosity shows no correlation. Tazamal ties the current spike partly to political calculation. “Polling for Trump is low, and the GOP is the sitting party, and they haven’t delivered on their promises,” she said. “So instead of focusing on institutional failures and policies they haven’t been able to put into place, they’re stirring up hate and bigotry towards a certain group, which is a routine tactic that they do.” Caleb Elfenbein, a Grinnell College professor who has mapped Islamophobic rhetoric for years, sees a small, organized network reactivating on a predictable schedule. “It really looks, and feels, like a very cynical effort to take advantage of a general sense of fear that can be activated at any given time,” he said. Whether it works for a GOP that polling indicates is likely to face heavy losses in November’s midterm elections is the open question hanging over this campaign. Republicans are simultaneously contending with an unpopular war with Iran and rising costs that have squeezed their approval ratings. Whatever happens, amid growing political mobilization among Muslim Americans and other groups, Tazamal does not expect the party to abandon this effort, or the Islamophobic rhetoric at the center of it. “I don’t think the GOP is going to do away with it,” she said. • This article was amended on 15 September 2026 to clarify the date of polling carried out by the Pew Research Center.

title: Obama reportedly urges Democrats to prioritize safety plan for AI
body_text: Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week. The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing. Obama’s comments follow a summer in which a band of rogue OpenAI chatbots hacked the company Hugging Face, towns across the country opposed datacenters and an AI researcher resigned in a viral social media post warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” AI leaders have recently expressed agreement that the race for technological superiority should slow, but have also sought to appease investors, whose stake in the technology is predicted to exceed $1tn in 2026 alone. “Once you are speaker,” Obama said to US House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York-Democrat, at the fundraiser Thursday. “I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” according to a transcript first reported by the New York Times. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.” Obama later added: “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,’” he said according to the Times. Obama made the remarks as the US closes in on the midterm elections and Congress has taken little action on AI. While prominent Democratic lawmakers, and some Republicans, have called to regulate the technology, Trump has attempted to aid the AI industry by introducing legislation that would ban state regulations (the bill did not move forward). Democrats face an open presidential field in 2028. One major flashpoint for the midterm elections is datacenters that power AI companies. Both parties have since begun running ads that oppose them, as one of the few issues, “Maga Republicans and liberal Democrats” agree on, according to an NPR analysis. On Sunday, while on a trip to his Irish golf course, Trump told reporters that a lot of “very negative forces” are ⁠bringing up concerns ⁠about AI that “won’t happen”, and that his main concern was that the US remain the industry leader, according to Reuters. “We’re leading China in AI. ‌We’re the ‌most sophisticated country in the world, ‌and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if ‌the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated. In the past, Trump has said on social media that anyone who opposes AI datacenters is likely “backwards and poor”. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he said on TruthSocial two weeks ago.

title: The American emperor’s new clothes?
body_text: Octavian (later Emperor Augustus), following his victorious battles of Illyricum and Actium, announced he would give 400 sesterces to adult male citizens. Will we see the US president wearing an emperor’s purple and gold toga soon (Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’, 10 September)? David Shannon Ashton under Hill, Worcestershire • Can we assume that the donations to Reform UK from the billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo (Report, 12 September) will be followed by some sort of cash offer for every adult in the UK should Mr Farage win the next election? Phil Thomas Frodsham, Cheshire • The crypto-billionaire Ben Delo told the Telegraph he wanted “a level playing field”. Presumably the cheques for the Greens and Lib Dems are lost in the post. Tim Mansfield Galgate, Lancaster • After “wild swimming” and “vertical drinking”, Joe Hyde asks: “Whatever next?” (Letters, 9 September). We have known the answer for ages: “lived experience”. Charles Foster Chalfont St Peter, Buckinghamshire • George Monbiot asks why Andy Burnham is taking a huge risk with fossil fuels (Opinion, 10 September). Maybe it is just another example of nominative determinism (Letters, 10 September). Andy Cook Honley, West Yorkshire • I am delighted to see that the nominative determinism discussion is getting out of hand. Frank Lawless Leeds • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war
body_text: “I will not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never end,” Donald Trump promised a crowd in Pennsylvania in 2024. While the disastrous conflict in Iran, which has escalated in recent days, may make it seem like the president has reneged on that promise, that’s inaccurate. It would be wrong to say that the president has dragged the US into yet another disastrous forever war in the Middle East because, as government officials keep insisting, what’s happening in Iran isn’t actually a war. “I wouldn’t call it a war,” JD Vance told reporters early this month, for example, after being asked whether the fighting in Iran might be over by the November midterms. “Right now, there is no active shooting.” Maybe not, but there has been quite a bit of active bombing. Earlier this month, a US missile strike hit a wedding at a private home in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old. That’s fairly restrained compared to the massacre in March when a US precision-guided missile hit an elementary school in Iran, killing 150 people, including 120 children, but it’s still something I would personally file under “possible war crimes”. But not only does the Trump administration keep insisting this isn’t a real war, they’re also adamant there aren’t any real crimes being committed: the vice-president would like to stress that you shouldn’t believe your eyes or ears when it comes to the civilian deaths being reported. Despite a weapons expert and a visual analysis by the New York Times concluding that the bomb that hit the wedding party in a residential area of the country was American, Vance has a hunch the whole thing might have been made up by some untrustworthy brown people. “The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” Vance said at that same press briefing, in relation to the wedding massacre. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.” The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it? A little skirmish? An interminable series of special military operations? A very bloody screw-up? Trump himself has called it a war on several occasions. Last Wednesday, for example, he said: “The war is going to end immediately after the election.” However, rather confusing matters, he also recently suggested he agreed with Vance that it wasn’t a full-fledged war. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump said last month. Those are some very expensive potatoes: the not-a-war already has a price tag of tens of billions. Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, has roughly estimated that it has cost the typical US household $1,200. And then of course there’s the human cost: the thousands of lives that have been lost. What we call this “military conflict” isn’t just semantics, it matters greatly. Not least because the constitution is very clear that a president can’t unilaterally start an official war on a whim; only Congress has the power to declare a war. Trump isn’t the first president to launch major military action without going to Congress for a declaration: Harry Truman classified the Korean conflict as a “police action” to bypass Congress and presidents since have engaged in similar semantic sleights-of-hand. But, as the historian and foreign relations expert Fredrik Logevall noted in an interview with the Harvard Kennedy School: “What’s extraordinary about President Trump in the current context is that he has not really bothered to even consult with Congress, never mind seek the approval of Congress.” In other words, he’s acting like a dictator. Trump, to be fair, has been clear that he’s exploiting the Truman Playbook. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say if you use the word ‘war,’ that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” Trump said at a fundraising dinner in March. “They don’t like the word ‘war’ because you’re supposed to get approval. So, I’ll use the word ‘military operation’, which is really what it is. It’s a military decimation.” Avoiding a formal declaration of war might also help the US government bypass certain “wartime” obligations to its service members and their families. Libby Klinner, the widow of an airman killed in combat operations against Iran in March, recently posted on Instagram that she wasn’t receiving certain benefits because the US wasn’t technically at war. “The Air Force recently told me that because we haven’t officially declared war, my kids and I aren’t eligible for some benefits,” Klinner wrote. “So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perceptions.” After this post went viral, it seems the government has stepped in smooth things over. Vance recently said the administration would ensure Klinner receives “what she is entitled to.” He added: “We will certainly work that on the back end.” The government might be able to fix Klinner’s benefits, but they’re going to have a hard time remedying the economic and political damage this not-a-war is inflicting. Trump’s popularity is plummeting, and a majority of Americans are fed up with this “small potatoes” conflict that has been going on for six months and making everyday life more dangerous and expensive. According to an estimate from Brown University last week, the conflict has cost Americans $100bn in extra energy costs. That bill is going up by $1m every two minutes. This week oil prices also climbed over $100 a barrel for the first time since July. Meanwhile, with hostilities escalating and no off-ramp in sight, it looks like Trump is out of options. All he has left is empty promises. The president has insisted that energy prices will tumble “right after the election” and, in a sign he is completely desperate, promised every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. The Trump administration can call the war whatever they like, but future generations will define it as a disastrous act of hubris. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears
body_text: The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Thirty state parties have a trained election protection director, with the goal of all states having one in place. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC, said the project is much more extensive and coordinated than the party has been in the past on election protection. “We didn’t want to be caught flat-footed on election day or leading up to election day,” she said. These volunteers will be trained to “be happy” and respond to any voter needs, including helping them find a polling location if they’re in the wrong place, or informing them they can cast provisional ballots if they need to, Kleeb said. They will also document whether others at the polls are hindering voters. “We don’t know if there are going to be a bunch of insurrectionist types out there trying to intimidate voters, but we’re going to be there happy with information, but we’re also going to be there trained to document if the other side is doing things that are violating the law,” she said. The party will additionally push out its first national early-vote campaign, telling voters to “bank their vote” by casting ballots early by mail or in person. This will include ad campaigns focused on communities at risk of Republican election interference. The state parties and the DNC typically run get-out-the-vote programs, but this year’s will include more explicit directions to voters – telling them to vote early, and not let a mail ballot sit on their kitchen counter for weeks before turning it in, Kleeb said. The party will also push for people to vote early in person. “We don’t know what Donald Trump is going to do. We’ve heard some of the things that he may do, but none of us can predict his behavior,” she said. “He’s so chaotic. All of us have witnessed certainly that. So the earlier you can vote, the better.” The third part of the project will spin up a “democracy defense network”, led by Democratic strategist Simon Rosenberg, designed to identify and counter tactics that can sway elections, including disinformation, dark money, manipulation via artificial intelligence and election subversion. The network will allow state parties to communicate with each other about these threats to share knowledge, with a goal to get ahead of such tactics before they gain traction.

title: Disaster insurance, datacenters, right to repair: meet the midterm candidates running on green policies
body_text: When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged. Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail. The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations. The climate crisis, however, is still rearing its head around the country, fueling the heatwaves, wildfires and floods plaguing communities around the US. It also lurks behind issues animating voters, from datacenter expansion to rising home insurance rates. And while some pundits have concluded from their polling and research that Americans don’t want to hear about global warming, other surveys directly contradict those findings. “Maybe people don’t rank climate as their main or top issue … but nobody really experiences everyday life like walking around the world rank-ordering the things that they care about,” said Aldana Cohen, who is also founding co-director of the thinktank Climate and Community Institute that calls for “green economic populism”. “What’s important is to learn how to embed the climate issue organically amidst the other issues that people care most about.” Some progressive and populist candidates in the US midterms are pushing back against climate-hushing, linking the issue to economic concerns and everyday struggles. Others aren’t speaking about it directly, but pushing for policies that could curb emissions. Such efforts could help build a mass base for climate policies, said Aldana Cohen. “If we want to decarbonize fast enough and adapt to the impacts that are already here, we’re going to need a robust majority that backs those policies,” he said. “Elite consensus alone will not suffice … we’re going to need like large numbers of people really enthusiastic about climate policies.” The Guardian spoke with three midterm candidates about how three issues with major environmental implications are shaping their campaigns. Single-payer disaster insurance Jane Kim, state director of the Working Families Party and a former San Francisco county supervisor, is running to become California’s next insurance commissioner. The little-noticed but highly influential position oversees the state’s home, auto and business insurance markets. The frontrunner in the race, she received 27% of votes in the June primary. Among her key proposals is a single-payer system for disaster insurance, which she began developing as climate-fueled wildfires ravaged the state. California wildfires have catalyzed homeowners’ insurance crisis. Companies have stopped writing new policies and non-renewed thousands of homeowners in high-risk areas, making coverage increasingly difficult to find. Homeowners can turn to the California Fair Plan, the insurer of last resort, but it provides limited fire coverage rather than the broader protection of a typical homeowners policy. title: Texas Democrat under fire for honoring convicted abuser Chris Brown at concert
body_text: The Democratic US representative Jasmine Crockett is under fire for honoring musician Chris Brown, a convicted abuser, with an official recognition at a Texas concert over the weekend. Crockett, a Texas congresswoman, awarded Brown and R&B musician Usher a congressional record recognition at a performance in Arlington, Texas, on Saturday. Appearing alongside Texas state representative Venton Jones, Crockett said she was there to “honor” Brown and Usher. “We are experiencing Black joy at the highest level,” she said, according to video from the concert. “And I wanted to make sure we document that at the congressional level. So let’s give it up again for Chris Brown.” A congressional record recognition is a ceremonial honor in which a member of Congress can enter a specific person or achievement into the official congressional record. Brown pleaded guilty in 2009 to felony assault against his then girlfriend, music star Rihanna. He also awaits sentencing in a UK incident in which prosecutors alleged he hit a music producer over the head with a bottle. Brown pleaded guilty to a charge of “affray” in that case. Crockett lost the Democratic primary for US Senate in Texas earlier this year to James Talarico, a state representative now running against Republican Ken Paxton in a race that’s considered a toss-up and a key target for Democrats. Since her loss, Crockett has so far not campaigned for Talarico, with some people online calling attention to her choice not to campaign with the Democratic Senate nominee and instead appear with Brown. Roxane Gay, the author, wrote on social media platform Threads: “What the hell is [Jasmine Crockett] thinking? This is such a bizarre and unacceptable misstep.” She later added that Crockett didn’t mention voting or endorse candidates in the appearance. “She just flew on stage and gave a known abuser of Black women (multiple allegations past and recent) a congressional honor,” Gay posted. Crockett has said she “will be campaigning down ballot” when asked in recent weeks by CNN’s Laura Coates about whether she would be campaigning with Talarico, saying she wanted to make sure that people in lower-profile races weren’t getting “overshadowed” by a focus just on the top of the ticket. Some defended Crockett, saying her appearing with Jones, the state representative, at the concert before thousands of people was using her platform to get voters to turn out for the down ballot. Crockett did not respond to a request for comment. Beto O’Rourke, a former Democratic congressman in Texas, defended Crockett’s decision to campaign for down-ballot candidates at a roundtable hosted by Bloomberg News in Dallas last week, before the Brown concert. “She’s helping him in what I think is the most effective way possible, which is this reverse coattails of boosting these down-ballot candidates,” O’Rourke said. “It’s up to her and at her discretion, but I would not be surprised if we don’t see her play a larger role in what’s about to happen in Texas and she will deserve so much of the credit when James Talarico wins, when Gina Hinojosa wins, for the work that she’s done, the people that she has engaged.” David Smith contributed reporting
