title: Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon call for curbs on AI at ‘pro-human’ summit
body_text: The progressive senator Bernie Sanders and rightwing strategist Steve Bannon have called for restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI) but offered competing visions for what they termed a “cold war” with China. Speaking at the “Pro-Human Assembly” in Washington on Tuesday, the ideological adversaries were united in warning of the potential dangers of AI and demanding stringent guardrails against Silicon Valley’s “oligarchs”. But the populist pair offered very different perspectives on how to resolve the AI race with China, which Donald Trump and other Republicans have cited to justify moving full speed ahead with the technology. Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, noted that Trump is due to host the Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington next week. Sanders called for international diplomacy and a global agreement, including with Beijing, to ban the development of super-intelligent machines. He told an audience gathered in the ballroom of a Washington hotel: “A super-intelligent AI that escapes human control will not be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem. “That is why I very much hope that at their AI summit next week, President Trump will negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on super-intelligence.” Sanders drew a comparison with US president Ronald Reagan and his Russian counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev seeking to avoid nuclear conflict at the height of the cold war, eventually signing a treaty that eliminated an entire class of missiles. He said: “They understood that a nuclear war would not be good for the Soviet Union, not be good for the United States, not be good for the world, and they came together for a nuclear treaty. With the survival of humanity at stake, they found a way to sign that treaty.” Bannon, who spoke directly after Sanders but did not share a stage with him, also used the cold war analogy but did not arrive at the same conclusion. The host of the War Room podcast and former White House chief strategist under Trump called for an aggressive economic and technological “quarantine” of China, demanding the immediate expulsion of Chinese nationals from US research laboratories, an end to the training of Chinese engineers and technologists and the total severance of capital flows. “Did our fathers and grandfathers, did they underwrite the Soviet Union?” Bannon asked. “Did they train Soviet Union scientists? Did they take Russian kids over here to college to let them go to the best universities and get the best degree? Did they have Wall Street slobbering to do their deals? Did they have every bank there to lend them money quicker than to lend anyone in this audience? “The answer is they did not. They stood up to the Soviet Union and the first thing to stand up to them was to choke them off and that’s what we have to do today to the Chinese Communist party. No deals, no agreements, you’re out of the AI business because we’re going to shut your ecosystem down.” Demanding immediate executive action to isolate Beijing’s tech sector, Bannon said: “No chips, no black marketing chips, no free ride off American technology, no steal on American tech … To hell with the Chinese Communist party.” Only then, Bannon argued, can the US have the time necessary to consider the proper regulation of the tech sector. He delivered a scathing verdict on major technology corporations and executives, accusing them of gambling with public safety for private profit. Bannon accused Silicon Valley of seeking to “socialise all the risk with the American people including potential bailouts” while keeping all financial upside. “The American people are not going to be supplicants to these tech oligarchs,” Bannon said, praising grassroots campaigns that previously defeated federal pre-emption bills aimed at blocking state-level AI regulations. Bannon has long praised Trump as a historic figure and endorsed his lie that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. But on Tuesday, while claiming that executive action is required rather than legislation by Congress, he made only a glancing reference to the president who has dismissed AI concerns as a “hoax” and “sick conspiracy”. Sanders, for his part, did criticise Trump and Congress along with the concentration of power in Silicon Valley. “Despite living in a so-called democracy, the public has had virtually no input into the AI revolution that is transforming the world in which they live,” he said. “Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing. Virtually all of the decisions regarding the development of AI have been made by a handful of the richest people in the world … whose chief goal is to achieve even more wealth and more power than they already have, no matter what the impact their work has on ordinary people.” Sanders said he would introduce legislation next week to permanently ban the development of artificial super-intelligence, an AI mind smarter than any human being, and put an immediate pause on advanced AI development until clear safety rules are in place. Recent surveys have found ⁠majorities of Americans worry that AI could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm. Residents in several states have also challenged ‌proposals for new data centres, a ‌critical component of the AI boom. The Pro-Human Assembly, taking place against a backdrop of growing bipartisan anxiety over AI risks, also heard from members of Congress, labour leaders and religious representatives. Congressman Greg Casar, who is co-sponsoring the legislation with Sanders, accused AI billionaires of deploying massive political spending to stifle regulation. “Even as the threat becomes clearer, there are many powerful people fighting to prevent action,” Casar told attendees. “AI billionaires are spending millions through the Leading the Future Pac to scare politicians into silence. The top Republicans who control the House of Representatives are not lifting a finger.” Casar added: “Leading in AI diplomacy does not mean waiting around for an international agreement on dangerous AI. Putting up guardrails now is the best way to show we are serious about getting to a deal.” Republican congressman Chip Roy similarly expressed scepticism over concentrating decision-making power within the executive branch or tech boardrooms. “The president yesterday said he should be making the decisions about AI. I disagree. I don’t think big tech CEOs should be making all the decisions about AI. “I don’t think Congress should be making all the decisions about AI. If we allow technology to fundamentally alter and transfer and change the way we make decisions about our society and our Republican form of government, then what do we have left?”

title: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war
body_text: The Republican congressman Thomas Massie on Tuesday proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. The proposal by Massie, an iconoclastic lawmaker who lost his primary earlier this year after Donald Trump and Hegseth urged voters to oppose him, may put House Republicans in a bind just weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, in which they are defending their control of Congress. Under the rules of the House of Representatives, the articles must be voted on by Thursday, forcing Republicans to weigh in on one of the most prominent advocates of the war with Iran, which has gone on far longer than Trump said it initially would, and grown unpopular with the public. “By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement after reading the text of his resolution on the floor of the House. “Secretary Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran. He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders, and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech. If we are to remain true to our oath to ‘support and defend the constitution of the United States’, Congress must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions.” In a statement to the Guardian, a Pentagon spokesperson did not directly address the allegations put forward in the impeachment articles, but hailed Hegseth a “transformative leader” who had “slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way”. “The entire department is unified behind the secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” the spokesperson, Kingsley Wilson, said. Massie’s resolution outlines eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer who as defense secretary has become a pugnacious defender of the president’s military politics. These include attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and ignoring a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict. The resolution also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary. The final two impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of violating the constitution through his involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House. Should the resolution pass, the impeachment articles would head to the Senate, where the Republican leadership would have to decide whether to hold a trial of Hegseth, who has maintained Trump’s loyalty even as other cabinet secretaries – including attorney general Pam Bondi and labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer – have been shown the door. The articles seem likely to attract many Democratic votes in the House. Massie has previously seized on unanimous Democratic support and the razor-thin Republican majority to push through a measure that forced the release of many files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein.

title: US House votes for third time to end Iran war after $38bn cost is revealed
body_text: The US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left America’s stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild. The final tally of 220-204 was similar to earlier votes, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats in calling for an end to the war. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto them. The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war before the midterm elections, where the war and America’s cost of living crisis are expected to hurt Republicans at the ballot box. Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress. “Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Democrat Seth Moulton before the vote. He added it was time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration”. Republican Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House foreign affairs committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat. Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending”, meaning decades of hostilities from Iran. The House first approved a war powers resolution in June and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but Republican senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch. While the constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also enables the president as the commander in chief to authorise some military actions. The war powers act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days. The vote late on Tuesday came as the CBO report found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. It estimated that the costs of the war will grow $3bn for every month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation. Much of the cost has come from missile defense. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and navy interceptors that the CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”. In a White House statement responding to reports of shortages, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. In August, Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true”. According to the CBO report, shortages would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains an arsenal of these and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has. The economic report came a day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn, and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. The Pentagon’s report did not address its own internal investigation of the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying results of the investigation that would show negligence in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes. The CBO report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and the CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been. In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding the CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out – including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs – $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above the CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs the CBO could not examine – a far larger secret share than in past war supplementals. The CBO added that it still could not estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

It estimated that the costs of the war will grow $3bn for every month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation. Much of the cost has come from missile defense. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and navy interceptors that the CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”. In a White House statement responding to reports of shortages, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. In August, Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true”. According to the CBO report, shortages would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains an arsenal of these and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has. The economic report came a day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn, and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. The Pentagon’s report did not address its own internal investigation of the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying results of the investigation that would show negligence in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes. The CBO report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and the CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been. In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding the CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out – including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs – $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above the CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs the CBO could not examine – a far larger secret share than in past war supplementals. The CBO added that it still could not estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

title: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat
body_text: After the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it significantly harder to vote by mail in the midterms, US election officials are redoubling their efforts to convince Americans it is safe to cast their ballots by mail. The supreme court’s Monday ruling, which sent Trump into an angry froth on Truth Social, averted what election officials of both parties said would be an administrative disaster for this year’s elections. Trump’s order would have required states to comply with cumbersome new rules, including redesigning mail-in envelopes and uploading lists of voters to the USPS, that were not feasible to implement before ballots started going out. The effort was seen as a push by the government to change voting policy as well as one to weaken confidence in voting by mail. “That is the whole intent of the president. He wanted to build doubt,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat who serves as the top election official in Nevada, where mail-in voting is widely used. “He wanted to create chaos.” Twenty-nine percent of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election and roughly one third cast a mail-in ballot in the 2022 midterms, according to researchers at the MIT election lab. Democrats were more likely than Republicans to cast a mail-in ballot. “There’s just concern: ‘Can we trust the mail?’ And I say yes, because it’s not the leadership or the management of the postal service that’s actually going to have their hands on the ballots, it’s the postal workers who are on our side,” Aguilar said. Nevada officials also plan to run a series of public service announcements to educate voters on the election process. In Wisconsin, election officials have faced questions about voters concerned their ballots won’t be delivered in time. Wisconsin law requires mail-in ballots to be delivered by the close of polls on election day in order to count and in the state’s April election there was an increase in late-arriving ballots. There have been higher rates of late-arriving ballots tossed this year, according to an analysis by the New York Times. Wisconsin election officials have encouraged people through county websites, social media, and notes attached to their ballots, among other things, to mail their ballots back sooner, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. “We’re really trying to encourage people to act sooner. So hopefully they take that to heart,” said Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin elections commission, which oversees voting in that state. “It’s hard to tell people, ‘No, really, you should trust the post office’ when they came up with this absolutely cockamamie rule that was going to eliminate absentee voting.” In a video released on Tuesday, Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin elections commission, said: “If you’re going to be returning your ballot by mail, please do so at least two weeks before the election. And you also may want to contact your municipal clerk to find out if there are other opportunities for you to return your ballot in your community. You may have drop-boxes or you may be able to return your ballot in person to your clerk.” Jane Kleeb, the president of the association of state Democratic chairs, said Democrats were making a more aggressive effort to encourage people to vote early in person while also emphasizing that if they want to vote by mail, they should return their ballots quickly. “We’re being honest with voters. We’re saying, ‘Look, normally you might have given three days to get your ballot to your election office, and now you should give a week,’” she said. A DNC spokesperson said the party “will continue to use every tool at our disposal to defend the right to vote, and we encourage Americans to make a plan to vote that best works for them and make their voices heard this November.” In Washington state, where everyone received a mail-in ballot, more than 20,000 votes were rejected in the August primary because they arrived late at an election office. “There is a sense of distrust,” said Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state. “Even though there is a victory in the courts, we still are urging our voters to put their ballot in a drop-box.” As lawsuits challenging the rule wound their way through federal courts this year, Adrian Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, publicly emphasized that the rule had not gone into effect yet and so that nothing around voting by mail had changed. Since the supreme court’s ruling preserved that status quo, he said, officials haven’t had to shift their messaging. While voters have raised questions about the proposed changes “we continue to tell them until there’s a change, there is no change,” said Fontes, a Democrat “We are still where we were. We never jumped on the paranoia bandwagon.” “It’s intentionally damaging to the entire elections administration process in this country,” said Fontes, a Democrat and the top election official in a state where voting by mail is widely used. “The administration, by their actions, have proven that they are hell-bent on driving American voters away from their own elections. And we’ve been working very hard to counter that.”

title: Kennedy Center to close as Trump threatens to block repairs over name dispute
body_text: Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the Kennedy Center would close “immediately” and threatened to cancel a planned renovation of the institution if federal courts did not allow his name to be placed on the front of the building. Trump’s ultimatum came shortly after the president’s handpicked board voted, again, to close the institution’s performing arts building in Washington, citing safety and financial concerns. In a Truth Social post, Trump said the board voted “almost unanimously” to close the riverside landmark “for Safety reasons, and so that I can begin the process of Reconstruction”. He then said he would block a $257m renovation project that Trump had previously touted to address what the center has described as “decades of deferred maintenance and critical infrastructure needs”. “The Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” Trump wrote. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.” The performing arts center, built as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, has been embroiled in a dizzying legal dispute over Trump’s desire to put his name on the building. Prior to the Tuesday meeting, a federal judge blocked the center’s board from adding Trump’s name to the venue, writing that it would violate his previous ruling ordering it to be removed. “Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” US district judge Christopher Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.” Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty, an ex officio board member and trustee of the center, who brought the legal challenge, said Trump’s efforts to rebrand the institution in his name was a reflection of the president’s “vanity” and a “ breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee”. “The board’s latest shutdown vote is more of the same failure and abuse that has characterized this administration’s treatment of the Kennedy Center,” Beatty said in a joint statement with attorneys Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky. “The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away. Now the board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We’ll see the defendants in court.” Beatty told MS Now on Tuesday that the president had thrown “a tantrum” in a phone call to the board when he learned that she had prevailed in court. “It was the most unprofessional thing that I’ve ever witnessed or been a part of it,” Beatty said. “He went into name calling,” she added, saying that Trump had called her dumb. “He said, ‘I think you’re incompetent,’ and I said, ‘I know you’re incompetent,’” the congresswoman recalled. “He said he was going to hold me responsible if something fell out of the ceiling and killed someone,” she added. “And I told him, I said, ‘You’re already killing people, we’re at war.’ “Then he wanted to talk about how great he was with developing and he didn’t know anything about me, but I had never done anything. This was the biggest thing I had done. So I reminded him that he had more bankruptcies than anybody in the room.” The board’s vote followed a weekend of dueling court filings. The board’s proposal called for closing the main building on safety grounds, describing it as unsafe for continued occupancy. Beatty’s lawyers disputed that characterization, arguing in a court filing that the safety consultants cited, Delta Consulting Group, “expressly disclaimed” reaching any such opinion. Eisencalled the board’s weekend document dump “an outrageous act of hostage taking”, writing on X: “Pay up or the Kennedy Center closes, and the price is Trump’s name on the building.” The board had also been expected to vote on a proposal related to adding Trump’s name. But in a notice filed on Monday in the US district court for the District of Columbia, government lawyers disclosed that Joe LaFauci, the center’s vice-president of board relations, told the board that Tuesday’s meeting was “now focused exclusively on the necessary closure of the center”, citing “recently exacerbated structural emergencies”. However, in the filing, the board said trustees “stand by the recognition resolution proposed and passed by the board on August 13 2026”. The now-shelved second resolution had listed 10 options for inscribing Trump’s name and the “Trump Kennedy Center Fund” beneath the center’s name on the exterior marble, tying various forms of credit to renovation, endowment or oversight of the building. After Trump’s name was added to the exterior of the building above Kennedy’s, Cooper ordered the president’s name removed, ruling in May that only Congress has authority to rename it, and the lettering came down in June. The board voted in August to reinstate an inscription and proceed with the closure. Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, posted a security video on Monday appearing to show debris falling in the center’s grand foyer, saying “the entire building is in this kind of shape” and that only Trump “can deliver the renovation on time and on budget”. Trump then shared the post on Truth Social. Lutnick’s wife, Allison, is a member of the president’s appointed board. Tuesday’s vote is the latest turn in a financial and legal fight that has dogged the center since Trump installed himself as chair in February 2025, firing the board and its longtime president, Deborah Rutter. Current leadership has blamed the crisis on mismanagement by Rutter’s team, alleging a “falsified” budget with $26m in “phantom revenue”, a claim Rutter and former board chair David Rubenstein have both denied, noting the center’s finances were independently audited.

title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe
body_text: Whenever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour into Trump’s marathon speech last Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared: “Only I can make this promise to you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Trump could make such a preposterous promise. Feeling very generous with other people’s money, the president promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe. I guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican. Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year. Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly against bread and circus bribes”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom caucus, called Trump’s promise a “socialist vote-buying scheme”. What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though the president once promised to eliminate the entire federal debt. Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations. But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled. When the president made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.” Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that, thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “a dividend of at least $2,000”. That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings could go directly to Americans. That didn’t happen either. Greene taunted Trump by writing on X, “$5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.” Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of our tremendous strength and success economically”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations. After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you. Unfortunately for Trump and every American, Trump’s promise to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s stocking will clash with one of his main promises – the $5,000 payments will increase consumer demand and that will inevitably push up inflation even though Trump repeatedly promised to cut prices. Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, issued a stern warning about Trump’s $5,000. “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2tn per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year treasury yield is approaching 5%,” MacGuineas said. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.” Kenneth Rogoff, a Harvard economics professor and former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, voiced even more alarm, telling PBS, “The US is already running an unsustainable deficit. This would only blow [it] up even more and increase the already high odds of a debt crisis over next five years.” With his $5,000 “dividend”, Trump is being his impulsive, myopic and reckless self, just like he was in plunging the US into war against Iran, leaving the nation’s economy and global relations in considerably worse shape than before the war. Trump’s $5,000 promise also risks spooking financial markets and nudging up interest rates. Every American – Republican, independent or Democrat – should see through Trump’s shamelessness. If his plan comes to pass, it might be a nice sugar high for many Americans, but it will do real economic damage – to inflation, interest rates and the nation’s debt – and it will also impose an unfair burden on our children and grandchildren. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations. After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you. Unfortunately for Trump and every American, Trump’s promise to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s stocking will clash with one of his main promises – the $5,000 payments will increase consumer demand and that will inevitably push up inflation even though Trump repeatedly promised to cut prices. Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, issued a stern warning about Trump’s $5,000. “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2tn per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year treasury yield is approaching 5%,” MacGuineas said. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.” Kenneth Rogoff, a Harvard economics professor and former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, voiced even more alarm, telling PBS, “The US is already running an unsustainable deficit. This would only blow [it] up even more and increase the already high odds of a debt crisis over next five years.” With his $5,000 “dividend”, Trump is being his impulsive, myopic and reckless self, just like he was in plunging the US into war against Iran, leaving the nation’s economy and global relations in considerably worse shape than before the war. Trump’s $5,000 promise also risks spooking financial markets and nudging up interest rates. Every American – Republican, independent or Democrat – should see through Trump’s shamelessness. If his plan comes to pass, it might be a nice sugar high for many Americans, but it will do real economic damage – to inflation, interest rates and the nation’s debt – and it will also impose an unfair burden on our children and grandchildren. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: How Jon Ossoff won the algorithm – and garnered Obama comparisons ahead of 2028
body_text: Delivering a speech in Atlanta last month, Jon Ossoff accused Donald Trump of corruption, incompetence and fecklessness, and peppered his remarks with substantive observations of dates and times and places. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One. The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall. After his remark went viral, stories about Trump’s young, exceptionally devoted, presidential aide Natalie Harp rippled through social and established media. Often enough, they were accompanied by an image of Ossoff, his sharp jawline captured from below as he looks into the middle distance. This photographic framing has increasingly been referred to as the “Ossoff angle”, perhaps in a disservice to myriad politicians from John F Kennedy to Barack Obama who also employed the technique, snapped at a low angle from a camera pit over the past century. While the approach is not new, it has helped the senator for Georgia to reach the social media feeds of users far beyond his state. Kathleen Hall Jamieson, professor of communication at Penn’s Annenberg School, likened Ossoff to Kennedy. The first millennial senator has mastered the medium of the moment, she suggested, much as Kennedy was the first president who really understood television. “How do you communicate that this is a new generation of leadership?,” Jamieson asked. “And how do you do that rhetorically? Because you can’t just stand up and say, ‘This is a new generation of leadership.’ “You have to have people draw that conclusion about you. And part of the way you do that is you master the media of the time, and you demonstrate that in the process you have leadership capacity and that you have the capacity to deal with the old order.” At 33 years, 11 months and four days, Ossoff was the youngest US senator sworn into the 117th Congress. At 39 today, and ever so slightly gray at the temple, he remains the youngest in a chamber with an average age of 65. The value of good lighting, a good background and a good angle in a social media post is not lost on a film-maker, as Ossoff was before turning to public office. The former documentarian has a knack for winning the algorithm with plain language, surfacing absurdities in an era of absurdities. While Trump is also a master of social media, the effect is different. His audience is generationally different. Trump, who regularly attaches infantile nicknames to his political enemies as a political marketing gimmick, calls Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman”, a tepid sobriquet which hasn’t yet landed. More recently, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned Super Pac, began running ads about Ossoff’s haircare and makeup regime using AI-generated videos of Ossoff in a salon chair. (Ossoff has spent about $1,200 on hair and makeup this election cycle – a drop in the bucket, given a fundraising haul of $81m up to June, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) disclosures.) Georgia elected Ossoff in a nail-biting runoff in January 2021 with control of the Senate on the line, amid the turmoil of Trump’s election dispute. His election, alongside fellow Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock, secured the Senate majority for Democrats. Rioters stormed the US Capitol the next day. Since taking office, Ossoff has built a high profile as an opponent of Washington corruption, maladministration and the so-called Epstein class. He grilled CIA director John Ratcliffe after Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, published a report that senior officials had shared sensitive information about future military strikes on Signal with him. He pressed Russ Vought, Trump’s budget director, after massive cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He questioned former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard on her presence at an FBI raid that seized 2020 ballots in Fulton county. His questioning of such Trump administration officials have proven as likely to reach wide social media audiences as anything he says on the campaign trail. Clips circulated of Ossoff repeatedly pressing intelligence director nominee Jay Clayton during a July 2026 hearing to say plainly whether the 2020 election was legitimate. Ossoff’s questions left Clayton sitting in silence at the hearing table, refusing to speak. “Your answers lack credibility,” Ossoff declared. “Your testimony lacks credibility. You’re being evasive and you’re not being candid or forthright. And everybody across the country is going to watch this and know that.” But outside of the spotlight, Ossoff has held hearings on child welfare and federal prison abuses both in Washington DC and across the state of Georgia. These relatively quiet issues tend to draw little media attention and less financial interest from funders, though they are a vital element of government oversight. “It is clear that Jon Ossoff believes what he is saying, and people – they get it,” said Charlie Bailey, chairman of Georgia’s Democratic party. “And so it not only matches up with their experience and their their anger and their frustration, they know he’s telling the truth. They know he’s saying what he believes, and that’s why he’s saying it, because he thinks it’s the right thing to do.”

title: First Thing: Houthis appear to target Mecca as House votes to end Trump’s war on Iran
body_text: Good morning. Saudi Arabia’s air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca yesterday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city. A spokesperson for the kingdom, which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen, said the security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”. Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage. Meanwhile, in Washington, the US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left the US stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild. Why is Pete Hegseth being targeted by lawmakers? Republican congressman Thomas Massie has proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. How is the Trump administration reversing decisions over arming Israel? Congress has been informally notified about a pending deal, with the US planning to deliver powerful 2,000lb bombs to Israel. The weapons prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago. All supporting acts withdraw from Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour of the US and Latin America have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opening act Macklemore, as backlash grows against his removal from the tour over onstage comments in support of Palestine. Grammy-winning Macklemore had said on stage he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, along with the words “free Palestine”. The remark prompted a petition calling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour from the Israeli-American Council and the opposition of some venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and a prominent donor to Israel. How has Ed Sheeran responded? In a lengthy Instagram post, the British singer said: “I have always used my platform and music to bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together … I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care. Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine.” NBC helicopter crash in LA kills at least three people, with others injured A news helicopter crash in a Los Angeles neighborhood has killed at least three people, after it hit the ground and burst into flames near the site of a bus crash that occurred hours earlier. The helicopter crashed near a one-storey commercial building in the neighborhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according the Los Angeles fire department. New report reveals prevalence of physical and sexual violence in US In their lifetime, more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence – and nearly half have experienced sexual violence, according to a new national study. The study, led by researchers from Tulane University’s Newcomb Institute and the University of California, San Diego, examined experiences of physical, sexual and intimate partner violence. The study found that 52% of US adults have experienced physical violence during their lifetime, including cases involving a gun or knife. The rate was the same among women and men: 52% for each. In other news … Nick Reiner will not face the death penalty if convicted of the killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, the Los Angeles county district attorney’s office announced. The US has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, in an announcement analysts warn will accelerate an arms race with Russia and China. Human remains have been discovered near Crystal Rapids in Arizona, over two weeks after a flash flood tore through the Grand Canyon. Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the US and in European nations supporting Ukraine, the FBI has claimed. The European Commission president has told Canada she wants to open the door for the country to become the EU’s first associate member. Stat of the day: US surgeon general nominee made $270,000 from supplement company Donald Trump’s nominee for US surgeon general, Dr Nicole Saphier, reported more than $200,000 in business income from a company she owns that sells dietary supplements, which some critics allege are akin to “snake oil”. Well Actually: Not glamorous, but common – how to manage dandruff Experts don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, but if you’re seeing light flakes on your scalp, over-the-counter products can help. Keren Landman explains how. Don’t miss this: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant women ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers – placing them in detention centers where they say it can be exceedingly difficult to access medical care. At the same time, the agency appears to have lost count of how many suffered a miscarriage. … or this: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for “talking” to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation. Climate check: Firefighters say US government is failing them amid intense wildfire season Firefighters battling enormous wildfires in the US say the federal government is failing them at a time when supercharged blazes have made their jobs exponentially more dangerous. Last Thing: Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner The owner of a New York City bodega was reunited with the store’s cat after a couple passing by the establishment five days earlier appeared to abduct the feline in plain view of a surveillance camera and ignited an intense grassroots search effort. title: House speaker calls early recess before midterms amid AI regulation frenzy
body_text: The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. It’s the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday. “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump. “We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. “Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.” More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards. In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place on Wednesday afternoon. A spokesperson for Johnson characterized the House speaker’s latest move as simply moving up scheduled votes, not canceling future votes. Speaking to reporters outside of his office on Wednesday, Johnson said he was modifying the schedule because “the House has done its work”. Johnson said he wanted members to return to their districts to spend time with constituents ahead of the election. “You’ve seen the statistics we’ve been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789,” Johnson said, repeating a claim he also made earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention. However, so far, the current session has fallen short of passing legislation to surpass the two previous House sessions, according to the fact-checking website Snopes. Johnson also addressed Massie’s impeachment resolution, calling it “a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention”. The House speaker insisted it would be “immediately” postponed and he would not address it before the recess because the US is in the middle of international conflicts. Lawmakers will likely face a busy legislative agenda when they return to Capitol Hill after election day in November. Among their priorities will be addressing Massie’s resolution on impeaching Hegseth because it was filed as privileged, which fast-tracks the resolution.

title: More Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into view
body_text: As the US war with Iran drags on, the ranks of Republicans signaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow. When the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trump proposed impeaching the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization. The rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. But they underscore the growing nerves among both the party’s most vulnerable and most disobedient lawmakers over continuing a conflict that appears to have accomplished little other than play into the hands of Democrats, who have spent the entirety of Trump’s second term arguing that only they can be trusted to lower costs for Americans. “I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” said the congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, one of the trio of Republicans who for the first time supported a war powers resolution. She was joined by another Iowa Republican, Zach Nunn, who justified his vote by noting his state “has already paid a devastating price” in the conflict, with two Iowans among the US soldiers killed by Iranian attacks as the war began. “Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” the congressman said. “Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.” Since the US joined Israel in attacking Iran at the end of February, Democrats have wielded war powers resolutions as a cudgel to get Republicans on the record about a conflict that polls indicate is not popular with the public. Their first three attempts failed, but in June, the fourth passed with the votes of two libertarian-minded Republicans – Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio – along with Tom Barrett of Michigan and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom occupy battlefield districts. The Senate later approved that measure, but Trump refused to abide by it. In July, the same lineup in the House passed a fifth war powers resolution, before Nunn, Miller-Meeks and Nancy Mace of South Carolina expanded the ranks of Republican objectors to seven in Tuesday’s vote. The two Iowans are among the Republicans considered most at risk of losing re-election in the November midterms, with Miller-Meeks having won her race two years ago by fewer than 800 votes. They also represent areas of a state where the market impacts of the war with Iran are pronounced, as Iowa farmers struggle with higher prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer, all of which have been compounded by Trump’s tariff regime. The House vote took place on the same day the New York Times and Siena University released polling that showed likely voters preferred Democrats over Republicans for Congress by nearly nine percentage point, a finding that lines up with other surveys. Democrats are helped in their quest to retake the House by the fact that Republicans control it with a tiny majority that may be exceedingly hard to defend in November, and has also enabled Republicans like Massie to seize on splits within the party to embarrass Trump and his ally the House speaker, Mike Johnson. Last year, Massie banded together with Democrats and a handful of Republican dissidents to force passage of a bill requiring the release of files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein. That intensified the president’s ire towards him, and Massie lost his primary to the Trump-endorsed Republican Ed Gallrein earlier this year. Now with even less to lose, the congressman appears to be trying to seize on splits within the House GOP to retaliate against Hegseth, who campaigned for Gallrein. Massie proposed the resolution on Tuesday, and House rules appear to require it be voted on by Thursday. The chamber was scheduled to be in session that day for the last time before the 3 November midterm elections, but on Wednesday morning, House Republican leaders canceled votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home early to face their constituents.

title: House votes to hold Leon Black in contempt over Epstein subpoenas refusal
body_text: The House of Representatives voted on Wednesday to hold billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress over his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. The action came a day after the committee voted unanimously to recommend that the House hold Black in contempt. Wednesday’s House vote passed under unanimous consent, meaning there was not a formal roll call, but no member objected to the contempt resolution. The Department of Justice will now decide whether to take action on the resolution, though it is not required to. Congress held former attorney general Merrick Garland in contempt in 2024, but the justice department did not act on it. But it did prosecute Trump advisers Peter Navarro and Steve Bannon after congressional referrals for contempt, and both men served prison time. In a statement on Wednesday, a justice department spokesperson said: “The Department of Justice is expecting to receive the referral from House oversight committee and takes allegations of contempt of Congress seriously. “For the past 18 months, the department has repeatedly said it will follow additional investigative leads in all matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein,” they added. “The US attorney’s office for the District of Columbia will review the referral of Mr Black carefully and will not hesitate to pursue additional cases where the evidence supports.” Black, whose name came up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017, first voluntarily appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview as part of its investigation in June, but the session ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities. His lawyers criticized the contempt resolution shortly after it passed Wednesday. “This an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black. The House of Representatives has rushed through every stage of this inquiry,” they said. “We intend to pursue our litigation challenging this action and will hold the committee and Chairman Comer accountable in the courts.” The committee, chaired by Republican James Comer, then issued two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce all NDAs “to which he is a party” and another requiring him to appear before the committee again for a deposition. Black did not appear for his scheduled 3 September deposition and did not produce all of the NDAs sought by the committee. He instead sued Comer and the committee, arguing that the subpoenas were “invalid” and exceeded the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. He also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein”. On Tuesday, Black’s attorneys said that the committee under Comer and the representative Robert Garcia, its top Democrat, had “lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power”. They described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens” and reiterated that Black “never abused a woman”, “was never blackmailed by Epstein” and “had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct”. On Wednesday morning, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse praised the House oversight committee for their vote. “Survivors have fought for years to bring the truth about Epstein’s network into the open and have helped create this moment of accountability,” they said on Wednesday morning before the House vote. “Congress now has an opportunity to build on that work by following the investigative leads contained in the Epstein files wherever they go and demanding answers from the powerful people connected to them.”

title: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
body_text: The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago. The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results. However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead. The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports. It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions. Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill. Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”. “Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries. The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members. “I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday. “I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.” The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote. “We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

title: ‘Pretend I’m on the ticket’: Trump hits campaign trail in bid to boost Republican hopes
body_text: Donald Trump returned to the campaign trail on Wednesday, imploring North Carolina voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” and “crush the communists” in the November elections at a rally in support of the Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley. Despite Trump’s deep unpopularity, Republicans hope to once again turn the president’s loyal following into a political force as the party confronts an unforgiving midterm landscape. “I’m not bragging, but when I’m on the ticket Republicans have always done really well,” Trump told supporters, speaking at the Gastonia municipal airport. “I just want you to go out and pretend I’m on the ticket, because essentially I am.” The rally, Trump’s first campaign event since the Republican party’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas last week where he debuted a similar message, was aimed at energizing the Make American Great Again (Maga) faithful behind Whatley, who is running in a crucial battleground race against the Democratic former governor Roy Cooper. With the Republican senator Thom Tillis retiring, Democrats see a rare opportunity to flip a seat in a state that has repeatedly dashed the party’s hopes in recent elections, but which could decide the balance of power in the Senate for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. To win control of the chamber, Democrats must prevail in at least four Republican-held seats. The president’s appearance in North Carolina on Wednesday underscored Republicans’ challenge in the state, where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 2008 but where polls have consistently shown Cooper ahead of Whatley. Nodding to Cooper’s edge, Trump claimed there was a misconception about the former governor’s politics, claiming he was a “radical” more closely aligned with his party’s left wing. “He tries to pretend he’s a moderate,” Trump said of Cooper. “He’s not.” During his hour-long remarks, Trump lavished praise on Whatley, his handpicked choice for Senate. The former Republican National Committee chair was a “ball-breaker” and “one of the greatest men I ever worked with in government”, the president said. “I had my choice of the whole country,” Trump said. “I chose Michael Whatley.” Whatley enthusiastically returned the embrace, praising Trump as the “greatest president of our lifetime”. By leaving no doubt about his loyalty to the president, Whatley is hoping Trump’s command of the Maga base can translate into broader support in a state where independent voters make up a large share of the electorate and where concerns about high prices, the economy and the administration’s handling of the war in Iran have complicated his party’s political prospects. In Gastonia, Trump sought to simplify the choice for voters. He cast the Senate contest as a referendum on Cooper’s governorship, arguing that the election was about “safety” and “bad management”. He invoked the killing of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee fatally stabbed on a Charlotte light rail train last year. Describing the attack in gruesome detail, Trump falsely claimed that the man arrested and charged with her murder, Decarlos Brown Jr, had been released from prison by Cooper. Dozens of mugshots appeared on a video screen as Trump bashed Cooper as a “murderer protector” and explicitly likened his playbook to the notorious “Willie Horton” ad used by George HW Bush’s 1988 presidential campaign against Michael Dukakis in a racially charged appeal to cast the Democratic nominee as weak on crime. “Years ago in Massachusetts, there was a governor named Dukakis, Michael Dukakis, you remember, who had a very substantial lead for president,” Trump said. “He was going to win easily, but he allowed a man named Willie Horton out of jail. Willie Horton was a bad guy, really bad guy. Same thing as this. Same exact thing.” Trump said Whatley was the “candidate of law and order” who preferred that criminals be “executed, arrested or deported”. Local Democrats held a news conference earlier on Wednesday to preempt some of Trump’s claims and denounce Whatley for supporting Trump’s agenda. “Why would Whatley back a war that is driving up prices for North Carolina families at a time when it’s already too hard for us to get by?” the Democratic state senator Woodson Bradley said. “Let’s not find that out, North Carolina. He’s already shown us everything we need to know.” In a reminder of the significant economic headwinds Republicans are facing, Trump spent time attacking the Federal Reserve, which on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point, its first increase since 2023. The Fed said persistent inflation warranted the move. Speaking to reporters on the tarmac before the rally, Trump called the central bank “very hostile” to him and said its officials were a “bunch of politicians”. “They’re doing the wrong thing,” he said, repeating several times that interest rates were “too high”. Robert Mackey contributed reporting

title: Trump and Rubio allies are vying for control of Cuba’s assets if regime falls
body_text: Spanish hotel chains. A Canadian mining firm. European shipping giants. Visa and Mastercard. Scores of foreign companies have been driven out of Cuba this summer over fear of being hit with potent, new secondary sanctions. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, told Axios last month there are “no escape valves” from his unprecedented pressure campaign against the island. But not everybody is losing out. A growing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets, charging top dollar to help clients navigate the ever-expanding web of sanctions, and positioning themselves for lucrative business opportunities in the case of regime collapse. Since an executive order signed by Donald Trump on 1 May drove Canada’s Sherritt International from its nickel and cobalt mining joint venture with the Cuban state, two rival US bids to buy out its stake have been presented to US authorities. Ray Washburne, the vice-chair of Trump’s 2016 Victory Committee who organized last week’s Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, is clashing with Albert Huddleston, another Texas oil tycoon with close ties to the White House. Both are hoping to swoop in, despite nine-figure claims on Sherritt’s Cuba holdings by Citigroup and Office Depot – Fortune 500 corporations. Washburne did not respond to the Guardian and the consortium group including Huddleston declined to comment. A similar approach is being pursued by Australia’s Antilles Gold Ltd, which after being blacklisted over its Cuba operations in June received the green light from the Trump administration to negotiate the transfer of its stake in a Cuban copper-gold mine to the New York-based, multibillion-dollar investment fund, Global Emerging Markets. “If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail,” said a person with several decades of experience in Cuba policy who requested anonymity. Sources tell the Guardian that several Trump Organization executives who had previously traveled to the island to explore real estate deals and who even registered the Trump trademark there in 2008 have in recent months returned to Cuba under the aegis of Dominari Holdings for meetings. The executives are said to have met with Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro, the grandson of former Cuban president Raúl Castro, dubbed “the Crab”, to explore opportunities amid the departure of Spanish hotel giants Meliá and Iberostar, which had been operating on the island since the 1990s. Neither Antilles nor Dominari returned calls for comment. But American investors aren’t the only ones sensing opportunity in Rubio’s effort to coerce the sanctions-battered country of his parents’ birth into becoming economically dependent on the US. Cubans have been living under an effective fuel blockade since January 2026: the Trump administration cut oil shipments to the island from the island’s main ally after abducting Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan president; it then nixed oil deliveries from Mexico by threatening tariffs on any country sending petroleum to the island. Treasury department-authorised oil exports from Florida and Texas to the island’s private sector, however – all but non-existent last year – have shot up to over $160m so far this year. Meanwhile, Florida shipping lines such as Crowley, a donor to Cuban-American Republican lawmakers from Florida, Mario Díaz-Balart and María Elvira-Salazar, seem to be beneficiaries of fresh sanctions that have hit foreign shippers and forced Cuba-bound commerce to reroute through Florida, according to informed sources who spoke with the Guardian. Crowley declined to comment. A spokesperson for Samaritan’s Purse said: “Details about aid for Cuba are still being developed and are not yet finalized.” Ironically, some of those who have called most vociferously for harsher sanctions are also cashing in. In July, Madrid-based Vima World SL, a leading player in the island’s food industry which partners with GAESA, the Cuban military conglomerate that controls large swathes of the island’s economy and has become the main target of the US squeeze, hired top Washington lobbying firm Continental Strategy – led by Cuban-American allies of Rubio who oversaw the maximum pressure Cuba policy as officials in the first Trump administration – for matters related to trade, foreign relations and the food industry.
