Lobbying disclosure forms filed in July by a newly formed group made up of former employees at the US taxpayer-funded Foundation for Human Rights in Cuba (FHRC), alongside longtime Republican lobbyist Otto Reich and the husband of top Rubio state department aide Viviana Bovo, indicate it is “advising [the] State Department on [an] economic development plan for a future free and democratic Cuba, including energy-sector development and compensation for owners of property/business expropriated by the Cuban government”. Reich and Tony Costa, the Foundation for Human Rights chairman, are involved in efforts to mobilize billions of dollars in private investment from wealthy Cuban exiles for a post-communist Cuba through the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC). To get their priorities heard by lawmakers and officials in Washington, FHRC and another attendee of the CANCC gatherings, Armando Labrador, a Miami-based plastic surgeon who regularly meets with state department officials and wants to become Cuba’s next leader, have paid DC lobbying firm The Cormac Group a combined $100,000 since December. For another US taxpayer-funded non-profit that had been the subject of an internal Biden administration inquiry that was quickly shut down by powerful House appropriators, the administration’s unprecedented economic siege could not have come at a better time. Just before the July release of a heavily criticized state department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the US, Digital News Association Inc received a fresh $250,000 contract from the US government’s office of Cuba broadcasting for “investigative journalism, research and media production”, after which its main site launched an online interview series repeating Trump administration claims of Cuba’s purported threat to US national security. Vima, Continental, Cormac and Digital News did not return calls for comment. “The cause is regime change,” said Erik Cartelle, a consultant working to connect prominent exiles with Rubio’s state department. “I have clients that want to do a lot of business in Cuba, and the administration is banking on Cuban-Americans going to Cuba and investing, but if there’s a deal that’s going to be had with the regime, it needs to take into account the diaspora’s wishes. You’ve got to listen to this community.”

title: Bad news this week for Trump – but Fox viewers might have missed it
body_text: Two breaking stories roiled US politics this week and immediately got big play on most news sites. The supreme court surprisingly rejected – for now – Donald Trump’s attempted restrictions on mail-in ballots, a blow to Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. And the investigative site ProPublica revealed that a Russian oligarch had helped to bankroll the Bahamas wedding of Trump’s son Donald Jr, to the tune of hundreds of thousands of dollars. The blockbuster story quickly became ProPublica’s most-read article this year and was covered heavily elsewhere. “There’s no looking away from this Trump scoop,” wrote CNN’s Brian Stelter. Unless you watched Fox News, of course. There, it was business as usual. The wedding blockbuster got barely a nod on Monday night: a mere minute on the rightwing network’s evening programming, as the progressive non-profit watchdog Media Matters reported. It was much the same for the vote-by-mail story. “The news broke during the 7 p.m. hour, but Laura Ingraham, a law school grad, didn’t bother to tell viewers,” Stelter noted. Neither did the other big-name Fox opinion hosts, Jesse Watters and Sean Hannity. You would have had to wait until 11.30pm for that 45-second report, Stelter wrote, even as it was a leading story in many other places. In subsequent days, Fox paid more attention to both stories, but mostly to hand the megaphone to Trump’s trashing of the justices who didn’t give him what he demanded. Fox News has long billed itself as the more balanced alternative to mainstream media, an antidote to what Trump constantly slams as “fake news”. But in fact, the network often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewers, who still number in the millions during primetime hours. “This is the ‘negative space’ of Fox News coverage, in which they pretend something is simply not happening,” Matt Gertz, who tracks Fox News at Media Matters, told me. “Trumpian corruption is the biggest part of this,” Gertz said. Thus the endless self-dealing and self-enrichment of Trump, his family and his allies are subjects left to others. Don Jr’s wedding falls squarely into this category. Normal news outlets are concerned with informing their audience. Fox’s network stars and executives have a different priority. “They are concerned with coddling their audience and maintaining the GOP’s political power,” as Gertz put it. They are also concerned with how Trump views the network and what he says about individual hosts or pieces. This is the well-known “audience of one” syndrome. Trump sometimes complains about Fox, but there’s little doubt that he’s watching closely, as he posts segments and praises individual hosts. The Fox News viewer, to some extent, is in a bubble and happy to stay there. This shows up in polls like a new one from Axios, in which 53% of respondents said the word “corrupt” describes Trump more than any other quality. (That’s followed by “dangerous”, “out of touch” and “cruel” – not exactly a rave review by the American public.) But an astonishing 23% said “corrupt” does not describe him. These people don’t seem to know about the cryptocurrency schemes, the insider trading, the pay-to-play pardons and the lavish gifts such as a $400m jet from Qatar. Or, of course, the Russian oligarch, close to Putin, who was somehow moved to finance a Trump son’s wedding. How could they not know? They could simply have their heads in the sand. Or they could think they’re staying informed while watching Fox as it once again explores its favorite primetime topics – race and gender in the WNBA, panic over commie Democrats, the evils of socialism and the troubles that come with illegal immigration. But some subjects do fall out of favor. Fox’s primetime hosts, who egged on Trump’s Iran war months ago and made it a favorite topic, have now added that quagmire to their “ignore it and maybe it will go away” list. Why? Because it’s unpopular and upsetting. Of course, so is Trump himself, which raises the vexing question of Fox’s exit strategy from the president the network has supported so diligently and helped at nearly every turn. No Fox, no President Trump, one might argue. But now, Trump, with his bottom-dwelling approval ratings and waning power, looks more and more like a problem for the network. So far, though, he’s one problem that Fox refuses to ignore. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s second term: ‘Has anyone ever done a worse job?’
body_text: Late-night hosts dug into Donald Trump’s attempts to sway the upcoming midterms and the Russian oligarch who bankrolled his son Donald Trump Jr’s second wedding. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host opened with news that Republicans skipped town early this week in order to dodge a vote on whether to impeach the “secretary of war”, Pete Hegseth. “They’re very good at dodging votes. They did this a couple weeks ago to dodge a vote on releasing the Epstein files,” Kimmel noted. “We are now 48 days from our president declaring a stolen election,” he continued. “He’s trying every trick to try to steal it himself. The supreme court foiled his plan to stop mail-in voting, so now he’s offering $5,000 to every adult if the Republicans win. Only if they win. Which is crazy – also crazy that he would give us our own money as some kind of a gift. “Also, remind me, aren’t Republicans the people who are always screaming about handouts?” he added before several clips of Trump and numerous conservative commentators decrying Democrats who, to quote Hannity, “take your hard-earned money and use it to buy power and votes for themselves”. “Those of us who did not vote for Donald Trump assumed he would be even worse the second time around, but even I had no idea he’d be this bad,” Kimmel added. “Has anyone ever done a worse job with anything? “Kitty and Jose Menendez did a better job of parenting their boys than Donald Trump has running this country.” In other news is “the president’s war – not the one in Iran, the one on the Kennedy Center”. On Tuesday, Trump’s handpicked board at the arts and culture institution voted to close for renovations, moments after a judge ruled that they could not add Trump’s name to the building without congressional approval. “So now the big baby says that if the supreme court doesn’t overturn that ruling and put his name on the wall next to the Kennedy’s, there will be no renovations at all,” Kimmel explained. “He’s holding the building hostage,” he added. “They really should call it the Melania Trump Kennedy Center.” The Daily Show And on The Daily Show, Josh Johnson reacted to reports that Hegseth’s Pentagon is seeking troops to attend his next speech who embody his specific vision of masculinity – men with a Hegseth-delineated “waist-to-height ratios” and “impeccable grooming standards”. “I’m sorry, is this guy still in charge of the military, or is he in charge of casting Love Island?” Johnson said. “I’ve never heard anyone say the phrase ‘waist-to-height’ ratio before,” he continued. “This man cannot count the number of missiles you need to fight a war with Iran, but when it comes to male physique, he’s A Beautiful Mind? “And asking for impeccable grooming is a little strange. But it’s nice to know that this administration is finally taking grooming seriously,” he quipped next to a photo of Jeffrey Epstein. In other “perfect specimens of masculinity” – Donald Trump Jr, who this spring got married (again) to Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson on a private island in the Bahamas … that was bankrolled by a Russian oligarch. Umar Kremlev, a former criminal turned boxing promoter turned associate of the Russian president, reportedly paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent the island and stage several parties with professional dancers and performances. “I don’t want to be culturally insensitive, but that name sounds like a knockoff James Bond villain,” said Johnson. “He’s a spy from the Kremlin – let’s call him Krem-lev. “But I’m getting distracted: a Russian oligarch with ties to Putin paid for the president’s son’s wedding weekend,” he added. “And this is a presidential family of billionaires, which means you just did corruption for the love of the game. “This whole family has been making billions off Trump’s presidency and they still can’t resist a freebie, whether it’s a Qatari jet or a post-wedding chocolate fountain.”

title: House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies
body_text: A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record. Salazar won re-election by a 20-point margin in 2024, but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.” First elected in 2020, the congresswoman is a champion of the Dignity Act, an immigration reform proposal in the House of Representatives that would create a pathway for some undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status. Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump before the 3 November elections, in which Democrats are vying to take back both the House and Senate. With gas prices high due to the war with Iran and Trump’s public approval low – including on key issues like handling of immigration – Democrats increasingly believe their candidates are competitive even in heavily Republican seats.

title: Jon Kyl, former Republican US senator who served three terms, dies aged 84
body_text: Jon Kyl, a Republican former US senator from Arizona who shepherded conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh through his confirmation hearing, died on Thursday at 84, his family announced. The cause was complications from a neurological disease, according to a statement. Last December, Kyl announced that he had been diagnosed with dementia. “We know that Jon belonged to all of Arizona, a state he loved and explored with vigor, curiosity and wonder. Serving his state and nation in Congress was a privilege and responsibility he honored and respected,” his family said. An attorney, Kyl won election to the US House in 1986 then the Senate in 1994, where he would serve three terms. He rose to become the Republican whip and served from 2007 until departing the chamber at the beginning of 2013, when his party was in the minority. title: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak
body_text: As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises, Robert F Kennedy Jr headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change. “But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said. He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once. “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” Recent polling suggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania. Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”. There is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends who are still at CHD. Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government. “We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” the CEO of the Children’s Health Defense, Mary Holland, said at the event on Thursday. Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism, spoke before and immediately after Kennedy. “I could not have imagined two years ago that Bobby [Kennedy] would be in the White House and that President Trump would be saying ‘divide up the MMR into three different’,” said Wakefield, who proposed the same strategy years earlier when he attempted to patent his own single measles shot to compete with the MMR. He stopped to laugh. “What drug was I on that morning?” Anti-vaccine activists had become nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy. But recent months have shifted vaccines back into the spotlight. “Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner,” Kane said. “Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.” The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. Several speakers explicitly linked vaccination to autism, despite decades of research showing no connection. Meanwhile, Kennedy also focused on the role of food systems in health, and touched on efforts to study electromagnetic fields and chem trails. He praised researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, who are now under investigation by their institution, as “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy attempted to fund their project in Guinea-Bissau looking at mortality after hepatitis B vaccination before local authorities cancelled the project. Their prior work on vaccines has been called “a house of cards” by other researchers. Mark Gorton, president of the Maha Institute, referred to himself as “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference”, adding that “only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough to raise awareness.” Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage”, said sen Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen Rand Paul, a Republican and physician from Kentucky, both rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death. Republican congressman Thomas Massie said he called Donald Trump soon after the election to ask for the agriculture secretary position. Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. Kennedy was nominated to HHS the next day, he said. Massie offered two pieces of advice to the anti-vaccine activists: Instead of trying to get rid of “clowns”, he said, “get the clowns who are here to do what you want. Get them to get in the clown car you want. And use pressure. Treat them like cattle.” Coverage of the measles outbreak is a “psy op” that is “meant to control what I think, what I do, what I believe, and what my attitude towards Bobby Kennedy ought to be,” said Tony Lyons, the publisher of books from Kennedy who now heads Maha Action. Kennedy was frequently invoked as a hero of the movement at the conference. “The truth is, he really is dangerous,” Lyons said, invoking the common refrain from scientists and experts. “I think Bobby Kennedy is the most dangerous individual to this system who’s come along in a generation,” he said to a burst of applause. This article was amended on 17 September 2026 to clarify that Kennedy led Children’s Health Defense for nearly a decade.

title: What Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting mean for the midterms
body_text: For the millions of Americans who vote by mail – almost a third of the country – the week began with significant uncertainty that they would be able to easily submit their ballot this fall, thanks to a March executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to restrict mail-in ballots. By Monday night, the supreme court restored a measure of order by rebuking the president and rejecting his plan – but Trump’s frothing response portends more danger for the rapidly approaching midterms. Trump’s March order forbade the US Postal Service from delivering mailed ballots to anyone the administration deemed ineligible. The Department of Homeland Security, working with the Social Security Administration, would have devised that list of supposedly ineligible, noncitizen voters. On its face, the move appeared plainly illegal. One expert told the Guardian’s Sam Levine, “This is a wholly unconstitutional EO,” because ultimately the federal government cannot set election rules; only states can. The plan was full of logistical problems, too. A whistleblower told Congress earlier this month that the Postal Service simply didn’t have the ability to implement the system safely, and that the whole plan was “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to Richard Blumenthal, the senator who handled the whistleblower complaint. State election officials also complained they would be unable to implement Trump’s restrictions this close to an election, even if they were deemed lawful. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin had already begun mailing out ballots before the supreme court ruled, and chaos would have reigned there and across the country had the court blessed Trump’s plan. But it didn’t – and that sent Trump into a furor. In a lengthy post on Truth Social, in which he called mailed ballots “corrupt and out of control”, he singled out the conservative justices who had gone against him on that issue and this year’s ruling on tariffs. (Only the justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from the mailed ballot ruling; Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, both nominated by Trump, did not.) “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” the president fulminated. His position is clear: the federal courts, the states that administer elections, the USPS – all of them should bow to his whims, regardless of what the constitution says. Trump has already shattered legal norms by appointing his former personal lawyer to head the Department of Justice and then continuing to treat him as a personal attorney. Just this week, in a remarkable scene at the White House, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, served the role of White House press secretary, answering a wide range of questions from reporters on behalf of the president. A day later, a smiling Blanche attended a Trump rally for the GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, flashing an enthusiastic thumbs-up from the crowd. The extraordinary danger of this moment is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process. Trump’s claims about mail-in voting are false, as the Guardian’s George Chidi explained. The Brookings Institution has found: “An average total mail voting fraud percentage across the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 general elections of only 0.000043%, or about four cases of mail voting fraud out of every 10 million mail votes.” But Trump has been obsessed with the issue since 2020, when mailed ballots – which are typically counted last – evaporated his slim lead in some key states on election night. (Incidentally, Trump has voted by mail at least three times since then.) And more Democrats than Republicans vote by mail, so restricting mailed ballots also tilts the playing field towards the GOP. State election officials are now working to assure voters that they can safely vote by mail this year, as Levine reported this week. But one can safely assume Trump will not stop pushing democracy to the brink. Watch this race: Florida’s 27th congressional district Trump won this Miami district by 15 points in 2024, when he aggressively promised a campaign of “mass deportations”. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican representative, easily held the seat, vanquishing her Democratic opponent by 20 points. But Salazar is distancing herself from Trump this time around. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she says to the camera in a remarkable ad released on Thursday. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” She is facing a significant challenge this year from Eliott Rodriguez, a Democrat and former news anchor. Fact check During Trump’s speech address at a rally in North Carolina on Wednesday, which the Charlotte Observer described in an op-ed as a “dark, divisive” speech, he painted the Tar Heel state as a crime-ridden hellhole. “So nobody used to think of North Carolina as a dangerous state, criminally dangerous,” Trump said. “It was like North Carolina, it was beautiful, it was apple pie, right? And now it’s one of the most violent and one of the worst in the whole nation.” (An interesting pitch to voters: your state is the worst.) But crime has fallen dramatically in North Carolina. Don’t take our word for it: only hours before Trump’s arrival in Gastonia, North Carolina, the White House blasted out a press release correctly noting: “In North Carolina, crime fell across all four major categories in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year, including a 12.4% drop in murders, an 18% drop in robberies and a 23% drop in motor vehicle thefts.” George Zornick is the Guardian’s US political enterprise editor

title: Trump’s authoritarian mindset can’t handle dissent from his appointees
body_text: “It’s not personal, Sonny. It’s strictly business,” Michael Corleone tells his brother, Sonny, in The Godfather. But for Donald Trump, it’s always personal. And he leaves this week feeling betrayed. First, the US supreme court rejected his effort to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” the president wrote on his Truth Social platform. “They are merely a shell of their original selves.” Then the Federal Reserve defied Trump by raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, marking its first rate hike in three years. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, described it as “a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision”. The president lashed out again but was careful to blame the board rather than Warsh. Trump told reporters he had spoken to the chair. “I said you might ⁠as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political.” It was an effort to rationalise a shock to the system for Trump, who instinctively assumes that anyone he appoints to high office will be eternally in his debt and automatically do his bidding. It is a view constantly reinforced by his cartoonishly loyal cabinet, from defence secretary Pete Hegseth to attorney general Todd Blanche, who was previously Trump’s personal lawyer. Blanche held a press conference in the White House Rose Garden on Tuesday and staunchly defended Trump. He was rewarded two days later when he attended a campaign rally in Gastonia, North Carolina, and heard Trump say of him: “He’ll go down as the greatest attorney general in the history of our country.” But the supreme court is a different matter. Its conservative majority includes three justices appointed by Trump during his first term. It has certainly given him plenty of wins in emergency appeals during his second term, lifting lower court orders that had blocked his crackdown on immigration, ban on transgender people serving in the military and dismantling of the education department. Perhaps that is why the defeats rankle and, to him, appear inexplicable. The justices struck down his far-reaching tariffs on nearly every other country and his restrictions on birthright citizenship while blocking his attempt to immediately fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook. Last week, the court refused to allow Missouri to use new elections maps redrawn at Trump’s urging to help Republicans gain an extra seat in the House of Representatives. Then came this week’s knockback of his administration’s planned restrictions on mail-in voting, which Trump has long condemned as fraudulent while continuing to vote by mail himself. Of the nine-member court, only justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented. For the authoritarian mindset, this does not compute. Trump has become accustomed to snuffing out the first sparks of dissent among Republicans in Congress before the flames of rebellion can spread. He has taken a scythe to government departments and entities such as the Kennedy Center, which he is now threatening to demolish. But not even he can control his own appointments when they serve in institutions protected by America’s system of checks and balances. The irony is that they might be saving Trump from his own worst impulses. The Fed’s intervention, for example, is aimed at curbing the rising prices that are hurting Trump politically. Warsh explained: “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.” It may only be a matter of time before Warsh’s honeymoon period ends and he feels the president’s wrath. But the Fed chair may also be aware that time is be on his side: every day brings Trump closer to the point at which Republicans begin looking beyond him to 2028. Last weekend, Mike Johnson, the House speaker, said only that Congress will “debate and discuss” Trump’s promise to give Americans $5,000 if Republicans retain control. On Thursday Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, forcefully criticised the president’s deportation agenda in a campaign ad. Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, says: “We’re starting to see institutions like the supreme court and the Republicans in the Senate more consistently resisting him. This is the beginning of the lame duck session for Trump. This is the entry point for where it’s going to be: a sour grapes moment in Trump’s political career.”

title: Trump administration sued over threat to deploy federal law enforcement at voting sites
body_text: A coalition of civil rights groups filed a lawsuit against Trump administration officials on Friday, seeking to stop them from threatening to deploy federal law enforcement officers to polling stations in the US midterm elections. The suit, led by the NAACP, alleges that by threatening to deploy law enforcement to survey elections and initiating new voter roll oversight, the Trump administration has violated a section of the Voting Rights Act which prohibits voter intimidation. “The result is predictable: voters across the country – particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, naturalized citizens and members of mixed-status families – are afraid to vote, help others vote and participate in civic life,” the plaintiffs wrote in the complaint. Plaintiffs cited other examples of voter intimidation, such as Donald Trump giving a primetime address to exaggerate claims of noncitizen voting, the administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operations in communities of color, and the president’s efforts to create a national voter eligibility list. Friday’s lawsuit is the latest attempt by groups to stop Trump from asserting more control over US elections as the country heads into what is expected to be a competitive midterm in November. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said “those who are here legally and not breaking other laws have nothing to fear” and denied that ICE was planning operations targeting polling locations. “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action,” the spokesperson added. DHS denied allegations of law enforcement engaging in racial profiling, calling the accusations “categorically FALSE” and insisting that targets of immigration enforcement were whether a person was in the US illegally, not by skin color, race or ethnicity. The FBI declined to comment for this story. ICE referred the Guardian to DHS. A White House official pointed to the administration’s past remarks denying any plan to deploy ICE agents to polls in November. Karoline Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, told reporters in February it was “not something I’ve ever heard the president consider”. Kiersten Pels, a justice department spokesperson, said in a statement: “The DOJ has never said it would send federal law enforcement to polling locations. Any suggestion otherwise is fearmongering.” Federal law states that no armed federal officers or members of the armed forces may be placed at a location where an election is being held. So far, the administration has not sent any armed officers or military members to polling locations. But recent mixed-messaging from top administration officials has raised concerns among election integrity advocates. In May, Trump did not rule out the possibility of sending the National Guard or ICE officers to polling locations. Kash Patel, the FBI director, told lawmakers this week that the FBI “will not shy away” from its efforts to ensure elections are safe and honest when asked whether he planned to send FBI agents the polls. “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation, we will, otherwise we won’t,” he added, noting that “we’re going to house our agents and intel analysts in our field offices”. Earlier this month, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, told reporters ICE would not be at polling locations to patrol but could be present if there was a threat or if they were serving a warrant to someone. “As a nation, we have no need for armed presence at polling locations – our elections are safe and transparent, which has been the hallmark of our democracy,” said Kristen Clarke, general counsel at the NAACP, in a statement after the lawsuit was filed. “Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period,” Clarke added. Friday’s lawsuit is at least the second of its kind. Last week a coalition of groups, led by the League of United Latin American Citizens, also sued the administration seeking to stop it from deploying ICE officers to polling locations.

title: Trump signs bill imposing sanctions on Russia and giving him more power to levy tariffs
body_text: Donald Trump on Friday signed legislation enabling sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending its war with Ukraine, and also giving him the power to impose additional tariffs on countries breaking the embargo. The US president signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law two days after it passed the House of Representatives in a bipartisan 262-159 vote, amid concerns the legislation gives him too much power. The Trump administration has previously been doubtful about imposing additional sanctions on Moscow but changed its stance after repeated attempts to end its four and a half year war against Ukraine have stalled. The bill named after the hawkish Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, who died in July, is aimed at depleting Russia’s ability to continue funding the war by targeting its natural gas and oil revenues, as well as countries that continue to buy Russian energy. The legislation imposes new sanctions on Russian political and military officials and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. In addition, it targets Russia’s fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite existing sanctions on its energy exports. But it also gives Trump wide leeway over its implementation, including which countries could face tariffs, and which tariff rates could be imposed. It also gives the president sweeping discretion over whether sanctions provisions can be waived against certain countries. Controversially, it allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy, including China, and on other countries that help Moscow to evade sanctions. The bill’s broad provisions were criticized by many Democrats, who complained that it gave Trump excessive authority to resort to tariffs, which he has already imposed on multiple countries despite a US supreme court ruling prohibiting him from doing so under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

title: US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over Greenland
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for much of his second term to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force. The full scope of the deal Trump described as “very important, historic, and special” was not immediately clear. But soon after his announcement in a post on Truth Social, the leaders of Denmark and Greenland issued statements indicating the deal would be signed by the three governments on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City next week. In his social media post, Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming that the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato. The announcement comes just weeks before November’s midterms, giving the president a foreign policy accomplishment he can tout to voters as the deeply unpopular war with Iran becomes an increasing political liability for Republicans vying to hang on to their narrow majorities in the House and Senate. The US has long had a military presence in Greenland – a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member – and has had a military base at Pituffik since the cold war. In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”. Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late on Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s previously stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”. Frederiksen said that what she called “a great agreement” for all three parties “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. Nielsen said it was “joyous” that the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base. Once agreed to, the pact would need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the Danish and Greenlandic statements said. Earlier in his term, Trump argued that the US needed control of Greenland for “economic security”, and has described ownership and control of the territory as an “absolute necessity”. The island had long been on the president’s radar as a target for purchase, and during his first term, in 2019, Trump confirmed reports he had been urging aides to find out how the US could buy Greenland, describing any sale as “essentially a large real estate deal”. Trump’s claims deepened divisions among the western alliance, with the Danish government repeatedly stating that Greenland was “not for sale”. When concerns over Trump’s annexation threats reached a fever pitch last year, the Guardian reported that the Danish government set up a “night watch” in the foreign ministry to monitor the US president’s pronouncements while Copenhagen sleeps. At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland. He threatened to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back. Strategically positioned between the US and Russia, Greenland is viewed as increasingly important for defense and is emerging as a geopolitical battleground as Arctic ice melts. The US vice-president, JD Vance, and his wife Usha, received a frosty reception when they visited US troops stationed at Pituffik space base last year, amid the White House’s aggressive campaign to take the mineral-rich island with roughly 56,000 inhabitants. Polling has found Greenlanders strongly oppose any effort to make Greenland a part of the US. Even so, a Trump administration insider dropped a hint online that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. Katie Miller, a former White House aide whose husband is Trump’s closest adviser, posted a map of Greenland covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”. Miranda Bryant contributed reporting

title: Kevin Warsh may be the adult in the room. But can he calm the US economy?
body_text: In the end, Kevin Warsh’s Federal Reserve acquitted itself well. For all the uncertainty he had sparked at the previous meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, when he refused to provide any indication of what he was prepared to do to tame stubborn inflation, the chair on Wednesday presided over a unanimous decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years. “Today’s action starts to show that we’re serious about this,” he said at the press conference after the meeting, with “this” meaning inflation in excess of the Fed’s 2% target for over five years. Welcome though it was, his embrace of economic orthodoxy nonetheless did little to dispel the Keystone Cops quality of governance in Donald Trump’s US. Warsh’s resolve – raising rates just a few weeks before elections that will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress – appeared even more resolute in the face of a veiled threat from White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett, who pointed out to his chums on Fox that “if you want an independent Fed, then one thing the Fed does is it stays out of the way of elections”. The central bankers’ parsimonious comments in the press conference following the meeting made a sharp contrast with the more unhinged commentary from other members of the administration, including the president himself, who earlier this month celebrated the resilience of the labor market with a mind-boggling threat to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” unless the Fed cut interest rates. Trump has yet to turn on Warsh in the way he did on his predecessor, Jerome “numbskull” Powell. But the signs are ominous. After the rate hike, Trump went ballistic – spewing more of the random, incoherent thoughts that have become his trademark. “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World,” he wrote on social media, despite recalcitrant inflation and a budget deficit that is likely to exceed $2tn this year. He again demanded the powers that be to “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” Yet more significant than the contrast between Warsh’s words and the incongruent economic rhetoric from the White House is the tension between the Fed’s decision on Wednesday and pretty much every other initiative from the administration, from the volley of tariffs against imports from everywhere to the war in Iran to Trump’s “promise” of $5,000 a head if he wins the midterms to treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s desperate efforts to pull interest rates down even as the Fed is raising them. All things considered, financial markets reacted relatively calmly to the day’s events. For sure, the S&P 500 index took a nosedive on Wednesday afternoon, closing some 0.4% lower at the thought that the Fed would likely now raise rates again in December and twice in 2027. The yield on the 10-year bond rose sharply, again surpassing 5%. But investors appear to have bought – for now at least – that whatever deranged policies may emerge from the rest of the administration, monetary policy will remain comparatively sane. Investors should probably remain on their toes, though. A rational Trump would probably thank Warsh for his hawkishness. There might be a plausible argument to keep rates where they were because inflation is driven by temporary forces, like a war. Yet had the Fed staid its hand, or – goodness forbid – cut rates as the president has demanded, the bloodbath in the treasury market would have been gruesome, as investors were forced to accept that the chair of the central bank would not stand up to the nut who appointed him. By contrast, by raising rates and demonstrating he is serious about curbing inflation, the Fed is likely to calm market jitters and reduce long-term inflation expectations, which will ultimately redound in lower yields on treasury bonds, allowing for lower interest rates on mortgages and other long-term loans that matter to businesses and consumers. More clown cars are likely on the way. In his fury on Wednesday, Trump again threatened to stop trading with countries that have a surplus with the US – a proposition so devoid of sense that it is hard to comprehend, let alone critique. The war in Iran is likely to continue throughout the administration, bringing more volatility to energy markets. Even Bessent seems to be losing his hold on reality. Vexed over rising treasury yields – which are raising the cost of servicing the government’s Brobdingnagian debts – the man whom markets believed would play the role of adult in the Oval Office on matters of economic policy has started to emulate the desperate government officials he once pummelled into submission. Bessent built a reputation in financial circles in 1996 as part of the team built by George Soros and Stanley Druckenmiller that pushed the British pound out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. They made a tidy profit by teaching hapless British ministers that however many pounds they bought to defend the exchange rate, they could never overcome a market determined to sell. Today, Bessent has taken the losing side of that trade, betting that he can buy enough treasuries to bring long-term interest rates down. The Fed on Wednesday likely helped Bessent’s cause. Still, the peculiar image of a central bank raising interest rates while the treasury secretary resorts to gunslinger tactics to lower them won’t restore trust in the creditworthiness of the United States. (“I am the house,” he proclaimed, hoping to achieve a steely gaze, rhetorically twirling and reholstering his revolver. “You can bet against me if you want.”) Can an unexpectedly solid Fed chair stabilize the ship of an American economy discombobulated by slapstick policymaking? Here’s hoping. But holding one’s breath may be a bad idea. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Hispanic voters’ support for Trump wanes over economy and immigration
body_text: Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Donald Trump in 2024 are discontented with his second-term economic and immigration policies, according to recent polling – indicating they may not be willing to support the president’s party in the midterm elections. Despite a record number of Hispanic voters casting their ballots for the Republican president, more than 65% said they are displeased with Trump’s handling of his job and 78% said they would prefer to see the Democratic party in control of Congress, according to a September poll from the New York Times/Siena University. “When we ask voters, ‘OK, what is shaping your opinion about the president?’ The cost of living was number one, number two was immigration enforcement and deportation in US cities, number three is back to the economy – wages,” Clarissa Martinez De Castro, the vice-president of the Latino Vote Initiative at UnidosUS, said. Frustration with the consequences of the administration’s current policies are driving Latino voters away from Republicans, said Mike Madrid, a campaign consultant, author and teacher who has been studying Latino voting patterns for 35 years. “There’s no renewed affinity or love for the Democratic party. They’re just extremely upset and disillusioned and angry, frankly, with Donald Trump,” Madrid said. “So they’re gonna leave the Republicans for the exact same reasons that they left the Democrats two years ago,” he added. Other polls support those findings. Approximately 63% of Hispanic respondents told a Fox News survey in September they plan to vote for the Democratic congressional candidate in their district. In an UnidosUS poll from April/May, 54% of Hispanic voters said they would vote for the Democratic House candidate, compared with 27% who said they would favor the Republican. The economy and cost of living are top concerns for Hispanic voters, polls show. Trump’s message of economic populism helped him get elected in 2024, but voters, including Republicans, have soured on his handling of the economy amid high inflation and rising costs. The Iran war has pushed gas prices past $4 per gallon on average. Inflation has risen over the last year and remained stubborn at 3.4%, elevating grocery costs. When asked about the recent polling of Hispanic voters, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said “hard-working Hispanic Americans are beginning to have some breaking room after four year of economic pain under the Democrats” and pointed to policies such as middle-class tax cuts, no tax on tips, overtime and social security and “defeating Biden’s inflation crisis”. Schuster said Trump was “honored to receive a record level of support from Hispanic Americans that helped fuel his landslide 2024 election victory” and that the president and Republicans in Congress would “continue fighting to make everyday life more affordable for working families”. Between October 2025 and May 2026, Hispanic voters’ favorability of Democrats in Congress increased by three percentage points, according to UnidosUS’s bipartisan poll of 3,000 Hispanic voters. Meanwhile, favorability toward Republicans in Congress only increased by one percentage point. Immigration is also an issue, especially since the Trump administration has deployed federal agents to Latino and Hispanic communities across the country. Some who have encountered immigration agents have accused the administration of racial profiling to target immigrants for deportation. But immigration is not the biggest issue for Latino voters – a misconception that politicians often make. In UnidosUS’s poll of 3,000, 17% said they wanted elected officials to prioritize increasing border security. Another 13% said they supported deporting all undocumented immigrants, regardless of how long they have been in the US. Those who voted for Trump are part of a larger cohort of “swing” voters who have no allegiance to a specific political party. They make up roughly 40% of the Hispanic electorate and are often misunderstood by politicians, Martinez said. “You have 40% of voters here for whom, many of them say, they don’t see the difference between the parties in terms of who really is going to be better,” Martinez said of the group. “That tells candidates: you have homework to do, and the clock is ticking,” she added. title: MS Now, CNN and Politico say reporters have been denied access to White House
body_text: Journalists from three US outlets were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning a day after Donald Trump said he would ban them from the executive branch complex in a move that has prompted outrage and shock from free-speech advocates. The outlets were television broadcasters MS Now and CNN as well as the political news website Politico. MS Now said a reporter and a cameraman had been denied access and had their White House press passes confiscated by the US Secret Service at a security gate outside the West Wing. CNN reported that its reporter Betsy Klein was also denied access and had her press pass seized too. Politico said White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett had received the same treatment. “The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now said, adding that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our first amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy”. It said: “We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the president, the administration and the issues that impact the American people.” CNN said in a statement: “We have a right under the US constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.” Politico’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, said in a statement to the Politico newsroom: “We stand by [Haslett] and all reporters here covering the White House … We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights.” Trump’s threat to banish CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House has brought condemnation from first amendment advocates and Democratic officials, among others, as the conflict between the US president and parts of the media sharply escalates ahead of November’s midterm elections. It has also thrown into stark relief Trump’s attack on press freedom in the US, which has unnerved civil liberties advocates. In a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon, Trump said he would order the removal of the news outlets “effective immediately” for what he claimed was “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and said he is considering banning more. Trump did not identify a single infraction, but said his decision was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it.” The White House Correspondents’ Association, which represents the White House press corps, condemned the move. “The constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” it said on social media. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting or approves of the questions its journalists ask.” The body said the issue is “about more than the rights of journalists” but about “the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office”. Trump has long clashed with the media over what he considers slanted coverage of his administration and himself personally, as well as describing a media environment in which the press and his political opponents are in collusion. Last year the Associated Press was banned form the White House after refusing to acknowledge an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America. After Friday’s ban was announced, CNN issued a statement saying that removing its reporters from the grounds could violate the law. “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” a spokesperson for the outlet said. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government.” Politico also issued a statement, saying it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones” and “will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them”. Jim Acosta, a former CNN reporter, accused Trump of “taking a meat axe to the free press in this country”. Speaking on MS Now on Friday, Acosta called the latest media bans “a slippery slope” and warned: “We are on the path to having a state media-like system in this country.” Acosta said the media should collectively oppose Trump’s ban. “Each of these news organizations should sue the White House, sue Donald Trump, and that other news organizations in Washington should band together and say, ‘We will not go to the White House and cover you and cover your administration. We’re banning you.’” Press freedom group PEN America said: “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the first amendment works. As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. “The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.”

title: As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails
body_text: Donald Trump’s sons, through a series of AI-linked defense and technology ventures, have picked up a $620m Pentagon loan, a Marine Corps robotics contract and an undisclosed air force drone deal in the past year. His longtime friend Michael Dell won a Pentagon contract worth nearly $9bn. And this week, as public support for artificial intelligence sinks to some of the lowest levels ever recorded, the president went to bat for the industry. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he posted on Truth Social Monday. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers.” It was the first of many aggressively pro-AI posts he would make this week. Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel. The administration frames its resistance chiefly as a matter of competitiveness. Trump and officials including David Sacks, who co-chairs his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, have repeatedly argued that new rules could slow US AI development when the country is racing China for dominance of the technology. Sacks said at a Politico summit on Wednesday that recent warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI about the technology’s risks amounted to political theater, manufactured by advocacy groups and the press, and said existing laws were largely sufficient. But many concerns are coming from inside the industry itself. In early September, Jacob Coxon – a researcher who spent three years working on the foundational training of AI models at both OpenAI and Anthropic – resigned and published a stark warning. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said colleagues privately believe the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic’s head of AI safety, Mrinank Sharma, separately resigned the same week, writing that “the world is in peril.” Those warnings coincided with a concrete demonstration of AI-enabled risk. A California cybersecurity firm disclosed this month that it had used artificial intelligence to build a self-spreading worm capable of hijacking WeChat accounts through a single unanswered call, and then automatically spreading through the victim’s contact list. The firm estimated the technology could compromise more than a billion devices within hours. Tencent, the Chinese tech giant that owns WeChat, patched the vulnerability before it was deployed and said no accounts were affected, but the firm noted that building the exploit, work it said would once have taken a larger team months, took roughly 10 days with AI assistance. Around the same time, JD Vance, speaking on a Christian podcast, described certain uses of AI as carrying “really, really weird spiritual dark energy” and said there are “things about the world” that leave him “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”. Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible. A poll released on Wednesday found just 11% of Americans support an AI datacenter being built in their own community, while 65% oppose one – including 52% of Republicans – and 57% say Trump has handled the issue of AI poorly, up seven points since March. The same day, the House voted 417-3 to require datacenters to bear the costs of the electricity-grid upgrades their operations demand, underscoring how concerns about AI’s infrastructure costs have moved from polling into Congress. If the federal government did enact regulations that ultimately damaged AI profits, it’s possible some members of the Trump family would feel the pain. Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump joined the investment firm Dominari Holdings last year and helped launch American Data Centers Inc, an AI infrastructure venture in which Dominari holds a minority stake. The deal came weeks after their father unveiled an expected $20bn datacenter pledge from Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani, and $500 bn in planned private sector AI investment, alongside an executive order unwinding Biden-era AI safeguards. Since then, the brothers have moved from infrastructure into defense contracting, most notably through Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet startup whose products are used in AI datacenters, drones and defense systems. Three months before the Pentagon announced its $620m loan to Vulcan in December – the largest the defense department’s office of strategic capital has ever issued – 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Trump Jr is a partner, quietly took a stake in the company. A ProPublica investigation found the loan request came not from Vulcan or the Pentagon but from Peter Navarro, a senior White House adviser and close friend of Trump Jr’s, and that Pentagon staff were told to move at an “unusually rapid pace”. “The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” one person involved in the deal told the outlet. Trump Jr’s spokesman, the Pentagon and Vulcan have all said he played no role in the deal and that the company received no political favoritism. Eric Trump, separately, serves as chief strategy adviser to Foundation Future Industries, the robotics startup behind the $24m Marine Corps contract; senator Elizabeth Warren called that award “corruption in plain sight”. A third venture, the drone maker Powerus backed by both brothers and having signed a new agreement with Pakistan’s army, also holds a $90m air force contract, and has separately pitched its technology to Gulf states amid Iran’s striking of US bases across the region. Drones are widely expected to increasingly utilize AI technology in the coming years. A Washington Post analysis in July found 15 companies tied to the brothers’ investment funds have generated at least $3.2bn in direct federal business since they got involved, but SpaceX and Anduril, the latter an AI-powered defense technology firm behind Lattice account for 97% of that figure, and 10 of the 15 companies already had government business before the Trump sons invested. Excluding SpaceX and Anduril, the remaining 13 companies had received $103m in direct federal funding and nearly $1.8bn in long-term commitments after the brothers’ investments. The pattern extends beyond Trump’s family to some of his closest technology allies. Sacks’s influence over Trump’s regulatory decisions has been substantial: in May, he reportedly persuaded the president in a last-minute call to scrap a planned executive order that would have subjected AI models to extended government review, overriding the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who had spent months negotiating the stronger version. His own financial position has drawn scrutiny inside the administration as a result. Sacks’s venture firm holds stakes in SpaceX and a range of AI startups, along with earlier investments in Meta, Palantir and Airbnb; federal ethics rules required him to divest only some of those holdings while he served as the White House’s AI and crypto czar, a post he left in March. Some administration officials have privately looked into whether Sacks could personally benefit from blocking new AI rules, the Wall Street Journal reported. The outlet reported that Musk pushed in the same direction, joining Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang last month in personally lobbying Trump against a proposed industry-funded AI oversight body, helping shelve the plan. Dell, a member of Trump’s science and technology advisory council and a longtime friend and donor to the president, saw his company win the nearly $9bn Pentagon contract in May, prompting ethics watchdogs to question whether his advisory role created an unaddressed conflict. The technology industry is not uniformly aligned behind Trump. Federal filings on OpenSecrets show the broader communications and electronics sector still sends roughly two-thirds of its political money to Democratic candidates and committees this cycle. Trump’s support among industry figures has come instead from a narrower group: OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman have given tens of millions of dollars to a pro-Trump super Pac and Trump’s inaugural committee, though have also donated to Democrats in the past. The Pentagon’s own account of its safeguards makes no distinction between a routine contractor and a company whose investors include the president’s son, which is a gap Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate last month. Next week, Trump is set to host the leaders of the country’s leading AI companies at the White House, a meeting arranged with the House speaker, Mike Johnson, that will coincide with a visit from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. In the meantime, the investments continue.

title: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways
body_text: Primary season has officially concluded in the United States, with Democrats leading the polls among voters amid widespread economic anxieties, a war with Iran and Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda continuing into the end of the year. Democratic and Republican voters have selected contenders for key races in the 3 November midterms that will decide the balance of power in Congress, and the future of both parties. Democrats have been rocked by the primary victories of leftwing candidates. Republicans have doubled down on backing the president’s policies, despite his low approval ratings. And both parties are navigating the fallout from a series of scandals that have forced some candidates from the race, while others decided to press on. Here’s a look back at what we learned over the past six months of primaries: Lawmakers fled the House in droves, ensuring a reshaped Congress in 2027 Viewed as the chamber of Congress most likely to change hands in the midterms, the House saw significant turnover this cycle, with 74 members departing, the most since 1992, according to a tally from the Pew Research Center. Some outgoing lawmakers retired, while others ran for other offices, but generally didn’t fare particularly well – only 13 made it through primaries for governorships, the Senate or other offices, with the remaining 15 were rejected by voters. Among representatives who sought re-election to the House, 11 lost their primaries, the second-highest total since 2022. Seven of these were Democrats, two of whom – Julie Johnson and Al Green – were unseated by other Democratic incumbents after they were redistricted by Texas Republicans to compete against each other. Leftists, especially Democratic socialists, rocked the party ... Of the five House Democrats who lost their primaries to newcomers, four were booted by leftist candidates with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In New York, Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair Adriano Espaillat fell to DSA member Darializa Avila Chevalier and congressman Dan Goldman was ousted by former DSA member Brad Lander, while DSA member Claire Valdez also won the primary to replace retiring congresswoman Nydia Velazquez. In Colorado, DSA member Melat Kiros unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette, and in Michigan, the DSA-endorsed Donovan McKinney beat congressman Shri Thanedar. All are expected to win their seats in the midterms, as their districts are heavily Democratic. “A lot of people were hoping that it was a blip, like oh well, this is a special case,” said the DSA-endorsed Chris Rabb, who is expected to be elected to the House after winning the Democratic primary in deep-blue Philadelphia. “We showed them a different way. So I think all of those things make this election cycle uniquely powerful in ways that most people could not anticipate, myself included.” The fifth sitting Democrat to lose renomination was John Larson. His challenger, Luke Bronin, 47, successfully argued to voters that it was time to replace the 78-year-old incumbent with a younger candidate. ... but centrists are on the frontlines The battle for the House will not be decided in safe blue seats, but rather the 21 districts that the Cook Political Report considers to be toss-ups.
