title: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous
body_text: Donald Trump’s speech on Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UN charter’s emphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address. For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influence negotiations where he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice. He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime. In July, he already vowed to destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself a threat to commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russian military commanders for doing precisely that in Ukraine. Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal. He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated a deal to constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trump ripped it up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran far closer to a nuclear weapon than ever before. Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls now predict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that he belittles. Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, although hundreds remain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting his might-makes-right beliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.” He noted the new agreement on Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member. He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there is no real war, only a rhetorical one. Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguably crimes against humanity. Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may be why Trump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”. It has been reported that Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’s statute. Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated. He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise the death toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues to kill Palestinians and block needed supplies, while Hamas has not disarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”. Indeed, the Trump administration has rejected a leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny this reality. He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues to occupy large swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’s mineral riches to the western market. title: Democrats accuse Susan Collins of corruption after bombshell ‘pay-to-play’ report
body_text: Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after a major media outlet reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Donald Trump derailed the inquiry. The article from the investigative newsroom ProPublica rocked the race for Collins’s Senate seat, which is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the chamber in the 3 November midterm election. The outlet reported that in the run-up to Collins’s successful bid for a fifth term in 2020, the head of her Super Pac had solicited a campaign donation from contracting firm Navatek, which demanded assurances of business from the government in return. Using a shell company, Navatek CEO Martin Kao later sent $150,000 to the Super Pac, then told other executives he had been informed Collins would ensure the firm won $32m in federal contracts. In late 2024, the FBI was moving towards investigating the arrangement, in what would have been a large-scale political bribery inquiry, but the agents leading the case were pushed out amid a wider purge of the bureau Trump ordered after returning to power last year, while a justice department office that oversees investigations of politicians was gutted. Collins has disputed the report, which her deputy chief of staff Annie Clark called “categorically false” and noted that Kao is currently in federal prison after pleading guilty to fraud charges. But it served as grist for Maine Democrats who hope they can finally convince voters to unseat Collins, who has represented the state since 1997 and survived repeated re-election challenges. “This is corruption of the highest order,” said Troy Jackson, the former state senate president and the Democratic nominee to take on Collins this year. “We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up.” Collins is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, but has a history of being a tenacious opponent. The last time Collins was on the ballot, in 2020, she beat her Democratic opponent Sara Gideon by eight percentage points, even as Joe Biden carried the state in the presidential race. Political forecasters consider her re-election campaign to be a toss-up, though recent polls have shown Jackson narrowly ahead. At a Wednesday press conference in Portland, the largest city, state Democratic party executive director Devon Murphy-Anderson accused the senator of misconduct as chair of the Senate appropriations committee, a powerful role that oversees federal spending and which Collins has used to channel significant investment to her state. “We sent Susan Collins to Washington to fight for us. Instead, it appears that she has sold us out yet again and gotten bailed out of trouble by the president of the United States,” Murphy-Anderson said. “It is not the first time that she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure that it is one of the last.” Addressing reporters separately, Collins’s campaign manager, Steve Abbott, denounced ProPublica’s reporting as based on “allegations from a guy who was awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense who was trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states directly”. He said that the justice department under Joe Biden had absolved the senator of the “pay-to-play” scheme that Democrats accuse her of. “In order for that claim to be true, you would have to disbelieve the Biden-led Department of Justice and the Biden-led FBI, who both investigated those contributions and the claims against Senator Collins, her campaign, and her federal staff, thoroughly, and found no basis to charge them,” Abbott said. Maine lies at the center of Democrats’ plans for retaking control of the Senate from Republicans, who won a 53-seat majority in the 2024 election. Beyond Maine, Democrats hope to win in at least three other states currently held by Republicans that voted for Trump two years ago, while also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire. Lance Dutson, a strategist who worked on Collins’s three most recent re-election campaigns, said the senator’s campaign in 2020 was so well-funded he found it “obviously absurd” that $150,000 would be viewed as a meaningful donation to her Super Pac. “In 2020, by the end of that race, campaigns were struggling to find places to spend money,” said Dutson, who is not involved with Collins’s re-election effort this year. He condemned ProPublica’s story as “a partisan hit piece” but said: “It’s definitely not helpful to have a story implying corruption show up in the newspaper in late September of an election year.” While Dutson argued the report is not a “silver bullet” for Collins’s foes, he warned that Trump’s low approval ratings – which have unnerved Republicans nationwide – present a significant complication for the senator’s re-election. “The headwind from Trump is very strong, as you know, and people are very upset about it,” he said. “This race is going to come down to Maine voters deciding whether that national argument is more important than the the direct relationship and the positive impact that Collins has had over the state.”

title: Diesel prices across Australia could surge beyond $3 a litre as Trump eyes cut to US fuel exports
body_text: Australian diesel prices could surge above $3 a litre if Donald Trump cuts off US diesel exports amid floundering negotiations with Iran. Fuel costs have risen to levels not seen since early April, adding to inflation risks and making another hike in interest rates all but certain. Canberra is recording the highest prices out of the capital cities, with diesel at 298.7c per litre and unleaded at 250c per litre on Thursday. Other cities’ prices were not far behind. Prices have risen nearly 40c a litre since the start of the month, adding $22 to the cost of filling up a vehicle with a 55-litre tank. Service stations have passed on steady increases from international refineries, which have struggled to secure cheap oil as ongoing hostilities in the Middle East prevent supply reaching global markets. The Brent crude oil benchmark price has held above US$100 per barrel for most of the last fortnight, reaching its highest point since May. Gulf countries’ exports of diesel have fallen to just a quarter of their prewar levels with the ongoing conflict preventing transit of fuel tankers through the strait of Hormuz and the smaller Bab al-Mandab chokepoint. Ukrainian attacks have cut off Russian supply, further restricting global oil flow. Shortages would worsen if the Trump administration banned US exports of diesel, which it is actively considering as a measure to suppress local service station prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ANZ bank analysts said limits would be especially disruptive as the US had stepped up its global diesel supply since the war began, now exporting more than 1.5m barrels a day. Australia almost entirely relies on overseas imports of diesel, with government data showing it brought in more than 18,400m litres from January to July 2026. Just 510.9m of the total came from the US, most of which arrived in April. Saul Kavonic, an analyst at MST Financial, predicted Australia would have to ration diesel and face prices of over $4 a litre within weeks of a US export ban, in comments to the ABC on Thursday. But Dr Lurion De Mello, from Macquarie University’s Transforming Energy Markets Research Centre, said Australia’s supply was still healthy. Australia’s stockpiles of diesel have fallen to 31 days’ worth of supply, where they were in March, down from 39 days’ worth in July. The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has said government-backed fuel purchases had slowed as existing storage facilities were full. De Mello said a US ban would push up prices as Europe, which relies on American diesel, would start competing with Australia for shipments from South Korea and other Asian refiners. “If you take any supplier out, globally, it puts pressure on prices to go up,” De Mello said. De Mello said Australia’s diesel prices could surpass $3.10 a litre but would be unlikely to reach $3.50 as long as Asian refiners continued to access oil. The Albanese government temporarily lowered the fuel excise in March when diesel prices surpassed $3.10 a litre but has not offered a second excise cut. High fuel costs would threaten industries that rely heavily on imported diesel, including farming and mining, and push up prices in food, manufacturing and transport industries. The Reserve Bank is expected to raise interest rates on Tuesday to 4.6%, a 14-year-high, in part due to upward pressure from fuel costs.

title: Oil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budget
body_text: Oil prices lurched upwards again on Thursday, creating a growing headache for UK policymakers ahead of John Healey’s budget next month. While Healey has been keen to present an upbeat picture of the UK’s economic prospects, Treasury sources concede the sharp jump in oil and gas prices means they have “less room” than a month ago. Officials are working “at pace” on a range of possible options for supporting consumers, particularly if high prices persist, feeding through into a sharp rise in the quarterly energy price cap in January. But any package is expected to fall far short of the costly across-the-board subsidies announced by Liz Truss in 2022, with the Treasury mindful of the measures already taken, including Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills. Options are believed to include shifting more green subsidies into general taxation, echoing the approach taken by Rachel Reeves, or targeting help at the poorest households – though some officials are sceptical about how effectively this can be achieved. The price of a barrel of Brent crude was up almost 5% at $108 on Thursday after reports of more military clashes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces. Donald Trump has given little indication of how, or when, the wider US-Israeli war on Iran could be brought to a close, despite the impact on gasoline prices in the US before crucial midterm elections. Senior UK government figures are also increasingly concerned about the prospect of interest rate rises, which could push up the cost of a mortgage just as Burnham has promised voters “breathing space”. After leaving interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week, the Bank of England said it expected the energy price cap to rise by as much as 24% in the new year. The Bank’s chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that rates would have to rise. “The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland. “On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.” Lombardelli’s warning was echoed by another member of the Bank’s monetary policy committee, the deputy governor Sarah Breeden, who told a conference at Imperial College London: “The larger and longer the shock, the more likely it is that we’ll see the material second-round effects that policy needs to respond [to].” Expectations of higher inflation and interest rates caused by rising energy prices are a key factor driving the global selloff in government bond markets – raising the cost of borrowing for the UK, alongside other economies. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, rose to 5.39% on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week. Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules. Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March. Healey has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn. Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts, but Treasury sources insist the budget will be narrowly focused. Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling, as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on. As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 10-year US treasury bonds surged to 5.17%, the highest level since 2007. Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.

title: Fossil-fuel firms in line for billions in benefits after answering Trump’s donation call
body_text: The fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190bn in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade after responding to Donald Trump’s pre-election call for major campaign donations, leaving American taxpayers to shoulder higher bills and public health costs associated with pollution, according to a new report. Released on Thursday by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate environment and public works committee, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, the report details what the senators describe as the fossil fuel industry’s expansive influence over the Trump administration. Pointing to Trump’s April 2024 fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago, Florida where he reportedly asked industry executives for $1bn in campaign contributions, in exchange for tax breaks and deregulations, the report said: “Big oil delivered in the hundreds of millions.” The senators said: “The Trump administration has delivered right back, handing polluters benefits worth hundreds of billions of dollars. That bargain came at a price, and American families are the ones paying it: higher energy bills and higher costs associated with increased damages from climate change and air and water pollution.” The senators also cited the Trump administration’s “near-total refusal to cooperate with legitimate congressional oversight”, saying it “complicated” their investigation. The estimate of $190bn savings for industry is calculated from existing tax breaks and subsidies over the next 10 years plus new benefits delivered by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to an analysis by Senator Bernie Sanders for legislation he proposed with Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to eliminate “handouts” for industry. In addition to an estimated $201m investment in Trump’s re-election campaign, industry executives contributed $19m to his inaugural fund, which the report described as “the largest political investment the industry has ever made”. In exchange, the report said Trump appointed 26 senior officials – all of whom had previously worked for fossil fuel, chemical, or other polluting industries – across various government agencies including the Environmental Protection Agency, as well as the energy and interior departments. The report also noted that the fossil-fuel industry secured various policies that would curb competition from clean energy, increase gas and coal consumption and “force Americans to spend at least $580bn in added fuel costs alone over the next three decades”. As part of Trump’s “big, beautiful” domestic spending bill, signed last July, the government created a $1bn direct subsidy fund for fossil fuels, using the Defense Production Act authority to “funnel taxpayer money into propping up fossil fuel projects” considered economically risky by private capital markets. The act also provides a permanent 20% business income deduction for oil and gas companies, which the report said would cost the government an estimated $737bn overall. The report further accuses the Trump administration of exempting companies from pollution controls, saying Trump “abused” the Clean Air Act by exempting more than 180 polluting facilities. The senators noted that “the rules at issue were designed to limit emissions of known neurotoxin and carcinogens”. It also highlighted that the Trump administration repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards and moved to roll back emissions rules for power plants and oil and gas facilities. While the Trump administration estimated the changes would save Americans $1.3tn, the report cites an EPA estimate of $1.5tn in additional fuel, repair and maintenance costs for consumers. Separately, the EPA estimated that the repeal would result in at least $580bn in additional fuel costs over the next three decades. Highlighting the impact of the fossil fuel industry’s influence on Trump and its consequences for the American public, the report stated that Trump’s “polluter-first agenda exposed Americans to price shocks on fossil fuels, heating, food production, and electricity; increased the cost of trucking food to grocery stores; and raised fertilizer prices for farmers”. One modeling estimate cited in the report found that average household energy bills could be $78 to $192 higher per year by 2035. Industrial energy costs, meanwhile, are projected to rise by between $7bn and $11bn over the same period. The report, however, said the sharpest increases could ironically fall on Republican-led states that lack state-level policies supporting renewable energy development. In addition to rising energy costs, the report pointed to the public health costs associated with Trump’s policies, noting that fossil fuel-related air pollution and climate-related harms cost approximately $820bn annually, or roughly $2,500 per person in additional health costs each year. “Even if Americans do not suffer from polluter-driven heart or respiratory disease, they pay more as health insurance companies spread around those costs,” the report said. Homeowner insurance costs are also rising as climate-driven disasters become more frequent and severe. The report noted that the average American homeowner now pays “about $2,948 per year in insurance premiums, nearly 12% higher than just one year ago”. The report also found that in 2025, fossil fuel companies paid more to shareholders than the direct damages attributable to extreme weather in the US, despite surges in hurricanes, wildfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts. Several environmental advocacy organizations have criticized the Trump administration in response to the report. Climate Power spokesperson Alex Glass told the Guardian: “This report lays it out in black and white. The Trump administration isn’t setting energy policy; the fossil fuel industry is writing it for them. Fossil fuel money bought access, and fossil fuel executives got the keys to the agencies meant to regulate.” Similarly, Mahyar Sorour, the director of beyond fossil fuels policy at the Sierra Club, said: “This report elevates a troubling reality: while fossil fuel companies throw money at politicians to fulfill polluters’ wishlists, American families are left paying for an energy system that puts corporate profits ahead of public health. “It’s time to make polluters pay.” Meanwhile, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s climate program, told the Guardian: “The campaign contributions to Donald Trump by big oil have paid dividends, and have allowed the fossil fuel industry to continue to pollute our communities … Every American family struggling with high costs is suffering because of the corrupt relationship between Donald Trump and the fossil fuel industry.”

title: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief
body_text: Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief. Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over. To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process. “Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath. Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.” Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk. He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said. Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence. When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating. A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US. The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”. The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory. Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone. “It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?” Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.” He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said. Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.” Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”

title: EU says Trump’s plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’
body_text: The EU has warned Donald Trump against plans to ban US diesel exports to the global market, saying the move would negatively affect Europe and the US. The European Commission has reacted with “concern” to reports this week that the US president could prevent diesel from reaching the global market. Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban to provide a temporary respite from high pump prices for US households before the midterm elections, after US diesel reached a record average of $6.52 (£4.93) a gallon. “I’ve said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” he said. Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the EU’s executive arm, said on Thursday “any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides” and the EU expected “close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets”. The EU made the diplomatic intervention as experts said that the potential export ban could be “devastating” for Europe, and traders scrambled to assess the continent’s reliance on imports from the US. The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has warned at an Economist event in New York that banning exports was a “blunt tool” that could harm US fuel supplies in the long term. For Europe, the ban could be far more damaging. US diesel exports have made up a third of the continent’s imports this year, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted. By August, the US supplied about half of Europe’s diesel imports. Pump prices have already climbed to record highs across Germany and the Netherlands, leading to calls for political leaders to protect households from rising costs. In the UK, motorists may be only days away from fresh all-time highs, raising concerns over the economic impact of further price hikes for hard-pressed households. The RAC said the average cost of diesel was 197.75p a litre on Thursday, up from 142.38p before the start of the Iran war. “A US export ban would be devastating for diesel supply in Europe, which would struggle to replace supply,” said Josh Michalowski, the head of European diesel pricing at Argus Media, a commodities data provider. Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices. So far the market for diesel cargoes has remained relatively quiet since reports of a potential US diesel ban emerged this week, according to Benedict George, the head of European products at Argus. He said traders were still weighing up the degree to which the White House might limit US exports. “If this prospect became even relatively serious [in the White House], it would be very serious for European markets. There would be some degree of panic given how reliant buyers have become on US cargoes,” George said. “There’s enough European diesel production to ensure that we wouldn’t run out, but losing US cargoes would mean buyers would have to compete with buyers in Asia for the few available cargoes from the Middle East and India, in what is already a very competitive global market.” The price of diesel has outpaced the rising price of global oil markets due to severe disruption to refineries in the Gulf and in Russia. The price difference – known as the “crack spread” – reached a record high earlier this month and could climb further still. “A US ban on diesel exports would pose a significant challenge for the UK, given the country’s growing reliance on American refined fuel,” said Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK. The UK has only four operating oil refineries after the closures of Grangemouth and Lindsey last year. Both produced diesel for the UK market. Pugh warned that losing almost 90,000 barrels a day of US distillate, or 18% of the country’s total consumption, would leave the UK even more exposed to global diesel prices. He added that, while shortages of fuel were unlikely immediately, a longer-term ban would make them a “real possibility”. Although the number of motorists driving diesel passenger vehicles has fallen, it remains the lifeblood of the UK’s agricultural and logistics sectors by fuelling heavy machinery, lorries and vans. The European Commission spokesperson said: “High-level contacts between the European Union and the US administration are ongoing.” A UK government spokesperson said: “Forecourts in the UK are being supplied with petrol and diesel as normal and we have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

title: Trump’s FDA nominee says MMR shot is ‘safe and effective’ at Senate hearing
body_text: Dr Heidi Overton, Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), has told senators the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind the president as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal”. At a confirmation hearing on Thursday, Overton described the MMR vaccine as “safe and effective”, adding: “It is our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak.” Asked whether any vaccine on the US market was unsafe, she said: “Every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective, according to the FDA.” Overton faced questions from Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican and physician who chairs the Senate health committee, whose vote is seen as pivotal. He had called her role in Trump’s August vaccine executive order “almost disqualifying”. The hearing comes as the US records its highest number of measles cases since 1991. When Cassidy asked what Overton would do if the president asked her to break those assurances on vaccine safety, she replied: “I would give him my best advice, and I would follow the statutory requirements for the role of FDA commissioner regarding individual product determinations for safety and efficacy.” When Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, asked whether she would have “the courage to stand up to” a president who he said “lies all of the time”, Overton did not answer directly. “I have worked for the president for a long time now, and earned his trust because I have been part of robust discussions to bring him the best advice,” she said. In her opening statement, Overton framed her agenda around speeding up drug development to protect US leadership in biotechnology. “We can protect America’s global leadership in biotechnology, but we have to act fast,” she said, pledging to make the FDA “the agency of the possible, rather than the impossible”. Overton, whose father leads a church in her home town of Gallup, New Mexico, has described Colossians 3:23 (“Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters”) as one of her life verses since childhood. Susan Collins, the Maine Republican senator, challenged her over the FDA’s August authorization of flavored vapes and nicotine pouches, including blueberry, mango and cappuccino. Collins said nearly 90% of young e-cigarette users choose flavored products. title: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
body_text: US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply. The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates, which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation. Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year. Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023. But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran. The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday. On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month. Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise. The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com, with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year. “A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith. High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership. Wages have not kept pace with higher inflation, and everyday costs are higher. The frustration is expected to show up in November’s midterm elections as Republicans struggle to maintain control of Congress. Nearly three-quarters of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, according to a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS, and two-thirds of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important” to their vote.

title: Americans living in Britain should vote – control of Congress is at stake
body_text: Americans in the UK should definitely ask for their US ballots and vote. As Kathryn Sikkink writes (Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change, 22 September), it’s easier than they may think and there are several compelling reasons to vote. One helpful website that wasn’t mentioned is votefromabroad.org. This nonpartisan website was launched 20 years ago, never keeps your data and provides 24/7 voter help that’s provided in person in 50 countries or via Zoom or email. Depending on the state in which they last lived, voters may be able to receive and return their ballot electronically. Control of Congress is at stake. Today, Republicans have a razor-thin majority in the House: 218 to 214. Many of these seats were determined by just a few hundred votes. Think of that in the context of the 298,268 voting-age US citizens in the UK that Sikkink references. Congress writes the laws and decides spending. It also investigates corruption, abuse and mismanagement in government. Even if the Democrats regain only the House of Representatives, they’ll have the power to stop some of the self-dealing and destruction of basic services. Decisions made in Washington affect Americans abroad, their families and their communities, and their votes help determine who makes those decisions. John Scardino Former vice-chair, Democrats Abroad UK

title: Democratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian elections
body_text: A group of 31 Democratic members of the US Congress has sent a letter to the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, criticising the Trump administration over “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections. Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing a technical tie between the incumbent leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro. In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed a series of measures the US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. They wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections in Argentina and presidential elections in Honduras and Colombia. In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who went on to win the second round. In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”. They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over his attempt to stage a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president was ultimately convicted and, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place. They also cited new tariffs that Trump imposed on Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well as plans by the US government to send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas. The Brazilian president has repeatedly complained that Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.” In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”. They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

title: Texas woman triumphs as court upholds acquittal in voting error case
body_text: The nearly decade-long case of a Black Texas woman who was sentenced to five years in prison in a controversial illegal voting case will end with an acquittal, the state’s highest criminal court said in a 5-4 decision on Thursday. The woman, Crystal Mason, has been appealing against the case ever since her 2018 conviction for casting a provisional ballot that ultimately wasn’t counted. In 2024, the Texas court of criminal appeals acquitted her in the case. The local prosecutor handling the case appealed that ruling to Texas’s highest criminal court, which initially agreed to hear it. But on Thursday, the court reversed itself, and said it would not hear an appeal, letting the acquittal stand. It did not offer any explanation for why. “After 10 long years of fighting, I am overwhelmed with joy and gratitude. It’s hard to put into words how excited I am right now. This journey has been long, exhausting, and emotional, but God has carried me through it all,” Mason, 51, said in a text message. Phil Sorrells, the Tarrant county district attorney, said in a statement: “Illegal voting remains a crime in Texas. “If there is evidence that someone knowingly violates our election laws in Tarrant County, we will investigate it and, when the evidence supports it, prosecute it,” he said. Mason was on supervised release – which is like probation – for a federal tax felony when she went to her polling place on election day in the 2016 presidential election. When she arrived, officials could not find her on the list of registered voters and offered her a provisional ballot, a safeguard required by federal law, to cast her vote. Mason decided to do so. Poll workers testified that they had Mason swear everything in the affidavit was true, though Mason has always disputed this occurred. Texas, like many US states, prohibits people with a felony conviction from voting if they are on probation. Even though Mason signed an affidavit saying she was eligible to vote, she maintained she did not actually read the language on it and was never told she could not cast a ballot. Federal probation officials testified at her 2018 trial they never told her she couldn’t vote. Prosecutors nonetheless argued Mason knew she was ineligible because she signed the affidavit and had sworn to poll workers that the information in the ballot was true. Mason has always maintained that testimony poll workers gave at her trial was not true. A judge found her guilty and sentenced her to five years in prison. The case triggered outrage because Mason consistently maintained it was an innocent mistake and the severity of her sentence. As Donald Trump sought to escalate claims about voter fraud after the 2016 race, many also saw the case as a local effort to make an example of Mason. “Civic participation without fear of imprisonment is a cherished right that is critical to our system of democracy. The highest criminal court in Texas affirmed that right by letting the lower court’s acquittal stand,” said Thomas Buser-Clancy, an attorney with the Texas chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent Mason. “Ms. Mason has spent nearly a decade defending her rights in Texas and today we see that her efforts have been successful not only in defending her own freedom, but also in protecting the ability of Texans across the state to participate in our democracy without fear.” Alison Grinter, another one of Mason’s attorneys, said the ruling was important given the upcoming midterm elections. “This really is a great day for Texas voters who can finally celebrate their right to go to the polls unafraid and undeterred by partisan intimidation and scare tactics,” she said. Because Mason was convicted of a criminal offense while on supervised release, she returned to federal prison for 10 months. During that period, she nearly lost her home to foreclosure and her teenage daughter was entrusted with running her household. Her college-age son left a football scholarship to return home and help with costs around the home. Mason has three children and also raised four of her brother’s children. She has 10 grandchildren. Four of the justices on the court wrote dissenting opinions, saying they believed there was sufficient evidence Mason knew she was ineligible when she cast a ballot. “The evidence presented by the State at Appellant’s trial for illegal voting was sufficient to show that Appellant ‘actually knew’ that she was ineligible to vote,” judge Lee Finley wrote in a dissent that was joined by judge Gina Parker. “The provisional voter affidavit, corroborated by the additional evidence presented by the State, leaves no doubt whatsoever that the trier of fact was presented with sufficient evidence to sustain Appellant’s conviction. This is not a close case.” Mason was not particularly political before 2016, but since her conviction, she has become much more politically engaged. In 2022, she opened a rally for Beto O’Rourke and worked to educate voters about their rights. Recently, she said, the wife of the current district attorney, Phil Sorrells, knocked on her door and asked her if she would consider voting for him this year. “The irony of that moment is something I will never forget,” she said. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026. An earlier version said prosecutors argued that Crystal Mason knew she was eligible to vote; this should have said ineligible.

title: Senate Republicans block Democratic effort to end US war with Iran
body_text: Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a Democratic effort to end the US war with Iran, voting down a House-passed war powers resolution as the conflict that has killed 19 American service members passed the 200-day mark. The measure, which passed the House last week with bipartisan support, failed in the Senate by a 49-50 vote. Senate Democrats, led by the minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and the senator Andy Kim of New Jersey, forced the vote under the War Powers Resolution, which allows lawmakers to bring such measures to the floor. The proposal attracted some Republican support, but not enough to pass. For the first time, Thom Tillis of North Carolina voted for the resolution, as did Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Susan Collins of Maine, who had backed previous efforts. But Bill Cassidy of Louisiana – whose vote was key to passage of a resolution in June – voted no, as did John Fetterman a Democratic senator of Pennsylvania, ensuring the measure’s defeat. Ron Wyden, the Democratic senator from Oregon, acknowledged the uphill fight for the minority. “We’re going to stay at it until we win,” he said. Democrats have kept up a steady pace of war powers resolutions ever since Trump ordered the US military to attack Iran in conjunction with Israel at the end of February. While one proposal passed in June, support for others has oscillated – in July, after a ceasefire in the conflict collapsed, the Senate voted 47-49 against advancing a war powers resolution, with Collins the only Republican in support. Tim Kaine, a Democratic senator from Virginia, who has been a leader of the war powers push in the Senate, said: “We’re going to keep doing them every week because we see Republican candidates out in the field now starting to change their position.” In recent days, Republicans running for key congressional and gubernatorial races in the 3 November midterm elections have called for an end to the conflict, which has worsened the inflation that Trump campaigned on ending. “They recognize how bad this is,” Kaine said of the Republicans. Yet most congressional Republicans remain unconvinced by the campaign to end the war. Dan Sullivan, the Republican senatorfacing a tough re-election contest in Alaska, said: “The war powers vote is about removing American forces from the region, and when there are troops in contact, I don’t believe in doing it.” Speaking before the vote, Kim, a former state department official who served in the Middle East, said Americans were “sick and tired of this reckless and expensive war”. “Democrats have taken action. We’ve come to this chamber 11 times in the past 208 days to try to bring this war to an end,” Kim said. He cited a congressional budget office report estimating the war cost nearly $40bn in its first four months, and said at least 19 US service members had been killed and more than 750 injured. Kim also said estimates showed higher petrol prices had cost American households about $900 each since the war began. “Chaos is not a negotiating tactic,” Kim said. “Trump is simply over his head here.”

title: California sheriff ordered to return ballots he confiscated in voter ‘fraud’ inquiry
body_text: California Republican sheriff Chad Bianco must return more than 650,000 ballots his department confiscated earlier this year in an unprecedented move that violated election law, a state supreme court ruled on Thursday. “Allowing law enforcement unfettered access to ballots, or the ability to handle and count them in secret, based on unregulated protocols, itself creates a substantial risk to election integrity,” the chief justice, Patricia Guerrero, wrote in a Thursday opinion. During a November 2025 special election, California voters passed Proposition 50, a redistricting amendment designed to counteract Republican-led gerrymandering in Texas. The measure easily passed statewide, and won in Bianco’s Riverside county by roughly 80,000 votes. After the election, a county citizen activist group claimed there was a discrepancy in the total vote count. Local election officials have said the complaint was unfounded. The Riverside county sheriff’s department launched an inquiry into the fraud claims, obtaining search warrants to assume custody of the ballots and other election materials. The Democratic attorney general of California, Rob Bonta, immediately launched a legal challenge, arguing Bianco had no authority over election materials and warning the seizure was designed to sow distrust in elections. He ordered Bianco to return the ballots, but Bianco did not. In court, Bianco’s attorneys argued the top prosecutor could not give directions to a sheriff about an active investigation. “Respondents’ arguments all boil down to the unsustainable view that the state’s chief law enforcement officer … must remain a mere bystander to an unprecedented sheriff’s investigation of undeniable statewide significance. As we have explained, that is not the case,” Guerrero wrote in a separate Thursday ruling. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, praised the court’s decision. “Today’s ruling affirms that in California we will defend democracy – using every branch of government,” he said in a statement. “People deserve to know their ballot is counted and secure, and in California we will do everything we can to protect that constitutional right – this year, and beyond.” Newsom on Saturday signed a bill that would prevent anyone from seizing ballots, as Bianco did. “The new laws I signed just last week add new protections so attacks like this cannot happen again,” Newsom said on Thursday. Bianco’s ballot investigation came as Donald Trump has repeatedly disputed the results of the 2020 election, citing unsubstantiated instances of fraud. His administration in January seized ballots and other documents from an election office in Georgia. Some Republicans have mirrored Trump’s rhetoric on voting in their states. Election officials and civil rights groups have been following the Bianco case carefully as they brace for the possibility that Trump or his allies may try to seize ballots in November.

title: Mary Peltola’s campaign says reports of her using slurs and shoving staffer are exaggerated
body_text: Mary Peltola’s campaign on Thursday downplayed a report that the Democratic nominee in Alaska’s pivotal Senate race shoved a staffer and used slurs, saying the article exaggerated her behavior, but acknowledging she struggled following the deaths of her husband and mother. The New York Times article published on Wednesday is based on text messages and interviews with nine former employees of Peltola, who served in the House of Representatives from 2022 till the beginning of last year and is now set to face the Republican senator Dan Sullivan in the 3 November midterm elections. In a statement, Harry Child, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign, said her behavior was affected by the stress of working in the House together with the death of her husband in a 2023 plane crash as well as her mother around the same time. “At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the US House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign – all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief,” Child said. “Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief. But she treats her staff with respect and care, and she maintains close positive relationships with her staff spanning her nearly 30 years in public service.” He added that “exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong”. The contest between the two-term senator Sullivan and Peltola, who lost re-election to the House in 2024, is seen as crucial to Democrats’s hopes of retaking the Senate in the midterms. Democrats must win at least four seats to gain a majority in the chamber, and have named Alaska as a top priority, in addition to Maine, North Carolina and Ohio. Sullivan called the behavior reported by the Times “sad” and “disturbing”. “Young Alaskans went through a lot of abuse and I’m sure there’s a hell of a lot more than was just reported in that story,” he told reporters at the US Capitol. Other former aides to Peltola who spoke to the Times stood by her conduct. “Mary Peltola is one of the finest human beings that I’ve ever worked for,” said Paul Horner, Peltola’s finance director in 2022, when she won both a special election to represent Alaska in the House and then a general election that year. Tyson Fick, a special assistant who had advised Peltola on fishing policy during her time in the House, called her “awesome and demanding”, but acknowledged she occasionally “raised her voice”. He said Peltola was dealing with grief during her time in Congress, and noted since she had previously worked on a commercial fishing boat, staffers who are not familiar with how people act in environments like that may have been misinterpreting her demeanor, the Times reported.

title: Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days
body_text: Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets. The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed. Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal. Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen. Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making. Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.” He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump. The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry. Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal. Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling. For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait. Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process. Earlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York. It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries. Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen. He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran. Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond. A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday. Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis. Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.” Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks. He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases. Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

title: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
body_text: Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest against Benjamin Netanyahu. Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as the Israeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly. The New York Post reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.” A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection. “Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said. “They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested. Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested. Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine. “They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly. Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza. The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views. “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said. “I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me. “But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added. Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon and Melissa Barrera. “I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,” she told Cannes film festival earlier this year. “There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

title: When Trump’s narrative meets voters’ realities
body_text: One of Donald Trump’s greatest talents – deployed during his time as a real estate tycoon, source and subject of tabloid gossip, reality TV protagonist, and president of the United States – is his ability to tell stories. With six weeks until the US midterm elections, he is likely to lean on this instinct more than ever. Rarely does the US president appear more comfortable than when behind a microphone, speaking without interruption, sometimes for multiple hours. Long before entering the White House, he wholeheartedly embraced social media as a means of crafting his narrative, going so far as to launch his own social network when booted off others. Earlier this week, his administration launched a YouTube channel, which critics quickly dismissed as a “state-run” TV network. Such platforms give Trump the ability to deliver his unfiltered narrative – unencumbered by open discussion, or its often tenuous relationship with the truth. Only when his stories leave the spaces where he has complete control, and enter the real world, do challenges arise. The president has long both courted and criticized the media, seeing the very publications and outlets he claims to loathe as opportunities to amplify his message. He bristles when they fail to do so. Last Friday, Trump abruptly announced a ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, setting up an acrimonious legal battle over press access. In the early hours of this morning, a federal judge ordered Trump to restore their ⁠access. “You said you weren’t going to cover me,” Trump told CNN, which had said no such thing, upon his arrival at the United Nations this week. “You shouldn’t be covering me.” *** Americans don’t need to tune in to Trump TV or log in to Truth Social to find out how much it costs to buy a home, feed their families or fill up their cars – factors that, time and again, have influenced which way they vote in elections. By the president’s telling, his controversial war on Iran has been about to end since not long after he launched it in February. Tariffs are meanwhile enriching the US economy. A new “golden age” is under way. When news outlets report otherwise, the president – a voracious media consumer – has a choice. He can engage with the message. The Iran war, more than 200 days since it started, is not over. The US economy is under pressure, despite a boost from vast investment into AI. And while the president and his allies seem to be doing OK, millions of Americans have yet to see tangible evidence that a “golden age” is under way. Or he can blame the messenger. Railing at all hours against the “Fake News Media”, Trump has filed lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the BBC and CBS, among others, over their coverage. “I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room does,” Trump claimed at July’s White House correspondents’ dinner. “Hmm,” he added. “Maybe not quite.” *** None of this marks a dramatic departure from the past 11 years, of course. But with Trump’s party facing a crucial electoral test in November, and Republicans increasingly nervous of an impending “bloodbath”, his hunger to control the narrative is set to grow. In this final stretch of the campaign, we can expect to see the president intensify efforts to hammer his narrative – from a purported “communist” infiltration of the Democratic party to a supposed economic boom across the nation – and attack those who dare to question it. This remarkably volatile president has shown a striking ability to stick to a message like glue in the final stages of an election. In 2024, this included relentlessly blaming Joe Biden for a surge in consumer prices, and promising Americans that he would fix it. We have a good sense of what it will include in 2026. After summoning Republicans for the party’s first ever midterm convention in Dallas this month – another chance to get behind a microphone, uninterrupted by reporters, or reality – Trump asked supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they were voting for him. In truth, his name will not appear on a single ballot paper. As polling day edges closer, the president is escalating his fights with the media. My colleague Chris Stein noted earlier this week that polls continue to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests. Once all votes are cast and counted, there is a world in which the president and his party retain control of Congress – defying frustration over the Iran war, concern over their handling of the economy and broader anger over the status quo – in an extraordinary display of political resilience. There is also a world in which they endure a painful rejection by voters and lose control of both congressional chambers, leaving Trump to serve out his second term as a lame duck in the White House. The president’s version of events is only likely to accept one of these outcomes. Quoted “Most people around the country, many of whom don’t even identify as Democrat or Republican or whatever, are 10 out of 10 pissed off, angry and willing to take that anger into action against the status quo.” – Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the Working Families party, a progressive third political party that has seen its endorsees winning bigger than ever this year Read more: ‘People are pissed off’: anger at the elite and the establishment is fueling this year’s midterms Meet the candidate: Brandon Herrera Brandon Herrera, a 30-year-old YouTuber with more than 4 million subscribers, has made a name for himself making outrageous pro-gun statements. He’s also the frontrunner in a race to represent Texas’s 23rd congressional district, where 23 people were killed in a mass shooting at a Walmart in 2019 and an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers in the Uvalde school shooting. Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015. Should he win the midterm election, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate. And while the president and his allies seem to be doing OK, millions of Americans have yet to see tangible evidence that a “golden age” is under way. Or he can blame the messenger. Railing at all hours against the “Fake News Media”, Trump has filed lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the BBC and CBS, among others, over their coverage. “I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room does,” Trump claimed at July’s White House correspondents’ dinner. “Hmm,” he added. “Maybe not quite.” *** None of this marks a dramatic departure from the past 11 years, of course. But with Trump’s party facing a crucial electoral test in November, and Republicans increasingly nervous of an impending “bloodbath”, his hunger to control the narrative is set to grow. In this final stretch of the campaign, we can expect to see the president intensify efforts to hammer his narrative – from a purported “communist” infiltration of the Democratic party to a supposed economic boom across the nation – and attack those who dare to question it. This remarkably volatile president has shown a striking ability to stick to a message like glue in the final stages of an election. In 2024, this included relentlessly blaming Joe Biden for a surge in consumer prices, and promising Americans that he would fix it. We have a good sense of what it will include in 2026. After summoning Republicans for the party’s first ever midterm convention in Dallas this month – another chance to get behind a microphone, uninterrupted by reporters, or reality – Trump asked supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they were voting for him. In truth, his name will not appear on a single ballot paper. As polling day edges closer, the president is escalating his fights with the media. My colleague Chris Stein noted earlier this week that polls continue to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests. Once all votes are cast and counted, there is a world in which the president and his party retain control of Congress – defying frustration over the Iran war, concern over their handling of the economy and broader anger over the status quo – in an extraordinary display of political resilience. There is also a world in which they endure a painful rejection by voters and lose control of both congressional chambers, leaving Trump to serve out his second term as a lame duck in the White House. The president’s version of events is only likely to accept one of these outcomes. Quoted “Most people around the country, many of whom don’t even identify as Democrat or Republican or whatever, are 10 out of 10 pissed off, angry and willing to take that anger into action against the status quo.” – Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the Working Families party, a progressive third political party that has seen its endorsees winning bigger than ever this year Read more: ‘People are pissed off’: anger at the elite and the establishment is fueling this year’s midterms Meet the candidate: Brandon Herrera Brandon Herrera, a 30-year-old YouTuber with more than 4 million subscribers, has made a name for himself making outrageous pro-gun statements. He’s also the frontrunner in a race to represent Texas’s 23rd congressional district, where 23 people were killed in a mass shooting at a Walmart in 2019 and an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers in the Uvalde school shooting. Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015. Should he win the midterm election, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate.
