title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
body_text: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”. Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver. Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board. The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU. “The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed. In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets. On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven. Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal. Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US. In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible. It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories. Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb. Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years. He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

title: US supreme court lifts restrictions on controversial voter database
body_text: The US supreme court has lifted restrictions on a controversial federal database of voters as Donald Trump seeks to impose tougher restrictions on voting ahead of November’s midterm elections. The ruling issued Friday by the chief justice, John Roberts, in the name of the court temporarily sets aside an injunction issued by US district judge Sparkle L Sooknanan, who ruled on 22 June against the Trump administration’s plan to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements – Save – database to vet voter registration eligibility. A federal appeals court later declined to pause that ruling. The ruling sends the case back to the DC circuit court of appeals to be heard. “Today’s decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections,” the League of Women Voters said in a prepared statement. “However, this case is not over. The D.C. district court ruled that the expanded SAVE program violated multiple laws. We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans’ voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands.” The case stems from an executive order issued in March 2025 with the stated purpose of improving enforcement of laws barring noncitizens from voting in US elections. Among its provisions, the order directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other agencies to make federal databases of citizenship information available to state elections directors. Other provisions of that executive order, like its demand to states to turn over their voter rolls to the federal goverment, remain bottled up in court. The League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and other groups sued to block the use of the Save database, arguing that it was riddled with inaccuracies, and that taking social security numbers from the Social Security Administration violation of the Privacy Act, Social Security Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. State officials had used social security numbers and other information obtained by DHS to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records. Federal law prevents state election administrators from systematically striking people from the voter rolls within 90 days of an election, with or without the use of the Save database. However, the Friday ruling notes that “all agree that the order prevents the Federal Government from using the modified SAVE program to conduct individualized inquiries, which are permitted under federal law during this period.” That distinction matters in light of a DHS whistleblower’s allegations that the department has as part of its “Unlawful Voter Initiative” directed federal agents to impersonate voters in violation of state laws, using social security numbers and other information to look up voter history on state websites. US senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, both California Democrats, sent a letter Monday to the state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, asking for an investigation. “As you know, the U.S. Department of Justice has been unsuccessful in its attempt to compel California to provide its voter information to the Trump Administration, raising serious questions about what this data is, how DHS obtained it, and whether they complied with the law in collecting and using this data,” the letter said. “The fact that the DHS data was compiled with something called ‘supplemental magic’ does not provide reassurance.”

title: Nearly 200 people wrongly identified on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens
body_text: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. In July, Donald Trump gave a speech saying DHS had found a combined 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls in Nevada, California, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Follow-up letters to each of those states weakened the claim, saying there only could be as many as 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls, including up to 15,903 in Nevada. In August, DHS officials told staffers in the Nevada secretary of state’s office that they had reviewed the numbers and confirmed only 185 were non-citizens. DHS officials said they still needed to review more than 14,000 records. But on Wednesday, Nevada election officials said they had reviewed the 185 records DHS sent them and confirmed they were US citizens. “As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Greg Ott, a deputy attorney general, wrote to DHS this week in an email obtained by the Guardian through a public records request. The message was first reported by the New York Times and Nevada Independent. In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson did not address whether the department still believed the 185 were non-citizens. The spokesperson said the agency “is providing a service to the citizens of Nevada”. “The list of 185 were simply a subset of individuals that had gone through a rigorous manual review process at that time of the call. The list shared with Nevada last month also included 6,218 individuals with the highest number of matching attributes to an alien in DHS records,” the spokesperson said. In his email, Ott lamented DHS had not been transparent about the methodology DHS had used to flag alleged non-citizens nor had it shared adequate information. When Nevada officials requested DHS provide the first name, last name, address, and any other data point DHS officials matched, the department said they were only going to provide the voter ID number. In Nevada, a voter registration number can belong to multiple people, he wrote. Each of Nevada’s counties used to maintain their own registration system, but Nevada recently transitioned to a single statewide voter registration system and gave voters new state voter identification numbers. “As a result, the same number may appear at different points in time in connection with different voter records,” he wrote. “The number also doesn’t tell us whether an individual was born in the United States, naturalized, derived citizenship through a parent, or holds any particular immigration status. Election records commonly reflect the information supplied during registration,” he added. “For example, if someone registered to vote in 1970, the registration record may be incomplete; the name, address, and date of birth may be incomplete, changed, entered differently, or shared by more than one person. A number that matches a voter record thus establishes only that a number exists in, or once existed in, a voter registration system.” The news outlet Votebeat also reported earlier this month that election officials in Pennsylvania have also pushed DHS for information on its basis for claiming there were as many as 14,576 non-citizens on its rolls. In an August letter obtained by Votebeat, Al Schmidt, Pennsylvania’s top election official, said DHS representatives had indicated they did not have “high confidence” in that number.

title: Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AI
body_text: Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped up their Washington summit on Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race. The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce. But despite the presence of top tech executives at a White House state dinner on Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. “It was such a layup,” said Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead. “I believe Xi Jinping would have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups. But he [Trump] didn’t want to; he has no interest in doing that.” It was the first visit to the White House by a Chinese president in more than a decade and Xi’s second state visit to the US. Three days of pomp and circumstance culminated on Friday with Trump and Xi drinking tea. Trump said ⁠the summit ⁠had produced great strides and that “our farmers are going to be happy,” but did not provide details. The pair then went to the National Archives, where Trump and Xi looked at the original Declaration of Independence, the constitution and Bill of Rights. Trump told reporters they were comparing China’s documents to America’s founding documents. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of. Theirs goes 6,000 years. So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250. But we’re very proud of our 250.” On Thursday, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. China aims to have next-generation smart terminals and AI agents reach more than 90% penetration by 2030. But Trump – who has repeatedly said the US must forge ahead to maintain its lead over China – appeared more focused on his push to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, later claiming on social media that Xi “seems to like” the term without divulging the substance of their discussions. Later Trump hosted a black-tie state dinner attended by titans of the tech industry. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator of Vermont, used social media to label a photo of Trump and Xi’s table with guests’ net worth: Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla ($928bn), Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ($3.5bn), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ($186bn) and Tim Cook of Apple ($3.1bn). Sanders commented: “A government of, by and for the billionaire class.” But their counterparts in the Chinese tech industry were not present and there was little sign of either country making even a symbolic gesture to apply the brakes. Khanna commented: “Trump didn’t have to have some groundbreaking treaty like Reagan and Gorbachev did [on nuclear weapons]. He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.” Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said. “Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.” The state visit underlined the contrast between Trump’s treatment of democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden is mockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said. But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May, when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference. Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.” Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI. Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate, said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.” Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December the Group of 20 summit will be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.” Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said. “Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.” The state visit underlined the contrast between Trump’s treatment of democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden is mockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said. But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May, when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference. Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.” Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI. Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate, said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.” Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December the Group of 20 summit will be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

title: White House claims pro-Trump ad it paid Fox to air was ‘public service announcement’
body_text: The White House on Friday defended its decision to use taxpayer funds to buy airtime on Fox News for a White House-produced, pro-Trump ad that some Democrats said could be illegal government propaganda aimed at influencing voters in the upcoming midterm elections. In a lengthy statement sent to news outlets, the White House press office insisted that versions of the ad, which feature audio of Trump urging voters to help him “defeat communism” and a whirlwind video review of his second term, were simply routine “public service announcements” like those produced by previous administrations. However, while the Trump administration ad features the president in almost every frame, and includes words of praise for him offered by a prominent supporter during the 2024 campaign, none of the advertising from three prior administrations the White House called similar featured any partisan messaging or showed images of Trump’s predecessors. By contrast, the 30-second version of the pro-Trump ad broadcast on Fox News this week uses audio of Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and a rapid-fire montage of images of Trump beneath the onscreen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN. In the original speech, Trump explicitly identified the enemy as “Dumocrat communists in Congress”. The last 10 seconds of the ad include text at the bottom the screen saying: “Paid for by the US government.” The ad aired on Fox News this week as Trump hosted the leader of the world’s largest communist nation, China, for a lavish state visit. In its new statement, the White House insisted that versions of the ad celebrating Trump, which were also posted on official government accounts on TikTok and YouTube before airing on Fox, “are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action. Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending – at home, at the border, and abroad.” In fact, the version of the ad broadcast on Fox clearly includes partisan messaging that celebrates Trump’s presidency and features his rhetoric comparing Democrats to communists in the run-up to congressional elections in which he recently urged supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and vote for his party. Unlike the initial versions of the ad posted on social media, the broadcast version includes onscreen text boasting about what Trump calls his accomplishments. “Largest tax cuts in history,” one slogan reads. “Reigniting American manufacturing,” says another. “Defend law and order and police,” comes next. The broadcast version of the ad also closes with a tribute to Trump from Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, who can be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sing Trump’s praises at the Republican national convention. While the White House argues that the ad is an “unapologetically American” public service announcement “aimed at the country – not a line on the ballot”, the actual images used are not of the grandeur of the country or its people, but just its current president. In fact, slowing down the rapid-fire montage reveals that the flash-frame imagery in the ad is exclusively of Trump commanding the stage in a bizarre mix of moments during his second term, including: overseeing the US military raid on Venezuela; hosting a state dinner for Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman; accepting the Fifa peace prize; pardoning a turkey; announcing a new class of US navy ships to be named for himself; attending a Kennedy Center performance; awarding the Fifa Club World Cup trophy; showing Cristiano Ronaldo his presidential walk of fame; and addressing McDonald’s owners. The paid advertising by prior administrations which the Trump White House compared its ad to on Friday were uniformly non-partisan public information campaigns. A 2002 Super Bowl ad from the White House office of national drug control policy, which connected drug use by young Americans to funding terrorist attacks, made no mention of political parties or then president George W Bush. A 2015 ad showing people how much money they could save by signing up for health insurance at healthcare.gov did not show or mention Barack Obama. A 2021 ad from the department of health and human services to promote the Covid-19 vaccine similarly made no mention of the president at the time, Joe Biden. The White House defense of its ad comes after the representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and constitutional scholar, suggested on social media that the ad may violate federal laws including the Hatch Act. “This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” Raskin wrote. “It is a Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it. It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns.” AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ads, told the Wall Street Journal that the pro-Trump ad aired on Fox News in New York City, Los Angeles, Miami and Washington DC, as well as on Newsmax in Chicago. The administration has spent at least $443,000 so far to air that ad, according to the Associated Press. AdImpact reported on Friday that the White House also paid to broadcast a second ad featuring Trump, with excerpts from his 3 July address at Mount Rushmore. The second ad, which aired on the rightwing network Newsmax on Friday, includes images of the president’s supporters waving Trump flags and ends with the president repeating a slogan he has used dozens of times to describe his second administration: “This is only the beginning of the golden age of America.” JMSN, the Detroit-born artist who wrote and performs the song Love Me, wrote on social media that it had been used “illegally”, because he was not approached by the White House for permission. “I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign,” the singer wrote. “I am looking at lawyers handling this.”

title: Trump cancels nearly $1bn in funding approved by Congress
body_text: Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1bn in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives. Trump’s office of management and budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending”. Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including non-profits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably. A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic president Barack Obama. Trump’s move was condemned by senator Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate appropriations committee. Collins said in a statement the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions”. “Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.” “This is theft from the American people, plain and simple,” Patty Murray, the Washington Democratic senator, who is vice-chair of the appropriations committee said in a statement. “These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people – not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families. Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because [Russell] Vought is saying their votes don’t count.” Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The government accountability office has called the maneuver, known as a “pocket rescission,” illegal. Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s constitutional power of the purse”. A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in 50 years by blocking $4.9bn in congressionally approved foreign aid. The US supreme court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending. The use of a pocket rescission fits part of a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the US government, eroding the power of Congress. The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

title: Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late?
body_text: Does Donald Trump secretly want Republicans to get annihilated in the midterms? Because he’s certainly acting that way. He continues to brush off concerns about the cost of living, saying last week that high gas prices are a very “inexpensive price to pay” for the war on Iran. And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after the midterms. But by the looks of his dismal polling numbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore. Still, despite the mess the Republicans have made of the country, I wouldn’t feel too optimistic about the Democrats returning to power: the party is famous for snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Instead of evolving, it has a tendency to do the same thing over and over again, expecting different results. See, for example, the fact that there are once again loud murmurings that Kamala Harris plans to run for president in 2028. The former vice-president hasn’t made any sort of official announcement yet – she told voters in Detroit this week that she’s still deciding what to do – but she seems to be testing the political waters through midterm campaigning. This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health. Harris will also be campaigning with the senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia next month and attending an event in Las Vegas with the Nevada attorney general, Aaron Ford, for his gubernatorial bid. Harris’s appearance in Michigan wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment attempt to be helpful; it was a highly calculated move designed to put her back on the national political stage. The New York Times reported this week that Harris’s aides had circulated a donor prospectus in July “that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028”. The document, which solicited funds for campaign travel, explained how Harris could boost midterm candidates. It also asserted that the current moment is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion”. But not everyone agrees it’s Harris’s time to shine. Numerous Democratic candidates have publicly stated that they don’t want Harris’s toxic brand anywhere near their elections. El-Sayed, meanwhile, seems to have decided that an alliance with Harris is mutually beneficial. It gives the progressive candidate an inroad into the establishment and might help him win more support with Black voters. Harris, who alienated many progressives and Arab Americans by her stance on Gaza, clearly thinks that associating with El-Sayed might improve her reputation among that cohort of voters. El-Sayed has said he opposes military aid to Israel and termed the situation in Gaza a genocide – as have numerous human rights groups and genocide experts. El-Sayed isn’t the only progressive that Harris appears to be trying to build bridges with. Last year, Harris offered only the most lukewarm of endorsements for Zohran Mamdani, stating: “He’s the Democratic nominee, and he should be supported.” Now that it’s clear that Mamdani embodies the political zeitgeist, she’s a lot more keen to be besties. In early July, Axios reported that Harris called up the New York mayor a couple of days after three leftwing candidates he’d endorsed won their primaries over establishment-backed candidates. In fact, Harris has been working the phones pretty hard. The same Axios piece noted that she’d reached out to a number of pro-Palestinian activists and Arab American leaders including James Zogby, founder and president of the Arab American Institute. He told Slate this week that the two had had a “long talk”, which he felt good about. In 2024, the Democrats took progressives for granted. They assumed that young progressives would show up to vote blue no matter who, even when the party treated them with disdain. Instead many of these voters stayed home. The Democrats are still loath to admit that Gaza was a factor in their defeat: a 2024 autopsy report released by the Democratic National Committee did not mention the issue once. However, it looks like Harris is waking up to the realization that her almost unconditional support for Israel hurt her in the previous election and is something she will have to rectify if she wants to run again. Particularly since polls show a record 60% of US adults now have an unfavourable view of Israel and the vast majority of Democrats support an arms embargo. Is all this too little too late for the former nominee’s brand? I don’t know. But it’s certainly too late for the tens of thousands of Palestinians the Biden-Harris administration were complicit in killing. The murder of nine women causes a reckoning in South Africa The bodies of nine women have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months. Some were naked or partially clothed. The apparent murders, which may be connected, have reignited protests about the country’s femicide rate, which is five times higher than the global average. Hundreds of demonstrators marched through Cape Town on Thursday, demanding an end to gender-based violence. Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to train wins Asian Games silver Fariba Hashimi was attacked with stones and had to train while disguised as a man when she first started cycling. Now based in Italy, Hashimi won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday and hopes to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles games. A Republican senator has warned that furries are infiltrating the aviation community “It’s terrifying when you think about this,” the senator Tommy Tuberville said this week. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal.” Tuberville seems to be referencing an incident in April when pilots were heard making “meow” sounds over an air traffic control frequency at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport. Is it possible they were maybe just mucking around? Or have the friendly really skies been taken over by a dastardly coalition of furries? Masked lesbian infighting went ultra-viral this week I wrote about the Last Ditch drama here. The dangers of AI are already here “The future is already here – it’s just unevenly distributed,” the science fiction writer William Gibson once said. And that is very true of AI. “We don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing,” Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein write in the Guardian. Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’ Lian Yunzhi is reportedly “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”. A day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza Sitting in her tent, warding off rats, Alaa watches videos of her three children, killed in an Israeli airstrike, on her cracked smartphone. She gave birth to a new baby boy, Waseem, shortly after the Guardian published this piece. Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium canceled due to nor’easter A hilarious development in the Ed “I’m not complicit in genocide” Sheeran tour story. Even the weather is sick of hearing him whine. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: White House blocks CNN from Air Force One in latest escalation with news media
body_text: The White House has blocked CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One on Saturday, impeding its TV press pool duties in the latest escalation of the administration’s battle with the news media. CNN had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, the network said on Friday. The White House confirmed CNN’s exclusion when it did not list the network on guidance sent to the press corps regarding Trump’s schedule for Saturday. CNN’s exclusion from Air Force One was first reported by the Washington Post. The White House did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment. The incident comes a week after Trump, a vocal critic of what he deems the “fake news media”, revoked White House access for CNN, Politico, and MS Now, citing unfavorable reports about his presidency. The Republican president published a post about the topic on his Truth Social platform early on Saturday which read: “Why should perpetrators of FAKE NEWS … be allowed access to a very sacred place, the White House? Despite my big Election Win, almost 100% of ‘TRUMP’ coverage is negative, and has been for years!” The post singled out CNN and MS Now, referring to the latter as MSDNC, which combined the outlet’s name with the Democratic National Committee. He published it days after a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low. The extraordinary access revocation prompted swift backlash from the White House press pool, who suspended their video coverage of Trump in protest. The press pool is a rotating group of journalists charged with covering presidential travel and disseminating written and multimedia reports to news outlets that may not be present at a given White House event. Since the beginning of Trump’s second administration in 2025, the White House has decided which outlets cover the president via the pool each day, a task previously coordinated by the White House Correspondents’ Association. In a joint statement Monday, the White House television pool said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” In a subsequent lawsuit, CNN, MS Now and Politico argued the White House ban was a violation of the first amendment. Meanwhile, the Department of Justice’s attorneys suggested the ban was in the interest of national security, pointing at media reports involving “sensitive” and “classified” information. The US district judge Timothy Kelly sided with the outlets, ordering the Trump administration to restore their White House access. CNN, MS Now and Politico’s journalists sought to enter the White House on Thursday morning, but were not granted entry until midday. Hours later, CNN’s editorial team along with an MS Now reporter were blocked from covering the state dinner commemorating Chinese president Xi Jinping’s visit.

title: ‘I’m not JD Vance’: the Appalachia memoir author running for Congress
body_text: Virginia’s sixth congressional district has been in Republican hands for over 33 years, but Beth Macy, a longtime reporter with the Roanoke Times and author of Dopesick, a powerful account of the opioid crisis that swept through Appalachia two decades ago, has a plan to change that. The plan, drawing on her experience as a reporter, is to canvass the district in the mountainous west of the state, knocking on doors, going to food pantries, meeting with veterans. It’s what any political hopeful might do, but with a twist: Macy carries her reporter’s notebook and jots down the good stories she’s been told. One came at a recent fundraiser: two couples whose land had been in the family for 300 years approached Macy to tell her that a datacenter had been proposed on land next door. Macy does an intro to camera: “Hey I’m Beth and I’m running for Congress.” Then they tell their stories that then get posted on social media. “It’s been really effective because it show the real issues that people care about and people who are independent or moderate Republican who are maybe changing their mind and starting to cross over …” she says. “If it’s enough, I don’t know.” Macy has challenged Republican congressman Ben Cline, who was elected by nearly 30 points in 2024, to three debates ahead of November’s vote. Cline agreed to participate in three, but then appeared to limit them to something less – candidate forums. Macy told her former paper that amounted to “a chicken-you-know-what response”. Many races in this cycle have been upended or at least complicated by the datacenter debate. Three hours to the north-east of Roanoke lies Loudon county, the data processing heart of the US. But this is farm county, typically Republican, and farmers are being buffeted by high diesel prices and fertilizer costs as well as the loss of immigrant workers. A sign on a country road to Glasgow, 30 miles north of Roanoke, read: “Farmers for Beth Macy: Protect Family Farms, Stop Data Centers.” Democrats hope Macy can pull of an upset win despite Virginia’s state supreme court striking down a voter-approved re-districting plan that would have helped the party. The decision has energized Democrats locally and with the political mood across the US turning against incumbents – but especially Republicans – Macy could pull it off. In Macy’s view, there is a more than a notional parallel between the opioid crisis and the data center issue. In the first, the public were told Oxycontin prescribed for pain relief was not addictive, only to find it was. In the second, data centers may be being foisted on the public without sufficient knowledge of their consequences to water and electricity supplies. “It’s the idea that this thing was done to people without their knowledge,” Macy says, pointing to the construction of a multi-building data center campus on a 312-acre site in Botetourt county, Virginia. “Only relatively recently did the people of Botetourt even find out they were doing it. “It’s just like when Purdue Pharma told doctors and conned congressmen with nice checks that their drug wasn’t addictive. It’s the same thing … they occluded the fact of the matter and how people were going to be hurt.” The opioid crisis, she points out, remained hidden from view for years because of the shame that addicts and their families carry, but the data center issue now blowing up in the faces of politicians from both political parties has changed the narrative. The amount of water that the Botetourt data center, codenamed “Project Raspberry”, would require only came to light after Henri Gendreau, founder of the Virginia-based news publication the Roanoke Rambler filed a public records request under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (VFOIA). Macy, 62, has published five books: Factory Man, about a furniture factory owner in rural Virginia: Truevine, about two Black brothers who were kidnapped and forced to perform in circus freak shows during the Jim Crow era; Dopesick, which later became a Hulu series; Raising Lazarus about the opioid crisis aftermath; and, last year, Paper Girl, a memoir about her Ohio childhood and the seeds of rising political division. That has brought a natural – though to her unwelcome – comparisons to Donald Trump’s vice-president JD Vance, whose 2016 memoir Hillbilly Elegy traced his upbringing and his mother’s heroin addiction in Ohio and became a launch pad for his political career. “Oh my God,” Macy exclaims, “I hate that comparison. I’m my own person, I’m not JD Vance. I’m 20 years older than he is. It’s not the exact same part of Ohio. He grew up with addiction and poverty. Okay, I’ll take that. Tough grandma, I’ll take that. But he mocked poor people for being poor and said it was a lack of masculinity and a lack of thrift. I would never blame poor people for their poverty.” In Paper Girl, Macy describes how she received a Pell Grant to go to Bowling Green state university, Hollins university and a fellowship in journalism at Harvard, much as Vance received a grant under the GI Bill to attend Ohio State and later a scholarship to attend Yale. “What I’ve tried to do is amplify the voices of people like me who don’t grow up with everything handed to them. He got out of that, went to Yale, became a venture capitalist, a senator and now the vice president, and now wants to yank up the ladder behind him,” Macy contends. Running as a Democrat in rural Virginia is of course very different from running under the same banner in a naturally blue or toss-up purple district. One of the hurdles a Democrat candidate running in a red district must address is the shortcomings of Biden administration policies. Macy acknowledges that Democrats the last time screwed up the border. “It was wide open and they sent Kamala [Harris] down there, or she was supposed to,” she said. Democrats, she says, have to talk about what they got wrong. She mentions the North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta) under Bill Clinton and the Communications Decency Act of 1996 that immunized websites and social media networks from responsibility for what is posted online. “We’ve got to talk about that stuff,” she says. “and we haven’t renewed immigration since 1996. We’ve got to have a solid H-2A program (for temporary or seasonal agricultural jobs) for folks. I’ve done a lot of solid reporting on tobacco workers who would love to go home once a year.” One aspect of Macy’s platform is to recognize that white-collar jobs filled typically by indebted college graduates are likely to disappear with AI, while the market for blue-collar or trades jobs will increase. “I think the trades are going to become highly coveted and you’re going to see people who might have gone to college or come from wealthier families go after the trade jobs. So I’m calling for free community college, and I think Google or all these data center companies should be paying for that.” Macy has called for a moratorium on data centers until “some kind” of AI czar can be found “to protect our jobs, our land, our electricity, our water, because it’s moving so fast now it’s endangering all of us.” Macy recently received an endorsement from the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US. She may be slowly opening the door in Virginia that has been closed to a Democrat for decades. At a fundraiser on a horse ranch – a largely favorable crowd – Macy says she believes Virginia voters who might have been resistant are loosening up. “They’re feeling the pain and they’re getting to know me a little bit ... I know what it’s like to worry that the electricity is going to get cut off, or might go hungry and eat government cheese, or my grandmother accepting food stamps.”

title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
body_text: Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. “They made a proposal but I reject it,” the US president told reporters at the White House. The president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported. Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”. During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would relieve pressure on global energy markets, and restart talks on its nuclear programme within seven days. In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”. That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday said “our conditions are clear and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled”. “We will not back down from them,” Araghchi said, state broadcaster IRIB reported. “We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.” Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York. After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.” Araghchi said on Sunday that the Iranians “saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators”. “We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them,” the foreign minister added. Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council. He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said. This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe. Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks. Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy. Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children. Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian. Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict. Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP

title: Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn
body_text: Election experts have warned Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce a crackdown on voting. With less than six weeks remaining until polls close, and control of US Congress in the balance, the post-election “counting window” is seen as as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. While the US president’s bid to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in ballots was rejected by the supreme court earlier this month, there is apprehension that Trump and his allies could use the period while votes are counted to amplify unfounded allegations in a bid to challenge results that don’t go their way. “I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they’re legally justified to do so or not,” Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, told a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice earlier this week. Some states take days – even weeks, in California’s case – to complete a count of votes after an election. Control of the House of Representatives and Senate may hinge on results in states with a delayed result. “That period, that waiting time, is where doubt begins to surface,” Durkovich said on Tuesday. “And when it is then amplified by foreign actors and, frankly, by domestic actors, it starts to cause distrust in the integrity of the process.” State-level elections officials are trying to prepare the public to understand the process now, to head off a manufactured controversy later, said Larry Norden, vice-president of the elections and government program at the Brennan Center. “To me, this is the biggest threat right now,” he said. “I think a lot of people may think just because they’re seeing all these headlines being thrown at them that things have changed – that it’s become more difficult to vote,” added Norden. “In the history of American elections in some ways, there have never been more options for the way that people can vote, and they are still in place going into this election.” Early voting eliminates most of the threats voters apprehend ahead of an election, he suggested. “The earlier they vote, the more secure they can feel that their vote is going to count, and I think that’s a really important message for us to be delivering to people.” The power of doubt about the validity of votes, and the risk of Trump unveiling “emergency” measures on ballots or voting machines around election day, looms large. “Every state in the country now has live ballots out,” said Ben Hovland, former chair of the Election Assistance Commission. “That really means the election is here, and it means that needs to be taken into consideration for any court rulings we’re looking at.” A supreme court decision this month upheld a lower-court injunction on the Trump administration using the US Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security to vet mail-in ballot deliveries. But groups such as the NAACP, the National Urban League and other rights organizations remain concerned about the Trump administration’s insistent claim – without evidence – that the 2026 midterm elections will be illegitimate unless the federal government intervenes. Normally, the Department of Justice and the FBI enter a “quiet period” just ahead of elections, to avoid influencing the results. That has not been the case this year. The Department of Homeland Security continues to pursue voter-roll lists in states that would not turn them over voluntarily. The federal government has asked states to retain their 2024 election documentation for later inquiries. And DHS is pursuing an independent “unlawful voter initiative” to find non-citizen voters on state rolls, one that an anonymous whistleblower told congress last week that is using “highly questionable data” and may be unlawful. The federal government’s claims of illegally-registered voters – claiming numbers that do not bear up under scrutiny – and Trump’s rhetoric alleging fraud without evidence, “back up a narrative of fraud to undermine confidence in the elections”, Hovland said. Much of the president’s election rhetoric revolves around foreign interference. Experts make a distinction between foreign influence – propaganda, essentially – and foreign interference , or directly manipulating vote counts. “It’s very important for people to understand that we don’t have any examples of a country trying to interfere in the electoral process, in that technical process,” said Beth Sanner, a former deputy director of national intelligence who is now director for geopolitics and strategy at International Capital Strategies. “It just didn’t happen,” she said. “It didn’t happen in 2020.” Election security has improved across the country, partially as a reaction to false claims about Trump’s 2020 defeat. “Every state audits its results,” said Geoff Hales, former chief of joint cyber defense collaborative partnerships at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA. “Election officials across the country have really taken cybersecurity seriously.” Despite the president’s insistence that the country faces a foreign threat to elections, Hale said the federal government has sharply cut staff and spending on elections security at CISA, and with it the technical assistance that once flowed to state election’s officers. “The federal support that used to be there has pulled back sharply,” he added. “This means that cybersecurity services have been reduced, funding for information sharing environments have been cut, the threat briefings about nation-state adversaries that used to occur dozens of times a year are occurring rarely or not at all.”

title: What Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in run-up to midterms: ‘We can’t just be anti-Trump’
body_text: In the run-up to the US midterm elections, Swing Left – a grassroots political group focused on electing Democrats to office – has spent time canvassing in dozens of districts across the country to hear from hundreds of thousands of voters. Now, with fewer than 40 days until the US midterm elections, the group’s executive director, Yasmin Radjy, sets out what she feels Democrats have been getting right and wrong this election cycle, and why these races are vital for the party’s future control of the US Congress in the years to come. We are now five weeks out. What do you feel have been, and will continue to be, the defining issues of these midterm races? Yasmin Radjy: The two things head and shoulders above everything else that we’re hearing about: one is a feeling like the system is broken, and soon after that are various issues around cost of living. The two are often related, but there are very few conversations where one or both of those issues are not coming up. Everyone’s gotten the memo that we need to talk about affordability. I don’t think there’s a Republican or a Democrat who’s not aware of that. The candidates who are really standing out this cycle again across the ideological spectrum, from Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan] to Mary Peltola [in Alaska]. And on the House map, Paige Cognetti [in Pennsylvania], to Amish Shah [in Arizona]. They are connecting those dots in a way that is specific and that is also mirroring the nature of those districts. What do you think the party needs to focus on to regain trust, and establish a clear sense of identity with voters moving forward – particularly after 2024? We have to follow up with people when they express urgency around the very real and material concerns that they have. When they express disappointment, we can’t pretend like everything is going great. We also need to acknowledge that a lot of the things we’ve been doing aren’t working. That requires having tough, not just conversations, but introspection, and openness to trying new things, testing new things and taking bigger, riskier swings than we’re accustomed to. On one of the must-win races you mentioned – the open Senate seat in Michigan – what do you feel voters are responding to with a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed? What do you think he needs to do in order to win over voters in that state that Trump won? I think something he is modeling is a “talk to everybody and engage with everyone” approach, not just talk to the people who already agree with you. I think he really won his primary because of organizing. In terms of the issues and themes in Michigan, what we’re hearing is very similar to elsewhere with subtle differences: both parties suck, and no politician cares about that voter, their community and people like them. That is ubiquitous. What he is able to speak compellingly on with a lot of authority is his feeling like the system is broken, and he is doing a good job of tying that to affordability and a whole host of other issues. I’m curious what you think might be the biggest obstacle for Democrats in this cycle? What could be getting in the party’s way? One is that we continue to not have a sufficiently clear answer, for a time when the winds are not blowing in our direction, of what Democrats stand for besides being anti-Trump. We need to start answering that now – and it’s OK if that answer has shades of difference in Michigan, Alaska and North Carolina. The second piece is we cannot assume our base will be with us again because of anti-Trump sentiment in a way that can sustain durable power. Something under-discussed that keeps me up at night is if we are not building long-term, durable power, by 2030 we are going to wake up to an election where, if we don’t have power in the states, we will not be able to win congressional majorities because of how bad redistricting will look. Population shifts are clear in California and New York – two big blue states essential for presidential math – and they will be losing electoral college votes starting in 2030. Texas and Florida are the inverse – they are going to gain power. If we don’t treat the midterms as our most important moment to build infrastructure while there’s money pouring in, while there’s energy to have a shot at winning tough Republican seats in a way we can sustain, we are going to lose without question in the future, because we will have squandered an opportunity. I want to discuss the concerns about progressives, from establishment Democrats. What’s your response to those in the coalition who question whether these progressive candidates have a real shot in battlegrounds that the party wants to either retain or flip? We have members who are Democratic Socialists of America members. We have members who think DSA is a huge threat to democracy – we’ve got the full gamut. Our perspective is that the fixation on ideology and the DSA-versus-centrist divide is a completely false binary. We need to win a majority, and there is a level of pragmatism among the grassroots that is underappreciated. The binary will crumble, not because it doesn’t exist in our institutions, but because that’s not how voters are. We talk to voters every day who might be DSA-aligned on healthcare and Blue Dog-aligned on the border, and it’s the same person. If we lead with genuine curiosity and openness to listening to voters, we immediately see that voters are idiosyncratic, strange and full of contradictions because they’re human. Linked to this, I’m thinking about James Talarico [the Democratic nominee for the US Senate seat in Texas] and Rob Sand [the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa]. They are showing a pivot in their messaging, particularly when it comes to trans rights. Do you feel that is a necessary strategy right now to court those swing voters, independents and moderates in newly competitive battleground states? I think when you go out and really talk to people, specifically on the issue of trans rights, most Americans want trans people to have rights – and the areas of discomfort range from lack of knowledge. Their worldview on trans issues is curated by Fox News, so there is an information gap. Most voters, including many Democrats, have complicated feelings about the trans people in sports issue. The answer is not to start repeating Fox News talking points. The way to talk about these issues – and this is what the data shows – is to break down the pieces: all Americans want every American to have a certain set of freedoms. The trans and sports issue is complicated, and it is not really a decision for governments, it’s a decision for the leagues. I think Sarah McBride is a perfect example of this – leading with grace, recognizing that changing hearts and minds takes time, and that people use clunky language along the way. Looking ahead, do you think Democrats are doing enough to respond to Donald Trump’s efforts to undermine elections in this cycle in particular? I would say there is an asymmetric investment in election protection right now. And that asymmetric investment is on the litigation front, it is on the donor-organizing and on the grassroots-organizing fronts. And I feel really confident and really relieved, candidly, that the amount of investment of time, talent and strategy has been placed on that. The flip side is the progressive ecosystem, overall, has not invested as much in the actual act of winning the election, and there is nothing more important for election protection than winning each competitive race by a big enough margin that Trump doesn’t have the incentive to try any kind of funny business. We are not where we should be in some of the most competitive races in the country in terms of dollars invested and volunteers ready to help that candidate, and to me, that is the most essential ingredient to election protection. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’
body_text: The US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized Donald Trump, his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary. “He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary. “John Cornyn’s a great member of the US Senate. Paxton has his challenges,” the retiring Tillis added. “We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in Texas if Cornyn had won.” Tillis pointed to the president’s involvement in the contest and described Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of Cornyn as an “unforced error” that has put the Senate seat at risk for the GOP. Trump endorsed Paxton just days before the Texas attorney general defeated Cornyn, a four-term senator, and advanced to face the Democratic candidate, James Talaricc, a in the general election on 3 November. The race had wide implications for Trump’s strength heading into November’s midterm federal elections. Paxton will now face Talarico, a pastor and state legislator whose message of peace and populism has attracted much attention. If he wins, Talarico would become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide office in Texas. When he chose to support Paxton over Cornyn, Trump highlighted the Texas attorney general’s record as a steadfast supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. Cornyn had previously said during the 2024 presidential campaign that Republicans should move on from Trump. In a social media post shortly before the election day, Trump said Cornyn had been “VERY disloyal” to him and implored voters in Texas to “REMEMBER!” Paxton, meanwhile, is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud, but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pre-trial diversion agreement. In July 2025, his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Tillis is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions. In April, he spoke out in defense of the Nato military alliance after Trump said he was “absolutely” considering withdrawing the US from it. “Any president that contemplates attempting to withdraw from Nato is not only fulfilling [Russian leader] Vladimir Putin and [Chinese premier] Xi Jinping’s greatest dreams but would be undermining America’s own national security interests,” Tillis said at the time. He also called for then secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem’s resignation after immigration agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis in January, calling her leadership “a disaster” during the last Senate hearing before her firing. Tillis was one of a small number of Republicans on Thursday to vote in favor of a Democrat-led war powers resolution that aimed to end the US war with Iran. Despite gaining some Republican support, the proposal failed to pass in the Senate by a 49-50 vote.

title: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’
body_text: Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued on Sunday that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting. Blanche offered no evidence for his claim that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate, rather than simply unflattering to the president. Pressed by the interviewer, Martha Raddatz, to point to a report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate. “Wait, give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that,” Blanche replied. “There’s not even a real dispute that the information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex. But on Saturday, CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One. “The president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told ABC. “That’s not the right way to describe it.” The continuing dispute between the administration and the White House press corps had appeared to be resolving before CNN was again blocked from providing pool TV coverage of Trump on Saturday. That was after outlets stood in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico by briefly refusing to provide any pool TV feeds of the president. On ABC, Blanche said it was not unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed on to the president’s plane. “The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One,” Blanche said. “This wasn’t a one-time denial of CNN. There’s all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying. “It’s not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it’s common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president.” What Blanche did not explain is that, before Trump’s second term, the choice of which correspondents were part of the pool covering presidential travel was left to the White House Correspondents’ Association and the broadcast networks that take turns providing camera crews. After Trump returned to office last year, the White House took control of which outlets would be permitted in the Oval Office, or on Air Force One, leading to increased access for partisan, pro-Trump journalists. Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”. Raddatz reminded Blanche that Trump himself said he had banned CNN, MS Now and Politico, because, he said, “they purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration”. In the ruling to temporarily restore the three banned outlets’ White House access for 14 days, US district judge Timothy Kelly said there was nothing in the record suggesting that revocation of the press passes was motivated by national security concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote in his ruling. Trump was faced with a gloomy political landscape with just over a month before the federal midterm elections in November. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low. But confidence in the news media polls lower, with just 28% expressing a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in newspapers, television channels and radio outlets to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, according to a 2025 Gallup survey. Bill Clinton recently commented on the battle between what the news media see as a crude effort at censorship and a denial of constitutional rights – and what the White House views as unfairly negative reporting. “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution – because none of us are immune from being pissed off. “But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is.” Blanche was asked what the US constitution’s first amendment – which guarantees the right to a free press – meant to him. “The law says – what the free press can do is they are free to report whatever they want,” Blanche remarked. “Of course, they can. But when it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house. It is a privilege and not a right to be there.” He added that “it is absolutely the president’s duty to make sure that the American people are hearing accurate news.”
