title: Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say
body_text: Federal regulators have been urged to stop the broadcast of White House advertisements promoting Donald Trump that critics say amount to government propaganda and violate laws against using public money to promote partisan causes. Public Citizen, an advocacy group, called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to intervene and block further airing of three ads it said were “designed to boost the image and character of Donald Trump” as part of the Republicans’ campaign for November’s midterm elections. “Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising,” the organization wrote. “Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads.” Broadcast stations cannot reject ads from legally qualified political candidates – but Trump is not technically a candidate, although he has urged voters to imagine that he is, on the November ballot. “Public Citizen strongly urges the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission to direct broadcasters to stop broadcasting these apparently illegal campaign advertisements and calls on individual broadcasters to cease airing the campaign advertisements,” the group wrote in a letter addressed to both agencies. “It is the greater responsibility of both the FCC [and] FTC and individual broadcasters to keep the airwaves fair and honest and operate in the ‘public interest, convenience, and necessity’.” The White House has labeled the ads – which began airing last week – “public service announcements” and has responded defiantly to criticism. It has established a webpage arguing for their use. Axios reported that more ads are set to broadcast, with Trump personally choosing which to use during the campaign for November’s midterms, which most polls suggest the Republicans are on course to lose. “This is just the beginning,” an administration official told Axios, which reported that the ads are being produced inside the White House. One is a rerun of a commercial aired by the Trump campaign before the 2024 presidential election and features black-and-white footage of him walking while his voice announces “the final battle”. He pledges to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and “rout the fake news media”. The only difference from the 2024 ad are the words “paid for the US government”. Another shows images of the president at various events while he is heard declaring “America will never be a communist country.” It takes place against the soundtrack of a choir signing the song Love Me. A third advertisement shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump declaring that “the United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.” The Wall Street Journal reported that the commercials were funded by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which is responsible for immigration enforcement and is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The DHS came under scrutiny early this year after a $200m advertising campaign that boosted Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary. Noem told a congressional committee that Trump had “signed off on the ads”. Her testimony reportedly infuriated Trump, who subsequently fired her. The latest Trump ads had aired more than 90 times across nationwide channels, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now and CBS by Sunday evening, the Journal reported. They were run during Saturday Night Live, Fox News Sunday and during several college and NFL football games. Public Citizen said the cost of the three ads already broadcast was estimated at more than $1m. “Donald Trump is not a candidate for any elective office. The FCC and broadcasters are not constrained by the special rule protecting candidate advertisements. “Although the White House contends these ads are ‘public service announcements’, and therefore may be paid for with taxpayer dollars, [they do not] meet the standard of a public service announcement. They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program.” On its website, the White House denounced the criticism as “highly dishonest” and likened the ads to previous public service announcements by previous presidents, dating back to Woodrow Wilson and Franklin D Roosevelt in the first and second world wars, and including the more recent administrations of George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden. “The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” says the statement, under the headline “Presidential public service announcements are nothing new.” “Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending – at home, at the border, and abroad.” The Guardian contacted the FCC and FTC for comment. Brendan Carr, the FCC chair and a close Trump ally, said on Wednesday that the ads fell “within standard practice” without raising “red flags” and did not require the commission’s intervention.

title: From mass raids to quiet crackdown: a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot
body_text: When federal agents fatally shot the US citizen protesters Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January during the nation’s largest immigration enforcement operation ever, it marked a turning point for the second Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. Donald Trump in his second term had sparked outrage and huge protests with federal immigration officers descending en masse on one Democratic-run city after another in what some leaders called militarized “invasions”. Los Angeles, Chicago, Charlotte, New Orleans, then Minneapolis saw lines of masked and armored officers swaggering into town to conduct street arrests, ambushes of day workers waiting in Home Depot car parks for hire, and neighborhood sweeps. Adults and kids were whisked off to detention and protests met with aggressive deployment of chemical spray, teargas, fists and batons. The killings in Minneapolis were the culmination of what appeared to many to be a federal shock force increasingly out of control while being defended by federal leaders – and public opinion broadly turned against this violence. There was a change of personnel and the administration flagged a switch to a “quieter” approach to immigration enforcement. But while large-scale theatrics on the streets waned, less visible enforcement is no less aggressive on the ground today and continues to ramp up in multiple ways. Here’s a timeline of how the administration’s anti-immigration campaign has evolved in recent months as Trump races to remove millions of people from the US. 2026 26 January Minneapolis madness leads to a changing of the guard Two days after Pretti was killed by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and 19 days after Good had been shot dead by an ICE agent, the US president announces that his “border czar”, Tom Homan, an immigration enforcement veteran, will deploy to Minnesota, while Gregory Bovino, the border patrol’s confrontational commander-at-large, suddenly stands aside. Bovino was the face and voice on the street of federal aggression; Good, Pretti and ICE watchers were the symbols of the resistance; and Liam Ramos was the image of collateral harm. 5 March Secretary of homeland security fired Kristi Noem becomes the first cabinet secretary fired during the second Trump administration when she loses her leading role at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Noem was tainted with scandals over her close relationship with senior adviser Cory Lewandowski and a $220m advertising campaign starring herself and using a firm with connections to her former staffer. She had also repeated a false narrative that Pretti “brandished” a gun at federal agents and called Renee Good a domestic terrorist. Weeks later, Bovino retires and tells the New York Times: “I wish I’d caught even more illegal aliens.” 24 March New face, new approach Markwayne Mullin, formerly a first-term senator from Oklahoma with “mixed martial arts fighter” on his résumé, is confirmed by the US Senate as the new DHS secretary. At his confirmation hearing, he says about immigration-enforcement officials: “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day.” Spring Empowering local police on the streets The DHS, in its own words, has “supercharged” efforts to work with local and state law enforcement via so-called 287(g) agreements. From January 2025 these deals mushroomed nationwide, from 142 to 2,315, with most modeled as a “taskforce”. They deputize local and state officials to actively enforce immigration laws during regular police work – normally under federal jurisdiction. By spring, this collaboration acts as a force multiplier for arrests, while allowing federal agents to avoid the spotlight as local cops take on more frontline duties. It also makes immigration enforcement harder to spot for protesters. May Pressure from the courts Attorneys and researchers start noticing immigration court dates being scheduled for unusually large groups of people with little to no notice, in what they say is a tactic to increase the number of deportation orders without ever giving someone an individualized hearing. These mass court dates balloon in June, affecting many thousands of people. Many more applicants struggle to find attorneys and prepare their now-rushed cases. Children are a particular target, too, being rushed through hearings as due process is undermined. 9 June Money, money, money After the longest DHS shutdown ever, congressional Republicans use a partisan process to provide the department with an additional $70bn, funding it for the rest of Trump’s second term in a move that critics say undermines accountability. All told, the DHS has received roughly a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding since Trump retook the White House. 25 June Scotus The US supreme court rules in favor of the Trump administration’s bid to strip temporary protected status (TPS) from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians who were legally in the US and protected from deportation. When Trump took office, 17 countries had active TPS designations, which allowed roughly 1.3 million people who were already in the US to live and work legally while it was unsafe for them to return home. But under his second administration, more than a million people who are generally law-abiding and often contribute economically to essential industries with significant labor shortages have already lost their TPS permissions. Now they face imminent risk of deportation to countries as dangerous as Afghanistan, Haiti and South Sudan if they do not qualify or cannot afford to apply for another immigration status. “We’re going after them right now,” Mullin has said of Haitians. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.” Summer 2026 Airport hazards ICE significantly increases its collaboration with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to detain immigrants with expired visas – many of whom have pending applications for green cards, asylum, employment-based visas, etc – at airports, sometimes near public spaces such as ticket counters or gates. However, the vast majority of arrests continue to occur where they are far less easy to detect and record on camera, such as in people’s homes and cars. July 2026 All paying off for ICE The DHS reports 49,571 immigration arrests, which sets a new monthly record for the second Trump administration, after previously doing so in June. A majority of the people arrested in July have no criminal history. Detentions also increase, with about 66,000 people in custody by the end of the month. Preliminary reports suggest immigration arrests in August have kept pace with July. 13 July Deadly days An ICE officer kills Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 26, in Biddeford, Maine, during a vehicle stop in which Durán was not the intended target, making him the 11th person fatally shot by federal immigration officials both on and off duty during Trump’s second term. The shooting comes days after federal agents similarly killed another immigrant father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston while he was driving his building crew to their job. The DHS briefly pauses most ICE traffic stops until Trump intervenes, posting online: “We CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!” In one 24-hour period, 13 to 14 July, three people die in ICE-involved incidents. August Even more local cops do ICE’s bidding Federal officials reach the milestone of 1,000 new 287(g) agreements since 26 January, expanding collaborations with local law enforcement agencies at an even faster clip than during the second Trump administration’s first year in office. August Visa applications All visas for people applying to immigrate to the US are paused for an unknown amount of time while officials undergo training around the new “public charge” policies. 1 September Big footprint in the Big Apple Mullin retroactively announces Operation Rotten Apple, which from 27 July to 29 August quietly rounded up nearly 2,200 immigrants across New York state. The operation is a case study in how aggressive immigration enforcement continues, including in Democratic-led “sanctuary” cities, without the previous theatrics. Summer into fall Suffer the children On August 1 the federal government ends its contract providing more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children with legal representation. At the same time, attorneys report that immigration judges are taking a “deport at all costs” approach to their young clients, who suddenly are not receiving the time they need for their pending applications to be adjudicated by other agencies before they are ordered removed from the US. Many of these kids qualify for a green card or other immigration status because they have been abused, abandoned, neglected, trafficked or otherwise severely mistreated, but their applications are often subject to backlogs and quotas that cause delays. In September, the Guardian reveals that Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, has been leading an unprecedented drive across several government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist, and, in some cases, flout federal law. Taken together, these policy changes are less showy but they have ramped up arrests, detentions and the number of people forced to leave the United States – and put millions more at immediate risk of the same. Many of these people have legal status or ongoing cases for winning or upgrading their legal status, or years of crime-free, honorable life in the US, but are being rounded up, often with little access to due process or attorneys who can help. This latest iteration of Trump’s mass deportation campaign is no longer defined by federal agents patrolling cities with smoke canisters in hand. It’s much more insidious but also more ruthless and effective – and it’s happening everywhere.

title: Trump ally urges administration to ‘step back’ and rethink immigration agenda
body_text: A close political ally of Donald Trump has broken from the administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda and recommended it “step back” to evaluate what it could do better. “To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” Jim Justice, a Republican senator of West Virginia, told Politico. “And in this situation, with all that’s going on and all the stuff, we probably got to step back from it and say: ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,’ and then adjust to that.” Justice, who also sits on the Senate agriculture committee, made his comments after three rancher associations condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity for negatively affecting agricultural communities. But his comments also come after an ACLU of West Virginia investigation found that about three-quarters of the more than 593 arrested by ICE in the state during “Operation Country Roads” in January had no criminal record. “Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years, and I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” Justice told Politico. Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda is a signature policy of his administration. Many voters indicated they wanted stricter immigration policies, but the intense tactics of federal agents have sparked anger nationwide. For ranchers in rural communities, ICE operations have had “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers” who assist in beef production and the cattle supply chain, the Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association said in a statement released last week. Dairy farmers have also recently raised concerns that ICE operations in rural areas could soon hurt their industries. “If we had a concerted effort to have enforcement activities within agriculture, you could really harm our ability to produce food to feed ourselves,” Rick Naerebout, the CEO of the Idaho Dairymen’s Association, told NPR. West Virginia is home to more than 22,700 ranchers, most of which are family-owned. Justice’s criticisms make him the latest Republican to distance himself from Trump in the lead-up to the midterm elections. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, recently ran a campaign advertisement telling Trump his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far”. The Guardian has asked the White House for a response.

title: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates
body_text: Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed up hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month. A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters. Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure. “The market had been tracing out a bullish formation, meaning the price pattern suggested that any positive catalyst could trigger a move higher and that’s exactly ⁠what happened,” said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. Traders now see a roughly 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from about a 45% chance, according to data ‌compiled by LSEG. The Federal Reserve is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023. Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy. US stock markets rose in early trading, but the S&P ended the day down 0.25% and the Dow fell 0.86%. The Nasdaq ended the day up 0.24%. Despite weakness in September, driven by bond market volatility and elevated oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict, the benchmark S&P 500 and the ‌Nasdaq were on pace for a second straight quarterly advance, if gains hold. On Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond held steady at 5.246%, a day after hitting its highest since June 2007. Crude oil prices rose on the day, with the December contract for Brent crude futures moving higher. There was also positive news from the jobs market. ADP, the US’s largest payroll supplier, said private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, higher than expected and up from 36,000 in August. On Friday, the labor department will release its latest monthly jobs tally, which is expected to show a gain of 84,000 for September, down from 162,000 in the prior month. Reuters contributed reporting

The Federal Reserve is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023. Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy. US stock markets rose in early trading, but the S&P ended the day down 0.25% and the Dow fell 0.86%. The Nasdaq ended the day up 0.24%. Despite weakness in September, driven by bond market volatility and elevated oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict, the benchmark S&P 500 and the ‌Nasdaq were on pace for a second straight quarterly advance, if gains hold. On Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond held steady at 5.246%, a day after hitting its highest since June 2007. Crude oil prices rose on the day, with the December contract for Brent crude futures moving higher. There was also positive news from the jobs market. ADP, the US’s largest payroll supplier, said private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, higher than expected and up from 36,000 in August. On Friday, the labor department will release its latest monthly jobs tally, which is expected to show a gain of 84,000 for September, down from 162,000 in the prior month. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Senate Democrats block datacenter energy bill, saying ‘toothless’ legislation ‘misses the mark’
body_text: Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation intended to offset the impact of datacenters on consumer electricity bills, calling it a “toothless” attempt to address a top voter concern ahead of November’s midterm elections. The Ratepayer Protection Act failed by a 57-to-43 vote, falling just shy of the 60 votes necessary to advance through the Republican-controlled chamber. Four Democrats – Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and both Georgia senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – joined Republicans in support of the measure. “Americans are calling for real solutions, real guardrails, real solutions on AI. Republicans’ toothless datacenter bill completely misses the mark,” the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said in a floor speech before the vote. Schumer assailed Trump for a meeting with top tech executives on Tuesday that the president said yielded a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. “Relying on ‘self-regulation’ is how we got into this mess,” Schumer added. Earlier this month, the House of Representatives had approved the bill by an almost unanimous vote. Datacenter construction and electricity consumption has grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has come increasing anxiety among voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills. The bipartisan legislation is an attempt by Congress to address those anxieties, and would have required electric utilities to consider adopting new standards so that datacenters pick up the costs of any necessary upgrades to transmission, generation and distribution, which can otherwise be transferred to households and businesses. It was proposed ahead of the 3 November midterm elections in which Democrats are campaigning on lowering the cost of living in their bid to regain control of the Senate and House. Its sponsor in the lower chamber was Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican who is a top target of Democrats, while the Ohio Republican Jon Husted championed the bill through the Senate. “It’s clear that big tech should be paying their own way, not passing the cost on to local communities and states – and this bill does that,” Husted said in a floor speech on Wednesday, urging Democrats to back the bill that the president had indicated he would sign. Though Ohio voted for Trump by an 11-point margin two years ago, recent polls have shown Husted trailing his opponent, the Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, who has accused the incumbent of bowing to the demands of the datacenter industry. While the proposal was seen as an attempt by Republicans Senate leaders to bolster Husted’s re-election chances, it also presented a quandary for the chamber’s Democrats, since voting it down could be seen as running counter to their pledges of lowering electricity bills. Nonetheless, the party’s leaders opted to oppose the measure, saying it would have been ineffective at actually addressing datacenters’ electricity consumption. The vote was one of the last the Senate is expected to take before the midterms. The chamber is scheduled to conclude its work on Friday, after which senators will return to their states to campaign.

title: Send us your questions about how the Iran war will affect US voters in the midterms
body_text: The war with Iran has had major implications for Americans’ wallets, government spending and US foreign policy. It’s also been key in reshaping the political landscape as it enters its seventh month before the 2026 US midterms. We’ll be hosting a live midterm election Q&A on Tuesday 6 October 2026 at 12pm EDT on the Guardian US site, with a panel of our politics and foreign policy reporters to help readers understand the costs of the war and political consequences for Trump and candidates running in November. If you have a question about how the war with Iran could shape midterm election results, we’d like to hear from you – and be sure to tune in to our live conversation on 6 October, as reporters may have an answer to your question. The US politics team is hosting a series of reader Q&As leading up to the November US midterm elections. See our first two conversations, here: The makeup of the Democratic party, plus key races to watch Who are the groups financially backing the candidates in the midterms? title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
body_text: With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”. On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use. Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF). Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa. “The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.” The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance. “Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations. “The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.” A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing on Brazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds. The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation. In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant). Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI. The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”. “Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.” Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects. The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped. A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president. A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches. One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria. And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations. The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year). The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship. The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News. The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.

title: Trump DoJ indicts 10 individuals on noncitizen voting related charges in Minnesota
body_text: The US Department of Justice indicted another 10 individuals on noncitizen voting-related charges on Wednesday as Donald Trump’s administration continues to pursue allegations of voter fraud raised by the president. In the sixth announcement of its kind this month, the attorney general, Todd Blanche, and homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said 10 people in Minnesota were charged with making false claims about citizenship to vote, or voting as a noncitizen. “Elections today are often decided by a small number of votes and that’s why these investigations and prosecutions matter,” Blanche told reporters during a press conference, in the latest attempt by senior Trump officials to heighten concerns about voter fraud. While there is no evidence that fraudulent voting is a substantial problem, Trump and his allies have repeatedly made unfounded allegations while claiming the electoral process is rigged against them. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative thinktank that often supports the administration’s initiatives, maintains a database of noncitizen voting – and identified 100 cases from 1982 to 2025. As the New York Times has noted, that represents 0.000008% of the 1.3bn votes cast in presidential elections over that period. Mullin went further than Blanche on Wednesday, suggesting that voting machines were not secure. “We’ve had some trouble with some machines,” he said, without providing evidence, but adding: “Can’t say that it was fraud or not fraud.” Administration officials have sought to support Trump’s longstanding unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in US elections through investigations and indictments related to election concerns. Trump has sought to undermine public confidence in US elections by promoting false claims of election fraud and making unverified claims of election insecurity. Earlier this year, the president heightened those claims in a primetime address. The US president has also pushed through a crackdown on voting, ostensibly to secure elections – despite experts assuring voters that elections are already secure. That includes directing his administration to implement new rules to restrict mail-in ballot voting, a method of voting Trump has criticized, to create a federal database of eligible citizens and force voters to provide proof of citizenship when voting in federal elections. Most of those actions have been challenged in court. Noncitizen voting is rare and often associated with administrative errors. In a September 2o26 report, the Center for Election Innovation & Research found that “sweeping allegations about possible noncitizen registration or voting appear to arise from misunderstandings, mischaracterizations, or outright fabrications about complex voter data.” Federal citizenship verification tools found that 0.04% of voter verification cases are returned as noncitizen, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Recently, New Jersey announced it found that more than 6,000 noncitizens had been falsely registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024, due to a system error. Of those, fewer than 340 voted. Since early September, the Department of Justice has charged at least 24 individuals across 10 states with similar charges. In most of those cases, the individuals charged are lawful permanent residents. The 10 individuals charged in Minnesota are all lawful permanent residents who either allegedly made false claims of citizenship to vote, or cast a ballot as a noncitizen, in the 2022 or 2024 general elections and 2026 primaries. At least three of the Minnesota defendants have pleaded not guilty to the charges. The Guardian has reached out to attorneys representing nine of the individuals indicted for comment. One defendant did not have an attorney listed on record. An attorney for Alan Barbu Kargb, a Liberian national with lawful permanent resident status who was charged with noncitizen voting and making false claims about citizenship to vote, declined to comment.

title: Senate blocks Republican bill restricting stock trades by US Congress members
body_text: The US Senate on Wednesday blocked a Republican bill restricting stock trading by members of Congress, after Democrats refused to advance a measure they said would let lawmakers keep their portfolios and was bundled with voter ID rules they called a “poison pill”. The 53-47 vote fell seven short of the 60 needed to open debate on the Stop Insider Trading Act, which the Republican-controlled House passed in July. Every Democrat and independent voted no, and the failure comes five weeks before the 3 November midterms. The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses and their dependent children from buying individual stocks. Democrats said that falls short of a ban because lawmakers could keep everything they already own, reinvest dividends into more shares and let a spouse or child trade on their behalf. Several also wanted the rules extended to the president and other White House officials, while others objected to the photo ID requirements for voting, which they said would make it harder for eligible citizens to cast ballots. Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, called the bill “a permission slip for corruption” and said Republicans had designed it to fail. He noted that a Senate committee advanced a bipartisan ban last year and accused Republicans of ignoring it. His deputy, Dick Durbin, dismissed the “meaningless” bill as “an inadequate congressional stock trading ban” and “Republican messaging”. Republicans said Democrats had picked politics over reform. Nebraska’s Pete Ricketts, who faces a tight re-election race, said on the Senate floor “we need to restore the faith of the American people” in Congress. Joe Gruters, chair of the Republican National Committee, accused Democrats of choosing to “protect the swamp” over voter ID and accountability and said “voters should hold them accountable in November”. The fight is the latest in years of failed efforts. The best known is the so-called “Pelosi Act”, introduced by the Republican senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, who said it would help restore trust in Congress by banning members from trading and holding stocks. A Senate committee advanced a reworked version 8-7, with Hawley the only Republican in favor, after the name was dropped and future presidents were added, though Trump was shielded. Trump attacked Hawley on Truth Social over the vote, and the bill never became law. Trump’s own trading has been eye-popping. The Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren and California representative Robert Garcia pointed to disclosures showing more than 14,000 stock trades in his first year back in office, worth up to $1.06bn, calling the volume “unprecedented” for a sitting president. Bloomberg reported that from January 2025 to June 2026, Trump made nearly 28,700 trades, compared with 22,200 by all lawmakers combined. Nothing in the filings shows insider trading, and they do not say whether Trump directed the trades himself. Lawmakers have faced similar questions, and a report by Common Cause found members of both parties made 13,324 trades worth $635.6m last year. In April 2025, Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Republican US representative, bought shares in Apple and Tesla just before Trump paused many of his tariffs and markets surged. Nancy Pelosi is one of the most closely tracked traders in Congress, and Trump called her out by name in February’s State of the Union speech. Yet Republicans and Democrats were evenly split among the 10 best-performing portfolios in Congress last year, while Pelosi ranked 28th, according to an analysis by Unusual Whales. title: Steve Hilton, Xavier Becerra clash in testy California governor’s race debate
body_text: Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton, the candidates running to be California’s next governor, clashed on Wednesday over taxes, immigration and regulating artificial intelligence in a testy debate held days before voters begin receiving their ballots in the heavily Democratic state. Hilton, the former Fox News host endorsed by Donald Trump, used the hourlong matchup, hosted by CNN in its studio in Burbank, California, to argue that Becerra, a former congressman who served as the US health and human services secretary during the Biden administration, was not actively campaigning and instead taking voters for granted. “He wasn’t even supposed to be the candidate,” Hilton, 57, said, referring to Becerra’s unexpected success after an unusually wild primary campaign. “I just want to ask every Californian: aren’t you tired of that?” Becerra, 68, pitched his experience as an asset, vowing to tackle the state’s punishing cost of living crisis while being a bulwark against the Trump administration’s policies. He accused Hilton of owing loyalty to Trump – and not the state that roundly rejected the president in each of the last three presidential elections. “If you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response,” Becerra said of Hilton’s reply to a question about regulating the development of AI. Hilton’s bid to succeed California’s term-limited governor, Gavin Newsom, is aimed at voter discontent with the political status quo in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican governor in two decades. But his pitch is complicated by his party identification and the president who has backed him. Though most Californians say the state is headed in the wrong direction, fewer than a quarter of likely voters approve of the president’s job performance, notably lower than the national average, and many cite “fight against Trump administration policies” as a priority. Recent polls show Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton, suggesting the onus was on the Republican hopeful to persuade voters partisan change was needed in Sacramento. The debate, the only scheduled face-to-face debate before the 3 November general election, comes just days before voters begin receiving their ballots by mail. Both candidates said they would oppose the so-called billionaire tax proposal, a November ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% tax on any California resident worth more than $1bn. Becerra’s opposition puts him at odds with progressives, including Senator Bernie Sanders, who will campaign for the measure in California this weekend. But they were at odds on Proposition 39, a ballot measure that would require voters to show a government-issued ID to vote in person. Like other Democratic leaders in the state, Becerra said he opposed the measure, calling it an initiative “backed by Donald Trump” that would make it harder for Californians to vote. Hilton said he supported the proposal, but insisted he had confidence in the state’s voting system despite Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of fraud. “I’ve got confidence in what we saw in the primary and in this process,” Hilton said. Without distancing himself significantly from Trump, whose Maga base he cannot afford to alienate, Hilton sought to draw subtle differences: “My whole aim here would be to lower the temperature.” An exchange over immigration policy became personal, when Becerra, the son of Mexican immigrants, accused Hilton, who grew up in England and was an adviser to the former UK prime minister David Cameron, of appearing to support measures that would “welcome immigrants who look like you” while wanting to “deport immigrants who look like me”. “What a disgraceful remark that was,” Hilton shot back. Becerra’s path to the general election was winding. After languishing in the low single digits for much of the race, he was catapulted to the front of the pack after the implosion of Eric Swalwell’s campaign amid a slew of sexual misconduct and assault allegations – claims the now former congressman denied. Becerra ultimately advanced first in the June primary, overcoming fierce opposition from his more progressive rival, the billionaire activist Tom Steyer. Hilton came in second, with Trump’s endorsement helping to consolidate conservative support and avert the risk of a Democratic lockout in the state’s non-partisan primary. But the president’s support risks being a liability in the general election as the unresolved war with Iran has spiked oil prices and kept US inflation stubbornly high. Since reaching the general election, Becerra has maintained a low profile, while Hilton has blitzed the state as he seeks to make inroads with voters who disapprove of Trump. “Thank you to CNN for bringing Xavier out of hiding,” Hilton said, slamming his opponent as a “career politician” who was the product of the “machine in Sacramento”. Becerra pushed back, arguing that the challenges facing the state and country were too great to risk rolling the dice on a political newcomer. “There aren’t training wheels in the governor’s office,” Becerra said, repeating a line he deployed in the primary. “You have to know how to do the job, and that’s why I’m asking California voters to vote for me for governor of state of California.”

title: Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn
body_text: The Trump administration has abandoned key security bodies meant to investigate direct threats to US elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, according to former officials and a recent report. While administration officials have been actively focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, other credible election threats appear to have been overlooked, the officials say. Between 2021 and 2024, the justice department’s election threats taskforce prosecuted 21 cases, such as that of Solomon Peña, a failed candidate for the New Mexico house of representatives who organized shootings at the houses of election officials, or Quintez Brown, who shot up a campaign meeting of Louisville’s mayor. Democrats and Republicans faced prosecution for harassing, intimidating and threatening elections workers, noted Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, now the executive director of the Oregon District Attorneys Association. Since then, the taskforce seems to have gone quiet. “While officials are being trained to handle threats, the federal deterrent meant to punish the people making them appears to have gone quiet,” Fisher said. “To date, no new cases have been prosecuted, and the [justice department’s] election threats taskforce appears to be defunct in practice.” Contacted for comment on the status of the election threats taskforce, the justice department referred to a series of nine media releases over the past five weeks describing indictments of foreign nationals on charges of election fraud and stolen identities. In an academic paper published in June, while she was studying at the Naval Postgraduate School, Fisher noted that the taskforce received more than 2,000 reports of election threats between 2021 and 2024. It opened more than 100 investigations into those threats. Trump administration officials began disbanding election investigative groups within the justice department, the office of the director of national intelligence and other agencies almost immediately after the president started his second term. The first day after Pam Bondi won Senate confirmation as attorney general, she eliminated the FBI’s foreign influence taskforce, which had been investigating influence campaigns waged by China, Russia and other adversaries. Administration leaders fired or reassigned personnel working on foreign election interference at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cisa). They also defunded Cisa’s training program for local officials to monitor and coordinate threats through the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center. Pleas from Democratic lawmakers during budget negotiations in 2025 to retain the taskforce and other election integrity assets went unheeded. “I’m less worried about jurisdictions’ ability to defend themselves in particular,” said Geoff Hale, a visiting fellow for election security at the Center for Democracy and Technology and former director at Cisa. “I’m more worried about the lack of an information-sharing environment across the community.” Federal cuts to these agencies’ monitoring and investigative apparatus leaves local agencies blind to broader patterns, he said. “The relationships and trust that Cisa had built up over 10 years, that was how the tapestry of security professionals that support elections across the country stayed in close contact and were able to close vulnerabilities to keep events and incidents from occurring in multiple locations.” Agencies working together with state and local election leaders offered regular warnings about suspicious activity, said Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, said at a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice last week. “This administration … has dismantled the entire apparatus that is responsible for detecting and holding these bad actors accountable,” she said. “That has all gone away at a moment when this administration is again claiming that the specter of foreign operations is … in play.” Meanwhile, Trump officials have been focused on some of the president’s longstanding personal grievances when it comes to election integrity. FBI agents swooped into Fulton county in January to seize ballots from the 2020 election, ostensibly as part of a continuing investigation into foreign election interference. Tulsi Gabbard, then the director of national intelligence, was present at the FBI raid. Similarly, the ODNI and the FBI seized elections materials in Puerto Rico, again while investigating foreign interference. Nothing has yet come of either event. But both cases led up to a primetime address by Trump on 16 July, in which he claimed China had acquired extensive voter information during the 2020 election cycle, characterizing it as an effort to influence and undermine the legitimacy of the 2018 midterm and 2020 presidential elections. Trump argued that US election databases and hardware had vulnerabilities to foreign adversaries, and that Venezuela had digitally manipulated its election results in ways that might be replicated in an American election. Trump’s claims could not be substantiated from the evidence presented. Since that address – and the public’s tepid response to the claims – the administration has pivoted to a dogged pursuit of noncitizen voters in American elections. The justice department has charged more than 90 people with voter-related fraud offenses, including 50 noncitizens in the last five weeks alone, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said on Wednesday, contrasting it with 13 cases brought under the Biden administration. “What we do at Department of Homeland Security is not controversial; we’re enforcing our nation’s laws,” said the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, who was also at the event. “Underneath the Trump administration, we will always protect the integrity of our election system and enforce our nation’s laws.”

title: Americans are paying millions for a batch of pro-Trump ads
body_text: The US government is spending millions of taxpayer dollars to get a blatantly partisan message in front of voters as the midterm elections loom. And while these TV ads aren’t explicitly campaign ads, they might as well be. They feature Donald Trump as a hero. They try to scare people into thinking that the US could become a communist country. They take shots at the news media and at vaguely described political enemies. Two Democratic senators, Patty Murray and Chris Murphy, on Tuesday aptly called them “a shockingly corrupt use of taxpayer dollars”. Their funding, through the Department of Homeland Security, may be illegal, according to experts, and is certainly unethical. They lack any hint of the public service message that the White House claims. In fact, they closely fit the defining characteristics of propaganda, as described by the government accounting office, including “self-aggrandizement” or “puffery”. But the agencies or institutions that could do something about them, including the supposedly independent FCC, are eager to do the president’s bidding. Brendan Carr, the FCC chair, is a proud Trump toady, with his thumb on the scale for every Trump project. Carr has shrugged off questions about the ads. They don’t raise any red flags for him; they are quite normal, and nothing that his agency intends to investigate. And with both houses of Congress held by Republican majorities, this startling use of taxpayer money will probably go unpunished – at least for now. “The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress,” said Donald Sherman, who heads Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (Crew) in Washington. However, as he told CNN, Congress “has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable”. Some Republican members of Congress have questioned the ads, but there’s no groundswell of bipartisan outrage so far. The Trump administration is responding to the criticism with its usual defiance, even planning to double down in the next few weeks. “This is just the beginning,” one administration official told Axios. The argument that these are not political ads is contradicted by an undeniable reality: one of them is a straight-up rerun of a Trump campaign commercial from before the 2024 presidential election. It differs, though, with the addition of an Orwellian coda, “paid for by the US government”. With its weirdly menacing tone, it shows black-and-white images of Trump walking as he promises to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and pledges to “rout out the fake news media”. Another ad shows images of Trump at public events with a voiceover insisting that “America will never be a communist country,” while the song Love Me plays in the background. (The R&B artist JMSN has said he didn’t authorize this use of his song and has made a cease-and-desist demand.) Another ad, reported Robert Tait of the Guardian, shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump bragging: “The United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.” The White House described that “love me” ad as “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. And, in a statement, it termed the various ads as “public service announcements”. They are playing to a big-tent crowd that Trump apparently thinks (or hopes) is persuadable. They’ve aired everywhere from pro-football games to Saturday Night Live. The Wall Street Journal reported that the ads, by last weekend, had aired more than 90 times across various networks – and political leanings – including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now and CBS. As corrupt as they appear to be, the ads do make a twisted kind of Trumpian sense. They are probably illegal and have garnered plenty of legitimate criticism. But what’s missing is accountability with actual teeth. As usual, he’s getting away with it. But the midterm elections could change that. With Trump’s approval ratings low and voters unhappy with misguided Iran war and soaring costs, Democrats could seize a majority in one or both houses of Congress. That might mean some restraints on Trump’s never-ending cascade of malfeasance. It’s no wonder he’s pulling out all the stops to make that nightmare go away. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: ‘Page one of repressive playbook’: critics warn of Trump’s conspiratorial attacks
body_text: Since the start of his second presidency, Donald Trump has often launched outlandish conspiratorial attacks on critics and foes that mock them and label their views as hoaxes, prompting scholars and legal experts to say Trump’s attacks endanger US freedoms, public health and science. Trump’s extensive use of conspiracy theories is the hallmark of an authoritarian leader that has weakened trust in the coming midterm elections, dangerously ignored scientific evidence, and often pushed for prosecutions of his political enemies in ways that seriously erode civil liberties, say critics. Trump’s conspiratorial and authoritarian-style tactics are palpable say critics, in his false claim that the US faces a “crisis of election security” to bolster his radical push for new curbs on voting rights, and his labeling of climate change as a “hoax” despite extensive scientific evidence that it’s a reality. To some scholars, Trump-backed conspiratorial claims have had a damaging impact on all levels of US society and democracy and are emblematic of how authoritarian leaders use conspiracies to justify repression. Steven Levitsky, the Harvard professor of government and the co-author of How Democracies Die, said: “Conspiracies are page one of the repressive playbook,” noting that Mao, Stalin, Putin and other authoritarian leaders have historically launched attacks on enemies by floating conspiracies. “They’re almost always used to justify repression,” Levitsky added noting that authoritarian leaders can simply allege conspiracies without providing any or only minimal “evidence”. In a notable twist, Trump charged in mid-September that some AI leaders and experts were engaging in a big “conspiracy” and perpetrating a “HOAX”, by urging strong safeguards to protect against potential extinction-level threats to humanity from this powerful new technology. Similarly, Trump without evidence disparaged critics of datacenters as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor”, and asserted he was the best “guardrail” to protect society from threats that unregulated AI pose. The investigation, which Trump has cheered on, has issued subpoenas to several former national security and law enforcement officials including ex-CIA director John Brennan and ex-FBI director James Comey. This sprawling inquiry has tapped some key Trump-allied election denialists for top posts. Notably, Trump recruited 81-year-old Joe diGenova, a former prosecutor who led the effort until he abruptly announced his departure on 10 September, and ex-White House lawyer Kurt Olsen. Both lawyers had worked to discredit the 2020 election results and Joe Biden’s win. The sudden move by diGenova to resign – after only five months on the job – raised questions about its direction and credibility. DiGenova’s departure followed that of another top prosecutor who was heading the investigation; Maria Medetis Long, a veteran national security prosecutor, resigned in April after reportedly voicing concerns about its direction. “The so-called Grand Conspiracy investigation turns prosecutorial practice on its head,” said ex-justice department inspector general Michael Bromwich who has represented ex-FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe in the inquiry. “It starts with designated targets, the president’s perceived enemies, and then searches for facts and bends the law to support the theory. Joe diGenova found that it was easier to be an outside propagandist cheering the theory from the sidelines than have the responsibility to build such a case with actual facts.” In other energy and environmental matters, Trump and his top officials have deployed bogus conspiracies and specious information to counter growing evidence of the risks posed by climate change from rising temperatures to dangerous storms worldwide. The Trump administration has moved hard to kill energy and environmental regulations aimed at fighting climate change, and simultaneously have promoted greater usage of coal, which Trump has lauded erroneously as “clean and beautiful”, and other fossil fuels that worsen climate change. Late last year, Trump energy officials issued emergency orders to keep open five ageing coal plants in Michigan and four other states that were scheduled to shut down, spurring some states to challenge the costly moves. In mid-September, a federal judge ruled that the energy department had exceeded its authority by ordering the Michigan plant to stay open past its retirement. Further, after years of conspiratorial attacks on wind energy by Trump, his administration in December announced it was pausing leases on five offshore wind projects on the east coast in a big blow to the industry. The five windfarms were slated to power over 2.5m homes and create 10,000 jobs. A federal judge in February issued a preliminary injunction allowing one of the five to stay open. “Trump’s decisions make no sense from either the perspective of environmental protection or the cost of energy,” Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard University science historian and professor of earth and planetary sciences, told the Guardian earlier this year. Dr Howard Frumkin, a professor emeritus of public health at the University of Washington told PBS: “It boggles the mind that the administration is rescinding the endangerment finding; it’s akin to insisting that the world is flat or denying that gravity is a thing.” In healthcare too, Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services (HHS) who has a long history of making factually erroneous claims about vaccine safety, have indulged in flawed and conspiratorial claims about vaccines. Trump declared flatly in August that the combined MMR vaccine for children could be “quite lethal”, but failed to offer scientific evidence to back his claim. Trump too has advocated breaking up longstanding immunizations into three separate shots that currently are not available in the United States. Even as the death toll from the worst outbreak of measles in decades rises, Kennedy on 16 September starred at a Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he spearheaded for almost two decades. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy told the gathering in an almost 90-minute talk. “You have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time.” According to recent polls about one-quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines in the wake of multi-year campaigns against immunizations by groups that once were fringe figures. From a historical perspective, Zelizer noted that conspiracy theories in American politics have a long history, but that before Trump “the role of presidents and other high-level elected officials had been to push back against this part of politics, rather than to amplify these ideas.”

title: White House airs new taxpayer-funded ad praising Trump’s war on Iran
body_text: The latest in a series of pro-Trump television ads aired using taxpayer funds in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a one-minute spot that celebrates Donald Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. The ad aired during a commercial break on Fox News on Wednesday night, according video posted online by MeidasTouch, a leftwing outlet. A copy of the new ad posted on social media by Medium Buying, a company that purchases airtime for Republican candidates, features audio taken from the president’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations in Iran. “This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States armed forces,” Trump can be heard saying over images of combat, some of which appear to be dramatizations or computer-generated. A cover version of John Lee Hooker’s Boom Boom provides the soundtrack. The audio then switches to comments made by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, in a briefing on the third day of the war. “He reminded the world, as he has time and time again, being an American means something unbreakable,” Hegseth says over slow-motion images of Trump walking down a corridor. “If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth says. “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it. Their war on Americans has become our retribution against their ayatollah.” As the words “Paid for by the US Government” appear at the bottom of the screen, the ad’s audio switches back to Trump’s call for regime change in Iran in his announcement of the war in February. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump can be heard saying, against a backdrop of dramatic music and images of Iranian Americans in New York celebrating the US strikes on 1 March. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take.” The images of Iranian Americans demonstrating in support of Trump’s war in New York City, marching down 42nd Street and holding signs that read “Thank you President Trump”, were all previously included in a White House video posted on YouTube on 4 March. The focus of the ad on speeches and images of celebration that all came in the first three days of the war, when it looked like Iran’s government could collapse, raises questions about why the administration is releasing it as the war enters its seventh month and continues to alienate many of Trump’s supporters.

title: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump
body_text: Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday. Diesel prices in the US have risen to record highs in recent weeks, adding to cost of living pressures that have helped push Trump’s approval ratings to a career low before next month’s crucial midterm elections. Energy analysts, however, have pointed to the war in Iran and wider disruption to global oil markets as the leading drivers of the price increases. Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have nevertheless emerged as an additional headache for Trump, with the attacks also contributing to tighter diesel supplies at a politically sensitive moment for the US president. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations. The Ukrainian president on Thursday also said the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, which has a range of 200km and was developed by the Ukrainian defence firm FirePoint, had been deployed for the first time. Zelenskyy accompanied the statement with footage of a missile launch, but did not disclose when or where the weapon had been used. Speaking at the Valdai discussion club, Vladimir Putin on Thursday acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had cost the country roughly 1% of its GDP. Earlier this week, Russia – traditionally the world’s second-largest diesel exporter – extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, adding further pressure to a global supply crunch. Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies, said it was unlikely Kyiv would stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure as long as Moscow continued its daily attacks on Ukraine. “There is no rationale for Ukraine to continue exercising restraint while it is being bombarded and major urban areas are under constant attack,” he said. “We need to deprive Russia of revenue,” he added. Zelenskyy has been pushing for a US-brokered energy ceasefire with Russia, but Putin has shown little interest in the proposal, instead vowing to intensify strikes on Ukraine. At Valdai, Putin called “absurd” a proposal he said was be discussed, under which Russia would stop striking Ukrainian vessels if Ukraine halted attacks on Russian oil refineries. In wide-ranging comments at the forum, Putin said Moscow was not on the verge of attacking foreign factories producing weapons for Ukraine, but that such facilities were something Russia’s military and intelligence services needed to monitor closely. He also ramped up his nuclear rhetoric, warning that Russia would consider using “all types of weapons” if its exclave of Kaliningrad was attacked, while insisting that Moscow had “no intention of attacking anyone”. Tensions over the exclave have risen this week, with Russia previously sending a letter to Nato warning it would be ready to resort to using nuclear weapons if the western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad. Meanwhile, Russia has continued its deadly missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, targeting energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and other businesses in an apparent effort to cripple the country’s economy and render Kyiv increasingly uninhabitable. A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday morning, but no one was injured because the children were sheltering in the basement, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. A key bridge in the Ukrainian capital was also hit, forcing authorities to suspend metro services and other public transport. Kyiv has experienced near round-the-clock Russian attacks in recent weeks, at times increasingly resembling a frontline city in what many see as the most challenging period for the capital since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Russia’s newer jet-powered drones have proved particularly difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, with success rates significantly lower than for the slower Shahed-type drones. The sustained attacks have revived fears of another winter with prolonged power and heating outages, after similar strikes last year left parts of Ukraine without electricity during temperatures that fell as low as -20C (-4F).

title: Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea?
body_text: Donald Trump seems to spend an unusual amount of time thinking about toilets. Back in 2019, he bizarrely claimed: “People are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times as opposed to once.” He repeated this claim at a Michigan rally the following year. “Ten times, right, 10 times,” Trump complained. “Not me, of course not me, but you,” he added while pointing at an unfortunate audience member. A couple of years later, he was back to the toilet talk: angrily disputing claims by the New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman that he’d once clogged a White House toilet by attempting to dispose of documents in it. I regret to inform you that the president is once again responsible for a national conversation about toilets. In a fitting encapsulation of Trumpism, explosive diarrhea has become a midterm talking point. Food recalls and stomach-churning parasites have been a mainstay of the news this year and Democrats are milking the issue. In August, for example, the Democratic party’s official Twitter/X account highlighted the number of foods that have been recalled in 2026 and demanded that RFK Jr resign from his role as health secretary. Last month (which happened to be Food Safety Month – who knew?), the Rhode Island congressman Gabe Amo argued that Trump’s cuts to the federal workforce had contributed to decreased food safety. Senator Elizabeth Warren similarly accused “slashed food safety agencies” of contributing to the “cyclospora outbreak” and demanded Trump be held accountable in November. To be fair, the number of food recalls during Trump’s second term is not remarkably different than it was under Joe Biden. What is different, however, is the scale of the problem. The US only recently declared the end of the largest ever recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak, which was linked to contaminated lettuce. That resulted in 570 hospitalizations and two ⁠deaths. Also different is the fact that, as Warren noted, the Trump administration seems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe. Ever since 1995, there has been a federal-state partnership called the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) which tracks infections caused by various pathogens, including Cyclospora. Starting on 1 July, however, the CDC downgraded this program so that mandatory surveillance for the 10 state health departments that participate in the program was limited to salmonella and E coli. This downgrading of pathogen surveillance didn’t cause the cyclospora outbreak, but it might have made it harder for health authorities to respond to it. And it’s not just food that the current administration is making less safe: the air we breathe and the water we drink are all getting more dangerous in the name of maximizing corporate profits. On Monday, for example, the Trump administration announced it was relaxing rules that govern how fuel-efficient auto companies have to make their new gasoline-powered cars and light trucks. The rationale given by Sean Duffy, the reality show star turned transportation secretary, is that removing stringent pollution-control requirements will reduce the average costs of new vehicles by $1,300. We’ll see if that actually happens (corporations are not keen on passing on cost savings), but even if it does reduce car prices, it’s going to cost consumers and the environment in other ways. Reduced efficiency will increase fuel spending, for one thing. And the change is poised to create more air pollution and worsen climate change. The Trump administration is also working to roll back regulation of toxic air pollutants. Earlier this year the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed weakening air pollution limits on ethylene oxide (EtO), a known carcinogen that is used to clean medical devices. A Biden-era rule finalized in 2024 required stringent testing for hazardous emissions and required emitters to cut the amount of EtO they were producing. If the EPA is successful in overturning these rules, then tons of the carcinogenic gas will continue to be released into the community. And it’s obviously not people in the vicinity of Mar-a-Lago breathing in the brunt of this poisonous air, is it? It’s people in largely low-income neighborhoods. Then there’s our water supply. A Biden-era rule set drinking-water limits for several Pfas (commonly known as “forever chemicals”). You know what happened next, don’t you? The Trump administration is trying to roll back those limits, arguing that the standards are expensive and legally flawed. They’ve also terminated a regulatory review of Pfas-contaminated sewage sludge fertilizer that is used on farmland. What does that mean?
