title: Trump and his allies credit deportations with record low crime. Experts disagree
body_text: Over the last year and a half, the US has seen a historic drop in homicides. Researchers and reporters are still puzzling through the complex set of reasons why - from the easing of pandemic-era stressors and the Biden administration’s investments in community-based violence prevention to policing and other factors. But for the Trump administration, there’s one easy explanation: increased immigration enforcement. As the midterm elections approach, the White House has been doubling down on this message, saying its crackdown against immigrants is why US crime rates are now falling. “We have the most secure border in the world, nobody comes in, unless they’re invited. Unless they have permission,” Trump said during a speech to the UN general assembly last week. “As a result, last year we achieved the largest drop in violent crime ever recorded.” JD Vance, the vice-president, made a similar claim at a rally in Iowa the week prior. “When you get the violent criminals out of your country you see the largest drop in violent crime in the history of the United States of America,” he said. “Murder rates, because we got the bad guys out.” But experts say this simply isn’t true. There’s no data that proves mass deportations or enhanced immigration enforcement leads to lower crime rates, and the research that does exist shows there is no relationship between immigrants – documented or not – and homicide rates in the US, experts say. “It’s a specious claim if you’ve never attempted to verify anything with actual facts and are willing to believe what the administration will tell you,” said Pratheepan Gulasekaram, a law professor at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “If you live in a fact-free world this is the type of nonsensical data you’re willing to imbibe.” In addition, the plummeting homicide rate the US is experiencing now didn’t start during Trump’s second term. It started in 2023, when Biden was president, researchers say. Even though there’s no evidence to back up the Trump administration’s claims, Gulasekaram said xenophobia is one reason why they resonate with many Americans. “There’s an intuitive appeal to that claim if you start with the premise that foreigners are so different from us and are the source of economic and social ills,” he said. “That feeds into that underlying sentiment and it becomes extremely sticky.” Other conservatives are echoing the White House’s unsubstantiated claims by making the same link between immigrants and crime. In a May Instagram video, Erich Pratt, vice-president of Gun Owners of America argued that Americans are “enjoying unprecedented safety”, because of the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. “It didn’t come from new gun restrictions,” he said in an email to the Guardian of the plummeting homicide rates across the US. “It came from a shift in priorities. President Trump implemented measures aimed at deporting violent gang members, ending catch-and-release policies for illegal aliens, and getting repeat offenders off the streets.” A Guardian analysis published in February showed that more than 75% of people who entered deportation proceedings for the first time had no criminal convictions. Only 34 of more than 18,400 people arrested by ICE between 2025 and June this year were convicted of killing someone, according to DHS data. The most common convictions were for illegal re-entry, driving under the influence and a category marked as “other”. It’s unclear how many undocumented migrants are currently in prison for murder convictions or have been convicted for killing someone since Trump took office. State prisons track demographic information such as age, race and type of conviction but, with the exception of Texas, immigration status is not one of them. And by the federal government’s own acknowledgment, there is no comprehensive or centralized data on the citizenship status of people incarcerated in local jails and state prisons, the government accountability office said in a 28 September report. Still, Trump has spent a decade claiming, without evidence, that undocumented migrants pose a safety threat to US citizens. In his 2016 presidential run, he repeatedly talked about the killing of Kate Steinle, a 32-year-old woman who had been killed in San Francisco the year before. The man accused of killing her was undocumented, but he was eventually acquitted. And during his 2024 run, he often spoke of Laken Riley, a nursing student who was killed while she was jogging. Her killer was an undocumented immigrant, and was sentenced to life in prison. Researchers say that stories like these have long been used to push for tougher immigration policies and more deportations. “The argument in their tragic cases is that they should have never been at risk because this person should have never been able to commit these crimes,” said Michael Light, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “But that’s more of a political disagreement than an empirical one.” Leaning on these kinds of anecdotes to determine immigration policy, and then claiming that they have led to public safety can cause misunderstandings of why homicides and other crimes have decreased, Light said. “There’s no question that they’ve increased enforcement and we’ve seen a historic decrease in homicides,” he said. “But the idea that immigration policy is the only thing that’s changed is problematic. And if we misdiagnose what’s actually driving the homicide decline, that’s going to lead to bad public policy.” This week, the Department of Justice announced a new $25m grant program to support people whose loved ones were killed or injured by undocumented migrants and fund law enforcement efforts to prevent future deaths. The Guardian approached the DHS and the White House to request any data or research that can prove a causal relationship between immigration enforcement and the declining homicide rate. Both agencies reiterated their claims that deportations are the reason homicides are down, but did not supply any evidence.

title: Lawmakers call for action on ‘plainly illegal’ taxpayer-funded ads to promote Trump
body_text: The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections. Two congressional Democrats, Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads. Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”. The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government. “President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.” The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable. The lawmakers say the ads may violate four sets of laws, and cited a provision in this year’s spending act that bars funds for “publicity or propaganda”, along with the Anti-Deficiency Act, federal criminal statutes on misusing public money and the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act exempts the president but covers executive branch staff, and the lawmakers argue that employees must have helped produce the ads. Raskin and Whitesides reject the White House’s description of the ads as public service announcements. They say nearly every claim in them is false, and that they are virtually identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ads. In one example, they say an ad credits Trump with reviving manufacturing, though the US has lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in his second term, according to a February report from Congress’s joint economic committee. They also challenge the White House’s argument that the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot, though at an August rally he urged supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot”. A White House spokesperson has called the ads “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. Trump said on Wednesday that he would “gladly pay the money” if the ads were found to be improper. Some Republicans have also raised concerns. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, and the senators Mike Rounds, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis have questioned the use of public money, while the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair, Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said the ads were appropriate. The ads are not the first administration advertising spending to draw scrutiny. Last year the Department of Homeland Security under Kristi Noem spent more than $200m on ads promoting her and Trump’s immigration policies. In March, Noem testified that Trump had approved the campaign (which the president denied to Reuters), and he then removed her from the secretary role, relegating her to special envoy of the “Shield of the Americas”.

title: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles amid Trump pressure
body_text: Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban. The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves. Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.” Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday. The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks. Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices. It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US. The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC. John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban. EC commission spokesperson Anna Kaisa Itkonen confirmed that EU member states will hold urgent talks with the commission on Friday to discuss a coordinated response. “The commission … is closely coordinating with EU member states to take stock of the situation and examine appropriate measures to tackle these high prices,” Itkonen added. Discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency. The US energy secretary Chris Wright said he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global fuel ⁠prices by drawing down its emergency diesel inventories. “This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go ⁠into to harvest season and we go into winter heating oil season,” he told Fox ⁠News. “Now’s the time to bring more ‌diesel to the market, and that diesel is available.” Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns. Earlier, a US official told reporters it was “in Europe’s best interest” to ⁠work with the US as it pursues options to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers. The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday. Releasing more stocks would represent a problem for European countries, which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues. “The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added. Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies. A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

title: Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors
body_text: By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, bestowed extraordinary influence on two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. The new project, which Hegseth dubbed “Project Meridian” in an event in Quantico, Virginia, on Wednesday, will be led by Pentagon official Emil Michael, a former Uber executive. As the Guardian has reported, Michael made millions in profits off non-public Musk company AI stock while in federal office – and while guiding the Department of Defense’s artificial intelligence efforts. Along with Luckey and Musk, Project Meridian will also include the Trump loyalist and former speaker of the House Newt Gingrich. Musk was one of the chief financiers of Trump’s 2024 victory, spending over a quarter of a billion dollars in the run-up to the election. Recent campaign records show he is still a major force in the coming midterms. His America Pac spent $3.4m attacking the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, for example. In the hotly contested Texas Senate race, America Pac spent $6.4m to oppose Democrat James Talarico and $1m to support the Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton. Musk’s SpaceX has been a crucial contractor for US space programs since 2018, and in the second Trump administration his company has emerged as key player in Trump’s pet Golden Dome ballistic missile defense project, a phenomenally expensive effort that could cost as much as $1.2tn. Musk dwarfs Luckey in resources and fame, but Luckey has achieved immense celebrity in the defense contracting and world. Initially a young celebrity in the tech world for inventing a virtual reality headset, Luckey later founded Anduril, a defense contracting company that has already won significant federal contracts. Luckey has also become of the most important “bundlers” for Republican candidates on the west coast, as the Guardian reported in August. One of the sources called him the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. Invitations to political fundraisers obtained by the Guardian show Luckey hosted and co-hosted events for candidates from Trump himself to Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, Mehmet Oz, Ted Cruz and others. The most recent event was on 22 August, where he and his wife co-hosted a $50,000-a-head effort to “Keep the Senate”, and listing guests John Thune of South Dakota, Mike Rogers of Michigan, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Jon Husted of Ohio. It is not necessarily a mystery what Musk and Luckey think about warfare’s future. The 34-year-old Palmer, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, UAVs, and space technology, has been already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare. Earlier this year, for example, he said he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through he crust of the earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. He has claimed that his company has “working prototypes of subterranean systems”. “Bringing major industry players into these types of positions at the Pentagon is not something new, but what feels different now is the substantial financial support these two have, and continue to, deliver for the Republican party,” said Brendan Glavin of Open Secrets, a non-partisan group that tracks campaign spending. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: DNC sues Trump administration over last-minute changes to overseas voting form
body_text: The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday. Until recently, the form, the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), gave overseas voters four options to choose from when describing their geographic location. Voters could say they needed an overseas ballot because they were on active military service, living outside the US with an intent to return, or living outside the US and uncertain about their return. The form also allowed voters to check a box if they were a US citizen who had never lived in the country (38 states and the District of Columbia allow citizens born abroad to vote in at least some elections even if they have never lived in the country). In August, as the deadline to send out overseas ballots approached, the Pentagon – the agency that oversees the form – submitted two emergency requests to modify the form. Among the changes, the Pentagon sought to eliminate the option allowing voters to say they were citizens who never lived in the US. The requests were quickly approved by the office of management and budget (OMB). NPR first reported the changes earlier this week. “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots. They know that Americans, both at home and abroad, are going to reject their destructive agenda, and they are scrambling to disenfranchise as much of the electorate as possible by any means necessary,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. A Pentagon spokesperson said: “The Department is committed to ensuring all Service members, their families, and overseas citizens have seamless access to the tools and resources to successfully exercise their right to vote from anywhere in the world. “To actively protect voting rights and eliminate voter confusion, FVAP.gov is routinely updated to ensure all online tools, federally-prescribed forms, and state-specific guidance remain streamlined, legally compliant, and simple to navigate. This includes updated online guidance on August 31 that clarifies instructions and voter eligibility requirements regarding the Federal Post Card Application and Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot,” the spokesperson said. The changes could confuse and discourage US citizens who have never lived in the country from registering and casting a ballot, experts said. “The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act guarantees US citizens abroad, along with service members and their families, the right to vote, and nothing in it requires a plan to return. Changing the form does not change that right. It changes whether a voter recognizes themselves on it,” said Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the US Vote Foundation, which works on helping overseas Americans vote. “If an overseas voter goes on to the FPCA website, goes to get their Federal Postcard Application to request their ballot, they’re going to see this form and they have to sign it under penalty of perjury,” said a DNC official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to candidly discuss the lawsuit. “They’re going to see that there is no longer the checkbox they’re used to checking. And the other options may not fit them accurately and they may not be able to comfortably or confidently sign that form and request their mail ballot.” In an August letter to the OMB, Sean O’Keefe, the deputy undersecretary of defense for personnel and readiness, said the department had recently become aware of the option on the form for citizens who had never lived in the US. The changes were necessary, he said, because the existing versions “may confuse voters about the information they are required to provide under federal law”. He added that the changes could not go through a normal process because the election was less than 90 days away, and therefore had to be rushed. Lawyers for the DNC said in its lawsuit that justification was pretextual and implausible. The government “has at least 15 years of experience issuing guidance to US citizens born and remaining abroad, reviewing public comments concerning use of the FPCA by these applicants, and modifying the FPCA to best serve these eligible voters”, they wrote. By rushing through the changes, the government violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal law that requires government agencies to carefully weigh the impact of rules changes before implementing them. The OMB also did not follow proper procedure by not allowing for public comment in the federal register. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington DC, asks a judge to declare the government violated the APA and to set aside the government’s changes to the form. There are an estimated 2.2 million US citizens living abroad who are eligible to vote, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (the highest number of eligible citizens are living in Canada and the UK). About 11% of eligible US citizens living abroad voted in 2024. It’s not immediately clear how many US citizens live abroad but have never lived in the country. A 2016 government report estimated there were about 11,590, though lawyers for the DNC believe the number has increased since then. The Pentagon changed the form as the Republican National Committee (RNC) has pushed to prevent US citizens who have never lived in the country from having their votes counted. Republicans have sued in nine states challenging the policy of counting ballots for these types of voters. While one North Carolina court agreed with Republicans, several other courts have rejected their arguments while other lawsuits remain pending. In August, around the time the Trump administration rushed through the change, the RNC put out a statement saying it was “leading the fight to shut down a loophole that allows certain people who have never lived in a state to vote in its elections. As the case heads to the Nebraska supreme court, the RNC is pushing to protect residency requirements and stop the spread of ‘never-resident’ voting nationwide.” “The RNC strongly agrees that every eligible US citizen should be able to vote. The difference is the DNC wants to extend voting rights to people who aren’t eligible. Enforcing citizenship and residency requirements isn’t disenfranchisement – it’s following the law,” Ally Triolo, the RNC’s communications director for election integrity issues, said in a statement. “Regardless of the number of people at issue, as the DNC, we want to defend the rights of Americans to vote – of eligible US citizens to vote at home and abroad,” the DNC official said. “It is simply offensive that the RNC is trying to outright disenfranchise eligible US citizens. And it is offensive that [the Pentagon] would be joining that campaign just before the election.”

title: Trump doesn’t rule out declaring state of emergency before midterm elections
body_text: Donald Trump deflected responsibility for misleading Americans about the length of the Iran war, dismissed low poll ratings as “fake numbers” and refused to rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency before the midterms, in a wide-ranging interview with Time magazine. When confronted with questions about the length of the Iran war, the US president blamed the media for reporting his remarks in which he said the conflict was projected to last “four to five weeks”, in March. “ … I think the press fed it to them,” Trump told Time when asked whether Americans misunderstood him. At the end of March, Trump had told Americans he planned to wind down the Iran war over the next “two to three weeks”. In May, Trump insisted that a peace deal with Iran was nearly finalized. The US president said that he could have ended the Iran conflict whenever but chose to extend it “because I wanted to go further”. For more than seven months, Americans have been grappling with higher everyday costs as a result of Trump’s war with Iran – from gas prices surpassing $4 per gallon to stubborn inflation hovering at 3.4%. Economic concerns, fueled by Trump’s conflict, have angered voters, most of whom say they are unhappy with the president’s handling of the economy and his job overall. Just 26% of adults said they approve of the economy under the Republican president, according to an Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll. Overall, just 31% of people said they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president. But when asked about his low approval rating during his interview with Time, Trump dismissed concerns. “They’re fake numbers,” Trump said. “I would beat anybody running today by 20 points. Your numbers, that you have, are fake. The pollsters are corrupt. They’re almost as corrupt as the writers.” The US president added: “See, I’m doing very well. I think I am. Look, we have the strongest economy.” Despite Trump’s assertion, Americans do not feel the same way. Approximately 74% of Americans told AP/NORC that the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs. Voters’ frustrations with Trump could affect Republican candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, particularly those closely aligned with the US president. Polls show many Democratic candidates making progress with voters, even in historically conservative states such as Texas. Trump brushed aside the likelihood of Democrats winning, telling Time magazine that, so long as he campaigns with candidates, Republicans could perform well. Some Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that Trump will again make allegations of election fraud if Democratic candidates outperform Republicans in the November elections. Trump refused to concede the 2020 presidential election after losing to Joe Biden. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump has claimed US elections are insecure and signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods – such as restricting mail-in ballot voting and requiring ID. He has previously refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement his desired regulations. Other administration leaders, such as the FBI director, Kash Patel, have not ruled out the possibility of deploying federal law enforcement officers to polling locations, which is against the law. When asked whether he would declare a state of emergency before the midterms, Trump told Time magazine: “I don’t rule anything out or in. We’ll see.” Trump further specified that while he’s never invoked the Insurrection Act, a 19th-century law that allows the president to deploy military troops domestically under specific circumstances, he “could use it”. “A lot of people think I should use it sometimes,” Trump said. Among other topics the president discussed with Time magazine, he responded affirmatively when asked whether he regretted appointing supreme court justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “What can I do? I put them in. They voted against me too often. I was very – I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they voted against me often,” Trump said. The supreme court often votes in favor of the Trump administration but it has ruled against the president – such as in the case challenging his sweeping tariffs and his efforts to roll back birthright citizenship.

title: US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains
body_text: US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady since last year, when it hit 4.5% in November. US jobless claims also inched lower for the fourth week in a row, the labor department said on Thursday. But a closer look at the data also reveals how not all Americans are experiencing the same labor market. Unemployment among Black Americans grew an entire percentage point to 7%, double the rate of white Americans. Though job growth slumped over the summer – the labor market unexpectedly contracted in July and figures in June and May were revised sharply down from initial reports – 162,000 jobs were added in August, the highest since March. Job openings and the number of hires have also remained little changed in August, according to the recent data from the labor department, as the “slow-hire, slow-fire” job market continues. Data from private employers released by the payroll firm, ADP, earlier this week had painted a much rosier picture of the labor market. It found that private sector hiring accelerated last month for the first time since May, carried by growth in the healthcare, education and hospitality industries, and private employers added 90,000 new jobs. The labor market has remained largely strong this year even as the US-Israel war on Iran has upped inflation, especially energy prices. Last month, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years, citing higher prices. At the time, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, emphasized the strength of the US labor market, which “is basically running consistent with full employment”, but he noted that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Though the data still reflects an overall solid jobs market, the September release cools expectations for the US Federal Reserve to increase rates again in its final meeting before the 3 November midterms. Most central bank officials penciled in at least one more rate hike before the year’s end, which is now more likely to come at the Fed’s December conference. But higher prices continue to be the biggest economic pain point for Americans. Mortgage rates accelerated to their highest level in three years on Thursday from 7% to 7.28%, the largest weekly jump since 2022. The 10-year treasury yield, which underpins mortgages and other loans, also reached a 24-year high as the recent global bond sell-off continued. Meanwhile, higher oil prices have cost Americans an estimated $936 per household.

title: Seth Meyers on Trump: ‘Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for?’
body_text: Late-night hosts dug into Donald Trump’s unpopularity with GOP midterm candidates and his insistence on having US taxpayers foot the bill for recycled campaign ads. Seth Meyers On Thursday’s Late Night, Seth Meyers noted dissent within the Republican party over Donald Trump’s hugely unpopular war with Iran. In the run-up to the midterms next month, several GOP candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas and Ashley Hinson in Iowa, have run ads calling the war a mistake, though not directly calling out Trump himself. “I’m sorry, you both supported the war, and now you want it to end? Who is that campaign ad for – you?” Meyers asked. “Also by the way, very cool and not at all cowardly to call for an end to the war while not naming the president who started it,” he continued. “But I get it, you guys are in a tough spot. Trump doesn’t care about anyone but himself. When it comes to Republicans running in competitive races, Trump is thinking ‘maybe I help them,’ or” to quote Trump speaking in the Oval Office this week about Iran, “maybe I blow them up.” Trump had previously endorsed Paxton, but “his endorsement came with some very strange and unusual caveats,” said Meyers. As Trump put it in one of many similar asides on Paxton: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” “How would you like to have Trump as your wingman?” Meyers laughed. “‘Excuse me, miss, my friend over there thinks you’re very attractive. He, on the other hand, is not attractive at all.’” Later in the segment, Meyers noted: “Trump’s own lackeys are slamming him, his poll numbers are bad, his TV ratings are worse, which is why he’s found a new and totally legal way to get his message out: just air campaign ads on national television using your taxpayer money.” New ads in support of the midterms aired this week that look suspiciously like Trump’s ads from 2024 yet paid for by the US government, raising concerns from Congress. “They literally took a campaign ad they used in 2024 and re-aired it on TV using taxpayer dollars,” Meyers fumed. “He’s $2bn richer than he was two years ago, just pay for it yourself, you cheapskate! Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for? If you went out to dinner with Trump, he’d order everything on the menu then say I forgot my wallet, then ask you for 50 bucks, then put it into his wallet in front of you.” Jimmy Kimmel And on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host reacted to a new report finding that consumer confidence is now lower than it was during the pandemic. “Remember the good old days, when we thought our parents were going to die of a highly contagious disease?” he joked. “But don’t worry, the president says our nation is doing really well.” In a post on Truth Social, Trump claimed the US was doing “better than ever before, but the Public just doesn’t know how well we’re doing. title: A Democratic upset is brewing in Alaska’s governor’s race as Trump’s popularity craters
body_text: This July, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins spent four days and 450 miles (725km) wending his way down the Yukon River in a 24ft Alweld skiff, a flat-bottomed aluminum boat built for shallow Alaska rivers. Starting in Koyukon Athabascan country, he passed through Indigenous Deg Hit’an communities like Anvik, before ending among the Yup’ik villages of the lower river, Russian Mission and Pilot Station among them. The boat carried him through 11 villages – some only reachable by water or small plane, and most with fewer than 300 residents, and fewer still who could recall the last time they had seen a candidate for Alaska governor, Republican, Democrat or independent. The 37-year-old former state representative is hopping on snowmachines – only people in the lower 48 call them snowmobiles – as well as boats and floatplanes to accomplish what Alaska Democrats have failed to do for nearly a generation: win the governor’s office. “Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.” Just two years after Donald Trump carried Alaska by 13 points, his approval rating there has collapsed – a net 21- to 22-point swing, among the steepest drops in any reliably Republican state he won. In August, Kreiss-Tomkins came in first ahead of his Democratic and Republican rivals in the state’s non-partisan primary. Now, “JKT”, as he’s known in his home town of Sitka, is betting that an old-fashioned exercise in retail politics – traveling the vast expanse of a state larger than Texas, California and Montana combined and asking voters for their support in person – will help him do it again in November. But a question looms over the race: how much of his strength is a reflection of the changing national political environment, and Americans’ broad dissatisfaction with Trump, and how much is particular to the candidates, personalities and particular electoral system of the last frontier? Unlike nearly every other US state, Alaska no longer holds a traditional party primary followed by a winner-take-all general election. Under the ranked-choice voting system adopted by voters in 2020, the top four candidates from an open primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference, and votes can transfer to their next-ranked candidate as lower-placed contenders are eliminated. Though reliably Republican, the state has a long independent streak. The outgoing governor, Mike Dunleavy, an early supporter of Trump, leaves office deeply unpopular, largely for his unfulfilled promise to increase the amount of oil-dividend money Alaskans are given each year; in 2026, every eligible Alaskan received $1,000, with an additional $200 energy relief payment. This localized frustration coupled with Trump’s sagging approval ratings, particularly on the economy, has created a potential opening for Democrats. A recent bipartisan AARP poll found Kreiss-Tomkins winning 40% of first-choice preferences, compared with a combined 41% for his three Republican opponents, Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, all of whom will appear on Alaska’s general election ballot. *** Kreiss-Tomkins grew up in Sitka, a fishing town of 8,500 where compromise is required. It’s wedged among the spruce and hemlock of the Tongass national forest and the open swell of the north Pacific, where you can’t escape political opponents in a town with just 14 miles of coastal road, accessible only by water or air. He entered politics in 2012, at the age of 22, winning a statehouse seat by defeating the Republican incumbent by 32 votes. “JKT is the clear frontrunner for governor not because of anything Trump did, but because he’s running a good campaign,” said Larry Persily, who has watched Alaska politics since the 1970s, first as the owner of the Wrangell Sentinel newspaper and later as an editorial page editor at the Anchorage Daily News. “He’s energized a lot of young people. His Republican opponents are just a sorry lot. The Republicans just put up a bunch of political losers.” Wilson, the top-finishing Republican candidate, would disagree. The Anchorage garbage-hauling entrepreneur, who finished third in August’s primary, is a former competitive figure skater and the great-niece of the late Republican governor Wally Hickel. She has secured endorsements from the Arkansas governor, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, one of Trump’s press secretaries during his first term, and Alaska’s own Republican congressman, Nick Begich – along with Byron Donalds, the Florida congressman running to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor there. Wilson casts Kreiss-Tomkins’s decade in elected office, and his elite educational background – he dropped out of Yale University in 2011, one credit short of graduating – as liabilities. “Alaskans are looking for fresh leadership from the private sector,” she said in an emailed statement. “Not another ‘experienced’ politician who will wreck our energy economy, raise taxes, continue to fail us on the PFD [permanent fund dividend], and sell out Alaska to advance their career.” Wilson’s relationship with one of her Republican rivals is tangled: she chaired Bronson’s 2020 campaign for Anchorage mayor. He won, arrived in office as a political newcomer, then spent his single term fighting the assembly over homelessness – at one point floating one-way plane tickets to the lower 48 for people living on the street – before losing re-election to the independent Suzanne LaFrance in 2024. Republican candidate Taylor’s route to the ballot has been stranger still. The former state attorney general was elevated to the final slot after Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, only to be disqualified four days later over an undeclared rental income disclosure; briefly replaced by his own running mate; then reinstated after a department of law review – conducted by the office he used to run – found trivial but, he claimed, similar issues among dozens of other candidates. The three Republicans’ competing campaigns have prompted efforts to consolidate conservative support behind Wilson. Alaska’s electoral history offers a precedent. In 1994, Democrat Tony Knowles won the governorship by just 536 votes after the conservative vote split between Republican nominee Jim Campbell and Jack Coghill, the sitting lieutenant governor, who ran on the Alaskan independence party ticket. Knowles, the last Democrat elected to the office, went on to serve two terms. *** The governor’s race is unfolding against a national backdrop of declining approval for Trump. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published in September put his approval at 32%, with dissatisfaction over living costs among the principal concerns. But national figures alone cannot explain what is happening in Alaska, where the statewide candidates are also confronting distinctly local issues. Electing a Democrat here is not as surprising as it is in some other red states, said Tom Kizzia, a longtime Anchorage Daily News reporter and Alaska historian. “It’s that Alaska iconoclasm that kicks in – the simmering resentment of big business ripping off our resources.” The common thread, in Kizzia’s telling, is not a particular political party, but rather a distrust of whoever is currently perceived as extracting Alaska’s wealth without giving enough back – a role historically filled by outside oil and mining interests, and one conservatives have often redirected toward the federal government instead. That history helps explain why Trump’s brand of politics has not translated into durable support for his allies on this year’s ballot. “Dunleavy hitched himself to the Maga wagon, which contained elements of that iconoclasm,” Kizzia says. “But Trump was mostly about non-Alaska things that don’t register strongly with Alaska voters.” What does register, he argues, is Dunleavy’s failure to deliver on a hefty permanent fund check, the annual payment that Alaskans receive from the state’s oil-wealth savings each October. Dunleavy promised to up the amount of these checks, and even to pay Alaskans retroactively. None of this has come to pass. This same unresolved grievance now faces all three Republicans running to succeed him. Kreiss-Tomkins argues for a dividend payment that can be maintained without destabilizing the budget. “I want a permanent fund dividend that is meaningful and sustainable. We don’t need an election-year promise that blows a hole in the budget and is mathematically impossible,” he said. His campaign blends the Alaska tradition of “visiting” with people, sometimes onboard his skiff retrofitted with a three-quarter-ply cabin with the amber varnish flaking off, with a volunteer operation nicknamed “Superpod”, built on the premise that someone responding to a campaign text should reach an actual human being rather than a bot. That emphasis on personal contact was apparent to Debbie Moderow, who operates sled dog kennels near Denali national park and in Anchorage. At a meet-and-greet in Anchorage attended by about 30 people, she watched Kreiss-Tomkins climb on to a folding chair to address the crowd. “He was brimming with energy and wisdom, young and bright-eyed, and it was obvious that he had been obsessed with government in a geeky way for a long time,” she said. “I immediately thought, this guy has a vision, and a way to chart the way forward at a time when our state desperately needs it.” Persily, the newspaper publisher, who keeps his 100-year-old Underwood manual typewriter atop a restored lead-type cabinet and pops in CDs for music, sees the campaign’s emphasis on face-to-face campaigning as significant. “Elections are determined by turnout,” he said. “If you can turn out people who wouldn’t otherwise vote, that will make the difference. The public in the state is looking for someone who is going to excite people who wouldn’t otherwise get engaged. On a boat, on a snowmachine, what have you – Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, from what I can see, is making that happen.” It hasn’t been without hiccups. Kreiss-Tomkins’s campaign has attracted criticism over its finances. He outraised the entire field during the primary, drawing substantial contributions from outside Alaska, including six-figure sums from employees of artificial intelligence companies. He has responded by emphasizing his proposed moratorium on new Alaska datacenters and his support for regulations intended to protect Alaskans from harms associated with AI. His position is that the donations reflect support for his proposals rather than an effort to influence them. Asked about his priorities in office, Kreiss-Tomkins returns to two concerns familiar to Alaskans: education and the cost of living. “Our top-of-mind campaign issues are supporting our schools and lowering everyday costs for Alaskans,” he said. Whether dissatisfaction with Trump translates into votes for Democratic candidates remains a separate question from whether Kreiss-Tomkins can assemble a coalition of his own. The governor’s race will test both possibilities, alongside the ability of Alaska’s ranked-choice system to accommodate three Republican candidates competing for many of the same voters. For Moderow, Kreiss-Tomkins’s relative youth is less significant than his years of experience in Juneau. “People frame it as giving a young guy a chance,” she said. “For me, it’s the opposite. It’s giving a professional an opportunity when Alaska needs a leader.”

title: How Trump changed the way US women vote
body_text: A decade ago, Donald Trump’s improbable presidential campaign was rocked – and nearly derailed – by the now-infamous Access Hollywood tape, a 2005 recording in which the real estate developer turned reality TV star boasted about kissing and grabbing women without their consent. “When you’re a star, they let you do it,” he said, a remark he later downplayed as “locker-room talk” before musing that the tape might be fake. (It wasn’t.) In the moment, it felt fatal – the ignoble end of an explosive campaign for the White House. Back then, Americans hadn’t quite grasped Trump’s capacity to shock but not surprise. Within days, the outrage receded, swallowed by two more “October surprises” – WikiLeaks released the hacked emails of Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and then-FBI director James Comey announced the bureau was reviewing new emails related to her private server. That November, voters punished the first woman to be nominated for president by a major party for her emails, among other grievances, real and imagined, and handed the presidency to the man who had boasted that he could “grab em by the pussy”. US women haven’t voted the same since, and next month’s midterm elections offer another test of their tolerance for Trump in the Trump era. Long divided by race and class, Trump’s rise – or perhaps Clinton’s defeat – splintered US women further, along lines of educational achievement and marital status. In 2016, Trump won white women overall, but Clinton prevailed among college-educated white women, a partisan reversal from the presidential election four years earlier. In 2018, suburban women voters “revolted”, propelling Democratic victories and sending a record 102 women to the US House of Representatives in what was hailed as another Year of the Women. A conservative backlash brewed. The Senate confirmed Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court after Christine Blasey Ford testified that he had sexually assaulted her when they were teens – a claim he vigorously denied. Gen Z grew up in the shadow of that collision. As a cohort, they are marked by a wide ideological gender divide, with gen Z women – many mobilized by the overturning of Roe v Wade – becoming more progressive and politically engaged, while their male peers drifted rightward into Maga and the “manosphere”. Anger over the loss of federal abortion protections helped forestall Democratic losses in the 2022 midterms. But the gender gap wasn’t enough to shatter the glass ceiling in 2024, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris – even after a jury found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation in a civil suit brought by writer E Jean Carroll. A gender divide once again looms over the midterm map that will determine the balance of power in Washington for Trump’s final two years in office. A recent New York Times-Siena poll found 65% of women disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job as president, compared with 52% of men. According to the survey, 57% of women would back the Democratic House candidate in their district, whereas only 45% of men said the same, a dynamic that played out across three key Senate contests surveyed in the poll – Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. Trump has maintained that he has empowered women throughout his business and political career. His chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is the first woman to ever serve in the role. But polling suggests women are deeply dissatisfied with the president’s second-term performance, including, according to one national poll, one in four women who voted for him. In Maine, Republican senator Susan Collins, long considered untouchable, is facing voters for the first time since Kavanaugh joined four conservative justices to end the constitutional right to abortion. Her Democratic opponent, logger-turned politician Troy Jackson, is working hard to ensure voters don’t forget that their senator cast a decisive vote to put him on the bench. The Times poll shows him leading among women voters by 53% to 44%. Trump has cast the November election as a referendum on his presidency. Will voters cement his power – or turn over control to Democrats, and grind his agenda to a halt? It all may depend on what US women want. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter,” Rick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, said about Trump’s final years in office. Read more: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes Watch this race: A Hobbs’ Choice in Arizona A “unity ticket”? In these partisan times? Katie Hobbs, the Democratic governor of Arizona, and John Giles, a former Republican mayor of Mesa, a populous Phoenix suburb, are giving bipartisanship a whirl in the battleground state. Facing a tough re-election, Hobbs tapped Giles – a vocal Trump critic who formally left his party in May to become an independent after endorsing Kamala Harris in 2024 – to be her running mate. Hobbs’ choice of Giles is an overture to the independents and moderate Republicans she will likely need to secure a second term. Once a reliably Republican stronghold, Arizona has elected a string of Democrats statewide since Trump was first elected. In 2020, voters there narrowly backed Joe Biden for president before swinging back to Trump in 2024. This year is the first time Arizonans will elect a lieutenant governor, after voters approved the second-in-command role in 2022. Hobbs faces Republican congressman Andy Biggs, a staunch Trump ally who played a prominent role in the effort to overturn Biden’s 2020 victory. Biggs has chosen Sine Kerr, a dairy farmer and former state senator as his running mate. In an age of political tribalism and populist rage, is the center a viable path to power for the unassuming Hobbs-Giles ticket? *** The US politics team is hosting a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms. cleaned_body_text: A decade ago, Donald Trump’s improbable presidential campaign was rocked – and nearly derailed – by the now-infamous Access Hollywood tape, a 2005 recording in which the real estate developer turned reality TV star boasted about kissing and grabbing women without their consent. “When you’re a star, they let you do it,” he said, a remark he later downplayed as “locker-room talk” before musing that the tape might be fake. (It wasn’t.) In the moment, it felt fatal – the ignoble end of an explosive campaign for the White House. Back then, Americans hadn’t quite grasped Trump’s capacity to shock but not surprise. Within days, the outrage receded, swallowed by two more “October surprises” – WikiLeaks released the hacked emails of Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and then-FBI director James Comey announced the bureau was reviewing new emails related to her private server. That November, voters punished the first woman to be nominated for president by a major party for her emails, among other grievances, real and imagined, and handed the presidency to the man who had boasted that he could “grab em by the pussy”. US women haven’t voted the same since, and next month’s midterm elections offer another test of their tolerance for Trump in the Trump era. Long divided by race and class, Trump’s rise – or perhaps Clinton’s defeat – splintered US women further, along lines of educational achievement and marital status. In 2016, Trump won white women overall, but Clinton prevailed among college-educated white women, a partisan reversal from the presidential election four years earlier. In 2018, suburban women voters “revolted”, propelling Democratic victories and sending a record 102 women to the US House of Representatives in what was hailed as another Year of the Women. A conservative backlash brewed. The Senate confirmed Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court after Christine Blasey Ford testified that he had sexually assaulted her when they were teens – a claim he vigorously denied. Gen Z grew up in the shadow of that collision. As a cohort, they are marked by a wide ideological gender divide, with gen Z women – many mobilized by the overturning of Roe v Wade – becoming more progressive and politically engaged, while their male peers drifted rightward into Maga and the “manosphere”. Anger over the loss of federal abortion protections helped forestall Democratic losses in the 2022 midterms. But the gender gap wasn’t enough to shatter the glass ceiling in 2024, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris – even after a jury found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation in a civil suit brought by writer E Jean Carroll. A gender divide once again looms over the midterm map that will determine the balance of power in Washington for Trump’s final two years in office. A recent New York Times-Siena poll found 65% of women disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job as president, compared with 52% of men. According to the survey, 57% of women would back the Democratic House candidate in their district, whereas only 45% of men said the same, a dynamic that played out across three key Senate contests surveyed in the poll – Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. Trump has maintained that he has empowered women throughout his business and political career. His chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is the first woman to ever serve in the role. But polling suggests women are deeply dissatisfied with the president’s second-term performance, including, according to one national poll, one in four women who voted for him. In Maine, Republican senator Susan Collins, long considered untouchable, is facing voters for the first time since Kavanaugh joined four conservative justices to end the constitutional right to abortion. Her Democratic opponent, logger-turned politician Troy Jackson, is working hard to ensure voters don’t forget that their senator cast a decisive vote to put him on the bench. The Times poll shows him leading among women voters by 53% to 44%. Trump has cast the November election as a referendum on his presidency. Will voters cement his power – or turn over control to Democrats, and grind his agenda to a halt? It all may depend on what US women want. title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves
body_text: Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel. The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday. Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets. Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices. The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban. Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November. Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”. He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days. “We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said. Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”. The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall. The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows. In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia. The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September. The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels. In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy. The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy. Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day. Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said a US ban on diesel exports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market. “The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC. “So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added. The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran. The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. • This article was amended on 4 October 2026. Walt Chancellor was speaking in response to the news of a potential US ban on diesel exports, not about the subsequent reaction by some European nations.

title: Georgia holds emergency meeting on AI exposing voters’ secret ballots
body_text: When voters cast their ballots, their votes are supposed to remain secret: from their family, their neighbors, and the government. But what if artificial intelligence could make secret votes visible? Last month, Max Springer, a postdoctoral research fellow at Princeton University’s Center for Information Technology Policy, tested the prospect of identifying voters based on their Georgia ballots with a $20 subscription to an AI large language model and data obtained from an Open Records Act request. “Within a couple of hours, I had a pipeline to analyze and identify secret ballots across the state of Georgia and the agent told me exactly what further information it would need to identify real voters’ ballots,” Springer wrote. “At no point did the agent refuse to comply or raise concerns over implementing the exploit.” The issue has raised alarms among Georgia’s election officials less than two weeks before early voting starts in the high-stakes midterm election that will determine control of the US Congress. Ballot secrecy is a democratic safeguard, allowing voters to shield their selection from anyone who might try to influence or intimidate them into voting a certain way. But Springer’s test showed that he could use AI to find out who people voted for, using Georgia’s public election records. Georgia’s state elections board held an emergency meeting on Thursday morning to discuss how artificial intelligence has made it easier to identify voters through their ballot code, leaving people more vulnerable. Georgia’s outgoing secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, locked down the tabulation data that someone might use to identify a voter, ordering any public release to redact the ID numbers after an election, which “substantially address[es] this flaw”, said Ben Adida, an MIT-trained cryptographer and the founder of the election technology non-profit VotingWorks, as he addressed the board on Thursday. Election workers make a record of every voter who comes through a polling place. Voters then choose candidates on a touchscreen, which then prints out a paper ballot. The voter feeds that ballot by hand into a scanner to be tabulated. “When a voter inserts their ballot into a tabulator, a digital record of that ballot is created. Think of it as a row in a spreadsheet. One row is one scanned ballot. It’s often called a cast vote record, or CVR for short. In order to later retrieve the CVR, the tabulator assigns a unique identifier to each CVR at the time of scanning.” The flaw shows up in how the machine records that ballot, Adida said. The identifying is not actually random enough. Using AI, the early-voting list and the cast-vote record file for each county, Springer, the Princeton researcher who says he’s never been to Georgia, could recover the voting order for 1.52m ballots, or 98.9% of in-person ballots in 114 of the 139 counties he examined. “In some of Georgia’s counties, I can determine the exact ballot cast by every voter at the vote centers – ballot secrecy is entirely lost,” he wrote. In places with few voters on any given day, like tiny Heard county, Springer said: “the agent was able to match the majority of the 650 early in-person voters to a specific ballot, and the rest to within a single swap.” About four years ago, election security researchers had discovered a flaw in the software used by Georgia voters that could connect a voter’s identity to their secret ballot. The fact that ballots have an identifying number assigned at all is a product of the political paranoia attending Georgia’s elections. An ID number for each ballot addresses a fear of unscrupulous election workers double-stuffing ballots through tabulator machines. But if the order of ballots can be paired with other information, like sign-in data when a voter checks into the precinct, or perhaps Flock camera imagery that shows when someone entered a building on a slow day, then that ballot can be synched up to a voter’s name. Representatives of the secretary of state’s office say they have been shouting into the wind for help with this problem for three years. Requests for money have been bound up in the long-running political feud between Raffensperger and conservative legislators positioning themselves in the orbit of Donald Trump and 2020 election skeptics. (Raffensperger has remained a top Trump target after refusing to overturn his defeat in the state’s 2020 presidential election.) Spokesperson Robert Sinners sent a litany of emails and phone records showing requests for an appropriation to upgrade Georgia’s voting system, to no avail. The governmental affairs committee secretary, Tim Fleming, now the Republican nominee for secretary of state, was on the receiving end of many of those requests. “We have presented numerous plans to the legislature for this – not, not just a patch, but an entire overhaul of the software to fix up any known vulnerabilities,” Sinners said. “Guess what we were gifted with from the legislature? A big fat goose egg.” Fleming did not respond to a request for comment. Other states use Dominion software for their elections. Every other state has either patched the software or withholds vulnerable voting data from public inspection. Georgia law has two competing imperatives. The Georgia constitution explicitly requires a secret ballot, and the law protecting ballot secrecy in Georgia is among the strongest in the country. However, Georgia law – with revisions driven by the election disputes of 2020 – also demands transparency for election records. Elections board member Salleigh Grubbs raised that latter point as she circulated a draft proposal that would call for poll workers to hold ballots in a tray before voters cast them into the machine, to shuffle the printed pages out of order as a way to defeat the problem. Grubbs said that Raffensperger’s fix – redacting the ID numbers in the cast vote record – violates the law. But county elections officials and other board members – including Janelle King, a conservative Republican – dismissed the proposal as equally problematic. “We are asking our election officials to completely retrain everybody that has been a part of this process up until this point on how to administer the election,” King said. “I also have major concerns about dropping our ballots into a secured box and then having other individuals scan my ballot. How do I know that in the shuffling something doesn’t fall out? I mean, I just have some major concerns about whether or not we are creating more problems while we are trying to address a problem.” With early voting around the corner, changes to processes now are “a day late and about $30m short,” Sinners added.

title: Republicans pull funding of Trump-backed Senate candidate in critical North Carolina race
body_text: A major Republican political action committee pulled the plug on financial support for its Senate candidate in North Carolina, Michael Whatley, according to multiple reports, as the party begins to triage resources amid increasingly dire midterm polling. The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the campaign arm of the Senate majority leader, John Thune, has withdrawn its ad spending in North Carolina to redirect support to other candidates, Semafor reported on Friday. The New York Times, CNN and other publications have confirmed the report with sources close to the fund. The retirement of Thom Tillis from the US Senate opened the door for Democrats to flip the seat. Former governor Roy Cooper, a venerable presence in the state’s politics, easily won the Democratic nomination. Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, was handpicked by Donald Trump and viewed as a more mainstream candidate than other Republican contenders in the closely contested state. The SLF had pledged $71m to hold North Carolina’s US Senate seat, and started targeting Cooper before he even won the nomination. The fund ran ads last year trying to link Cooper with the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee, in an unprovoked attack onboard a light-rail train in Charlotte. Cooper was not in office at the time of the attack. The Pac’s advertising in North Carolina has consistently focused on crime and public safety, featuring a series of interviews with crime victims. Ronald Hayes, whose son Shemar was murdered in 2024, appeared in one such ad. Hayes later said he had been “swindled” by the SLF, believing he was going to appear in an advertisement against gun violence and not a political campaign ad. The SLF had planned to spend $30m more supporting Whatley. But polling data presents an increasingly difficult political map for Republicans trying to hold control of the Senate. Republicans have a 53-47 majority today. With the vice-president, JD Vance, as a tiebreaker, Republicans can afford to lose no more than three seats to keep control. The Cook Political Report rates the North Carolina Senate race as “leans Democratic”. Seven other races are toss-ups; five are currently held by Republicans, including seats in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Roger Marshall, the senator from Kansas, is facing a stiff challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor. Cook rates the race as “leans Republican”. The SLF reportedly will redirect its North Carolina spending to support Marshall. Cooper has persistently maintained a polling lead over Whatley despite the deluge of political ads. An AARP poll released on Monday gave Cooper an 11-point lead, consistent with other recent polls. Cooper has never had less than a four-point lead on Whatley in any poll this year. In-person early voting starts on 15 October in North Carolina.

title: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
body_text: Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party. Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!” In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state. The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol. “This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing. Malin was one of several speakers who reminded the people gathered of the history and fight for voting rights in the state, from the 1890 constitution, which disenfranchised Black voters and ushered in an era of Jim Crow, to the 1964 efforts of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic party and the work of Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer and others. Following the rally, those gathered marched to the capitol holding signs, their chants of “Leave our maps alone” and “Whose maps? Our maps” echoing through the capitol building. An hour before the hearing was scheduled to begin, the room was full, with some people leaning against the walls. Others sat in an overflow section outside and watched the proceedings on television screens. Prior to the proceedings, house Democratic leader Robert Johnson, who is Black, encouraged audience members to ensure that they made the historical record. “This is testimony,” said Johnson, one of several Democratic lawmakers who showed up to observe or speak at the proceedings. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.” The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, is primarily made up of white men. It consists of 16 Republicans, all of whom but one are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. The committee did not answer questions, provide information about how the redistricting process would look on their end or explain how citizens’ testimony would affect their decision. And in a room full of dozens of Black men and women, six of the first 10 speakers were white. The first Black woman called to give her testimony was the 15th person to speak. Overall, 67 people spoke. Each person was given two minutes to speak. The proceedings lasted just under two hours. State auditor Shad White, who is considering a gubernatorial run, created controversy almost as soon as he began his comments. “The delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does,” White said, as members of the audience booed. Bennie Thompson, who is Black, is Mississippi’s lone congressional Democrat. White, Reeves and other Republicans in the state have openly targeted Thompson and his district. Through continued boos, White said that there was a “silent majority” of people who “want better representation for the Mississippi delta”, and not someone who is “focused on running the January 6th committee”. Jesse Otto Smith, who was born and raised in Mississippi, said that the stakes of the redistricting hearing were personal. “I’m 76 years old. My father was born in 1926 – he couldn’t vote. My grandfather was born in 1891 – he couldn’t vote. That’s why I’m here. My great-grandfather was born as an enslaved man, considered less than a human, in 1861 – he couldn’t vote. He was a piece of property,” he said. “That’s why I am here. My mother graduated from Rust College, grew up in Starkville, but couldn’t go to school at Mississippi State, paid taxes without representation.” Walter Boone, who is white, called the redistricting efforts “Mississippi plan 2.0”. “The original Mississippi plan culminated in our 1890 constitution, and we cannot ignore that history. I’m not a scholar or trained historian, and even I know that Mississippi has been here before,” he said. “Our first reconstruction ended in much the same way, through a culmination of redistricting and fraud. Our Black elected representatives were stripped of their offices, and Black constituents did not see another person represent them that looked like them for 75 years.” Lauren Wilson, a sophomore at Tougaloo College from Tupelo, spoke in opposition to redistricting. She asked why the committee held hearings about redistricting, but not for Medicaid expansion or any of the myriad issues in the state. “If I’ve learned one thing from history, if I’ve learned one thing from the Lord, if I’ve learned one thing from my educators and my pastors, I’ve learned no matter who holds the position, the people hold the power,” she said. “The pharaoh had the position, but Moses had the power. Woodrow Wilson had the position, but Ida B Wells had the power. Lyndon B Johnson had the position, but Martin Luther King had the power. “We stand today before the committee who has to make a decision on redrawing the lines that seek to disenfranchise the people. So I want you to know that even though tonight you have the position, we hold the power.” The full legislature is expected to convene in a special session later this year to redraw the state legislative maps. While those maps would not affect November’s midterm elections, lawmakers will likely target Thompson’s seat before he is up for re-election in 2028.
