I’m trying to help elect Republicans.” Cruz, in turn, denied he was thinking about 2028 yet and suggested Vance may have a chip on his shoulder. “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz told Politico on Saturday. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes.” Yes, please continue making whatever comments you like, JD! In fact, I’d strongly suggest you take it up a notch and remind people of Cruz’s greatest hits. There was the time he fled to Cancún on holiday when his state, Texas, was facing deadly, record-breaking freezing temperatures, for example. And the time his official Twitter account “liked” a pornographic tweet (apparently it was “a staffing issue, and it was inadvertent”). And there’s the longstanding joke, which started with a meme in 2013, that Cruz is the Zodiac killer. Obviously, this was baseless, but it went viral because apparently it is believable. Indeed, a 2016 poll found that 10% of voters in Florida thought Cruz was the Zodiac killer and an additional 28% said they were not sure. That said, Vance should be careful about what he dishes out: he’s been the subject of a few memes himself. Who can forget the (completely unfounded) viral rumours about the vice-president having sexual relations with a couch? While Vance and Cruz may be butting heads now, I suspect they’ll eventually kiss and make up. They are pragmatists, which is a polite way to say soulless opportunists. They had similar journeys when it comes to Trump, for example. In 2016, Cruz called Trump, who nicknamed him Lyin’ Ted, a “serial philanderer” and a “pathological liar”. Around the same time, Vance wondered if Trump was “America’s Hitler” and called him “the most-raw expression of a massive finger pointed at other people”. Now, of course, it’s a very different story. Vance is veep and Cruz has become such a staunch Trump ally that the president calls him Beautiful Ted. With the news as grim as it is, you’ve got to find satisfaction where you can. And it’s certainly satisfying to watch Vance (who absolutely does not fornicate with furniture) and Cruz (who is definitely not the Zodiac killer) feud. Ultimately, though, it may turn out that we don’t have to worry about either man come 2028. MS Now’s Rachel Maddow thinks the president may follow the authoritarian playbook and install a family member as his successor. “If he wants [his family] to not end up in jail or prosecuted or having their … gains investigated … he’s got to make sure that the next president is also a Trump,” Maddow opined on a recent podcast. Potus himself has said “there could be” a Trump dynasty and seemed to suggest his daughter-in-law Lara may be his successor. Take a seat on a comfy couch for this one, JD: you’re going to have a tough time trumping a Trump. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: California to ‘actively monitor’ for possible threats after Trump said Iran could ‘take out’ LA and San Diego
body_text: California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, on Tuesday directed the state’s emergency preparedness center to “actively monitor” possible threats to the state after Donald Trump suggested Iran could “take out” the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. Trump has faced a chorus of condemnation from Democratic leaders in California after his comments at a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, which the White House has suggested were being taken out of context. At the president’s rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Trump claimed that high prices due to the war with Iran are a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. He went on: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded the line. “Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs,” Newsom said in a post on X, adding that the state’s threat-assessment center would be on heightened alert “in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California”. From the governor’s press office account, he taunted California Republicans for their “radio silence” in response the president’s bombastic remark. But one Republican House candidate, Jim Desmond, who is running in a competitive San Diego-based seat, pushed back. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our commander in chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond, a former mayor of San Marcos, said in a statement. It is a notable rebuke from a Republican in a closely watched contest that could help the party retain their razor-thin majority in the lower chamber. Desmond is set to face Marni Von Wilpert, a lawyer and member of San Diego’s city council, for the state’s 48th congressional district – which was redrawn in response to Proposition 50. Desmond, also a navy veteran, said that he “served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war”. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage,” he added. He joined a string of prominent Democrats who called out the comments. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, said: “The nuclear annihilation of an American city is no laughing matter.” Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor vying to succeed Newsom, said he wasn’t surprised by the president’s comments. “Donald Trump is a known commodity – you know how he acts, you know how he behaves,” Becerra told reporters at a campaign event in Los Angeles on Tuesday. But he took a jab at Republicans who “profess that they should be the leaders of our state” but were. not willing to “stand up to Donald Trump”. Becerra’s Republican rival, Steve Hilton, did not return a request for comment. But many Trump supporters dismissed the uproar. Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit to resemble Trump’s border wall, lives in San Diego and was at the rally in Nebraska. He said by phone on Tuesday: “I defend his comments absolutely. It is not inappropriate to mention something like that now because you have to take it in the context in which it is spoken. If you look at that context, it’s appropriate for a rally in which the president is addressing his base.” Marnell added: “The Democrats have a long and storied history of flying off the handle at any remark that President Trump makes, and this is just another chapter in that history, and I ascribe no significance to it, and in two days no one will be talking about it.” Darrell Issa, a Republican congressman who represents parts of southern California, did not directly respond to an inquiry about Trump’s remarks, but defended the president in a statement, saying he had “taken historic and concrete action to eliminate the nuclear threat, protect every inch of our homeland, and ensure Iran never threatens America or her allies ever again”. Paula Whitsell, chair of the Republican party of San Diego county, criticized what she called the “biased media” for taking the president’s remarks “completely out of context”. “No one should believe for a single moment that he wants ANY American city attacked,” Whitsell said in a statement. “The president was simply speaking to his belief that confronting Iran is worth it to eliminate the threat to our country and named two cities as an example of what could happen if we don’t act, not as an invitation for them to be attacked.” The White House also insisted that Trump was being willfully misinterpreted. Steven Cheung, its director of communications, posted on X: “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” The White House’s “Rapid Response 47” account called the Los Angeles Times newspaper “buffoons” and insisted that Trump was saying the US is “fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon – which they would if they had the chance.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. A previous headline implied it was Trump’s suggestion to “take out” LA or San Diego. Trump suggested that Iran could do so.

title: Jon Stewart on Trump and AI tech bros: ‘Stop lying to us’
body_text: Late-night hosts took aim at Donald Trump’s close ties to the AI industry and his flailing attempts to lure midterm voters. Jon Stewart On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart spoke about how AI had been a “great concern lately” and how the biggest AI leaders meeting at the White House seemed to suggest that something important was being done about it. But instead, the president went against many of his previous statements against tech bros to announce that they would be self-policing their actions. “They’re tyrants!” Stewart said in response. “I thought you hated these guys?” He asked “how can you justify letting the tech giants police themselves?” as well as “why can’t we just fucking slow this down rather than let people regulate something they have a clear conflict of interest in regulating?” When asked about the positive impact of AI, many of the key figures said that it would be used for the greater good but Stewart spoke instead about how it’s mostly being used at this moment. “So in the future we will use AI to cure diseases but right now it’s mostly murder, surveillance and surge pricing for the McRib,” he said. He added: “I’m getting the sense that you guys might be full of shit” before moving on to the topic of jobs and how they will be affected by the rise of AI. Many key tech figures have found themselves unable to fully answer how employment will be affected while also suggesting it won’t be a problem. “They can’t answer the jobs question in a straightforward manner,” he said, Stewart added: “My guess is that they’ll still have jobs when this is done”. He played a clip of Elon Musk claiming that AI will actually lead to a universal high income for us all. “If we let them do enough unfettered capitalism, we can apparently capitalism our way to socialism,” Stewart said. But he questioned why that money isn’t coming to us now. “Don’t call us welfare queens, just call us early adopters,” he joked. “Stop lying to us,” he added. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host spoke about flu season being more dangerous than ever, with a rise in other diseases, including the plague in Russia. “No worries, the gang who brought polio back is on the case,” he joked after showing a clip of Trump speaking about the story. Kimmel reminded viewers that the president is “a doctor but also Jesus” in reference to his AI social media posts. The host reminded viewers that the midterms are close and “you’d better be registered to vote” as Trump is trying to “save the Republican majority and his marriage”. Polls suggest his party won’t do well but if he can’t inspire the vote, “he’s gonna buy it from you” with the president repeating his claim that every American will receive $5,000 if Republicans win. “Why not make it five million dollars?” Kimmel asked before saying that Trump is “more likely to run a 5K than give it to us”. Trump has also been trying to tank Democrat James Talarico’s campaign as he is “one of the strongest candidates we’ve seen in a long time”. He is also still trying to make “dumocrat” happen even though “not one time has it gotten a laugh”. Taxpayer money has also been used for Trump ads and the FCC chair, Brendan Carr, has not found that to be a problem. Kimmel said it was “hard to see anything when your head is that far up the president’s ass”. Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers spoke about Trump claiming he is a “high IQ person” at a recent rally. “This dude thinks he’s a genius because he passed a dementia test,” he said. Trump, who is “obsessed with his own intelligence”, has recently spent time attacking Senator Tom Cotton as he has opposed a bill to establish year-round daylight savings time. The president raged against it to the press, complaining about the annoyance of changing clocks. “Nobody changes their clock any more!” Meyers countered before saying that Trump must be using his “stove as an alarm clock”. “We don’t just decide to make it dark earlier for no reason,” he said before suggesting Trump’s talk of light and dark made him sound like a Neanderthal. But Trump “desperately needs a win no matter how small” and recently gave out Cotton’s cell number on social media. “Never give Donald Trump your cell, you gotta be more careful with that,” Meyers said. Meyers said that Trump’s circle was now just “weirdos and losers”, which is what happened when you spend “a decade devoting yourself to someone with no fixed principles, allegiances and loyalties”.

title: Election deniers stoke Trump-driven ballot security fears before midterms
body_text: Prominent election deniers have spent recent weeks stoking fears over US election security before next month’s midterms, echoing claims pushed by Donald Trump to justify asserting more control over voting. On conservative-friendly media outlets, former or current officials who tried to bolster the US president’s false claims of mass voter fraud in 2020 have in recent weeks made fresh allegations of election vulnerabilities. Cleta Mitchell, a former politician who tried to help Trump overturn the 2020 election results, capitalized on recent reports that voting machines in Georgia had a privacy vulnerability to assert the state was not doing enough to secure voters’ ballots. “The problem in Georgia is that they use a version of these machines where … the machine doesn’t count the choices. The machine actually counts a QR code,” Mitchell told the conservative strategist and longtime ally Steve Bannon in an interview on Friday. Ed Martin, the controversial former US pardon attorney, repeated claims from top administration officials that voting machines, which used parts manufactured in China and other countries, were “compromised”. Other election deniers have planted seeds of doubt about the predicted outcome of the 2026 midterm elections. Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, which established and published Project 2025, told Fox Business in September that predictions Democrats could flip the Senate were “a psyop” – a term popularized by online theorists to describe something they believe authorities are doing to influence people covertly. “I think that this prognosticating is a psyop by so many of these polling firms. In order to do what? To depress conservative turnout,” Roberts said. In conducting media hits about election integrity, some prominent election deniers also revealed that the Trump administration was continuing its effort to assert greater power over states, which are responsible for running elections. Martin told Eric Bolling of Real America’s Voice on Monday that Trump had met with Tina Peters, a politician convicted of crimes related to her efforts to interfere with 2020 election results. “Just hours ago, maybe two hours ago, Tina Peters, you know, from Colorado, was in the Oval Office meeting with the president on election integrity, and they were talking about the plans,” Martin said. “The president is taking it seriously. If the Congress won’t pass the Save America Act, and they won’t, then the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do,” Martin added. Trump has sought to undermine public confidence in US elections by promoting false claims of election fraud and making unverified claims of election insecurity. Earlier this year, the president tried to heighten those claims in a prime-time address. The president has attempted to crack down on voting, ostensibly to secure elections – despite experts assuring voters that elections are already secure. That includes directing his administration to implement new rules to restrict mail-in ballot voting, a method of voting Trump has criticized despite using it himself, create a federal database of eligible citizens, and force voters to provide proof of citizenship when voting in federal elections. Most of those actions have been stalled by court challenges. The supreme court has allowed the administration to move forward with compiling a federal database of eligible voters. Mitchell told Bannon she had “on good authority, from some of the highest levels in the Trump administration”, that the justice department was inquiring with the Georgia secretary of state about voter data it shares with two non-profit groups. She accused the states, including Georgia, of being “hypocrites” for refusing to share voter data with the federal government.

title: Disney accuses Trump officials of ‘blatant violations’ of constitution amid FCC battle
body_text: Lawyers for Disney accused the Trump administration of “blatant violations of the US constitution” and censorship on Tuesday in the first court hearing over the Federal Communications Commission’s early review of the media giant’s eight local television station licenses. District judge Loren AliKhan seemed unswayed by government arguments that the order to force Disney’s ABC to apply years early to renew local television station licenses was tied to an investigation into parent company Disney’s hiring practices. ABC, Disney and its station group filed suit against the FCC in August, seeking to block the US media regulator from taking any further steps to punish or pressure the network in connection to the order. In its lawsuit, ABC argued that the FCC’s actions – taken at the behest of the Donald Trump-appointed chair, Brendan Carr – were actually intended to chill the network’s speech, which the president and Carr have argued is tilted against the administration. In legal filings and during Tuesday’s hearing, the network cited past threats by the president and the FCC chairman that jeopardized the licenses of television networks, including ABC on several occasions, for editorial purposes. “These are blatant violations of the US constitution,” the prominent trial lawyer Beth Wilkinson, arguing on behalf of ABC, told the judge during the approximately two-hour hearing. She said ABC faced a “chilling effect” that has affected – and will continue to impact – its editorial decision-making, as the network steers clear of political bookings and any other programming decisions that could spark further ire from the Trump administration and Carr. “That chilling effect has been happening and will happen every day,” she said, causing “irreparable harm” to the network and its ability to broadcast independent news for the benefit of the American people. ABC has said it has stopped booking politicians on the daytime talkshow The View and chose to air a July speech by Trump on its streaming platform so as not to antagonize the president. “Our editorial decisions are being affected right now,” Wilkinson said, noting the significance of decisions about how to cover next month’s pivotal midterm elections. “We are watching everything we do … We have already altered our conduct because of the fear of retaliation.” She also noted that ABC recently chose to air a Jimmy Kimmel-conducted interview with Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube, rather than television, “because the FCC has no control over YouTube”. Dimitar P Georgiev, representing the FCC defendants, argued that “there is no reason to believe the early renewal order has prompted changes to the plaintiffs’ editorial decisions”. He also argued that the US district court for the District of Columbia was not the proper jurisdiction for the case, saying that ABC could instead appeal any adverse decision to the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia. ABC is seeking a decision from the judge to enjoin the FCC from taking any further actions against the network’s licenses. “We are asking to stop pure retaliation, putting us in a process that we should never have to be in,” Wilkinson said. In what Wilkinson called a “fatal admission”, Georgiev said the license renewal process “is not about the licenses”, but is instead a “tool” to expedite the commission’s review of ABC for potential violations of federal equal opportunities regulations. The lawyer also said the FCC could choose to end the license review process early if ABC is able to satisfy its document requests. Considering that the FCC opened its employment practice investigation into Disney last year, with requests for documents ongoing since then, the judge asked: “Why is it only in the summer that you determined that their responses were woefully inadequate?” She also questioned why the commission required the company to submit renewal applications for all eight of its stations simultaneously. And she noted past comments by Carr about the network’s licenses, including a remark in July, when he had said ABC’s decision not to carry the president’s speech that month on its linear channel could factor into the license investigation. “It strikes me with all the comments that this was merely over a discovery dispute, what made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Judge AliKhan asked lawyers for the FCC, whom she asked for a list of some of the other enforcement actions the commission could have taken short of calling up the network’s licenses early. And she noted that there was “some daylight” in the FCC’s arguments, considering that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) inquiry was handled by the commission’s enforcement bureau, while the license order was made by the media bureau. The judge ended the hearing without issuing an order, saying she would take the matter “under advisement”.

In legal filings and during Tuesday’s hearing, the network cited past threats by the president and the FCC chairman that jeopardized the licenses of television networks, including ABC on several occasions, for editorial purposes. “These are blatant violations of the US constitution,” the prominent trial lawyer Beth Wilkinson, arguing on behalf of ABC, told the judge during the approximately two-hour hearing. She said ABC faced a “chilling effect” that has affected – and will continue to impact – its editorial decision-making, as the network steers clear of political bookings and any other programming decisions that could spark further ire from the Trump administration and Carr. “That chilling effect has been happening and will happen every day,” she said, causing “irreparable harm” to the network and its ability to broadcast independent news for the benefit of the American people. ABC has said it has stopped booking politicians on the daytime talkshow The View and chose to air a July speech by Trump on its streaming platform so as not to antagonize the president. “Our editorial decisions are being affected right now,” Wilkinson said, noting the significance of decisions about how to cover next month’s pivotal midterm elections. “We are watching everything we do … We have already altered our conduct because of the fear of retaliation.” She also noted that ABC recently chose to air a Jimmy Kimmel-conducted interview with Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube, rather than television, “because the FCC has no control over YouTube”. Dimitar P Georgiev, representing the FCC defendants, argued that “there is no reason to believe the early renewal order has prompted changes to the plaintiffs’ editorial decisions”. He also argued that the US district court for the District of Columbia was not the proper jurisdiction for the case, saying that ABC could instead appeal any adverse decision to the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia. ABC is seeking a decision from the judge to enjoin the FCC from taking any further actions against the network’s licenses. “We are asking to stop pure retaliation, putting us in a process that we should never have to be in,” Wilkinson said. In what Wilkinson called a “fatal admission”, Georgiev said the license renewal process “is not about the licenses”, but is instead a “tool” to expedite the commission’s review of ABC for potential violations of federal equal opportunities regulations. The lawyer also said the FCC could choose to end the license review process early if ABC is able to satisfy its document requests. Considering that the FCC opened its employment practice investigation into Disney last year, with requests for documents ongoing since then, the judge asked: “Why is it only in the summer that you determined that their responses were woefully inadequate?” She also questioned why the commission required the company to submit renewal applications for all eight of its stations simultaneously. And she noted past comments by Carr about the network’s licenses, including a remark in July, when he had said ABC’s decision not to carry the president’s speech that month on its linear channel could factor into the license investigation. “It strikes me with all the comments that this was merely over a discovery dispute, what made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Judge AliKhan asked lawyers for the FCC, whom she asked for a list of some of the other enforcement actions the commission could have taken short of calling up the network’s licenses early. And she noted that there was “some daylight” in the FCC’s arguments, considering that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) inquiry was handled by the commission’s enforcement bureau, while the license order was made by the media bureau. The judge ended the hearing without issuing an order, saying she would take the matter “under advisement”.

title: S&P 500 and Nasdaq surge to record highs after AI chipmaker rally
body_text: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at a record high after a rally around AI chipmakers and a dip in US treasury yields. At market’s close, the S&P 500 was up 0.58%, topping 7,800 for the first time in its history. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 0.45%, while the Dow, which is slightly down from its record high in August, climbed 0.49%. Investors appeared optimistic after recent developments for chipmakers including Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that showed growth in the markets for the chips used to power AI. Wall Street has also grown more optimistic that the US Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its next board meeting in October. Job figures from September showed underwhelming growth in the labor market, and multiple Fed officials have said the next interest rate increase can probably wait. The optimism in the stock market, largely coming from continuing investment in AI, has defied other signs of instability in the US economy and global politics. The US bond market, typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, has been in turmoil in recent weeks. US bond yields, or the return an investor receives when a bond matures, reached recent highs amid concerns over high inflation and interest rates. The yield for 10-year US treasury bonds on Monday reached 5.349%, the highest since April 2022, before dipping back down on Tuesday. For American consumers, higher energy prices continue to be a major pain point. While gas prices have dipped over the last week, prices are still about $1.20 a gallon on average higher than a year ago. Diesel, which is used to fuel trucks, buses and trains, has also gone down from record high but is still over 40% higher than a year ago. The economy is expected to be a top issue in the upcoming midterm elections, with many voters expressing frustration over high prices. Donald Trump, who has been stumping for Republican candidates across the country, has been trying to paint a different picture for voters. At a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump said that “our nation is doing better now than it’s ever done” and that gas prices would fall below $1.85 a gallon “in no time”.

title: Trump says he is weighing suspension of federal gas tax
body_text: Donald Trump said on Tuesday his administration was considering suspending the federal gasoline tax, a sign the president is noticing voter anger over fuel costs a month before the midterm elections. “We’re thinking about that,” Trump said when asked whether the tax should be suspended. Any suspension would require an act of Congress. The president cannot unilaterally suspend the federal tax. Trump first raised the idea in May, as the Iran war pushed fuel prices sharply higher. Pump prices have stayed high since. The national average for regular was $4.3685 a gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA, more than a dollar above where it stood a year ago. The federal tax is 18.4¢ a gallon on gasoline and 24.4¢ on diesel. Dropping it would cut about 4% from the price of a gallon of regular. The tax also brings in more than $23bn a year for highways and public transit. Asked about the midterms, Trump said he expected Republicans to “do very well”. He said his rallies, were “changing things around” because voters were hearing “what the Republicans have done”. “Prices are now coming way down,” he said. “And oil, as soon as the war is over, which will be soon, will be coming way down.” He gave no date for the end of the war and did not say how a tax suspension would pass Congress.

title: ‘Not exactly his favorite senator’: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
body_text: Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine, pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times. Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans, saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator. Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate. Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform. Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion. “Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways. “He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?” Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992. Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”. Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine. “I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.” Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border. “I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.” Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

title: Skepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’
body_text: Donald Trump has long sought to portray himself as a man of steel, from the White House photoshopping Trump to look like Superman, to enacting tariffs on steel and approving the sale of US Steel to Japan’s Nippon Steel with a ”golden” share given to the US government. Most recently, the Trump administration announced plans to construct the largest steel plant in the US, a $15bn plant in Lee county, Iowa, to be built by India-based Mesabi Metallics. But the project and claims surrounding it have incited skepticism over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record and the financial history of Mesabi Metallics’ parent company, Essar Global. The plant had originally been scheduled to be built in Minnesota, a state that usually votes for Democrats. The shift to Iowa – where Republicans are struggling in the midterms – has also attracted attention. Doug May, who worked for 43 years as a steelworker at a mill in Granite City, Illinois, characterized the announcement as “political pandering” given the timing and how tariffs are hurting Iowa farmers. “He pulled the same thing in 2018, just before an election, when he announced that $10bn Foxconn project,” May said. That project, in swing state Wisconsin, failed to produce the jobs Trump and Foxconn had promised. May argued Trump was using the steel industry as a campaign strategy, while ignoring the work the United Steel Workers have done to push to save the industry, including filing more than 150 trade cases over the past decades to combat unfair trade practices that harm US workers. More than 40 domestic steel producers in the US filed for bankruptcy in the late 1990s. “We, the steel workers in Granite City, served as the best foot soldiers lobbying Congress, holding rallies and campaigns, to raise awareness to the cheating of foreign steelmakers and the need for stronger trade enforcement during that era,” added May. “Arguably, we played a very important role in saving domestic steel.” Essar Global first proposed building a steel plant with a $1.65bn investment in the Mesabi iron range in north-east Minnesota when they purchased Minnesota Steel in 2007. By 2016, Essar Steel Minnesota had filed for bankruptcy, following construction delays and financing issues at its Nashwauk, Minnesota, project, where its iron ore mine, which is supposed to fuel the Iowa steel plant, is located. In efforts to get rid of its debt, Essar Global sold off assets, including the completion of a sale of Essar Oil for $12.9bn to a Russia-controlled energy company. Mesabi Metallics briefly changed ownership to Virginia billionaire Thomas Clarke, before he lost control of the company in 2018, with Essar Global regaining control, but then losing its mining leases in 2021 when the state of Minnesota revoked them after a missed deadline. “This plant that has been 20 years in the making,” said Mark Dayton, former governor of Minnesota who dealt with Mesabi Metallics in the state through their bankruptcy proceedings. “I had, a decade ago, a very bad experience with Essar Steel because they started this plant, raised lots of expectations and hopes up north, and then went into default and went into bankruptcy and the like,” he said. Dayton said it did look like the plant was “actually proceeding, which is great if they’re going to actually complete building this plant”. But he added: “I’m skeptical of the announcement in Iowa this close to the election. That’s going to require $15bn of investment. I’d like to see that money on the table from Essar before they start to bring a shovel.” Some, including May, see echoes of Trump’s Foxconn announcement in June 2018. Ahead of the 2018 midterm elections, Trump described plans by the Taiwanese electronics contract manufacturer to open a gargantuan site outside Milwaukee as “the Eighth Wonder of the World” and said the plant “will provide jobs for much more than 13,000 Wisconsin workers”. Trump’s promises came as his approval ratings with the public were low, with Democrats poised to take advantage and regain control of the House. The site currently has about 1,100 employees and became an albatross around the necks of its backers as Foxconn’s ambitious plans failed to materialise. This time around, Trump’s approval ratings are even lower than they were in 2018 and Democrats are expected to regain control of the House and possibly the Senate. Trump has claimed “they’ve already started building” the plant, though a local NBC news affiliate in Iowa reviewed county records and disputed this claim. “The review found no major property purchases tied to the project this year. County officials say they don’t have details from the company about its plans. No permits have come before supervisors,” TV6 Investigates reported. A site location has not been disclosed by elected officials or Mesabi Metallics, with steel production aimed to begin in 2030. Mesabi Metallics did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In Iowa, the state’s Sierra Club chapter criticized the special state legislature session called for by the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, to expand government subsidies the state can provide to Mesabi Metallics for the project. The state government is experiencing budget shortfalls, with more than $1bn in deficits the past two years. “Any time we step up incentive programs above and beyond what we’re giving, our revenues are going to be downgraded. And I understand there’s going to be jobs and economic activity around this, but the state is hurting financially,” said Pam Mackey Taylor, director of the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club. “Do we need to really double the incentives that other large projects get to support this steel project?” The Iowa governor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In a special session, the Iowa legislature approved $1.36bn in tax incentives over 10 years to Mesabi Metallics. The steel plant is projected to create 1,750 permanent jobs and support up to 6,000 construction jobs. The White House did not comment directly on the steel plant’s move to Iowa or on White House senior communications strategist Jason Miller’s past work as a registered foreign lobbyist for Mesabi Metallics. Mesabi Metallics paid at least $240,000 SHW Partners, a government relations firm led by Miller, according to lobbyist disclosure records. The government of India also paid his firm $150,000 per month for “strategic counsel, tactical planning and government relations assistance on policy matters before the US government”, with the contract beginning in April 2025. Miller said the contract with India stopped in June 2026 and claimed the lobbying for Mesabi Metallics was domestic, not foreign, and ended in July 2026. “Taking a lobbyist who’s on the payroll of a foreign government and companies with huge government contracts and putting him inside the White House will create a three-headed beast of divided loyalties,” said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate at Public Citizen, in a statement on Miller’s appointment to a White House role. In response to Miller’s lobbying work and criticisms of it, Miller said: “Public Citizen is a bunch of America-hating fake news soy boy losers who prefer new investments go to China and not the US, and respectfully, they can get rekt. Not only did I deregister from Mesabi Metallics months ago, I took the additional step of recusing myself from having anything to do with their announcement at the White House.” A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said in an email: “No president has done more to revive American steelmaking than President Trump, whose 50 percent Section 232 tariffs on steel is driving record investments into this key sector. Those tariffs, along with the Administration’s other pro-growth and pro-investment policies, are not going away anytime soon.”

title: Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law
body_text: Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “millionaire tax” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was signed into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it. An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A coalition of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions. Facing dwindling federal funds under the Trump administration yet home to substantial tech-industry wealth, including prominent billionaires such as Bill Gates, Steve Ballmer and, until recently, Jeff Bezos, Washington has joined other states and municipalities by turning to its wealthiest earners as a source of revenue. Massachusetts, Maine and New York already impose a unique tax rate on millionaires, and Hawaii passed a similar measure in May. California, whose resident billionaires possess a collective net worth hovering above $2tn, will see voters decide on a proposed one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth. The measure is opposed by most billionaires as well as Gavin Newsom, the governor; some progressive groups also question the long-term benefits of the one-off tax. Washington’s governor, Bob Ferguson, has said he would veto any effort to expand the millionaire tax to encompass lower-earning households. And, after decades of voter-rejected efforts to reform the state’s tax structure, which has historically lacked an income tax and instead levied sales taxes, property taxes and fees, Washingtonians in recent years have approved new progressive revenue streams, including a capital gains tax. Advocates claim that the millionaire tax is part of a clear mandate to better align the state’s largely regressive tax code with its progressive values. *** The statewide fight over an income tax really began in the 1930s, according to the Washington state senate majority leader, Jamie Pedersen, an architect of the millionaire tax. Nearly 100 years ago, the state’s supreme court ruled that income taxes constituted a property tax, hamstringing efforts to diversify beyond flat-rate excises. By 2002, a state commission led by Bill Gates Sr concluded that Washington’s tax code was uniquely regressive, and called for a state-level income tax. But, in 2010, voters still voted by wide margins against a proposed tax for those earning above $200,000; Steve Ballmer, Microsoft’s then CEO, was the leading contributor to the campaign opposing the tax, and the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, ranked fourth. A reliance on sales, property and other taxes leaves the state with “the second-worst tax code in the nation when it comes to who actually pays as a share of their income”, said Emily Vyhnanek of the Washington State Budget and Policy Center, a non-partisan research group. Those in the lowest-earning quintile spend up to 13.8% of their annual income on state taxes, while those in the top 1% currently spend about 4%, they said. In 2021, lawmakers passed a 7% tax on capital gains above $250,000, which survived a constitutional challenge and a conservative-led ballot initiative aiming to overturn it in 2024. The initiative’s resounding defeat was “some indication that voters were willing to vote for something that the opponents labeled as an income tax”, Pedersen said. By 2025, facing a nearly $15bn shortfall over the ensuing four years, Democratic lawmakers debated new ways to tackle the state’s structural budget problem, and landed on the high earners’ income tax. Lawmakers had “99.9% certainty” that conservative groups would challenge the tax through a ballot initiative, Pedersen said. *** Brian Heywood, a conservative hedge fund executive and the founder of Let’s Go Washington, a political action committee, has helped spearhead and fund initiative 645, the ballot initiative to overturn the millionaire tax. Let’s Go Washington is behind two other proposals, including a campaign to ban trans girls from participating in girls’ sports at school. Opponents have expressed alarm at the initiative and have dubbed it “the most extreme proposal of its kind”, as it would require girls to undergo “verification of biological sex” during sports physicals, potentially through genital exams. Pedersen suggested that advocates interested in overturning the millionaire tax may “have figured out Brian Heywood” and may be “trying to distance themselves from his pretty toxic brand”. The state supreme court is also slated to hear a legal challenge to the tax early next year, which will test the validity of the new income tax against state-constitutional and legal precedent. ••• Recent polling suggests that the initiative is likely to fail. In a survey of Washington residents, research firm DHM found 57% of respondents opposed repealing the tax. Kara Krnacik, who helped lead the survey, said Washington residents may be growing more open to an income tax below the million-dollar threshold: 41% of respondents said they were in favor of an income tax that might eventually extend to those making $100,000 or more, up from 36% in November 2025. But if the tax is overturned, lawmakers face a “very stark reality”, Pedersen said, and may have to find revenue through “inferior alternatives” such as hiking the sales tax rate, or enacting a statewide payroll tax. Meanwhile, if the tax survives, Pedersen said lawmakers may begin to scrap or reform other regressive taxes in Washington, including its business taxes. “I think it’s really significant that you do not see almost any major business that is aligning itself with the initiative 645 folks,” Pedersen said. Public disclosure records suggest the initiative’s opponents have outspent its supporters by more than 50%; and major labor unions in the state have contributed more than $6m to the campaign defending the tax. In addition to new legal challenges, Heywood said he had begun to consider ways to circumscribe how unions receive and disburse funds in the state.

title: Trump administration sued over plans to send election monitors to voting sites
body_text: The Trump administration has been sued over its plans to deploy “a historic number” of election monitors to polling stations during next month’s midterm elections. The bid “stands to jeopardize” the elections and could “interfere with the right of voters to participate in the election free from intimidation”, according to the NAACP, which filed a lawsuit against Harmeet Dhillon, head of the justice department’s civil rights division, who has said she hopes to send 1,000 monitors to midterm polling sites in November. “To be clear, there is no federal statute that gives the US Department of Justice [DoJ] the right to send their so-called ‘election monitors’ to polling sites across the country, and this administration has made clear its intent to disrupt and interfere with the way elections are run in our country,” said Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, who served in Dhillon’s role under Joe Biden. The NAACP lawsuit seeks to force the Trump administration to release records regarding the deployment of the monitors. The NAACP said it requested such records under the Freedom of Information Act on 1 September, but said the Department of Justice had failed to comply. “The timely release of these documents is critical to protecting voter rights and ensuring election integrity,” the NAACP said in a statement. On Sunday Todd Blanche, the attorney general, confirmed that election monitors will be sent to all 50 states. Speaking to Fox News, however, he downplayed the role of the monitors. “Since the 60s, the Department of Justice has monitored elections. Every single election’s been monitored,” Blanche said. “This administration, President Trump, is doing the same thing that every single administration has done in our generation, multiple generations.” In a statement a justice department spokesperson said: “Department election monitors comply with all legal and ethical requirements, including the requirement that they not interfere with the voting process, and their work is consistent with longstanding department practice of monitoring elections for compliance with federal law.” The monitors have raised concerns, however, from within the Republican party. In August Mark Gordon, the Republican governor of Wyoming, criticized the behavior of two election monitors who he said arrived at a polling station during the state’s primaries earlier this year without notice, and attempted to examine voting machines. “It was aggressive, unexpected, disruptive – certainly didn’t seem to show respect for the state,” Gordon told the New York Times. “We’re going to get to the bottom of it as best we can.” The justice department spokesperson said: “AAG Dhillon had a cordial meeting with Gov Gordon, the Wyoming Attorney General, and the county clerk for Laramie County. We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were ‘aggressive’ or did anything improper. The discussion with the Governor and his team was helpful and we look forward to having a presence in Wyoming in the general election.” “During the primary season, we saw monitors deployed with no notice to the public or jurisdiction, and no clear evidence that they were there for a legitimate civil rights purpose,” Clarke said. “Americans deserve to know whether the justice department is abusing its law enforcement powers to the detriment of voters and the election officials tasked with running our elections. Americans deserve transparency on the justice department’s increasingly evolving and unwieldy plans. With election day just weeks away, the NAACP is seeking judicial intervention to ensure transparency and to safeguard the fundamental right to vote.”

title: ‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible
body_text: Donald Trump was in Nebraska on Monday, and though his long rally speech had elements of a performance, this was no Bruce Springsteen album. He offered another dark meditation on a world spiraling out of control, one in which the destruction of American cities is increasingly a possibility, unless Americans trust him to use the vast powers of the presidency to annihilate his foes. The president drew fury when he suggested that Iran could launch a nuclear attack and “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego. California leaders reacted with scorn at Trump’s alarmism. Governor Gavin Newsom denounced Trump as “deranged and dangerous”, while the mayors of Los Angeles and San Diego, Karen Bass and Todd Gloria, objected strenuously to putting their cities in harm’s way, even if only in his feverish imagination. Perhaps the worst problem with Trump’s speech – and there were many – was not that it vividly daydreamed about Armageddon-on-the-Pacific. It was just so delusional that it had almost no basis in fact at all. It is inherently destabilizing when a nation’s leader cannot be trusted to make an accurate statement, and the situation is especially troubling when the nation is the United States, the defender of the rules-based order since 1945. First, the claim itself. When read inside the transcript, the words don’t make a great deal of sense. It’s almost like scat singing as the president goes into his famous “weave”, his word for the way he lurches from one half-formed thought to another, like a rodeo clown on a bucking bronco. “[Kamala] stole a lot of things that didn’t work out too well. But I want, I wanna see, I wanna see a tremendous victory. You wanna see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the word, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. “They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s, this is a very small price to pay, and it’s gonna be over very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.” If he was talking about the war as being “almost over with”, then he’s certainly wrong, as the conflict drags into its eighth month with no sign of resolution. But if he was talking about the midterms, then he’s correct that it will end soon, and not well for him. In effect, he now has to go into the reddest part of a red state to sustain his vanishing popularity. Monday night’s rally was held at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds, in Hall county, Nebraska, which had a population of 62,895 in 2020. Even farmers are wary of this war, which has raised the price of fertilizers and diesel. The language about LA and San Diego was to be fair, quite vague. Presumably, he was worried that Iran’s nuclear program might be able to target LA or San Diego. But by saying “let them …” it almost sounded like he was encouraging them to, as when John F Kennedy, in Berlin, held up that city as a model of courage and said: “Let them come to Berlin,” in both English and German). In either case, there is no possibility of it happening, as his military advisers know, and as even he must know at some level. Iran does not have a nuclear weapon, nor can its missiles reach the United States, on either the east or west coast. Furthermore, it is the height of irresponsibility to even discuss such an unimaginable threat. All foreign leaders understand that any attack on the United States with a nuclear weapon would result in an overwhelming counterattack. It’s called deterrence. It is that knowledge – and the cautious way in which previous American presidents have talked about nuclear weapons – that has helped to preserve the peace all these years. We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad. The rest of the speech was also a mess. There was a lot of red-baiting, despite the fact that the cold war ended in 1991. There were the usual schoolyard insults, in this case lobbed toward the Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (“I call him Alfred E Neuman”) and Georgia senator Jon Ossoff (“he looks like Pee-wee Herman to me”). And more pot-stirring, with no basis in fact. Often, his claims undermined each other, as Trump claimed both that Iran has been rendered toothless (“we’re kicking Iran’s ass”) and that it remains a lethal threat, capable of destroying our second- and eighth-largest cities. Which one is it? Over and over, we have heard that Iran’s nuclear program has been “obliterated”. But if so, why are we still at war? The rest of the speech was the usual farrago of distortions and lies, as the most casual effort to factcheck shows. “We want honest,” Trump said at one point, confusingly. Yes, we do. But whether we are going to get it, is another question entirely. Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

title: Paxton admits Trump’s Iran war and US gas prices are plaguing Republicans in leaked audio
body_text: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted privately that rising fuel prices as a result of Donald Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms in the latest leaked audio recording. Asked what issues were “dragging” his campaign at a closed-door fundraising event, Paxton replied, “It’s not tariffs … it’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” according to an audio recording shared with Axios. “When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch,” Paxton said. Paxton acknowledged affordability was Republicans’ “biggest problem” heading into next month’s election, citing polling numbers that indicate Democrats are ahead in many competitive races – including his own. Trump has tried to change the narrative around affordability, insisting his administration has done more to lower everyday prices for Americans than Democrats. Trump, who picked Paxton to run as the Republican in the Texas Senate race, will join Paxton at a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday evening. But Paxton appeared to recognize the uphill battle facing Republicans, telling people at the closed-door events that “so many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable”. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t, you know, I don’t know what’s behind some of the decisions,” Paxton said. The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment. Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for Paxton’s campaign, said in a statement that the Texas attorney general’s comments were “a non-story”. “The attorney general said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” Cercy said. “President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families’ pockets with a bigger child tax credit and larger deductions for health care and buying a home. Texans need immediate relief, and everyone knows James Talarico will raise your taxes,” Cercy added. Recent polling from the Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research indicates most adults blame Trump for poor economic conditions. Approximately 74% of Americans said the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs. In the audio recording, obtained by Axios, Paxton said he was trying to help lower costs in ways that he could, such as through his proposed tax cut plan that includes healthcare and housing write-offs. Axios’s reporting is just the latest leaked audio clip of Paxton being critical of his own party. Earlier this week, Politico reported that Paxton privately admitted to people at a closed-door event that outside forces in Washington DC were controlling much of his campaign messaging. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from DC,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico. Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican midterm convention “dropped” his polling numbers. Paxton is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico. Polls show Paxton and Talarico are neck-and-neck, but Talarico has a small lead over the Texas attorney general.

In the audio recording, obtained by Axios, Paxton said he was trying to help lower costs in ways that he could, such as through his proposed tax cut plan that includes healthcare and housing write-offs. Axios’s reporting is just the latest leaked audio clip of Paxton being critical of his own party. Earlier this week, Politico reported that Paxton privately admitted to people at a closed-door event that outside forces in Washington DC were controlling much of his campaign messaging. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from DC,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico. Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican midterm convention “dropped” his polling numbers. Paxton is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico. Polls show Paxton and Talarico are neck-and-neck, but Talarico has a small lead over the Texas attorney general.

title: Will Trump’s rallies lift the Republicans?
body_text: With fewer than 30 days until the US midterm elections, Donald Trump seems determined to still be centre stage despite poll fears that after 3 November he may end up a lame-duck president as a Democratic blue wave sweeps the country. Our Washington bureau chief, David Smith, has been watching how the president is playing to Republican voters at the start of a blitz of cross-country rallies. It’s, at best, a mixed picture. As David reports, Trump’s self-belief and message to voters to “pretend” his name is on the ballot reveal a man out of touch with ordinary Americans’ worries about the cost of living and whose promises that the war with Iran will soon be over ring ever more hollow. And then there are the candidates, more of whom are shying away from their earlier allegiances to a president whose approval ratings continue to slide. Republican analysts view Trump’s contribution to the midterm campaign as more of a hindrance than help, David discovers. And it’s a view shared by some voters Stephen Starr spoke to in Ohio. All of which bodes ill for JD Vance, whose “one more chance” messaging is unpicked by columnist Sidney Blumenthal as a strategy that only underlines the view of voters, like the ones in Stephen’s piece, who will vote for change and an America that is not like it is now. I hope that this week’s cover story primes you to make sense of the midterms. And it comes with an early reminder that due to our printing deadlines, Guardian Weekly won’t carry news of the results immediately but we will provide in-depth analysis of what they mean in our 13 November issue. title: The most shocking part of Trump’s comments is what our reaction says about us
body_text: Donald Trump’s campaign rallies can be repetitive. Very repetitive. He calls himself the “greatest” president leading the “greatest” movement inside the “greatest” economy. He rails against “Dumocrats” for the “transgender mutilization” of children. He lambasts the “fake news” and reheats election lies. He describes illegal immigration as an “invasion” and recites the poem The Snake. If we were all frogs being slowly boiled alive, we’ve now reached the stage of blackened toad. After a decade of this, presidential utterances that would once have caused outrage are met with a shrug. We are no longer shockable. Or so we thought. On Monday, speaking at a rally in Nebraska, Trump seemingly suggested that Iran, which he long accused of pursuing nuclear weapons, could “take out” the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. “I want to see a tremendous victory,” the US president told supporters of his war on Iran, launched almost eight months ago. “You want to see a tremendous victory because it verifies all the things we did. “And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial,” he added, in an apparent reference to higher prices. “It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.” Trump went on: “They can take out a city. Let them take – let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s – this is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.” Perhaps the only thing more chilling than a commander-in-chief musing about the deaths of millions of Americans under mushroom clouds was the sound of his supporters cheering at the line “let them take out”. After all, the question of the Trump era has always been: what does this say about us? Democrats had a field day. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut called it “such a sick, evil thing to say”. The independent senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont accused Trump of saying the small price to pay was the “annihilation of two major American cities”. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, called Trump “deranged and dangerous” and put the state’s threat-assessment centre on alert. Forty-three members of Congress from California jointly called on the president to apologise. Even a group called Astronauts for America felt compelled to issue a statement of condemnation. But most Republicans remained silent (a sentence written countless times in recent years). The White House communications director, Steven Cheung, claimed that Trump “was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped”. Some of Trump’s critics allowed that perhaps this time he had merely spoken clumsily, rather than diabolically. Aaron Blake of CNN argued that the comment was “incoherent, not malicious”. Yet the central formulation was undeniable: “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” All you have to do is imagine another president uttering those words and imagine the response. Obama would have faced accusations of treason and potential impeachment; Biden would have been written off as an old man suffering dementia. But what to make of Trump? The comments were a jumbled word salad that raises familiar questions about the 80-year-old’s mental acuity. Last week, for example, inviting attenders of a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration to walk the floor of the new White House ballroom, he warned: “Don’t fall over the edge because it’s a long way down. And only a Hispanic could survive that fall.” Listening to Trump at a rally these days is akin to listening to Lucky in Samuel Beckett’s absurdist play Waiting for Godot: “Given the existence as uttered forth in the public works of Puncher and Wattmann of a personal God quaquaquaqua with white beard quaquaquaqua outside time without extension who from the heights of divine apathia divine athambia divine aphasia loves us dearly with some exceptions for reasons unknown but time will tell …” The way in which the president singled out Los Angeles and San Diego underlined his decade-long project of division. Indeed, for years California has been Republicans’ idea of the bastion of woke decadence, the quintessential “enemy within”. We’ve grown used to the president’s campaigns of retribution against Democratic power centres, but such othering is dangerous in any society. Trump has a willing accomplice in JD Vance, who is quietly pursuing a rally schedule of his own. Speaking in Lakeland, Florida, the vice-president responded to the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon, who is Black, after she called herself a socialist, saying: “Then get the hell out of here. You don’t belong in America if those are your views.” Vance, who is 42 and potentially rehearsing for a White House bid, speaks less incoherently than his boss. He has also shown more willingness to acknowledge voters’ struggles and plead with them to give Republicans more time to get the job done. But history will remember that, even as Trump unravelled before the world’s gaze, Vance remained loyal, and was among his chief enablers. It is their task to normalise Trump, whose approval ratings continue to test fresh lows, and sanewash his statements so that Americans forget what a catastrophically abnormal chapter this is. The worst horror of all in Nebraska was not what the president said, but what Republicans and others failed to say in response. Lawrence O’Donnell, a host on the MS Now network, warned viewers on Tuesday: “You live in a country, you live in a world tonight, where it is no longer news that the president of the United States appears to be insane. It remains the single most important ongoing news story of this era.”

title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too
body_text: For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates. Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That would require flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck. Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remain unpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of a red undertow rather than a blue wave. Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populist James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such as Maine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with $700m of advertising booked since the start of September. Mr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasingly distancing themselves from the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as “elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him are changing their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing. Outrageously, Mr Trump has used taxpayer-funded adverts to laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts to restrict mail-in voting – used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it. Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But should Democrats manage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.

title: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government
body_text: Donald Trump distanced himself from two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans. On Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”. “They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” The president’s comments came after the New York Times reported that LaCivita and Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, an autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to assist the government ahead of elections over the weekend. Sources told the newspaper that each adviser was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars. LaCivita and Blair are meanwhile working with Maga Inc, the Trump-backed SuperPac assisting Republican candidates in November’s US midterm elections. Both men have long histories with Trump, and the US president has praised them separately on social media. LaCivita joined Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign in 2022, after leading a pro-Trump Super Pac called Preserve America. In 2024, Trump wrote on Truth Social that LaCivita was “THE BEST” co-campaign manager alongside Susie Wiles, who now serves as the White House chief of staff. Blair worked for Trump’s 2020 campaign in Florida and was the political director of Trump’s 2024 campaign. He joined the president at the White House as deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs. In April, Trump called Blair “one of the brightest political minds” while announcing that Blair would leave his White House position, briefly, to join Maga Inc and assist Republicans in the midterms. Trump said Blair would return to the White House after the midterms. Trump’s statement distancing himself from the two advisers comes as Maga Inc prepares to ramp up efforts to assist Republican candidates in next month’s elections. Public polls indicate Democrats are leading Republicans in several key competitive races. That is largely attributed to widespread disapproval over Trump’s handling of the economy and cost of living. A spokesperson for Maga Inc told the New York Times that Blair and LaCivita remained engaged with midterm efforts while traveling, saying the two “hosted a team call with race captains on Saturday morning to go over recent survey data”. The Guardian has contacted Maga Inc for comment. Despite polling showing waning voter enthusiasm for Republicans, the party has a cash advantage over Democrats. At the end of August, Maga Inc had more than $415m cash on hand. Several Super Pacs tied to Maga Inc have begun launching multimillion-dollar ad blitzes.

title: Democrats sue to stop Trump from using taxpayer funds for self-promoting ads
body_text: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington DC to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda. The ads promoting Donald Trump, including one recycled from his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement that Trump was misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November. Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes.” After a bipartisan backlash to the use of public money to promote himself during the final month of the midterm campaign season, Trump claimed on Monday that he would direct the Maga Inc Super Pac he controls to pay for the ads instead. The next day, however, the White House said Trump’s political action committee would not reimburse taxpayers for the money it had already spent on the ads. Then, when the government unveiled a fifth ad in the series, celebrating Trump’s military intervention in Venezuela, it was also paid for by the US government. The DNC complaint, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, alleges the ads violate federal law, including a ban on congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”. “President Trump personally directed this illegal activity. The White House office crafted the partisan campaign. The office of management and budget shifted $20m to pay for it. And US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has carried it out. These unlawful actions are ultra vires and violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),” the complaint states. The suit also notes the first ad in the series features an image of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, awarding Trump the so-called “Fifa peace prize” to support its case that the ads all violate a prohibition on the use of taxpayer funds for “self-aggrandizement”. In February, Trump shared a racist video on social media that portrayed him as a lion and Barack and Michelle Obama as apes.
