The press, the pundits, and the mainstream party strategists keep behaving as if every Jew cares about Israel – and all Jews care about is Israel – and a candidate must be pro-Zionist or lose the elusive Jewish vote. We saw this during the campaign of the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Forthright support for Palestinian self-determination had long been central to his politics, and to his appeal to progressives. But Mamdani was running for mayor, not president. His brilliant stroke was affordability – a theme that is easily understandable, widely relatable, and capable of making socialist solutions sound reasonable. Nevertheless, from the moment he appeared, the press, from the New York Times op-ed page to college newspapers to the international Jewish press, made the election a referendum on Israel – and, more perniciously, on Islam. Mamdani’s Democratic primary opponent, former governor Andrew Cuomo, attacked him with flagrant Islamophobia, conflating his critique of Israel with antisemitism and signalling that his faith was a danger to Jews. The fearmongering did not defeat Mamdani. In the end, only a third of Jews voted for him; in Hasidic neighborhoods, 90% went for Cuomo. But progressive Jewish organizations including Jewish Voice for Peace and Jews for Racial and Economic Justice endorsed him. He won in almost every racial and class demographic and pulled in three-quarters of voters under 30. What’s the lesson here? The youth vote – plus the Black vote, the Hispanic vote, the working-class vote, etc – plus good ideas and a great campaign put Mamdani over the top. Furthermore, an analysis by Good Authority concludes that no position on Israel, pro or con, is driving Jews out of the Democratic party. Now Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, is shlepping the burden of this vaguely defined, perpetually disgruntled “Jewish vote”. After narrowly winning the primary, he apologized to members of the Jewish community for a statement he made after a Lebanese-born naturalized citizen rammed his truck into a large synagogue, injuring a guard. The apology came after El-Sayed clumsily linked the man’s antisemitism to Israeli violence in Lebanon, saying: “Hurt people hurt people.” It was an inoffensive adage among, say, prison abolitionists. But to some Jews, it sounded as if El-Sayed felt more sympathy for the perpetrator than for his targeted victims. The Republicans have taken advantage of these fissures, attacking El-Sayed with a combination of Islamophobia and the usual hypocritical condemnations of antisemitism. At their midterm “convention”, El-Sayed’s opponent Mike Rogers claimed, falsely, that the Democrat had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. And while El-Sayed definitively distanced himself from the leftwing Israel critic Hasan Piker – a Twitch streamer the press began to cover obsessively – speaker after speaker hammered on the connection between the two men. These tactics appear to be falling flat. A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that most Michiganders have never heard of Piker. The poll found that El-Sayed leads his opponent by 39 points among voters 44 and younger, who are far more critical of Israel’s policies than their elders. That generational split is also pronounced among Jews. El-Sayed has the endorsements of JVP and IfNotNow, an organization that attracts many young Jews who are painfully rejecting their parents’ Zionism, as well as Vermont’s Jewish senator, Bernie Sanders. While Rogers has been collecting pledges of votes from Jewish Michiganders, more than 600 “Michigan Jews for Democracy”, including elected officials and rabbis, have signed a letter in support of El-Sayed. Recently, Mamdani repeated his condemnation of Benjamin Netanyahu as a war criminal who should be arrested in advance of the Israeli prime minister’s visit to New York to address the UN. That revived Zionist fury toward the mayor, but Jews both supportive and critical of Israel – and Mamdani – held noisy rallies. The reason for Mamdani to keep trying to speak to both sides is not to win the mythical Jewish vote. It is to make common cause with people who don’t want Israel swept into the sea but also cannot abide a Jewish ethnostate whose survival depends on occupation and apartheid. That said, if El-Sayed were the Islamist Jew-hater his enemies claim he is, it should be obvious to a lot more Jews. If it were obvious to a lot more Jews, Aipac would not have had to pour $32m – unsuccessfully – into Stevens’ campaign or contemplate pouring more into supporting Rogers in the general election. And of course, the “Arab American” or “Muslim vote” is no more unanimous than the hypothetical Jewish vote. To be frank, the whole discourse stinks. It boils down to “support the Muslim” or “support the Jew”, as if this were some ancient racial animosity – natural enemies “fighting”, as Trump said of the Palestinians and Israeli Jews, “for a thousand years”. Not only is this contention untrue. Such thinking obviates politics, the effort to understand a problem and convince others that your solution is best. It is not good for the Jews – or for anyone. And it is deadly for a secular, pluralistic democracy. Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

title: Targeting Trump: how Democrats plan to investigate the president if they win Congress
body_text: In August, Jamie Raskin renewed his demand that Jared Kushner hand over documents about the overlap between his informal role advising Donald Trump on foreign policy and the private equity firm he runs after an earlier request was ignored. Five of the 11 companies that Elizabeth Warren, Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden wrote to about Donald Trump’s IRS settlement – including the Trump Organization and World Liberty Financial – never answered at all. Of course, none of them had to. That all changes if Democrats win the House and Senate in November. Control of the chamber would not only give Democrats the gavels, but they would be handed bigger staffs and the power to subpoena documents and testimony – and they have been unusually candid about how they plan to use it. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked his priorities in September: the Trump family’s businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s handling of vaccines. Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee and its likely chair, calls the potential scope of the work “gargantuan”. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, has promised to “hold the crooks accountable”. Here are eight of the most consequential investigations, what Democrats have already demanded, and where they could hit a wall. The family business Garcia ranks Trump family corruption first on his list for the oversight committee, while Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Kushner and Trump Jr. On 25 August, Raskin wrote to Kushner, renewing a demand for documents on his dual roles as an informal foreign policy adviser to Trump and the head of a private equity firm that does business with foreign governments. He has been chasing Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, since 2023, when he said it took $2bn from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund after Kushner left the White House. There is also the $400m plane that Qatar gifted Trump, a Trump Jr wedding party that was partly funded by a Russian oligarch, and several multimillion-dollar defense contracts won by the extended Trump family that will draw more scrutiny. The IRS settlement In May, the Department of Justice settled the president’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS with an order barring the agency from auditing past returns of Trump, his family and related companies. Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House ways and means committee, and Raskin demanded documents on the negotiations, the roles of the justice department and treasury officials, and safeguards against fraud, with a 27 May deadline ahead of the appearance of the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, before Neal’s committee. In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the finance committee, and 12 other finance Democrats on 22 May called for a bipartisan investigation into the settlement and the administration’s decision to bar the IRS from auditing Trump, his family and businesses. At a hearing, Wyden pressed Bessent on whether the audit immunity remained in effect, which he declined to answer. On 7 July, Wyden, Warren and Schumer wrote to 11 companies, including Kalshi and Polymarket, asking whether they intend to rely on the settlement as protection against audits, given Trump Jr’s financial ties with the companies. Raskin and Garcia, meanwhile, demanded correspondence between Trump’s lawyers and the justice department over his reported $230m claim for past investigations. A federal judge has said the order conflicts with federal law, according to Warren’s office, and the legal fight is unresolved. Crypto and betting markets Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, opened a preliminary inquiry and wrote to executives behind the $Trump memecoin and World Liberty Financial, asking about ownership and investment structure. Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, asked the Office of Government Ethics to review a reported deal involving World Liberty, Binance and a UAE state-backed fund. Warren, Blumenthal, Gary Peters, Dick Durbin and Wyden demanded hearings after disclosures showed Trump earned more than $1.2bn from crypto ventures, including about $588m tied to World Liberty token sales. In the House, Maxine Waters, the top Democrat on the financial services committee, has called for legislation to “end the President’s crypto profiteering and recoup his ill-gotten gains”. On prediction markets, the July letter to Kalshi’s chief executive noted that Trump Jr was a “strategic advisor” to the company, and seven House Democrats asked the oversight chair, James Comer, to subpoena the markets over suspicious trades tied to the Iran war. This one has the most bipartisan appeal: the Republican senator John Curtis asked the Senate judiciary committee to subpoena Trump Jr over his Kalshi and Polymarket ties, and Comer opened his own insider-trading investigation. Epstein and the emails Thanks to a tag-team effort by representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it has deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is now facing a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (but not always) acting in concert to subpoena witnesses and hold them in contempt when they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress. The Pentagon and the wars Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family. The sharpest look so far is a January letter from Warren, Blumenthal and Andy Kim. It lists companies backed by 1789 Capital, the venture firm Trump Jr joined as a partner: Cerberus ($45m), PsiQuantum ($10.8m), Firehawk Aerospace ($4.9m) and Vulcan Elements ($10m, plus a reported $620m loan). It also cites a $12.8m contract to Unusual Machines, a drone company in which Trump Jr holds a stake. The senators asked whether the Vulcan loan was competitive, which officials Trump Jr screened for Pentagon jobs, and for every contact between defense department officials and Trump Jr since 5 November 2024. A later Pentagon reply, they wrote, showed no safeguards against such conflicts. Vulcan and the Pentagon have denied Trump Jr had any involvement in the loan. On the war, Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, led his colleagues in demanding that Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth, Steve Witkoff and Kushner testify on the Iran war, and forced a vote to subpoena them. He also demanded documents on Venezuelan oil revenue routed into a Qatar account. In 2025, Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, pressed for an expanded inspector general investigation of the defense secretary’s use of Signal. He and Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House armed services committee, objected to a Hegseth memo routing Pentagon communications with Congress through his office. Immigration enforcement and who profits In March, Raskin and Warren led 52 lawmakers in writing to six companies tied to ICE’s warehouse detention plan: CoreCivic, Geo Group, GardaWorld Federal, Gosin Group, KVG LLC and PNK Group. They asked for expected profit margins, lobbying efforts and donations to Trump’s campaign or cabinet officials, by 13 April. The plan carries a $38.3bn price tag and aims to hold nearly 100,000 people by November. The lawmakers flagged ICE paying $129m for a Georgia facility, nearly five times its assessed value, and a contracting official who came from Geo. Garcia’s oversight Democrats wrote separately to Geo about Corey Lewandowski’s dealings, after reports he sought personal payments from contractors. Peters, the retiring top Democrat on the Senate homeland security committee, led a letter seeking every DHS contract that the border czar, Tom Homan, may have influenced, after reports of a bribery investigation. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the House homeland security committee, would take the matter up there. Warren’s Wall Street If Democrats flip the Senate, now-ranking member Elizabeth Warren would be positioned to chair the banking committee, and private credit is her likeliest target. On 13 May, she wrote to Bessent and the SEC chair, Paul Atkins, on how deregulation has increased private credit risks, with responses due by 26 May. In July 2025 she asked Bessent to run a stress test of the market, which he did not do. She has also written to ratings agencies including S&P, Moody’s and Fitch over reportedly inflated private credit ratings. When Blue Owl restricted withdrawals from a fund, she called for higher bank capital requirements for private credit exposures, transparent data from the firms and a stress test. The wildcard Impeachment hangs over all of it. Trump was impeached twice in his first term and acquitted both times. Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing in and nothing out, while the Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”. Even if Jeffries does not ultimately pursue impeachment, Trump could force his hand. Nancy Pelosi held off leftwing calls for impeachment for months after she became speaker of the House after the 2018 midterms, but when Trump tried to get Ukrainian leaders to pursue an investigation of Joe Biden – and then incited the January 6 attack on the Capitol – Pelosi relented and oversaw two different impeachments.

title: Democratic Senate candidate responds to anti-trans attacks pushed by Republicans
body_text: Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina, has responded to persistent efforts by Republicans to make trans athletes in women’s sports a wedge issue in the race. In a restrained direct-to-camera statement, Andrews – a pediatrician – outlined her opposition to “biological men playing in women’s sports”, as her party pushes back against Republican attacks. “I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing in women’s sports, and I don’t support and haven’t ever performed gender surgery for minors,” Andrews said in a new ad. Andrews’ video, in which she wears a white lab coat with a stethoscope around her neck, was in response to recent attacks from Donald Trump and an aggressive ad, paid for by a super political action committee (Super Pac) supporting her Republican opponent in South Carolina, Darline Graham. The ad claims Andrews “is for they/them” and frames a transgender person as predatory toward a child. Republicans are using anti-trans issues, such as keeping trans women off women’s and girls’ sports teams, to try to thwart Democrats in the upcoming midterms. Trump has pushed the issue for years. A landmark supreme court ruling earlier this year handed Trump a key “culture war” victory by upholding laws in two conservative states excluding transgender girls and women from competing in female sports. Andrews, who has previously been vocal in her support of trans people, used her response ad to directly address Republican criticisms and claims as the party pushes anti-trans attacks against Democrats nationwide. Some Democrats running in competitive districts have shifted their tone on the issue of trans rights, particularly on the issue of trans athletes in women’s sports. Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, seeking re-election in a district that voted for Trump in 2024, recently aired an ad touting that she “voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools” and “boys should not play in girls’ sports”. Congressman Don Davis of North Carolina, running for re-election in a district that also backed the president in 2024, released an ad saying: “There’s real concerns about fairness and safety; that’s what I believe states should decide what’s right for protecting women and girls.” Blake Gendebien, the Democratic candidate running in a primarily Republican district in New York, released an ad stating that “boys shouldn’t play on girls’ sports teams” while also highlighting that the topic was a non-issue in the district. “The thing is, in 20 years raising a family here, I haven’t heard this issue come up. Not once,” Gendebien said. “But internet trolls like [the Republican candidate] Anthony Constantino use it to rile people up.” In 2024, pro-Trump groups seized on conservative opposition to the Biden administration’s trans inclusive policies to attack former vice-president Kamala Harris, the then Democratic presidential candidate. “Kamala’s agenda is they/them, not you,” a voiceover said in one widely seen pro-Trump ad. The ad attacking Andrews in South Carolina uses nearly identical language as the pro-Trump one two years ago. How Democrats should respond to Republicans’ anti-trans attacks has divided some. Equality Pac, the fundraising arm of the congressional equality caucus focusing on electing LGBTQ+ people, told Axios it disapproved of Kaptur’s handling of her response to the anti-trans attacks. The Pac called Kaptur’s language “unacceptable” and said it was “absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time”, referring to her ad in which she called transgender girls “boys”. Last month, the Human Rights Campaign – an LGBTQ+ advocacy group – wrote a Substack article to help guide Democrats on how to best respond to anti-trans rights attacks. “Turning on a vulnerable community is not a winning political strategy – and it’s exactly what Trump, [Elon] Musk, and MAGA want,” it wrote. “It legitimizes their side and weakens ours. And it harms transgender people.” The group pointed to the Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown’s response to anti-trans attacks as a good example of how to handle those attacks. Brown released an ad last month featuring voters who dismiss the anti-trans issues, and instead redirected attention to affordability issues under Brown’s competitor, and the incumbent senator, Jon Husted. “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” one voter said in Brown’s advertisement. The Human Rights Campaign said Brown “didn’t play into MAGA’s hands” and “let voters do the talking” in the video.

title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional. Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website. Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors. In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”. “But if it is anything close to objective,” they continued, “the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her”. Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers. Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property. Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations. In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired. Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April. Congress created the Fed to be an independent and non-partisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy. Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.

title: Federal judge rules against Trump DoJ’s policy of collecting state voter rolls
body_text: A federal judge ruled on Friday that the US justice department’s policy of collecting states’ unredacted voter rolls to check them against a federal immigration database is unlawful. The ruling, by the US district judge Sparkle Sooknanan, was a setback for Donald Trump, who has pushed his administration to ramp up investigations into non-citizen voting ahead of the November midterm elections, with control of Congress at stake. The department’s list maintenance policy, adopted to comply with the president’s election integrity executive order, violated privacy laws and risked disenfranchising voters, Sooknanan said. “The court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more – a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans,” Sooknanan wrote in the 78-page ruling. Sooknanan said the policy not only violated federal laws, but also that the justice department did not have the authority to enact it because Congress gave the states, not the federal government, control over the maintenance of their voter rolls. “Behind all the window dressing, the challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote,” Sooknanan wrote. “But Congress has left that authority where our constitution has always placed it: with the states.” Sooknanan wrote that her ruling “does not prevent the federal government from taking lawful steps to support states’ efforts to maintain accurate voter rolls” and did not prevent states from maintaining their own. Sooknanan previously ruled against the administration in June, limiting the its ability to create a database of Americans’ information. The US supreme court later temporarily set aside her decision. The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit, brought by the government watchdog group Common Cause, came after the justice department requested voter information from states in May. Roughly 18 states complied, handing over information that included voters’ full names, birth dates, residential addresses, and state driver’s license numbers or the last four digits of their social security numbers. Sooknanan said the department “improperly” disclosed and maintained records. The administration wanted voter roll information to compare with immigration data, to ensure non-citizens are not registered to vote. But Sooknanan said the justice department “failed to consider the risk that its use of citizenship records known to be unreliable would lead the civil rights division to demand that states remove US citizens from their voter rolls”. In her ruling, she cited two people who had been incorrectly removed from their state’s voter roll list because they had been wrongly identified as non-citizens. “This is a victory for voters and yet another loss for the Department of Justice. It’s time the Trump administration stop these desperate attempts to seize voters’ private data and take control of our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of Common Cause.

title: Trump says he picked ‘devoted fan’ Katie Zacharia to be next press secretary
body_text: Donald Trump on Friday announced that he had picked Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary, lining up a conservative commentator he called a “devoted fan” to be his most prominent spokesperson. Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after the birth to her second child. “It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia,” the president wrote in a social media post on Truth Social. “She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump added. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia has been selected for the role. The Guardian has reached out to Zacharia for comment. Zacharia’s selection puts her at the heart of the White House’s efforts to shape the public narrative around Trump’s second term, as his approval rating falls to record lows, and his party fights to maintain control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections. Trump has asked supporters to vote like his name is on the ballot, turning the election into a referendum on his presidency amid widespread economic discontent and an unpopular war with Iran. Zacharia previously worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and now serves as a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns Truth Social, the president’s social network, on which he made the announcement about her selection official. The appointment came as a something of a surprise in Washington, after weeks of building speculation about who the president might choose to replace Leavitt. Several reports suggested Scott Jennings, the conservative TV pundit was an “an early favorite” for the role, though skeptics noted that his past criticism of the president would likely be an issue. Zacharia, a California native, has been involved in Republican politics for years. She attended Pepperdine University and served as president of her school’s College Republican organization. She interned in the White House’s office of political affairs during the second Bush administration as well as at the Republican National Committee. She obtained her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. Prior to joining DHS, Zacharia worked as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative nonprofit focused on “election integrity”. The organization is headed up by Trump ally and diplomat Ric Grenell. Zacharia was a frequent join Fox News commentator, often promoting or defending the US president’s policies while harshly criticizing Democrats. She is married to film producer Tyler Zacharia. They have four children. In his Truth Social post, Trump praised Leavitt, who he said had done a “fantastic job” in the role. On Monday, Fox News announced that Leavitt would join the network as an on-air contributor. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration,” Trump wrote, adding: “Good luck Katie!”
